The representative of the Philippines raised concerns with this measure. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/678.1.  Thank you to the United States and Russia for including this item in the agenda. Allow me to read out the position of the chemical industry association of the Philippines which we in government fully endorse.2.  The Philippines is of the view that the proposed regulation has serious implications on the trade of titanium dioxide which is used extensively as raw material in the manufacture of paint products, cosmetics, pharmaceuticals and even food.3.  The EU Commission's classification, labelling and packaging (CLP) regulations may create panic, fear and paranoia among consumers as well as potential disastrous financial loss to companies engaged in the manufacture of products containing titanium dioxide in various levels of composition.4.  Specifically, we believe the proposed classification and required labelling has the potential to result in a significant impact on international trade. This impact is expected despite serious and ongoing concerns by global experts on the underlying rationale being used to advance this action:The rodent toxicity studies used to support the classification do not support a finding that TiO2 should be considered a human carcinogen.The scope of the proposed classification is excessive. The classification would apply to TiO2 regardless of the physical form. Even though the rodent toxicity studies were performed with TiO2 as a respirable dust, the proposed classification would still apply when TiO2 is embedded in a liquid or solid matrix as in paints and coatings or present in any waste.An alternative mechanism to minimize any hazard exposure to TiO2 dust is through the use of an appropriate occupational exposure limit.The social and economic impact of such a classification is enormous, for international trade and within the EU, compared to the negligible (or non-existent) benefit for human health.5.  The EU would be advancing an unfounded interpretation of the UN Globally Harmonised System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals (GHS) under its Classification, Labelling and Packaging (CLP) regulation. This interpretation has not been advanced by any other national regulatory body that has been undertaken the same risk management, and the unwarranted hazard and precautionary labelling it would require in the EU markets for widely used consumer products like paint and coatings, is not required anywhere in the world. For these reasons, it is critical for the EU to provide the rationale as to why such a significant, unique and highly disruptive interpretation has been made.6.  The economic cost of the trade disruptions is substantial, if not staggering, and wholly unnecessary.7.  We therefore call on the EU to indefinitely defer adoption of the proposed regulation when the REACH Committee meets on 1 July.

The representative of Australia raised concerns with this measure. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/645.1.  As previously noted in this Committee, Australia recognises the European Union's (EU) right to regulate for public and occupational health and safety, we also recognise that appropriate classification and labelling for hazardous substances and mixtures can address legitimate public and occupational health concerns.2.  Australia would be interested in an update on the EU's internal processes to consider the proposed changes to the classifications of Titanium Dioxide (TiO2) and cobalt, including any relevant timelines, particularly given we understand there have been several postponements of a REACH Committee vote on these matters.3.  As per WTO TBT Agreement commitments, we would urge the EU to ensure that any regulation to address concerns about the possible hazards associated with TiO2 and cobalt is no more trade restrictive than necessary, and does not unduly impact trade in goods which contain TiO2 and cobalt.4.  Australia would like to reiterate the possible implications of the classification of Titanium Dioxide (TiO2) as a suspected carcinogen:as previously noted, TiO2 is a premium pigment that is used in the manufacture of a wide range of products, most commonly paint and coatingsthe classification may create unnecessary obstacles to international trade for TiO2 and products containing TiO2Australia suggests that alternative regulatory measures are available to address the EU's concerns that would more directly address the potential health hazards of TiO2, without affecting trade.5.  The Australian industrial chemicals regulator, the National Industrial Chemicals Notification and Assessment Scheme (NICNAS), has undertaken assessments on the risks of TiO2 (excluding nano particles of TiO2), and as previously noted has found:exposure to TiO2 in a finished product through dermal, inhalation and oral routes presents limited risks to human healthappropriate work health and safety controls are adequate to protect public and workers' health and safety in relation to TiO2 inhalation exposurethe NICNAS information sheet on nanoparticles of TiO2 stated that there is some evidence that breathing in large quantities of TiO2 nanoparticles over a long period of time may cause toxic effects due to impairment of normal lung clearance mechanisms, but the studies available (up to 2012) do not provide sufficient evidence to conclude that TiO2 causes lung tumours in humansif a classification is proposed for TiO2, it should be limited to nanoparticles of TiO2 (<100 nm in size), and only through the inhalation routethere should be clear evidence that the carcinogenicity is from TiO2 and not from the insoluble nature of TiO2 nanoparticles causing lung overloading.6.  Australia would also like to express its interest in the EU's proposed classification of cobalt as a Category 1B carcinogen for all routes of exposure, in addition to a Category 1B reprotoxin and Category 2 mutagenas noted by other Members this may create unintended downstream consequences and unnecessary obstacles to international trade for goods containing small amounts of cobalt and nickel, such as stainless steel productswe note that Australia is also an exporter of nickel and cobalt to the EU - in 2017-18 Australia exported AUD 16 million worth of nickel ores to the EU, along with AUD 6.5 million of nickel articles and AUD 92 million of cobalt mattes.Australia asks that the EU take this into account as it considers a holistic risk assessment profile for the reclassification of cobalt.7.  The Australian industrial chemicals regulator, NICNAS, has assessed cobalt under its Inventory Multi-tiered Assessment and Prioritisation (IMAP) scheme, and concluded it is a likely carcinogen for inhalation in a work health and safety contextwe would like to suggest that consideration be given to removing 'all routes of exposure' from the proposed Category 1B Carcinogen classification of cobalt metal, for example applying an interim classification for the inhalation route only in the absence of further scientific evidenceconsideration could also be given to exempting uses where the cobalt is bound and not bioavailable, for example in alloys like stainless steel.

The representative of Japan shared others' concerns on the EU's titanium dioxide regulation. In the EU's 14th adaptation to technical and scientific progress (ATP) proposal of the CLP regulation, the provisions for titanium dioxide and mixtures containing titanium dioxide were of concern. In particular, the proposed draft regulation classified the powder mixtures containing 1% or more of titanium dioxide as a carcinogen regardless of whether or not exposure of titanium dioxide by inhalation could occur. This could inappropriately broaden the scope of products to be regulated. Labelling requirements could even affect products containing titanium dioxide with low inhalation risk such as toner cartridges. In addition, those products had not been classified as a carcinogen in other countries' systems along with Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals (GHS). The EU was requested to reconsider the classification criteria in order to limit the scope to products where titanium dioxide inhalation exposure risk existed. Japan also asked that the EU ensure that the regulation would not be more trade-restrictive than necessary.

The representative of New Zealand said that New Zealand acknowledged and supported the right of all WTO Members to regulate to achieve legitimate health objectives. However, any regulation to address concerns about the possible carcinogenicity of titanium dioxide must be proportionate and not unduly restrict trade in goods containing titanium dioxide. He invited the EU to explain how it had ensured that the draft regulation was helping to achieve the EU's environmental and human health protection objectives, whilst not being more trade restrictive than necessary. He also asked whether the European Union had considered less trade-restrictive alternatives and, if so, on what basis it had been decided not to adopt such alternatives.

The representative of the Russian Federation raised concerns on the CLP regulation, in particular with respect to the proposed classification of cobalt. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/700 (below).1.  The delegation of the Russian Federation would also like to thank the EU delegation for the bilateral work in Moscow and Brussels on this issue.2.  However, with deep regret, we have to express our raising concern with regard to the proposed classification of cobalt according to the draft of the 14th ATP to CLP adopted by the European Commission on the 4th October 2019.3.  First, we have to highlight the absolute lack of transparency of this classification's elaboration process as there are no minutes, summaries or any other publicly available official information about the CARACAL meetings that took place in July and September. Moreover, both the membership and the basic rights of the third countries within the frameworks of those meetings are limited. In addition, as far as we understand the EU's explanation of the process, the third countries represented at the CARACAL must coordinate their joint position. Such state of things seems strange to us. If the above understanding is correct, then it unfairly limits the stakeholders' rights and their opportunities to express their opinion.4.  Second, we know that the comments of the third countries and even Europe's own business associations on cobalt classification have been completely side-lined and ignored, as the classification has already been adopted by the Commission but there has yet been no response from the European Commission during the "consultation" period. We have to point out to the Commission that it resorts to a consultation practice and routinely ignores stakeholders. 5.  Third, in the context of our bilateral work with the Commission, it has openly resorted to the hazard – based approach, which directly contradicts the UN GHS, considered to be the best international practice. In accordance with the Art. 2.4 of the Agreement on TBT, technical regulations should be based on the international standards and best practices.6.  Fourth, the Commission has confirmed the lack of scientific data to classify cobalt metal as carcinogen 1 b for all routes of exposure, but it still deems it possible to classify cobalt in such an unjustifiable manner. Due to the lack of well-grounded scientific evidence, we consider this measure to constitute an unnecessary obstacle to trade to fulfil the requirements under the Art. 2.2 of the Agreement on TBT, even bearing in mind the fact that the measure will be implemented as labelling requirement.7.  Fifth, we are deeply concerned that a new draft of the 14th ATP, that had not been notified in the WTO, was published on the official website of the Commission on the 26th of August 2019. That draft stated that the Commission had received more than thirty comments on cobalt, however, from the Commission's point of view, these were not strong enough to reconsider the Commission's position on the proposed classification. Moreover, as we know now, the Commission moved to the 14th ATP adoption on the 4th of October 2019. We have to point out that the abovementioned document fails to provide any explanation to the Commission's dismissal of the arguments and provides no justification whatsoever for such an approach.8.  Sixth, we are aware of the statement, made by the DG-Envy during the bilateral meeting with the delegation of another third country about possible exemptions. For instance, medical devices, due to their critical importance, are not likely to be covered by the proposed measure. There have been other examples as well. We have to remind the Commission that neither REACH nor CLP contain provisions that allow such exemptions. For this reason, we ask for clarification, because, as far as we can understand the current situation, DG - Environment has either misled those delegates or proposed to implement exemptions that are illegitimate according to the WTO rules, including the Art. 2.1 of the Agreement on TBT and the I Art. of the GATT 1994.9.  Seventh, the Commission has failed to produce the results of the socio-economic analysis of the consequences of the proposed cobalt classification, which goes against international best practice as well as the Commission's own policy.10.  Eighth, we ask the EU delegation to give us information about the replies on the letters sent to the European Commission. 11.  It is with deepest regret that we have to observe that the cobalt metal classification is only the first step, taken by the Commission, towards applying these deeply flawed unscientific approaches for classification of chemicals and mixtures to other chemicals with the explicit purpose to distort global trade, disrupt manufacturing and added value chains creation. 12.  Taking into account these factors, we question if the Commission's actions and approaches are consistent with the WTO rules, which demand well-grounded scientific data when elaborating technical regulations in according with the Article 2.2 of the Agreement on TBT.13.  In conclusion, we ask the EU delegation to reconsider this classification, to take into account its socio-economic consequences provided by both the Russian delegation and global industry, the results of the planned scientific studies as well as the comments made by other WTO delegations, stakeholders, the European and foreign manufacturers of steel, stainless steel, nickel, and multi-metallic alloys and products.14.  On that note, we also formally ask you to provide us with access to all the documents of the past CARACAL meetings including minutes, summaries and any other relevant information. Moreover, the Russian Federation would like to submit an application for participation in the CARACAL's meetings. We would appreciate some practical help from our European partners on this subject.

The representative of Mexico thanked the EU for the bilateral meeting held the previous day regarding the proposed classification of titanium dioxide as a possible carcinogen category II, as notified in document G/TBT/N/EU/629 in December 2018. The feedback from the EU seemed to indicate that the regulation would not have an impact on the paint sector as the classification would not apply in cases where titanium dioxide was present in a product in solid or liquid form. There would be an impact if there were special labelling requirements to indicate that a product contained titanium dioxide. Considering that the use of titanium dioxide was crucial for the production of 90% of paints, additional investments would be needed to adjust the labelling, which could also lead consumers to falsely believe that the products were dangerous. This could be incompatible with the principle of proportionality established in Article 2.2 of the TBT Agreement as it would impose more onerous requirements on the paint sector than necessary in light of the objectives pursued by the EU. If the proposed classification did not cover products containing titanium dioxide in solid or liquid form, she wondered why the labelling of paints would need to indicate presence of titanium dioxide, creating additional burdens for the paint sector. In this context, Mexico requested that the EU reconsider its proposal and also share information on the following steps to be taken regarding the regulation, its final publication and entry into force.

The representative of Canada, noting the concerns raised by Russia and Mexico, reiterated concerns raised in previous meetings. Canada continued to be concerned with the potential disruption on trade in various products that the measure could create and was disappointed that the EU had not found it necessary to perform an impact assessment on the potential downstream effects of the regulation. The measure would foreseeably result in stricter requirements under other regulations, beyond simple labelling requirements, which could in turn have a significant impact on trade from Canada. It also remained unclear how products containing cobalt and titanium dioxide would be treated once the regulation came into force. Canada thanked the EU for the useful information and clarification provided during various bilateral meetings and for responding to Canada's comments. It also remained unclear how products containing cobalt and titanium dioxide would be treated once the regulation came into force. Canada thanked the EU for the useful information and clarification.

The representative of the United States raised concerns regarding on the CLP regulation including with respect to titanium dioxide and cobalt. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/704 (below).1.  The United States' concerns with the EU's CLP regulations for the classification and labeling of chemicals and products are well known. First, we are concerned about the lack of transparency of how the EU notifies and conducts public consultations on chemicals via the CLP regulation, both within the EU and to the WTO.Second, the EU's WTO notifications tend to come only after its own scientific and regulatory committees have completed their sometimes years-long reviews, raising transparency concerns regarding consideration of international stakeholder input at an early and appropriate stage in the development of a regulation.For highly complex products, such as chemicals, where the science of assessing hazards and risks is quickly evolving and scientific studies can take years, this is a missed opportunity to meaningfully integrate international participation and comments, bringing the consultative intent of the EU's WTO notifications into question.Third, we are disappointed that in the cases of specific substances such as TiO2 and cobalt, the EU has not sought to consult with, much less address, the concerns of many WTO Members, who have provided substantive comments on the proposed classification and labeling requirements.2.  The U.S. specifically inquired for TiO2 as to why ECHA did not follow well-established methodologies to test inhalation toxicity—and why the Commission continues to side-step relevant international standards for chemical classification and labeling such as the UN Globally Harmonized System for the Classification of Chemicals that would allow for the management of any "potential hazard" from TiO2 particles without disrupting trade.3.  The United States has several questions regarding the delegated act that is now pending legislation with the European Parliament and the EU Council of Ministers: The delegated act adds a new amendment to the CLP Regulation on the criteria used to classify and to label all substances henceforth—not just TiO2 and cobalt. This amendment, Note W, states that when the carcinogenic hazard of a substance arises from inhalation of respirable dust, that this is not a "criterion for classification:" Can you explain this amendment, and how it will affect the classification of all substances—not just TiO2—with respirable dust? [If relevant, following EU response] Why does the delegated act still propose that TiO2 be listed as a carcinogen via inhalation in Annex VI, if it cannot be classified based on inhalation of "respirable dust?"4.  We also take note of the concerns from downstream industries, such as the toy industry, who have stated that they find the TiO2 labeling requirements in the delegated act confusing—particularly as it requires a hazard label for all liquid and solid mixtures containing TiO2, even when there are other EU regulations that govern the safety of chemicals when used in these products. For example, why do toys such as finger paint have to carry a hazard label even when they are considered safe under the EU Toy Safety Directive?5.  We would also appreciate if the EU could confirm if stainless steel will be considered a case requiring further evaluation under Article 12 of the CLP Regulation, and not subject to the cobalt classification and labeling requirements, as the Commission did not have enough information to determine if there is a risk of cobalt exposure via metal compounds.6.  Given the extent of the concerns and comments expressed by many WTO members as to the trade disruptions of the EU's actions on TiO2 and cobalt, as well as the CLP regulation more broadly, we ask that the ECHA and the Commission consider how it can bring greater transparency and consideration of WTO members and industry inputs in the future.

The representative of Australia recognized the European Union's right to regulate for public and occupational health and safety and that appropriate classification and labelling for hazardous substances and mixtures could address legitimate public and occupational health concerns. Australia and other Members had raised concerns on multiple occasions in the TBT Committee and other fora that the proposed regulation was more trade-restrictive than necessary. Australia understood that the proposed classifications had been adopted and would enter into force in late December or early January if there were no objections from the Council or Parliament. The new classifications had the potential to create unintended downstream consequences and unnecessary obstacles to international trade in products containing titanium oxide and cobalt. The actual impact of the new classification was unclear, particularly with regard to downstream products containing small amounts of titanium dioxide or cobalt. For example, the classification of cobalt (as category 1B carcinogen for all routes of exposure, with a concentration limit of 0.1%) would appear to capture some types of stainless steel. As stainless steel was very common, the potential for the classification to have unintended consequences affecting trade was high. Australia urged the EU to ensure that regulations to address concerns about the possible hazards associated with titanium dioxide and cobalt were no more trade restrictive than necessary.

The representative of Japan shared the concerns raised by other Members regarding the proposed changes to the CLP regulation, especially with respect to provisions for mixtures containing titanium dioxide. The proposed draft regulation could inappropriately broaden the scope of products to be regulated as it classified powder mixtures containing 1% or more of titanium dioxide as carcinogen regardless of whether exposure to titanium dioxide by inhalation could occur. In addition, labelling requirements would even affect products containing titanium dioxide with low inhalation risk such as toner cartridges. What is more, these products had not been classified as carcinogen in other countries' systems or in the Global Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals (GHS). Therefore, Japan requested that the EU reconsider the classification criteria in order to limit the scope to products where titanium dioxide inhalation exposure risk existed and ensure that the regulation was not more trade-restrictive than necessary.

The representative of New Zealand shared other Members' concerns about the EU's titanium dioxide regulation and referred the Committee to New Zealand's statement delivered at the previous TBT Committee meeting. Although the regulation was nearly finalized despite ongoing concerns, New Zealand reiterated its view that any regulation to address concerns about the possible carcinogenicity of titanium dioxide needed to be proportionate and not unduly restrict trade in goods containing titanium dioxide. New Zealand wished to understand more about the labelling requirements that would be introduced to determine what implications they might have on trade.

The representative of the Russian Federation raised concerns with this measure. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/731.European Union - Regulation (EC) No 1272/2008 (CLP Regulation)statement by the RUSSIAN FEDERATION to the committee on technical barriers to tradE26 – 27 FEBRUARY 20201.  The Russian delegation raises deep concern in respect of the cobalt and titanium dioxide classification under the 14th Adaptation to the technical progress to the CLP Regulation adopted by the European Commission on 4 October 2019. 2.  We stress that carcinogenicity of cobalt is not doubted and accepted by the Russian Federation and the Russian and Global industries, but only for inhalation route of exposure. Cobalt classification for other routes of exposure is not justified due to the fact that the relevant scientific data do not exist and the classification for all routes by default proposed by the Commission is not appropriate. 3.  As for the concern, the European Commission rushed this classification without scientific justification and necessary assessment of its economic consequences, disregarding deep concerns raised by the Member-states of the EU itself and ignoring the comments made by the WTO members. Moreover, the Commission has chosen to ignore the concerns of the Global and even its own European industries, which are involved in manufacturing, use, and disposal of the products containing cobalt and titanium dioxide. In this sense, the 14th ATP is yet another example of highly inappropriate implementation of the CLP Regulation as it contradicts the EU's own communication on the precautionary principle application (COM (2000) 1, section 6.1, item 16) that states "the implementation of the approach based on the precautionary principle should begin with a scientific evaluation, as complete as possible, and where possible, identifying at each stage the degree of scientific uncertainty". In this particular case, the Commission has chosen not to follow the principles declared earlier by the Commission itself.4.  It seems that the EU side did not deny the fact that their proposed measure was not based on scientific data and the classification of cobalt for all routes of exposure was simply applied by default, however the Article 2.2 of the Agreement on TBT explicitly requires scientific justification when elaborating technical regulations.5.  As far as UN GHS is concerned, we stress that while the Commission applied the hazard-based approach, which is a necessary step in classifying a substance, it becomes inappropriate and misleading if no risk assessment follows it. Hazard identification does not mean that health risks actually do exist for particular material/application/route of exposure. The UN GHS clearly stipulates that regulations should be based only and exclusively on full assessment of actual risks. Based on this, the cobalt classification case can be regarded as an inappropriate and flawed implementation of UN GHS by the Commission.6.  As far as appropriate scientific data are concerned, we take note that the relevant scientific study of cobalt carcinogenicity for the oral route of exposure has already been initiated by the global cobalt industry. While the Commission was repeatedly informed about the industry's commitment and intention to conduct this study, this fact had not been taken into account either and the Commission chose to rush its classification without providing any grounds as for the reasons for such urgency. Moreover, we also take a specific note that, to the best of our knowledge, there has never yet been a case when the Commission amended a classification, which had entered into force within the frameworks of REACH and CLP Regulations, when new scientific information disproving such an overly restrictive classification arrived. In this regard, we request the European Union to confirm that the Commission will expediently amend the current classification accordingly if the results of the study for cobalt metal carcinogenicity for the oral route of exposure are negative. Also, we request the Commission to outline fully the existing legal and regulatory procedure that enables the Commission to amend such overly restrictive classifications of chemicals and describes the relevant legislative procedures of the relevant processes. 7.  As for transparency and inclusiveness, we have to point out that the information on the discussions within CARACAL's meeting and their outcome is unacceptably limited and restricted. 8.  There is no substantive information on the discussions during these meetings that is being made public. There are no publicly available minutes of CARACAL meetings, nor statements made by participants, nor other documents. In this regard, the procedure is absolutely non-transparent. For this reason, we request the Commission to provide us with the relevant information on this issue. 9.  As for economic implications, the adopted cobalt classification will have a negative impact on broad manufacturing, supplying and recycling the wide range of products. Apart from cobalt itself, this non-scientific classification directly affects the markets for copper, nickel, steel, and stainless steel, as these materials contain trace fractions of cobalt. In practical terms, it makes it impossible to recycle these materials, which renders ineffective the EU own policies on resource efficiency, energy efficiency, recycling, and reduction of waste. The examples of the negative implications of this classification are numerous that they have been provided within the meetings of the Committee on TBT and the Council for trade in goods as well as bilaterally by the Russian Federation, other nations, as well as the industry itself, including the Cobalt and Nickel institutes. However all the presented data have never been considered, nor taken into account, nor even commented on. Basically, they have remained ignored and unaddressed.10.  Finally, within the frameworks of the scrutiny process and discussions on the 14th ATP to the CLP that took place during the European Parliament plenary sittings on 22 January 2020, the European Conservatives and reformists group raised an objection with respect to this document. Earlier, several Member Countries, namely Germany and the Czech Republic, expressed their concerns with respect to the 14th ATP in November 2019 and therefore, the scrutiny process was prolonged until 4 February 2020, despite the fact that initially the scheduled date was 4 December 2019. Today, we do not have any information regarding formal steps of adoption and implementation of this regulation. Bearing all these facts in mind, one has to conclude that the Commission has failed to conduct a comprehensive consultation on the proposed measure with the Member-states of the EU because these issues keep occurring during the final approval stages at the level of the European Parliament and the Council.11.  The Russian Federation has deep concerns regarding the approach that the European Commission intends to take with respect to classifying other chemicals, alloys, and mixtures. In this regard, we request the European Commission to revert to science and good practice, as well as to follow its own declared principles. 12.  In addition, we kindly remind the distinguished delegation of the European Union that they still have to provide some substantive response to the letters of the Russian Federation signed by the Minister of Economic Development to the European Commission sent to them in September 2019.

Summary: The representative of Australia recognized the EU's right to regulate for public and occupational health and safety, and that appropriate classification and labelling for hazardous substances and mixtures could address legitimate public and occupational health concerns. Australia and other WTO Members had raised concerns on multiple occasions, in this and other forums, that these measures were more trade restrictive than necessary.Australia was disappointed that the regulations had been adopted without fully taking into account the concerns expressed by WTO Members and industry bodies, although it welcomed the narrower scope for the TiO2 regulation to powder form only. Australia's concerns focused on the potential of these regulations to create unnecessary obstacles to international trade in products containing titanium oxide and cobalt. The representative of the United States stated that its concerns with the EU's proposed 14th Adaptation to Technical Progress to the CLP regulation for the classification and labelling of cobalt were well known. With the Adaptation to the ATP pending final adoption before the EU Parliament as a delegated act, the US asked the EU to provide clarifying guidance to industry that metal compounds containing trace amounts of cobalt and, in particular, stainless and other specialty steels were not currently covered in the ATP restrictions on the use of cobalt. As noted by the EU in the original notification of the draft cobalt restriction to the WTO, the Commission did not yet have sufficient information to determine whether there was a risk of cobalt exposure via metal compounds.Given how disruptive this classification could be to trade in products such as stainless steel and other specialty steels, the US asked the Commission to issue clarifying guidance that these uses would not be subject to these restrictions until the completion of the good faith testing efforts by US and EU industry, along with the appropriate EU authorities, to determine whether there was an actual health risk. The US requested the EU to provide a timeline for when it would communicate that the ATP cobalt restrictions no longer applied to metal compounds containing trace amounts of cobalt and, in particular, stainless and other specialty steels.

StatementSubmitted:
Thank you, Chair

The Russian Federation would like to thank the EU for its active work on the gastric fluid bioelution protocol (i.e. EURL ECVAM submission to OECD) and its commitment to incorporate it into the Article 12 of the CLP Regulation (i.e. DG Envi and DG Grow now convening a bioelution expert group under CARACAL to discuss the incorporation of bioelution test data into regulations). We do believe that this approach will be helpful in limiting the negative impact of the current unjustified classification of the cobalt metal on a wide range of cobalt-containing products.

At the same time, the Commission has failed to adopt bioelution at the level of OECD. In this regard, application of bioelution and mitigating the negative consequences of such a strict classification of cobalt on alloys and compounds appear to be problematic. Therefore, the measure at issue seems to be more trade restrictive than necessary and will have the negative impact on manufacturing and trade in a wide range of cobalt containing products at upstream and downstream as well as distort the global value added chains.

The 14th ATP was adopted on the 18th of February 2020 and applies from the 1st of October 2021. The European Commission rushed this classification without full scientific justification and necessary assessment of its economic consequences, ignoring the comments made by the WTO members and even disregarding deep concerns raised by the Member-states of the EU itself.

Moreover, the Commission has chosen to ignore the concerns of the Global and even its own European industries, which are involved in manufacturing, use, and disposal of the products containing cobalt and titanium dioxide. In this regard, the 14th ATP is yet another example of a highly inappropriate implementation of the CLP Regulation by the Commission as it contradicts the Commission’s own Communication on the precautionary principle’s application. In accordance with COM (2000) 1, section 6.1, item 16 (I quote) “the implementation of the approach based on the precautionary principle should begin with a scientific evaluation, as complete as possible, and where possible, identifying at each stage the degree of scientific uncertainty” (the end of the quote). Indeed, the precautionary principle should be applied in cases where it is not possible to complete a comprehensive risk assessment because there is no sufficient data, and where the regulator therefore makes conservative assumptions about potential hazards of certain chemical. Nevertheless, the precautionary principle can still only be invoked once a full scientific assessment has been made. In the case of cobalt classification, the Commission admits that it has not made a full scientific assessment, as there has been absence of complete scientific data (e.g. oral carcinogenicity study considered together with existing epidemiological data), therefore under the circumstances, any scientific assessment is simply impossible.

As a result, the current classification of cobalt for all routes of exposure is not based on a complete set of scientific facts, and has been adopted in direct contradiction to the Commission’s own guidelines on the proper application of the precautionary principle.

We note hereby that the provisions of the Agreement on TBT explicitly require scientific justification when elaborating, adopting, and applying technical regulations.

The statement of the Commission that any negative consequences will be largely mitigated by the application of the Generic Concentration Limit (GCL) of 0,1 % is factually incorrect. Firstly, the average content of cobalt impurity in stainless steel is several times higher than that and even in some cases of carbon steel and some alloys, can still be problematic. Secondly, the current GCL of 0,1 % is being set temporarily only and if it is to be revised in favor of the initially proposed Specific Concentration Limit, which was even more stringent than the current GCL by an order of magnitude, the consequences would be even more dire. Moreover, the Commission further admits that the methodology behind the derivation of the concentration limits (I quote) “was considered questionable” (the end of the quote).

Besides, the EU notified to the WTO the draft regulation amending Annex XVII to REACH Regulation (G/TBT/N/EU/714). According to the document, cobalt metal was included in the list of CMR category 1 B in order to prevent contacts of the general population with it. We note hereby that the draft legislation does not provide any exemption and steel articles will be covered by these restrictions as the Commission was not able to adopt the gastric bioelution protocol at the OECD, which resulted in it remaining in uncertainty.

As for economic implications, the adopted cobalt classification will have a significant negative impact on manufacturing, supplying, and recycling of a wide range of products. Apart from cobalt itself, this non-scientific classification directly affects the markets for copper, nickel, alloys, steel, and stainless steel, as these materials contain traces of cobalt.  In practical terms, it also makes it impossible to recycle these materials efficiently, which renders ineffective the EU own policies on resource efficiency, energy efficiency, recycling, circular economy, and reduction of waste. The examples of the negative implications of this classification are numerous and they have been provided within the meetings of the Committee on TBT and the Council for trade in goods as well as bilaterally by Russia and the industry itself, including the Cobalt and Nickel institutes. However all the presented data have never been considered, nor taken into account, nor even commented on. Basically, data have remained ignored and concerns have remained not addressed.

We urge the EU to revoke the measure and rely on available scientific data and arguments made by Russia and European and Global industries. StatementSubmitted:
As previously noted in this Committee, Australia recognises the European Union’s (EU) right to regulate for public and occupational health and safety. We also recognise that appropriate classification and labelling for hazardous substances and mixtures can address legitimate public and occupational health concerns.

However, Australia and other WTO Members have raised concerns on multiple occasions in this and other forums that these measures are more trade-restrictive than necessary.

Our concerns have focused on the potential of these regulations to create unnecessary obstacles to international trade in products containing titanium dioxide and cobalt, as well as the raw materials themselves.

While the EU has provided some information on the downstream consequences for TiO2, we have yet to receive a clear response to our concerns regarding products containing trace amounts of cobalt. Despite concerns raised by Australia and other Members, the EU has retained the classification of cobalt as a carcinogen through all routes of exposure, rather than limiting the classification to inhalation only. This means a larger number of products are potentially affected by the regulation, and there is therefore a greater risk of unintended downstream consequences. For example, stainless steel is a common product which may contain trace amounts of cobalt in concentrations greater than the generic limit of 0.1 per cent applied in the regulation.

We continue to urge the EU to ensure that regulations to address concerns about the possible hazards associated with TiO2 and cobalt are no more trade restrictive than necessary.

StatementSubmitted:
In August, the European Union notified a draft regulation proposing changes to Part 3 of Annex VI of the Regulation (EC) No 1272/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council on Classification, Labelling and Packaging of Substances and Mixtures (CLP), which introduce a stricter classification of reproductive toxicity to  2-ethylhexanoic acid (2-EHA) from Repr. 2 to Repr. 1B. If adopted, the modification would take effect in the first semester of 2022.

The revaluation process was initiated in 2014, when ECHA requested new studies to be carried out, specifically an Extended One-Generation Reproductive Toxicity Study (EOGRTS). A Substance evaluation (SeV) process was then carried on by Spain, which recommended maintaining the previous classification of reproductive toxicity (Repr.2, H361d). At the time, the only modification suggested was the introduction of an explanatory note, which clarified the fundamentals of the classification in question.

The competent authorities then opened a public consultation for the submission of comments on the dossier resulting from the SeV and additional information by authorities of other Member States and members of the private sector. During this period, Germany and France submitted a reclassification proposal to Repr. 1B, based on analysis of analogy (also called “read-across”) with the substance valproic acid.

            The use of read-across relies on the assumption that, due to the presence of similar chemical aspects, the substances in question will have similar effects when exposed to the same tests, and thus, will reveal the same toxicity. According to our private sector, this does not seem to be the case. The reproductive toxicity studies specific to 2-EHA, which contradict the applicability of read-across with valproic acid, make up the best technical information to support the classification of reproductive toxicity, as they are a direct analysis of the substance, without relying on assumptions of similarity. Studies specific to 2-EHA conclude that the most appropriate classification would be the Repr. 2, and the more restrictive classification adopted by the EU is not justified.

In addition to the higher costs associated with the registration process of chemicals classified as 1B, it is estimated that the reclassification will have a negative impact on the preferences of importers of the substance, who will have the wrong indication of its actual level of risk. We believe that, if adopted, these regulatory changes would be more trade-restrictive than necessary to fulfill the EU legitimate objectives of health protection.

In light of the above,


	Could the EU explain why it chose to adopt the read-across methodology when there are reproductive toxicity studies specific to 2-EHA that do not support the conclusion underlying draft regulation G/TBT/N/EU/826?
	Could the EU indicate whether it will consider not changing the classification of said substance?
	Does the EU consider postponing the adoption of the new reproductive toxicity classification for 2-EHA until the competent authorities can analyze the private sectors’ comments on the read-across studies and the GHS standards for 2-EHA?

We believe, therefore, that these regulatory changes would be more trade-restrictive than necessary to fulfill the EU legitimate objectives of health protection. Brazil thanks the EU for its statement in our last meeting, clarifying procedural aspects of its legislation. We also appreciate the written reply to the comments from our private sector in the public consultation. In this sense, we would like to ask if the EU could provide an update on the status of the proposal, regarding the current and next steps of the process towards adoption and entry into force.

StatementSubmitted: In August 2021, the European Union notified a draft regulation proposing changes to Part 3 of Annex VI of the Regulation (EC) No 1272/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council on Classification, Labelling and Packaging of Substances and Mixtures (CLP), which introduce a stricter classification of reproductive toxicity to 2-ethylhexanoic acid (2-EHA) from Repr. 2 to Repr. 1B. The revaluation process was initiated in 2014, when ECHA requested new studies to be carried out, specifically an Extended One-Generation Reproductive Toxicity Study (EOGRTS). A Substance evaluation (SeV) process was then carried on by Spain, which recommended maintaining the previous classification of reproductive toxicity (Repr.2, H361d). At the time, the only modification suggested was the introduction of an explanatory note, which clarified the fundamentals of the classification in question. The competent authorities then opened a public consultation for the submission of comments on the dossier resulting from the SeV and additional information by authorities of other Member States and members of the private sector. During this period, Germany and France submitted a reclassification proposal to Repr. 1B, based on analysis of analogy (also called “read-across”) with the substance valproic acid. The use of read-across relies on the assumption that, due to the presence of similar chemical aspects, the substances in question will have similar effects when exposed to the same tests, and thus, will reveal the same toxicity. According to our private sector, this does not seem to be the case. The reproductive toxicity studies specific to 2-EHA, which contradict the applicability of read-across with valproic acid, make up the best technical information to support the classification of reproductive toxicity, as they are a direct analysis of the substance, without relying on assumptions of similarity. Studies specific to 2-EHA conclude that the most appropriate classification would be the Repr. 2. The EU has claimed that its analysis has considered studies specific to 2-EHA and not only read-across ones. Brazil is still concerned, though, that the more restrictive classification adopted by the EU is not justified. Brazil would also like to note that, according to the EU, the reclassification of the product as 1B would not entail higher costs associated with the registration process of chemicals. Nevertheless, the reclassification will still have a negative impact on the preferences of importers of the substance, who will have the wrong indication of its actual level of risk. We believe, therefore, that these regulatory changes would be more trade-restrictive than necessary to fulfill the EU legitimate objectives of health protection. Brazil thanks the EU for its statement in our last meeting, clarifying procedural aspects of its legislation and informing that if there would be no objection for the European Parliament and the Council, the measure should be published in the second half of April. In this sense, we would like to ask if the EU could provide an update on the status of the proposal, regarding the current and next steps of the process towards adoption and entry into force.

The delegation of the Russian Federation provided the following statement. Russian Federation reiterates statements made during the previous meetings of the TBT Committee and CTG with regard to the cobalt classification as a carcinogen 1b for all routes of exposure. We stress that this measure was adopted in the absence of sufficient scientific justification, neither laboratory nor epidemiological, without taking into account grounded comments and opinions of the WTO Members and business community. At the same time, we appreciate efforts of the EU on adoption of the gastric bioelution protocol at the EU and the OECD levels. However, the EU has not adopted this methodology and has not incorporated its use into the CLP Regulation as a regular practice of classifying alloys and compounds that will allow to exclude many cobalt-containing products from the scope of further restrictions which will be developed within the framework of the implementation of this classification decision. We urge the European Union to adopt this methodology as soon as possible.
