The representative of Indonesia continued to raise concerns with this measure. The full statement is contained in document G/TBT/W/641 (below).1.  The Government of Indonesia is disappointed with the adoption of Delegated Regulations, effective on 12 May 2019, as the implementation of the Amendment of EU Directive of Renewable Energy. The Delegated Regulation negates all the inputs and considerations provided by the Government of Indonesia and other Palm Oil Exporting countries2.  The Government of Indonesia received a letter on 3 May 2019 stating that the EU-RED II and Delegated Regulation are not intended to limit the importation of oil palm products to the EU. In addition, it was also stated that the technical requirements contained in the Delegated Regulations are beyond the scope of the WTO TBT Agreement. 3.  We beg to differ with the EU on this important issue. The requirements stipulated in the delegated regulation are technical regulations to a product and or group of products which are clearly fall under the TBT agreement. Some provisions, such as the 2008 base year determination and determination of the annual average rate of expansion of global production areas and the determination of production area conversion thresholds above areas with high carbon stocks used as the basis for calculating ILUC high and low risk, are clear indication that these are technical regulations that should be met by producers of biodiesels in order to help with EU environmental achievement. 4.  The structure, design, and expected operation of this standard are expected to discriminate biodiesels generated from palm oil against other biodiesel products produced within EU members countries, such as rapeseed and sunflower. Moreover, the expected operation of this regulation will also curb the demand of palm oil biodiesels and create unnecessary barriers to trade in contravene with the TBT Agreement.5.  The RED and Delegated Regulations stated that biofuel feedstocks which have a significant annual expansion rate of production areas, the level of consumption will be limited to the consumption level in 2019. Moreover, vegetable oils that do not meet ILUC criteria will be phased out gradually up to 0% in 2030. This is certainly a discriminatory practice that violates the National Treatment principle (article III: 4) and general elimination of quantitative restriction (article XI: 1) GATT and articles 2.1 and 2.2 of TBT Agreement.6.  The EU continued denial that this issue is fall under TBT Agreement is alarming and threatening the credibility of TBT Committee. Moreover, it is also threatened the credibility of EU Proposal on Procedures to Enhance Transparency and Strengthen Notification Requirements. If, pragmatically, members start denying that a de facto standard or technical regulation is not a standard or technical regulation under the TBT Agreement, all the STCs in this committee would need to be decided by the Dispute Settlement Body.7.  In addition, Indonesia firmly believes that any weighting on the sustainability issues should not covers only deforestation. It shall also take into account the overall aspect of sustainable development which include environmental, social, and economic aspect. This is a global commitment under Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 2030, of which the EU has committed to and shall obliged to. 8.  The palm oil crops have a very high productivity. It produces up to 10 times more compared to other vegetable oils with a smaller land use rate. EU intention to phase out of palm oil biodiesel will only increase sharply the demand for other vegetable oils which will lead to massive land clearing. Due to this reason, we expect the EU to review the policy of limiting the use of palm oil to prevent further environmental degradation.

The representative of Ecuador continued to raise concerns with this measure. The full statement is contained in document G/TBT/W/650 (below).1.   Ecuador supports the position of Indonesia, Colombia and Malaysia, and agrees with the analysis conducted.2.   We consider that the ILUC methodology proposed by the European Union (EU) is unilateral since it has not been extensively discussed or endorsed at international level or sufficiently disseminated, and can therefore be considered as a new technical requirement that would covertly affect palm oil production and marketing processes. Ecuador observes a clear technical barrier to trade in this methodology.3.   It is clear that the EU is seeking to meet legitimate climate‑related goals, as are all the other countries that signed the Paris Agreement, and they are working in accordance with their own national agendas to eliminate deforestation from supply chains as part of their commitment to and support for alleviating the effects of climate change. However, the rural development capacities of predominantly agricultural countries should not be limited, and the restriction of trade through the extrajudicial application of national agendas based on non‑consensual measures cannot be justified by a legitimate environmental objective.4.   In this regard, any environmental measure for fulfilling the European climate agenda must be accompanied by the commitment to make it compatible with the multilateral trading system – in other words, ensuring that the measure would not constitute a means of arbitrary or unjustifiable discrimination, or a disguised restriction on international trade.5.   Like Colombia, Ecuador considers that the criteria established would directly affect oil palms but not fuels produced from other types of vegetable oil, for instance rapeseed oil or sunflower‑seed oil, which is inconsistent with the obligation contained in Article 2.1 of the TBT Agreement and Article I:1 of the GATT 1994. Moreover, since the proposed measure favours vegetable oils produced in the EU, it also violates the principle of national treatment contained in Article 2.1 of the TBT Agreement and Article III:4 of the GATT 1994.6.   The delegated act, established pursuant to Article 26 of the Directive, provides for specific standards on biofuels, bioliquids and biomass fuels produced from food or feed crops, to address what it refers to as emissions produced by indirect land‑use change (ILUC). This methodology and the characterizations applied through the establishment of general, specific and additionality criteria for the certification of biofuels, bioliquids and biomass fuels are not and have not been the subject of any agreement or multilateral negotiations, especially with countries that supply the raw materials.7.   It should be recalled that under the Paris Agreement related to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), each country establishes its own targets to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. These are the "nationally determined contributions" (NDCs), in which each country, while retaining its sovereignty and observing the principle of common but differentiated obligations in line with its development capacities, establishes its system for controlling the expansion of crops at the expense of forests, forage or vegetation with high carbon stock. In this regard, Ecuador considers that the Directive and the subsequent delegated act run counter to the letter and spirit of the Paris Agreement, especially Article 3 thereof, which recognizes "the need to support developing country Parties for the effective implementation" of the Agreement.8.   The lack of definition of certain terms relating to ILUC certification in the EU regulations means that it is difficult for Ecuador to comply with these standards that require significant technical and financial investment, as well as going beyond commitments made at the bilateral or multilateral level.9.   To date, the European Commission has not included the ILUC methodology in its calculations of greenhouse gas emissions, and therefore fails to comply with the principle of national treatment. Third countries cannot be expected to apply a methodology that provides no certainty regarding the hypotheses used, benchmarks for oil palm plantations, estimates of greenhouse gas emissions in the production of palm oil, or projections concerning the types of land to be used for the expansion of oil palm crops. Calculations of deforestation have been carried out from a global perspective without considering differences that exist between individual cases.10.   In this regard, it is important to emphasize that Ecuador has made significant progress in meeting its national targets and commitments for mitigating the effects of climate change, as it is currently a world leader in the implementation of policies, measures and actions for reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation (REDD+). This commitment has also been made by the Ecuadorian palm‑growing sector, which signed an agreement to move towards sustainable, deforestation‑free oil palm production, with a roadmap setting out clear zero‑deforestation goals and commitments.11.   Ecuador is also the second country in the world to have met the requirements established by the UNFCCC to gain access to performance‑based payments for reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation. It is therefore fundamental that such achievements made in the context of international commitments be taken into consideration when establishing this type of restriction.12.   Specifically, in its REDD+ Action Plan "Forests for Good Living", Ecuador set itself the goal of reducing greenhouse gas emissions from deforestation, as evidenced by the results achieved. Our average gross annual rate of deforestation was 94,353 hectares in the period 2015‑2016, compared with 129,943 hectares in the period 1990‑2000, representing a decrease of 27%. This has amounted to a reduction of over 29 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent between 2009 and 2014.13.   Attention should also be drawn to the socio‑economic effect that unilateral measures can have on the oil palm sector in Ecuador, which produced approximately 560,000 tonnes of crude palm oil in 2018, the gross production value of which was USD 326 million, representing around 3% of agricultural GDP. There are approximately 6,568 palm oil producers, of whom 88% are small producers with less than 50 hectares under production and 51% are small producers in small‑scale family farming with less than 10 hectares under production.14.   The importance of this sector lies in its economic contribution to the country, with foreign exchange earnings from exports of around USD 226 million in 2018. Palm oil occupies fifth place in agricultural exports from Ecuador. The sector accounts for some 120,000 direct and indirect jobs throughout the production chain, jobs which are stable in terms of time since the productive lifespan can be around 25 years. The oil palm sector pays the unified basic wage plus all statutory benefits.15.   In view of the above, Ecuador calls on the EU to consider its proposal regarding ILUC, since internationally agreed provisions exist regarding the control of deforestation, gas emissions and climate change. Environmental measures adopted by Members must not cause additional obstacles to trade, especially when there are binding parameters agreed upon at international level to measure countries' effectiveness in protecting the environment.16.   Another point to bear in mind is that, in accordance with the TBT Agreement, measures adopted by Members should be based on international standards providing clear definitions, not on unilaterally established definitions which require additional technical and economic outlay to implement them and affect developing countries.

The representative of Costa Rica reiterated his delegation's support for the concerns raised by preceding speakers. In particular, Costa Rica was concerned about the criteria proposed for the determination of indirect change in the use of the soil, and the certification of a low risk of indirect change in the use of the soil in relation with biofuels. As pointed out at previous meetings of the TBT Committee, Costa Rica was a pioneering country committed to the protection of the environment. It was one of the few countries that had been capable not only of reforesting but also of reversing the trend to deforestation. Today Costa Rica had one of the few decarbonized electricity systems in the world: in 2017 some 99.5% of Costa Rica's electricity had been generated without using fossil fuels – the highest percentage in 30 years. Costa Rica applauded the efforts of the EU to establish an effective policy for the use of renewable energy sources. Nevertheless, these efforts could not be detrimental to product marketing conditions on the basis of criteria that lack scientific foundation. Costa Rica trusted that European authorities would be able to recognize the special nature of palm oil cultivation in Costa Rica and other areas of Latin America.

The representative of Malaysia continued to raise concerns with this measure. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/691 (below).1.  Malaysia remains very concerned with the development of the Directive (EU) 2018/2001 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 December 2018 on the promotion of the use of energy from renewable sources and the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/807 of 13 March 2019.2.  The development has negatively impacted the Malaysian oil palm industry because this had resulted in several countries in the European Union and non-European Union enforcing legislation to single out and discriminate biodiesel produced from palm oil to be not eligible for incentives and tax exemption against biodiesel produced from other vegetable oils. 3.  We have been engaging with the European Union in all possible fora to provide scientific evidence, facts and information as well as to exchange views to find a mutually beneficial and mutually acceptable way forward to ensure continued market access for Malaysian palm biodiesel. 4.  Although we appreciate the European Union for their willingness for open discussion and dialogue, the continuous engagements have not resulted in a fair treatment for palm oil produced in Malaysia.5.  We urge the European Union to observe the principles of fairness, justice, openness, transparency and non-discrimination in conducting international trade. We also urge the European Union to provide an equitable treatment across all oil crops biofuels and bioliquids in line with the principle of non-discrimination which stipulates that a member shall not discriminate between "like" products from different trading partners.6.  Malaysia is committed to realising the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and its 17 Sustainable Development Goals. The Sustainable Development Goals are a universal call to action to end poverty, protect the planet and ensure that all people enjoy peace and prosperity. In this context, the oil palm industry plays a very important role in contributing positively and constructively towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals. 7.  In March 2019, the Government of Malaysia had agreed with the new policy in ensuring that Malaysian oil palm is cultivated in a sustainable manner. The measures included to cap oil palm cultivated area to 6.5 million hectares; to put a stop on conversion of permanent forest reserved area; to halt planting of oil palm in the new peatland area and further strengthen regulations with regard to existing oil palm cultivated on peat; and to make available oil palm plantation maps for public access that demonstrate further transparency in the supply chain.8.  Malaysia wishes to emphasise that the Malaysian oil palm industry is committed to produce palm oil in accordance with sustainable principles and criteria under the Malaysian Sustainable Palm Oil (MSPO) certification scheme, which will be implemented on a mandatory basis by 31 December 2019. 9.  Malaysia has put in place policy framework and legislation to ensure sustainable development balancing the protection of the environment and socioeconomic development. This is evident through the implementation of various programmes and initiatives for conservation and preservation of forests and biodiversity including among others, national forestry initiatives namely, The Central Forest Spine and Heart of Borneo, reforestation through replanting of forest tree species, establishment of wildlife corridors and reduction of greenhouse gas (GHG) emission.10.  The Central Forest Spine covers 5.3 million hectares in Peninsular Malaysia and the Heart of Borneo is a trilateral cooperation between Brunei, Indonesia and Malaysia covering an area of over 20 million hectares. These initiatives help to strengthen the world's resilience to climate change by conserving carbon sinks and creating a huge green lung for the world while at the same time protecting the livelihoods for the forest dependent communities.11.  Malaysia continues to maintain 55.3% of its land area under forest cover which exceeds the commitment of Malaysia to retain at least 50% pledged at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992. 12.  The Malaysian Budget 2020 which was tabled on 11 October 2019 had also included the strategy on promoting environmental sustainability. The Government of Malaysia had allocated budget for preservation of Malaysia's pristine forests and natural biodiversity as well as protection of endangered species such as Malayan tiger and orang utan which demonstrate our commitment and seriousness in taking action to address the issue. 13.  Also, we will commence a survey project that aims to undertake a new population survey of the Orang Utan and pygmy elephants in Sabah. This survey will bring together wildlife experts, scientists and researchers to take part in an extensive study on the population of the state's iconic wildlife.14.  Currently, Malaysia has also committed to plant 1 million forest tree species within the next 10 years particularly in degraded lands in Sabah as well as protecting the wildlife population which the projects will be sponsored primarily by the palm oil industry players. 15.  We urge the European Union to acknowledge and recognise the efforts and commitment in contributing towards protection and conservation of forest and biodiversity and production of Malaysian palm oil in a sustainable manner.16.  We remain fully committed to negotiating in a sincere and constructive manner in ensuring a non-discriminatory treatment against palm products and to prevent the unnecessary barrier for market access of palm products into the European Union. 17.  We look forward to the positive response from the European Union.

The representative of Colombia  continued to raise concerns with this measure. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/697 (below).1.   We wish to reiterate our concern regarding Directive (EU) 2018/2001 of the European Parliament and of the Council, which establishes that, as from 2021, first‑generation biofuels shall account for a share of no more than 7% in the transport sector, and that first‑generation biofuels posing a high risk of indirect land‑use change (ILUC) shall have their contribution to the renewable energy share gradually reduced to 0% by 2030. In Colombia's view, these provisions are inconsistent with the national treatment and MFN obligations set out in the GATT 1994 and Article 2.1 and 2.2 of the WTO TBT Agreement.2.   Colombia appreciates the intention of the European Union (EU) to adopt a public policy aimed at protecting the environment through the promotion of the use of energy from renewable sources. Nevertheless, this environmental policy should be applied in a manner that is non‑discriminatory and not more restrictive than necessary, and should not create an unnecessary obstacle or disguised barrier to trade that indirectly affects entire economies and populations dedicated to agriculture and agro‑industry.3.   We also wish to express our concern regarding the delegated act issued by the European Commission, which establishes criteria for identifying high ILUC‑risk biofuels and for certifying low ILUC‑risk biofuels.4.   We would first like to draw attention to the ILUC methodology, which has no valid or internationally recognised scientific basis for measuring the environmental impact of a production activity. Nor are there any calculations of the expected reduction in greenhouse gas production, and the Commission did not take into account other methodologies that have been validated and tested internationally in this area. It is also important to conduct an impact assessment – one that takes into account the potential scope of a measure that sets out criteria for determining the high ILUC‑risk feedstock for which a significant expansion of the production area into land with high carbon stock is observed.5.   With regard to the classification of certain high ILUC‑risk biofuels, the considerations are not technically appropriate, since: (i) the level of deforestation associated with these products is not always high in all producing countries; and (ii) some countries, such as Colombia, have land available to increase the agricultural production area without resorting to deforestation. Furthermore, products shown by international studies to be the greatest contributors to deforestation, such as soy, rapeseed and even livestock, are not considered to present a high ILUC risk. The European standard could even, by virtue of the delegated act, benefit producers of these goods who have engaged in deforestation, since excessive growth would not be recorded.6.   In order to establish criteria to define the high ILUC risk, the delegated act uses the reference made in the annex "Worldwide production expansion of food and feed crop". Accordingly, palm oil crops would be excluded from the outset due to their excessive growth, without the use of any broader classification indicators to ensure that the process is effective and applied in the same manner to other crops used in the production of biofuels. It should be noted that this EU standard could also run counter to the commendable aims of environmental conservation, as the oil would then come from other crops that require a larger area to obtain similar results in terms of production volume.7.   With regard to the certification mechanism, the delegated act states that biofuels may only be certified as low risk if they meet a number of criteria, such as "additionality measures", which only allow for the certification of additional oil, meaning that a large part of current production could not be certified.8.   Furthermore, the definition used for small‑scale producers (small holders) is a cause for significant concern. These producers are defined as "farmers who conduct independently an agricultural activity on a holding with an agricultural area of less than 2 hectares for which they hold ownership [or] tenure rights". In Colombia's view, this classification has no technical or scientific basis and substantially diverges from the standards used by international organizations such as the FAO. It should be recalled that the classification of small‑scale producers differs in each country, in accordance with economic and social conditions. In addition, certification based on this methodology would generate unjustified costs for producers, given that the criteria is not aligned with any internationally recognized standard and the methodology is not used on a global basis.9.   Furthermore, this measure constitutes de facto discrimination under Articles I and III of the GATT, which prohibit discrimination between like products of different foreign origins and like products of foreign and national origin. In this context, it is important to highlight the extensive economic and technical scope for substitution that exists among vegetable oils. We wish to draw particular attention to the manner in which the Directive and the delegated act establish that a feedstock may present a high ILUC risk on the basis of indicators, criteria and definitions that de facto discriminate against palm oil, but exclude from the prohibition like feedstock, much of which is produced locally in European territory. Similarly, these criteria are applied across the board to all producers, without recognizing the specific features and differences in production methods and processes in different jurisdictions.10.   The delegated act also constitutes de facto discrimination under Article 2.1 of the TBT Agreement, given the competitive relationship between like products of foreign origin, such as soy, and of domestic origin, such as rapeseed. The measure also violates Article 2.2 of the TBT Agreement, which requires Members to refrain from adopting technical regulations that create unnecessary obstacles to international trade, and fails to fulfil the requirements of the "necessity test" through which its compliance with this Article is assessed. The delegated act does not permit countries with low ILUC threat indicators to be excluded from the measure and, in addition, excludes feedstock that threatens sustainability. Therefore, the measure, as it currently stands, is not effective in meeting its environmental protection objective and creates an unnecessary obstacle for palm oil.11.   We also wish to refer to the findings of the Panel in DS332 (Brazil – Retreaded Tyres), where it was concluded that in order to comply with Article XX(b) of the GATT 1994, it is necessary to establish the existence not just of risks to the environment generally, but specifically of direct risks to human, animal or plant life or health; it is therefore clear that this measure is designed to address other concerns, including environmental issues, and overlooks the link to other variables that are taken into account in this Article, even being discriminatory since there is evidence of an environmental impact on other activities that have not been regulated.12.   The measures adopted by the EU discourage the use of biofuels produced from sustainable palm oil (as even 100% sustainable oil cannot count towards renewable energy targets on account of being "high ILUC‑risk") and have a disproportionately negative impact on countries such as Colombia, an environmentally responsible producer of this product.13.   Thus, while, on a global scale, palm oil meets the criteria established in the delegated act for its categorization as a high ILUC‑risk feedstock, there are significant regional differences regarding the impact that the expansion of oil palm production has had in terms of deforestation.14.   Colombia requests the EU to conduct a thorough review of the delegated act in 2021, in order to adopt an approach that enables sustainable palm oil to contribute to the EU's renewable energy targets.15.   We once again welcome the opportunity to comment on this matter and request the EU to clarify how it reconciles this discriminatory treatment against palm oil‑producing countries with its WTO obligations concerning national and MFN treatment. We look forward to the EU's response to the concerns raised.

The representative of Ecuador continued to raise concerns with this measure. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/689 (below).1.1.   Ecuador thanks Indonesia, Colombia and Malaysia, and agrees with the analysis conducted.1.2.   The delegated act provides for specific standards on biofuels, bioliquids and biomass fuels produced from food or feed crops, to address what it refers to as emissions produced by indirect land‑use change (ILUC).1.3.   Various studies have found the methodology of existing ILUC models, the basis on which the EU defines ILUC in this measure, to be problematic.1.4.   In general, ILUC methodologies used for calculations (such as IFPRI, CARB, GLOBIOM) operate on inadequate budgets and outdated data, since they use historical information and do not incorporate the most recent data and scientific evidence as a matter of course.1.5.   As it is based on such methodology, the EU standard automatically labels crops which had historically experienced deforestation as being of high ILUC risk, while completely setting aside data that show recent progress which has led to innovation and the implementation of improved legislation and better practices by producing countries1.6.   In its current form, the regulation has a dual effect:On one hand, it creates arbitrary discrimination between similar biofuels, some of which are from crops that are less productive per hectare than oil palm, such as rapeseed and sunflower, but these are nonetheless not considered as being of high ILUC risk. This is inconsistent with obligations under Article 2.1 of the TBT Agreement and in Articles I:1 of the GATT 1994. On the other hand, it favours the use of raw materials of European origin, in violation of the principle of national treatment contained in Article 2.1 of the TBT Agreement and Article III:4 of the GATT 1994.1.7.    As there is no current consensus among scientists on ILUC methodology, instead of its unilateral adoption by the EU, the proposed methodology should be extensively discussed at the international level, and endorsed multilaterally, and especially with the participation of the developing countries that provide raw materials.1.8.   There is currently no certainty regarding the hypotheses used, benchmarks for oil palm plantations, estimates of greenhouse gas emissions in the production of palm oil, or projections concerning the types of land to be used for the expansion of oil palm crops. Calculations of deforestation have been carried out from a global perspective without considering differences that exist between individual cases.1.9.   The ILUC methodology used for calculations must recognize that palm oil can be of low ILUC risk when produced sustainably.1.10.   In this regard, it is important to emphasize that Ecuador has made significant progress in meeting its national targets and commitments for mitigating the effects of climate change, as it is currently a world leader in the implementation of policies, measures and actions for reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation (REDD+). This commitment has also been made by the Ecuadorian palm‑growing sector, which signed an agreement to move towards sustainable, deforestation‑free oil palm production, with a roadmap setting out clear zero‑deforestation goals and commitments.1.11.   Ecuador is also the second country in the world to have met the requirements established by the UNFCCC to gain access to performance‑based payments for reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation.1.12.   Specifically, in its REDD+ Action Plan "Forests for Good Living", Ecuador set itself the goal of reducing greenhouse gas emissions from deforestation, as evidenced by the results achieved. For instance, our average gross annual rate of deforestation was 94,353 hectares between 2015 and 2016, compared with 129,943 hectares in the period 1990 to 2000, representing a decrease of 27%. This has amounted to a reduction of over 29 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent between 2009 and 2014.1.13.   It is fundamental that such achievements made in the context of international commitments be taken into consideration. ILUC methodology used for calculations should provide incentives, not penalize countries that have made great efforts to produce sustainable palm oil.1.14.   Attention should also be drawn to the socio‑economic impact that this measure could have on developing countries that produce palm oil. In Ecuador the palm oil sector is comprised of approximately 6,500 producers, of which 88% have fewer than 50 hectares under production, while 51% are small producers in small‑scale family farming with fewer than 10 hectares under production.1.15.   This sector earned around USD 226 million in 2018, occupying fifth place in agricultural exports from Ecuador. The sector accounts for some 120,000 direct and indirect jobs throughout the production chain.1.16.   In view of the above, Ecuador calls on the EU to change its ILUC methodology, and the way in which it is using the measure in question to single out palm oil for exclusion. We understand that the EU is seeking to meet legitimate goals as part of their commitment to, and support for, alleviating the effects of climate change. Nonetheless, any environmental regulation for fulfilling the European climate agenda must be compatible with the multilateral trading system ‑ in other words, it must ensuring that the measure would not constitute a means of arbitrary or unjustifiable discrimination, or a disguised restriction on international trade.

The representative of Guatemala said that as a producing country of palm oil, Guatemala shared the concerns and understood that this method did not limit the use of palm oil but acted as a disincentive of its use as it was discriminated against when compared with other vegetable oils, and particular those produced in the EU, meaning that there were fewer advantages for this type of oil. Stating that in 2017 palm oil had been positioned as the sixth export product from Guatemala, she said that the impact of these new measures would affect bilateral trade as the EU represented one of its main trading partners. The production sector was making the necessary efforts to generate sustainable production, implementing policies at the private level and estimating GHG emissions in palm oil production, thereby demonstrating its priority and commitment to these issues. Additionally, it was considered necessary to differentiate between palm oil production and production conditions worldwide; it was not possible to condemn those whose daily livelihood depended upon it. Guatemala reiterated its commitment to achieve the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals and supported the certification of sustainable palm oil with the aim of achieving the millennium goals.

The representative of Costa Rica expressed support for concerns raised by other Members regarding the changes made to the EU text. He also expressed concern regarding the criteria which had been set for the determination on changes in soil use and also regarding biofuels. As previously stated, Costa Rica was very committed to protecting the environment and was amongst the few countries that had been able to reverse deforestation, therefore benefitting from a very low carbon fuel system. While understanding the EU's need for renewable energy legislation, Costa Rica believed that it was important that such legislation should not be made on grounds having no scientific basis. The EU was therefore requested to look at low risk biofuels and on that basis to recognize the advantages of palm oil in Costa Rica and other Latin American countries.

StatementSubmitted: MALAYSIA’S STATEMENT TECHNICAL BARRIERS TO TRADE (TBT) COMMITTEE MEETING13-14    MAY 2020 Malaysia regrets having to continue raising our concern on the Directive (EU) 2018/2001 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 December 2018 on the promotion of the use of energy from renewable sources and the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/807 of 13 March 2019 which have negatively impacted the oil palm industry and Malaysia’s trade interest. The European Union continues to reiterate that the legislation does not represent an import prohibition of biofuels and bioliquids produced from palm oil. However, this is tantamount to a barrier and de facto ban of the use of palm oil as feedstock for the production of biofuels and bioliquids for use in the European Union.  The development of such regulation has negatively impacted the oil palm industry and Malaysia’s trade interest. This has resulted in several countries to enforce legislation to discriminate biodiesel produced from palm oil against biodiesel produced from other vegetable oils in terms of fiscal incentives without substantiated by scientific evidence.  The measure is to believe has culminated into a technical barrier to trade that distorts the market and pricing system. This is a measure which is against the principle of free trade that is unfavourable to palm oil. We remain troubled as this creates the arbitrary or unjustifiable discrimination disguised restriction on international trading of palm oil and its products. This is taking into consideration that the delegated regulation creates unnecessary obstacles which are more trade restrictive than necessary and more burdensome for producers of palm oil based biofuels and bioliquids including Malaysia.   We have been engaging with the European Union in all possible fora to provide scientific evidence, facts and information as well as to exchange views to find a mutually beneficial and mutually acceptable way forward to ensure continued market access for Malaysian palm biodiesel.  Although we appreciate the European Union for their willingness for open discussion and dialogue, the continuous engagements have not translated in a fair treatment for palm oil produced in Malaysia. We urge the European Union to observe the principles of fairness, justice, openness, transparency and non-discrimination in conducting international trade. We also urge the European Union to provide an equitable treatment across all oil crops biofuels and bioliquids in line with the principle of non-discrimination which stipulates that a member shall not discriminate between “like” products from different trading partners. Malaysia is committed to realising the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and its 17 Sustainable Development Goals. The Sustainable Development Goals are a universal call to action to end poverty, protect the planet and ensure that all people enjoy peace and prosperity. In this context, the oil palm industry plays a very important role in contributing positively and constructively towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals.  Apart from that, in March 2019, the Government of Malaysia had agreed with the new policy in ensuring that Malaysian oil palm is cultivated in a sustainable manner. The measures included to cap oil palm cultivated area to 6.5 million hectares; to put a stop on conversion of permanent forest reserved area; to halt planting of oil palm in the new peatland area and further strengthen regulations with regard to existing oil palm cultivated on peat; and to make available oil palm plantation maps for public access that demonstrate further transparency in the supply chain.  Malaysia wishes to emphasise that the Malaysian oil palm industry is committed to produce palm oil in accordance with sustainable principles and criteria under the Malaysian Sustainable Palm Oil (MSPO) certification scheme, which has been implemented on a mandatory basis since 1 January 2020.  Malaysia reiterates its commitment made at the Rio Summit in 1992 to retain at least 50% of the land area under forest cover and has put in place policy framework and legislation to ensure sustainable development balancing the protection of the environment and socioeconomic development. This is evident through the implementation of various programmes and initiatives for conservation and preservation of forests and biodiversity including among others: The Central Forest Spine covers 5.3 million hectares in Peninsular Malaysia and the Heart of Borneo is a trilateral cooperation between Brunei, Indonesia and Malaysia covering an area of over 20 million hectares. These initiatives help to strengthen the world’s resilience to climate change by conserving carbon sinks and creating a huge green lung for the world while at the same time protecting the livelihoods for the forest dependent communities; A survey project that aims to undertake a new population survey of the orang utan and pygmy elephants in Sabah. This survey will bring together wildlife experts, scientists and researchers to take part in an extensive study on the population of the state’s iconic wildlife; and Replanting of one million forest tree species within the next ten (10) years particularly in degraded lands as well as protecting the wildlife population which the projects will be sponsored primarily by the palm oil industry players. On the other hand, Malaysia is now in the midst of setting up a specific fund for green initiatives, especially for tree planting and wildlife conservation. We urge the European Union to acknowledge and recognise the efforts and commitment in sustainable production of Malaysian palm oil as well as our contributing towards protection and conservation of forest and biodiversity. We remain fully open and committed to negotiating in a sincere and constructive manner in ensuring a non-discriminatory treatment against palm products and to prevent the unnecessary barrier for market access of palm products into the European Union.  Malaysia will continue to monitor the development and we look forward to the response from the European Union. Thank you.1

Preocupación Comercial Específica N.º 61. Unión Europea - Modificaciones de la Directiva 2009/28/CE, Directiva sobre energías renovables (ID 553):

 

Deseamos referir a los Miembros a los documentos G/TBT/W/650 y G/TBT/W/718, que recogen las declaraciones hechas por el Ecuador sobre este tema en las reuniones de este Comité de junio y noviembre de 2019, y febrero de 2020.

Mi delegación se ve obligada a reiterar su preocupación con esta normativa europea y con la metodología de cálculo del Cambio Indirecto del Uso del Suelo – ILUC en la que se encuentra basada, sin fundamento sólido de evidencia científica.

La UE afirma que esta normativa no constituye una prohibición de importación de aceite de palma ni de biocombustibles producidos a partir del aceite de palma.  Sin embargo, aunque no haya una prohibición explícita, la forma en que está diseñada la norma conlleva este efecto.

Por una parte, se genera una discriminación arbitraria entre biocombustibles similares, algunos de los cuales provienen de cultivos menos productivos por hectárea que la palma aceitera, como la colza y el girasol, que sin embargo no están considerados como de alto riesgo de ILUC.  Ello podría ser incompatible con la obligación consagrada en el párrafo 1 del artículo 2 del Acuerdo OTC y en el párrafo 1 del artículo I del GATT de 1994.

Cualquier medida ambiental para cumplir con la agenda climática europea debe ser compatible con el sistema multilateral de comercio, es decir, que no constituya un medio de discriminación arbitrario o injustificado, o una restricción encubierta del comercio internacional.

The representative of Colombia raised concerns regarding labelling requirements of food products and the use of "palm oil-free" labels, in particular. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/467 (below).1.   Colombia notes that there have been a variety of measures and campaigns, both at European level and within its member States, against the use or consumption of palm oil in different products, in which palm oil is identified as harmful to health and destructive to the environment.2.   One of these measures involves "negative labelling" used by some companies to attract more consumers, where the label highlights nutritional and health properties that the items in question do not possess (unvalidated by the competent authority), such as, for example, the indications "palm oil free" or "no palm oil" promoted in the EU, for instance through the International Palm Oil Free Certification Accreditation Programme.3.   Colombia believes that these practices (i) stigmatize the use of palm oil; (ii) lack scientific justification; (iii) discriminate against palm oil as opposed to like products; (iv) disregard the processes developed by the palm oil agro‑industry under international environmental sustainability standards. Consequently, they constitute disguised technical barriers that are inconsistent with the national treatment and MFN obligations in Article 2.1 of the TBT Agreement and in Articles I:1 and III:4 of the GATT 1994.4.   It seems to us that EU Regulation No. 1169/2011 establishes the illegality of misleading claims on the packaging of products for human consumption. Chapter V stipulates that such labelling: (i) shall not mislead the consumer; (ii) shall be based on relevant scientific data; (iii) shall be objective and non‑discriminatory; (iv) shall not be applied in such a way as to create obstacles to the free movement of goods; and (v) shall not lead to unfair competition.5.    Moreover, this Regulation – which has been in force since December 2014 – requires that the origin of the oil used as an ingredient be specified; in other words, it is not enough simply to indicate "vegetable oils", but the type of oil has to be specified, for example palm oil, sunflower seed oil, olive oil, etc.6.   Similarly, since 13 December 2016, the nutrition claim is required not to mislead buyers as to the characteristics of the food. Nor can it attribute special properties to food, such as the prevention of possible health risks.7.   Furthermore, Article 36 in Chapter V states that food information provided on a voluntary basis (a) shall not mislead the consumer; (b) shall not be ambiguous or confusing for the consumer; (c) shall be based on the relevant scientific data.8.    According to Regulation No. 1169/2011, member States may require food business operators placing on the market in their territory foods bearing such information to notify the competent authority of the use of an additional form of expression or presentation and to provide them with the relevant justifications regarding the fulfilment of the requirements.9.   At the same time, Regulation No. 1925/2006 requires that the manufacturer or the person placing such foods on the market to provide the authority with "a model of the label used for the product".10.   In view of the above, Colombia would like to know what kind of surveillance, control and monitoring systems the European authorities use to check the additional nutrition claims on the label indicating that the product is palm oil free. How can the European authorities guarantee the accuracy of the information provided on the labels of products claiming to be palm oil free prior to their placement on the market, since there is no international reference standard by which the EU health authorities can verify the presence or absence of palm oil in the products marketed in their territory?11.   Colombia would also like to know what laboratory analyses the European authorities require of companies to verify whether or not products contain palm oil so that they can approve these nutrition claims on food labels. What analytical methods have been validated and accredited to carry out these analyses and confirm the accuracy of the claims? Is there any official EU document setting out the procedures for verifying and assessing the nutrition claims on the label? Finally, what laboratory accreditation scheme does the EU use to conduct tests to determine that the products are palm oil free?12.   All of this leads us to the conclusion that although the legislation in force is clear in prohibiting information that could mislead the consumer, it permits the use of negative labelling that is inconsistent with the rules governing consumer protection and unfair competition in that it provides the erroneous signal that palm oil is harmful to health and destructive to the environment, while at the same time implying that unlike palm oil, other oils are healthy and environmentally friendly.13.   In other words, negative labelling, rather than informing the consumer, becomes a form of deceptive advertising devoid of any technical justification, aimed at attracting followers and consumers by exhibiting nutritional properties that have not been duly verified by the competent authorities, thereby clearly misleading the consumer.14.   In conclusion, Colombia considers that the European authorities have been remiss in their surveillance and control in connection with the verification and acceptance of additional claims that are being used to attribute to products special properties that have not been verified and scientifically substantiated, in particular the negative labelling "palm oil free", which ultimately constitutes a disguised trade restriction designed to discriminate against palm oil as opposed to other similar oils and has been accepted as deceptive advertising in violation of the national treatment and MFN obligations contained in Article 2.1 of the TBT Agreement and Articles I:1 and III:4 of the GATT 1994.15.   Finally, Colombia appreciates this opportunity to make these observations, and looks forward to the EU's replies to its questions.

The representative of Colombia reiterated concerns with the EU's regulations about the use of "Palm Oil Free" labelling. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/599 (below).1.   Colombia reiterates its concern, already raised in documents G/TBT/W/467 and G/TBT/W/577, regarding the measures and campaigns, both at European level and within EU member States, against the use or consumption of palm oil in different products, in which palm oil is identified as harmful to health and destructive to the environment.2.   One of these measures involves "negative labelling" of certain products, where the label highlights nutritional and health properties that the items in question do not possess (unvalidated by the competent authority), such as, for example, the indications "palm oil free" or "no palm oil" promoted in the EU.3.   Colombia believes that these practices (i) stigmatize the use of palm oil; (ii) lack scientific justification; (iii) discriminate against palm oil as opposed to like products; and (iv) disregard the processes developed by the palm oil agro‑industry under international environmental sustainability standards. Consequently, they constitute disguised technical barriers that are inconsistent with the national treatment and MFN obligations in Article 2.1 of the TBT Agreement and in Articles I:1 and III:4 of the GATT 1994.4.   Regulation (EU) No. 1169/2011, which relates to food labelling, makes the provision of food information mandatory, including in relation to fats. We note that the expression and presentation of "fats" covers "saturates", "mono‑unsaturates" and "polyunsaturates". The mandatory food information does not specify whether the fat originates from palm oil or another source. Hence the negative label "palm oil free" does not constitute mandatory food information and is contrary to the provisions of the regulation.5.   Similarly, it seems to us that the same regulation establishes the illegality of misleading claims on the packaging of products for human consumption. Chapter V stipulates that such labelling: (i) shall not mislead the consumer; (ii) shall be based on relevant scientific data; (iii) shall be objective and non‑discriminatory; (iv) shall not be applied in such a way as to create obstacles to the free movement of goods; and (v) shall not lead to unfair competition.6.   Moreover, Directive 2005/29/EC prohibits unfair business‑to‑consumer commercial practices and covers misleading commercial practices, which are a feature of this particular case. The Directive provides that a commercial practice shall be regarded as misleading if it contains false information and is therefore untruthful or information which, even if correct, is likely to deceive the average consumer and cause him to take a transactional decision that he would not have taken otherwise. The above types of misleading information relate, inter alia, to the main characteristics of the product (its benefits, risks, composition, geographical origin, the results to be expected from its use, etc.).7.   Lastly, account must be taken of the international standard Codex Stan 1‑1985[1] (General Standard for the Labelling of Prepackaged Foods), which establishes that any information may be shown on the label, provided that it is not in conflict with the mandatory requirements, including those relating to claims and deception established in Section 3 (General Principles) of that standard. This international standard also indicates that "[p]repackaged food shall not be described or presented on any label or in any labelling in a manner that is false, misleading or deceptive or is likely to create an erroneous impression regarding its character in any respect".8.   In view of the above, Colombia would like to know what kind of surveillance, control and monitoring systems the European authorities use to check the additional nutrition claims on the label indicating that the product is "palm oil free". How can the European authorities guarantee the accuracy of the information provided on the labels of products claiming to be palm oil free prior to their placement on the market?9.   In conclusion, Colombia considers that the European authorities have been remiss in their surveillance and control in connection with the verification and acceptance of additional claims that are being used to attribute to products special properties that have not been verified and scientifically substantiated, in particular the negative labelling "palm oil free", which ultimately constitutes a disguised trade restriction designed to discriminate against palm oil as opposed to other similar oils and has been accepted as deceptive advertising in violation of the national treatment and MFN obligations contained in Article 2.1 of the TBT Agreement and Articles I:1 and III:4 of the GATT 1994.10.   Colombia appreciates this opportunity to make these observations, and looks forward to the EU's replies to its questions.[1] See in particular section 3 and section 7.1 of Codex Stan 1‑1985.
