Allowing food exporters to apply this labelling in the absence of scientific evidence creates unfair and unnecessary barrier to trade. Indonesia encourages the EU to be consistent with EU Regulation 1169 Chapter V Article 36 point 2, which states that "(a) it shall not mislead the consumer, as referred to in Article 7; (b) it shall not be ambiguous or confusing for the customers, and (c) it shall, where appropriate, be based on the relevant scientific data."4.  Article 18 (1) of the Regulation provides that the list of ingredients shall include all substances that are used to manufacture the food product and not the substance that is not used in manufacturing or preparing the food product. While Article 9 and 21 of the Regulation require foodstuff producers to make clear of the presence of certain substance in the labelling of the food products, it is only limited to substances that are causing allergies or intolerances, in which, according to Annex II of the Regulation does not include palm oil as a substance that is causing allergies or intolerances. Therefore, mentioning palm oil as a substance that is absence from the list of ingredients of foodstuffs is also contravening the Regulation. 5.  Moreover, based on EU Regulation 1924/2006 on nutrition and health claims made on foods, the EU does not give authorization to food producers in claim related to carotenes contain in the palm oil due to the fact of the insufficient scientific evidence. This is on the contrary with current situation on which the EU allowing food producer to use palm oil free labelling without scientific justification. 6.  Indonesia emphasizes the EU to refer to the International Codex standards related to general food labeling (GENERAL STANDARD FOR THE LABELING OF PREPACKAGED FOODS CXS 1-1985), especially regarding the basic principles of labeling not mislead and not related to other products that confuse consumers.7.  We believe that free palm oil label, exploited by non-governmental bodies within the EU, without accurate scientific evidence on the impact of palm oil in food products on human health is a mere black advertisement to mislead and deceive the customers. Therefore, Indonesia urges the EU to apply the principle of non-discrimination on the treatment given to palm oil compared to other vegetable oils (sunflower, soybean, rapeseed oil). 8.  Indonesia emphasizes that the EU need to be consistent with the WTO TBT Agreement in Article 2.1 on non-discrimination, Article 3.4 and 3.5 on measures by local governments and non-governmental bodies that shall be in line with the WTO TBT Agreement. Indonesia urges EU to take necessary action to ensure that their NGOs and local governments apply measures consistently with EU Regulation 1169 and WTO TBT Agreements.

The representative of Costa Rica repeated his delegation's concerns relating to the widespread use on the European market of labels including wording such as "palm oil free". As previously stated, Costa Rica considered that there was no proper scientific justification for generally maintaining that products manufactured with palm oil were harmful to health and that therefore there was no basis for allowing the inclusion of wording of this kind on the packaging, As such, his delegation deemed that the EU had committed an oversight in allowing this additional statement, resulting in non-compliance with the principles and legitimate objectives of the TBT Agreement.

The representative of Honduras shared the concerns raised by Colombia and Indonesia and underlined the importance of the palm oil sector for Honduras, with many thousands of permanent jobs and farmers relying on this product. Palm oil was controlled in Honduras, including by regulations protecting forests and only a very minimal impact on the environment from this product had been observed. She thanked the EU for the bilateral meeting.

The representative of Thailand registered his delegation's interest in palm oil free labels, recalling the concerns raised at the March 2019 TBT Committee meeting. Thailand would continue to monitor the development of this concern in the TBT Committee.
The representative of Malaysia continued to share concerns raised by other Members under this STC.
The representative of Guatemala continued to share concerns raised by other Members under this STC. Guatemala referred the Committee to its previous statements.

The representative of Ecuador supported the concern raised by Colombia and Indonesia with regard to the practice of labelling food products as being "palm oil free", insofar as it generated a negative campaign against those products in particular, without a technical or scientific basis. Her delegation considered that from the nutritional standpoint, this labelling constituted an unfounded negative generalization, implying that palm oil was somehow harmful to health or nutritionally inferior to other similar vegetable oils. From the environmental standpoint, this labelling implied that palm oil per se was less ecological or sustainable than other similar vegetable oils, without considering the particular circumstances of African palm producing countries such as Ecuador, for example, where palm oil was produced responsibly and sustainably, as explained at some length in her delegation's statement concerning STC 23*. Although the labels did not include explicit references to nutritional properties or the possible environmental consequences of consuming palm oil, Ecuador was of the view that the negative allusion was implicit in the message through its very ambiguity and had a dissuasive effect on the consumer which in turn had an unfair and discriminatory impact on the product. These actions fell within the context of misleading commercial practices, as mentioned by Colombia in its statement, since even though the information was factually correct it might lead the consumer to take a decision that he or she would not otherwise have taken. Ecuador called on the EU to provide information concerning the control procedures it carried out to ensure that the information in the labels on the products indicating that they were palm oil free did not infringe its own domestic legislation in force and did not result in unjustified discrimination against the product. Ecuador thanked the EU for the bilateral meeting.*European Union — Amendments to the Directive 2009/28/EC, Renewable Energy Directive

The representative of Indonesia reiterated its concerns about the use of "Palm Oil Free" labelling by several food product companies in the EU and referred the Committee to its statement in the previous meeting. Indonesia continued to be concerned about the EU's inconsistency with their own Regulation (EU) 1169/2011 on food information, in particular food labelling, Article 7 and 36, and EU Regulation 1924/2006 on nutrition and health claims made on foods. Indonesia emphasized that the EU should abide by Article 2.1 of the TBT Agreement on non-discrimination, as well as Articles 3.4 and 3.5 on measures by local governments and non-governmental bodies.

The representative of Guatemala shared concerns expressed by other palm oil producing Members. The labelling "palm oil free" or "does not contain palm oil", generated a label with negative impact and discouraged the consumption of palm oil and not the other vegetable oils produced in the EU, constituting discrimination. She said that this type of labelling provided misleading information and supported other types of oil, making it difficult for Guatemala's oil industry. These measures ignored the efforts made by Guatemalan palm oil agribusiness to have sustainable production and comply with international environmental sustainability standards.
The representative of Malaysia registered its interest in this STC and would continue to monitor its development in the Committee.

The representative of Colombia reiterated previously raised concerns with the adverse trade effect the measure could have on its palm oil industry, in particular the use of negative labels which Colombia considered was not being applied in consideration of consumer protection. Colombia looked forward to receiving information from the EU on the matter.

The representative of Costa Rica echoed Indonesia's concerns regarding the use of "palm oil free" labelling, which Costa Rica believed had no scientific justification. Costa Rica maintained that it was unjustified to use language on packaging indicating that food produced with palm oil was harmful to health and therefore that the measure was not in line with the TBT Agreement.

The representative of Australia recognized the right of governments to take measures necessary to protect public health and emphasized the importance of compliance with the TBT Agreement, in particular with the national treatment obligations and Article 2.2. He stressed that Australian exporters faced ongoing uncertainty regarding the implementation and certification requirements under the notification and needed clearer guidance in order to be able to comply. Australian exporters were also concerned about the impact of the requirements on their business, in particular, the cost involved in additional testing and the potentially long wait times for test results. Australia noted that the Certificate of Analysis must include an analysis of the liquor in accordance with the Thai Industrial Standard for Wine, Fruit Wine and other Fermented Beverages (TIS 2089-2544). In Australia, wine production was governed by Standard 4.5.1 of the Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code. His delegation asked whether Thailand would recognize official certificates guaranteeing compliance with Australia's requirements. He further requested clarification on whether testing of all 14 items listed in the Thai Industrial Standard was required if the use of the relevant material was not permitted in Australia or if the limit in Australia was the same or higher than that specified in the Thai Industrial Standard.
The representative of the United States supported the comments of Australia on the measure.

The representative of Japan expressed an interest in the issue and currently was carefully reviewing the measure, including examination of the impact on businesses. Any information by Thailand would be appreciated.

The representative of the European Union raised concerns about the regulation, in particular concerning the certificate of analysis and possible impact of trade in alcoholic beverages. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/522 (below).1.  The European Union would like to support the concerns expressed by Australia with regard to certain elements in the new Thai requirement to provide a Certificate of Analysis for the marketing of fermented[1] and distilled[2] alcoholic beverages (wines, spirits, beer). While sharing the importance of ensuring the protection of public health, the European Union notes that the testing criteria and methods foreseen for the issuing of the Certificate of Analysis raise concerns as to their possible undue impacts on trade in alcoholic beverages. 2.  The European Union welcomes the recent issuing by the Thai authorities of a notification extending the grace period for the entry into force of this requirement until 15 September 2018. The European Union understands that the Thai authorities are reflecting on how to clarify the requirements for the Certificate of Analysis, so to ensure that it does not create undue restrictions to trade. 3.  We would be grateful for an indication by Thailand on the envisaged next steps in this respect, in particular on whether it intends to allow for Certificates of Analysis to be issued in line with the standards of the country of origin or with international standards, for both distilled and fermented products. The European Union would also welcome further clarification on the envisaged frequency for the submission of the Certificate of Analysis for imported products, also noting that for domestic products such certificate has to be submitted only once. 4.  Once finalised, we invites Thailand to notify this requirement to the TBT Committee, reasonably ahead of its entry into force, so as to allow Members to become acquainted with it and submit comments.[1] TIS 2089-2544 for wines, TIS 2090-2544 for beer.  [2] TIS 2088-2544 for distilled spirits.

The representative of the United States noted that Thailand had not yet notified the measure, despite flagging at the March 2017 Committee meeting that it would do so, to enable trading partners the opportunity to comment. She did however express appreciation that Thailand had issued guidelines to the measure in March 2018 and that full implementation had been deferred until September. Nevertheless, the guidelines did not clarify a number of her delegation's concerns, such as what testing was required. Given that full entry into force was due in September 2018, Thailand was urged to notify the measure as soon as possible in an effort to resolve US concerns before trade became impacted, and requested that Thailand delay enforcement until trading partners' concerns had been taken into account.

The representative of the European Union expressed concern with regard to certain elements in the Thai requirement to provide a Certificate of Analysis for the marketing of fermented and distilled alcoholic beverages (wines, spirits or beer). Whilst supporting the importance of ensuring the protection of public health, the EU was nonetheless concerned that the testing criteria and methods foreseen for the issuing of the Certificate of Analysis may unduly impact trade in alcoholic beverages. Her delegation appreciated that the grace period for submitting samples or certificates of analysis after importation had been extended until 14 September 2018. Also appreciated was the adoption on 22 March 2018 of implementing guidelines on the submission of alcohol beverages samples for quality compliance testing as part of the import licence application, in particular the clarification that samples had to be submitted only once, unless there was a change in the production process, and that their size should be of at least 0.50 litres. Furthermore, she expressed appreciation for the openness of the Thai Excise Department to address remaining concerns. Based on a recent discussion on 18 June between her delegation and the Thai Excise Department in Bangkok, Thailand had indicated its intention to amend the Thai Industrial Standards Institute (TISI) standards and accept producer self-certifications as of 15 September 2018. Pending the amendment of TISI standards, market surveillance would take into consideration the differences in testing methods and thresholds in international standards (including exemptions for sweet wines in OIV standards) in order to avoid market disruptions. The EU requested confirmation on these next steps and remained available to work with Thailand on the review of the TISI standards, including through discussions at expert level on substances for which testing was not foreseen in international standards. Thailand was encouraged to notify the requirement to the TBT Committee, sufficiently in advance to allow Members to become acquainted with it and submit comments in accordance with Article 2.9.2 of the TBT Agreement.

The representative of Japan expressed concerns on this issue and recalled Thailand flagging at the March 2018 Committee meeting that the competent authority was in the process of preparing a TBT notification for the measure. His delegation sought an update on the notification and requested that a sufficient comment period be provided. In addition, Thailand was urged to amend the issue appropriately and sufficiently before entry into force, taking into account Members' comments.

The representative of New Zealand acknowledged and supported Thailand's right to introduce new regulations to address specific public health concerns. Her delegation appreciated that in seeking to address the harmful use of alcohol, the technical regulation was directed towards achieving a legitimate public health objective. She stated, however, that New Zealand exporters faced ongoing uncertainty regarding the implementation of the regulations and were keen to work with the Thai government and importers to comply with the new requirements. Thailand was requested to update Members on the progress of any implementing guidance.

The representative of the European Union reiterated concerns raised in the previous TBT Committee meeting.* The EU appreciated the extension of the grace period to submit samples or certificate of analysis within 30 days of importation (from 14 September 2018 to 14 March 2019) and asked Thailand to confirm the Thai Excise Department's intent to set its own standards and accept producer self-certifications. On 10 October, the Thai Excise Department had shared, for consultation, the draft forms of Certificate of Analysis for distilled and fermented spirits to be filled-in by relevant certifying bodies in the countries of origin. The forms provided details on the limits for each regulated substance to be certified by those relevant certifying bodies. It was noted that the limits were similar to TISI limits and that no details had been provided regarding the analytical methods. The EU had recently provided comments on the draft forms to the Excise Department. The EU remained available to work with Thailand on the review of the standards, including through discussions at expert level on the regulated substances and the methods of analysis to address the differences between the standards of the Excise Department and internationally accepted practices.

*G/TBT/M/75, paras. 4.263 et 4.264.

The representative of Mexico was particularly concerned about the Certificate of Analysis (CoA) that the Thai authorities were planning to introduce in March 2019 and that would be necessary to obtain an import licence. Mexico's concern was underpinned by the following considerations: Regarding levels of methanol in Tequila: In accordance with the Certificate of Analysis, products had to comply with the provisions of the Decree on Industrial Product Standards of 1968, Notification of the Ministry of Industry No. 2927 of 2001 on Distilled Spirits Standards (TIS 2088- 2544), which established maximum permitted physical and chemical levels for alcoholic beverages and the associated test methods. The guidelines established in this Decree presented significant difficulties for Tequila in the Thai market, primarily because the maximum level of methanol permitted under the Decree was lower than the maximum level of methanol permitted under Official Mexican Standard NOM 006-SCFI-2012, Alcoholic Beverages-Tequila-Specifications. Lack of information on the CoA: The new certification measure had not been notified to the TBT Committee; this could constitute a violation of Article 2.9 of the TBT Agreement. Moreover, criteria and guidelines for the implementation of the measure had not been made known. There was therefore significant uncertainty as to how the measure would be implemented. Analysis procedure: samples of alcoholic beverages had to be analysed by the Thai authorities using an extensive procedure that was unnecessary since the CoA could be issued by the authorities of the country of origin. This certificate could be attached to the product before it left the country of export thereby eliminating the need to issue one in Thailand – avoiding both time and costs of an additional procedure. In light of these considerations, and taking account of the provisions of Article 2.2 of the TBT Agreement, Thailand could be introducing measures that constituted unnecessary obstacles to trade since it intended to implement regulations that could be considered more restrictive than necessary. In view of the above, Mexico requested that Thailand share with the Committee (i) its reasoning and the basis used to establish such low maximum permitted levels of methanol; and (ii) the status of the CoA notification issued to WTO Members and confirm whether the date of entry into force remained March 2019.

The representative of Canada supported concerns raised previously regarding Thailand's excise tax act of 2017, specifically pertaining to certain elements of the certificate of analysis required for imported alcoholic beverages. Canada was also of the view that Thailand should formally notify the WTO of the new measures to provide a rationale for the proposed measures and a reasonable time for Members to comment.

The representative of Australia recognized the right of governments to take measures necessary to protect public health. Nevertheless, Australia wished to emphasise the importance of compliance with the TBT Agreement and particularly the principle of national treatment and Article 2.2 of the Agreement. Australian exporters faced ongoing uncertainty regarding the implementation and certification requirements under the notification. It was understood that the requirements had changed and Australia requested that these be notified to the TBT Committee to enable the engagement of trading partners. Australian exporters were also concerned about the impact of the requirements on their business, particularly the cost involved in additional testing, and the potentially lengthy delays for test results. In addition, Australia noted that Thailand had circulated a proposed Certificate of Analysis with two self-declaration options, which would require Australia's regulatory body to certify that the goods meet the required Thai industrial standard. Certification of the composition of elements in liquor without testing was against best practice and was unworkable in Australia. The proposed Certificate of Analysis required the inclusion of analysis of the liquor in accordance with an updated Thai Industrial Standard for Wine, Fruit Wine and other Fermented Beverages (TIS 2089-2544). Some proposed levels did not sufficiently account for naturally occurring elements or minimum detection levels in laboratory testing. In Australia, wine production was governed by Standard 4.5.1 of the Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code. Australia would appreciate consideration of whether Thailand would recognize official certificates guaranteeing compliance with Australia's requirements. Specifically, Australia asked for clarification on: (i) the expected implementation process for the option on the proposed certificate to submit products for testing to the Thailand Excise Department including costs, timeframes and import tax and warehousing implications; and (ii) the length of validity of a Certificate of Analysis.

The representative of Chile shared the concerns expressed by previous speakers with respect to the regulatory system being introduced by Thailand. Chile was particularly concerned that the regulation had not been notified to the Committee and Thailand was invited to proceed with this notification given the affects it could have on the Chilean industry, which had expressed concern.

The representative of the European Union welcomed the notification by the Thai authorities, on 15 November 2018, of the Ministerial Regulation entitled "Liquor Importation Permission" (B.E. 2560 (2017)). The EU was currently examining the Regulation in detail, with a view to providing comments. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/638 (below).1.  The European Union welcomes the notification by the Thai authorities, on 15 November 2018, of the Ministerial Regulation entitled "Liquor Importation Permission" (B.E. 2560 (2017)), and is currently examining the Regulation in detail, with a view to provide comments. The European Union notes that the Regulation entered into force on 16 September 2018. 2.  The European Union would like to reiterate its previous concerns with regard to certain elements in the Thai requirement to provide a Certificate of Analysis for the marketing of fermented[1] and distilled[2] alcoholic beverages (wines, spirits or beer). While sharing with Thailand the important objective of ensuring the protection of public health, the European Union notes that the testing criteria and methods foreseen for the issuing of the Certificate of Analysis raise concerns as to their possible undue impacts on trade in alcoholic beverages. 3.  The European Union appreciates that the grace period for submitting samples or Certificates of Analysis within 30 days from importation has been extended from 14 September 2018 to 14 March 2019. In addition, the European Union welcomes the adoption, on 22 March 2018, of implementing guidelines on the submission of alcohol beverages samples for quality compliance testing as part of the import license application. 4.  Furthermore, the European Union appreciates the openness of the Thai Excise Department to address remaining concerns through discussions held in June 2018 with the EU Delegation in Bangkok, as well as through the consultation, in October 2018, on the draft forms of Certificate of Analysis for distilled and fermented spirits, to which the European Union provided comments. 5.  As specific concerns on the measure, the European Union considers that some of the analytical requirements are unclear (for instance, fusel oil or ferrocyanide), while many others, such as ethyl carbamate or iron, are not applicable to wines under OIV international standards since there is no scientific evidence justifying their regulation. 6.  In addition, some of the proposed limits would represent a trade barrier for EU wines. For example, the limits on aldehyde proposed by the Thai authorities would prevent the imports of Sherry. The limits on sulfites may prevent the imports of exceptionally sweet wines such as Sauternes, Tokaj and Passito. Furthermore, the methods of analysis are diverging from international OIV ones, which may lead to testing errors, to the detriment of food business operators. These strict requirements appear not proportionate when compared to EU requirements for imports of wines. We would appreciate if Thailand could provide detailed scientific justifications for the limits of the regulated substances that are more restrictive than the relevant international standards. 7.  The European Union understands that the intra-agency consultations held by the Excise Department with a view to set its own standards for alcoholic beverages have been concluded. According to our information, the Excise Department is preparing to amend Ministerial Regulation B.E. 2560 from 2017 and to issue a Notification introducing the new set of standards. In this regard, the European Union would like to invite Thailand to notify the draft Regulation and the new set of standards to the WTO TBT Committee in a manner that allows reasonable time for other WTO members to comment. 8.  In addition, we would like to kindly request the extension of the grace period giving more flexibility in the submission of alcohols samples or certificates of analysis beyond 19 March 2019. This would allow proper public consultation with a view to gather wider public opinions on the new set of standards and potential changes in the certification procedures to take place. The European Union remains available to work with Thailand on the review of the Thai standards, including through discussions at expert level on the regulated substances and the methods of analysis, in order to address the differences between the standards of the Excise Department and internationally accepted practices. [1] TIS 2089-2544 for wines, TIS 2090-2544 for beer.[2] TIS 2088-2544 for distilled spirits.

The representative of New Zealand acknowledged and supported Thailand's right to introduce new regulations to address specific public health concerns. New Zealand appreciated that in seeking to address the harmful use of alcohol, the technical regulation was directed toward achieving a legitimate public health objective. However, New Zealand exporters remained uncertain on certification requirements. She asked that Thailand advise whether acceptance of other recognized industry certification, which achieved the objective of these measures, was being considered. New Zealand remained keen to work with the Thai Government to ensure New Zealand exporters met Thailand's objectives under these regulations through the least trade restrictive means.
The representative of Mexico urged Thailand to clarify the issues raised and to notify any changes to the TBT Committee.

The representative of the European Union raised concerns with this measure. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/659 (below).1.  The European Union welcomes the notification by the Thai authorities, on 15 November 2018, of the Ministerial Regulation entitled "Liquor Importation Permission" (B.E. 2560 (2017)), entering into force on 16 September 2018. 2.  With reference to the concerns previously raised by the European Union regarding certain elements in the Thai requirement to provide a Certificate of Analysis for the marketing of fermented[1] and distilled[2] alcoholic beverages (wines, spirits or beer) under the aforementioned Regulation, the European Union would like to thank the Excise Department for its efforts in addressing our concerns. 3.  The European Union welcomes the adoption, on 22 March 2018, of implementing guidelines on the submission of alcohol beverages samples for quality compliance testing as part of the import license application. In addition, the European Union appreciates that the grace period allowing for flexibility in submitting samples or Certificates of Analysis within 30 days from importation has been extended first from 14 September 2018 to 14 March 2019 and then, subsequently, to 14 September 2019. 4.  Furthermore, the European Union appreciates the openness of the Thai Excise Department to address remaining concerns through discussions with the EU Delegation in Bangkok, as well as through the consultation, in October 2018, on the draft forms of Certificate of Analysis for distilled and fermented spirits, to which the European Union provided comments. 5.  The European Union welcomes the enactment of a new Ministerial Regulation on Liquor Importation permission and of the Excise Department's Notification on the standards of imported alcohol, both taking effect from 5 June 2019. According to the new Ministerial Regulation, the standards from the Thai Industrial Standards Institute (TISI) are replaced by the reference standards determined by the Director General of the Excise Department in the Excise Department's Notification. 6.  The European Union appreciates that the final list of standards is identical to those in the draft presented to the EU Delegation in March 2019. This means that the discrimination in the standards in favour of domestic artisanal products is now eliminated and that our comments on the limits of certain substances are significantly taken on board. We understand that under the new system, certificates of analysis will generally be valid for three years while the certificates of analysis issued under the previous Ministerial Regulation remain valid until June 2022. 7.  That being said, there remain some systemic concerns as regards the existing differences in the regulated substances and methods of analysis between that of the Excise Department and that of the OIV. The European Union remains available to work with Thailand on the review of the Thai standards, including through discussions at expert level on the regulated substances and the methods of analysis, in order to address the differences between the standards of the Excise Department and internationally accepted practices, which may interrupt future trade flows of European alcohol products safe for marketing globally. 8.  In this regard, the European Union would also like to invite Thailand to notify the new Ministerial Regulation and the new set of standards to the WTO TBT Committee as soon as possible.[1] TIS 2089-2544 for wines, TIS 2090-2544 for beer.[2] TIS 2088-2544 for distilled spirits.

The representative of Japan requested that Thailand provide the latest information on this issue. Japan requested that Thailand amend this ministerial regulation appropriately and provide sufficient scientific evidence and background before its entry into force. Comments from Members should also be taken into account.

The representative of the United States recalled that on 18 June 2019, Thailand had notified its Ministerial Regulation entitled Liquor Importation Permission (No.2) B.E. 2562 (2019) amending the Ministerial Regulation entitled Liquor Importation Permission B.E. 2560 and Notification of the Excise Department Prescribing Quality Standards for Imported Liquor to the WTO TBT Committee as G/TBT/N/THA/548 and G/TBT/N/THA/549, respectively. As of 5 June 2019, all alcohol beverage imports required a certificate of analysis confirming the product's compliance with a series of maximum limits for contaminants, food additives, and chemical attributes. The US appreciated the bilateral discussions held to date with the Government of Thailand but remained concerned about its certificate of analysis requirement for alcohol beverages, which could be burdensome for US alcohol beverage exporters. She noted that testing for all the requested substances was not standard practice in the US, and federal laws prohibited the use of certain substances, such as Ferro cyanide. Further she noted that Thailand's measure appeared to be related to food safety given its focus on maximum limits for additives and contaminants. Thailand was therefore urged to also notify its measure to the SPS Committee and provide the required scientific justification for its certification and testing requirements. The US hoped for the opportunity to continue to engage with the Government of Thailand on this requirement in the Committee and bilaterally, and to find a mutually agreed upon solution to satisfying this requirement.

The representative of the European Union raised concerns with the measure. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/687 (below).1.  The European Union welcomes the enactment of a new Ministerial Regulation on Liquor Importation permission amending the previous Regulation and of the Excise Department's Notification on the quality standards for imported liquor, both taking effect from 5 June 2019 and notified to the TBT Committee on 18 June 2019 (references THA/548 and THA/549). According to the new Ministerial Regulation, the former standards from the Thai Industrial Standards Institute (TISI) are replaced by the reference standards determined by the Director General of the Excise Department in the Excise Department's Notification. 2.  The European Union would like to thank the Thai Excise Department for its efforts in addressing our concerns regarding certain elements in the Thai requirement to provide a Certificate of Analysis for the marketing of fermented and distilled alcoholic beverages (wines, spirits or beer). 3.  Furthermore, the European Union appreciates the openness of the Thai Excise Department to address remaining concerns through discussions with the EU Delegation in Bangkok, as well as through the consultation, in October 2018, on the draft forms of Certificate of Analysis for distilled and fermented spirits, to which the European Union provided comments. 4.  The European Union appreciates that the final list of standards is identical to those in the draft presented to the EU Delegation in March 2019 and that the discrimination in the standards in favour of domestic artisanal products is now eliminated. EU comments on the limits of certain substances are significantly taken on board. We understand that under the new system, certificates of analysis will generally be valid for three years while the certificates of analysis issued under the previous Ministerial Regulation remain valid until June 2022. 5.  That being said, there remain some systemic concerns as regards the existing differences in the regulated substances and methods of analysis between that of the Excise Department and that of the OIV. 6.  In this context, the European Union would appreciate the clarification by Thailand on the meaning of the "equivalent test methods" concerning the Standard for Analysis of Beer, Wine and Sparkling wine made from grapes and fermented liquor and Distilled Liquor. The European Union would like to know in particular whether international OIV methods of analysis are recognised as "equivalent test methods" for Wine and Sparkling wine made from grapes and fermented liquor. The European Union considers that the harmonisation of the Thai Quality Standard for Imported Liquor with internationally recognised standards is important to avoid unjustified trade barriers. 7.  Moreover, the European Union would like to get confirmation from Thailand on the possibility for EU exporters to use the EU "wine export certificate" proving compliance with EU rules of origin, health and authenticity in order to show compliance with the new Thai standards. 8.  The European Union remains available to work with Thailand on the review of the Thai standards, including through discussions at expert level on the regulated substances and the methods of analysis. The European Union considers that it is crucial to address the differences between the standards of the Excise Department and internationally accepted practices, which may interrupt future trade flows of European alcohol products safe for marketing globally.

The representative of Japan asked Thailand to provide the latest information on this issue and requested that Thailand amend this Ministerial Regulation appropriately and sufficiently with scientific background before entry into force, taking into account comments from Members.

The representative of Canada supported Thailand's efforts in addressing specific public health concerns related to import of alcoholic beverages. Canadian industry remained interested in the Certificate of Analysis requirements implemented by Thailand due to the possible undue impact on trade in alcoholic beverages. Canada would be interested in receiving additional information on work of the regulatory body on determining the testing standards and levels being introduced. Further, Canada would be interested in receiving clarification regarding acceptance of foreign certifications issued by accredited laboratories, which would achieve the objectives of these measures. Canada was keen to work with Thailand to ensure Canadian industry meet Thailand's objectives under these measures through the least trade restrictive ways.

The representative of Australia recognized the right of governments to take measures necessary to protect public health. There was also the importance of compliance with WTO obligations, in particular the requirements that measures not be implemented in a nondiscriminatory manner and in a way that was no more trade restrictive than necessary. She said that Australian exporters faced ongoing uncertainty regarding the implementation and certification requirements under the regulations. Understanding that the requirements had changed, Australia requested that these be notified through the WTO to enable the engagement of trading partners. Australian exporters were also concerned about the impact of the requirements on their business, in particular the cost involved in additional testing and the potentially lengthy wait times for test results. In Australia, wine production was governed by Standard 4.5.1 of the Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code. She said that Australia would appreciate the opportunity to outline the Australian approach whereby the regulatory requirements imposed on wine makers were proportionate to wine's low food safety risk. Australia would also welcome the opportunity to discuss alternative pathways for satisfying the requirements of the Thai regulation including: recognition and acceptance by Thailand of Australian production techniques; acceptance of certificates issued by Australia's wine regulator, Wine Australia, in place of Certificate of Analysis; and the possibility of capturing the Australian practices that meet the Thai regulation in a bilateral agreement. Finally, she thanked Thailand for its ongoing engagement with Australia on the issue and looked forward to further cooperation.

The representative of Chile asked Thailand to consider accepting the APEC certificate in order to facilitate trade, explaining that it was a regulatory measure guaranteeing health and safety that everybody aspired to. She said that the sanitary measures of the country of origin must be respected and acknowledged the very different conditions for production determining the acceptable limits for additives. Chile assured that the safety and health of consumers would be guaranteed as the measures were checked in the countries of origin.

The representative of New Zealand acknowledged and supported Thailand's right to address public health concerns, in particular the harmful use of alcohol, and as such he said the technical regulation was directed towards achieving a legitimate public health objective. However, New Zealand exporters continued to face uncertainty with regards to certification requirements and had concerns about the impact of the additional testing requirements on the ability to gain timely certification for exports. New Zealand requested clarification as to whether acceptance of other recognized industry certification achieving Thailand's objectives was being considered. New Zealand remained eager to work with the Thai government to ensure New Zealand exporters met Thailand's objectives under these regulations through the least-restrictive means possible.

StatementSubmitted:
THAILAND – Certificate of Analysis for the Import of Alcoholic Beverages

Thank you, Chair,

As mentioned in the previous TBT Committee meeting, the European Union welcomes the enactment of a new Ministerial Regulation on Liquor Importation permission and of the Excise Department's Notification on the quality standards for imported liquor, both taking effect from 5 June 2019 and notified to the TBT Committee on 18 June 2019 (references THA/548 and THA/549). According to the new Ministerial Regulation, the former standards from the Thai Industrial Standards Institute (TISI) are replaced by the reference standards determined by the Director General of the Excise Department in the Excise Department's Notification.

The European Union thanks Thailand for its efforts in addressing our concerns regarding certain elements related to the Certificate of Analysis for the marketing of fermented[1] and distilled[2] alcoholic beverages (wines, spirits or beer). For instance, the discrimination in the standards in favour of domestic artisanal products is now eliminated and EU comments on the limits of certain substances are significantly taken on board. However, since there still remain some systemic concerns, the European Union submitted written comments on 20 December 2019, noting the existing differences in the regulated substances and methods of analysis between that of the Excise Department and that of the International Organisation of Vine and Wine (OIV).

In this context, the European Union would appreciate the clarification by Thailand on the meaning of the “equivalent test methods” concerning the Standard for Analysis of Beer, Wine and Sparkling wine made from grapes and fermented liquor and Distilled Liquor. Could Thailand confirm whether international OIV methods of analysis are recognised as "equivalent test methods" for Wine and Sparkling wine made from grapes and fermented liquor? The European Union considers that the harmonisation of the Thai Quality Standard for Imported Liquor with internationally recognised standards is important to avoid unjustified trade barriers.

Moreover, the European Union would like to get confirmation from Thailand on the possibility for EU exporters to use the EU “wine export certificate” proving compliance with EU rules of origin, health and authenticity in order to show compliance with the new Thai standards. Furthermore, the European Union would appreciate confirmation that the Thai authorities accept laboratory results from foreign laboratories.

The European Union remains available to work with Thailand on the review of the Thai standards, including through discussions at expert level on the regulated substances and the methods of analysis. The European Union considers that it is crucial to address the differences between the standards of the Excise Department and internationally accepted practices, which may interrupt future trade flows of European alcohol products safe for marketing globally. 

Thank you, Chair.

 


[1] TIS 2089-2544 for wines, TIS 2090-2544 for beer.

[2] TIS 2088-2544 for distilled spirits.

The EU thanked Thailand for its efforts in addressing its concerns regarding certain elements related to the Certificate of Analysis for the marketing of fermented and distilled alcoholic beverages (wines, spirits or beer). For instance, the removal of the discrimination in the standards in favour of domestic artisanal products. StatementSubmitted:
Thank you, Chair,

The European Union would like to thank Thailand for the reply of 24 April 2020 to the comments submitted in December 2019 as regards the Notifications G/TBT/N/THA/548 and 549 notified on 18 June 2019.

The European Union welcomes the information concerning the consultation with stakeholders and the meetings held with Embassies, including the Delegation of the EU in Thailand, prior to the entry into force of the concerned regulations. However, such public consultation does not preclude Thailand from the obligation to notify the draft regulations to the TBT Committee at an early appropriate stage providing a reasonable commenting period to the Members in line with Articles 2.9.2 and 2.9.4 of the TBT Agreement.

The European Union understands that Thailand recognises OIV methods of analysis as "equivalent test methods" for Wine and Sparkling wine made from grapes and fermented liquor insofar as the issuing authority can confirm that the amounts of substances in the products do not exceed the limits set by the Excise Department. If it is not the case, the importer shall submit samples of the wine to the Excise Department laboratory, a Government laboratory or a private accredited laboratory in Thailand. The same reasoning applies for the acceptance of the ‘EU wine export certificate’ in order to show compliance with the new Thai standards.

As for the recognition of other ‘equivalent test methods’, the European Union would like to seek further clarification regarding the principles applied by Thailand for the acceptance of test methods accredited according to the ISO/IEC 17025 standards.

The European Union fully concurs with Thai authorities in the protection of consumer health as the main driver for the establishment of maximum level of substances for liquors. In this respect, the European Union reiterates the recommendation to adopt scientifically based international standards and test methods such as, for wine, those of the International Organisation of Vine and Wine (OIV) that protect consumers’ health while avoiding unjustified trade barriers.

In particular, we would highlight the specific burden that the analysis of non-typical parameters would represent for small export volumes.

The European Union reiterates its willingness to work with Thailand on the review of the Thai standards with the objective of ensuring their alignment with international standards. The ongoing work by the OIV on the update of the international standard for certificates of analysis should also be taken into account in this respect. The European Union considers that it is crucial to address the differences between the standards of the Excise Department and internationally accepted practices, which may be an obstacle for future trade flows of safe alcohol products. 

Thank you, Chair.

The representative of the United States raised concerns regarding India's scheme for testing and certification of telecom equipment. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/540 (below).1.  India notified the India Telegraph (Amendment) Rules, 2017 to the WTO on 6 December 2017 for a 60-day comment period noting the proposed date of adoption of this amendment was 5 September 2018 with entry into force 1 October 2018. US industry commented through the Indian domestic consultation on 23 October 2017 with its Indian trade association counterparts.2.  The certification requirements cover a wide range of telecom equipment, and include a disparate array of technical requirements. We note exemptions for research and development, demonstration activities and personal travel equipment. Categories of testing covered by the essential requirements are radio frequency safety, EMI/EMC and security. 3.  The amendment requires testing and certification for all telegraph equipment by a Telecom Engineering Center (TEC) designated domestic conformity assessment body (CAB), any TEC recognized CAB of an MRA partner, or by one of the four Government of India Regional Telecommunications Engineering Center (RTEC) laboratories. 4.  Once again, we are taking the floor to express concerns about how Indian imposes duplicative, local testing and certification requirements on products, which other WTO Members accept through Suppliers Declaration of Conformity (SDOC), ILAC accredited laboratories or the IECEE CB Scheme. Acceptance of SDOC or recognition through international conformity assessment schemes are less trade restrictive means of achieving India's legitimate objectives of safety and security.5.  While we are appreciative that India will accept test results from ILAC accredited laboratories located outside India until 1 March 2019, we are unsure why that practice could not continue past that date.6.  The United States is also interested in better understanding how to pursue the MRA partner option, and which WTO Members are India's current MRA partners. We have not seen notifications of MRAs by India, under Article 10.7.7.  It also appears that the TEC has been given the authority to add to the list of essential requirements and modify other testing requirements at any time; creating a high degree of uncertainty for OEMs. Industry is also concerned there are not enough laboratories in India accredited to the scope of testing required by the certification program. As a result, significant backlogs of products waiting to be tested will delay products time to market. OEMs will incur additional fees for TEC certification on products that have already been tested and certified.8.  We are concerned there maybe overlapping certification requirements between this measure and the Compulsory Registration Order managed by MEITY. Have the agencies coordinated to eliminate duplicative testing? 9.  The United States recognizes India's concerns about security. However, we strongly urge the Ministry of Telecommunications to reconsider implementing the TEC certification in a less trade restrictive means for accepting test results from conformity assessment bodies or suppliers.

The representative of the United States raised concerns with India's Testing and Certification of Telegraphs. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/596 (below).1.  The United States is concerned with the provisions contained in The Indian Telegraph (Amendment) Rules. Particularly, the proposed certification procedures will produce overlapping and conflicting testing requirements that are expected and are likely to result in unnecessarily burdensome costs for foreign companies selling telecommunications equipment in the Indian market. 2.  The mandatory testing requirements for telecommunications equipment under the TEC Procedure for Certification of Telecommunication Equipment is a redundant burden for international OEMs (Original Equipment Manufacturers) doing business in the Indian market. 3.  The United States recognizes India's concerns about security. However, we strongly urge the Ministry of Communications Department of Telecommunications to reconsider implementing the TEC mandatory domestic testing requirements, and to continue following standard international best practices. 4.  These best practices include accepting test results from internationally accredited labs and suppliers' declarations of conformity (SDoC) — standards that are utilized by many WTO Members with leading-edge ICT industries. 5.  With these concerns in mind, we urge India to address the following questions: Given that the October 2018 enforcement date has passed, we understand that the testing requirements will actually be implanted in phases. Is this accurate? If so, what is the anticipated date(s) of enforcement for the various testing requirements? We understand that test lab results for ILAC accredited labs will be accepted until 31 March 2019. If this is accurate, what makes the ILAC accredited lab test results unacceptable after 31 March 2019? What is the justification for not continuing to accept such test results after 31 March 2019? At the June 2018 TBT Committee meeting, India indicated it was reviewing the overlap between the CRO and the Indian Telegraph (Amendment) Rules to re-assure there would not be duplicate testing requirements. Could you please provide an update on this review?6.  In closing, we see no justifiable reasons for implementing in-country testing requirements for telecommunications equipment. We urge India to work with Industry to understand the testing and certification procedures of manufacturers that comply with existing international standards. India should accept suppliers' declaration of conformity (SDoC) and test results from certain bodies accredited through a recognized international system.

The representative of the United States recalled concerns expressed at the November 2018 meeting with the provisions contained in rules governing telecommunications-related equipment. Namely, the US was concerned that the proposed certification procedures would produce overlapping and conflicting testing requirements through the Telecommunications Engineering Center (TEC) and under the Compulsory Registration Order (CRO) that were expected to result in unnecessarily burdensome costs for foreign companies selling telecommunications equipment in the Indian market. The US recognized India's desire to ensure the integrity and security of the country's communications network. However, the US urged India to reconsider implementing domestic testing requirements, and to continue following standard international best practices, including the acceptance of ILAC-accredited lab results. She reported that the TEC had announced that the enforcement date of the testing and certification requirements had been postponed with no new date of enforcement having been announced. The US asked if India could confirm the postponement and asked if TEC would continue to accept test results from international ILAC accredited labs past thestated deadline of 31 March 2019.

The representative of the Republic of Korea supported the comments made by the US. It was stressed that, according to the regulation, the product needed to be tested in a TEC-designated testing laboratory in India, and after undergoing necessary certification procedures, TEC certification mark had to be attached on the product. The enforcement date was August 2019, but a testing laboratory for the mandatory testing fields such as LTE, LTE-A radio (RF), Internet Protocol Version (IPv6), and GPS, had not been designated. Also, designated testing laboratories for SAR and 2.4 GHz RF were not enough, which made it difficult to acquire the certification. Moreover, global manufacturers would be applying for the certification all at the same time – right after the enforcement date, and Korea worried that it would take a long time. Therefore, Korea requested India, in respect of the amendment of Indian Telegraph Rules: (i) to designate a testing laboratory for all the fields; (ii) to ensure that no technical barriers to trade due to lack of designated laboratories resulted; and (iii) to grant a grace period of at least six months after designating a testing laboratory for all the fields. It was also important that the designated laboratories had sufficient resources to cope with the testing and certification demands, so the exporting companies could comply with the regulation.

The representative of China expressed concern that ever since 2014, Chinese companies which applied for TSA certification on civil aviation security screening equipment had been treated unequally compared to US domestic companies or those in other Members. Thirdly, according to Article 5.1.2, conformity assessment procedures should not be prepared, adopted or applied with a view to or with the effect of creating unnecessary obstacles to international trade; however, in China's view, TSA certification was undertaken in an unpredictable, unclear manner, having negative impacts on China's exports and creating unnecessary obstacles to international trade. The representative of Mexico raised concerns on the regulation, notified on 31 August 2016 in document G/TBT/N/IDN/110, establishing the safety and quality criteria, and the labelling and advertising requirements for domestically produced and imported alcoholic beverages distributed in Indonesia. She said that according to safety standards in the regulation, the maximum methanol content in alcoholic beverages should not exceed 0.01% of the volume of the product. The regulation also included a definition of tequila and recognized the regulations applicable to this product, as well as its physico-chemical parameters. Her delegation was therefore concerned about the uncertainty and lack of clarity with regard to whether the regulation's maximum permitted level of methanol in alcoholic beverages applied to Mexican tequila, as the provisions of the regulations applicable to tequila allowed for higher maximum methanol levels. Furthermore, the regulation included provisions prohibiting any type of advertising in any media, thus restricting advertisements, and displays of alcoholic beverages at authorized points of sale. Her delegation was concerned that this provision could infringe Article 2.2 of the TBT Agreement of the WTO, as it indirectly affected the advertising and marketing of this type of product in Indonesia and created unnecessary barriers to trade. In light of the above, Mexico requested Indonesia to: (i) clarify whether the maximum permitted level of methanol established in the regulation also applied to tequila; and (ii) explain the logic behind the implementation of restrictive measures on the advertising of alcoholic beverages.

The representative of Mexico noted that it had not submitted comments during the public consultation period for this draft regulation, notified on 13 September 2017 as G/TBT/N/COL/228, as it had not identified any sensitive issues that might affect Mexican industry. However, the final regulation issued through Resolution No. 721 on 16 April 2018 (notified in G/TBT/N/COL/228/Add.1), expected to enter into force nine months after publication, contained provisions which indirectly affected Mexican industry, in particular the toy industry, absent from the draft regulation initially notified in 2017. She said that Mexico's concern related to the last paragraph of Article 3 of the resolution, which stipulated that not only must such batteries and cells be certified in order to comply with the regulation in question, but that they must also be removed from products. The Mexican toy industry used the "try me" system, enabling users to test products before purchasing them. She noted that if batteries and cells had to be removed from battery-powered products, this system would cease to work. Mexico was of the understanding that Colombia was the only country to have such a requirement, meaning that it would no longer be possible for the toy industry to carry out one type of production process to meet regional requirements, thus forcing industry to establish a special production process for Colombia, and considerably increase costs. In light of Article 2.2 of the TBT Agreement, Mexico considered that this requirement would create an unnecessary barrier to trade, as the inclusion of batteries and cells in products (provided such batteries and cells were certified) would not be misleading and would not jeopardize human life, health, or safety, animal or plant health, or the environment. Furthermore, based on Article 2.9.2 of the TBT Agreement, although the draft regulation met the requirement concerning notification to the TBT Committee and providing a consultation period, it had not included, from the outset, the provision on battery removal, indirectly impacting on all imported products that included such batteries and cells. While emphasizing that Mexican industry was in favour of the requested certification of batteries and cells, but was opposed to their removal from imported products, Colombia was requested to consider revising its regulation to allow for battery-powered products to be imported together with batteries and cells, provided such batteries and cells were certified, as this did not affect the fulfilment of the legitimate objective stated by Colombia.
The representative of the United States expressed support for Mexico's comments.

The representative of Mexico raised concerns about the draft Ecuadorian Standardization Institute Technical Regulation (RTE INEN) No. 088 (1R), "Surface tension agents" notified to the TBT Committee on 6 March 2018 in document G/TBT/N/ECU/117/Rev.1, for which the public consultation process had ended on 27 May 2018. The draft regulation established the requirements to be met by surface tension agents intended for use, with a view to protecting the environment and preventing practices likely to mislead end users. Her delegation was concerned that the draft technical regulation only recognized one test method to demonstrate compliance with the biodegradability requirement and one method to determine the phosphate content, despite the international recognition of several methods to demonstrate the compliance of both requirements. Concerning biodegradability, the draft regulation only recognized tests carried out on the final product whereas internationally, both tests on the final product and tests on ingredients were recognized. Mexico believed that by recognizing tests on ingredients, it would be possible to eliminate tests on certain groups of ingredients the properties of which had been proven at international level to be biodegradable, which would prevent both the duplication of tests and increased costs in the certification processes prior to exportation. She explained that this type of "filter" had been implemented in Mexican Standard NMX Q 901 CNCP 2016. Concerning phosphate content, the draft regulation also only allowed for one test method. Mexico considered that by accepting only one of the many internationally recognized methods in order to meet the aforementioned requirements, the draft regulation may be creating a technical barrier to trade, as it appeared to violate Articles 2.2 and 2.3 of the TBT Agreement, insofar as it established requirements that may be more trade restrictive than necessary. Mexico was also concerned that the provision that conformity assessment tests must be conducted through an accredited certification body in Ecuador could be in violation of Article 5.1 of the TBT Agreement, as the draft regulation imposed more restrictive conformity assessment processes for imported products. In light of the above, Ecuador was requested to: (i) allow for compliance with the biodegradability requirement to be demonstrated through the two internationally recognized test methods (tests on the final product and on surfactants), thereby preventing the duplication of tests by exempting groups of surfactants that had proven to be biodegradable from further tests; (ii) include all internationally recognized tests proven to demonstrate biodegradability and phosphate content, or provide a rational explanation for not including them; and (iii) accept declarations of conformity from providers and/or recognize tests conducted by foreign conformity assessment bodies.

The representative of Switzerland expressed concern regarding the Indonesian National Standard SNI 2973: 2011 and certification requirements for the import of biscuits, as notified to the TBT Committee on 20 April 2016. The representative of China raised concerns with the EU's Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council laying down rules and procedures for compliance with and enforcement of Union harmonization legislation on products and amending relevant regulations. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/578 (below).1.  The provision is discriminatory against emerging business models such as cross border e‑commerce. Cross-border e-commerce, by which goods are sold via parcels to consumers around the world, is a rapidly growing area of the economy. By simplifying trade, cross-border e-commerce provides EU consumers significant benefits from access to a greater variety of goods at low prices. Requiring every merchant around the world who sells any goods into the EU via cross-border ecommerce to designate a compliance person within the EU, will severely restrict benefits to EU consumers from cross-border e-commerce, as well as SMEs worldwide. 2.  It is quite difficult for E-commerce sector and small-size companies to designate an economic operator in EU. EU require certification to ensure the safety of products, it is not necessary to require additional measure which will make unaffordable cost to e-commerce operator and small-sized companies.3.  Article 14.3(b) gives the market surveillance authorities the power to audit the system, but this power is beyond the surveillance for the product itself; nor does it clearly state the objective, criteria and procedure for audit, and it is difficult to ensure that so many EU market surveillance authorities can exercise this power in a fair and effective manner, manufacturers will have great difficulties in responding to the system audits of so many EU market surveillance authorities.4.  According to the draft, market surveillance authorities can unconditionally enter the economic operators' workplace and examine, seize, take or obtain copies of information, data or documents, irrespective of their storage medium; and even seal any premises or seize any information, data or documents (Articles 14.3(d), 14.3(e)), which are relevant to economic operators Trade secrets, information security risks, etc. The articles extend too much power of law enforcement to the power of judicial adjudication. Most European market surveillance authorities are non-government agencies. Although they are authorized by the government, the power to close the premises and seize the information, data and documents of the operators is only the jurisdiction of the state authority. Otherwise, it will lead to the abuse of power and the chaos of the market.5.  So we propose to delete Article 14.3 (b), 14.3(d), 14.3(e)(2) and 14.3(e)(3) and emphasize in articles of Chapter 5 that market surveillance authorities are required to the most strict implementation of laws and regulations, the principle of professional business confidentiality.

The representative of Canada, echoing China's comments, was also concerned that the measure may restrict trade because of the requirement contained in Article 4 that each exporter designate a person responsible for compliance information located in the EU. According to the measure, this designated responsible person would be required to provide compliance information – their name and contact information on the product label - and cooperate with market surveillance authorities where appropriate. His delegation considered that this requirement could create financial and administrative burdens for exporters, particularly SMEs, by requiring them to find and employ an EU-based person or entity to act as a representative for them.

In addition, regulations such as the RoHS Directive and the RED Directive have labelling requirements, again requiring the application of physical labels, adding unnecessary costs.5.  It is proposed to add a clause in Article 4.4 that "allows the enterprise to inform the consumer of the name, trademark, contact information and postal address of the economic operator through online or electronic means".6.  The Union testing facility is critical to the technical execution and interpretation of the Regulation, ensuring consistency between test standards and test results. The representative of the European Union thanked Chile for the opportunity to send written comments on the notification G/TBT/N/CHL/442 and proceeded to summarize those concerns. It was noted that the draft law would not allow cheeses made from milk powders or from recombined/reconstituted milk to be labelled as "cheese" but only as "milk product similar to cheese", meaning that cheese made from products other than milk, such as milk powders, would not be allowed to be commercialised as cheeses and economic operators would have to relabel their products specifically for the Chilean market. He warned that this would result in an unnecessary burden and would likely have an adverse impact on international trade. The EU referred to Codex General Standard for Cheese, CODEX STAN 283-1978, which, in relation to the essential composition of cheese, referred to the use of raw materials such as "Milk and/or products obtained from milk". His delegation was of the view that on the basis of this Codex standard, both liquid milk and/or preserved milk (in the form of milk powder, concentrated, etc.) may indeed be used in cheese manufacture. 3.10. The EU invited Chile to take into account its concerns and to reply to its written comments. Chile was also encouraged to apply to the greatest extent possible the international standards adopted by CODEX. Finally, the EU enquired about the state of play of the preparation of this legislative piece.

The representative of the United States voiced support for the EU on this issue and would follow developments of the regulation closely. Her delegation looked forward to receiving Chile's response to their comments on the notified measure.

The representative of New Zealand said that her delegation acknowledged and supported Members' right to regulate to achieve legitimate health objectives, including Chile's efforts to protect the health of consumers. However, New Zealand considered that Chile's specific proposed legislation was not consistent with CODEX Standards and, consequently, that it constituted an unnecessary barrier to trade. New Zealand urged Chile to correct such inconsistencies. In New Zealand's view, Chile's proposed measure was inconsistent with CODEX standards for the following reasons: a. It did not allow cheeses made from milk powders, or from other products obtained from milk, to be labelled as "cheese" but only as "milk product similar to cheese". This would mean that cheese made from products other than milk, such as milk powders, would not be allowed to be commercialised as "cheese", which was inconsistent with Codex General Standard for Cheese, CODEX STAN 283-1978. According to CODEX STAN 283-1978 raw materials for cheese manufacture should be "milk and/or products obtained from milk". This Codex Standard placed no restriction on the use of milk powders and/or other products obtained from milk as raw materials for cheese production. b. It contained unclear definitions for "milk" and "reconstituted milk". It also included new terms that were not, however, defined, such as "liquid milk" or "milk enhanced with reconstituted powdered milk". Furthermore, the proposed definitions did not align with CODEX STAN 206-1999 (Codex General Standard for the Use of Dairy Terms).

The representative of New Zealand acknowledged and supported the rights of all Members to regulate for the protection of human health and safety. However, New Zealand was concerned that Chile's law establishing rules on the marketing and labelling of dairy products might be more trade restrictive than necessary to fulfil a legitimate objective and at odds with internationally accepted Codex standards. Specifically, New Zealand was concerned that Chile's proposed definition of "cheese" was overly restrictive in requiring extra labelling for cheese that was manufactured with milk powder, despite Codex standards for cheese placing no restrictions on the use of milk powders and reconstitution for cheese manufacturing. New Zealand was also concerned by the exclusion of protein standardisation in Chile's proposed definition of "natural milk," as protein standardisation was an important and commonly used step for keeping milk of consistent quality and taste throughout the year. While appreciating Chile's notification of the measure, New Zealand was very concerned that Chile had decided to proceed with implementing the law by publishing the final regulation a month before the end of the 60-day comment period, putting into question fulfilment of its obligations under the TBT Agreement to allow a reasonable time for Members to make comments and to take these comments into account. Therefore, New Zealand strongly urged Chile to reconsider the regulation and bring it into alignment with Codex standards to avoid creating an unnecessary obstacle to trade, as per Article 2.2 of the TBT Agreement.

The representative of the United States said that while appreciating Chile's notification of its revised draft law on dairy products in September 2019, the US was very concerned that the law appeared to have been approved and published in Chile's Diario Oficial on 2 November 2019, more than three weeks before the deadline provided for comments. It was of particular concern in light of comments provided by trading partners on previous versions of the law. The US and other trading partners had provided significant comments in 2018 on notifications G/TBT/N/CHL/442 and G/TBT/N/CHL/458, which were related to this law. It appeared that the notification of the measure to the WTO at such a late stage was a mere formality, rather than a meaningful opportunity to submit comments that Chile would take into consideration prior to implementation of the measure. An initial review of the published law indicated that Chile had taken neither the US comments nor concerns raised during previous TBT Committee Meetings into consideration. The US had concerns with Chile's proposal to require labelling of reconstituted dairy products and the restriction of using reconstitution in cheese production, both of which appeared to be inconsistent with Codex standards. The US asked Chile to explain its rationale for not adhering to Codex standards in the development of the measure and also what steps it intended to take to ensure that trading partners' comments were taken into account, in light of the fact that the measure had been finalized and whether it was possible for Chile to amend the measure. Finally, the US asked that the implementation of the draft law be delayed pending confirmation with trading partners that their concerns, and particularly the inconsistencies with Codex, had been taken into account in a revised version of the measure.

New Zealand acknowledges and supports the rights of all WTO Members to regulate for the protection of human health and safety.
	However, New Zealand is concerned that Chile’s draft law establishing rules on the marketing and labelling of dairy products may be more trade restrictive than necessary to fulfil a legitimate objective and at odds with internationally accepted CODEX standards.
	Specifically, New Zealand is concerned that Chile’s proposed definition of “cheese” is overly restrictive in requiring extra labelling for cheese that is manufactured with milk powder, despite CODEX standards for cheese placing no restrictions on the use of milk powders and reconstitution for cheese manufacturing.
