StatementSubmitted: The United States maintains that it has serious concerns with CSAR and the consistency of some of its implementing measures with certain WTO obligations, including the treatment of imports; overly burdensome and disproportionate information requirements; lack of procedures to ensure the protection of confidential and proprietary information; duplicative in-country testing; and continued challenges with transparency in the development and implementation of the CSAR measures.    However, China finalized several additional technical guidelines in late August. While we are in the process of reviewing these, could China please clarify the implementation timelines of these measures, in light of Announcement Number 34’s intent to extend the transition period?  We reiterate our request from the last two committee meetings that China provide clarity on NMPA’s Announcement Number 13 of 2023, issued in January on matters related to the notification and inspection of general cosmetics. Our understanding is that firms manufacturing in China will have the option of self-testing for general cosmetics, if they have a cosmetics production license and they meet additional conditions. Could China please confirm?  We also ask that China clarify whether importers will also be given the option to self-test.  Further, if these requirements and procedures were not included in previously notified measures, would China please notify them to the WTO TBT Committee? As we have long noted, U.S. industry faces pressing challenges in trying to comply with China’s often unrealistic implementation timelines for CSAR and its conflicting technical regulations – complicated further by the lag from prior Covid-19 shutdowns over the past three years, and the testing backlog at labs in China.  In prior meetings, we asked that China consider extending the national CSAR implementation deadlines for the notified measures contained in CHN/1459, 1515, 1526, and 1525, including extending the deadlines that have already gone into effect.  We appreciate that China’s March 27 announcement extended the deadlines for cosmetics ingredients filings, and we urge that China provide further flexibility in extensions across the other measures, given the aftereffects of the pandemic and the requirements for in-country testing.    We also ask that China consider how it can rely upon international recognition schemes for conformity assessment to reduce the timelines for companies to comply. We understand that China may be drafting some provisions regarding overseas inspections. We again ask China the same question from the June meeting: is China able to provide a timeline on when these provisions will be notified for public comment?  U.S. companies remain eager for a means to engage with NMPA on questions arising from CSAR implementation, including regarding the new requirements and use of NMPA’s new online platforms for product and ingredient filings. Does China have any plans for this? Finally, we refer to previous U.S. statements for other unresolved issues and unanswered questions. We ask that China discontinue its practice of responding to requests for clarification by merely reiterating CSAR’s requirements and instead acknowledge and resolve the specific, tangible concerns expressed by the United States and many other WTO members.

StatementSubmitted: The United States maintains that it has serious concerns with CSAR and the consistency of some of its implementing measures with certain WTO obligations, including the treatment of imports; overly burdensome and disproportionate information requirements; lack of procedures to ensure the protection of confidential and proprietary information; duplicative in-country testing; and continued challenges with transparency in the development and implementation of the CSAR measures.  In its response to WTO Members at the November 2023 TBT Committee, China stated that for cosmetics efficacy claims “the efficacy claim evaluation test method does not limit the selection of internationally recognized foreign regulations or technical standards, such as OECD or ISO.” We ask that China clarify how companies using OECD or ISO standards can comply with China’s requirements when registering or notifying their cosmetics, in place of a Chinese standard?  Further, we understand that China has been updating parts of the Safety and Technical Standards for Cosmetics, which was notified to the TBT Committee as a draft in 2022. Could China provide an update on timing for issuing the finalized Safety and Technical Standards regulation for cosmetics?  We reiterate our request from the last three committee meetings that China provide clarity on NMPA’s Announcement Number 13, issued in January 2023 on matters related to the notification and inspection of general cosmetics. Our understanding is that firms manufacturing in China will have the option of self-testing for general cosmetics, if they meet certain conditions. Could China explain further what the requirements are for self-testing? Will importers also be given the option to self-test?  Further, if these requirements were not included in previously notified measures, would China please notify them to the WTO TBT Committee? As we have long noted, U.S. industry faces pressing challenges in trying to comply with China’s often unrealistic implementation timelines for CSAR and its conflicting technical regulations.  We urge China to consider how it can rely upon international recognition schemes for conformity assessment to lessen the burdensome timelines for companies to comply. We understand that China may be drafting some provisions regarding overseas inspections. We again ask China the same question from prior TBT Committee meetings: is China able to provide a timeline on when these provisions will be notified for public comment? U.S. companies remain eager for a means to engage with NMPA on questions arising from CSAR implementation, including regarding the new requirements and use of NMPA’s new online platforms for product and ingredient filings. Does China have any plans for this? Finally, we refer to previous U.S. statements for other unresolved issues and unanswered questions. We ask that China discontinue its practice of responding to requests for clarification by merely reiterating CSAR’s requirements and instead acknowledge and resolve the specific, tangible concerns expressed by the United States and many other WTO members.

Summary: The representative of the Republic of Korea provided the following statement. The Republic of Korea reiterates its existing concerns on the followings: "Cosmetics Supervision and Administration Regulation," "Specifications for Cosmetic Efficacy Claim Evaluation," "Specifications for Registration and Filing of New Cosmetic Ingredients," "Cosmetics Labeling Administration" and "Specifications for Cosmetic Registration and Filing." We acknowledge China's policy aims in strengthening the regulations on cosmetics to guarantee quality and safety, and to protect consumers' health as well. We truly know that it is not easily achievable to strike a balance between consumers' safety and market access. Nevertheless, we remain concerned that the international practices and China's "Cosmetic Supervision and Administration Regulation" and its measures are not in full harmony. Cosmetic industrial stakeholders are also worried if their intellectual property rights could be infringed since the Chinese government requests much more specific information than the general scope in controlling the cosmetics market. As for cosmetics being exported into China, it is mandatory that the overall "safety evaluation" reports on each ingredient be submitted for the registration and filing. This requirement, however, could act as a trade barrier as it may be hard for the industry to get prepared by the current deadline, May 2024. In this regard, we would like to request some extension from the date 1 May 2024 for submission of draft versions. In accordance with the Chinese regulations, test reports submitted shall be issued by the testing laboratories accredited by the China Metrology Accreditation (CMA). Japan would like to request that China continue to address not only the matters in the statements in the meetings, but also all of the matters uploaded on the e-Agenda that refer to past statements.1. Tests conducted for cosmetics test reports required by the “Cosmetics Registration Filing Information Management Regulations” must be conducted by testing laboratories that are located in China and that have obtained CMA (China Methodology Accreditation) certification. Japan has received responses from China stating that it does not prohibit or restrict foreign laboratories from obtaining CMA based on the “Administrative Measures for the Accreditation of Inspection and Testing Institutions”. However, Article 4, Article 14, etc. of the aforementioned Administrative Measures explicitly stipulate that only testing laboratories within the territory of China can qualify for CMA. Consequently, this does not meet Japan’s request to accept the test results of foreign laboratories with testing capabilities equivalent to laboratories that have obtained CMA. As Japan has repeatedly stated, location is essentially irrelevant to testing capability, therefore Japan would like to continue to request that China treat foreign laboratories with capability equivalent to the laboratories located in China that have obtained CMA as equal and also accept test results of such foreign laboratories as being equally valid, regardless of where they are located. 2. Regarding the efficacy claim evaluation methods required by the “Specifications for Cosmetic Efficacy Claim Evaluation”, China responded at the past meeting that “Based on the principle of equivalence the efficacy claim evaluation test method does not limit the selection of internationally recognized foreign regulations or technical standards, such as the ISO or OECD.” However, the test methods applied to the efficacy claim evaluations of special cosmetic products such as sunscreens are limited to the ones listed in the Safety and Technical Standards for Cosmetics. Similarly, China requires microbiological, physical, chemical and toxicological tests to be conducted in accordance with the test methods specified in the Chinese national standards and relevant regulations, and in the case of using a test method which is not specified in the national standards and the regulations, China additionally imposes the verification of equivalence with the test methods specified in the national standards and regulations, and storage of the test results in preparation for inspection. Japan would like to request that China treat internationally accepted methods such as those from the ISO or OECD as equal to the methods stipulated in China’s national standards or relevant regulations. If they are not regarded as equivalent test methods, Japan would like China to clarify why they are not treated as acceptable.3. Also, Japan considers that the efficacy claim evaluation methods required by the Specifications are more stringent and restrictive than necessary for the purpose of efficacy claim evaluation to guarantee the scientific validity and reliability and protect consumer legal interests. Japan reiterates its request for the implementation of a flexible framework considering internationally recognized practices akin to the example included below.For example, “Attachment 1, Requirements of Cosmetic Efficacy Claim Evaluation Item” specifies four types of evidence. It specifically stipulates which evidence can be used for each efficacy claim. In contrast, according to the internationally recognized practice, the types of evidence for each efficacy claim are determined individually by cosmetics registrants and filers based on the specific wording of claims and scientifically valid testing method for each one, as the types of evidence depend on the specific wording of claims.Furthermore, the “Provisions for the Supervision and Administration of Toothpaste” announced in March 2023 stipulate that the efficacy claim evaluation of toothpaste must "conform(s) to laws, regulations, mandatory national standards, technical norms and relevant requirements for quality safety and efficacy evaluation regulated by the National Medical Products Administration”. Particularly, human efficacy claim tests are required for anticavity, control of dental plaque, anti-dentin hypersensitivity and reduction of gum problems. This necessitates retesting of many products, including even ones that have been approved to be effective overseas without human efficacy claim tests.As with cosmetics, according to the abovementioned Provisions , human efficacy claim tests relevant to toothpaste must be conducted in China, and given these circumstances, we are concerned that retesting will take a long time and affect many toothpaste products currently on the market. Japan would like to request a flexible framework of using results from in vitro tests using oral-derived bacteria, cells, and tissues and open literature, as international practices adopted to confirm efficacy claims.4. The “Announcement on Matters Relating to the Implementation of Toothpaste Regulation and Simplification of Filing Requirements for Listed Toothpastes (announcement No.124, 2023)” published in September 2023 stipulates that submission of evidence of efficacy claims will be required for products that are to be on the market from 1 December, 2023. However, many of the specific items required for filing, such as applicable claims on efficacy, methods of human tests as efficacy claim evaluation, toxicological testing, positive lists on ingredients etc., have not been stipulated in the “Standards of Information File for Toothpaste Notification” that came into force in December 2023, therefore it is obviously impossible to comply with this requirement. In addition, delays in updating the application system have also been an obstacle in complying with regulations. To ensure that the measures are consistent with Articles 5.8 of the TBT Agreement, Japan requests that China clarify the implementation of the measures in detail and operate the application system in a proper and practical manner.5. Regarding the “Interim Measures on the Administration of Overseas Inspections of Cosmetics”, Japan recognizes that overseas inspections have already been conducted despite the fact that related TBT notifications have not been made in advance. Japan requests that the final version of the measures be published immediately. Also, Japan requests a flexible framework regarding the following concerns Japan has repeatedly expressed, so that overseas inspections are not more stringent and restrictive than necessary:?Clarification of specific purposes for conducting overseas inspections and which laws and regulations are used to assess conformity. Also, assurance that the inspections will not be more trade restrictive than necessary to achieve the purpose of protecting human health.?Information related to research and development is the most important confidential information for companies, but it is not information that directly affects product safety assurance. Furthermore, inspections within China are limited to the production sector and this indicates that it is not necessary to conduct inspections of R&D sections. Therefore, Japan requests exclusion of R&D departments of companies that may possess confidential information from the subject of overseas inspections and assurance that confidential information will not be disclosed to persons other than those who are necessary for the legitimate purpose of the inspections.6. The “Administrative Measures on Cosmetic Labeling,”?promulgated on 3 June 2021 stipulates the labeling items and methods to be displayed on the product label, and when the content of the label is slightly changed, the label must be revised. In order to avoid excessive burdens related to revising labels, Japan requests that the labeling items and methods be reasonably determined so that they ensure safety, quality, etc.In particular, Article 7 of the Administrative Measures requires the indication of “producers,” “registrants or filers,” and in the case of imported products, a "responsible person in China" on the product labels of cosmetics and toothpaste. However, the “Cosmetics Supervision and Administration Regulation” and the “Provisions for the Supervision and Administration of Toothpaste” clearly stipulate that registrants and filers are fully responsible for quality, safety and efficacy claims of products. In order to clarify responsibilities and avoid confusion among consumers, Japan would like to request that the labels of cosmetics and toothpaste indicate only “registrants or filers,” as a single responsible person and if needed, a "responsible person in China" as a contact person can be added, and that China delete content requiring the indication of producers.Also, Article 12 stipulates that regarding the labeling of all ingredients in cosmetics, only ingredients with a content of 0.1% or less can be listed in random order. This is contrary to the internationally recognized practice in which ingredients with a content of 1% or less are allowed to be listed in random order. Japan would like to request that China assure that the rules for labeling follow the internationally recognized practice, including for toothpaste, so as not to be more trade restrictive than necessary for the purpose of demonstrating the safety and efficacy of products to consumers.7. Japan understands the purpose of the sample retention system, and Japan is not against sample retention per se. However, “Public Notice Related Matters of Provisions for the Supervision and Administration of Cosmetics Production and Distribution” (No.140, 2021), requires that, regarding products imported to China by foreign registrants or filers, domestic responsible persons must retain samples of each batch of cosmetics. Registrants or filers are essentially responsible for the cosmetics, and since samples of imported products are stored in the country of origin, requiring an additional sample to be stored in China places an excessive burden only on imported products in terms of cost and storage space. Even in the case of imported cosmetics, Japan would like to request that China accept that samples need not be retained in China if the testing system can be utilized immediately when problems occur.8. Sales certification to prove that the products have been sold in the country of production or where the registrants or fillers are located is imposed only on imported cosmetics. Japan requests that China treat imported products no less favorably than products produced in China, in other words, Japan requests that China abolish the obligation to acquire the sales certification for imported products.9. Japan recognizes that transition periods are set in all relevant regulations but disagrees that the transition periods are of sufficient length. Japan strongly requests that China provide an adequate grace period of at least one year after promulgation of all relevant regulations and guidelines in order to prevent market turmoil and in order to enable cosmetics registrants and filers to adapt cosmetics to new requirements.

Particularly, human efficacy claim tests are required for anticavity, control of dental plaque, anti-dentin hypersensitivity and reduction of gum problems. This necessitates the retesting of many products, including even ones that have been approved to be effective overseas without human efficacy claim tests. According to the abovementioned Provisions, human efficacy claim tests relevant to toothpaste must be conducted in China, and given these circumstances, we are concerned that retesting will take a long time and affect many toothpaste products currently on the market. Japan would like to request a flexible framework of using results from in vitro tests using oral-derived bacteria, cells, and tissues and open literature, as international practices adopted to confirm efficacy claims.4. The "Announcement on Matters Relating to the Implementation of Toothpaste Regulation and Simplification of Filing Requirements for Listed Toothpastes (announcement No.124, 2023)" published in September 2023 stipulates that submission of evidence of efficacy claims will be required for products that are to be on the market from 1 December 2023. However, many of the specific items required for filing, such as applicable claims on efficacy, methods of human tests as efficacy claim evaluation, toxicological testing including oral mucosa irritation testing, positive lists on ingredients etc., have not yet been stipulated in the "Standards of Information File for Toothpaste Notification" that came into force in December 2023 and "Announcement of the National Medical Products Administration on the Incorporation of 15 Test Methods Including the Test Method for pH Value of Toothpaste into the Technical Specification for Cosmetic Safety (2015 edition) (announcement No.13, 2024)" published in March 2024, therefore it is obviously impossible to comply with this requirement. In addition, delays in updating the application system have also been an obstacle in complying with regulations. To ensure that the measures are consistent with Articles 5.8 of the TBT Agreement, Japan requests that China clarify the implementation of the measures in detail through their publication etc. and operate the application system in a proper and practical manner. 5. Regarding the "Interim Measures on the Administration of Overseas Inspections of Cosmetics", Japan recognizes that overseas inspections have already been conducted despite the fact that related TBT notifications have not been made in advance. Japan would like to request that China clarify when the final version of the measures will be published. Also, Japan requests a flexible framework regarding the following concerns Japan has repeatedly expressed, so that overseas inspections are not more stringent and restrictive than necessary: Clarification of specific purposes for conducting overseas inspections and which laws and regulations are used to assess conformity. Also, assurance that the inspections will not be more trade restrictive than necessary to achieve the purpose of protecting human health. The "Interim Measures on the Administration of Overseas Inspections of Cosmetics," released for public comment in November 2019, stated that China could conduct inspections of research and development departments. However, in view of the purpose of inspections to confirm the quality control status of cosmetics production, Japan considers it unnecessary to conduct inspections of R&D departments that are not directly involved in production. Accordingly, Japan requests deletion of the provisions stating that China may inspect R&D departments from the final version of the measures by its publishment.6. The "Administrative Measures on Cosmetic Labeling," promulgated on 3 June 2021 stipulates the labelling items and methods to be displayed on the product label, and when the content of the label is slightly changed, the label must be revised. In order to avoid excessive burdens related to revising labels, Japan requests that the labelling items and methods be reasonably determined so that they ensure safety, quality, etc. In particular, Article 7 of the Administrative Measures requires the indication of "producers," "registrants or filers," and in the case of imported products, a "responsible person in China" on the product labels of cosmetics and toothpaste. However, the "Cosmetics Supervision and Administration Regulation" and the "Provisions for the Supervision and Administration of Toothpaste" clearly stipulate that registrants and filers are fully responsible for quality, safety and efficacy claims of products. In order to clarify responsibilities and avoid confusion among consumers, Japan would like to request that the labels of cosmetics and toothpaste indicate only "registrants or filers," as a single responsible person and if needed, a "responsible person in China" as a contact person can be added, and that China delete content requiring the indication of producers. Also, Article 12 stipulates that regarding the labelling of all ingredients in cosmetics, only ingredients with a content of 0.1% or less can be listed in random order. This is contrary to the internationally recognized practice in which ingredients with a content of 1% or less are allowed to be listed in random order. Japan would like to request that China assure that the rules for labelling follow the internationally recognized practice, including for toothpaste, so as not to be more trade restrictive than necessary for the purpose of demonstrating the safety and efficacy of products to consumers.7. Japan understands the purpose of the sample retention system, and Japan is not against sample retention per se. However, "Public Notice Related Matters of Provisions for the Supervision and Administration of Cosmetics Production and Distribution" (No.140, 2021), requires that, regarding products imported to China by foreign registrants or filers, domestic responsible persons must retain samples of each batch of cosmetics. Registrants or filers are essentially responsible for the cosmetics, and since samples of imported products are stored in the country of origin, requiring an additional sample to be stored in China places an excessive burden only on imported products in terms of cost and storage space. Even in the case of imported cosmetics, Japan would like to request that China accept that samples need not be retained in China if the testing system can be utilized immediately when problems occur. 8. Sales certification to prove that the products have been sold in the country of production or where the registrants or fillers are located is imposed only on imported cosmetics. Japan requests that China treat imported products no less favourably than products produced in China, in other words, Japan requests that China abolish the obligation to acquire the sales certification for imported products. 9. Japan recognizes that transition periods are set in all relevant regulations but the transition periods are unreasonably short. Japan strongly requests that China provide an adequate grace period of at least one year after promulgation of all relevant regulations and guidelines in order to prevent market turmoil and in order to enable registrants and filers to adapt cosmetic and toothpaste products to new requirements. In addition, Japan recognizes many of the recent public consultation periods on guidelines and other matters related to the implementation of the "Cosmetics Supervision and Administration Regulation" are extremely short. Japan requests that China provide sufficient time for public consultation to review and submit comments with necessary consideration on guidelines and other matters related to the implementation of the "Cosmetics Supervision and Administration Regulation".

StatementSubmitted: The United States maintains that it has serious concerns with CSAR and the consistency of some of its implementing measures with certain WTO obligations, including the treatment of imports; overly burdensome and disproportionate information requirements; lack of procedures to ensure the protection of confidential and proprietary information; duplicative in-country testing; and continued challenges with transparency in the development and implementation of the CSAR measures.  For the most part, our entire statement from March remains valid. Rather than repeat it here, we will refer China and others to that statement and ask that China provide responses to each of the questions raised.  We also ask that China discontinue its practice of responding to requests for clarification by merely reiterating CSAR’s requirements and instead acknowledge and resolve the specific, tangible concerns expressed by the United States and many other WTO members.
Summary: The representative of the United States provided the following statement. The United States maintains that it has serious concerns with CSAR and the consistency of some of its implementing measures with certain WTO obligations, including the treatment of imports; overly burdensome and disproportionate information requirements; lack of procedures to ensure the protection of confidential and proprietary information; duplicative in-country testing; and continued challenges with transparency in the development and implementation of the CSAR measures. For the most part, our entire statement from March remains valid. We will refer China and others to that statement and ask that China provide responses to each of the questions raised. We also ask that China discontinue its practice of responding to requests for clarification by merely reiterating CSAR's requirements and instead acknowledge and resolve the specific, tangible concerns expressed by the United States and many other WTO Members.

The representative of the United States expressed full support for the objective of managing the public health challenges related to drunk driving. However, her delegation was concerned by the lack of transparency in the development of the proposed amendments to Korea's Public Health Promotion Act. It was also noted that many aspects of the measure were currently unclear, including the timeline for implementation and the technical requirements for the new labels which could result in an unnecessary disruption to trade in US alcohol beverage products to Korea. In December 2018, the US had requested via the TBT Enquiry Point that Korea notify the revisions under consideration to its Public Health Promotion Act, including the details of its new graphic warning label requirements for beverage alcohol. She noted that Korea had not notified the amended measure and asked Korea to commit to doing so before adoption.

The representative of the United States expressed full support for the objective of managing the public health challenges related to drunk driving. However, her delegation was nonetheless concerned with various aspects of the proposed measure. The US understood this measure to include, among others, the following requirements: (i) a warning on the label to the effect that driving under the influence of alcohol was "equivalent to murder;" and (ii) a picture on the label depicting a traffic accident or other harmful effects of driving under the influence of alcohol (including a warning photo). The US also had federal mandatory health warning requirements for alcoholic beverages. Federal regulations required that any alcoholic beverage containing 0.5% alcohol or higher have a Health Warning Statement on the label. US regulations set out a number of requirements relating to the font and appearance of the Health Warning Statement, including that it be legible, appear on a contrasting background, and be separate and apart from all other label information. However, there was no federal requirement in the US for a graphic warning (i.e., a picture) on alcoholic beverage labels. The US also supported several public-private partnership initiatives related to combating the harmful use of alcohol and driving under the influence of alcohol. The 2015-2020 US Dietary Guidelines did not recommend that individuals start or increase drinking for any reason and, if alcohol was consumed, the Guidelines stated that it should be consumed in moderation - up to one drink per day for women and two drinks per day for men - and only by adults of legal drinking age. It had come to US' attention, however, that Korea had recently taken other steps to address drinking and driving. In December 2018, a bill to amend Korea's Road Traffic Act had been passed by the National Assembly. This amendment reduced the allowable blood alcohol level for driving under the influence of alcohol and instituted the revocation of an individual's driving license if their blood alcohol level was found to be above 0.08%. Had Korea considered allowing time to analyse the impact of this measure before making additional changes to its labelling requirements? Could Korea consider other, less trade-restrictive means to achieve its objective, such as its domestic initiatives to reduce drinking and driving?

The representative of Japan was concerned that Korea had not presented any detailed warning statements and graphics showing the dangers of drunk driving, nor a date of entry into force of this Amendment. Japan asked Korea to present a full English text of this amendment, as early as possible. Japan also asked Korea to indicate how long the transition period for this Amendment would be, which should be adequate in order to avoid any confusion. Japan also stated that related international standards, such as "CODEX General Guidelines on Claims" (CAC/GL1- 1979), should be taken into consideration for the amendment.

The representative of the European Union said that her delegation supported the concerns raised by others and invited Korea to provide further details about the health warning statements and also to respond to the comments sent to the Korean enquiry point.

The representative of Mexico said that, although her delegation recognized the objective of reducing the impact related to the abuse of alcohol consumption and the need to educate the people in this regard, it nonetheless considered that there were different alternatives to the warning statements proposed by Korea, that might be more effective without being more unnecessarily trade restrictive. Mexico asked Korea to examine the results of other recently implemented and less traderestrictive measures.

The representative of Canada said that, while Canada and the Canadian wine industry supported the goal of minimizing the potential harm associated with the misuse or abuse of alcohol, it was nonetheless concerned that this regulation may have an impact on trade, especially for smaller producers. As a wine-producing country, Canada was interested in receiving further clarity and information on the measure in order to ensure that that any unnecessary disruption to trade in Canadian alcoholic beverages to Korea could be avoided.

The representative of Australia said that, while his delegation recognized the right of government to take measures necessary to protect public health, it on the other hand emphasized the importance of compliance with WTO obligations, in particular the requirements that measures be implemented in a non-discriminatory manner and in a way that would not be more trade restrictive than necessary. Australia sought clarification as to the evidence on which the draft amendments and labelling requirements were based and how the proposed measures would contribute to public health objectives. Australia asked Korea to provide guidance on the final wording of the warning statements and images that were required to appear on alcoholic beverages, as well as the specifications, such as size and placement, required for the warning statements and images. Australia would also appreciate clarification from Korea on: (i) the expected timeframe for implementation of the measures; and (ii) whether exemptions or a transition period would apply for products that were already in market or in transit when the new measures were implemented.

The representative of the United States reiterated that the US fully supported Korea's objective of managing public health challenges related to drunk driving. In March 2019, Korea notified the WTO of its newly proposed labelling requirements for alcoholic beverages, to which the US had submitted comments. At the June 2019 TBT Committee meeting, Korea indicated that it would respond to those comments and the US asked when the response might be forthcoming. It was the US understanding that Korea's proposal included, among other requirements: (i) a warning on the label that driving under the influence of alcohol is "equivalent to the act of killing"; and, (ii) a picture on the label depicting a traffic accident or other harmful effects of driving under the influence of alcohol (including a warning photo). To reiterate the US comments submitted on the measure, while fully supporting Korea's objective of mitigating public health challenges associated with driving under the influence of alcohol, the US was concerned that Korea's proposed graphic warning label requirement may be more trade restrictive than necessary to achieve Korea's legitimate objective. She asked what evidence Korea had considered when determining the specific language required on the label, and when determining the need for a graphic of a car accident in addition to a warning statement. The US queried whether Korea intended to notify implementing regulations outlining the details of its proposal prior to enforcement, and whether WTO Members would have the opportunity to comment. The US described its federal mandatory health warning requirements for alcoholic beverages, namely that federal regulations require that any alcoholic beverage containing 0.5% alcohol or higher include a Health Warning Statement on the label. US regulations also set out several requirements relating to the font and appearance of the Health Warning Statement, including that it be legible, appear on a contrasting background, and be separate and apart from all other label information. There was no federal requirement in the US for a graphic warning (i.e., a picture) on alcoholic beverage labels. The US supported several public-private partnership initiatives related to combating harmful use of alcohol and driving under the influence of alcohol. The 2015-2020 US Dietary Guidelines did not recommend that individuals start or increase drinking for any reason and, if alcohol was consumed, the Guidelines stated that it should be consumed in moderation - up to one drink daily for woman and two drinks for men - and only by adults of legal drinking age.

The representative of the European Union also had concerns with this measure and invited Korea to provide further details about the health warning statements, and to respond to the comments sent by the EU to the Korean TBT enquiry point in June.

The representative of the Japan echoed concerns raised by the US. Korea had not offered any detailed information on the warning statements and pictures showing the dangers of drinking and drunk driving, and the date of entry into force of this Amendment. Japan requested Korea to provide an overall explanation of the Amendment including the above detailed information as soon as possible. In addition, Korea had not indicated the length of the transition period for this Amendment. Japan requested Korea to update the Committee on the transition period and to ensure an adequate period to avoid any confusion. Finally, Japan asked Korea to take into consideration the relevant international standards for the Amendment, including "CODEX GENERAL GUIDELINES ON CLAIMS" (CAC/GL1-1979).

The representative of Australia recognized the right of Members to take measures necessary to protect public health. In this regard, Australia appreciated Korea's efforts to address a legitimate public health concern. Australia asked Korea to provide guidance on the final wording of the warning statements and images that are required to appear on alcoholic beverages, as well as the specifications, such as size and placement, required for the warning statements and images. Australia also requested clarification from the Republic of Korea on the expected timeframe for implementation of the measures, and whether exemptions, or a transition period, would apply for products already on the market or in transit when the new measures would be implemented.

The representative of Canada stated that as an exporting country of alcoholic beverages, Canada remained interested in the implementation of this regulation due to its possible impact on trade, especially for small producers. At the last TBT Committee, Korea indicated that the specifics with respect to the enforcement (such as whether or not it would be enforced, the detailed contents, and enforcement date) had not yet been determined. Korea also stated that it would consider the re-notification to the TBT Committee after the specific enforcement date and the revised draft were confirmed. Canada requested that Korea update the Committee on this proposed measure, in particular with respect to the timing of the planned re-notification in order to ensure that any unnecessary disruption to trade was avoided.

The representative of Mexico reiterated its concerns expressed at previous meetings. Mexico also supported the concerns expressed by the US and other Members and requested an update and more information from Korea on the designation of accident photographs, and the question of the re-notification of this measure.

The representative of the United States thanked Uruguay for their bilateral meeting and noted their support of Uruguay's objectives of reducing diet related non-communicable diseases. She stated that the final decree as notified may, however, not be based on robust scientific evidence, be more trade restrictive than necessary to achieve a legitimate objective, did not appear to consider the relevant international standards, and may contribute to consumer confusion. She further asked whether positive health claims would be allowed for foods such as yogurts, cereals, or oatmeal which were required to carry the warning label but may also contain other nutrients, be fortified, or make other positive contributions to an overall diet. In addition, she noted that the United States had not received a response to its 2017 comments on the draft decree and asked whether Uruguay had reviewed evidence-based international standards to determine if they would fulfil Uruguay's public health objectives. Although the US had listed international standards in communication with Uruguay, the original draft document did not mention Codex standards being utilized or evaluated, while the final decree only mentioned the Pan American Health Organization's Nutrient Profile Model. The United States further asked whether Uruguay had considered that the required black and white octagonal "stop sign" symbols and the new requirement that they contain the initials MPH in addition to the statement that the product was in "excess of" a specified nutrient may cause consumers to avoid products that could be part of a healthy diet. She asked whether studies in Uruguay had demonstrated that this interpretive approach was more effective than presenting nutrient and calorie information on labels based on serving size portions of the product, and whether Uruguay had evaluated any alternative labelling schemes, or a voluntary approach.
The representative of the European Union noted interest in this regulation and asked for a written reply to the comments the delegation would send.

The representative of Guatemala reiterated concerns over the creation of divergent labelling of packaged food without taking into account the Codex Alimentarius. She noted that this worked in favour of large firms with the capacity to create labels for different markets and consequently discriminated against MSMSEs and SMEs. While recognizing Members' legitimate objectives in this domain, she highlighted that technical regulations should not be any more restrictive than necessary.
The representative of the European Union shared the concerns expressed by the US and asked that Uruguay provide a written reply to the EU comments.
The representative of Colombia supported the concerns raised and follow it with interest.

The representative of Guatemala supported the concerns raised and follow it with interest. Costa Rica referred the Committee to the statement delivered at the previous TBT Committee meeting, circulated in document G/TBT/W/613.

The representative of Costa Rica supported the concerns raised and follow it with interest. Costa Rica referred the Committee to the statement delivered at the previous TBT Committee meeting, circulated in document G/TBT/W/613.

The representative of the United States supported Uruguay's public health objectives of reducing modifiable behavioural risk factors associated with non-communicable diseases. However, in the context of the June 2019 US-Uruguay Trade and Investment Framework Agreement talks, several remaining concerns were raised about the 29 August 2018 final decree notified to the TBT Committee. In particular, she said the decree may contribute to consumer confusion and Uruguay did not appear to have considered less trade-restrictive alternatives. The US reiterated its request that Uruguay consider whether the required black and white octagonal "stop sign" symbols, and the decree's new requirement that the symbols must contain the initials MPH in addition to the statement that the product was in "excess of" a specified nutrient, may cause consumers to avoid products that could be part of a balanced diet, such as low- and no-calorie sweetened foods and beverages. The US again urged consideration of whether alternative labelling schemes or a voluntary approach could provide consumers with similar information in a manner less burdensome and costly for producers while still achieving Uruguay's valid health objective. The US also urged Uruguay to provide a transition period of at least two years, given the complexities involved in adjustment by manufacturers to new food labelling schemes.

The representative of Costa Rica supported the concerns raised by the US. Costa Rica questioned the scientific base of Uruguay's labelling system and was concerned that it departed from Codex standards. He requested updated information from Uruguay and referred to Costa Rica's statement at the March 2019 Committee meeting contained in G/TBT/W/613.

The representative of the United States raised concerns with the EU's measure on chlorothalonil. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/607 (below).1.  The United States thanks the European Union for the bilateral meeting and would like to continue to express ongoing concerns with the EU's approach to pesticide regulation, and specifically with the December 2018 Draft Commission Implementing Regulation concerning the non-renewal of the approval of chlorothalonil. 2.  Chlorothalonil is a broadly effective fungicide used on many horticultural products in the US, most significantly cranberries and almonds. 3.  Following the EU's summary removal of MRLs for Chlorothalonil in 2014, the US cranberry industry suffered significant crop losses due to the loss of this effective crop protection tool, without any corresponding food safety benefits. To regain access to this important tool the US cranberry industry invested significant resources generating new data to support an import tolerance application for submission to EFSA, to allow for the use of chlorothalonil on cranberries destined for export to the EU.4.  The United States was pleased that EFSA acknowledged no consumer risk and in 2016, the EU established an import tolerance harmonized with the US tolerance of 5 mg/kg for cranberries.5.  Given that EFSA so recently evaluated this substance and found no risk to consumer health, even at a level twice the current import tolerance, we would request that the EU maintain its current standard for residues on cranberries at 5 mg/kg.6.  Can the EU confirm that no action will be taken on chlorothalonil MRLs prior to the conclusion of a comprehensive risk assessment to support any changes to existing MRLs and import tolerances?7.  The US almond industry has also expressed concern about the loss of chlorothalonil from its pest management programs, as producers rely on a robust rotation of fungicides to manage resistance and protect against crop damage and unnecessary food waste. 8.  The uncertainty created by the nonrenewal of chlorothalonil creates a burden for US growers who are making crop protection decisions for their 2019 crops. The uncertainty causes particular difficulties for producers of commodities with longer shelf lives (e.g., dried fruits, nuts), for which there may be significant periods between application, harvest, processing, and distribution. 9.  More generally, the United States has repeatedly expressed concern that the EU, by focusing on data gaps and adopting hazard-based standards for regulation, may not fulfill its obligation to conduct risk assessments. The United States has also repeatedly expressed its concern regarding the process for product registration approvals and establishment of MRLs, as well as the overly restrictive timelines involved. 10.  We believe that the EU's process for approving and establishing residue limits for active substances creates unnecessary barriers to trade. We request that the EU establish risk-based approaches, which comport with the principles of non-discrimination, transparency, necessity, and predictability.

The representative of Colombia raised concerns with the EU's measure on chlorothalonil. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/600 (below).1.   On this occasion, with the aim of promoting agricultural development and facilitating foreign trade with the European Union (EU), we would like to draw the attention of the EU to a subject of great importance for the agricultural sector in Colombia. We would be grateful if you would take our comments into consideration.2.   Colombia wishes to express its concern regarding the measure notified by the EU through document G/TBT/N/EU/625 of 4 December 2018, relating to the non‑renewal of the approval of the active substance chlorothalonil. This substance is key to pest control for a wide range of crops, and banana exports would be especially affected by the measure, since chlorothalonil is used for the control of Black Sigatoka, a fungus known to devastate banana crops.3.   Our country is the fifth largest banana exporter in the world. In 2017, our total production amounted to 1.87 million tonnes, with exports worth USD 850 million. A total of 80% of exports go to the EU, especially Belgium (575,000 tonnes), Italy (270,000 tonnes) and the United Kingdom (242,000 tonnes). Colombian banana producers are a major source of employment and development. The banana industry in the main producing regions of Urabá, Magdalena and Guajira accounts for 35,000 direct and 100,000 indirect jobs.4.   The possible adoption of this measure is a source of concern, since the decision to withdraw marketing approval for the substance, without maximum residue levels (MRLs) being affected for the moment, is based on a precautionary principle in response to concerns mainly relating to carcinogenicity classification and a lack of data on the magnitude and toxicity of metabolites.5.   The above is corroborated by Regulation (EC) No. 1272/2008 of the European Parliament: "Additionally, chlorothalonil is classified as carcinogen category 2 in accordance with Regulation (EC) No. 1272/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council while in the conclusion of the Authority it is indicated that chlorothalonil should be classified as carcinogen category 1B. For the representative uses considered, residue levels as referred to in point (b) of Article 18(1) of Regulation (EC) No. 396/2005 could not be confirmed for plant and animal products due to lack of data on the magnitude and toxicity of metabolites that are included in the residue definition for risk assessment. Consequently, the requirement set out in Points 3.6.3 of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No. 1107/2009 is not fulfilled." It is indicated that no danger or risk has been determined for the metabolites concerned. Hence there is a need to request further information and complete the corresponding risk assessment and then take a decision regarding unacceptable health risks for potential consumers.6.   Colombia considers that the classification decision should be taken by the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) as the competent EU authority in this field, whose opinion should be made available before member States are asked to take a decision on the renewal of the approval of chlorothalonil.7.   In view of the information gaps, it is impossible to establish criteria for acceptance or rejection of the compound. However, before imposing a ban, the EU should be encouraged to fill the information gaps and obtain a risk assessment based on data, not uncertainty.8.   In view of the above, we are faced with a violation of Article 2.2 of the TBT Agreement – which provides that technical regulations shall not be more trade‑restrictive than necessary to fulfil a legitimate objective – since, as demonstrated above, there is insufficient information to establish criteria for acceptance or rejection of the chlorothalonil compound, its impact on health not having been clearly established in scientific terms. Furthermore, we wish to mention that any technical adoption of an alternative to this active ingredient for the banana industry in Colombia will require at least six months. We therefore consider that the time defined for withdrawing this active substance from the production of bananas and other products is not viable since there are currently no studies on possible replacements for it.9.   It is important to mention that the change in the regulations would also seriously affect other crops which are exported to the EU, such as: plantains (47,816 tonnes), cape gooseberries (5,863 tonnes) and cocoa (1,796 tonnes) (approximate quantities exported in 2018).10.   Without chlorothalonil, fruit pest control would be more difficult and exports of Colombian bananas and other crops to the EU market would be adversely affected, which, in turn, would have a major social and economic impact in the producing regions. Non‑renewal of the approval of the active substance chlorothalonil restricts the range of chemical pesticides for use with agricultural products, a situation that is not compatible with tropical agriculture, which is biodiverse in terms of pests, diseases and weeds and cannot be compared with agriculture at European latitudes. Seasonality alone makes European agriculture significantly different from our own agricultural reality.11.   It is therefore essential that the EU uses the risk assessment approach in decision‑making with regard to the application of this measure, since there is insufficient scientific evidence to determine the various toxicological aspects that may affect human health, and the thresholds for safe use of the active substance chlorothalonil are unknown.12.   In light of the above, Colombia requests the EU to maintain the registration of chlorothalonil in the EU, since it is a vital substance for managing resistance development and has been assessed for many years as suitable for authorization and use at the global level. It is important that the measures adopted are based on scientific evidence and international standards and also take account of the biodiverse agriculture of countries such as Colombia, which cannot be compared with that of European latitudes, where the climatic conditions and seasons are very different. The foregoing is in accordance with the terms of the TBT Agreement, which provides that any measures established must not be more trade‑restrictive than necessary or create unnecessary obstacles to trade.

The representative of Guatemala expressed concern with respect to the measure notified in G/TBT/N/EU/625 of 4 December 2018, with respect to the non-renewal of the approval of the active substance chlorothalonil, a substance generally used by some agricultural producers as a fungicide to control certain pests. Her delegation reiterated its belief that the EU should take a risk-assessment approach based on sufficient scientific evidence in determining control levels, particularly those established in the Codex Alimentarius. Guatemala considered that changes to agricultural practice required a more extensive process and that it was important to be adaptable in seeking alternatives as regards the use of pesticides. She pointed out that as these processes were lengthy, transitional periods should be set accordingly. Guatemala associated itself with Colombia's request to maintain the approval of chlorothalonil in the EU, and with the concerns previously expressed by other Members. She also called upon the EU to offer solutions and alternatives for tropical countries in respect of their ability to adapt in this area. Referring to the indication in the EU's notification that the maximum residue levels (MRLs) for pesticides containing chlorothalonil may be revised in the future, clarification and information about the work plan envisaged was requested, as well as the arguments being put forward in that regard.

The representative of Brazil shared Colombia's concerns, in particular the fact that the EU's decision was founded only on a hazard-based approach, without a proper risk analysis. The nonrenewal of approval for chlorothalonil by the EU did not take into consideration that it was currently authorized in 109 countries, and that the MRLs allowed by Codex could reach up to 70 mg/kg, depending on the product. In this context, he reiterated Brazil's concerns with the fact that some analyses conducted by the European Food Safety Agency (EFSA), whose results on the genotoxicity of substances were founded on a hazard-based approach, had led to the non-renewal of certificates and subsequently to the reduction of MRLs. The case of chlorothalonil, he said, had a negative impact on Brazil's trade of agricultural products, such as banana, coffee, citrus fruits, papaya, watermelon, among others, which used this substance for pest control. He recalled that for all those commodities, Brazil adopted MRLs below those established by Codex, in line with concerns related to consumer safety. Finally, Brazil reiterated its systemic concern with the fact that issues relating to the nonrenewal of agricultural pesticides were being dealt firstly in the TBT Committee. He said that in many cases the communication of non-renewal of approval of important substances for trade of agricultural commodities was notified in the TBT Committee as an announcement of the future reduction of MRLs in the SPS Committee. In this context, Brazil asked the EU about the eventual next steps regarding the possible reduction of MRLs for chlorothalonil and that this be notified to the SPS Committee as soon as possible.

The representative of Panama reiterated his delegation's continuing concern, already expressed in the TBT Committee as well as the SPS Committee, on measures being taken by the EU which appeared to go beyond Codex Alimentarius scientific evidence.

The representative of Paraguay expressed concern with the measure as in Paraguay, chlorothalonil was classed as a low-risk pesticide and sold freely. It was used for several key products exported from Paraguay, such as corn, wheat, rice and soya and whilst not the main input of phytosanitary products for the pest control of such crops, it was considered as a component in the rotation of these products to address handling shortfalls and prevent resistance to other active substances. Her delegation deemed that the categorization of chlorothalonil as carcinogenic, carried out by the EFSA, was based on inconclusive claims. The proposal to eliminate the use of this active substance had once again been based on a hazard assessment rather than a consumer risk assessment, and, once again, did not comply with relevant international standards. It was felt that rather than providing a genuine solution or fulfilling the objective of health protection, this situation would result in unnecessary barriers to trade. Paraguay also expressed concern with the pattern of action taken by the EU, starting with the prohibition of the marketing of a substance and then moving to the amendment of the MRLs for that substance. Her delegation believed that such amendments established levels that were equivalent to a prohibition of the use of the substance and did not ensure import tolerances. The EU was urged to comply with the international commitments that it had undertaken in the WTO, and to carry out risk assessments rather than hazard assessments when making this type of decision.

The representative of Canada thanked Colombia for bringing the issue to the attention of the Committee as chlorothalonil was registered for use in field and orchard crops in Canada. She said that a growing number of active substances were not being renewed in the EU due to incomplete or insufficient information to complete a risk assessment and excluded health and environmental concerns. Canada considered this a worrisome trend that may affect agriculture and food imports in the EU given the lack of clarity on how import tolerances would be established following a nonrenewal decision due to lack of such information. Her delegation encouraged the EU to indicate what information was needed to complete and conclude its risk assessment.

The representative of Ecuador was aware that the decision currently only mentioned the placing of the substance on the market and not of an MRL for this product. Her delegation nevertheless expressed concern over the fact that specific measures could be taken regarding the MRLs and that such measures could be very restrictive. In Ecuador, she said, active chlorothalonil registers were kept for several agricultural products, but the substance was especially used as a technological tool to help control Black Sigatoka in bananas. The EU was requested to take into consideration the fact that Ecuador's banana exports accounted for 2% of overall GDP and approximately 35% of agricultural GDP. According to registers of the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock (MAG), about 162,236 hectares had been cultivated with bananas, representing 4,473 banana producers (small (3,480), medium-size (800) and large (193)). Ecuador therefore urged that, before a final decision was taken on implementing the measure and another on possible assessment of the MRLs, the European Commission consider all existing data, as well as comments submitted to it, with due regard for the implications on the food-producing sector of developing countries.

The representative of Costa Rica raised concerns with the EU's measure on chlorothalonil. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/612 (below).1.   Costa Rica supports the trade concern raised by Colombia with regard to the draft Implementing Regulation proposed by the European Union concerning the non‑renewal of the approval of the active substance chlorothalonil.2.   The use of this active substance is an essential part of agricultural production in Costa Rica. The non‑renewal of its approval would cause serious problems for the Costa Rican production sector, as there are currently no substitute or similar phytosanitary products with a better environmental or toxicological profile.3.   Chlorothalonil is used to control pests of economic importance, particularly in the production of bananas. Costa Rica is the world's second largest exporter of bananas, with sales amounting to an estimated USD 1 billion, representing around 2% of GDP and 38.6% of agricultural GDP. Banana production in the country also creates 40,000 direct jobs and around 100,000 indirect jobs. The main destination for exports is the European Union, where over 50% of the fruit produced in Costa Rica is sent, which further illustrates the impact that the implementation of this measure would have.4.   The measure proposed by the European Union is based on the alleged risk that chlorothalonil may pose to both health and the environment. In this regard, it is important to point out that domestic producers apply good agricultural practices based on the requirements established by widely‑recognized certification organizations such as Global Gap, Rainforest Alliance and Fair Trade.5.   Furthermore, extensive sampling of bananas conducted by the Laboratory for the Analysis of Agrochemical Residues of the State Phytosanitary Service has demonstrated the absence of chlorothalonil residues, thus confirming that good practices have been applied and that there are no risks to health or the environment.6.   Lastly, I wish to emphasize that the non‑renewal of the approval of chlorothalonil proposed by the European Union is not based on a risk assessment, as required under Article 2.2 of the Agreement on Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT Agreement). This non‑renewal has been put forward on the basis of concerns and issues for which no conclusive results have been obtained, as indicated by the European Union in its notification of the measure.7.   Chlorothalonil was previously approved for use in the production of agricultural goods intended for the European Union. On the basis of this approval, our farmers began using the substance in banana production. A significant number of jobs in less developed areas depend on this crop.8.   Lastly, Costa Rica strongly urges the European Union to carry out a risk assessment before implementing the non‑renewal of the approval of chlorothalonil. Furthermore, any discussion on the possible public health effects related to this substance should be held within the multilateral framework, as part of the work carried out in the Codex Alimentarius, which has established the permitted chlorothalonil tolerances for different agricultural products.
The representative of Honduras expresses its trade interest in the issue and asked the EU for more information on the criteria used for the implementation of the measure.

The representative of Colombia raised concerns with this measure. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/661 (below).1.   Colombia wishes to express once again its concern at the approach adopted by the European Union (EU) with regard to the regulation of pesticides and, specifically, regarding the measure notified through document G/TBT/N/EU/625 of 4 December 2018, relating to the non‑renewal of the approval of the active substance chlorothalonil. This substance is key to pest control for a wide range of crops, and banana exports would be especially affected by the measure, since chlorothalonil is used for the control of Black Sigatoka, a fungus known to devastate banana crops.2.    This matter has already been brought before this Committee in document G/TBT/W/600 and, since it is considered of great importance for the agricultural sector in Colombia, we are grateful to the EU for taking our comments into consideration, in order to promote agricultural development and facilitate trade between the two parties.3.   Our country is the fifth largest banana exporter in the world. In 2017, our total banana production amounted to 1.87 million tonnes, with exports worth USD 850 million. A total of 80% of exports go to the EU. Colombian banana producers are a major source of employment and wealth in rural areas. The main banana‑producing regions in Colombia account for 35,000 direct and 100,000 indirect jobs.4.   The possible adoption of this measure is a source of concern, since the decision to withdraw marketing approval for the substance is based on a precautionary principle in response to concerns mainly relating to carcinogenicity classification and a lack of data on the magnitude and toxicity of metabolites.5.   The above is corroborated by Regulation (EC) No. 1272/2008 of the European Parliament, which indicates that no danger or risk has been determined for the metabolites concerned. Hence there is a need to request further information on the compound, complete the corresponding risk assessment and then take a decision regarding health risks.6.   Colombia considers that the classification decision should be taken by the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) as the competent EU authority in this field, whose opinion should be made available before Member States are asked to take a decision on the renewal of the approval of chlorothalonil.7.   Moreover, in view of the information gaps, it is impossible to establish criteria for acceptance or rejection of the compound. However, steps should be taken to seek additional information before a ban is imposed.8.   In view of the above, we are faced with a violation of Article 2.2 of the TBT Agreement – which provides that technical regulations shall not be more trade‑restrictive than necessary to fulfil a legitimate objective – since there is insufficient information to establish criteria for acceptance or rejection of the chlorothalonil compound, its impact on health not having been clearly established in scientific terms. Furthermore, the search for an alternative to this active ingredient for the banana industry in Colombia may take at least six months. We therefore consider that the time determined for withdrawing this active substance from the production of bananas and other products is not viable since there are currently no studies on possible replacements for it.9.   Without chlorothalonil, fruit pest control would be more difficult and exports of Colombian bananas and other crops to the EU market would be adversely affected, which, in turn, would have a major social and economic impact in the producing regions. It should not be forgotten that this is a particular situation in tropical agriculture, which is biodiverse in terms of pests, diseases and weeds and cannot be compared with agriculture in European latitudes. Seasonality alone makes European agriculture significantly different from our own agricultural reality.10.   In view of the above, Colombia requests the EU to maintain the registration of chlorothalonil in the EU, since it is a vital substance for managing resistance development and has been assessed for many years as suitable for use at the global level. It is important that the measures adopted are based on scientific evidence and international standards and also take account of the biodiverse agriculture of countries such as Colombia, which cannot be compared with that of European latitudes, where the climatic conditions and seasons are very different. The foregoing is in accordance with the terms of the TBT Agreement, which provides that any measures established must not be more trade‑restrictive than necessary or create unnecessary obstacles to trade.

The representative of  the United States raised concerns with this measure. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/671 (below).1.  The United States remains concerned with the EU's approach to pesticide regulation, and specifically with the December 2018 Draft Commission Implementing Regulation concerning the non-renewal of the approval of chlorothalonil. 2.  Chlorothalonil is a broadly effective fungicide used on many horticultural products. As stated in the March TBT Committee meeting, following the EU's removal of MRLs for Chlorothalonil in 2014, the U.S. cranberry industry suffered significant crop losses due to the loss of this effective crop protection tool, without any corresponding food safety benefits. To regain access to this important tool the U.S. cranberry industry invested significant resources generating new data to support an import tolerance application for submission to EFSA, to allow for the use of chlorothalonil on cranberries destined for export to the EU.3.  The United States was pleased that the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) acknowledged no consumer risk and in 2016, the EU established an import tolerance harmonized with the U.S. tolerance of 5 mg/kg for cranberries. There continues to be no consumer risk at this residue level.4.  The U.S. almond industry has also expressed concern about the loss of chlorothalonil and other substances from its pest management programs, as producers rely on a robust rotation of products to manage resistance and protect against unnecessary crop damage and food waste. 5.  Will the EU take U.S. and other nations' comments into consideration in the final regulation?6.  The United States has also repeatedly expressed its concern regarding the process for product registration approvals and establishment of MRLs, as well as the overly restrictive timelines involved. 7.  The uncertainty created by the nonrenewal of chlorothalonil creates a burden for U.S. growers who may have already made crop protection decisions for their 2019 crops. The uncertainty causes particular difficulties for producers of commodities with longer shelf lives (e.g., dried fruits, nuts), for which there may be significant periods between application, harvest, processing, and distribution. 8.  More generally, the United States has repeatedly expressed concern that the EU's focus on data gaps and adopting hazard-based standards for regulation, may not fulfill its obligation to conduct risk assessments. Many data gaps cited by the EU are not problematic for other scientific organizations or regulating bodies that conduct risk assessments. 9.  Can the EU confirm not to take action on chlorothalonil MRLs prior to the conclusion of a comprehensive risk assessment to address data gaps and support any changes to existing MRLs and import tolerances? While the EU claims the purpose of the nonrenewal of approval was not to amend MRLs, its common practice has been to remove MRLs immediately following nonrenewal of approval.10.  How did the EU determine that the nonrenewal would not be more trade restrictive than necessary?11.  We believe that the EU's process for approving and establishing residue limits for active substances raises significant concerns. We continue to request that the EU establish risk-based approaches, which comport with the principles of sound science, non-discrimination, transparency, and predictability.

The representative of Ecuador raised concerns with this measure. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/649 (below).1.   Ecuador expresses its concern at the measure notified by the European Union (EU) to the WTO (G/TBT/N/EU/625) regarding the draft Commission Implementing Regulation concerning the non‑renewal of the approval of the active substance chlorothalonil and the withdrawal of existing authorized plant protection products containing chlorothalonil from the market.2.   Even though this EU measure currently only refers to the placing of this substance on the market, we do wish to express concern since the next step will be measures that restrict maximum residue levels (MRLs) for this product, which could have a serious impact on the marketing of bananas.3.   Ecuador is the world's leading banana exporter, trading with around 85 international markets, including the EU as one of its main trading partners.4.   Banana exports from Ecuador account for approximately 35% of agricultural GDP, with over 160,000 hectares under cultivation for bananas and nearly 4,500 banana producers, 75% of whom are small producers.5.   Banana production in Ecuador occurs largely in the context of the household economy and the "popular and solidarity economy", which means that the sector contributes to job creation and poverty reduction. The country's banana sector accounts for between 2 million and 2.5 million jobs at various stages of the value chain.6.   Most plantations in the country are high‑tech and many meet international quality standards with ISO, HACCP (Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point), Rainforest Alliance or GLOBALG.A.P. certification. To date, 80,000 hectares of banana crops have GLOBALG.A.P. certification. Another 16,000 hectares have Rainforest Alliance certification and 10,000 hectares are Fairtrade‑certified.7.   Under the terms of the Andean regulations on the registration and control of chemical pesticides for agricultural use, the toxicological, ecotoxicological and agronomic specifications for obtaining the registration of a pesticide in Ecuador must be science‑based and developed according to internationally recognized methods and protocols, with standardization and acceptance by international reference organizations.8.   These are subjected to technical assessment by our National Technical Committee on Pesticides, – comprising the Ecuadorian Agency for Agricultural Product Quality Assurance (AGROCALIDAD) and the national health and environment authorities –, which analyses everything relating to active ingredients. The technical assessment determines the parameters for: authorized use (specific interaction between crop and pest concerned), dosage, water consumption, method of use and withholding period for the registered product. The objective is to provide guidance for the correct use and handling of the product as part of good agricultural practices, to prevent and minimize health and environmental risks, and to ensure the biological effectiveness of the product.9.   In the light of the above, Ecuador requests the EU, before taking a final decision on implementation of this measure and another on possible assessment of MRLs, to consider all existing data and the comments submitted to the European Commission in order to avoid any undue impact on the food production sector in developing countries.

The representative of Brazil shared the concerns raised by Colombia and the US and regretted the EU's decision to base this measure on a hazard-based approach, without a proper risk analysis and compliance with long-standing scientific principles. The non-renewal of approval for chlorothalonil did not take into consideration that it was currently authorized in 109 countries and that the MRLs allowed by Codex could reach up to 70 mg/kg, depending on the product. This issue had negative impacts on Brazil's exports of agricultural products, such as banana, coffee, citrus fruits, papaya, watermelon, amongst others, which used this substance for pest control. For all these commodities, Brazil adopted MRLs below those established by Codex, in line with concerns related to consumer safety. Brazil reiterated concerns with the fact that some hazardbased analyses conducted by the European Food Safety Agency (EFSA) had led to the non-renewal of certificates and subsequently to the reduction of MRLs. Finally, in line with the presentations made by Brazil during the June 2019 thematic session on transparency, he reinforced Brazil's systemic concern with the fact that issues related to the nonrenewal of agricultural pesticides were being dealt with firstly in the TBT Committee. In many cases the communication of non-renewal of approval of important substances for trade of agricultural commodities was notified in the TBT Committee as an announcement of the future reduction of MRLs in the SPS Committee. As this situation stands, Brazil would continue to raise and support these concerns in both committees.

The representative of Panama continued to raise concerns expressed at past meetings of the TBT and SPS Committees regarding the reduction of the maximum levels of active substances by the EU, specifically the active substances chlorothalonil and buprofrezin. Since 1987, Panama had adopted the maximum levels of active substances recommended by Codex, which were internationally recognized by WTO Members as the standards for world food safety and the promotion of fair trade. Although every Member was free to take measures necessary to ensure the safety of its citizens, these measures should not be unnecessarily strict, to the point of adversely affecting trade.
