The representative of the United States expressed appreciation for the opportunity to speak with Saudi Arabia on her delegation's very strong concerns regarding the Saudi Food and Drug Authority's (SFDA) draft regulation that all food and beverage products could not exceed maximum added sugar limits established by SFDA (G/TBT/N/SAU/1108 and Add.1). The US also appreciated that since initial notification, Saudi Arabia had informed Members that implementation would be suspended until further notice. Her delegation was concerned that if implemented, the measure would disrupt the export of a wide range of popular food and beverage products to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, making most forms of popular carbonated beverages, ice cream, jams and preserves, confectionary, chocolate candy, energy drinks, and many juices unavailable to consumers there, as many of these products required a certain level of added sugar as a preservative or stabilizer. She warned that as in many cases there was no viable alternative, the product would not be able to enter Saudi Arabia through authorized channels. Moreover, she said, the sudden removal of these products from the market would negatively affect Saudi producers, retailers, importers, and consumers and if implemented, the regulations would cause several companies to shut their Saudi Arabian food production operations and lay off their employees. Whilst appreciating Saudi Arabia's desire to address obesity and non-communicable diseases (NCDs), such as diabetes, as part of its Healthy Food Strategy, the US nevertheless questioned the sufficiency of the scientific evidence used as justification for the regulation, the limits prescribed, the specific objectives of the regulation, and the process by which this draft would meet those objectives. The US was also concerned about how the draft regulation aligned with Saudi Arabia's proposed new regulations on Front of Package Nutrition Labelling (FOPNL) and yet to be notified regulations on maximum limits on salt. Her delegation asked Saudi Arabia to notify these regulations to the WTO and added that they were unclear and did not reflect consultation with private-sector stakeholders, noting the cumulative effect of increasing uncertainty and unpredictability for a range of US and multinational companies. Whilst appreciating the suspension of implementation of the draft regulation, the US requested Saudi Arabia to work with stakeholders and trading partners to ensure that measures took into account scientific and technical information for meeting specific health objectives while minimizing potential negative economic impacts. She flagged that her government would be providing technical comments in response to the April 2019 notifications of the regulation to the TBT and SPS Committees, a process industry groups would be actively involved in, and urged Saudi Arabia to take those comments into account.

The representative of Switzerland pointed to the ample scientific evidence demonstrating the effects on human health of too much sugar over a prolonged period and therefore supported Saudi Arabia's objective in principle. He drew attention to Switzerland's "Nutrition Strategy 2017-2024" which sought to improve public health awareness through a variety of measures, including through the engagement of foodstuff producers and suppliers, a better education, and the promotion of a varied and balanced diet with less sugar. His delegation also welcomed initiatives to develop relevant international standards with the view to reducing sugar content in day-to-day diets, in particular for added sugar. Switzerland was concerned, however, with the lack of scientific evidence to support the draft regulation, for example, concerning the quantity of added sugar in food products. Saudi Arabia was asked to provide more information on the scientific basis of the measure. Also of concern were the economic implications if the regulation was implemented. It was unclear to Switzerland to what extent food producers could adjust the recipes and production lines to meet the upper sugar limits for foodstuffs and asked whether Saudi Arabia had received feedback from private sector stakeholders on this particular aspect. He then asked if Saudi Arabia had considered other less trade-restrictive measures to reach its policy objective, questioning why private sector stakeholders had not been more widely engaged in the consultation process. Bearing in mind the important technical knowhow of producers and suppliers of foodstuff, which could help design effective regulations, Saudi Arabia was encouraged to engage with private sector stakeholders to ensure a transparent process.

The representative of the European Union raised some of the most important points included in written comments on the measure that would be sent to Saudi Arabia, in particular the expected compliance difficulties due to the lack of an analytical method to distinguish naturally present and added sugar. The EU also noted that Foods for Special Medical Purposes and Infant formula and Follow-up formula should be excluded from the scope of the draft. In addition, her delegation enquired whether the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia had considered alternative, less trade-restrictive policies to reduce the sugar content in foods placed on the national market, such as economic measures facilitating healthier food choices and restricting consumption of added sugar or control of food advertising and marketing. Finally, the EU considered that the limits currently proposed may be technically challenging, particularly within the short timeframe proposed. Consequently, some key product categories currently exported from the EU to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia would no longer be able to access the market on 1 January 2020 and in this context, the EU invited Saudi Arabia to consider a transition period of at least three years for the notified provisions.

The representative of the Russian Federation expressed support for public health concerns that may be caused by unhealthy diet but believed that such concerns could be addressed in a less trade-restrictive manner. His delegation considered that the upper limit for added sugar required in the draft of the technical regulation of Saudi Arabia was more trade restrictive than necessary. Specifically, sugar content requirements set out in the document were not technologically achievable with regard to confectionery, for instance for chocolate and candies, among others. These requirements would therefore constitute a de facto ban, severely disrupting international trade in confectionary. It was noted that the document developed by the WHO, referred to by Saudi Arabia, only set recommendations for daily sugar consumption and did not lay down any requirements for sugar content in food products. Saudi Arabia was therefore requested to specify the scientific basis for such requirements in general and more specifically the basis for sugar content requirements in particular food products. Without such scientific data, he said, the measure could not be considered as justifiable, and based on international standards, practices and recommendations, his delegation was inclined to consider it as arbitrary. The Russian Federation remained open for consultations with the delegation of Saudi Arabia to discuss ways to revise the draft measure.

The representative of the United States reiterated that this measure would disrupt the export of a wide range of popular food and beverage products to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. While appreciating Saudi Arabia's desire to address obesity and non-communicable diseases (NCDs), such as diabetes, as part of their Healthy Food Strategy, and as noted in comments dated 14 June 2019, the US had questions about the sufficiency of the scientific evidence used as justification for the regulation, the limits prescribed, the specific objectives of the regulation, and the process by which this draft would meet those objectives. While acknowledging the suspended implementation of the draft regulation, the US strongly urged Saudi Arabia to be transparent and work closely with stakeholders and trading partners to ensure that revised measures took into account scientific evidence for meeting specific health objectives while minimizing potential negative economic impacts. The US was also concerned on the cumulative effect of the draft regulation on maximum added sugar limits and Saudi Arabia's other proposed measures on Front of Package Nutrition Labelling (FOPNL) and maximum limits on salt. The current status of these measures was unclear, increasing uncertainty and unpredictability for many US companies. Saudi Arabia was requested to provide an update on the status of the FOPNL measure, notified as G/TBT/N/SAU/1105.

The representative of Switzerland joined the US in raising concerns over the proposed sugar upper limits in food products and recalled its position from the last meeting of the TBT Committee. Switzerland remained concerned over the impact on trade if the regulation were implemented and called on Saudi Arabia to continue to engage with trading partners and the private sector in a transparent process to assure that the measure was not more trade restrictive than necessary, and to take such consultations with stakeholders into account. Also of concern was the fact that the draft regulation in general and quantities of added sugar in food products in particular were not based on scientific evidence; more information on the scientific basis of this measure was therefore requested. Switzerland encouraged Saudi Arabia to consider less trade restrictive alternatives, including through the engagement of foodstuff producers and suppliers, the provision of better information to consumers, and the promotion of a varied and balanced diet with less sugar, and to allow for a reasonable transitional period, taking the technical challenge of the requirements into account. While it was acknowledged that the implementation of the draft regulation had been postponed and that the sugar upper limits seemed to be voluntary for the time being, the status of the regulatory process remained unclear. Switzerland requested an update on the regulatory development of this measure and its timeline.

The representative of the Russian Federation shared concerns raised by the US and recalled the statement made during the previous meeting of the TBT Committee. He requested information on the state of play of the revision as well as the nature of the proposed amendments. Russia remained open for bilateral work with Saudi Arabia on this issue.

The representative of the European Union reiterated interest in the draft technical regulation on Added Sugar Upper Limit in Some Food Products, notified in G/TBT/N/SAU/1108, and referred to its detailed written comments. While fully sharing the legitimate objective of public health protection, the EU encouraged Saudi Arabia to consider alternative, less trade restrictive policies to reduce the sugar content in foods placed on the national market. Concerning the revision process of the draft announced in the previous TBT Committee meeting, Saudi Arabia was invited to duly take into account in that process the comments and statements of the EU and other WTO Members. Most importantly, compliance with the proposed sugar limits would cause serious technical difficulties for the industry producing some of the products covered by the draft measure, particularly within the short timeframe proposed. Consequently, some key product categories currently exported from the EU to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia would no longer be able to access the market. Finally, the EU requested an update on the state of play of the notified draft.

The representative of the Russian Federation thanked the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia for the bilateral engagement and for notifying the intention to withdraw this measure. While sharing the public health objectives contained in the draft measure, Russian requested that Saudi Arabia confirm that the measure had indeed been withdrawn.

The representative of the United States raised concerns with the measure. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/668 (below).1.  The United States thanks Uruguay for notifying its Resolution on Analytical Specifications Related to Exogenous Water in Imported Wine Products to the WTO TBT Committee on 14 March 2019, as G/TBT/N/URY/27, and its subsequent revision on 25 March 2019, as G/TBT/N/URY/27/Rev.1.2.  We recognize Uruguay's delayed entry into force of this measure from 1 March 2019 to 1 June 2019, but the United States continues to have strong objections to the Resolution and finds the delay inadequate for exporters to adjust to new requirements, particularly when those requirements remain unclear.3.  The United States thanks Uruguay for its 13 May 2019, response to our TBT comments. However, several concerns and questions remain.4.  Uruguay indicates in its TBT notification that the objective of this measure is the "Prevention of deceptive practices and consumer protection." The United States maintains that the Resolution continues to raise questions regarding its consistency with Uruguay's WTO obligations, such as whether it is more trade-restrictive than necessary to fulfill a legitimate objective under Article 2.2 of the WTO Agreement on Technical Barriers to Trade. The United States would appreciate a clear explanation of how a prohibition on imported wine containing "exogenous water" furthers Uruguay's objective.5.  Does Uruguay believe that wine quality cannot be assured in cases where very limited amounts of water are used in winemaking? What information is Uruguay using as the basis for this concept?6.  Our TBT comments raise questions about the definition of exogenous water and whether Uruguay would consider U.S. winemakers' technical use of water in accordance with U.S. law to be exogenous. A clear definition of the term is necessary in order for trading partners to know if wine exports from their markets are affected by this measure.7.  Uruguay's notification references the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) product code 67.160.10. This ISO product code refers to all alcoholic beverages, including beer, wine, spirits, etc. Would Uruguay please define the scope of products subject to this Resolution?8.  We understand Uruguay's 13 May response to U.S. comments to indicate that Uruguay objects to the establishment of tolerances that allow for a maximum amount of water because the existence of a tolerance could allow winemakers to use the existence of a tolerance as an economic tool. 9.  The U.S. does not allow the addition of water to increase the volume of wine. However, where water is added to facilitate the solution or dispersal of a material, the volume of water added, whether the material is used singly or in combination with other water based treating materials, may not total more than one percent of the volume of the treated wine, juice or both wine and juice from which such wine is produced. We understand that Uruguay intends to require the U.S. to comply with this measure while not requiring compliance from other countries, which allow for water additions but do not set an upper limit. Can Uruguay please explain its rationale for this distinction?10.  In its 13 May 2019 response to our TBT comments, Uruguay indicated that a certificate from the competent authority would be required. The United States notes that the U.S. competent authority for alcoholic beverages, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB), does not issue certificates related to water content in wine. Furthermore, we understand that to evaluate the results of the oxygen isotope analysis required by Uruguay, a robust database of values in the country of export is required. Neither the U.S. government nor U.S. industry is aware of an adequate database of wine values that takes into account vintage, varietal, appellation of origin or age of U.S. vines. The United States asks Uruguay to reconsider this certification requirement entirely, including whether such a certificate would be issued by the competent authority or industry.11.  As set out in our comments on Uruguay's revised notification, we would also like to remind Uruguay of its commitments as a WWTG Member and, thus, a Party to the WWTG Agreement on Mutual Acceptance of Oenological Practices (MAA), which entered into force, for Uruguay, on 1 May 2018. According to MAA Articles 5(2) and 5(4), Uruguay's new requirement should not apply to wine imports from the eight other WWTG Members: Argentina, Australia, Canada, Chile, Georgia, New Zealand, South Africa, and the United States. 12.  We thank you for your consideration of these concerns and look forward to discussing this further.

The representative of Chile raised concerns with the measure. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/647 (below).1.    Chile would like to raise a trade concern regarding a measure notified by Uruguay to the TBT Committee, as follows:2.   On 14 February 2019, the National Grape‑Growing and Wine Production Institute (INAVI) of the Republic of Uruguay issued the resolution, under Act No. 005/2019, implementing the requirement to submit certification attesting that, as part of the import procedure, a certificate be submitted for all wine products attesting that the shipment contains no percentage of exogenous water. This was communicated to the Committee through Notification G/TBT/N/URY/27, indicating that it was an emergency notification, and its revised version G/TBT/N/URY/27/Rev.1, published on 14 March 2019 and 25 March 2019, respectively, with entry into force from 1 May 2019 (in accordance with the aforementioned Rev.1).3.   INAVI considers that the presence of exogenous water in wine, whatever its percentage, is illegal. Moreover, the resulting wine will be considered artificial and will therefore be unable to enter Uruguay.4.   As everyone knows, Members have the responsibility under the WTO's TBT Agreement to meet the obligations established therein, and to comply with the Decisions and Recommendations adopted by the WTO's TBT Committee.5.   According to Notification G/TBT/N/URY/27/Rev.1, Uruguay corrected the reasons for urgency, notifying under Article 2.9.2 of the TBT Agreement, set a deadline of 25 April for comments, and postponed entry into force until 1 May 2019. On 25 April, INAVI issued a statement indicating its decision to postpone entry into force of the measure until 1 June 2019. It should be emphasized that the requirement to set a period of at least 60 days for comments was not met.6.   Chile sent comments on 8 April 2019, through the official contact point for the TBT Agreement in Uruguay. A reply was sent on 13 May, which referred explicitly to only three of the seven comments sent by the Government. Comments sent by the industry (Wines of Chile) and the Association of Oenologists did not receive any response.7.   The main observations regarding the obligations of the TBT Agreement are as follows:8.   Chile recognizes the importance of the contribution of international standards to improving efficiency of production and facilitating the conduct of international trade. In this regard, it appreciates that Uruguay considers, as indicated in its notified resolution, the International Organisation of Vine and Wine (OIV) as an international reference body for recognition regarding the preparation and evaluation of the conformity of wine.9.   By means of recommendations, the OIV also proposes technical, regulatory or economic resolutions to the governments of member countries aimed at maintaining the development of the production and marketing of wines and other vine‑based products.10.   Chile has been an OIV member State since 1952, adopting into its legislation the oenological practices and treatments that all correspond to resolutions published and recommended by the OIV and are relevant to the practical reality of Chilean grape‑growing and wine production, thereby harmonizing these practices and treatments with international standards.11.   In this context, the OIV considers and recognizes the variability of expression and production in the global wine industry, in view of the differences in the soil and climatic conditions of wine‑producing countries. In recognition of this geographical and climatic diversity, OIV resolutions are established by the consensus of all member States.12.   Accordingly, the oenological practices and treatments authorized by Chile correspond to those recommended by the OIV, but only those that are relevant to grape‑growing and wine production in Chile are adopted.13.   The resolutions recommended by the OIV concerning oenological practices and treatments involve the implicit use of water as a universal solvent for various additives and processing aids, on the understanding that certain substances must first be dissolved in water before being added to the wine‑making and preparation processes for the production of quality wines without affecting the genuineness of the product.14.   Chile considers that the resolution adopted by INAVI in Uruguay could be a discriminatory measure if this regulation establishes that water originating from these oenological practices is of exogenous origin and is thus considered a technical obstacle to international trade.15.   Chile hopes that the successful trade in wine will be maintained. It also wishes to highlight the good trade relations and cooperative spirit that exist, as reflected in the recent signature of the free trade agreement between the Chile and Uruguay.16.   It should also be noted that Article 2.2 of the TBT Agreement provides that Members shall ensure that technical regulations are not prepared, adopted or applied with a view to or with the effect of creating unnecessary obstacles to international trade. For this purpose, technical regulations shall not be more trade‑restrictive than necessary to fulfil a legitimate objective, taking account of the risks non‑fulfilment would create. Under this provision, Uruguay would need to clarify the nature of the legitimate objective established in the TBT Agreement which it seeks to fulfil with the application of the new regulation.17.   Moreover, Article 2.9.1 of the TBT Agreement provides that Members shall publish a notice in a publication at an early appropriate stage, in such a manner as to enable interested parties in other Members to become acquainted with it, that they propose to introduce a particular technical regulation; and Article 2.9.4 of the said Agreement provides that Members shall, without discrimination, allow reasonable time for other Members to make comments in writing, discuss these comments upon request, and take these written comments and the results of these discussions into account.18.   Under this international commitment entered into by Uruguay under the said Agreement, Chile requests Uruguay to explain whether it has incorporated the comments received concerning the development of this regulatory process.19.   Regarding the date of entry into force of the proposal, namely 1 June 2019, it should be emphasized that, under Article 2.12 of the TBT Agreement, Members shall leave a reasonable interval between the publication of technical regulations and their entry into force, except in the case of certain urgent circumstances; this is not the case here and it has restricted market access for wine.20.   It should be recalled that the Ministerial Decision on Implementation‑Related Issues and Concerns, adopted on 14 November 2001 in Doha, provides that, subject to the conditions specified in Article 2.12, the phrase "reasonable interval" shall be understood to mean normally a period of not less than six months, except when this would be ineffective to fulfil the legitimate objectives pursued. The TBT Committee stresses the importance of the Doha Ministerial Decision with respect to Article 2.12 on technical regulations.21.   Furthermore, while noting that Article 2.12 already includes reference to developing country Members and their specific needs, the Committee encourages Members to provide an interval of more than six months, when possible, between the publication of technical regulations and their entry into force so that producers, in particular in developing country Members, have sufficient time to adapt to the new requirements. This was not done by Uruguay.22.   In the light of the above, the measure in question is considered to be an unnecessary obstacle to trade and to infringe Article 2.2 of the TBT Agreement, inasmuch as the said objective could be fulfilled in a manner less restrictive to trade.23.   We kindly request Uruguay to revise this measure, to reply to all the comments issued through the contact point and to align the measure with the rights and obligations of the TBT Agreement, and also with good international regulatory practices and the recommendations of this Committee.

The representative of South Africa raised concerns with the measure. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/643 (below).1.  South Africa provided comments on Uruguay's notifications G/TBT/N/URY/27 of 14 March 2019, and G/TBT/N/URY/27/Rev.1 of 25 March 2019. We thank Uruguay for their response of 13 May 2019 on our comments.2.  South Africa still has various concerns with Uruguay's regulation regarding exogenous water.3.   In the notified regulation, there is no tolerance or admissibility percentage of exogenous water in the produce indicated. This means that any exogenous water, whether through permitted oenological practices, such as additives or the accidental addition through filtration and wine transfer will be prohibited.4.  Although South African regulation does not allow the dilution of wine with water, it however, permits various oenological practices such as Bentonite swelling, yeast rehydration, malolactic bacteria rehydration, isinglass preparation, concentrated grape must addition, enzyme activation etcetera, that need to be dissolved or activated in water. Similar oenological practices are permitted by many other wine producing countries.5.  It would be helpful if Uruguay could please provide a definition for the term "exogenous water" as used in Uruguay's Resolution. Clarity is also required whether Uruguay considers irrigation water used in the cultivation of grapes as "exogenous" water?6.  We understand that certification will only be required for products imported into Uruguay from countries whose legislation accepts the presence of "exogenous water". Will Uruguay compile a list of these countries and will this list be made publicly available?7.  It is our understanding that the required analysis cannot differentiate between exogenous water used for oenological practices and exogenous water used for dilution. Uruguay's new regulation is not clear on how water used for oenological practices is to be accommodated in the regulation and subsequent analysis. Water permitted for oenological practices, cannot be regarded as illegal. 8.  Uruguay's regulation will require that a detailed database of the water and wine in each region of the exporting country is maintained on a continuous basis. South Africa does not have such a database for the water and wine in each of its wine producing regions. It currently does not have any laboratory in South Africa that is able to perform oxygen isotope analyses. The establishment of a representative database will be exorbitantly expensive, and it will only be used for wines exported to Uruguay. The analysis that will be compared with the detail in the database will never be 100% accurate as all sources of water cannot be covered by the analysis. 9.  The enforcement of this regulation will make it impossible for South Africa to export wine to Uruguay.10.  South Africa is also concerned that Uruguay did not provide a "reasonable interval" of at least six months between the adoption date of the regulation and its entry into force as Ministers agreed to interpret a "reasonable interval" as stated in paragraph 5.2 of the Doha Ministerial Decision of 14 November 2001[1] on Implementation-related issues and concerns related to the Agreement on Technical Barriers to Trade and also recommended by the Committee[2].11.  South Africa is interested to know why the six-month period between adoption and entry into force of the regulations as decided by Ministers could not be adhered to. Why is this time ineffective in fulfilling the legitimate objective pursued?[1] WT/MIN(01)/17 para 5.2[2] G/TBT/1/Rev.13 section 5.3.1.10

The representative of Australia expressed support for the concerns of other Members regarding Uruguay's implementation of new certification requirements for exogenous water in wine. He emphasized the importance of compliance with WTO obligations, in particular the requirements that measures be implemented in a non-discriminatory manner and in a way that was no more trade restrictive than necessary. He explained that in Australia, wine producers were permitted under the Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code to add water to dilute high sugar musts to aid in fermentation. The addition of water was done in minimal circumstances, for technical necessity, in small volumes to aid fermentation during periods of difficult seasonal conditions. Australia asked Uruguay to clarify the term 'exogenous water' and whether the use of water, permitted in Australia under the Food Standards Code, would be considered 'exogenous water'. Noting that the objective of the new measure was the 'prevention of deceptive practices and consumer protection', his delegation sought clarification on how the proposed measure would contribute to those objectives.

The representative of New Zealand expressed concern that Uruguay's measure may be more trade restrictive than necessary to fulfil a legitimate objective. His delegation requested that Uruguay reconsider its new regulation so that it did not become an unnecessary barrier to trade, as per Article 2.2 of the TBT Agreement. He pointed out that his country, like Uruguay, had a cooler climate, arguing that the addition of exogenous water was not necessary for New Zealand winemakers at that time, although it was acknowledged that climate change may eventually mean reviewing that decision. Whilst New Zealand did not allow this practice in the winemaking process, his delegation recognized that other countries may require this process due to differing climates and underlined that New Zealand made no restrictions in imported wine based on the practice. Moreover, it was recognized that countries permitting this practice through climatic necessity had strict controls over its use. In the Board of the National Grape-Growing and Wine Production Institute (INAVI) Resolution of 14 February, Uruguay referenced the OIV's method of determining isotopic ratios of oxygen in wine as the basis for its new requirements. Many WTO Members were not members of the OIV, and New Zealand did not recognize the OIV as an international standard setting body, as outlined in TBT Decision on Principles for the Development of International Standards, Guides and Recommendations with relation to Articles 2, 5 and Annex 3 of the Agreement. Whilst acknowledging that Uruguay had re-notified the draft regulation to the WTO to allow for a longer comment period, his delegation remained concerned that the proposed date of entry into force was 1 June, which New Zealand considered gave Uruguay insufficient time to take comments into account, as well as exporters to readjust practices. Uruguay was requested to delay the entry into force in accordance with Article 2.12 of the TBT Agreement, providing at least a six-month transition period between the date of final publication of a technical regulation and entry into force, so that comments submitted to the Uruguay TBT enquiry point could be taken into account.

The representative of the United States thanked Uruguay for bilateral technical exchanges and its agreement that for US wine it would not require the certificate established by the Resolution, nor any declaration or proof regarding exogenous water. Technical uses of water in winemaking permitted by the US and other countries did not lead to deception or the undermining of consumer protection. She urged Uruguay to recognize that those countries were not allowing the addition of water to dilute or increase the volume of wine and not to impose requirements related to exogenous water on imports from those countries. As a party to the World Wine Trade Group (WWTG) MAA, Uruguay was required to permit imports of wine produced by another party in conformity with the producing party's laws, regulations and requirements relating to oenological practices and the mechanisms to regulate them.

The representative of Australia referred to concerns raised in the June Committee meeting and expressed support for the concerns of other Members regarding Uruguay's implementation of new certification requirements for exogenous water in wine. Australia emphasized the importance of compliance with WTO obligations, in particular the requirements that measures be implemented in a non-discriminatory manner and in a way that was no more trade restrictive than necessary. He pointed out that in Australia, wine producers were permitted under the Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code to add water to dilute high sugar musts to aid in fermentation. The addition of water was done in minimal circumstances, for technical necessity, and in small volumes to aid fermentation.

The representative of New Zealand expressed concern that Uruguay's measure may be more trade restrictive than necessary to fulfil a legitimate objective. She said that like Uruguay, New Zealand had a cooler climate and the addition of water to high sugar must to facilitate fermentation was currently not necessary for their winemakers, although climate change may eventually force a review of that decision. While New Zealand did not allow this practice in its own winemaking process, it was recognized that other countries may require this process due to differences in climate. New Zealand did not make any restrictions based on this practice in imported wine and acknowledged that countries allowing it due to climatic necessity exercised strict controls over its use. Uruguay was therefore asked to reconsider its regulation so that it did not act as an unnecessary barrier to trade, as per Article 2.2 of the TBT Agreement.

The representative of Indonesia raised concerns about the development of the Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) Category Rule (CR) for intermediate paper products. Indonesia noted the EU's effort to standardize Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) conduct and to share PEF information with the public. His delegation requested an update on the final draft of Product Environmental Footprint Category Rules (PEFCR) as circulated in 2016. He recalled that the draft PEFCR stated that around 88.5% of the timber used for EU pulp came from EU-27 countries, while the rest was imported mainly from Russia, Belarus and Norway. The majority of tree species in Europe consisted of pine, spruce and fir, for which the planting and harvesting cycle in the temperate and boreal regions was significantly longer than 20 years, exceeding the maximum period for inclusion in the Land Use Change (LUC) impact assessment stated above. On the other hand, he said, in tropical countries like Indonesia, the plantation trees used for the pulp and paper industry were fast-growing species such as Acacia Sp. and Eucalyptus Sp, with planting and harvesting cycles ranging from five to seven years. In his delegation's view, this constituted unfair discrimination against pulp and paper products from tropical countries like Indonesia. The currently proposed accounting standard for LUC effectively exempted the European plantation industry from having to factor in LUC in the LCA for their products. By contrast, since the plantation industry for pulp and paper in Indonesia and in many other developing countries had only begun in the early 1990s, almost all of Indonesian timber sources would be included in emissions due to LUC under the current criteria. This created a fundamental disadvantage for the pulp and paper industry in Indonesia and other developing countries which had established plantations in the 1990s compared to the industry in Europe, where most plantations had been established more than 20 years previously and before January 2008. Indonesia requested clarification on how the reference date of January 2008 and the cut-off period of 20 years had been chosen and argued that they appeared to be arbitrary and unfair. Indonesia claimed that the values had been developed based on the circumstances of the European pulp and paper industry, where LUC emissions would not be required, and that the pulp and paper products coming from tropical developing countries, where LUC emissions were likely to be included, would not be able to achieve those values. Indonesia believed this was an area in which the PEFCR could become a non-tariff trade barrier for Indonesian pulp and paper products entering the EU market. Indonesia urged the EU to respond to their concern accordingly, including on the status of PEFCR.

The representative of China raised concerns with this measure. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/651 (below).1.  We noticed that the EU issued a number of eco-design regulations on servers and data storage products, washing machines, washer dryers. These Requirements stipulate the ecological design requirements, conformity assessment and market supervision verification procedures for related products.2.  We appreciate the EU's efforts in ecological protection. But we have the following concerns:3.  There are significant uncertainties in the scope of products subject to the regulations. And some terms will cause misunderstanding thereby unnecessary obstacles to trade. We hope that the EU will:clarify whether the washing machines without heating function are subject to the eco‑design requirements. cancel requirement of Maximum delivery time of necessary spare parts (it stipulates the manufacturer or importer shall deliver the necessary spare parts for household washing machines and household washer-dryers to professional repairers within 15 working days after having received the order. We think spare parts delivery is a commercial concern, and it should be adjusted by market demand. 15 days is impossible for overseas manufacturers, that will cause unnecessary cost for trade thereby barrier to trade).  re-adjust the formula of EEI. 4.  We hope that the EU will clarify whether the eco-design requirements and specific applicable methods are applicable to the dishwashers without drying function. It is strongly recommended that the EU cancel the time limit requirement for the delivery of necessary spare parts and extend the transition period for the effective date of the regulations.5.  The test methods for some parameters in the regulations are inconsistent with international standards, and it is even missing. Some clauses are beyond the limits necessary to achieve legitimate goals. We hope that the EU can: clarify whether the test method for lumen maintenance rate can adopt the international standard test method (IEC 62612);give clear and definite test method for the scintillation flicker level (Pst LM) and the stroboscopic effect visibility (SVM); adjust the light source energy efficiency rating table; and extend the transition period to avoid unnecessary impact on trade.6.  We want to make the following suggestions:Based on the text of 2009/125/EC (3), it is suggested that the EU delete Annex 1 (12) (e), i.e. the requirement of "having the same number of available processor sockets and number of available processor sockets populated" in the definition of "server product family".Based on the principle of harmonization with market demand, it is suggested that the verification procedure on a randomly selected or ordered model configuration for market surveillance purposes be consistent with the eco-design requirements (Annexes II 2.1 and 2.2).The regulation requires manufacturers to provide product information when the server-related products are put on the market. It is suggested that the EU clarify that electronic manuals in the form of website links, QR codes, electronic CD-ROMs, etc., can be taken as the attached information carriers for environmental protection considerations.

The representative of China reiterated concerns on EU ecodesign requirements on light sources notified in G/TBT/N/EU/606 and G/TBT/N/EU/607, household dishwashers notified in G/TBT/N/EU/611 and household washing machines notified in G/TBT/N/EU/615. For the ecodesign requirements for light sources, in accordance with Article 2.4 of the TBT Agreement, China recommended using IEC standards for colour consistency and calculation of lumen maintenance factor of LED lights. The EU was asked to clarify the test method for the "Pst LM" value of "Flicker for LED and OLED MLS" and "SVM" value of "Stroboscopic effect for LED and OLED MLS". China also recommended that the EU allow for a transition period to avoid any negative impacts on trade. China found that there was a major discrepancy when comparing the light efficiency parameters set by the ecodesign requirements and the energy labelling regulation (G/TBT/N/EU/607). Light sources with the best available technology in terms of efficacy according to the ecodesign requirements could only meet the energy efficiency class D of the energy labelling regulation. The EU was strongly urged to adjust energy efficiency rating in the energy labelling regulation. China also suggested that the EU give a clearer definition on products subject to the ecodesign requirements on washing machines and washer dryers and clarify whether washing machines without heating function were subject to the regulation. In the notified ecodesign requirements on household washing machines, there was a provision that 'manufacturers or importers shall deliver the necessary spare parts for household washing machines and household washer dryers to professional repairers within 15 working days after having received the order". There was a similar provision in the ecodesign requirements for household dishwashers. As spare parts delivery is a pure business practice, and such requirements would be very difficult for overseas manufacturers, China strongly recommended that the EU revoke such requirements so as to avoid unnecessary barriers to trade.

The representative of China reiterated concerns raised in previous meetings* and asked the European Union if it had any updated information on the eco-design requirements on light sources and household washing machines.

*G/TBT/M/79, para. 2.294.

StatementSubmitted:
China would like to reiterate our concerns on EU eco-design requirements on light sources, and household washing machines.

For the eco-design requirements for light sources, in accordance with Article 2.4 of the TBT Agreement, we recommend EU use IEC standards for colour consistency and calculation of lumen maintenance factor of LED lights. We suggest that EU clarify the test method for the “Pst LM” value of “Flicker for LED and OLED MLS” and “SVM” value of “Stroboscopic effect for LED and OLED MLS”. For the testing of verification tolerances, we recommend EU use the current international standards such as IEC62717:2014+AMD1:2015 and IEC62612:2013+AMD1:2015+AMD2:2018. We also recommend EU to cancel the tolerance requirement of the “related colour temperature [K]” to avoid unnecessary obstacles to trade.

Comparing the light efficiency parameters set by the eco-design requirements and the energy labelling regulation (G/TBT/N/EU/607), there is a major discrepancy. Light sources with the best available technology in terms of efficacy according to the eco-design requirements could only meet the energy efficiency class D of the energy labelling regulation. We therefore strongly recommend EU to adjust energy efficiency rating in the energy labelling regulation.

We suggest EU give a clearer definition on products subject to the eco-design requirements on washing machines and washer dryers, and clarify whether washing machines without heating function are subject to the regulation.

In the notified eco-design requirements on household washing machines, there is a provision that “manufacturers or importers shall deliver the necessary spare parts for household washing machines and household washer dryers to professional repairers within 15 working days after having received the order”. There is a similar provision in the ecodesign requirements for household dishwashers. As spare parts delivery is a pure business practice, such requirements would be very difficult for oversea manufacturers, we strongly recommend EU revoke such requirements so as to avoid unnecessary barriers to trade.

The representative of China provided the following statement. We suggest that: (i) the EU clarify whether washing machines without heating function are applicable to this regulation. The draft regulation requires that the washing process of household washing machines should include an "ECO 40-60" washing cycle, but washing machines without heating function are designed without the function of "ECO 40-60", which means it cannot be tested according to the standard; and (ii) the EU cancel the requirement for spare parts delivery time. We believe that the delivery time for spare parts is a business practice and should not be stipulated and implemented as a regulation, and this measure is not feasible especially during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The representative of Guyana raised concerns with this measure. The full statement is contained in G/TBT/W/640 (below).1.  Guyana takes note of a notification by the European Union, under document G/TBT/N/EU/432/Rev.1, of a new regulation on the definition, description, presentation, labelling of spirit drinks, the use of the names of spirit drinks in the presentation and labelling of other foodstuffs, the protection of geographical indications of spirit drinks, the use of ethyl alcohol and distillates of agricultural origin in alcoholic beverages, and repealing its Regulation (EC) No 110/2008.2.  In this new regulation, the EU has strengthened restrictions on the use of the word "Agricultural" in all languages, to rums produced from sugarcane juice in the overseas departments of France (Martinique, Guadeloupe etc.) and Madeira.3.  This restriction was already in place in the repealed regulation, and indeed this wording has existed in the EU rum definition since the first EU Spirits Regulation of 1989. However, the new text appears to strengthen the provision substantially. The wording in the repealed regulation is as follows: 4.  The new regulation states that: 5.  The specific effect of this new wording, taken in conjunction with stricter rules on sales denominations, would be to prevent the use in the EU market by Guyana and other CARIFORUM producers of the word "Agricultural" in the languages of the region (English, Spanish, French and Dutch). Guyana believes that this measure, the revised Spirits Definition, would constitute an unnecessary restriction to trade in rum exports from CARIFORUM States, resulting in significant erosion of export volumes of the product in the EU and possibly other markets. 6.  The Cariforum rum industry of the ACP Caribbean States[1] is the largest non-mineral export industry for the region and its premier export product. It is one of the largest agri-based foreign exchange earners for the grouping and a substantial employer. 7.  The EU is a traditional and important export market for Caribbean branded and bulk rum. In 2017 the EU imported € 125 million in spirits and liqueurs from CARIFORUM, making it the single largest product export to the EU.8.  As the region where the product distilled from sugar cane materials first came to be known as rum, many Caribbean countries have a lengthy and diverse history of rum production both from molasses and from sugar cane juice or syrup.9.  Guyana believes it would be possible for the EU to fulfill its objectives in a less trade restrictive manner, to avoid unnecessary restrictions to trade, whilst protecting the interests of the GI French/Madeira producers, by limiting the restriction to the French language version of "Agricultural" only. This is the word "Agricole" and is the word in common use by the producers concerned. 10.  Though the ACP Caribbean industry transmitted its concerns to the EU on this issue, informally and in writing on several occasions between mid-2017 and February 2019, it does not seem that these concerns were taken into account. The first formal and substantive response to the ACP Caribbean was only received two days after its adoption by the EU Council on 09 April 2019.11.  We would further point out that the TBT Agreement mandates due consideration of comments and a minimum of 60 days, and more in the case of developing countries, has been recommended as being a reasonable time frame for Members to make comments and to take these written comments and the results of discussions into account. In its official notification to the WTO dated 12 December 2018, the EU indicates that it provided only 30 days for comment. The EU has not justified this regulation as an emergency measure. 12.  Therefore, Guyana urges the European Union to reconsider its measure, along the lines of Cariforum written comments and concerns transmitted, with a view to ensuring that the proposed measure does not create unnecessary obstacles to exports from developing Cariforum country members. As necessary, CARIFORUM would welcome further engagement with the EU on this matter with a view to resolving the issues as soon as possible.[1] Antigua and Barbuda; the Bahamas; Barbados; Belize; Dominica; the Dominican Republic; Grenada; Guyana; Jamaica; Saint Kitt and Nevis; Saint Lucia; Saint Vincent and the Grenadines; Suriname and Trinidad and Tobago, together known as the CARIFORUM.

The representative of the United States expressed support for the development and enforcement of a well-defined medical device regulatory system assuring the safety and performance of medical devices. However, her delegation had serious concerns regarding the implementation of the MDR and IVDR, and US industry was worried about its continued access to the EU's $125 billion medical device market, $20 billion of which was supplied by US products. She stated that the implementation of MDR/IVDR was behind schedule, raising two particular concerns for industry: (i) the insufficient number of Notified Bodies (NBs) performing certification activities under the MDR/IVDR; and (ii) the insufficient number of implementing acts drafted by the EU, needed to provide details to industry about how to ensure compliance of their products with the new product standards. She asked for an update on how many of the 58 NBs accredited to test and certify products under old directives were currently designated as operational under the new MDR and IVDR, and how many were expected to be designated as operational by the end of 2019. It was her delegation's understanding that DG GROW expected no more than 12 NBs to be designated as operational by the end of 2019, a number the US deemed inadequate to provide sufficient capacity to ensure continued regulatory approvals by May 2020 and May 2022. The US was concerned that as only two of the eighteen implementing regulations had been issued, EU standardizing bodies could not begin work on developing the standards industry may use to comply with the MDR/IVMDR. Given this backlog, US industry maintained that the product standards necessary for compliance with the MDR could not be completed before the deadline. The US considered that the MDR and IVDR provisions for warehousing and a grace period, intended to provide transitional relief, were insufficient. The warehousing provision was insufficient because buyers and producers could not predict demand, making it difficult to warehouse the right amount of product to meet that demand through the implementation delays. Moreover, warehousing was expensive, degradation was common with medical technology, and the technology itself could quickly become obsolete. She added that the grace periods were insufficient because CE mark product registrations compliant with the old directives may expire before the end of the grace period, in 2024. Given these concerns, the US urged the EU to delay implementation by three years to allow for US exporters to adapt to the new requirements. If not possible, the EU was urged to allow for legacy products currently deemed safe to be sold on the market until 2024 and to ask NBs to provide new products, requiring testing for the first time, with priority access to testing and CE marking certification over products being re-certified to the new requirements.

The representative of Canada echoed the points raised by the US related to the implementation of this measure, notably the insufficient number of Notified Bodies (NBs) and expressed interest in hearing any additional information and clarification the EU could provide. Representatives of the Canadian medical devices industry had also informed his delegation of their concerns with regard to certain aspects of the measure.

The representative of Japan expressed Japan's support for the development of medical device regulations setting high standards of quality and safety for medical devices. However, Japan had serious concerns on the implementation of the MDR from May 2020. Firstly, the EU had not provided necessary and sufficient information, or completed implementing acts, for manufacturers to comply with the new system. Secondly, the number of Notified Bodies designated (by EU countries) to perform certification activities under MDR was insufficient. As of 7 November, only seven Notified Bodies had been designated. While the number of Notified Bodies had increased since June 2019, it was still insufficient to certify the volume of products that would fall under the MDR. Furthermore, the currently designated Notified Bodies had not started accepting MDR applications of new products in Japan. Thirdly, the classification of devices such as reusable surgical instruments had been changed to class 1 devices, meaning that manufacturers must involve Notified Bodies in conformity assessment in addition to self-certification. However, there was no transition period for these devices. Since the implementing acts and Notified Bodies were still inadequate, it would not be possible for manufacturers to comply with the MDR for these devices before May 2020 and Japanese manufacturers would be unable to export to the EU not only new products, but also the newly classified class 1 products which would require an audit by Notified Bodies. These issues could potentially create a substantially trade restrictive barrier. Japan requested that the EU postpone the date of application for a minimum of two years and undertake some reforms to allow Japanese manufacturers to comply with the requirements of the MDR.

The representative of China said that the lack of sufficient numbers of conformity bodies to perform certification, was making it very hard for companies to get certificates in time and the EU should therefore extend the transitional period to two years. As some medical devices in the List B catalogue already had CE certification, duplicated certification tests could be avoided with simplified procedures for such products.

The representative of the United States supported the development and enforcement of a well-defined medical device regulatory system that assured the safety and performance of medical devices. However, there were serious concerns regarding the implementation of the MDR and IVDR. US industry was worried about its continued access to the EU's USD 125 billion medical device market, $20 billion of which was supplied by US products. As MDR/IVDR's implementation was behind schedule, there were two main concerns. Firstly, the insufficient number of Notified Bodies (NBs) designated to perform certification activities under the MDR/IVDR. With only five Notified Bodies currently designated, including one based in the UK, could the EU provide an estimate as to when all 58 will be operational? US understanding was that DG GROW expected no more than 20 Notified Bodies to be designated as operational by the end of 2019. This was insufficient to ensure continued regulatory approvals by May 2020 and May 2022. Smaller companies appeared disproportionally affected by the insufficient number of designated Notified Bodies. Secondly, the EU had drafted an insufficient number of the implementing acts needed to provide details about how industry can ensure their products comply with the new product standards. As of 16 September 2019, only two of the 18 implementing regulations had been issued and a third had been drafted. As a result, EU standardizing bodies could not begin work on developing the standards that industry may use to comply with the MDR/IVMDR. The MDR and IVDR provisions for warehousing were insufficient to provide relief during the transition. Buyers and producers could not predict demand, making it difficult to warehouse the right amount of product to meet that demand through the implementation delays. Moreover, warehousing was expensive, degradation was common with medical technology, and the technology itself quickly obsolete. Further, the MDR and IVDR provisions for grace periods to provide relief during transition were also insufficient. The grace periods were insufficient because CE mark product registrations compliant with the old directives could expire before the end of the grace period, in 2024. Japan would like to express its support for the development of medical device regulations setting high standards of quality and safety for medical devices. First, the EU has not provided necessary and sufficient information, or completed guidance documents, for manufacturers to comply with the requirements of MDR.

With respect to the list of “Ongoing Guidance Development within MDCG (Medical Devices Coordination Group) Subgroups”, Japan requests that the EU promptly provide guidance documents which are necessary for product development processes. Especially, guidance documents categorized as “Significant change”, “Clinical Investigations and Evaluation (CIE)” and “Post-Market Surveillance and Vigilance (PMSV)” are essential information for manufactures.

Furthermore, Japan would like to request that the EU establish a consultation desk for guidance documents and updated Q&A.

Second, the number of operational notified bodies designated to perform certification activities under MDR is insufficient. Japan recognizes that, since last November, the number of designated notified bodies has increased from 7 to 14, including 11 notified bodies for Medical Devices. StatementSubmitted:
1. The EU notified the Proposal for a Regulation of the in vitro diagnostic medical devices (G/TBT/N/EU72) on October 23, 2012, and notified the first reading of the revision of the regulation (G/TBT/N/EU/72 add.1) on Mar 23, 2017.

On May 5, 2017, the EU issued the regulation (EU) 2017/746 on in vitro diagnostic medical devices (IVDR), repealed Directive 98/79/EC (IVDD) and Commission Decision 2010/227/EU, which shall apply from May 26, 2022.

2. China raised concerns at the 80th  TBT Committee meeting, proposing EU to speed up the authorization of testing agencies, simplify the certification process and postpone the implementation time. The EU replied that?Based on current information available, estimates indicate that approximately 20 Notified Bodies might be designated under the Medical Devices Regulations by the end of the year. Notified Bodies have increased their resources by an average of 50% for the assessment of medical devices and by up to 200% for the assessment of IVDs?. For the concern about simplification of the certification process?the EU did not respond.

We appreciate EU for the reply?but after a careful study for the number of Notified Bodies, we believe that it is not enough for manufacturers to quickly obtain CE certification. Therefore, we present the following comments. 

2.1 Postpone the implementation of IVDR for 2 years.

According to estimates, about 85% of the in vitro diagnostic medical devices entering the EU market must be assessed by Notified Body to obtain a CE certificate for the purpose of compliance with IVDR regulations, rather than in the form of "self-declaration"?while the proportion is only 15% for compliance with IVDD regulations. Even a large number of in-vitro diagnostic devices have obtained valid IVDD certificates, they still need to be re-certified according to the requirements of new products.

However, at present, the EU has announced only 3 Notified Bodies, and has neither issued, nor updated the list of EU harmonized standards, nor the more detailed certification guidelines, and no laboratory has been authorized by the EU reference laboratory yet. If such a situation continues, it will be difficult for manufacturers to rectify according to the list of harmonized standards, as well as to conduct tests in authorized laboratories and obtain certificates issued by the notified body in a timely manner. Therefore, we propose to postpone the implementation of IVDR from May 2022 to May 2024.

2.2 Provide a simplified certification for devices that have been CE certified.

Products (with List B and above risk) that have been on the market or have been in use for many years, have continuous quality and safety assurance, as they have been CE certified according to the IVDD regulations. For these products, in light of continuity of IVDD and IVDR regulations, we suggest EU to provide a simplified certification so as to ensure a smooth transition of regulations.

2.3 Expedite the announcement of laboratory authorization and preparation.

According to the classification requirements of the IVDR regulations, in addition to applying for a CE certificate for exporting high-risk products to the EU, inspection at an authorized laboratory is also required. Therefore, manufacturers need to consider the laboratory resources in advance while applying for product certification. However, the EU has not announced any laboratories that have been authorized. As the certification of high-risk products takes a relatively long time, manufacturers can't choose the suitable laboratory and make corresponding preparations, which will make it more difficult to be certified.

2.4 Accelerate the establishment of the EUDAMED medical device database.

According to the requirements of the IVDR regulations, all medical device manufacturers that export to the EU need to apply for SRN (Single Registration Number) in EU medical device database before obtaining the CE certificate. At present, EU has not confirmed the medical device database and the relevant SRN guidelines for application, which has made medical device manufacturers unable to properly prepare application materials and complete the preparatory work for CE certification.

StatementSubmitted: European UnionProposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on Medical Devices, and Amending Directive 2001/83/EC, Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 and Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 & Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on in Vitro Diagnostic Medical DevicesG/TBT/N/EU/71/Add.1; G/TBT/N/EU/72; G/TBT/N/EU/72/Add.1STC#45 Statement Thank you for your detailed update on the status of MDR and IVDR implementation during our bilateral meeting last week.  The United States supports the development and enforcement of a well-defined medical device regulatory system that assures the safety and performance of medical devices, especially now given the global health crisis we are facing. The one-year delay in implementation of the MDR provided some necessary relief.  However, several issues remain regarding implementation of both the MDR and IVDR, and U.S. industry remains concerned about its continued access to the EU’s $125 billion medical device market, $20 billion of which is supplied by U.S. products.  Given pandemic-related travel restrictions are making in-person audits difficult we urge additional consideration be given to allow virtual audits for both the MDR and IVDR. We are concerned that the lack of audits will become a serious bottleneck.  While we note that 17 Notified Bodies (NBs) have been approved to assess conformity to the MDR, it is still significantly less than the number of Notified Bodies that were approved under the MDD.  We ask for continued attention to the approval process to ensure Notified Body applications continue to move through the review process. We also note that there are currently only four NBs approved to assess conformity to the IVDR.  If practical solutions cannot be found to address these looming bottlenecks, we recommend serious consideration also be given to a significant extension in implementation of MDR and IVDR. We are also concerned about the status of standards that companies can use to demonstrate compliance with the essential requirements.  We understand that many of the standards in the Commission’s standardization mandate are not based on the latest international standard.  A presumption of conformity is important to support market access in practical terms.  We note that in preparation of the implementation of MDR, the Commission selected the Classificazione nazionale e internazionali (CND), a Unique Device Identifier (UDI) system that is not harmonized with the well-established UDI system that utilizes the Global Medical Device Nomenclature (GMDN).  GMDN was developed with the support of the International Organization Standardization and the International Medication Device Regulators Forum, and is widely adopted by the medical device industry and is used by over 70 national medical device regulators to support their activity.  We are concerned that EU’s selection of CND, because this selection will undermine the interoperability of the two UDI systems for tracking and reporting purposes, and will pose several significant obstacles to the medical device and healthcare community. Furthermore, the Commission has not made any progress on mapping CND to GMDN and has not addressed interoperability concerns. An additional consequence of the Commission’s adoption of CND is that it could encourage other regulators and entities, like the World Health Organization to adopt CND, creating duplicative requirements for the medical device industry.

China thanks EU for former replies, but still, there remain concerns about the IVDR. We are looking forward that EU could give consideration to our following requests.

1. To postpone the transition deadline of IVDD and IVDR for 2 years.

According to estimates from our industry, about 85% of the in vitro diagnostic medical devices entering EU must obtain a CE certificate after a technical documents review by a Notified Body, rather than adopting the form of "self-declaration". The proportion was only 15% in the case of IVDD. For a large number of in-vitro diagnostic devices that have already obtained valid IVDD certificates, they still need to be re-certified according to the requirements as new ones. Therefore, manufacturers are facing a huge amount of certification work in the period before the implementation. However, at present, EU has only announced 3 Notified Bodies, and has neither issued nor updated the list of EU harmonized standards, as well as more detailed certification guidelines, moreover, no laboratory has been authorized by EU reference laboratory yet.

Importantly, considering the pressure on national authorities of EU member states, Notified Bodies, manufacturers and other actors, as well as the impact of COVID-19 epidemic on the implementation of the IVDR, it would be more difficult for manufacturers to rectify conduct tests in authorized laboratories and obtain certificates issued by the notified body in a timely manner. Manufacturers will face major difficulties in completing conversion review of all the products before the implementation of IVDR. Therefore, China asks EU to postpone the deadline of transition period from May 2022 to May 2024.

2.2 To provide a simplified certification procedure for devices those have obtained CE certification.

Products (with List B and above risk) that have been on the market or have been in use for years have continuous quality and safety assurance, as they have been CE certified according to IVDD. China asks EU to provide a simplified certification procedure as some other members when issuing detailed guidelines for IVDR, so as to ensure a smooth transition of regulations. 

2.3 To expedite the announcement of laboratory authorization and preparation.

According to the classification requirements of the IVDR, in addition to applying for a CE certificate for exporting high-risk products to EU, inspection at an authorized laboratory is also required. Therefore, manufacturers have to consider the available laboratories in advance while applying for product certification. However, the EU has not announced any authorized laboratories. As the certification of high-risk products takes a relatively long time, manufacturers have no choice on suitable laboratory and make the corresponding preparations impossible, which adds difficulties in certification .

2.4 To accelerate the establishment of the EUDAMED medical device database.

According to the requirements of the IVDR regulations, all medical device manufacturers exporting to the EU have to apply for SRN (Single Registration Number) in EU medical device database before obtaining the CE certificate. Yet, EU has not confirmed the medical device database and the relevant SRN guidelines for application, which has prevented manufacturers from properly preparing application materials and completing the preparatory work for CE certification.

Additionally, we appreciate and support the continued utilization of remote audits to alleviate the assessment backlog and ultimately ensure patients’ continued access to much needed medical devices and in vitro diagnostic tools. The U.S. has previously expressed concerns regarding implementation of the in-vitro diagnostics regulation (IVDR), and the continued access of U.S. firms to the EU market.  In particular, we are concerned about the number of Notified Bodies (NBs) approved to assess conformity to the IVDR, with only six such NBs approved as of October 2021. However, we note the recent notification by the EU to the TBT committee proposing a delay in the implementation of IVDR. We appreciate the recognition of the challenges around building adequate certification capacity under the legislation’s timeline. We are still studying the proposed timeline and scope of products covered under the new notification, and we understand that the delayed implementation provides for a staggered extension based on the class of IVDR. Can you please provide a brief explanation of the new proposed timelines? We hope the Commission will continue to work with the United States as well as stakeholders to address any future challenges with IVDR implementation to avoid unintended adverse effects on patients. We understand that the Commission intends to create harmonized European standards to demonstrate compliance with EU legislation rather than use existing international standards. We urge the Commission to use internationally recognized standards where possible to avoid duplicative efforts and additional burdens on manufacturers to comply with separate harmonized standards- one for the EU and others for other international regulatory authorities. We note that in preparation for the implementation of the MDR, the Commission announced in January 2020 that a new nomenclature system, the European Medical Device Nomenclature (EMDN) system would be created to be the basis of the European Database on Medical Devices (EUDAMED). EUDAMED will include a Unique Device Identifier (UDI) module. The EMDN is based on the CND (Classificazione nazionale e internazionali), which is not harmonized with the well-established Global Medical Device Nomenclature (GMDN).[1]  The United States uses the GMDN as the basis for our Global Unique Device Identification Database (GUDID). GMDN was developed with the support of ISO and the then Global Harmonization Task Force (now the International Medical Device Regulators Forum) and is widely adopted by the medical device industry and used by over 70 national medical device regulators to support their activity.  We are concerned that the Commission’s selection of EMDN will undermine the interoperability of the two UDI systems (EUDAMED and GUDID) for tracking and reporting purposes and will pose several significant obstacles to the medical device and healthcare community. Furthermore, the Commission has not addressed interoperability concerns, and has not made any progress on mapping EMDN to GMDN so as to harmonize the UDI systems and reduce duplication for industry. An additional consequence of the Commission’s adoption of EMDN is that it has encouraged other regulators and entities, like the World Health Organization, to adopt EMDN, creating duplicative requirements for the medical device industry, and thus possibly harming public safety. The EU has repeatedly stated in bilateral discussions and in published documents that it intends to map its nomenclature system to GMDN, but we have yet to see any action by the EU that demonstrates an attempt to map to GMDN.  In fact, the EU recently published its European Medical Device Nomenclature for public consultation which does not propose any steps toward mapping to GMDN.  Could the EU explain what actions it is taking to map EMDN to GMDN? [1] The European Commission announced its decision to adopt CND via guidance: https://ec.europa.eu/health/sites/health/files/md_topics-interest/docs/md_emdn_eudamed_nomenclature_en.pdf

The representative of Japan provided the following statement. 1. We appreciate the June update of the MDCG guidance publication plan. We request that public consultation be carried out prior to the publication of the MDCG guidance, and that the guidance that is published be made mandatory with a transition period. The mapping plan for EMDN (European Medical Device Nomenclature) and GMDN (Global Medical Device Nomenclature) mentioned in the MDCG guidance publication plan is still N/A (Not Applicable). We request that a publication schedule be set and that they be published as planned. Post-marketing surveillance and vigilance are required by the MDR. Though the plan for publication of guidance on post-market surveillance and vigilance has been described, we request that it be published promptly. 2. In June, we stated that we had received reports from many companies undergoing technical document review that there had been no progress since the start of the review, which was in all cases a lengthy period, and that it was not foreseeable that the review would be completed and certificates issued by the date of application of the MDR. Many companies also reported that despite more than one year having passed since the start of the technical document review, it remained incomplete and we also requested an investigation into the cause of the delay and an explanation of the measures undertaken to improve the situation. However, there has been no improvement. We would like the regulatory authority to continue to investigate the cause and take measures for improvement.3. In June, we stated that the MDR requires strict clinical evaluation of Class I, IIa and IIb medical devices. In order to prevent the MDR from becoming more trade-restrictive than necessary, we requested that you consider simplifying the clinical evaluation requirements for Class I, IIa, and IIb medical devices in the same way as Japan's premarket certificate or the U.S. 510(k) regulations. We request that you continue to consider this matter. 4. We welcome that the European Commission has proposed a Regulation amending the transition period for the IVD Regulation on 14 October 2021. We deeply appreciate that such a proposal to extend the transition period for three to five years depending on risk classifications of products needed to be certified by notified bodies. We are confident that this proposal would eliminate our grave concern that many of the IVD devices placed on the market would not be certified by the end of the transition period due to a lack of capacity to address the issue on the part of the notified bodies. Meanwhile, since only one guidance document on IVD has been issued since June 2021, we would again request prompt issuance of the guidance documents and provision of a timeline for their issuance as early as possible, as was requested in the previous (WTO/TBT) meeting. 5. As for the harmonized standards of European regulations, despite the publication plan not being disclosed in the EU Official Journal, they were suddenly promulgated. Therefore, Japanese companies need to hastily develop a conformity plan and take action after the harmonized standards are promulgated. We request the release of the plan for the development and publication of harmonized standards for MDR and IVDR.

StatementSubmitted:
China thanks to the EU for the new notification, but still remain concerned about the IVDR. We are looking forward to the consideration of and reply to our following suggestions.

1. It is recommended that the new proposal to extend the IVDR transitional period could enter into force and the legislative process could issue without delay.

2. It is recommended to announce the laboratory authorization and preparation.

According to the classification requirements of the IVDR regulation, in addition to applying for a CE certificate for exporting high-risk products to the EU, an authorized laboratory is also required for inspection. Therefore, manufactures need to consider the allocation of laboratory resources in advance while applying for product certification. However, the EU has not announced the laboratories that have been authorized. In addition, the certification of high-risk products takes a relatively long time, and manufacturers cannot choose the suitable laboratory configuration and optimize them, which will increase the difficulty of certification.

3. It is recommended to introduce guidelines under the IVDR regulations.

For example: 

1) The In Vitro diagnostic code and classification guidelines for enterprises to conduct classification sampling and determine the number.

2) Technical guidelines under IVDR regulation, such as detailed technical guidelines of clinical performance evaluation, performance analysis of special products, certification of systems and supporting consumables, etc.

3) Detailed guidelines on how modifications are determined.

StatementSubmitted: The United States continues to support the development and enforcement of a well-defined medical device regulatory system that assures the safety and performance of medical devices. The United States appreciates the amended transitional provisions adopted by the European Parliament and Council of the European Union last year for a staggered rollout of the in-vitro diagnostics regulation (IVDR).
