StatementSubmitted: Colombia es consciente de la importancia de alimentos libres de exceso de residuos de plaguicidas que cumplan con recomendaciones internacionales de inocuidad. Sin embargo, la prohibición y posterior no renovación de sustancias activas como Mancozeb, Clotianidina, Tiametoxam y Clorotalonil está generando traumatismos en el sector agrícola exportador de nuestro país. Aunque nuestras autoridades sanitarias realizan grandes esfuerzos con los sectores productivos explorando alternativas de cumplimiento de los requisitos, la búsqueda de sustancias sustitutas de aquellas que han sido prohibidas o se encuentran en proceso de modificación, requiere de tiempo e inversión, más aun cuando los posibles sustitutos se ven cada vez más reducidos también debido a cambios regulatorios fitosanitarios en la Unión Europea. Un caso típico de este asunto, y no es el único, es la disponibilidad de una alternativa al mancozeb que también está limitada porque se han prohibido en el mercado europeo otras sustancias de uso similar, como el clorotalonil. En este contexto, resulta fundamental que la no renovación o la modificación de sustancias activas tengan en cuenta los procesos y métodos de la producción en los países que podrían verse afectados. De otra manera, se estaría desconociendo el artículo 2.2 del Acuerdo sobre Obstáculos Técnicos al Comercio que señala que los reglamentos técnicos no deben ser más restrictivos de lo necesario en la búsqueda de su objetivo legítimo. Este tipo de acciones también parecen ser contrarias al art. 12.3 del Acuerdo sobre Obstáculos Técnicos al Comercio, el cual indica que se deben tener en cuenta las necesidades especiales, financieras y comerciales de los países en desarrollo para que los reglamentos, las normas y los procedimientos de evaluación de la conformidad no se conviertan en obstáculos innecesarios a las exportaciones. En este sentido, coincidimos con argumentos expuestos en este Comité relacionados con que la Unión Europea haga consistentes los Límites Máximos de Residuos con los límites establecidos en el marco del Codex Alimentarius y que otorgue a los agricultores de terceros países un trato no menos favorable que el otorgado a los agricultores europeos.  Así las cosas, y en beneficio no solo en los países en vías de desarrollo sino en beneficio del sistema multilateral de comercio ya bastante golpeado por estas y otras medidas, invitamos a la Unión Europea a buscar y apoyar soluciones para que nuestros productores agrícolas puedan continuar abasteciendo la demanda europea de alimentos.
Summary: The representative of Colombia provided the following statement. Colombia is aware of the importance of foods free from excess pesticide residues that comply with international safety recommendations. However, the ban on active substances such as mancozeb, clothianidin, thiamethoxam and chlorothalonil, and the subsequent non?renewal of the approval of these substances, are hitting our country's agricultural export sector hard. While our health authorities are going to great lengths with the productive sectors to explore alternatives to meet the requirements, the search for substances to replace those that have been banned or whose approval is being modified requires time and investment, especially when potential alternatives are also becoming scarcer owing to changes to phytosanitary regulations in the European Union. A typical example of this, but not the only one, is the limited availability of an alternative to mancozeb, on account of similar substances, such as chlorothalonil, being banned in the European market. In this context, it is vital that the non?renewal or modification of approval for active substances takes into account production processes and methods in countries that could be affected. Failing to do so would violate Article 2.2 of the TBT Agreement, which stipulates that technical regulations shall not be more trade?restrictive than necessary to fulfil a legitimate objective. Failing to do so also seems to violate Article 12.3 of the TBT Agreement, which states that account should be taken of the special financial and trade needs of developing countries, with a view to ensuring that regulations, standards and conformity assessment procedures do not create unnecessary obstacles to exports. In this regard, we agree with arguments presented in this Committee expressing the need for the European Union to bring maximum residue levels into line with the levels established within the framework of the Codex Alimentarius and to treat farmers in third countries no less favourably than it does European farmers. This being the case, and for the benefit of not only developing countries but also the multilateral trading system, which has already been hit hard by this and other measures., we invite the EU to follow the recommendations for good regulatory practices, according to which rules should be based on clear and objective information, and open dialogue with stakeholders, transparency and reduction of market distortions.

StatementSubmitted: The United States remains concerned with the European Union’s Commission Regulation 2023/334 regarding the reduction of maximum residue levels (MRLs) for clothianidin and thiamethoxam, notified to the TBT Committee as G/TBT/N/EU/908 on June 6, 2022.  The United States is concerned that this precedent-setting regulation lacks sufficient technical justification to fulfil its environmental objective, and undermines the expertise of national competent authorities and good agricultural practices worldwide.  Given the critical importance of pesticides such as clothianidin and thiamethoxam for the production of crops that are exported to the EU from the United States and other WTO Members, we are concerned that the reduction of these MRLs to the limit of determination (LOD) poses a significant obstacle to trade.  As the EU has previously recognized, global environmental challenges cannot be achieved by prescriptive, one-size-fits-all approaches that are narrowly tailored to the conditions in one country or region.  The United States welcomes the EU to instead pursue a collaborative approach to protecting pollinators, using appropriate international venues to advance a shared understanding of this global challenge.  The United States respectfully reminds the EU that environmental considerations are not included in the Codex Committee on Pesticide Residue (CCPR) assessment process for establishing MRLs, and are hopeful that the EU will move away from the attempt to use pesticide MRLs as an environmental safety management tool.  The United States urges the EU to refrain from using pesticide MRLs outside of their intended purpose, which is to allow regulators to monitor the lawful applications of pesticides and to ensure consumer food safety.  We also remind the EU that the lack of predictability that results from the consideration of import tolerance requests on a “case-by-case” basis, as in the case of this regulation, unnecessarily increases uncertainty for farmers globally and limits farmers’ ability to protect crops from pests and diseases.  The United States recalls that the European Food Safety Authority’s (EFSA) most recent review of clothianidin and thiamethoxam MRLs recommended MRLs that were safe for consumers.  We respectfully ask the EU to share the scientific and technical information evaluated by EFSA that demonstrates how the reduction of these MRLs to the LOD for products produced outside of the EU protects pollinators, including bees. Given the lack of global consensus about the factors that negatively affect pollinator health, including the health of bees, and in the absence of scientific or technical information indicating how the reduction of MRLs to the LOD for products produced outside of the EU contributes to the objective of protection of pollinators, including bees, the United States requests that the EU refrain from additional attempts to achieve global environmental outcomes through pesticide MRLs and to restore prior MRLs for clothianidin and thiamethoxam.
Summary: The representative of the United States provided the following statement. The United States remains concerned with the European Union's Commission Regulation 2023/334 regarding the reduction of maximum residue levels (MRLs) for clothianidin and thiamethoxam, notified to the TBT Committee as G/TBT/N/EU/908 on 6 June 2022. The United States is concerned that this precedent-setting regulation lacks sufficient technical justification to fulfil its environmental objective, and undermines the expertise of national competent authorities and good agricultural practices worldwide. Given the critical importance of pesticides such as clothianidin and thiamethoxam for the production of crops that are exported to the EU from the United States and other WTO Members, we are concerned that the reduction of these MRLs to the limit of determination (LOD) poses a significant obstacle to trade. As the EU has previously recognized, global environmental challenges cannot be achieved by prescriptive, one-size-fits-all approaches that are narrowly tailored to the conditions in one country or region. The United States welcomes the EU to instead pursue a collaborative approach to protecting pollinators, using appropriate international venues to advance a shared understanding of this global challenge. The United States respectfully reminds the EU that environmental considerations are not included in the Codex Committee on Pesticide Residue (CCPR) assessment process for establishing MRLs, and are hopeful that the EU will move away from the attempt to use pesticide MRLs as an environmental safety management tool.The United States urges the EU to refrain from using pesticide MRLs outside of their intended purpose, which is to allow regulators to monitor the lawful applications of pesticides and to ensure consumer food safety. We also remind the EU that the lack of predictability that results from the consideration of import tolerance requests on a "case-by-case" basis, as in the case of this regulation, unnecessarily increases uncertainty for farmers globally and limits farmers' ability to protect crops from pests and diseases. The United States recalls that the European Food Safety Authority's (EFSA) most recent review of clothianidin and thiamethoxam MRLs recommended MRLs that were safe for consumers. StatementSubmitted: Costa Rica desea apoyar nuevamente esta preocupación comercial, presentada originalmente por Kenia, sobre el interés de la UE de establecer límites máximos de residuos (LMR) para la clotianidina y el tiametoxam como mecanismos para alcanzar objetivos medioambientales. Costa Rica reitera que, en términos generales, su política nacional está alineada con el objetivo de la UE de priorizar la protección del medio ambiente, la lucha contra el cambio climático y el desarrollo económico sostenible, como único vehículo viable para salvaguardar el futuro de nuestro planeta. Sin embargo, en ningún caso la consecución de estos objetivos debe ir en detrimento del multilateralismo y de las obligaciones fundamentales que sustentan esta Organización. El Acuerdo sobre Obstáculos Técnicos al Comercio define claramente los objetivos que pueden cumplir legítimamente los reglamentos técnicos, las normas y los procedimientos de evaluación de la conformidad. Desde la perspectiva de Costa Rica no hay certeza  de qué objetivo legítimo podría justificar la revisión de un LMR, cuestión relacionada con la seguridad alimentaria y la protección de la salud humana, que entra en el ámbito de aplicación del Acuerdo MSF. Por lo tanto, tenemos dificultades para entender la notificación de la UE G/TBT/N/EU/908, debido al hecho de que esta notificación, aunque propone reducir los LMR de clotianidina y tiametoxam, se notificó al Comité OTC y no al Comité MSF.Costa Rica no concuerda con la UE en la afirmación de que la notificación antes mencionada se justifique en una "preocupación medioambiental de [carácter] mundial". Entre los objetivos legítimos del Acuerdo OTC, no podemos encontrar preocupaciones ambientales de carácter mundial como justificación de una medida cubierta por este Acuerdo. Abordar las preocupaciones medioambientales de carácter mundial es también una cuestión de la máxima importancia para Costa Rica. Sin embargo, no está claro cómo este objetivo entra en el ámbito de aplicación de los Acuerdos MSF y OTC.  Por último Costa Rica agradece a la UE sus explicaciones sobre esta preocupación.
Summary: The representative of Costa Rica provided the following statement. Costa Rica wishes once again to support this trade concern, which was originally raised by Kenya and relates to the EU's intention to establish maximum residue levels (MRLs) for clothianidin and thiamethoxam as mechanisms to fulfil environmental objectives. Costa Rica reiterates, as it has done at previous meetings of this Committee, that, broadly speaking, its national policy is aligned with the EU's objective of prioritizing environmental protection, the fight against climate change and sustainable economic development, as the only viable path to secure the future of our planet. However, under no circumstances must achieving these objectives come at the expense of multilateralism and the fundamental obligations that underpin this Organization. The TBT Agreement clearly sets out the objectives that technical regulations, standards and conformity assessment procedures may legitimately fulfil. From Costa Rica's perspective, it is unclear which legitimate objective might justify the revision of an MRL, which is a matter related to food security and the protection of human health and therefore falls within the scope of the SPS Agreement. In that connection, we are struggling to understand EU notification G/TBT/N/EU/908, due to the fact that, although this notification proposes reducing the MRLs for clothianidin and thiamethoxam, it was submitted to the TBT Committee and not to the SPS Committee. Costa Rica does not agree with the EU's claim that the above-mentioned notification is justified by a "global environmental concern". Among the legitimate objectives of the TBT Agreement, we cannot find global environmental concerns as justification for a measure covered by this Agreement. Addressing global environmental concerns is also a matter of the utmost importance for Costa Rica. However, it is unclear how this objective falls within the scope of the SPS and TBT Agreements. We thank the delegations that support this concern and endorse their statements. Lastly, we request and would welcome more detailed explanations from the EU regarding this concern.

StatementSubmitted: Indonesia reiterate that the Draft Commission Regulation as regards maximum residue levels for clothianidin and thiamethoxam, notified under G/TBT/N/EU/908 amending Regulation (EC) No. 396/2005, will have a serious impact on farmers in developing countries producing products exported to the European Union, as it will restrict farmers from using certain technologies useful for producing agricultural commodities economically, as has been raised at previous meetings.Indonesia also reminds that Maximum Residue Levels (MRLs) is an international trade standard related to food safety and consumer protection. The Imposition of MRLs for environmental protection deviates from the purpose of MRLs themselves.Every country, including Indonesia, has unique sustainable agriculture goals and challenges. In addition to climate challenges, agriculture in our country has high pest and disease pressure due to the combination of heat, humidity, and plant-disturbing organism pressure from various pests, diseases, and plant weeds. To overcome these problems, various methods, tools, and technologies are needed so that agriculture can sustainably meet the world's growing food and feed needs. Therefore, in accordance with regulations implemented by the government, we continue to promote more sustainable and good agricultural practices and food systems by emphasizing the combination of the best methods and techniques to achieve adequate and more sustainable production. Therefore, regulatory decisions relating to pollinator protection should take into account the uniqueness of each country's ecology and agricultural landscape, and be assessed by each country's regulators based on a scientific approach.Indonesia understands that this draft regulation does not require non-EU countries to ban the use of clothianidin and thiamethoxam in their own territories and the aim is that food and feed consumed in the EU does not contribute to the global decline of pollinators. However, lowering the MRL to the Limit of Quantification (LoQ) is an indirect measure to avoid the use of thiamethoxam and clothianidin by countries that have different agricultural practices to control pests resulting in different but safe residue levels. We believe that non-EU countries have their own regulatory frameworks that recognize the safety of these products in use.Indonesia has adopted Codex Alimentarius standards for setting MRLs through the Indonesian National Standard (SNI), and all other crops have MRLs currently set higher than 0.01 mg/kg, except for palm oil and cocoa products. However, any new levels applied will pose a risk to our export products, as even small exceedances that are perfectly safe for human consumption could lead to refusal of shipments to the EU or return and destruction. This will result in high cost for our producers and the uncertainty process will make it less attractive due to the higher risk of rejection. We would like to appreciate the data from the EU annual monitoring program for pesticide residues in 2019, all analyzed samples originating from Indonesia, had clothianidin or thiamethoxam levels lower than the LoQ, except for tea products. We highlight a very significant decrease in MRLs for tea products, from Codex Standards and EU Regulations, which are 400 times and 14 times lower for Thiamethoxam and Clothianidin, respectively. Referring to Codex, the MRLs for Thiamethoxam and Clothianidin are 20 mg/kg and 0.7 mg/kg, whereas under the EU Regulation, the MRL should be 0.05 mg/kg. This will be a significant obstacle for Indonesian tea farmers which could lead to loss of Indonesian tea exports to the EU.Indonesia hopes that the European Union can take this into consideration and refer to the MRLs in existing international standards as a reference for setting MRLs for clothianidin and thiamethoxam in or on certain products.

We highlight a very significant decrease in MRLs for tea products, from Codex Standards and EU Regulations, which are 400 times and 14 times lower for Thiamethoxam and Clothianidin, respectively. Referring to Codex, the MRLs for Thiamethoxam and Clothianidin are 20 mg/kg and 0.7 mg/kg, whereas under the EU Regulation, the MRL should be 0.05 mg/kg. This will be a significant obstacle for Indonesian tea farmers which could lead to loss of Indonesian tea exports to the EU. Indonesia hopes that the European Union can take this into consideration and refer to the MRLs in existing international standards as a reference for setting MRLs for clothianidin and thiamethoxam in or on certain products.

StatementSubmitted: El Paraguay reitera su preocupación por la pretensión de la UE de utilizar los LMR de Clothianidin y Thiamethoxam, no para proteger a los consumidores europeos, sino como un medio para regular el uso de neonicotinoides en los procesos y métodos de producción en terceros países, en honor al tiempo. Me limitaré a señalar solo algunos comentarios y a reiterar algunas de las preguntas no respondidas:La imposición de las restricciones al comercio internacional establecida en este reglamento restará competitividad a los agricultores de Paraguay y de la región frente a los de Europa, quienes no tienen que enfrentar las mismas plagas y condiciones climáticas para producir alimentos y pueden beneficiarse de autorizaciones de emergencia para seguir utilizando estas sustancias.En honor al tiempo me permito actualizar brevemente solo los principales puntos señalados con ocasión de la anterior reunión del Comité y las preguntas no respondidas.Con respecto a los comentarios remitidos por escrito a la notificación dentro del plazo previsto por el Paraguay y varios otros miembros: ¿Podría la UE aclarar como son tenidos en cuenta los comentarios remitidos por los miembros? Para este caso pero en general como solicitamos para la PCE ID 580 sobre consultas internacionales. En especial teniendo en cuenta el poco tiempo transcurrido entre el fin del periodo para remitir comentarios y la decisión del Comité Permanente de Plantas, Animales, Alimentos y Piensos de la UE (ScoPAFF) que aprobó sin modificaciones la propuesta de reducción de los LMR para estas sustancias.Con respecto a la mención equivocada de mi país en la versión final del reglamento 2023/334: Aunque requirió el doble de tiempo del que se tomo ScoPAFF para analizar los comentarios de varios miembros, agradezco la publicación de un corrigendum. Hasta la fecha, sin embargo, en la página oficial de la UE aún no se cuenta con una versión actualizada por lo que al consultar el Reglamento sigue la referencia equivocada al Paraguay en el pie de página 19.Con respecto a las autorizaciones de emergencia: Seguimos sin recibir respuestas a las preguntas sobre cuánto tiempo se tarda en aprobar una autorización de emergencia y cuál es el costo promedio del proceso de aprobación de una autorización de emergencia para entender cómo las autorizaciones de emergencia son compatibles con la obligación de no discriminación.La UE insiste en que esto depende de los miembros que son miembros de la OMC también por derecho propio asi que traslado la pregunta a la República Checa, o Rumania dado que la más recientes autorizaciones de emergencia para estas sustancias son de ese país quizás podrían brindar esta información.Con respecto al fallo del Tribunal de Justicia de la UE (TJUE) del 19 de enero de 2023: Tampoco recibimos respuestas sobre como afecta este fallo a las autorizaciones de emergencia en general y en especial a las autorizaciones para estas sustancias, en especial teniendo en cuenta que identificamos al menos 5 autorizaciones de emergencia con periodos de validez posteriores al fallo e incluso, al menos una autorización de emergencia para la sustancia Thiamethoxam fue otorgada luego de la sentencia.La Autorización fue otorgada por República Checa el 4/04/23 para el periodo 20/04/23 al 16/07/23.Aunque no hay nuevas autorizaciones de emergencia luego de esta, esto podría estar relacionado a los Summary: The representative of Paraguay provided the following statement. Paraguay reiterates its concern about the EU's claim to use the MRLs for clothianidin and thiamethoxam, not to protect European consumers, but as a means to regulate the use of neonicotinoids in production processes and methods in third countries. In the interest of time, I will limit myself to making only a few comments and repeating some of the unanswered questions. The restrictions on international trade imposed by this Regulation will make farmers in Paraguay and the region less competitive than farmers in Europe, who do not have to contend with the same pests and climatic conditions to produce food, and who can benefit from emergency authorizations to continue using these substances. In the interest of time, I shall simply provide a brief update on the main points made at the Committee's previous meeting and the unanswered questions. With respect to comments on the notification submitted in writing within the time limit by Paraguay and several other Members: Please could the EU clarify how the comments submitted by Members are taken into account? That is, how they are taken into account in this case, but also in general, as we asked with regard to STC ID 580 on international consultations. In particular, bearing in mind the short time that elapsed between the end of the comment period and the decision of the Standing Committee on Plants, Animals, Food and Feed (SCoPAFF) of the EU, which approved the proposal to reduce the MRLs for these substances without amendments.With respect to the erroneous reference to my country in the final version of Regulation 2023/334, while it required twice as much time as it took SCoPAFF to analyse the comments of a number of members, I welcome the publication of a corrigendum. To date, however, a revised version is still not available on the official EU website so when consulting the Regulation, the erroneous reference to Paraguay remains in footnote 19. With regard to emergency authorizations, we still have not received responses to the questions on how long it takes to approve an emergency authorization and what the average cost of the approval process for an emergency authorization is in order to understand how emergency authorizations are compatible with the non-discrimination obligation. The EU insists that this depends on the members that are also WTO Members in their own right, so I would like to direct the question to the Czech Republic or Romania, given that the most recent emergency authorizations for these substances were issued by the Czech Republic; maybe they could provide this information. Likewise, with respect to the ruling of 19 January 2023 of the Court of Justice of the EU (CJEU), we have not received responses explaining how this ruling affects emergency authorizations in general and authorizations for these substances specifically, especially since we have identified at least five emergency authorizations that were valid for periods after the ruling and at least one emergency authorization for thiamethoxam that was granted after the judgement. This authorization was granted by the Czech Republic on 4 April 2023 for the period from 20 April to 16 July 2023. Although there have been no new emergency authorizations after this, this may be because of the times of year when the substances are required, and not because of the ruling itself, so the clarification is still required.Concerning import tolerances, I would like to use the example of another substance, tricyclazole, which, despite the fact that the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) considered that import tolerances and "the proposed MRLs (in this case for rice) are fully supported by data and safe for consumers". And yet a number of member States did not support the approval of the draft Regulation submitted by the Commission. The draft fell short of the majority required in SCoPAFF and in the Council, and is likely to be vetoed in the European Parliament, meaning that the obligation to base measures on scientific principles has not been met. If member States fail to vote in favour of import tolerances when MRLs are set with the objective of protecting human health, how can the Commission argue that requesting import tolerances is a feasible way forward for MRLs set with environmental objectives (for example, those covered by this Regulation)? With respect to the extraterritoriality of the measure, I do not think it is necessary to reiterate how this measure fails to recognize the ability of national authorities to establish regulatory frameworks based on sound science, which are applied to registration processes in order to assess the risks of pesticides and their uses, including the assessment of the risk to the environment and to pollinators. I will only ask the EU how this is consistent with its obligations under WTO rules and under its founding agreements. These and other questions were submitted to the EU as part of the corresponding trade concerns raised in the SPS Committee, in document G/SPS/GEN/2140. We look forward to receiving responses shortly.The representative of Paraguay provided the following statement. Could the European Union highlight any new developments or new information presented with respect to this trade concern as the statement is identical to that of the June meeting.

StatementSubmitted: Australia reiterates our concerns about amendments to Regulation 396/2005 arising from Commission Regulation 2023/334 regarding maximum residue levels for clothianidin and thiamethoxam in or on certain products. The amendments consider environmental impacts in exporting countries when setting import MRLs and assessing requests for import tolerances.Australia recognises the right of WTO Members to regulate agricultural imports in a manner that protects animal, plant and human health and the environment. However, Members are also bound by WTO obligations. Specifically, Article 2.2 of the Agreement on Technical Barriers to Trade stipulates that regulations are not to be more trade-restrictive than necessary, taking into account science-based risk assessments.Australia does not support using MRLs on imported products to achieve environmental outcomes outside the EU’s borders. This extra-territorial approach impacts the ability of third countries to implement environmental policies consistent with their unique environmental circumstances.National authorities of third countries are best placed to ensure that pesticide application is undertaken in a responsible and sustainable manner in each country, and in accordance with their unique environment.It is important to note that the Codex Committee on Pesticide Residue (CCPR) assessment process for establishing MRLs does not include environmental conditions. Australia urges pesticide MRLs – as an important international standard for trade – to be used within the scope of their intended purposes, which is to ensure food safety and human health. Australia is concerned about the limitations of the 2018 European Food Safety Authority risk assessments cited by the EU in the draft regulation. These studies have been used to support a link between the lowering of MRLs to the limit of determination and pollinator health. We request the EU provides robust scientific evidence in support of this conclusion.Australia also requests the EU provide information on the health of pollinators in all trading countries where the new MRLs are likely to apply. The EU may wish to consider restricting the new MRLs only to those countries where it has robust evidence to support its policy objective.Australia has a robust regulatory framework for agricultural and veterinary chemicals, providing Australian farmers with safe access to the pesticides they need to maintain productivity and profitability while looking after Australia's unique environment. This approach aligns with the principles set out in the statement by Cairns Group members on the contribution of the multilateral trading system to support sustainable and resilient agriculture and food systems (G/AG/GEN/222). The Statement highlights the crucial role of a resilient agriculture sector in feeding the growing population and a science-based and inclusive approach to collectively address environmental challenges.We look forward to continuing to engage with the EU on this important topic.

StatementSubmitted: Colombia es consciente de la importancia de alimentos libres de exceso de residuos de plaguicidas que cumplan con recomendaciones internacionales de inocuidad. Sin embargo, la reducción y/o no renovación de sustancias activas como Mancozeb, Clotianidina, Tiametoxam y Clorotalonil genera traumatismos en el sector agrícola exportador, en particular de países en desarrollo. Estos temas han sido tratados en múltiples ocasiones en este Comité, sin tener por parte de la Unión Europea una solución, a pesar de haber planteado varios elementos, como por ejemplo: La búsqueda de sustancias activas sustitutas requiere de tiempo y recursos, más aun cuando los posibles sustitutos se ven cada vez más reducidos debido a otros cambios regulatorios en la Unión Europea. Las medidas parecen desconocer el Acuerdo sobre Obstáculos Técnicos al Comercio, el cual señala que los reglamentos técnicos, las normas y los procedimientos de evaluación de la conformidad no deben ser más restrictivos de lo necesario, convirtiéndose en obstáculos innecesarios a las exportaciones. Coincidimos con la necesidad de hacer consistentes los Límites Máximos de Residuos con los límites establecidos en el marco del Codex Alimentarius y que se brinde a los agricultores de terceros países un trato no menos favorable que el otorgado a los intra comunitarios. Para Colombia es claro, como lo mencionó en la pasada Conferencia Ministerial, que el Sistema Multilateral está en crisis por varias razones, entre ellas por este nuevo proteccionismo, entendido como medidas unilaterales al amparo de objetivos legítimos, que se convierten en restricciones al comercio. Así las cosas, y en beneficio no solo en los países en vías de desarrollo sino en beneficio del sistema multilateral de comercio ya bastante golpeado por estas y otras medidas, invitamos a que se busquen y apoyen soluciones para que nuestros productores agrícolas puedan continuar abasteciendo la demanda europea de alimentos.
Summary: The representative of Colombia provided the following statement. Colombia is aware of the importance of foods free from excess pesticide residues that comply with international safety recommendations. However, the reduction and/or non-renewal of active substances such as mancozeb, clothianidin, thiamethoxam and chlorothalonil has a severe impact on the agricultural export sector, particularly in developing countries. These matters have been addressed on multiple occasions in this Committee; the European Union has yet to offer a solution despite various points being raised, which include the following: The search for alternative active substances requires time and resources, especially when potential alternatives are becoming scarcer owing to other regulatory changes in the European Union. The measures appear to be in breach of the Agreement on Technical Barriers to Trade, which states that technical regulations, standards and conformity assessment procedures must not be more restrictive than necessary or become unnecessary obstacles to exports. We agree that there is a need to bring maximum residue levels into line with the levels established within the framework of the Codex Alimentarius and to treat farmers in third countries no less favourably than European Union farmers. It is clear to Colombia, as was mentioned at the Ministerial Conference, that the multilateral system is in crisis for various reasons, which include this new protectionism in the form of unilateral measures that seemingly pursue legitimate objectives and that become trade restrictions. We therefore call for efforts to be made to seek out and support solutions that would allow our agricultural producers to continue meeting European demand for food, to the benefit not only of developing countries but also the multilateral trading system, which has already been hit hard by this and other measures.

StatementSubmitted: EUROPEAN UNION - DRAFT COMMISSION REGULATION AMENDING ANNEXES II AND V TO REGULATION (EC) NO 396/2005 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL AS REGARDS MAXIMUM RESIDUE LEVELS FOR CLOTHIANIDIN AND THIAMETHOXAM IN OR ON CERTAIN PRODUCTSIndonesia thanks the Members that raised and supported this trade concern. We reiterate the position that we previously expressed and continue to have concerns over the same issue. Indonesia understands that this draft regulation does not require non-EU countries to ban the use of clothianidin and thiamethoxam in their own territories and the aim is that food and feed consumed in the EU does not contribute to the global decline of pollinators. However, setting import MRLs below the International standard such as Codex, and assessing requests for import tolerances as means to regulate the use of pesticides in the production processes and methods in the third countries, can become unnecessarily barrier to trade. This extra-territorial approach will impact the third countries’ agricultural exports, such as palm oil, cacao, tea products, mangoes etc. We also believe that non-EU countries have their own regulatory frameworks that recognize the safety of clothianidin and thiamethoxam in use based on scientific evidence, data and the implementation of international standards.Indonesia also echoes the concerns raised by other members, in that the EU’s adoption of this regulation could be considered as using MRLs beyond their intended purposes, which is food safety. MRLs are food standards and should be assessed considering consumer food safety. For the pollinator risk assessment, robust data was presented to different authorities worldwide demonstrating the safety of thiamethoxam when used according to label directions (i.e., US EPA, Canada PMRA, India Ministry of Agriculture). Hence, the EU’s decision to use pesticide MRLs to tackle environmental safety management tool cannot be justified.Lowering the MRL is not the best way to protect pollinators as the two things are not connected. The residue level in a crop does not correlate to the safety for non-target species or the local environment. There are many situations where the residues in nectar and pollen pose low risk to bees, e.g. seed treatments, pre-flowering foliar applications, or where crops are not visited by bees, e.g. these are harvested before flowering. Growers who in moving to earlier applications to reduce risk of contravening MRLs there is an increased risk that this overlaps with the end of flowering despite clear product labelling to avoid applications during flowering. In fact, the EU in 2013 in connection with implementing restrictions for the use of thiamethoxam (and two other NNI’s) foliar uses after flowering in the registered crops continued to be allowed. Pollinator decline is multifactorial and cannot be associated exclusively to pesticides use. When talking about pesticides, its protection is relying on the correct product use, according to label recommendations and Best Management Practices adopting mitigation measures when applicable. The Government of Indonesia (Ministry of Agriculture), working together with the crop protection industry, has commitment in equipping the country’s farmers with practical skills on effective and efficient use of plant protection products through Stewardship activities. Such activities are carried national-wide in a continuous and sustainable manner to ensure pesticides are applied and managed correctly according to label recommendations. Indonesia already has pesticide registration regulations that refer to international standards. Only products that have met technical and administrative requirements can be registered and permitted for use in Indonesia. This shows that Indonesia has adequate capability and capacity in managing pesticides.We request EU to review this regulation with addressing the inputs of substantive changes from members and using the international standard such as Codex Alimentarius as a reference for setting MRLs for clothianidin and thiamethoxam in or on certain products.

StatementSubmitted: India reiterates its concerns regarding lowering of existing MRLs for clothianidin and thiamethoxam by EU. During the last meeting, in its reply, the EU acknowledges that non-EU countries may face production conditions and pest pressures di?erent from those in Europe. However, EU has not granted exemption to those countries where the use of clothianidin and thiamethoxam cannot be avoided due to (a) di?erent soil and other production conditions and including pest pressures and environmental conditions; and (b) non-availability of e?cacious alternative pest control products. A blanket universal prohibition without taking into account the di?erences in the conditions prevailing in di?erent countries is inappropriate. India request EU to develop a methodology whereby di?erence in the conditions of the production and pest pressures are taken into account and appropriate derogations are granted.The EU’s ban on the imports of seeds treated with clothianidin and thiamethoxam is based on a study conducted by the EFSA. The EFSA’s study concludes that there are different levels of risks associated with different crop types and exposure. The EFSA’s study only looks at a limited number of crop types and has not examined the impact of the use of clothianidin and thiamethoxam on crops which are not attractive to bees. Several crops grown in India – such as wheat, rice, potatoes, oats, tomatoes, etc. are either non-attractive to bees or have very low attractiveness as per a study conducted by the United States Department of Agriculture.[1] The EU is urged to consider granting exemptions to the use of these active substances on crops that are not attractive to bees.The EU’s measure is not limited to only those types of usage of active substances that pose the highest level of risk to the population of bees but is a blanket ban, which could cover situations with very low or negligible risk. Since the EU’s measure imposes a blanket ban on imports of all seeds using clothianidin and thiamethoxam, the level of protection granted exceeds what is necessary to ful?l the objectives, and therefore creates an unnecessary obstacle to international trade.The Maximum Residual Limit (MRL) of active substances, which has been revised by the EU through the said noti?cation exceeds the international standards for the same. India is concerned that the EU is adopting protection levels that far exceed what is required by the EU to meet its legitimate objectives.India requests the EU to take into account the concerns raised by India and amend the concerned regulations suitably.[1] https://www.usda.gov/sites/default/?les/documents/Attractiveness-of-Agriculture-Crops-to-Pollinating-Bees-Report-FINAL-Web-Version-Jan-3-2018.pdf.

StatementSubmitted: The United States remains concerned with the European Union’s Commission Regulation 2023/334 regarding the reduction of maximum residue levels (MRLs) for clothianidin and thiamethoxam, notified to the TBT Committee as G/TBT/N/EU/908 on June 6, 2022.  The United States is disappointed that the EU has not provided a substantive response to the legitimate concerns raised by multiple Members in this Committee.  We remain deeply concerned that this precedent-setting regulation lacks sufficient technical justification to fulfil its environmental objective and undermines the expertise of national competent authorities and good agricultural practices worldwide.  Given the critical importance of pesticides such as clothianidin and thiamethoxam to produce crops that are exported to the EU from the United States and other WTO Members, we are concerned that the reduction of these MRLs to the limit of determination (LOD) poses a significant obstacle to trade.  As the EU has previously recognized, global environmental challenges cannot be achieved by prescriptive, one-size-fits-all approaches that are narrowly tailored to the conditions in one country or region.  [Bilateral] The United States recalls that during the November 2023 WTO TBT Meeting, the EU had stated that there is no additional information on their position that the classifications of pesticides are harmful to pollinator health when used outdoors. The U.S. would like an update on if this stance has changed.
Summary: The representative of the United States provided the following statement. The United States remains concerned with the European Union's Commission Regulation 2023/334 regarding the reduction of maximum residue levels (MRLs) for clothianidin and thiamethoxam, notified to the TBT Committee as G/TBT/N/EU/908 on 6 June 2022. The United States is disappointed that the EU has not provided a substantive response to the legitimate concerns raised by multiple Members in this Committee. We remain deeply concerned that this precedent-setting regulation lacks sufficient technical justification to fulfil its environmental objective and undermines the expertise of national competent authorities and good agricultural practices worldwide. Given the critical importance of pesticides such as clothianidin and thiamethoxam to produce crops that are exported to the EU from the United States and other WTO Members, we are concerned that the reduction of these MRLs to the limit of determination (LOD) poses a significant obstacle to trade. As the EU has previously recognized, global environmental challenges cannot be achieved by prescriptive, one-size-fits-all approaches that are narrowly tailored to the conditions in one country or region. The United States urges the EU to refrain from using pesticide MRLs outside of their intended purpose which is to allow regulators to monitor the lawful application of pesticides and to ensure consumer food safety. The US recalls that the EFSA review of clothianidin and thiamethoxam MRLs recommended MRLs that were safe for consumers. We therefore reiterate our request for the EU to share the scientific and technical information evaluated by EFSA that demonstrates how the reduction of these MRLs to the limit of determination for products produced outside of the EU protect pollinators, including bees. Given the lack of global consensus about the factors that negatively affect pollinator health, including the health of bees, and in the absence of scientific and technical information indicating how the reduction of MRLs to the limit of determination for products produced outside of the EU contributes to the objective of protecting pollinators, the United States requests that the EU refrain from additional attempts to achieve global environmental outcomes through pesticide MRLs and to restore prior MRLs for clothianidin and thiamethoxam.

The representative of Ecuador provided the following statement. Ecuador wishes to express its concern about the measures being taken by the European Union to protect pollinators by lowering maximum residue levels (MRLs) for neonicotinoids (clothianidin and thiamethoxam), which were notified in document G/TBT/N/EU/908 in July 2022. Pesticides are one of the most important inputs in global agroindustrial development. They have allowed agricultural productivity to increase significantly in order to meet the growing demand for food and have helped producers reduce their operating costs and post-harvest losses, enabling them to access and compete in markets with better quality and prices. They also improve crop efficiency, preventing extensive land use and helping meet food demand and sustainability targets. One of the objectives of the European law in establishing MRLs is to "ensure a high level of consumer protection". The new regulatory proposal would distort the objective of Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 by changing the approach from protecting the "European consumer" to "environmental factors" in third countries, where agricultural production conditions differ from those of the European economic bloc. The EU's regulatory proposal is inconsistent with Articles 2.2, 2.4 and 12.3 of the WTO Agreement on Technical Barriers to Trade and the GATT 1994, as it infringes on the regulatory powers of third countries in environmental matters, exerting a disproportionate impact and failing to recognize third countries' jurisdiction in this area. In the Codex Alimentarius, both clothianidin and thiamethoxam still have valid MRLs above the limit of quantification.This proposal creates non-tariff barriers to trade and disregards the regulatory policies of Latin American countries, which set the conditions for food production and agricultural activity in their jurisdictions by their sovereign will, according to their differences in terms of geography, ecosystems, agricultural output, scientific capabilities and so forth. Controlling nematodes and insects is extremely important for banana production. Growers who have had problems with nematodes report that their productivity has fallen to around 38 metric tonnes per hectare (MT/ha) compared to 45 MT/ha for a plantation with adequate nematode management, which represents a 7 MT/ha drop in production. It may be said, then, that a grower's yield can fall by up to 16% because of nematodes. Thiamethoxam is effective against nematodes and black aphids in banana plants. It also leaves significantly less residue in the environment and decomposes much faster than other products. According to the Rainforest Alliance, the risk from the use of thiamethoxam in banana cultivation has been mitigated and there have been no reports of direct harm to bee populations. Furthermore, according to Phillips McDougall in "Evolution of the Crop Protection Industry since 1960" (April 2019), obtaining just one compound to be used as a pesticide can take more than 11.3 years of research and development on average and can require significant private investment.As this is a measure that applies to third countries, the EU needs to carry out an analysis of the impact that not having these substances as a means to protect their crops would have on farmers in both member countries and third countries, before establishing new levels. It follows that this measure would have a direct impact on the production and marketing of agricultural products of third countries, hence the call to maintain the current MRLs. We also urge the EU to notify these measures to the WTO Committee on Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures in parallel, considering that they lower the MRLs for active substances (clothianidin and thiamethoxam) used for pest control in the agricultural sector. Lastly, Ecuador thanks the EU for the information regarding its financing of various research projects as part of the Horizon Europe programme to find alternatives to chemical pesticides for integrated pest management. In this regard, we urge the EU to consider the needs of each country when providing this technical assistance and ensure that it is tailored to each trading partner, bearing in mind that the realities of each territory are different.

StatementSubmitted: El Paraguay reitera su preocupación por la pretensión de la UE de utilizar los LMR de Clothianidin y Thiamethoxam, no para proteger a los consumidores europeos, sino como un medio para regular el uso de neonicotinoides en los procesos y métodos de producción en terceros países, en honor al tiempo. Summary: The representative of Paraguay provided the following statement. Paraguay reiterates its concern about the EU's claim to use the MRLs for clothianidin and thiamethoxam, not to protect European consumers, but as a means to regulate the use of neonicotinoids in production processes and methods in third countries. I will limit myself to making only a few comments and repeating the questions: With respect to written comments submitted on the notification within the time limit provided for Paraguay and several other Members: Please could the EU clarify how the comments submitted by Members are taken into account? That is, how they are taken into account in this case, but also in general, as we asked with regard to STC ID 580 on international consultations. With regard to emergency authorizations: We still have not received responses to the questions on how long it takes to approve an emergency authorization and the average cost of the approval process for an emergency authorization in order to understand how emergency authorizations are compatible with the non-discrimination obligation. The EU continues to insist that this depends on its members, who are Members of the WTO in their own right, so I will once again direct the question to the Czech Republic and Romania, who granted the most recent emergency authorizations, and to other Members that, according to official EU information, have granted emergency authorizations for these substances since the prohibition of all outdoor uses, namely Austria, Belgium, Croatia, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Hungary, Lithuania, Poland, Slovakia and Spain. Could these Members please provide information on their internal processes for granting emergency authorizations? We understand that, following the ruling of the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) on 19 January 2023, new emergency authorizations will not be granted for these substances, yet we have identified at least five emergency authorizations valid for periods after the ruling, and at least one emergency authorization for thiamethoxam was granted after the ruling, thus the question remains. Concerning import tolerances: I should like once again to use the example of the import tolerance requested for tricyclazole. Although the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) considered that the import tolerance and proposed MRL, in this case for rice, are "fully supported by data and safe for consumers", they failed to secure the necessary majority and were eventually rejected. If member States do not vote in favour of import tolerances when MRLs are set with the objective of protecting human health based on scientific evidence, how can the Commission argue that requesting import tolerances is a feasible way forward for MRLs set with environmental objectives (for example, those covered by this Regulation)? Lastly, with regard to the erroneous reference to my country in the final version of Regulation 2023/334, I once again welcome the publication of a corrigendum. We should be grateful if the erroneous reference to Paraguay in footnote 19 could be amended, and a revised version of the Regulation made available on the official EU website, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/334/oj.

StatementSubmitted: Colombia es consciente de la importancia de alimentos libres de exceso de residuos de plaguicidas que cumplan con recomendaciones internacionales de inocuidad. Sin embargo, la reducción y/o no renovación de sustancias activas como Clotianidina y Tiametoxam, Clorotalonil y Mancozeb, genera traumatismos en el sector agrícola exportador, en particular de países en desarrollo. Estos temas han sido tratados en múltiples ocasiones en este Comité, donde se han planteado varios elementos, como por ejemplo: 1. La búsqueda de sustancias activas sustitutas requiere de tiempo y recursos, más aun cuando los posibles sustitutos son cada vez más escasos debido a nuevos cambios regulatorios en la Unión Europea. 2. Las medidas adoptadas parecen desconocer el Acuerdo sobre Obstáculos Técnicos al Comercio, el cual señala que los reglamentos técnicos, las normas y los procedimientos de evaluación de la conformidad no deben ser más restrictivos de lo necesario. 3. Pueden hacerse consistentes los Límites Máximos de Residuos con los límites establecidos en el marco del Codex Alimentarius. Para Colombia es claro, como lo mencionó en la pasada Conferencia Ministerial, que el Sistema Multilateral está en crisis por varias razones, entre ellas por este nuevo proteccionismo, entendido como medidas unilaterales al amparo de objetivos legítimos, que se convierten en restricciones al comercio. Así las cosas, y en beneficio no solo en los países en vías de desarrollo sino en beneficio del sistema multilateral de comercio, debemos buscar soluciones que permitan a nuestros productores agrícolas continuar abasteciendo la demanda de alimentos.
Summary: The representative of Colombia provided the following statement. Colombia is aware of the importance of foods that are free from excess pesticide residues and that comply with international safety recommendations. However, the reduction and/or non-renewal of active substances such as clothianidin, thiamethoxam, chlorothalonil and mancozeb has a severe impact on the agricultural export sector, particularly in developing countries. These issues have been addressed on multiple occasions in this Committee, where several points have been raised, including the following: 1. The search for alternative active substances requires time and resources, especially when potential alternatives are becoming scarcer owing to new regulatory changes in the European Union. 2. The adopted measures appear to be in breach of the Agreement on Technical Barriers to Trade, which states that technical regulations, standards and conformity assessment procedures shall not be more trade-restrictive than necessary. 3. Maximum residue levels can be aligned with the levels established within the framework of the Codex Alimentarius. It is clear to Colombia, as was mentioned at the recent Ministerial Conference, that the multilateral system is in crisis for a number of reasons, including this new protectionism that manifests itself in unilateral measures that seemingly pursue legitimate objectives and that become trade restrictions. We must look for solutions that enable our agricultural producers to continue meeting the demand for food, to the benefit of not only developing countries but also the multilateral trading system.

StatementSubmitted: Indonesia reiterates once again its concerns related to maximum residue levels for clothianidin and thiamethoxam in or certain products.The EU Regulation 2023/334 that lowers trade-facilitating Maximum Residue Limits (MRLs) for thiamethoxam and clothianidin will have a serious impact on farmers in non-EU countries like Indonesia. The potential negative trade-offs of the regulation have not been assessed before establishing this unilateral approach.This Regulation will be counterproductive in creating a sustainable food system in Indonesia. This is because, as a tropical country, agriculture in Indonesia is exposed to pests and diseases that are different from those found in the agriculture in the European Union (EU) countries. To comply with such EU Regulation, Indonesia’s farmers whose agricultural products are exported to the EU and use the active ingredients of thiamethoxam and clothianidin, need adjustments to their plant protection practices. This adjustment will have implications for costs, transition time for adjusting agricultural practices, and cause a decrease in yield and quality due to adjustments of practices that are not suitable for agriculture conditions in Indonesia.The implementation of MRL in Indonesia adopts the internationally recognized Codex Alimentarius (Codex) standard, in addition to the local MRL standard which has been published in regulation number: SNI 7313:2008. This implementation that has adopted the international standards must be respected because the MRL levels set for both thiamethoxam and clothianidin have been assessed and decided based on the agriculture conditions of pests’ pressure and good agriculture practices in Indonesia.Indonesia understands that the Regulation does not require non-EU countries to prohibit the use of clothianidin and thiamethoxam in their own territories. However, the reduction in MRL will require farmers whose agricultural products (oil palm, cocoa, tea, mango) are exported to the EU to adjust their crop protection practices to fulfill to such regulation. The new MRL level, if implemented, will put trade at risk. Even when the go beyond the small limits that are completely safe for humans, could result in shipments being refused entry into the EU/returned or destroyed. This uncertainty makes it less attractive for Indonesian exporters because the risk of rejection is much higher, which manifests as a trade barrier.As also previously explained, Indonesia is a tropical country which has different pest and disease challenges on agricultural land compared to European Union countries. Therefore, the MRLs set are adapted to the agricultural conditions in Indonesia. The draft EU regulation which requires changes to the MRL of thiamethoxam and clothianidin could threaten agricultural production levels and the costs incurred by farmers due to the need to change crop protection practices which may not fit with Indonesia’s agricultural conditions.Globally the number of beehives has increased by 50% over the last 50 years (FAO statistics) and the land dependent on pollination has increased by 300%. Bee populations have seen healthy growth and their role is critical for agriculture.The amount of residues must be safe for the consumer and is set according to the ALARA principle: As Low As Reasonably Achievable. MRLs are trading standards, or legal thresholds, ensuring trading nations that the food is safe for consumption. MRLs do not correlate to environmental exposure.EU Regulation 2023/334 that lowers trade-facilitating Maximum Residue Limits (MRLs) for thiamethoxam and clothianidin to the technical zero is an example of a unilateral trade measure with extra-territorial reach. While MRLs are intended to protect the human health of EU consumers and also enabling trade, the EU is using MRLs to protect environmental factors outside of the EU, thereby disabling trade.As part of the EU’s Green Deal and Farm to Fork Strategy, the EU unilaterally introduced the use of environmental factors into the EU MRL-setting process, thereby regulating product use outside the EU. When the lowered MRLs apply after the transition period, imported products are no longer allowed to contain detectable levels of residues of thiamethoxam and clothianidin. This means that Indonesia’s growers cannot de facto use those pesticides if they want to maintain the EU as an export market for their produce. However, those pesticides were assessed for their risks to pollinators and are legally registered in Indonesia, meaning a de facto ban.The EU Regulation 2023/334 is viewed as violating Article 2.2 of the TBT Agreement, which prohibits measures that are more trade restrictive than necessary to pursue a legitimate objective (regardless of whether they are discriminatory). As a prohibition on sale (and de facto on importation), the EU measure is clearly trade restrictive, and for precisely the same reasons mentioned above, it does not pursue a legitimate objective.MRLs are “the highest level of a pesticide residue that is legally tolerated in or on food or feed when pesticides are applied correctly in accordance with Good Agricultural Practice”, i.e. the approved pesticide label, according to Codex Alimentarius. The Indonesian government, through the Ministry of Agriculture, collaborates closely with the crop protection industry in regular training for farmers regarding the appropriate and safe use of crop protection products (stewardship). This stewardship activity program includes practices for applying pesticides according to the product recommendations and appropriate application methods to support sustainable agriculture practices.The EU Regulation 2023/334 is not consistent with international principles and obligations established by Codex Alimentarius and referenced by WTO Agreements, creating non-tariff trade barriers. Leaving aside the fact that MRLs are not a proxy for environmental exposure, such as pollinator health, the EU Regulation 2023/334 discriminates against foreign producers and is extra-territorial in its intent. The EU thereby ignores assessments undertaken by non-EU countries under their own regulatory system. The EU Regulation 2023/334 can set a negative precedent for other measures that will follow the same approach as already announced by the EU, thereby hindering agricultural trade.Indonesia shares the global goal of protecting the biodiversity globally and looks forward to continuing to work with the EU in multilateral fora towards this outcome. However, there is no one-size-fits all model to achieving this goal. Indonesia hence does not support the EU Regulation 2023/334 and strongly encourages the EU to make greater reliance on the efforts of JMPR and the Codex in establishing safe and harmonized levels of pesticide residues in agricultural products.

Summary: The representative of Paraguay provided the following statement. In the interest of time, Chair, I will refer to Paraguay's interventions on STC ID 393 and STC ID 580 with regard to the establishment of import tolerances and international consultations. We simply reiterate the question as to how comments submitted by Members are taken into account. This is particularly relevant as we noted from the notification of this measure that, despite the large number of substantive comments received from various Members, around 20, the PAFF Committee approved the Regulation, without amendments, only 23 days after the end of the comment period. However, I would like to focus here on emergency authorizations and reiterate that we still have not received responses to the questions about how long it takes to approve an emergency authorization and the average cost of the approval process for an emergency authorization. It is essential to understand how emergency authorizations are consistent with the obligation of non-discrimination. At previous meetings and in written questions sent to the EU, we requested its members provide information, since the EU insists this is their responsibility. We even provided a list of those members from whom such information is requested, as according to official EU records they have granted emergency authorizations for these substances after they were banned for outdoor use. However, the EU has reminded us that, while emergency authorizations are the responsibility of its members, individual EU members do not respond in the WTO. We are therefore once again requesting that the EU provide us with this information. We wish to take this opportunity to draw attention to a new emergency authorization granted by Romania for thiamethoxam which came into force almost exactly one year after the ruling of the Court of Justice of the EU (CJEU) of 19 January 2023. The EU informed this Committee that, pursuant to that ruling, new emergency authorizations would not be granted for any use of these substances but, especially, as a seed treatment, as the ruling specifically addressed this type of use.As we have already indicated in previous statements, the questions in this respect are still valid, since the absence of new emergency authorizations was not necessarily due to the ruling, but to the periods in which the substances are needed owing to pest pressure, and for which, to quote the Romanian emergency authorization, "there are no viable alternatives". We are in full agreement with this statement. We also concur with the good agricultural practices mentioned in the risk mitigation section of the emergency authorization. This is one of our recurring arguments, raised in the comments on the notification and at every meeting in which this trade concern has been discussed. However, this has not been accepted, and the MRLs have been lowered to the LOQ, not to protect European consumers or because residues in products imported by the EU may affect pollinators within its borders, but as a means to regulate the use of neonicotinoids in production processes and methods in third countries. We also agree with Romania that the use of neonicotinoids, applied in a correct and controlled manner in the case of agricultural crops, does not endanger the environment or pollinators and respects all the health standards in force. This was mentioned in the note submitted to the Council of the European Union requesting an exception from the ban on the use of these substances. The note also states, as have other WTO Members of this Committee that are honey producers, that the use of the substances did not in any way affect the number of bees in Romania. We agree with these statements with regard to neonicotinoids, but also, more generally, with regard to all substances where approval has been suspended and MRLs have been lowered without a proper risk analysis and without complying with scientific principles.Lastly, I must point out under this trade concern that the final version of Regulation No 2023/334 erroneously mentions my country. Although a corrigendum has already been published on the official EU website, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/334/oj , for which we are grateful, a revised version is not yet available. Footnote 19 of the Regulation still contains an erroneous reference to Paraguay. We should be grateful if this could be amended. We understand the red tape and the delays and difficulties that may arise. All countries face them. And it is particularly understandable in bureaucracies as large as that of the European Union. But given that the same bureaucracy considered 23 days sufficient to analyse substantive comments from some 20 Members and two months for the corrigendum, it is, in our view, a little unreasonable that one year and four months later we still do not have a corrected version in the official repository of EU regulations.The representative of Paraguay provided the following statement. I would just like to thank the European Union for its comments. We had indeed reviewed the EFSA opinions on the emergency authorizations and we find, as EFSA does, that they are justified when there are no chemical alternatives, which is exactly what WTO Members have been claiming, but we do not have the option. We draw attention to the fact that the European Union referred, yet again, to the ruling, but Paraguay's entire statement was, once again, based on an emergency authorization that came into force exactly one year after the ruling. So we would request more information on how the European Union proposes to deal with these new emergency authorizations, approved after the ruling. This is not the first such authorization, it is the second, but it is the most recent.

StatementSubmitted: Australia reiterates our concerns about amendments to Regulation 396/2005 arising from Commission Regulation 2023/334 regarding maximum residue levels for clothianidin and thiamethoxam in or on certain products. The amendments consider environmental impacts in exporting countries when setting import MRLs and assessing requests for import tolerances. Australia recognises the right of WTO Members to regulate agricultural imports in a manner that protects animal, plant and human health and the environment. However, Members are also bound by WTO obligations. Specifically, Article 2.2 of the Agreement on Technical Barriers to Trade stipulates that regulations are not to be more trade-restrictive than necessary, taking into account science-based risk assessments. Australia does not support using MRLs on imported products to achieve environmental outcomes outside the EU’s borders. This extra-territorial approach impacts the ability of third countries to implement environmental policies consistent with their unique environmental circumstances. National authorities of third countries are best placed to ensure that pesticide application is undertaken in a responsible and sustainable manner in each country, and in accordance with their unique environment. It is important to note that the Codex Committee on Pesticide Residue (CCPR) assessment process for establishing MLRs does not include environmental conditions. Australia urges pesticide MRLs – as an important international trade standard – to be used within the scope of their intended purposes, which is to ensure food safety and human health.  Australia is concerned about the limitations of the 2018 European Food Safety Authority risk assessments cited by the EU in the draft regulation. These studies have been used to support a link between the lowering of MRLs to the limit of determination and pollinator health. We request the EU provides robust scientific evidence in support of this conclusion. Australia also requests the EU provide information on the health of pollinators in all trading countries where the new MRLs are likely to apply. The EU may wish to consider restricting the new MRLs to only those countries where is has robust evidence to support its policy objective. Australia has a robust regulatory framework for agricultural and veterinary chemicals, providing Australian farmers with safe access to the pesticides they need to maintain productivity and profitability while looking after Australia's unique environment. This approach aligns with the principles set out in the statement by Cairns Group members on the contribution of the multilateral trading system to support sustainable and resilient agriculture and food systems (G/AG/GEN/222). The Statement highlights the crucial role of a resilient agriculture sector in feeding the growing population and a science-based and inclusive approach to collectively address environmental challenges. We look forward to continuing to engage with the EU on this important topic.
