Summary: The representative of Mexico provided the following statement. The delegation of Mexico refers to the Draft Food Safety and Standards (Alcoholic Beverages) Amendment Regulation, 2023, notified to Members of the Committee on Technical Barriers to Trade in document G/TBT/N/IND/271, and refers to the communication sent by the Government of Mexico to the Government of India on 4 August 2023. In this connection, the delegation of Mexico would like to express the following concerns and requests: The draft Regulation excludes drinks made from wine and beer from the definition of ready-to-drink/low alcoholic beverages, which could contravene Article 2.2 of the TBT Agreement, by creating an unnecessary obstacle to the trade in such products. The Government of India is therefore requested to provide the technical and scientific evidence underpinning the definition of ready-to-drink/low-alcoholic beverages proposed in the Regulations. Furthermore, the Regulation could hinder trade for third-country producers wishing to export ready-to-drink/low-alcoholic beverages, as it imposes a maximum limit of 8% of alcohol by volume (ABV), which would impede market access for new products.India is therefore requested to provide the technical and scientific evidence underpinning the decision to set the maximum alcohol content of ready-to-drink/low-alcoholic beverages at 8% ABV. In addition, India is requested to provide the technical and scientific evidence or the international standards underpinning the decision to set maximum limits with respect to the physico-chemical specifications to be met by alcoholic beverages marketed in India. Lastly, the delegation of India is kindly requested to clarify whether the specifications for "country liquors" are applicable to imported liquors, and to provide a response to the comments submitted by the Government of Mexico during the public consultation period on the Regulation. The delegation of Mexico thanks the delegation of India for giving its consideration to this statement.

The representative of the European Union provided the following statement. The EU would like to thank India for notifying this measure allowing thus other WTO Members to make comments in writing, discuss them, and take these comments and discussions into account. The EU provided its comments on 1 September; however, it did not yet receive any reply from India to the questions raised therein. Therefore, the EU would like to reiterate its comments as follows. The draft Food Safety and Standards (Alcoholic Beverages) Amendment Regulations, 2023, add the category of "ready-to-drink beverages" and while the EU welcomes the Indian authorities' objective to provide ready to drink beverages (RTDs) with a legal framework, the EU has concerns regarding the proposed definition, particularly: (i) the range for the content of alcohol, (ii) ingredients, and (iii) the recognition of nitrogen as a permitted additive for RTDs.First, as regards the definition, it does not seem to be in line with international standards and could create unnecessary barriers to trade, as defined by the Article 2.2 of the TBT Agreement. Namely, limiting RTDs to beverages having less than 8.0% of alcohol ABV will have the effect of excluding a significant part of the RTDs range from the Indian market. The proposed limit of the alcohol content of RTDs is not in line with the Codex Alimentarius in which RTDs are included in the Food Category 14.2.7 (Aromatized alcoholic beverages) and which specifies that "most of these products contain less than 15% alcohol", and not 8% as proposed in the Indian Regulation. The Codes, actually, recognize that some traditional non-standardized aromatized products may contain even up to 24% alcohol. Therefore, the EU suggests deleting the proposed maximum 8% ABV level for RTDs, or increasing it to at least 15% ABV, in order to align the definition with Codex and ensure that imported products will not be excluded from the Indian marketplace. Second, the list of ingredients that can be used to produce RTDs appears to be too restrictive and would exclude many RTDs produced by third countries to be marketed in India. For instance, RTDs can be mixtures of different spirit drinks categories (vodka and liqueur), or mixtures of a spirit drink and wine (liqueur and white wine). According to the Codex Alimentarius, RTDs are defined as prepared cocktails and "mixtures of liquors, liqueurs, wines, essences, fruit and plant extracts, etc.". Hence, the EU suggests amending the proposed definition, in order to align it with Codex and to allow the addition of any alcoholic beverage to produce RTDs.Third, the proposed definition does not explicitly allow the use of liquid nitrogen for RTDs, whereas Codex Alimentarius does so. The EU therefore suggests amending the definition to allow the use of nitrogen in RTDs to avoid creating a barrier to innovation. Lastly, the EU invites the authorities of India to clarify whether "ready-to-drink" and "low-alcoholic beverage" must both be stated on the label or whether they can be stated in a mutually exclusive manner. The EU kindly asks the authorities of India to review the entire definition of RTDs and align the draft Regulation to Codex, unless there are objective justifications for such deviations, which the EU would like India to provide information on. With regard to nitrogenated beer, the EU welcomes the acknowledgement of "nitrogenated" or "nitro" beer. Nevertheless, the EU notes that the proposed amendment in Column No 8, table 3 in Article 1(8) does not mention the category "nitro beer", but merely "strong". The EU suggests that the alcohol bands be broadened, so that beers with alcohol content lower than 5% ABV are also recognized as "nitro" beers. The EU suggests a "nitro beer" category with "strong" and "regular" columns mimicking the approach taken for the existing beer and draught beer categories. Furthermore, to be able to accommodate "nitro" beers with lower carbonation levels, the carbon dioxide ranges should be amended as 0.75-3.6 v/v. With climate change policies requiring initiatives for decarbonation, the availability of further lower ranges will grow. Their prohibition from the Indian market would not be justified from both brewing science and environmental perspectives. The EU would be grateful if the above-mentioned comments could be taken into account and replied to before adoption of the notified draft.

StatementSubmitted: The EU would like to thank India for notifying this measure allowing thus other WTO members to make comments in writing, as well as to responding in writing on 1 March 2024 to the comments sent by the EU on 1 September 2023.From the reply received the EU understands that majority of the comments on ready to drink beverages (RTD) have been accepted by the FSSAI and will be reflected in the revised draft.Furthermore, India provided clarification that nitrogen is already permitted at GMP level for this category, as per the Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011, as well as that nitrogenated beer, as regular category (with ethyl alcohol content up to 5% abv) is already specified under Craft Beer in the regulations, while the notified draft proposes additional 'strong category' for the craft beer.The EU would like to thank India for taking into consideration its comments and is looking forward to India’s notification of the revised draft as an addendum to the original notification, facilitating the EU's assessment of the revised draft.

StatementSubmitted: The United States thanks India for notifying its Draft Food Safety and Standards (Alcoholic Beverages) Amendment Regulations, 2023 to the WTO TBT Committee. We offer the following statement for your consideration. The proposed regulation refers to “ready-to-drink/low alcoholic beverages” as a single category, yet ready-to-drink beverages and low alcohol beverages often have different attributes. For instance, ready-to-drink cocktails can have various alcohol by volume ranges, some that are low-alcohol, but some that are above the proposed 8.0% alcohol by volume limit. The United States would appreciate clarification on India’s definition of this category and encourage that these terms not be used interchangeably.  The United States also requests the basis for setting the alcohol by volume range for ready-to-drink alcoholic beverages between 0.5 and 8.0% alcohol. This range is potentially restrictive of other types of ready-to-drink cocktails and would create a barrier for new, innovative products to access the Indian market. Would India consider a higher threshold to not unnecessarily hinder other types of ready-to-drink beverages that fall above this range? The United States also requests the reasoning for excluding wine and beer from India’s definition. Without including wine and beer-based cocktails, the draft regulation would differentiate between spirits-based ready-to-drink beverages from other types of alcoholic ready-to-drink products that fall within the specified alcohol by volume range. Codex Alimentarius, in their definition of “aromatized alcoholic beverages,” does not differentiate between alcohol sources and classifies “beer, wine and spiritous cooler-type beverages, low alcoholic refreshers” as a single category.  In addition, it is unclear whether products made outside of India would be considered Country liquors/Indian liquors for the purposes of these regulations. Part 2 defines Country liquors as “alcoholic beverages obtained from distillation of fermentable carbohydrates of agricultural origin.” The United States is concerned that U.S. alcohol beverages fitting this definition might be treated differently from domestic products Finally, we would also appreciate a response to the comments submitted by the United States on August 4, 2023, during the public consultation period as well as an update on the status of the draft regulation. The U.S. delegation thanks India for their attention to this statement and looks forward to your response.

StatementSubmitted: La delegación mexicana hace referencia al Proyecto de Resolución N°02/23- Reglamento Técnico Mercosur sobre Definiciones relativas a las bebidas alcohólicas (con excepción de las fermentadas), sus materias primas y procesos de fabricación (Derogación de la Resolución GMC N°77/94), notificada ante los Miembros del Comité OTC con las nomenclaturas G/TBT/N/ARG/444 y  G/TBT/N/URY/85, asimismo, se hace referencia a la comunicación remitida por el Gobierno de México al Gobierno de Argentina el 10 de agosto de 2023 y por medio de la cual, se expresaron comentarios respecto al Reglamento del Mercosur. Asimismo, la delegación mexicana quisiera expresar que si bien, el Gobierno de México reconoce los esfuerzos de los socios comerciales del Mercosur para mantener actualizadas las regulaciones técnicas, sobre todo, las de una industria en constante evolución como es la industria de las bebidas alcohólicas, es importante asegurar que la actualización de reglamentos técnicos, considere aquellos elementos de regulaciones previas que continúen vigentes, con el objetivo de mantener el flujo comercial.Al respecto, la delegación de México, solicita conocer la razón por la cual, no se incluye la definición de Tequila en el Reglamento, toda vez que el Reglamento que se pretende derogar sí la incluye. Asimismo, se señala que el no considerar al Tequila como una bebida alcohólica (no fermentada) podría contravenir el principio de proporcionalidad, estipulado en el artículo 2.2 del Acuerdo OTC, al constituir un obstáculo innecesario por modificar las condiciones existentes del comercio.Por último, la delegación de México solicita a la delegación de Argentina, conceder una respuesta a los comentarios compartidos por el Gobierno de México en el periodo de consulta pública del Reglamento. Muchas gracias por la atención a esta declaración.
Summary: The representative of Mexico provided the following statement. The Mexican delegation refers to draft Resolution No.02/23 - MERCOSUR Technical Regulations on definitions relating to alcoholic beverages (except fermented beverages), their raw materials and manufacturing processes (Repealing GMC Resolution No.77/94), notified to the members of the TBT Committee in documents G/TBT/N/ARG/444 and G/TBT/N/URY/85. We also refer to the communication sent by the Government of Mexico to the Government of Argentina on 10 August 2023, containing comments on the MERCOSUR Regulations. We would also like to say that, while the Government of Mexico recognizes the efforts of MERCOSUR trading partners to keep technical regulations up-to-date, particularly the regulations of ever-changing industries such as the alcoholic beverage industry, it is important to ensure that elements of previous regulations that remain in force are taken into account when updating technical regulations, in order to maintain trade flows. In this connection, the delegation of Mexico would like to know why the definition of tequila is not included in the Regulations, considering that it is included in the regulations to be repealed. Failure to consider tequila as an (unfermented) alcoholic beverage could contravene the principle of proportionality, stipulated in Article 2.2 of the TBT Agreement, as it creates an unnecessary barrier to trade by modifying existing trade conditions. Lastly, the delegation of Mexico requests the delegation of Argentina provide a reply to the comments submitted by the Government of Mexico during the public consultation period on the Regulations.

StatementSubmitted: The United States believes that this is a technical regulation as it regulates product characteristics for derived products and it includes conformity assessment procedures in its due diligence requirements. As such, the United States believes this measure is within the scope of the TBT Agreement. As a leader in addressing deforestation, the United States has been committed to conserving critical ecosystems and addressing drivers of global deforestation since the early 1900s.   Based on this experience, the United States emphasizes that deforestation is a global issue that requires cooperative approaches by national competent authorities and civil society organizations rather than unilateral action.  For this reason, the United States has strong concerns with the EU’s unilateral approach in this space. Specifically, we are deeply concerned that the EU’s approach may not be well-calibrated to effectively address root causes of deforestation and that it may adversely impact trade by imposing significant costs and burdens to global supply chains without providing measurable benefits to curb global deforestation.  While we are still evaluating the full impact, it is our understanding that the EU’s regulation will add billions in costs for a variety of industries, in both markets, and potentially complicate supply chains without producing a sufficiently  tangible benefit to the global fight against deforestation from each affected industry or market.  We understand that the regulation has been formally adopted and published in the EU’s Official Journal; however, additional work must be done to develop the country benchmarking methodology and implementing guidance for Member States. We request continued consultations between our technical experts to discuss ways this regulation can be better calibrated to address global deforestation and avoid imposing undue burdens on any producers that a party can demonstrate do not contribute to global deforestation.  Given that this regulation is expected to have a significant impact on international trade, the United States respectfully requests that the EU delay implementation of this regulation, notify the regulation to the WTO TBT Committee, provide adequate time for stakeholder comment, and take those comments into account before implementing the final regulation.  The United States looks forward to further technical dialogue on this regulation. (In rebuttal to the EU's argument that the Deforestation-Free Products Regulation does not lay down product characteristics or their related processes or production methods, and is therefore not a TBT measure):The United States disagrees with the EU’s position regarding the TBT Agreement’s definition of technical regulation.  The United States notes that operators will be required to exercise due diligence requirements prior to placing relevant products on the EU market, and it appears that these due diligence requirements will be used by the EU to determine those relevant requirements in the regulation are fulfilled.   Specifically, Article 15 of the regulation describes how EU competent authorities will examine mandatory due diligence statements to determine that the relevant requirements in the regulation are fulfilled.

StatementSubmitted: India is concerned with European Union’s “Regulation on deforestation-free products” (Regulation (EU) No. 995/20102) (“Regulation”). The EU’s omission to notify the Regulation to the Committee on Technical Barriers to Trade (“TBT”) raise serious questions with respect to the compliance with the TBT Agreement. India believes that the Regulation would have a disproportionate impact on countries with agrarian economies that have significantly large population and vast tracts of forest land. Though the Regulation claims to contribute to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (“SDG”), it is noted that the Regulation would, in fact, have an adverse impact on the achievement of other SDGs such as ‘no poverty’ (SDG1), ‘zero hunger’ (SDG2) and ‘reduced equality’ (SDG10).The EU has failed to disclose the scientific basis on which it has selected the seven ‘relevant commodities’ and the evidence to demonstrate that the targeted seven products pose a high risk to deforestation. Additionally, the retroactive cut-off dates and the burdensome due diligence processes, including annual reviews, are some of the specific concerns that would affect the trade in the relevant commodities between India and EU. The EU has unilaterally introduced a three-tier risk assessment system under which every country would be assessed and categorised into High, low or standard risk countries.  No objective criteria have been disclosed for the risk assessment model. There is a high risk that the risk assessment could turn out to be highly subjective. Further, EU shall not be the sole arbiter of the efforts of other Members for reducing the environmental impact of deforestation activities. The provision relating to cooperation with third countries is vague and lacks any substantive methodology for implementation. India is concerned that the Chapter relating to the country benchmarking system and cooperation with third countries confers an unreasonable amount of discretion to the Commission to assess the risk level of countries, without any accountability or transparency. India believes that the cumbersome implementation mechanism provided in the Regulation does not address the policy objectives sought to be achieved. The due diligence obligations in the Regulation apply to operators’ that ‘place a relevant commodity in the Union market’. The burden on an operator would increase manifold for collecting data conducting due diligence, assessing the risk, providing information to the competent authorities in the EU market, maintain the data for a period of five years etc. There are legitimate concerns that even the exporters/producers that follow ‘deforestation-free’ agricultural practices may be denied access to the Union market if the ‘operators’ in the Union market (to whom the exporters/producers supply their products) are unwilling to comply with the due diligence requirements. The ban on ‘placing a product in the Union market’ unless they are ‘deforestation-free’ appears to be excessive, and India is concerned that the EU has made insufficient attempts to consider less-trade restrictive alternatives to meet its objectives.India urges EU not to implement the Regulation before arriving at a consensus with trading partners on the definitions, scope of products covered, cut-off date, due diligence, risk assessment, etc.

StatementSubmitted: En primer lugar, Colombia quisiera expresar que comparte los objetivos de reducir la deforestación y la degradación forestal a nivel global, como parte de los esfuerzos para promover la sostenibilidad y combatir el cambio climático.  Sin perjuicio de lo anterior, tenemos inquietudes respecto a que la implementación de esta medida y su cumplimiento se conviertan en barreras al comercio para algunas exportaciones, a pesar que ellas tengan baja o ninguna relación con la deforestación. Menciono lo anterior por la existencia de sectores clave de exportación colombiana como bovino, cacao, café, palma aceitera, caucho, soja, que estarían sujetos a la exigencia de una declaración de debida diligencia para demostrar su condición de estar libres de deforestación. En este contexto, hay preocupaciones relacionadas con la implementación de la medida porque podría haber potencial multiplicidad de modelos de debida diligencia, además de pérdida de relevancia de certificaciones que ya miden tales riesgos de deforestación. De otro lado, esta legislación no tiene en cuenta las circunstancias y capacidades locales, las legislaciones nacionales y los mecanismos de certificación de los países productores en desarrollo. Es claro que el modelo "único para todos" de la Unión Europea, basado en la debida diligencia y la trazabilidad, descuida las variadas condiciones locales, imponiendo altos costos a las naciones exportadoras, a los productores y a los consumidores. Los efectos más perjudiciales de esta reglamentación se derivan de las excesivas tareas administrativas relacionadas con la geolocalización, los requisitos de trazabilidad, certificaciones y procedimientos aduaneros. En este contexto, coincidimos con Estados Unidos cuando menciona que la deforestación es un problema global que requiere enfoques cooperativos en lugar de acciones unilaterales.  Finalmente, quisiera reiterar que Colombia valora los objetivos ambientales y está comprometida con los esfuerzos para combatir la deforestación y defender los compromisos multilaterales, por supuesto bajo principio de responsabilidades comunes pero diferenciadas. También estamos dispuestos a un diálogo constructivo para lograr un equilibrio entre los objetivos de conservación y las necesidades comerciales. Por ello hacemos un llamado a que se realice una revisión detallada y objetiva del Reglamento para asegurar que cumple con los principios y obligaciones de la OMC y a considerar alternativas menos restrictivas que puedan lograr el objetivo deseado sin generar obstáculos innecesarios al comercio internacional.
Summary: The representative of Colombia provided the following statement. First, Colombia would like to state that it shares the objectives of reducing deforestation and forest degradation at the global level, as part of its efforts to promote sustainability and combat climate change. Nevertheless, we are concerned that the implementation and enforcement of this measure could become barriers to trade for some exports, even when these exports bear little or no relation to deforestation. I say this because some key Colombian export sectors, such as cattle, cocoa, coffee, palm oil, rubber and soy, would be required to provide a due diligence statement to demonstrate that they are deforestation-free. In this context, there are concerns about implementing the measure because there could potentially be multiple models of the due diligence statement, and certification that already takes such risks of deforestation into account could lose its relevance. On the other hand, this Regulation does not take into account local circumstances and capacities, national legislation and certification mechanisms in developing producer countries. It is clear that the European Union's "one-size-fits-all" model, based on due diligence and traceability, disregards the varying local conditions, imposing high costs on exporting nations, producers and consumers. The most harmful effects of this Regulation stem from excessive administrative tasks related to geolocation, traceability requirements, certification and customs procedures. We therefore agree with the United States that deforestation is a global problem that requires a cooperative approach rather than unilateral action. Lastly, I would like to reiterate that Colombia values environmental objectives and is committed to efforts aimed at combating deforestation and defending multilateral commitments, of course under the principle of common but differentiated responsibility. We are also ready to engage in constructive dialogue in order to strike a balance between conservation objectives and trade needs. We therefore call for a detailed and objective revision of the Regulation to ensure that it complies with WTO principles and obligations and for consideration of less restrictive alternatives that could achieve the desired goal without creating unnecessary barriers to international trade.

StatementSubmitted: El Paraguay reafirma sus compromisos con los objetivos y principios ambientales. En particular, enfatizamos con vehemencia nuestro compromiso en combatir la deforestación y la degradación forestal.Sin embargo, nos preocupa la manera en que la norma europea aborda estas cuestiones.El Paraguay agradece a la Unión Europea la sesión informativa realizada durante la Semana Ambiental, la circulación del documento WT/CTE/GEN/30, la reciente publicación de un documento con preguntas frecuentes y las discusiones bilaterales. Sin embargo, persisten las preocupaciones y consultas de los miembros, como se puede apreciar por la cantidad de preguntas y preocupaciones comerciales específicas de las que es objeto esta medida.Este reglamento y otras medidas unilaterales con supuestos objetivos ambientales y un claro impacto comercial se están discutiendo en varios órganos de esta institución, incluso en el Consejo General. La UE ya ha anunciado que organizará una nueva sesión informativa durante la próxima reunión del Comité de Comercio y Ambiente. Esperamos que la UE pueda responder a las preguntas e inquietudes presentadas en alguno de estos espacios, ya que lo que necesitamos los miembros es un diálogo y que las preocupaciones sean tenidas en cuenta y no una exposición unilateral sobre sus medidas.Permítame, presidenta, concluir mi intervención instando nuevamente a la UE "a cooperar de manera eficaz y establecer un diálogo productivo con sus interlocutores en materia de comercio y desarrollo sostenible para abordar conjuntamente el impacto de la legislación de la UE y sus instrumentos de aplicación, incluido el apoyo para facilitar el comercio".Además, adelanto que enviaremos junto con otros miembros preguntas por escrito a la UE sobre esta medida en el marco del Comité de Comercio y Medio Ambiente.
Summary: The representative of Paraguay provided the following statement. Paraguay reaffirms its commitment to environmental objectives and principles. In particular, we are at pains to stress our commitment to combating deforestation and forest degradation. However, we are concerned about how European legislation addresses these issues. Paraguay thanks the European Union for the information session held during Environment Week, the circulation of document WT/CTE/GEN/30, the recent publication of a document with frequently asked questions, and the bilateral discussions. However, concerns persist, as evidenced by Members' concerns and queries, as seen from the number of questions submitted in the various bodies of this Organization, including the General Council. This Regulation and other unilateral measures that supposedly have environmental objectives and a clear impact on trade are being discussed in several bodies of this Organization, including the General Council. The EU has already announced that it will organize a new information session at the next meeting of the Committee on Trade and Environment. We thus hope that the EU will be able to respond to the questions and concerns raised in one of these forums, as what Members need is a dialogue and for their concerns to be taken into account, not a unilateral presentation on EU measures. Allow me, Chair, to conclude my statement by calling on the EU once again to engage in "effective cooperation and meaningful dialogue with its partners in the areas of trade and sustainable development to jointly address the impact of EU legislation and its implementing instruments, including providing support to facilitate trade". In addition, I would like to let you know that, together with other Members, we will forward written questions on this measure to the EU within the framework of the Committee on Trade and Environment.

StatementSubmitted: Australia recognises the critical importance of forests and shares international concerns about the rate and impact of global deforestation on climate and biodiversity. Australia supports measures that address global deforestation and forest degradation. As a signatory to the Glasgow Leaders’ Declaration on Forests and Land Use and the Forests and Climate Leaders’ Partnership, Australia is committed to halting and reversing net forest loss and land degradation by 2030. Australia has been progressively increasing the area of its own forests since 2008. Nevertheless, Australia and other WTO members remain concerned the European Union’s (EU’s) deforestation measures are more restrictive than necessary and will create unnecessary barriers to international trade, through costly and time-consuming obligations that will result in administrative and compliance burdens.  Australia is also concerned about the lack of clarity surrounding critical aspects of the EU’s deforestation regulation (EUDR ), including relevant definitions, country risk ratings, how assessment of compliance will be undertaken by competent authorities, including the evidence used to support deforestation status and the process of review. These uncertainties mean no party can yet be confident of its absolute compliance with the regulation.   Like many countries, Australia’s forest definition applies specific metrics that align with internationally agreed terms with thresholds (tree height and canopy cover) adapted to our extensive forest estate distributed across a broad range of geographic landscapes and climatic environments. The ‘one-size-fits-all’ definition used in the EUDR does not address Australia’s diverse and unique forest ecosystems.  Australia is equally concerned that the Forest Observatory maps must accurately reflect the status of Australia’s forests. The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences (ABARES) has reviewed the first version of maps and notes that the Forest Observatory records a higher area of forest than is recognised in the Forests of Australia 2023 dataset. Given the difference between the EUDR definition of forest and the Australian definition, including the former having a greater height threshold of 5 metres rather than 2 metres and excluding land predominately under agricultural use, we would expect that the forest area mapped by the Forest Observatory would be substantially less.  Further, Australia is still seeking clarity around certain definitions in the regulation and their application, particularly in relation to land predominantly used for agriculture. Extensive grazing land in Australia does not appear to have been removed from the EU 2020 forest dataset, despite meeting the EUDR definition of ‘agricultural use’. Given the direct impact that application of these definitions will have on the Forest Observatory dataset and subsequent implementation of the EUDR, this highlights the outstanding need for the EU to provide greater clarity regarding this inconsistency. Australia has sought and would welcome technical exchanges with relevant experts in the European Commission (EC) as soon as possible to further discuss improving the accuracy of this important resource. Australia believes the classification of a conversion of plantation forest to agricultural use as ‘deforestation’ and linked trade restrictions are unjustifiable, and potentially contrary to the aims of the EUDR. This would limit land decision flexibility, noting that plantation establishment is often a commercial decision influenced by factors such as market demand which can change. It may perversely disincentivise landholders to consider plantations given these potential trade implications of having to maintain land as a forest in perpetuity or otherwise face trade limitations.  Australia also remains concerned about the development of country risk ratings, having received no response from the EU on the country report that was submitted in June 2023. As the risk rating will have a direct bearing on the compliance impost to exporters, Australia remains concerned about the limited compliance timeframe until entry into force of the regulation in December 2024.  Australian producers and exporters of affected commodities and products will need to develop fit-for-purpose traceability systems to record and transfer geo-location data throughout their supply chains to meet EUDR requirements. This will be complex, costly and time intensive to achieve, and particularly challenging for bulk commodities that typically mix produce from multiple locations in the transport process. In addition, some derived products captured in the regulation, such as leather for example, are already in production. Affected industry sectors in Australia are expressing increasing concerns about the uncertainty surrounding EUDR compliance, reiterating the need for expeditious release of guidance documents. Australia requests the EU provide specific guidance for producers and exporters of affected commodities and products as soon as possible.  Australia notes the EU is developing guidelines for implementation of the regulation by its Member States. Australia requests information on the regulatory approaches to be taken by EU Member States be provided to third countries as soon as possible, including the process for review in the event of detained consignments.  Noting Australia will have product on water in October 2024 that will be subject to the due diligence obligations, and fundamental pieces of information remain outstanding to ensure compliance, Australia requests the EU delay implementation until these key uncertainties have been addressed.  At a minimum Australia requests a delay in enforcement of penalties for non-compliance whilst the EU completes the guidance, processes and systems that are fundamental to adherence to the regulation. This would ensure producers, companies and operators who make best endeavours to comply are not unfairly penalised and provides competent authorities adequate time to implement and evenly enforce the regulation.  Australia recalls that the EU stated this regulation is “outside the scope of the definition of a technical regulation” at the November 2023 TBT Committee when this measure was first raised as a specific trade concern. The EU indicated the regulation “does not “lay down” or otherwise prescribe, positively or negatively, “product characteristics”. The Regulation only refers to conditions that have to be met before placing the products on the EU market or exporting products from the EU market.” Australia disagrees with this assessment, which is why we consider appropriate to again speak to the matter at this meeting. The definition of a technical regulation in Annex 1 is: a “Document which lays down product characteristics or their related processes and production methods, including the applicable administrative provisions, with which compliance is mandatory.” Australia considers a requirement to be “deforestation-free” to be a product characteristic. Additionally, the regulation is prescriptive in relation to products’ ‘related processes and production methods’.

StatementSubmitted: Canada supported this STC at the last Committee meeting in November 2023, and the decision to raise it at this meeting reflects our serious and growing concerns with the implementation of the measure.  With the entry into force of the Regulation now less than 9 months away, there is little time for the EU to address the many concerns and unanswered questions raised by Canada and other Members regarding the unnecessarily trade disruptive effects of the measure. As noted previously, Canada shares the EU’s desire to stem deforestation globally and recognizes the scope and scale of what the EU is undertaking regarding deforestation free supply chains. However, Canada is concerned that some of the compliance measures proposed in this regulation will result in barriers to trade for Canadian exports of several important products, even though they are at low risk of having stemmed from deforestation. Based on information provided thus far by the European Commission, it seems clear that in particular the geo-location requirement of the Regulation will be unworkable for many Canadian exporters, particularly of composite or bulk products such as paper, soy beans, or wood pellets.  While we respect the aims of the regulation, and understand the desire for traceability, we ask that the EU consider a more flexible approach to meeting some of these compliance objectives.  We urge the EU to consider delaying the entry into force of this Regulation given the large number of uncertainties around how the Regulation will be enforced, and the country benchmarking process.  Reducing unnecessary and unintended effects on trade, particularly when sourcing agricultural and forest products that originate from countries with well-managed, stable forest area, is critical at this time of global economic uncertainty. To that end, it is imperative that complex regulatory requirements such as those included in the Regulation are well thought through and feasible.

StatementSubmitted: EUROPEAN UNION - REGULATION (EU) 2023/1115 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL ON THE MAKING AVAILABLE ON THE UNION MARKET AND THE EXPORT FROM THE UNION OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES AND PRODUCTS ASSOCIATED WITH DEFORESTATION AND FOREST DEGRADATION AND REPEALING REGULATION (EU) NO 995/2010Indonesia remains deeply concerned about the development of the European Green Deal, particularly the EUDR, which entered into force on June 29, 2023.We believe the EUDR may potentially violate the WTO rules, due to its unilateral and discriminatory nature – as well as creating unnecessary trade barriers. Summary: The representative of Indonesia provided the following statement. Indonesia remains deeply concerned about the development of the European Green Deal, particularly the EUDR, which entered into force on 29 June 2023. We believe the EUDR may potentially violate the WTO rules, due to its unilateral and discriminatory nature - as well as creating unnecessary trade barriers. These ultimately will undermine the confidence in a rules-based multilateral trading system. Indeed, there are many aspects in the EUDR that needs to be carefully reconsidered prior to its implementation in December 2024. We have raised these valid concerns in many different occasions, both in bilateral and multilateral settings. Such concerns have also been raised by other producers of these particular products and commodities that are associated with deforestation and forest degradation. However, it seems that there have been no concrete steps taken by the EU to address these concerns. Today, we are compelled to raise the following issues: First, the launch of the EU Observatory and Forest Degradation (EUFO) and the Global Forest Map 2020 on 8 December 2023. We believe that this Map does not reflect the dynamics and complexities of forests in different regions and countries. Indeed there is a gap between the Global Forest Map and our official map due to the difference of parameter in the classification of the land. We have presented a preliminary analysis of this gap during last month's Ad-hoc Joint Task Force Meeting on EUDR between Indonesia, Malaysia, and the EU. On-site land verification with our national authority is, therefore, very critical. Indonesia has developed a forest inventory platform called SIMONTANA, which has been used as a reference in the FAO's State of the World's Forest Publication. We urge the EU to consider similar recognition to SIMONTANA. Second, the due-diligence provision in the EUDR, which tends to be discriminatory in nature, contradicts the basic principles of multilateral trading system, and potentially affects the producing countries' interests, including Indonesia. The EUDR is estimated to affect more than USD 5 billion-worth of Indonesia's commodity exports to the EU. In addition, the EUDR imposes additional burden to our smallholders. Based on data from the Indonesian Ministry of Agriculture, at least more than 12 million hectares of land area and 19 million tons of commodities managed and produced by smallholders would be affected by EUDR. As such, we have repeatedly asked the EU to consider granting smallholders a postponement or a flexibility in the EUDR implementation.We urge the EU to explain concrete mitigation measures to address the concerns of our smallholders - who may be excluded from global supply chain - not because they have deforested their land - but because they lack the capacity to prove their compliance to the excessive and ever-stringent sustainability criteria imposed. Third, mutual recognition of standard between producer countries and the EU. Mutual Recognition Agreement (MRA) is a good form of an inclusive and collaborative approach, as it also encourages countries to develop their standards from within according to their own needs and avoiding unjustified restrictive and discriminative measures. We believe our national certification scheme is already quite comprehensive, and urge the EU to provide a room within the EUDR for MRA on commodities covered by the Regulation. We still have many questions regarding the EUDR, including on clear timeline and details in the EUDR implementation, and competent authorities in the EU that may provide assistance in this regard. We are also still not clear whether these measures will bring more benefits instead of creating more unnecessary disguised trade barriers. Let me close by underlining that in order to be more effective, stronger collaborative efforts in addressing climate change are needed, instead of punitive ones - including technology transfer, investment in relevant sectors - in line with the principle of Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR). Indeed, we need to see more burden-sharing in fighting climate change, and work together to prevent burden-shifting - especially policies aimed at shifting disproportionate responsibilities to Members that historically have contributed less to climate change.

StatementSubmitted: India wishes to reiterate its concerns regarding EU’s Deforestation Regulation [(EU) 2023/1115 adopted by the European Union on 31 May 2023.India believes that the Regulation would disproportionately impact countries with agrarian economies that have signi?cantly large populations and vast tracts of forest land.India reiterates that the lack of scienti?c basis for the selection of the seven ‘relevant commodities’, the retroactive cut-o? dates, burdensome due diligence processes and annual reviews, are some of the speci?c concerns that would a?ect the trade in the relevant commodities between India and EU. All these aspects of the measure make the regulation far more trade-restrictive than what is necessary to meet the legitimate objectives of the EU.The three-tier risk assessment system under which every country would be assessed and categorised into high, low, or standard risk countries is a patent violation of Article 2.1 TBT Agreement since it discriminates between ‘like products’ based on the country of origin. Further, it is reiterated that no bjective criteria have been disclosed for the risk assessment model. There is a high possibility that the risk assessment could turn out to be extremely subjective.The provision relating to cooperation with third countries is vague and lacks a substantive methodology for implementation. India is concerned that the Chapter relating to the country benchmarking system and cooperation with third countries confers an unreasonable amount of discretion to the Commission to assess the risk level of countries, without any accountability or transparency.India believes that the cumbersome implementation mechanism provided in the Regulation does not address the policy objectives sought to be achieved. The due diligence obligations in the Regulation apply to ‘operators’ that ‘place a relevant commodity in the Union market’. The burden on an operator would increase manifold for collecting data conducting due diligence, assessing the risk, providing information to the competent authorities in the EU market, maintaining the data for ?ve years etc. There are legitimate concerns that even the exporters/producers that follow ‘deforestation-free’ agricultural practices may be denied access to the Union market if the ‘operators’ in the Union market are unwilling to comply with the due diligence requirements for reasons of additional costs of compliance. The ban on placing a product in the Union market’ unless they are ‘deforestation-free’ ‘appears to be excessive. India is concerned that the EU has made insu?cient attempts to consider less-trade-restrictive alternatives to meet its objectives. The measures are excessive and result in unnecessary obstacles to international trade.

StatementSubmitted: The United States is deeply concerned that the European Union finalized the EU Deforestation-free Supply Chain Regulation (EUDR) without notifying the regulation to the WTO nor providing any opportunity for stakeholder comments to be taken into account. The United States reiterates that the EUDR falls within the scope and obligations of the TBT Agreement. As a leader in addressing deforestation, the United States is disappointed that the EU continues to pursue its unilateral and punitive approach despite the legitimate concerns raised by more than a dozen Members in this Committee. The United States is concerned that rather than acknowledging good forestry practices or encouraging better production practices, the EUDR simply increases costs and burdens for all producers, regardless of forestry practices. The United States emphasizes that instead of addressing global deforestation, this regulation’s most tangible impact will be increased compliance burdens and market distortions that may result in substantial consequences for global supply chains and food security. As such, the EUDR may in fact undermine global efforts to tackle deforestation and climate change by increasing costs, creating market inefficiencies, and disrupting supply chains.  In December 2023, the EU issued a Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) document that may ease some of the compliance burdens imposed on specific U.S. producers; however, the United States is concerned that, in part because it is not legally binding, the FAQ document does not alleviate stakeholder uncertainty, and does not address the fundamental concerns raised regarding the regulation.  Given that this regulation is expected to have a significant impact on international trade, the United States urges the EU to delay implementation of this regulation, and subsequent enforcement of penalties, until stakeholder and trading partner concerns have been addressed through all available administrative, regulatory, or legislative mechanisms.The United States reiterates our request for the EU to notify the regulation to the WTO TBT Committee, provide adequate time for stakeholder comment, and take those comments into account before implementing the final regulation. We understand that the regulation has been formally adopted; however, substantial gaps remain for U.S. producers to be able to comply with this regulation.  Therefore, we request continued consultations between our technical experts to discuss ways this regulation can be better calibrated to address global deforestation and avoid imposing unnecessary burdens on producers.  We look forward to working with our EU counterparts and like-minded partners to identify and resolve several remaining issues so the EUDR does not cause unnecessary disruptions to trade. REBUTTALThe United States is concerned and, frankly, disappointed that the European Union refuses to respond to the substantive questions and concerns raised by multiple Members of this Committee. The EU frequently notes its efforts to provide transparency; however, avoiding significant concerns raised by Members of this Committee only amplifies concerns that Member concerns are not being taken into account. Moving forward, we expect the EU to make a legitimate effort to respond to Member concerns and strongly urge the EU to delay implementation of the EUDR until stakeholder concerns are addressed through all available administrative, regulatory, and legislative mechanisms.The United States appreciates the EU’s position regarding the TBT Agreement’s definition of technical regulation.  The United States notes that the regulation specifies that products that are made with or contain certain listed commodities are prohibited, and requires operators to exercise due diligence to demonstrate that they meet the regulation, prior to placing relevant products on the EU market.   Specifically, Article 1 of the regulation states that it lays down rules for specific products with the characteristic that they are made from listed commodities. Article 3 prohibits those products unless they meet certain requirements, including due diligence requirements. Article 9 and Article 15 of the regulation describes how EU competent authorities will examine mandatory due diligence statements to determine that the relevant requirements in the regulation are fulfilled.

StatementSubmitted: México comparte el objetivo de combatir el calentamiento global y reconoce la iniciativa de la Unión Europea para actuar en consecuencia y reducir la deforestación de bosques a nivel mundial. No obstante, el Reglamento establece estándares para demostrar que un producto está libre de deforestación que resultan discriminatorios por la dificultad y altos costos de implementación para los productores, sobre todo, de países en vías de desarrollo.La implementación del Reglamento trae consigo más afectaciones a la sociedad en su conjunto que los beneficios que podría generar pues impacta directamente sobre uno de los sectores, históricamente, más precarizados: el sector agrícola, sobre todo cuando se trata de productores pequeños y locales.México se suma a las preocupaciones expresadas por otros Miembros en este y en anteriores Comités y está convencido que existen mecanismos más efectivos para aminorar los efectos del calentamiento global.
Summary: The representative of Mexico provided the following statement. Mexico shares the goal of combating global warming and acknowledges the steps taken by the European Union to act accordingly and reduce deforestation worldwide. However, the Regulation establishes standards for demonstrating that a product is deforestation-free which are discriminatory, owing to the difficulty and high costs of implementation for producers, especially those from developing countries. The implementation of the Regulation poses more disadvantages to society as a whole than possible benefits, since it directly impacts the agricultural sector, which has historically been one of the most precarious sectors, and especially small and local producers. Mexico echoes the concerns expressed by other Members in this and previous meetings and is convinced that more effective mechanisms exist for curbing the effects of global warming.

StatementSubmitted: El Paraguay reafirma sus compromisos con los objetivos y principios ambientales. En particular, enfatizamos con vehemencia nuestro compromiso en combatir la deforestación y la degradación forestal.Sin embargo, nos preocupa la manera en que la norma europea aborda estas cuestiones.Este reglamento y otras medidas unilaterales con supuestos objetivos ambientales y un claro impacto comercial se están discutiendo en varios órganos de esta institución, incluso en el Consejo General.El Paraguay agradece a la Unión Europea las sesiones informativas realizadas, la publicación de un documento con preguntas frecuentes y las discusiones bilaterales. Sin embargo, persisten las preocupaciones y consultas de los miembros, como se puede apreciar por la cantidad de preguntas y preocupaciones comerciales específicas de las que es objeto esta medida. Instamos nuevamente a la UE a cooperar de manera eficaz y establecer un diálogo productivo con sus interlocutores en materia de comercio y desarrollo sostenible para abordar conjuntamente el impacto de la legislación de la UE y sus instrumentos de aplicación, incluido el apoyo para facilitar el comercio.Hago referencia para su inclusión en las minutas de esta reunión bajo esta preocupación comercial a las preguntas que el Paraguay junto con otros miembros presentamos en el marco del Comité de Comercio y Medio Ambiente bajo signatura WT/CTE/GEN/33 para las cuales esperamos respuesta por escrito como prueba de la transparencia y verdadero espíritu de diálogo y cooperación de la Unión Europea, considerando que el mismo reglamento incluye a la OMC entre los foros para Cooperación con Terceros Países.De no recibir las respuestas por escrito en el ámbito en las que las presentamos nos veremos obligados a replicarlas en todos los órganos en que existan preocupaciones comerciales específicas sobre esta medida.
Summary: The representative of Paraguay provided the following statement. Paraguay reaffirms its commitment to environmental objectives and principles. In particular, we are at pains to stress our commitment to combating deforestation and forest degradation. However, we are concerned about how European legislation addresses these issues. This Regulation and other unilateral measures with supposedly environmental objectives and a clear impact on trade are being discussed in several bodies of this Organization, including the General Council. Paraguay thanks the European Union for the information sessions, the publication of a document with frequently asked questions and the bilateral discussions. However, Members' concerns and questions remain, as can be seen from the number of specific questions and trade concerns raised in relation to this measure. What we social stakeholders need is dialogue rather than an explanation or presentation of the measure by the European Union. We once again call on the EU to engage in effective cooperation and meaningful dialogue with its partners in the areas of trade and sustainable development, in order to jointly address the impact of EU legislation and its implementing instruments, including a study on possible support to facilitate trade. I refer to the questions put by Paraguay and other Members during the Committee on Trade and Environment in document WT/CTE/GEN/33, for their inclusion in the minutes under this trade concern. We look forward to written responses as evidence of the European Union's transparency and spirit of dialogue and cooperation, considering that the same regulation includes the WTO in forums for cooperation with third countries. The failure to receive written responses within the framework of the Committee will leave us with no choice but to repeat our questions in all bodies where there are specific trade concerns about this measure, including this Committee. In fact, today I thought about reading the 10-page document in this meeting as it had been forwarded to several Members, announcing a long intervention by Paraguay. However, I noted that the document containing the questions was circulated after the previous meeting of this Committee, so it did not seem fair to me, along with the TBT delegations, to proceed in this way without first giving the European Union the opportunity to reply to the questions. However, in the absence of responses, we will do so in the next meeting so we might have to envisage an additional day. In any case, we have already announced this in the Council on Trade in Goods, so if we do not receive the replies, we will read the 10 pages in that forum.The representative of Paraguay provided the following statement. I did not want to lose the opportunity to support what the US has just said. We said it before, in the previous meeting, for other STCs. We are constantly hearing from the EU their openness and transparency for the measures, and yet we see no responses to our concerns or questions. Frankly, the only effort we see is to reshuffle a little bit the answer but it is still the same answer as in the previous meeting but in a different order and that is all the effort we are seeing to respond to ours and several other Members' concerns and questions. So we kindly ask the EU to provide more detailed responses to our concerns both in this Committee but also in others.The representative of Paraguay provided the following statement. We did analyse the Frequently Asked Questions and the guidelines. There are several questions that are not answered, that is why we submitted a document in the CTE a few months ago and the answer we got there was that we will not be receiving a reply in writing so we have looked into that and we have participated in all the dialogues and also in a document circulated by the EU in the CTE (WT/CTE/GEN/30) about deforestation, but there are still questions unanswered, which is why we pose them here and in other documents. We thank the effort but we insist in the ones that have not been answered yet.

StatementSubmitted: New Zealand appreciates the opportunity to continue our engagement on the EU’s Deforestation Regulation – both here and in Brussels. As we have said before in this and other fora we, like others, share the EU’s desire to address deforestation, and to halt and reverse global forest loss.  We are, however, unconvinced about the effectiveness of the EU's approach and we are deeply concerned about the significant impact that the EU's implementation of these regulations will have on global trade. We are particularly concerned at the high compliance burden this regulation will impose on countries and producers whose systems are not linked to deforestation. It is our firm view that this is not the most trade facilitative approach to achieve the objective of protecting global forests.We are also concerned about the wide range of outstanding questions and issues that would need to be addressed before implementation, including legal clarity around definitions, the operation of information systems and competent authorities’ processes.These outstanding issues severely limit the ability for suppliers and operators to prepare for implementation, and make it hard for us to envisage that it could take effect on 30 December, without causing significant disruption to global supply chains.  It is on this basis that we join others in requesting that the date for the commencement of the due diligence obligations is deferred while stakeholder concerns are addressed and in order to allow more time for the Commission to clarify the outstanding issues to avoid trade disruption.Finally, we hold a systemic concern about the prescriptive nature of the measure and the disregard for local conditions of production. New Zealand believes that a more effective approach would involve WTO members working together collectively, rather than contributing to the proliferation of unilateral initiatives which cause trade disruption and risk fragmenting the international trading system. We encourage Members to collaborate, including at the WTO, to consider how trade facilitation and other trade levers can be used to address global challenges such as deforestation.
Summary: The representative of New Zealand provided the following statement. We are, however, unconvinced about the effectiveness of the EU's approach and we are deeply concerned about the significant impact that the EU's implementation of these regulations will have on global trade. We are particularly concerned at the high compliance burden this regulation will impose on countries and producers whose systems are not linked to deforestation. It is our firm view that this is not the most trade facilitative approach to achieve the objective of protecting global forests. We are also concerned about the wide range of outstanding questions and issues that would need to be addressed before implementation, including legal clarity around definitions, the operation of information systems and competent authorities' processes. These outstanding issues severely limit the ability for suppliers and operators to prepare for implementation, and make it hard for us to envisage that it could take effect on 30 December, without causing significant disruption to global supply chains. It is on this basis that we join others in requesting that the date for the commencement of the due diligence obligations is deferred while stakeholder concerns are addressed and in order to allow more time for the Commission to clarify the outstanding issues to avoid trade disruption. Finally, we hold a systemic concern about the prescriptive nature of the measure and the disregard for local conditions of production. New Zealand believes that a more effective approach would involve WTO Members working together collectively, rather than contributing to the proliferation of unilateral initiatives which cause trade disruption and risk fragmenting the international trading system. We encourage Members to collaborate, including at the WTO, to consider how trade facilitation and other trade levers can be used to address global challenges such as deforestation.

The concerned EU Regulation has the effect of laying down the product characteristics and therefore, is a technical regulation. India reiterates the concerns raised in the previous meetings. India urges EU to address the concerns raised by a wide range of WTO Members.

StatementSubmitted: The United States shares the European Union’s commitment to combatting deforestation but remains deeply concerned that the European Union continues to avoid meaningful engagement in this Committee regarding Members’ concerns on implementation of the EU Deforestation-free Supply Chain Regulation (EUDR). The United States reiterates that the EUDR falls within the scope and obligations of the TBT Agreement and should be notified to the TBT Committee. Given that this regulation will be enforced on December 30, 2024, the United States is increasingly concerned that the EU appears woefully unprepared to implement this regulation.  We have identified four critical issues that must be resolved for U.S. producers to be able to comply with the EUDR. First, the EU’s December 2023 FAQ document does not provide sufficient information for producers to understand nor comply with the EUDR. The United States is concerned that without clear guidance, the EUDR may result in market distortions that could have substantial consequences for global supply chains and food security. Second, despite the EUDR’s December 2023 deadline, many EU Member States have not designated a competent authority to enforce the regulation. The United States is concerned that the lack of EU competent authorities may lead to uneven application of the EUDR. Third, the EU has yet to develop the information system for producers to provide mandatory due diligence statements. Without this system in place, producers will not be able to submit the information necessary to comply with the EUDR.  Finally, following difficulties conducting its risk benchmarking, the EU made an interim decision to classify all countries as standard risk. This approach fails to recognize responsible forestry stewardship, as demonstrated in the United States, and will simply increases costs and burdens for all producers, regardless of forestry practices. Providing low or no-risk producers expedited entry into the EU market without providing due diligence statements would be the most effective way to incentivize deforestation-free trade.  Failure to address these issues before the enforcement of the EUDR could have significant negative economic effects for U.S. producers and EU consumers. For example, the majority of “cellulose fluff” used to make diapers and feminine hygienic products in the EU derives from sustainably managed U.S. forests. According to industry, should EUDR go into effect as scheduled, EU consumers will face a significant shortage of both groups of products by the end of 2025.  Therefore, United States urges the EU to delay implementation of this regulation, and subsequent enforcement of penalties, until at least 24 months after the EU has developed the elements necessary for producers to be able to comply with the EUDR. Given that this regulation is expected to have a significant impact on international trade, the United States reiterates our request for the EU to notify the regulation and any implementing guidance to the WTO TBT Committee, provide adequate time for stakeholder comment, and take those comments into account before implementing the final regulation. We reiterate our request to the EU to hold consultations between technical experts to discuss ways this regulation can be adjusted to more effectively address global deforestation and avoid imposing unnecessary burdens on producers. The United States, again, encourages the EU to work with like-minded trading partners to resolve these remaining issues and identify other barriers to implementation so the EUDR does not cause unnecessary disruptions to trade.

StatementSubmitted: As noted previously, Canada shares the EU’s desire to stem deforestation globally and recognizes the scope and scale of what the EU is undertaking regarding deforestation free supply chains.However, Canada is concerned that some of the compliance measures proposed in this regulation will result in barriers to trade for Canadian exports of several important products even though they are at low risk of having stemmed from deforestation. We urge the EU to consider delaying the entry into force of this Regulation given the large number of uncertainties around the Regulation itself, how it will be enforced and implemented, and the country benchmarking process. We also highlight the need for transparent and science-based criteria in the regulation to prevent discrimination against products from countries whose forests and forest management systems may not have been considered when this regulation was written, but whose forests are managed sustainably and in accordance with the laws of the country of harvest.  We also note the potential negative impact on the livelihoods of small-scale producers and indigenous communities in exporting countries. Reducing unnecessary and unintended effects on trade, particularly when sourcing agricultural and forest products that originate from countries with well-managed, stable forest area, is critical at this time of global economic uncertainty. To that end, it is imperative that complex regulatory requirements such as those included in the Regulation are well thought through and feasible.
