StatementSubmitted: 1. Japan expresses its concern about the revision of the F-gas regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/573 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 7 February 2024 on fluorinated greenhouse gases, amending Directive (EU) 2019/1937 and repealing Regulation (EU) No 517/2014) following its previous statement.2. Japan has concerns about this regulation regarding the safety risks and lower energy efficiency associated with the use of propane gas expected to be used as a substitute for F-gases, as well as restricting the use of next-generation F-gases, such as HFO refrigerants, with a low greenhouse effect. Therefore, we strongly urge for appropriate regulation design, including the safety exemptions and the review clause based on technological development, as described below.(1) Banning of all F-gases  As pointed out in our last statement, the regulation bans all F-gases, including HFO refrigerants, and it will accordingly make "split air-conditioning equipment and heat pumps using F-gases," including imported products, de facto unable to be put on the market in the future, since utilizing flammable natural refrigerants in them is technically more difficult from the viewpoint of safety risks and other factors. For this reason, they will be disadvantaged compared to "self-contained air conditioning equipment and heat pumps using natural refrigerants," which are the main domestic products of the same category in Europe.  Although the purpose of the regulation is to reduce greenhouse gases (GHGs), banning all F-gases uniformly including even those with low GWP such as HFO refrigerants would not necessarily contribute to the purpose. In addition, no risk impact assessment of the safety risks associated with the use of highly flammable refrigerants and the greenhouse effect associated with the use of F-gases with low GWP has been conducted. Consequently, the regulation may not have been designed to be sufficiently relevant for the purpose.  Therefore, the less favourable treatment for split air-conditioning equipment and heat pumps, which are the main products outside Europe, cannot be said to be solely based on legitimate regulatory distinctions, and would therefore be inconsistent with Article 2.1 of the TBT Agreement.  Furthermore, the regulation bans the use of all F-gases even when no alternative refrigerants are available. In addition, even though the purpose of the regulation is to reduce GHGs, the regulation bans all F-gases uniformly including those with low GWP which actually contribute to the purpose from the standpoint of “responds to concerns about the use of PFAS or substances breaking down to PFAS as well as other environmental considerations”. This is different from the purpose of the F-gas regulation, and regulations that address these concerns and considerations should be considered under the PFAS regulation.  These may be inconsistent with Article 2.2 of the TBT Agreement as they are more trade-restrictive than necessary to achieve the legitimate objective.(2) Impact assessment  The content of the revised regulation is significantly different, including the addition of banning all F-gases at 12kW or less, from that of the former regulation, for which the assessment was done in 2022, and an appropriate assessment in accordance with the content of the revised regulation has not been conducted. Therefore, the EU should conduct an appropriate impact assessment in a manner that is consistent with the content of the revised regulation, including the banning of all F-gases incorporated therein at the stage of final negotiation.Specifically, the following assessments should be conducted.??Impact Assessment of Continued Use of F-gases  -Impact Assessment on Global warming of low-GWP F-gases (GWP less than 150)??Impact Assessment of Banning all F-gases and using alternative refrigerants (especially for highly flammable refrigerants (propane))  -Assessment of the safety of each type of equipment  -Assessment of the safety during their entire life cycle (including installation, disposal, etc.)   -Assessment of the energy efficiency impact of using alternative refrigerants (global warming impact, cost impact, etc.)(3) Exemption  In the “Reply from the European Union to the Comments Received from Japan Regarding Notification G/TBT/N/EU/1031”, the EU stated that "these restrictions target only equipment, for which non-fluorinated and energy efficient alternatives exist today." We understand that the implementation rules will be specified based on Article 11(5). At that stage, we would like the EU to take appropriate measures therein based on the actual conditions of safety when using alternative propane refrigerant and other relevant factors.  In particular, equipment such as split air-conditioning equipment and heat pumps of over 6 kW up to and including 12 kW have no alternative refrigerants due to safety reasons, as the use of highly flammable propane refrigerants have a risk of combustion or explosion. We ask these categories to be considered as exemptions.(4) Safety Requirement  Regarding the “Safety Requirement” defined in Article 3 (42), we have concerns about which specific laws and non-legally binding acts are applicable. We ask that the EU provide us with the details of the applicable laws and acts regarding Article3(42), including the details of the provision and the timeline for their application.(5) Review of the regulation in view of trends in technological development  A review of the regulation should be conducted as soon as possible including the impact assessment in the above (2). In particular, the use of next-generation F-gases, such as HFO refrigerants, which have comparable greenhouse effect to propane gas and are currently under technological development should be properly assessed and considered, as technological development of these refrigerants may be impeded by the future uncertainty of the regulation.(6) Opinions of Industry Stakeholders  We request that the EU properly consider the opinions of industry stakeholders on both the impact assessment and detailed design of the implementation.
Summary: The representative of Japan provided the following statement. Japan expresses its concern about the revision of the F-gas regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/573 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 7 February 2024 on fluorinated greenhouse gases, amending Directive (EU) 2019/1937 and repealing Regulation (EU) No 517/2014) following its previous statement. Japan has concerns about this regulation regarding the safety risks and lower energy efficiency associated with the use of propane gas expected to be used as a substitute for F-gases, as well as restricting the use of next-generation F-gases, such as HFO refrigerants, with a low greenhouse effect. Therefore, we strongly urge for appropriate regulation design, including the safety exemptions and the review clause based on technological development, as described below. (1) Banning of all F-gases. As pointed out in our last statement, the regulation bans all F-gases, including HFO refrigerants, and it will accordingly make "split air-conditioning equipment and heat pumps using F-gases," including imported products, de facto unable to be put on the market in the future, since utilizing flammable natural refrigerants in them is technically more difficult from the viewpoint of safety risks and other factors. For this reason, they will be disadvantaged compared to "self-contained air conditioning equipment and heat pumps using natural refrigerants," which are the main domestic products of the same category in Europe. Although the purpose of the regulation is to reduce greenhouse gases (GHGs), banning all F-gases uniformly including even those with low GWP such as HFO refrigerants would not necessarily contribute to the purpose. In addition, no risk impact assessment of the safety risks associated with the use of highly flammable refrigerants and the greenhouse effect associated with the use of F-gases with low GWP has been conducted. Consequently, the regulation may not have been designed to be sufficiently relevant for the purpose. Therefore, the less favourable treatment for split air-conditioning equipment and heat pumps, which are the main products outside Europe, cannot be said to be solely based on legitimate regulatory distinctions, and would therefore be inconsistent with Article 2.1 of the TBT Agreement.Furthermore, the regulation bans the use of all F-gases even when no alternative refrigerants are available. In addition, even though the purpose of the regulation is to reduce GHGs, the regulation bans all F-gases uniformly including those with low GWP which actually contribute to the purpose from the standpoint of "responds to concerns about the use of PFAS or substances breaking down to PFAS as well as other environmental considerations". This is different from the purpose of the F-gas regulation, and regulations that address these concerns and considerations should be considered under the PFAS regulation. These may be inconsistent with Article 2.2 of the TBT Agreement as they are more trade-restrictive than necessary to achieve the legitimate objective. (2) Impact assessment. The content of the revised regulation is significantly different, including the addition of banning all F-gases at 12kW or less, from that of the former regulation, for which the assessment was done in 2022, and an appropriate assessment in accordance with the content of the revised regulation has not been conducted. Therefore, the EU should conduct an appropriate impact assessment in a manner that is consistent with the content of the revised regulation, including the banning of all F-gases incorporated therein at the stage of final negotiation. Specifically, the following assessments should be conducted. - Impact Assessment of Continued Use of F-gases - Impact Assessment on Global warming of low-GWP F-gases (GWP less than 150) - Impact Assessment of Banning all F-gases and using alternative refrigerants (especially for highly flammable refrigerants (propane)) - Assessment of the safety of each type of equipment - Assessment of the safety during their entire life cycle (including installation, disposal, etc.) - Assessment of the energy efficiency impact of using alternative refrigerants (global warming impact, cost impact, etc.) .(3) Exemption. In the "Reply from the European Union to the Comments Received from Japan Regarding Notification G/TBT/N/EU/1031", the EU stated that "these restrictions target only equipment, for which non-fluorinated and energy efficient alternatives exist today." We understand that the implementation rules will be specified based on Article 11(5). At that stage, we would like the EU to take appropriate measures therein based on the actual conditions of safety when using alternative propane refrigerant and other relevant factors. In particular, equipment such as split air-conditioning equipment and heat pumps of over 6 kW up to and including 12 kW have no alternative refrigerants due to safety reasons, as the use of highly flammable propane refrigerants have a risk of combustion or explosion. We ask these categories to be considered as exemptions. (4) Safety Requirement. Regarding the "Safety Requirement" defined in Article 3 (42), we have concerns about which specific laws and non-legally binding acts are applicable. We ask that the EU provide us with the details of the applicable laws and acts regarding Article3(42), including the details of the provision and the timeline for their application. (5) Review of the regulation in view of trends in technological development. A review of the regulation should be conducted as soon as possible including the impact assessment in the above (2). In particular, the use of next-generation F-gases, such as HFO refrigerants, which have comparable greenhouse effect to propane gas and are currently under technological development should be properly assessed and considered, as technological development of these refrigerants may be impeded by the future uncertainty of the regulation. (6) Opinions of Industry Stakeholders. We request that the EU properly consider the opinions of industry stakeholders on both the impact assessment and detailed design of the implementation.

StatementSubmitted: While the United States appreciates that the EU notified the F-Gas proposal to the WTO TBT Committee, we continue to have significant concerns. Among them that the document notified to the WTO did not reflect the most accurate and recent version of the measure, and stakeholder comments were not taken into account.  While the written response transmitted to the United States and our industry on April 9th was thorough, it notably did not address the following concerns and questions: First, while the U.S. supports the objective of updating the EU’s F-gas Regulation to phase down certain HFCs (Hydrofluorocarbons) that contribute to global warming, we would appreciate more information as to why the EU included timelines to ban many products and services that utilize HFOs (Hydrofluoroolefins) and HCFCs (Hydrochlorofluorocarbons) despite the benefits, including avoiding greenhouse gas emissions, and before determining if there are viable alternatives in the marketplace. Further, these gases and their technological applications’ contributions to the avoidance of global warming are recognized by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change and the World Meteorological Organization, as well as international standards bodies. Can the EU explain why Annex IV of the Provisional Agreement in some cases extended or exempted the transition timeline for certain products and equipment, particularly when alternatives that are below the proposed GWP thresholds are widely available? We note for example in the 2022 Impact Assessment, cited by the EU in its written response, that the EU did not assess the market availability of F-gas alternatives in the marketplace, for many products. Instead, the regulation sets a deadline of 2030 to conduct an evaluation of whether the proposed phase-outs of low to zero GWP of F-gases  that have not yet gone into effect should be amended, due to a lack of viable alternatives.  This impact assessment further notes that natural gases are an EU led technology, while low GWP F-gases were developed by other nations. We should note that the United States manufactures and trades in these heating, air conditioning, refrigeration, and foam technologies with the EU. This decision to phase out F-gas technologies, before determining if proposed alternatives are viable, is already creating considerable uncertainty for manufacturers. Will this report and any subsequent amendments to Annex IV and its phase out timelines be subject to public consultation?  We strongly encourage the EU to move up its planned 2030 technological review as early as possible, and to include assessment of both what is technologically available in the marketplace and what will lead to the greatest increase in avoided emissions. The EU recently announced that its revised draft REACH PFAS Restriction proposal, which may impact HFOs, is not expected before the end of 2024.  Why then has the EU opted to phase out HFOs via the F-gas regulation, in advance of REACH?  Will the REACH process consider the environmental benefits of HFOs, in terms of avoided greenhouse gas emissions?  How will the EU ensure that the two regulations do not present contradictory or duplicative requirements for industry?   Will the REACH proposal take into account that the Montreal Protocol’s Environmental Effects Assessment Panel considered the use of HFOs in air conditioning and heating equipment, in relation to potential TFA emissions, and found a minimal risk to human health and the environment? As this measure moves into implementation, we would appreciate continued engagement to address stakeholder concerns.
Summary: The representative of the United States provided the following statement. While the written response transmitted to the United States and our industry on 9 April was thorough, it notably did not address the following concerns and questions: First, while the US supports the objective of updating the EU's F-gas Regulation to phase down certain HFCs (Hydrofluorocarbons) that contribute to global warming, we would appreciate more information as to why the EU included timelines to ban many products and services that utilize HFOs (Hydrofluoroolefins) and HCFCs (Hydrochlorofluorocarbons) despite the benefits, including avoiding greenhouse gas emissions, and before determining if there are viable alternatives in the marketplace. Further, these gases and their technological applications contribute to the avoidance of global warming and are recognized by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change and the World Meteorological Organization, as well as international standards bodies. Can the EU explain why Annex IV of the Provisional Agreement in some cases extended or exempted the transition timeline for certain products and equipment, particularly when alternatives that are below the proposed GWP thresholds are widely available? We note for example in the 2022 Impact Assessment, cited by the EU in its written response, that the EU did not assess the market availability of F-gas alternatives in the marketplace, for many products. Instead, the regulation sets a deadline of 2030 to conduct an evaluation of whether the proposed phase-outs of low to zero GWP of F-gases that have not yet gone into effect should be amended, due to a lack of viable alternatives.This impact assessment further notes that natural gases are an EU led technology, while low GWP F-gases were developed by other nations. We should note that the United States manufactures and trades in these heating, air conditioning, refrigeration, and foam technologies with the EU. This decision to phase out F-gas technologies, before determining if proposed alternatives are viable, is already creating considerable uncertainty for manufacturers. Will this report and any subsequent amendments to Annex IV and its phase out timelines be subject to public consultation? We strongly encourage the EU to move up its planned 2030 technological review as early as possible, and to include assessment of both what is technologically available in the marketplace and what will lead to the greatest increase in avoided emissions. The EU recently announced that its revised draft REACH PFAS Restriction proposal, which may impact HFOs, is not expected before the end of 2024. StatementSubmitted: On October 26, 2023, Saudi Arabia announced the draft of technical regulations for electric vehicles.We submitted the comments on December 21, 2023, and received a reply from Saudi Arabia on January 10, 2024. Summary: The representative of China provided the following statement. On 26 October 2023, Saudi Arabia announced the draft of technical regulations for electric vehicles. We submitted the comments on 21 December 2023, and received a reply from Saudi Arabia on 10 January 2024. Since then, at the 93rd WTO/TBT meeting, we submitted an STC and received a reply from Saudi Arabia. We would like to make a response to Saudi Arabia's reply. StatementSubmitted: China noticed that the EU notified the Proposal for a Regulation of the  European  Parliament and of the  Council on the safety of toys and repealing the Directive On October 4, 2023.About this regulation, we are concerned about some articles like Article 5 on the toys' risk to the safety or health of users or third parties, Chapter 4 Product Passport, and some requirements on new chemicals. We consider them will greatly increase the compliance complexity and compliance costs in product design, raw material improvement, testing and certification, digital management system construction, and other aspects, which may lead to a large number of enterprise exports being interrupted, causing a significant blow to small and medium-sized toy enterprises. So we have 3 recommendations: (1) publicly disclose relevant technical information or evaluation methods for evaluating the psychological and mental health, well-being, and cognitive development of children with toy products, or remove this requirement. (2) Taking into account the overall costs of enterprises (including toy companies outside the EU), focus more on the supervision of product safety and weaken the requirements for product passports. (3) Release toy chemical requirements guidelines for enterprises, especially small and medium-sized enterprises; And provide compliance consulting on production, labeling, and packaging to alleviate the burden on enterprises in terms of compliance, inspection, testing, and certification.
Summary: The representative of China provided the following statement. China noticed that the EU notified the Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on the safety of toys and repealing the Directive on 4 October 2023. About this regulation, we are concerned about some articles like Article 5 on the toys' risk to the safety or health of users or third parties, Chapter4 Product Passport, and some requirements on new chemicals. (2) Taking into account the overall costs of enterprises (including toy companies outside the EU), focus more on the supervision of product safety and weaken the requirements for product passports. StatementSubmitted: The notified regulation introduces generic bans for the most harmful chemicals in toys, and requires that a product passport including the compliance information is created for toys.China concerns that:(1)Based on the requirements of Article 5, China holds that due to socio-cultural and individual cognitive differences, there is a great deal of subjectivity in judging mental health and a lack of relevant international standards, and the present draft provides no criteria for such judgments, which is not conducive to the implementation of enterprises and may cause problems for the supervisory authorities;(2)Regarding 2(g) of Article 17, setting up a 10-year passport validity period for such a large number of toy products which have a very limited lifespan,is not necessary and will increase the burden of maintenance on enterprises.there are a huge number of substances or mixtures to be banned by (EC) No 1272/2008 in the toy safety regulations. PFAS only, exceeds 10,000 types and a considerable part of them do not have detection methods, making it difficult to effectively supervise them in practice. According to Article 2.2 of the WTO/TBT Agreement China mainly has 4 recommendations(1)the EU further clarify the specific requirements of this provision and provide universal standards for determining the risks posed by toys to children, so as to facilitate reference and implementation by enterprises when designing and producing toys, and also to facilitate better supervision by regulatory authorities(2)the EU provide a scientific basis for this provision and suggests that the EU set different validity periods for product passports corresponding to different toy product classification.(3).it is recommended to retain the approach of the original Toy Safety Directive, which exempts completely inaccessible toys, not limited to " toy components necessary for electronic or electric functions of the toy ".(4).China recommended that the European side maintain EN71-12 nitrosamines and nitrous substance requirements, solving compliance difficulties of copper alloys, stainless steel, crayons through exemptions.For other suggestions, please refer to our comment submitted on 20th May 2024. We hope to receive a reply from the European side again and fully consider the Chinese opinions in the legislative process of toy safety regulations.
Summary: The representative of China provided the following statement. The notified regulation introduces generic bans for the most harmful chemicals in toys, and requires that a product passport including the compliance information is created for toys. China is concerned that: (1) Based on the requirements of Article 5, China holds that due to socio-cultural and individual cognitive differences, there is a great deal of subjectivity in judging mental health and a lack of relevant international standards, and the present draft provides no criteria for such judgments, which is not conducive to the implementation of enterprises and may cause problems for the supervisory authorities; (2) Regarding 2(g) of Article 17, setting up a 10-year passport validity period for such a large number of toy products which have a very limited lifespan, is not necessary and will increase the burden of maintenance on enterprises. There are a huge number of substances or mixtures to be banned by (EC) No 1272/2008 in the toy safety regulations. PFAS only, exceeds 10,000 types and a considerable part of them do not have detection methods, making it difficult to effectively supervise them in practice.According to Article 2.2 of the WTO/TBT Agreement China mainly has 4 recommendations. (1) the EU further clarify the specific requirements of this provision and provide universal standards for determining the risks posed by toys to children, so as to facilitate reference and implementation by enterprises when designing and producing toys, and also to facilitate better supervision by regulatory authorities. (2) the EU provide a scientific basis for this provision and suggests that the EU set different validity periods for product passports corresponding to different toy product classification. (3) it is recommended to retain the approach of the original Toy Safety Directive, which exempts completely inaccessible toys, not limited to "toy components necessary for electronic or electric functions of the toy". (4) China recommended that the European side maintain EN71-12 nitrosamines and nitrous substance requirements, solving compliance difficulties of copper alloys, stainless steel, crayons through exemptions. For other suggestions, please refer to our comment submitted on 20 May 2024. We hope to receive a reply from the European side again and fully consider the Chinese opinions in the legislative process of toy safety regulations.

StatementSubmitted: The United States submitted comments on the proposed modifications to NOM-181 on yogurt in November 2021 and remains concerned about the physical-chemical specifications for yogurt and the deviation from CODEX guidelines. We would like to request that Mexico please provide an updated timeline for the procedural next steps for NOM-181. Could Mexico please share when its response to U.S. comments will be published in the Official Gazette? Additionally, could Mexico share when the final draft standard is expected to be published to the Diario Official?  Could Mexico confirm that the final draft will be amended to include milk protein concentrates and whey protein concentrates as approved enrichment ingredients for yogurt? We continue to have several significant concerns and questions about this measure’s scope and implementation and requests that Mexico indefinitely delay implementation of this measure.

StatementSubmitted: On 5 October 2023, the EU notified the European Common Criteria-based cybersecurity certification scheme (EUCC) to WTO (G/TBT/N/EU/1019). China submitted our comments through the enquiry point of China in November 2023, and received a response on 28 February 2024. On 7 February 2024, the Official Journal of the EU officially promulgated the Regulation (EU) 2024/482. As the Regulation covers specialized IT and ICT equipment, such as integrated circuits, smart cards, network equipment and so on, we reiterate the following comments on the Regulation (EU OJ version).China appreciates the EU’s cybersecurity certification requirements for IT and ICT equipment, but according to Article 2.9.4 of the WTO/TBT Agreement, from the perspective of not creating unnecessary trade barriers, China would like to make the following concerns:1. It is proposed to unify the validity period of EUCC certificates to 5 years to ensure that the validity period of certificates issued by different CBs for the same type of product is consistent. For Articles 12.1&12.2 of Chapter II, different validity periods will cause confusion. If the CB of the EU countries can set different validity periods of certificate based on the characteristics of the certified product, then it is very likely to result in different validity periods of certificate for the same type of product, which will affect the uniformity of the EUCC certification scheme and the mutual recognition within the EU, which may create unhealthy market competition.2. For Chapter III, it is proposed to clarify the certification mechanism for Protection Profiles(PP) as well as the following questions:(i)The certification process of PP;(ii)Which organizations will be responsible for the development of PP of EUCC? Can the manufacturers/the ITSEF develop such PP and apply for certification?(iii)Is there any PP applicable to the EUCC Substantial and EUCC High(AVA_VAN.3), such as PP that has been issued under SOG-IS MRA, CCRA? Or will the PP of Substantial and High(AVA_VAN.3) level be developed under the EUCC scheme?(iv)If the products are identified as requiring High(AVA_VAN.4 or AVA_VAN.5) certification, how will the certification be carried out when there is no corresponding PP standard in Annex I&II?3. It is proposed to clarify the notification method for certificate holders in the description of “Certification holders shall notify the purchasers of the ICT products about the suspension of certificates” in Article 30.3 of Chapter V.4. It is proposed to delete the requirement as “store the specimen of the certified ICT product” in Article 41.2 of Chapter VII. The EU CE marking is a basic requirement for product of the EU NLF. None of its relevant Regulations, such as RED Directive(2014/53/EU), RED DA[ (EU) 2022/30], Low Voltage Directive(2014/35/EU) or EMC Directive(2014/30/EU), stipulates the retention period requirement for certified product specimen. 5. It is proposed to clarify the certification schemes of alternatives when EUCC puts into force on 27 February, 2025. Article 49 of Chapter XI does not clarify whether the lightweight CC certification scheme developed by each country will be replaced(such as CSPN in France, BSZ in Germany, LINCE in Spain, etc.). If national certification requirements mentioned above still exist after EUCC’s implementation, it will cause confusion and a burden of repeated certification for the industry.6. It is proposed to clarify how to define the certification level of TOE(Target of Evaluation) for composite evaluation certification based on CC certification standards.7. The EUCC High certification standard shall timely match market demand and provide guarantees for product market access. For Article 48.2 &3 of Chapter X and Recital (31), it is proposed that the EU clarify the amendment mechanism for ANNEX I&II, such as procedures, frequency, etc. Meanwhile, it is proposed that the EU give full consideration to whether the amendment mechanism for the High-level(AVA_VAN.4 and AVA_VAN.5) certification standards(ANNEX I&II of Regulation) matches the demand of the corresponding certification market. Also it is proposed that the updated PP certification standards shall be published on the EUCC certification website simultaneously so that the industry can quickly obtain information.8. ANNEX IV.4/3 stipulates that Article 13 of Chapter III of the Regulations applies when the patch involves a significant change to a certified product and involves a previously undetected vulnerability (i.e., the vulnerability has previously been determined to have no critical impact on the security of the ICT product). It is recommended to specify pre-conditions for triggering certificate audit in ANNEX IV.4/3 to better guide manufacturers to carry out the certificate maintenance activities based on the patch management requirements.9. It is proposed to either work on the perfection of the provision of ANNEX IV.4/4 and provide guidance for the product patch management process, or the European Commission should require relevant agencies such as ENISA to release relevant guidance to facilitate manufacturers. 10. It is proposed to clarify the circumstances when the Conformity Assessment Body may not apply the relevant documents in ANNEX I&II. Article 7.2 of Chapter II stipulates that the Conformity Assessment Body may ask NCCA for not using the State-of-the-art document for assessment in certain circumstances and with certain reasons. NCCA will give approval if it’s rational. NCCA will also notify ECCG(European Cybersecurity Certification Group) of the information and fully consider opinions of ECCG, but the preconditions in the current Regulation are not clear enough.11. It is proposed to clarify the criterions of conformity for certification in Article 28.1 of Chapter V and provide its regulatory provisions/standards. Article 28.1 of Chapter V stipulates that when the PP or the certified ICT product is inconsistent with the requirements of the Regulation and (EU)2019/881(CSA), CB shall inform the certificate holder of the certification consistency issue and require the certificate holder to take fixes. However, the Article does not specify the specific regulations and standards for reference, which leads to difficulty in implementation. Besides, the definition of “non-conformity” is not clear.
Summary: The representative of China provided the following statement. China noticed that the EU notified the European Common Criteria-based cybersecurity certification scheme on 5 October 2023, and submitted our comments in November 2023, and received a response on 28 February 2024. China noticed that the EU officially promulgated regulation on 7 February 2024. China wants to reiterate concerns, meanwhile, China suggests that the EU may check the concerns and comments that were raised earlier on the e-Agenda.This time, China mainly has three kinds of concerns: 1. China asks the EU to make some modifications to Article 12.2 of Chapter 2 to unify the validity period of EUCC certificates to ensure that the validity period of certificates for the same type of product is consistent. And to delete the requirement "store the specimen of the certified ICT product" in Article 41.2 of Chapter 7. 2. China asks the EU to make some clarification on the certification process of PP, and the certification schemes of alternatives when EUCC puts into force on 27 February 2025, and the scope of application of AVA_VAN.5, whether it applies to both military and civilian products; for the applicability of civilian products and explain its rationality and provide the scope of civilian products to which AVA_VAN.5 applies, and provide graded management strategies and related requirements based on the level of security vulnerabilities. 3. China suggests that the EU further improve the information security measures for ENCC certification, and introduce a graded certification strategy into the EUCC certification system, allowing products with low-security risks to undergo self-assessment of compliance, and recognize the results of CC certification and announce the starting time for implementing the certification, and include key information and the reference standards, evaluation procedures, testing methods and effectiveness of certification data of certification bodies in the reporting scope, and timely disclose it on the network security certification website to ensure that the security performance of ICT devices is correctly tested and evaluated.

StatementSubmitted: As the top dairy export market for the U.S., the United States values Mexico as a trading partner and has a vested interest in any changes to Mexico’s dairy regulations. StatementSubmitted: INDIA – PLYWOOD AND WOODEN FLUSH DOOR SHUTTER (QUALITY CONTROL ORDER), 2023Indonesia would like to thank India for its notification related to the Plywood and Wooden flush door shutter (Quality Control) Order 2023 as G/TBT/N/IND/274 on June 8th, 2023 to the TBT WTO Committee. Indonesia thanks India for the bilateral meeting held on 11-12 January 2024 with the Bureau of Indian Standard (BIS), however there has been no significant progress regarding the concerns raised by Indonesia. India already forces this regulation on 29th February 2024 and not provided any explanation regarding Indonesia’s questions. India also did not notify the addendum to the WTO TBT Committee Secretariat regarding the implementation of this Quality Control Order.Referring to the notifications, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, Ministry of Commerce and Industry – India, has issued 10 standards regulations on plywood and wooden flush door shutters where the products must be certified according to Indian Standards and the manufacturer is required to undergo certification by the Indian Standards Bureau (BIS) under Foreign Manufacturer Certification (FCMS), before the product allowed to enter the Indian market.Related to the implementation of the regulation, Indonesia had sent inquiries through India Enquiry Point seeking clarification and explanation on the legitimate objective of this QCO on August 3rd, 2023 but not yet replied. Indonesia would like to seek further clarification on the following matters:This regulation has the same pattern as the implementation of other QCO’s by India Government which have leave problems for business actors. The measure resulted in the cessation of export of Indonesian products to India, and impacted heavy losses for business actors.The transition time of the regulation is insufficient for producers to be able to meet the requirements set out in the QCOs. With a large number of regulated products, the need for physical testing, and the factory inspection requirements at production sites, we concerned about the possibility of queues and backlogs of product certification applications coming into the BIS, which could slow down the certification process and hinder the export process. In this regard, we request India to postpone the implementation of this QCO to 36 months (3 years) after promulgations; We understand that the BIS acts as National Standards Body as well as Certification Authority and grants License for Conformity Assessment Scheme under Compulsory Certification of at least for 609 products, applies to both domestic and imported products. Given the magnitude role and responsibilities of BIS, can BIS provide options to cooperate with Product Certification Bodies from Indonesia or Laboratories that have been accredited by the Indonesia National Accreditation Body signatory of International Accreditation Forum (IAF)? If yes, kindly explain the regulatory references and processes for cooperation and conducting mutual recognition arrangement with BIS.Indonesia suggest India open the option of international recognition for conformity assessment results and/or conformity assessment bodies (inspection bodies) from the country of origin to speed up the audit and certification process and also reduce the cost of certification.Indonesia also urges India to notify the stipulated technical regulations to the secretariat, in accordance with Article 2.9.2 of the TBT Agreement.

StatementSubmitted: The United States thanks the European Union for continued dialogue on its regulation regarding wine denominations of origin, protected geographical indications, labeling, and certification requirements for imported wine, notified to the WTO on February 6, 2023, as G/TBT/N/EU/952. We appreciate the EU’s efforts to develop the Q&A guidance document that addresses many of the United States’ concerns and supports implementation of the new wine labeling regulations. We also acknowledge the EU’s TBT National Enquiry Point which has been responsive to U.S. comments. Despite the clarity provided by the Q&A guidance document, the United States remains concerned that the current guidance does not provide a uniform format for digital labels or QR codes across the EU. The United States notes that creating multiple labels for the EU market may be confusing for EU consumers and would be costly and burdensome to U.S. exporters. Providing unique labels for each Member State may be challenging as wine that enters the EU in one Member State is often distributed to multiple Member States.  The United States requests that the EU approve a language-free modality for identifying QR codes that will be accepted by all Member States, in order to assure uniform implementation and alleviate confusion. Given that this regulation will apply to wines produced after December 8, 2023, the United States is concerned that Member State authorities may have difficulty assessing when a wine was produced.  To avoid misinterpretation, we ask that the EU issue official guidance to Member State authorities clarifying that the U.S. 2023 vintage and non-vintage, and blended wines from 2023, were produced before the enforcement date and are exempt from the new labeling regulations. This is critical as there have already been reports of importers requiring compliance of exempt wines. Given that U.S. wine producers need significant lead time to design and print new labels, we ask that the EU provide quick and favorable consideration to the United States’ requests so that U.S. wine producers will have adequate time to comply with the new requirements.

StatementSubmitted: The United States appreciates our dialogue with the European Union on its new wine labeling requirements, notified to the WTO on February 6, 2023, as G/TBT/N/EU/952. We are taking the floor for the final time in this Committee to share progress and remaining concerns related to this measure. The United States has raised this regulation with the EU on a variety of occasions including in this Committee, the U.S. – EU Wine Dialogue, and bilateral meetings. In these discussions, we have appreciated the constructive engagement with the EU to address many of our concerns and to ease compliance for U.S. exporters. Specifically, the United States thanks the EU for issuing its Q&A guidance document, which helped to address many U.S. stakeholder concerns and has facilitated implementation of the new wine labeling regulations.  The EU also issued official guidance to EU Member State officials to confirm the continued validity of the Simplified Export Certificate for U.S. wines.  Despite positive developments, uniform implementation remains the United States’ primary concern. The EU has clarified that the word “ingredients” must accompany QR codes for ingredient labeling and can be provided in any one EU official language. The United States requests that the EU provide official guidance to Member States encouraging the acceptance of just the word “ingredients” in one official EU language to identify QR code labels.  This one word, one language approach will alleviate confusion and promote uniform implementation across Member States.  The United States further encourages the EU to pursue all available administrative, regulatory, and legislative mechanisms to provide a language-free modality to identify QR codes with mandatory ingredient information to prevent the need for multiple country-specific translations. The United States welcomes continued collaboration with the EU to address questions and clarifications from the United States to promote smooth implementation of this regulation as 2024 vintage wines from the United States enter the European marketplace.

StatementSubmitted: Korea expresses gratitude for the opportunity to submit following requests and comments on the "Kingdom of Bahrain Technical Regulation on Commercial Air-Conditioners - Minimum energy performance requirements and testing requirements" (hereinafter, Regulation) which was notified in 2020 as G/TBT/N/BHR/575 and published in Bahrain official gazette on November 9, 2023.  Firstly, Korea requests that necessary measures be taken to ensure that the registration is not rejected when registering products using the AHRI certificate according to PATH A program as outlined in Article 6.2 of the Regulation. The AHRI certificate does not display essential information for registration, such as energy efficiency and detailed model names. Therefore, concerns have been raised that submissions of the AHRI certificate as is, in accordance with PATH A, may lead to registration rejections.  Secondly, regarding the PATH B program as outlined in Article 6.3 of the Regulation, Korea requests information for the implementation of the PATH B procedures, including a list of accredited testing laboratories and clarification on whether manufacturers' own test results are recognized. Thirdly for products that are large in size and must be exported in a semi-manufactured form to be assembled and installed in Bahrain, Korea requests information on whether these products are subject to certification. Additionally, Korea asks for guidance on the registration procedure for these products. The three requests mentioned align with the comments Korea submitted to the Bahrain WTO TBT Enquiry Point on nine occasions from 2020 through November 2022, in response to Bahrain's G/TBT/N/BHR/575 notification in 2020. Finally, Korea kindly requests the provision of updated information regarding the registration requirements outlined in Article 9 of the Regulation to the WTO Members.

StatementSubmitted: A new measure has been implemented in Qatar, imposing new obligations for all processed food products exported from Korea and the Philippines to attach Certificates of Conformity (CoC) per every shipment.  The Korean government and the exporters need to be aware of the necessity of this measure and be given the opportunity to provide opinions in prior to the implementation, but it is regrettable that the process has not been carried out formally and transparently. Moreover, due to the new obligations imposed by Qatar, Korean exporters are spending a great amount of time and money for the issuance of CoC upon every shipment, and there are concerns that this may consequently become a trade barrier. On February 21, 2024, the Korean government officially requested the Qatari government for a bilateral consultation to discuss on this matter, and we wish to have the discussion as soon as possible to come up with reasonable solutions.

StatementSubmitted: The United States thanks Mexico for its November 27 notification to the TBT Committee of G/TBT/N/MEX/527, draft measure regarding the use of the IFT seal on products, equipment, devices or apparatus for telecommunications and broadcasting.  As mentioned in our comments submitted on January 26, it is our understanding that this proposal, as written, will add significant compliance costs and logistical complexities for businesses due to the redesign of product labels, especially for small-sized equipment. Further, it is our understanding that these costs are not considered in the Regulatory Impact Analysis.  It is also our understanding that this measure was published as final in Mexico’s Federal Register on December 26, 2023, one month before the deadline for comments under the WTO notification. Can Mexico clarify how it intends to take comments received pursuant to the WTO notification into account, when the measure is already published as final? Can Mexico share when it intends to respond to stakeholder comments?  We’d like to remind Mexico of its WTO and USMCA Technical Barriers to Trade and USMCA Good Regulatory Practices obligations to not only provide a comment period of at least 60-days for stakeholder comments under normal circumstances, but also to take those comments into account before finalizing the measure. We also request that IFT consider providing a one-year transition period to give producers sufficient time to adapt their products or methods of production to the new requirements. Can Mexico please provide an update on the status of the measure, and any steps Mexico is taking to address stakeholder concerns?

StatementSubmitted: India would like to convey its concerns regarding the TBT noti?cation G/TBT/N/IDN/151 issued by Indonesia on October 25, 2022. India requests Indonesia to clarify the procedure to be followed in the case of exporters from Non-MRA countries. India requests Indonesia to take into account the concerns raised by India and amend the standards suitably.

StatementSubmitted: The EU remains deeply concerned by the increasing number of Quality Control Orders (QCOs) issued by India across many sectors. The EU would like to recall that the majority of QCOs introduced by India appear to have a protectionist orientation and consequently raise questions regarding their compliance with the WTO’s TBT Agreement obligations. The EU is particularly concerned by the fact that QCOs usually prescribe India-specific standards where international standards already exist. The EU would like to remind India that article 2.4 of the WTO TBT Agreement requires members to use international standards, where they exist, as basis for their technical regulations, except, when such international standards or relevant parts would be an ineffective or inappropriate means for the fulfilment of the legitimate objectives pursued, for instance because of fundamental climatic or geographical factors or fundamental technological problems.Furthermore, QCOs prescribe mandatory conformity assessment procedures that are more restrictive than necessary to fulfil their legitimate objective. They cause extra burden and economic cost to the EU industry as a result of unnecessarily cumbersome procedures, including mandatory factory inspections, sample testing in Indian laboratories, to obtain necessary permissions or licences for products already tested and certified under established international standards and schemes. There is no provision for a streamlined process on the basis of existing certification from any international body. The European Union would like to express its concerns about India’s Furniture Quality Control Order (G/TBT/N/IND/318). On 27 November 2023 the EU sent comments on this notification to India. Unfortunately to this date no official reply to EU comments was received. The EU would appreciate it if India could prepare an official reply to EU comments. The EU would like to highlight the importance of its statement in this Committee, especially in the light of no answer to official comments on this notification. We do hope that India’s reply will be comprehensive.The EU supports the objective of the Indian authorities to ensure that only products with a high level of quality are placed on the market. However, this Quality Control Order (QCO) sets mandatory requirements on quality and performance which will lead to over engineered products, demanding separate production lines, with at best marginally better consumer utility benefits and will have an impact on the cost of the product. In addition, the Indian certification process required to be able to put products in the Indian market are extremely cumbersome and costly, leading to yearlong go-to-market delays. The standards specified by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) contain many technical requirements and associated tests that are exceptional in nature (in the range of 30 to 40 different conformances) on materials, surface finish, dimensions, construction, stability, performance, and endurance tests. Certain mechanical test parametric requirements deviate significantly from international standards and contain requirements to satisfy extreme use conditions. Overall, deviations from the international norm will result in deterioration in consumer welfare. For any industry to adopt these standards significant changes to design, materials, and production methods have to be made. This will lead to costs escalations - a cost that will ultimately be borne by the consumers. This makes these technical requirements exceptional, going beyond what is justifiable from a quality point of view and difficult to comply with even for larger industry players. This QCO will disrupt the supply chains as it will demand double or separate production lines and inventory management, dilute the economies of scale operating benefits to companies and lower product price benefit to customers.The EU welcomes the extension of the period given to comply with the notified draft from 6 to 12 months, as notified on 13 October 2023 in G/TBT/N/IND/318/Corr.1. However, as the certification process to place furniture products on the Indian market is complex and currently takes approximately 2 years, the EU kindly asks the Indian authorities to consider a longer transition period of at least 24 months during which certification would stay voluntary. Sufficient time is also needed to increase the capacities for testing and certification on the Indian side.As the notified draft foresees longer transition period for SMEs, the EU would like to know whether that exemption applies also to foreign SMEs.The QCO will require increased capacity needs. Each manufacturing unit will need to set up facilities for routine testing of raw materials, in-process tests and finished product tests. The BIS scheme requires each unit to be fully equipped to carry out all tests. With the range of tests prescribed in the standard, a fully equipped laboratory will cost upwards of 114 k€ per unit. Other costs include BIS certification fee (approximately 20-25 k€ per overseas factory), testing of surveillance samples, cost of additional manpower. Further compliance costs are approximately 20-25 K Euro per overseas factory location plus annual renewal and label costs. In addition, there are currently no accredited and certified labs for the notified mandatory Indian furniture standards and the assigned certification scheme that can support companies. To cope with the size of industry, India would need heavy investments in testing infrastructure in all states. Moreover, the size of industries that BIS has traditionally handled are relatively small. The EU experience shows that timelines for the BIS marking program, especially for overseas manufacturers, is one to two years as seen recently with toys QCO. In comparison, domestic companies were certified in 3-6 months. Bringing the lead time up to par with domestic manufacturers would mean allowing foreign manufacturers to use the same online system (Manak Online Portal) used by domestic manufacturers, instead of having to submit hard copies. StatementSubmitted: On 21 November 2023, the EU submitted comments on Australia’s notification G/TBT/N/AUS/163. Given that to date no official reply was received, the EU would like to recall its key concerns related to the proposed changes to the Industrial Chemicals General Rules and Categorisation Guidelines. The EU is concerned that the new industrial chemicals (IC) rules go beyond what is required in international practice and do not provide for sufficient safeguards to protect intellectual property. In some cases, the new rules may put the protection of trade secrets in jeopardy, for example in case of fragrances, either due to disclosing the chemical identity or ingredient use, concentration used in the product formulation and import volume. The EU would like to know what safeguards does Australia envisage to ensure the appropriate protection of trade secrets when implementing the new rules?The EU is concerned that there are many introduction types that are unable to use INCI names, which could potentially deter the trade of cosmetic products to Australia. Furthermore, the proposed definition of “eligible INCI plant extract name” is not clear and falls short of providing a pathway for the operator to determine whether an INCI name will be accepted or not. The EU would like to propose to Australia to consider a universal acceptance of INCI names by Australia’s Industrial Chemicals (General) Rules to avoid barriers to trade. The EU would also like to note that chemical assessment reports of certain chemicals listed with Specific Information Requirement (SIR) in AICIS inventory are not publicly available. This difficulty remains a practical hindrance to the access to the Australian market. The EU would like to know the reasons for the lack of direct access to these reports, which are necessary for compliance checks. The EU would like to ask the Australian authorities to consider including the public availability of these reports as part of its work plan.

StatementSubmitted: The EU would like to recall its previous statement on this specific trade concern.  The European Union remains concerned that Australia’s industrial chemicals (IC) rules go beyond what is required in international practice and do not provide for sufficient safeguards to protect intellectual property. The EU notes these changes took effect on 24 April 2024 with the new rules, have only been in effect under the new rules and that stakeholders raised these issues in the notified consultation. In some cases, the amended rules may put the protection of trade secrets in jeopardy, for example in case of fragrances, either due to disclosing the chemical identity or ingredient use, concentration used in the product formulation and import volume. The EU would like to know what safeguards does Australia envisage to ensure the appropriate protection of trade secrets when implementing the amended rules?The EU would like to urge AICIS to commit to urgently work with the regulated entities to identify and implement the best regulatory solution for the IP issues in the Rules. The EU also calls on Australia to ensure that AICIS would not pursue compliance action until a solution for IP issues is implemented.The EU is concerned that there are many introduction types that are unable to use INCI names, which could potentially deter the trade of cosmetic products to Australia. Furthermore, the proposed definition of “eligible INCI plant extract name” is not clear and falls short of providing a pathway for the operator to determine whether an INCI name will be accepted or not. The EU would like to propose to Australia to consider a universal acceptance of INCI names by Australia’s Industrial Chemicals (General) Rules to avoid barriers to trade. The EU notes that 'Proper Names' are now removed from the Rules. The EU would like to ask Australia to provide an explanation as to why this removal was decided, given that industry was using 'proper names' to defend using INCI names when no other chemical names are available. In real practice, the removal is contrary to AICIS’ intention to increase the acceptance of INCI names.Some specific INCI non-acceptance scenarios are especially puzzling given the extreme complexity in the new Rules. For example, even when INCI names are acceptable for a specific circumstance where the introducer knows the name of the chemical, the same name cannot not be necessarily used if the introducer does not know the name of the chemical (i.e. chemical name could be IP). It is a newly introduced requirement. It is unclear why this difference exists and there has been no logical explanation provided by AICIS.Given the large number of different introduction scenarios and the individualised chemical names acceptance for each scenario, it is now extremely difficult for the industry to gauge the 'real-world' impacts of these new rules. The industry needs more time to test how the new Rules work in order to have better assessment of the impact regarding INCI name acceptance. The EU would also like to note that chemical assessment reports of certain chemicals listed with Specific Information Requirement (SIR) in AICIS inventory are not publicly available. This difficulty remains a practical hindrance to the access to the Australian market. The EU would like to ask the Australian authorities to consider including the public availability of these reports as part of its work plan.

StatementSubmitted: The recent entry into force of Cookware and Utensils Quality Control Order, 2023, covering a wide spectrum of products, caused heavy disruptions to EU companies importing such products to India. The Quality Control Order covers cooking utensils, serving utensils, table utensils and storage utensils. It impacts any utensils manufactured from aluminium or its alloys in wrought form which can be used for cooking, baking, serving or storing of solid/ semi-solid/ liquid food, water and household provisions. It also covers inset type stainless steel sinks used for domestic purposes, as well as rigid metal containers made of tinplate which can be hermetically sealed for packing of thermally and non-thermally processed foods and drinks like fruit vegetable and dairy. Finally, also aluminium cans for beverages up to 500-ml capacity for packing of beer and carbonated beverages fall under this QCO.The objective for the introduction of this QCO is the protection of human health and safety. While the EU supports this objective, it finds the provisions of the QCO too stringent and too trade-restrictive in comparison to the declared objective. The entry into force of this QCO disrupted the supply chains and availability of concerned products to customers. Adapting the range of products in order to recover the articles that are not readily available with the Indian suppliers takes around 12-18 months. For this reason, the EU would like to ask India to consider a transition period that would allow the industry to prepare for the change brought about by this QCO. In the current situation the stocks in the warehouses need to be scrapped. This leads to losses and does not serve the interest of end users.The consequence of this QCO will in most cases lead to over engineered products, and to setting up of separate production lines for India only.  It will also impact affordability by making the products more expensive. In addition, the Indian certification process required to put products on the Indian market is extremely cumbersome and costly, leading to yearlong go-to-market delays.

StatementSubmitted: The EU takes note of the publication of the Cookware, Utensils and Cans for foods and beverages (Quality Control) Order, 2024 on 14 March 2024, which superseded the Cookware and Utensils (Quality Control) Order 2023, notified by India as G/TBT/N/IND/258.The European Union notes with regret that India failed to notify to this Committee the 2024 Quality Control Order and thus making it impossible to send comments on this measure. The EU calls on India to comply with transparency provisions stemming from the TBT Agreement, and to notify the Cookware, Utensils and Cans for foods and beverages (Quality Control) Order, 2024 as soon as possible, providing the customary 60 days for comments.The Quality Control Order covers cooking utensils, serving utensils, table utensils and storage utensils. It impacts any utensils manufactured from aluminium or its alloys in wrought form which can be used for cooking, baking, serving, or storing of solid/ semi-solid/ liquid food, water, and household provisions. It also covers inset type stainless steel sinks used for domestic purposes, as well as rigid metal containers made of tinplate which can be hermetically sealed for packing of thermally and non-thermally processed foods and drinks like fruit vegetable and dairy. Finally, also aluminium cans for beverages for packing of beer and carbonated beverages fall under this QCO.The objective for the introduction of this QCO was the protection of human health and safety. While the EU supports this objective, it finds the provisions of the QCO too stringent and too trade-restrictive in comparison to the declared objective. The EU welcomes the delayed entry into force of this QCO set for the 1st of September 2024. However, the date of entry into force can only be indicated after the notification to the TBT Committee and the expiry of the commenting period. The EU notes that India gives additional time for compliance to small (1.12.2024) and micro (1.3.2025) enterprises. StatementSubmitted: California’s Farm Animal Confinement measure was initially notified to the WTO TBT committee on June 7, 2021, followed by several addenda and a notification of the final measure on September 12, 2022. Massachusetts’ Prevent Cruelty to Farm Animals measure was notified as a proposed measure on June 29, 2021 and we understand it is currently in effect.Canada would like to thank California, Massachusetts and the U.S. federal government for their bilateral engagements on California’s Proposition 12 and Massachusetts’ Question 3.Unfortunately, our core concerns remain unaddressed.Canada is a strong proponent of animal welfare, as evidenced by our comprehensive Codes of Practice for the care and handling of farm animals.We also support the right of governments to develop requirements for food production within their own jurisdictions.Nevertheless, Canada is concerned about the emerging patchwork of subnational regulations across the U.S., which mandate prescriptive agricultural production practices for food to be sold within a State, including imported products.California and Massachusetts’ measures prohibit the sale of specified food products, such as types and cuts of meat, where animals were not housed in the exact manner prescribed in their respective regulations.Overall, Canada is concerned that:These measures are not based on evidence or international standards and do not  consider the entire welfare needs of animals. These measures are not outcome-based and do not provide an opportunity for the recognition of equivalence.A patchwork of diverging subnational regulations, mandating highly-prescriptive production practices, has the potential to severely restrict trade in agriculture and agri-food products in the U.S.These measures set a concerning precedent: They signal the ability of each state to restrict the sale of any product that is not produced in an exact manner, irrespective of evidence, outcomes or international standards. If this continues to be replicated in other States or other regulatory areas, participating in the U.S. market will become unmanageable.Less trade restrictive alternatives do not seem to be taken into consideration.To reiterate, Canada strongly supports the proper care and handling of farm animals in agriculture production. However, Canada feels that these measures do not achieve that objective and establish a concerning precedent of a patchwork of subnational regulations that restrict trade.We urge the U.S. to consider mechanisms to address the growing patchwork of regulations and ensure trade is not unduly restricted.
Summary: The representative of Canada provided the following statement. California's Farm Animal Confinement measure was initially notified to the WTO TBT committee on 7 June 2021, followed by several addenda and a notification of the final measure on 12 September 2022. Massachusetts' Prevent Cruelty to Farm Animals measure was notified as a proposed measure on 29 June 2021 and we understand it is currently in effect. Canada would like to thank California, Massachusetts and the US federal government for their bilateral engagements on California's Proposition 12 and Massachusetts' Question 3. Unfortunately, our core concerns remain unaddressed. Canada is a strong proponent of animal welfare, as evidenced by our comprehensive Codes of Practice for the care and handling of farm animals. We also support the right of governments to develop requirements for food production within their own jurisdictions. Nevertheless, Canada is concerned about the emerging patchwork of subnational regulations across the US, which mandate prescriptive agricultural production practices for food to be sold within a state, including imported products. California and Massachusetts' measures prohibit the sale of specified food products, such as types and cuts of meat, where animals were not housed in the exact manner prescribed in their respective regulations.Overall, Canada has five main concerns. 1. These measures are not based on evidence or international standards and do not consider the entire welfare needs of animals. 2. These measures are not outcome-based and do not provide an opportunity for the recognition of equivalence. 3. A patchwork of diverging subnational regulations, mandating highly-prescriptive production practices, has the potential to severely restrict trade in agriculture and agri-food products in the US. 4. These measures set a concerning precedent: they signal the ability of each state to restrict the sale of any product that is not produced in an exact manner, irrespective of evidence, outcomes or international standards. If this continues to be replicated in other states or other regulatory areas, participating in the US market will become unmanageable. 5. Less trade-restrictive alternatives do not seem to be taken into consideration. To reiterate, Canada strongly supports the proper care and handling of farm animals in agriculture production. However, Canada feels that these measures do not achieve that objective and establish a concerning precedent of a patchwork of subnational regulations that restrict trade. We urge the US to consider mechanisms to address the growing patchwork of regulations and ensure trade is not unduly restricted.

Summary: The representative of China provided the following statement. StatementSubmitted: The EU would like to thank China for notifying this measure to the WTO, to which the EU submitted comments on 12 April 2024. We look forward to receiving a reply from China in the near future. In addition to those comments, the EU seeks clarification on the following items: Lot codes – as Chinese law already protects against tampering of production dates on labels, would it be possible to have lot codes also protected from tampering, so as to enhance product traceability by allowing companies to conduct recalls where necessary? Translations – the EU appreciates that trademarks will benefit from an exemption from translation into Chinese, however an extension of this exemption for geographical indications (GIs) would also be appreciated. Additionally, the obligation for non-mandatory information in a foreign language to correspond to that in normal Chinese characters could give rise to different interpretations and cause problems at enforcement level. Stock exhaustion clause – could China allow for a stock exhaustion clause for products placed on the market prior to the entry into force of revised GB7718?  Transition period – the EU would appreciate if a transition period of at least 18 months could be foreseen. Other – industry has identified concerns about the minimum size and height requirements for certain labelling elements, such as lot codes and units of measure, and the requirement to have both the production date and shelf life labelled on the product would pose challenges to existing production processes. Finally, we understand that there is separate labelling text being prepared by the State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) and a new version of GB7718. Will both of these be subject to public consultations and notified to the WTO?  The EU would like to emphasise that alignment and consistency, including in terms of entry into force dates and transition periods, are essential in order to avoid conflicting requirements and the need for multiple labelling changes.  The EU thanks China in advance for information/confirmation on the above issues.

StatementSubmitted: The United States values ongoing conversations with Colombia as a partner under our Trade Promotion Agreement (TPA) and in bilateral consultations in this forum to find agreement on an issue that we estimate will have a significant impact on the autos and automotive parts sector. The associated regulations were notified to the WTO TBT Committee as: G/TBT/N/COL/254, G/TBT/N/COL/257, G/TBT/N/COL/257/Add.1, G/TBT/N/COL/258. We acknowledge that our vehicle safety regulators from NHTSA have had positive discussions with their ANSV counterparts over the past years.  However, multiple engagements in the past 6 months between our regulators at both staff and senior levels has yet to yield a solution to a series of measures within these regulations that will go into effect as early as this August. The United States requests that implementation of the draft technical regulations be delayed until our vehicle safety regulators from NHTSA and their ANSV counterparts have resolved the certification issues that are still being discussed.    If these measures go into effect in August, vehicles manufactured to U.S. Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS) would ultimately face serious and costly impediments in order to comply with the required third-party certification, which would require duplicative testing and has an unproven ability to certify compliance to U.S. standards.  In addition, Colombia has not provided any safety justification for requiring such duplicative testing, nor have they provided evidence of any performance verification benefits.  We see no reason that Colombia’s proposed certification structure would be more robust than the regulatory, monitoring, and enforcement systems currently provided by the United States.  ANSV has not provided evidence of actual safety issues with products subject to NHTSA’s compliance authority and NHTSA remains committed to addressing concerns with every road vehicle product sold in the U.S. market. As part of its safety mission, NHTSA remains firmly committed to addressing concerns with every road vehicle product sold in the U.S. market. FMVSS are robust, research-driven vehicle safety requirements, and vehicles manufactured to them are among the safest in the world.  FMVSS are developed following good regulatory practices via a thorough public notice and comment process, making them some of the most scientifically vetted automotive safety standards in the world.    In addition, we note that nine automotive industry associations from six countries sent a letter in March expressing concerns about the trade restrictiveness of ANSV’s regulatory plans.  As the industry associations noted in their letter, the evidentiary basis for ANSV’s acceptance of Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS) solely for products built in the United States is unclear.  Automotive goods built in compliance with U.S regulations and standards are manufactured in countries across the globe.  Colombia has not provided evidence of any issue with products manufactured outside of the United States to U.S. standards. Likewise, FMVSS is as widely accepted outside the United States as are 1958 Agreement regulations outside of Europe.  In fact, many countries accept both standards equally. In our extensive bilateral exchanges on this issue, Colombia has not identified any safety concerns that would justify preference for the 1958 Agreement.  We note that in an April letter from ANSV to NHTSA, ANSV states that its goal is moving towards sole acceptance of the 1958 Agreement to support harmonization. Adoption of 1958 Agreement regulations while excluding harmonization with the FMVSS does not result in harmonization.  It results in the opposite.  While the United States supports greater regulatory alignment in order to reduce technical barriers to trade, the United States notes that Colombia’s pursuit of regulatory alignment with the 1958 Agreement alone are counterproductive to the goals of harmonization and result in creating additional technical barriers to trade that did not previously exist.    U.S. industry has proposed an alternative solution that we believe meets ANSV’s legal mandates. We believe that Colombia’s proposed measures would result in expensive, duplicative testing.  These measures would also limit consumer access to safe, high-quality vehicles and parts in the Colombian market, and increase costs to consumers.  We also note that this compliance issue is not specific to vehicles and their parts, and dates as far back as 2014, when the United States was among several other WTO Members who raised concerns with Colombia’s approach to standards acceptance, as laid out in the law implementing the National Quality Subsystem notified as G/TBT/N/COL/201, and Colombia’s product standard law, Decree 1074 of 2015, which requires third-party certification for high-risk products like vehicles and vehicle parts.  During the November 2014 TBT Committee meeting, the United States raised concerns that products were designated as "medium" or "high" risk without any associated risk assessment.  Now, this designation made without an associated risk assessment has led to a series of regulations that disadvantage products that are manufactured to arguably some of the highest standards of safety. We strongly encourage ANSV to continue working with the United States and industry on a solution that addresses both Parties’ concerns regarding conformity assessment.  The United States again requests that Colombia postpone implementation of the regulations until an acceptable resolution is reached.

StatementSubmitted: The United States thanks Canada for its willingness to engage on Québec’s Bill 96. As we mentioned in our February 2, 2024, WTO Enquiry Point message, we have concerns that this measure and its draft implementing regulation have not been notified to the WTO TBT Committee for stakeholder comment given its likely significant impact on trade.  We’d like to remind Canada of its WTO obligation to ensure that the technical regulations of local governments on the level directly below that of the central government are notified to the WTO TBT Committee, and that such notifications take place at an early appropriate stage, when amendments can still be introduced and comments taken into account. We’d further encourage Canada to ensure 60 days for stakeholder comments to make sure that stakeholders are able to fully convey their input. It is our understanding that Québec only accepted written comments physically submitted to the Minister of French Language, did not allow for the electronic (online) submission of comments, and only provided a 45-day period for comment on the draft implementing regulation for Bill 96 that was published on January 10, 2024. Given the significant impact this measure will have on trade, does Canada plan to notify Bill 96 and its draft implementing regulation to the WTO with a corresponding comment period of at least 60 days, and with an option for electronic submission of comments, so that interested WTO Members can provide comments when they can still be taken into account in the development of the final regulation?  Can Canada please provide an update on the status of the measure, and any steps Québec is taking to address stakeholder concerns?
