StatementSubmitted: Japan shares the concerns with other members on China’s regulation on registration and administration of overseas manufacturers of imported food (GACC Order No. 248).(If the US makes some requests to China)?In concrete terms, firstly, it is unclear what type of information is required for the registration. For example, while Article 10 enumerates the items required for the registration, GACC’s CIFER system also requires the HS code and CIQ code for facility registration, neither of which are listed in Article 10. ?Secondly, the scope of Decree 248 is unclear. It should be noted that GACC frequently changes the list of commodities for which facility registration is required. As a result, we are facing frequent changes regarding whether an item is subject to Article 7, registration by the Government, or Article 9, registration by private entities. Moreover, in connection with the first issue Japan raised, when an item designated under Article 7 becomes subject to Article 9, the registered HS code and CIQ code are sometimes deleted in the CIFER system without notice along with the application under Article 7 being transcribed to the application under Article 9, or vice versa. ?Accordingly, Japan considers that these issues cause unnecessary obstacles to trade. When a commodity is exported to China, Customs Office reviews not only whether the commodity comes from registered facility but also whether the commodity matches with Chinese HS code and CIQ code that were input at the time of registration. The issue is that the current CIFER system does not accept an application to add or modify the HS code and CIQ code to the record of the already registered facility. So when a commodity is changed from an Article 7 registration to an Article 9 registration in accordance with the change in the operation of Decree 248, and part or all of the registered HS code and CIQ code are deleted at the timing of the change, the HS code and CIQ code cannot be newly entered; this results in hindering exports. Japan also encountered another case. Although Article 2 of Decree 248 stipulates that the scope of the Decree is the registration of the facilities that manufacture, process or store food, GACC recently required an exporter to register the fishing vessels that have no processing nor storage equipment. This issue also highlights a lack of transparency concerning the registration process under Decree 248. The SPS Agreement requires as one of its obligations that sanitary and phytosanitary measures be based on scientific principles and an appropriate risk assessment, and that such measures should not be more trade-restrictive than necessary to achieve the appropriate level of protection. Japan is concerned this regulation is more trade-restrictive than necessary, considering the excessive burden this regulation imposes on both foreign competent authorities and private entities that manufacture, process, and store food items to be shipped to China. Lack of transparency creates unforeseeability of the trade with China. We suggest that China take account of the comments and concerns from WTO members.  (In case the US makes further request to China)?Japan also requests China to allow imports from registered facilities regardless of registered commodities till July 1st, 2023 as a grace period for CIFER system enough for manufactures to complete registration without stress, and to set contact points for exporters to communicate with GACC directly and correct their registered information by themselves. Furthermore, Japan requests China to hold an information session concerning operation of the Decree so that the manufacturers may register smoothly.
Summary: Sharing the concern, Japan sought clarification from China on the type of information required for registration following discrepancies between the information contained in Article 10 of the regulation, and the information available on the CIFER system as well as the scope of Decree 248. Japan noted that the list of commodities for which facility registration was required changed frequently, which resulted in unnecessary barriers to trade. Recalling the obligations established in the SPS Agreement, Japan requested China to take Members' comments into account, provide a grace period until 1 July 2023 to allow imports from registered facilities, establish contact points between exporters and China's customs authority, and hold an information session on the operation of the Decree.

StatementSubmitted: China's Administrative Measures for Registration of Overseas Producers of Imported Foods and Administrative Measures on Import and Export Food Safety  (G/TBT/N/CHN/1522) (G/SPS/CHN/1191)March 2022 WTO SPS Committee - Statement by the United States The United States notes that China’s Decrees 248 and 249 came into effect on January 1, 2022.  The United States is concerned with China’s lack of response to requests for scientific justification for these measures and explanation of how these measures will address food safety and public health concerns. The United States again requests China to provide any risk assessments that informed the development of these decrees.  The United States is particularly interested in assessments that justify the identification of high-risk products and the application of these measures to low-risk products. The lack of guidance provided by China is causing considerable confusion for exporters and competent authorities. This confusion is leading to inconsistencies in China’s implementation and enforcement of the measures and causing negative trade impacts.  While China has provided some clarification, much more is needed. In addition, U.S. agencies have been working to resolve issues with shipments frequently being held up at ports in China due to the repeated broadening of the scope of harmonized tariff codes subject to the measures. Meanwhile, companies accumulate demurrage and other port fees while they await resolution, and Chinese consumers face higher prices for safe food.  As we have raised in interventions at every meeting of this Committee since June 2020, any measure of this magnitude requires far more time for producers, exporters, and competent authorities to implement.  Therefore, we ask that China take the following steps to facilitate trade: First, allow entry of all products from registered facilities until July 1, 2023. This additional time will allow facilities to accurately enter or update product information in their online registration.Second, provide a point of contact at the General Administration of Customs of China (GACC) for facilities to contact directly with concerns about the online registration system.Third, hold an informational session in Geneva for trading partners to learn more about GACC’s implementation of the Decrees.
Summary: The United States reiterated its concern regarding China's lack of response to requests for scientific justification and clarification on how the measures established in Decrees 248 and 249 would address food safety and public health concerns. The United States urged China to provide the risk assessments used in the development of the Decrees. Noting instances of shipments held at Chinese ports due to a broadening of the scope of HS codes subject to the measure, the United States requested China to allow entry of products from registered facilities until 1 July 2023, to provide a contact point at China's customs authority to address concerns regarding the online registration system, and to hold an information session in Geneva on the implementation of the Decrees. The United States submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2004.

StatementSubmitted: Australia respects the right of all WTO members to address the safety and quality of imported food products in accordance with the SPS Agreement and based on international standards and guidelines. Australia acknowledges China’s efforts in facilitating implementation of measures under its Regulation on Registration and Administration of Overseas Manufacturers of Imported Food (Decree 248).  Australia remains concerned over the burden imposed on regulatory authorities and exporting businesses in meeting the requirements of the Decree, in particular for low risk processed food products.  Further, Australia reminds China of its obligation to provide notification through the WTO of all future regulation changes to ensure transparency and enable trading partners to effectively implement requirements.   While some implementation issues are unavoidable, Australia remains concerned about the number of issues and delays surrounding the registration of food producers within China’s systems. For example, it is taking more than three weeks for GACC to approve minor changes (such as minor typographical name changes) that are submitted through the CIFER system. Some of these changes are the result of incorrect information entered by GACC.   It is also not clear the length of time it will take GACC to approve new registrations in the system or what the inspection requirements are for new registrations. Will documentation review or virtual inspections be utilised to allow trade to commence for new registrants?  Australia has establishments across a range of commodities wanting to trade with China who stand willing to meet all requirements under Decree 248, however it is not clear what is required for them to complete the registration process.  Australia is ready to work collaboratively with China to address the ongoing implementation issues and to ensure that food safety is upheld while facilitating undisrupted trade.
Summary: Australia reiterated its concerns regarding delays and requirements in the registration processes of China's Regulation on Registration and Administration of Overseas Manufacturers of Imported Foods (Decree 248), in particular for low-risk processed food products. Australia reminded China of its transparency obligations to notify all future regulation changes, and highlighted a number of current challenges relating to the registration of food producers in China Import Food Enterprise Registration (CIFER) system, including the uncertainty in the length and requirements of new registrations approvals. Australia expressed its willingness to work collaboratively with China to ensure food safety while facilitating undisrupted trade.

StatementSubmitted: China’s new “Regulations on the Registration and Administration of Overseas Producers of Imported Food”, has come into effect since January 1st, 2022. Although Japan fully filled in and filed the registration form including the list of items to be manufactured at the facilities, some facilities were registered lacking some product codes filed at the time of application. Some other facilities have not been registered yet without notice of reasons that should be provided in a written form under Article 14 of the registration.? ? As basic obligation, SPS Agreement requests Members that SPS measures are based on scientific principles and risk assessment, and are not more trade-restrictive than required to achieve the appropriate level of sanitary or phytosanitary protection. Japan expresses its concern that information on scientific justification or risk assessment of the new regulation by China has yet to be provided. Japan requests China to provide information on scientific justification or risk assessment of the new regulation imposes the significant burden on foreign authorities and operators, it is more trade-restrictive than necessary? ? The practice of China’s authority for the new regulation could have a significant negative impact on trade with Japan and other Members. Since the measures taken by China lack transparency and risk creating an excessive burden on foreign manufactures, many of the Members, including Japan, raised this issue as a Specific Trade Concern or voiced their support for such concerns. Japan would request China to improve the operation of the registration as well as to make the procedures transparent based on the Members’ remarks at the prior formal meetings.?? Specifically, Japan would request China (1) for registered facilities to be allowed to export any items regardless of the registered product codes until July 1, 2023, (2) to facilitate the registration of new facilities and the correction of the registered contents of facilities, (3) to ensure that registration of facilities or product codes is completed without undue delay, (4) to provide appropriate explanations, time frames, and detailed guidelines about the operation of the regulation including the registration system, and to respond to uncorresponded questions, (5) to establish an enquiry point for interested parties and competent authorities.?
Summary: Japan reported problems with the registration of its facilities for which information had been filed at the time of application. Recalling the obligations established in the SPS Agreement, Japan highlighted that China had not provided scientific justification or risk assessment for its new regulation, which lacked transparency, was burdensome, and restricted trade more than necessary. Japan requested China to allow registered facilities to export any items regardless of the registered product codes until 1 July 2023; to facilitate the registration of new facilities and the correction process; to ensure that registration of facilities or product codes was completed without undue delay; to provide appropriate explanations, time frames, and detailed guidelines about the operation of the regulation; and to establish an enquiry point for interested parties.

StatementSubmitted: Thank you, Chair.Canada joins other Members in continuing to raise significant concerns and challenges with China's administrative measures for the registration of overseas manufacturers of imported food. I refer to Canada’s previous interventions on this item, which remain valid.It remains unclear how China’s Decrees 248 and 249 will contribute to achieving China’s appropriate level of protection and Canada remains concerned that China’s Decrees will negatively and unnecessarily impact trade.Canada remains concerned that the new administrative measures are overly burdensome and unjustified, as they do not appear to be based on an assessment of risks using the risk assessment techniques developed by international organizations, and go beyond the extent necessary to protect against food safety risks. Canada notes that the implementation of the online China Import Food Enterprise Registration (CIFER) system, which was not notified by China to the WTO, will create further barriers to trade including significant financial impacts on both industry and foreign competent authorities. Prior engagement by China with trading partners would have limited the disruptions and concerns being raised by competent authorities and industry stakeholders.Despite repeated requests from trading partners, there remains limited engagement, limited information, and minimal guidance from Customs China regarding the implementation of the CIFER system, which is resulting in continued uncertainty and concerns. As a result, exporters are now encountering delayed clearance of their shipments as companies are unable to register or update their registration in the CIFER system. The registration process in the CIFER system is overly detailed and confusing, lacking a step by step guidance and defined timelines for both competent authorities and industry. As many questions remain regarding the registration process, Canada calls on China to create a single contact or enquiry point for both industry and competent authorities, or to work directly with companies for the completion of their registration. Additionally, Canada expects China to add to the CIFER system, without undue delay, all Canadian products and establishments previously approved by China, but currently not on the list of approved Canadian products and facilities eligible to export to China. Canada strongly urges China to outline all timelines in a transparent manner and develop clear guidance documents to address the questions and concerns from both industry and competent authorities.Canada remains deeply concerned about the unnecessary impact these measures are having on trade. In conclusion, Canada calls on China to provide Members with additional information and clarification on the requirements under  Decrees 248 and 249 and the CIFER system immediately.   Thank you, Chair
Summary: Canada reiterated its concern regarding China's administrative measures that, in its view, were overly burdensome and went beyond the extent necessary to protect against food safety risks. China had not notified the implementation of the online CIFER system, which would create further barriers to trade. Stressing that the registration process in the CIFER system was overly detailed and confusing, Canada requested China to establish a single enquiry point or to work directly with establishments for the completion of their registration. Canada urged China to add to the CIFER system all Canadian products and establishments previously approved by China without undue delay, and to provide further information and clarifications on the implementation of Decrees 248 and 249 and on the CIFER system.

StatementSubmitted: China's Administrative Measures for Registration of Overseas Manufacturers of Imported Foods  (STC 485)June 2022 WTO SPS Committee - Statement by the United StatesThe United States remains deeply concerned with China’s lack of response to requests for scientific justification or an explanation of how Decrees 248 and 249 will address food safety and public health concerns, and requests any risk assessments that informed the development of these decrees.  The United States remains particularly interested in assessments that justify the identification of high-risk products and the application of these measures to low-risk products. The United States notes that the lack of guidance provided by China and inconsistencies in China’s implementation and enforcement of the measures continues to cause considerable confusion for exporters and competent authorities.  The inconsistent and changing application of these administrative measures is directly leading to disruptions in trade.  U.S. agencies continue to face administrative burdens as they work to resolve issues with shipments held up at ports in China.   As we echo statements raised in every meeting of this Committee since June 2020, any measure of this magnitude requires far more time for producers, exporters, and competent authorities to implement.  Therefore, we again ask that China take the following steps to facilitate trade: First, the General Administration of Customs of China (GACC) should continue to use existing government-to- government facility registration processes, as outlined in Article 11 of Decree 248, and not require facilities to enter information online, where such pre-established processes exist. Second, allow entry of all products from registered facilities until at least July 1, 2023 without requiring complete registration information or competent authority intervention. This additional time will allow facilities to accurately enter or update product information in their online registration. Third, provide a central point of contact at the GACC for facilities to contact directly with concerns about the online registration system. Facilities should be able to communicate with this point of contact in English from outside of China, and the point of contact should not refer general registration questions to satellite GACC offices at individual ports. Fourth, hold an informational session in Geneva for trading partners to learn more about GACC’s implementation of the Decrees. We note that GACC’s requests for additional detailed information from facilities and competent authorities, such as process-specific food safety plans and photographs on an establishment-by-establishment basis, create additional administrative burdens for exporters and appear to be unnecessary and unjustified.  We look forward to China’s response to these specific requests and comments.
Summary: The United States reiterated its concern regarding China's lack of response to requests for scientific justification and clarification on how the measures established in Decrees 248 and 249 would address food safety and public health concerns. The United States urged China to provide the risk assessments used in the development of the Decrees. The United States requested China to use existing government-to-government facility registration processes, to allow entry of products from registered facilities until 1 July 2023, to provide a contact point at China's customs authority to address concerns regarding the online registration system, and to hold an information session in Geneva on the implementation of the Decrees. The United States submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2044.

StatementSubmitted: The EU would like to reiterate its concerns about the implementation of Decree 248 of the General Administration of Customs of the People's Republic of China.The EU does not question the wish of China to ensure that imported food products come from legitimate sources. We overall share and support this objective.While China has provided guidance information, and engaged on a dialogue with the EU, problems persist with the lengthy and burdensome mechanism set up by China to register exporting businesses, including: (1) cases of shipments being held up at ports in China due to erroneous or missing information in CIFER; (2) cases of establishments in the meat, dairy and fishery sector that were notified to GACC before the deadline of 31 December and remain unregistered; (3) lack of clarity about the scope and category of products that are covered, which keep expanding; and (4) the obligation put on competent authorities and businesses to consult CIFER almost permanently to be able to follow all the changes made by China to the structure of the CIFER system and to individual registrations, as well as to be informed about the deadlines to re-register individual establishments.Therefore, the EU urges China to:Maintain an open dialogue to solve implementation issues pragmatically and expeditiously;Facilitate new and old registrations by continuing to provide supporting material, guidance documents in English, including on how competent authorities have to verify the establishments that were registered under the fast track procedure;Facilitate amendments/corrections to existing registrations;Facilitate the management by competent authorities and businesses of the changes in CIFER, of the information requested by China and of the deadline to register establishments by introducing an automatic e-mail notifications system in CIFER.The EU would like to thank China for the openness and ongoing dialogue to solve the technical issues related to Decree 248. However, important implementation issues need to be solved in order to eliminate all disruptions to trade as soon as possible and before 1 July 2023.
Summary: The European Union reiterated its concerns and stressed that China had set the lengthy and burdensome mechanism to register exporting businesses. The European Union emphasized the lack of clarity regarding the expansion of product coverage, and the frequent changes introduced in the CIFER system. The European Union urged China to maintain an open dialogue to solve implementation issues, to provide guidelines on registration in English and on the verification of establishments registered under the fast-track procedure, and to facilitate amendments to existing registrations and the management of changes to existing registrations in order to solve this issue before 1 July 2023.

StatementSubmitted: Japan would like to reiterate its concerns about the implementation of China’s new “Regulations on the Registration and Administration of Overseas Producers of Imported Food,” which entered into force in January this year. We appreciate China’s efforts to try to implement this measure smoothly. However, Japan remains concerned that the new regulations lack transparency and impose a significant burden on foreign authorities and manufacturers, due to reasons that Japan and other Members have expressed repeatedly at previous meetings of this Committee. Japan reiterates that one of the fundamental obligations under the SPS Agreement is the requirement that Members ensure their SPS measures are based on scientific principles and appropriate risk assessments, and that the measures are not more trade-restrictive than required to achieve an appropriate level of SPS protection. Japan therefore requests that China improve its registration procedures, and make the procedures appropriately transparent, based on the remarks made by Members at this and previous SPS Committee meetings.Specifically, Japan requests that China: (1) Explain the scientific justification for introducing the new regulations, including the results of the risk assessment they relied on.(2) Notify the Members promptly of any changes in the operation of its regulations or China Import Food Enterprise Registration (CIFER) system, including changes to product codes (HS?CIQ) used in the system, which will or might affect exports. Should any changes occur, we also ask that GACC provides a reasonable transitional period.(3) Permit, as an interim measure, previously registered facilities prior to the introduction of the new regulation, to export all items, even when there are incorrect or incomplete product information, until July 1, 2023.(4) Add all product codes (HS?CIQ) that are currently missing from the product code list shown on the system before the end of this year.(5) Establish an enquiry point for interested parties and competent authorities, and hold an information session in Geneva for concerned Members regarding implementation of the regulations, by the end of this year.(6) Respond to unanswered questions within a reasonable time.Japan thanks China for its prompt attention to resolving these issues in an appropriate and timely manner.
Summary: Recalling the obligations established in the SPS Agreement, Japan expressed concerns regarding China's administrative measures for registration of overseas manufacturers, in force since January 2022, which lacked transparency, were burdensome, and restricted trade more than necessary. Japan requested China to provide a scientific justification of its new measures; to notify any change in the operation of China Import Food Enterprise Registration (CIFER) system; to allow registered facilities to export any items regardless of the registered product codes until 1 July 2023; to add all missing product codes to the system before the end of 2022; to establish an enquiry point for interested parties; and to respond to unanswered questions within a reasonable time.

StatementSubmitted: November 2022 WTO SPS Committee   –  U.S. Statement on China’s Administrative Measures for Registration of Overseas Manufacturers of Imported Foods (26 November 2019) (STC ID 485)The United States remains deeply concerned with China’s continued lack of response to the numerous requests for scientific justification or an explanation of how Decrees 248 and 249 will address food safety and public health concerns and requests any risk assessments that informed the development of these decrees.  The United States remains particularly interested in assessments that justify the identification of high-risk products and the application of these measures to low-risk products.The United States notes that the lack of guidance provided by China and inconsistencies in China’s implementation and enforcement of the measures continue to cause considerable confusion for exporters and competent authorities. The inconsistent and changing application of these administrative measures is directly leading to disruptions in trade.  U.S. agencies continue to face administrative burdens as they work to resolve issues with shipments held up at ports in China. Additionally, China’s General Administration of Customs, GACC, appears to require foreign competent authorities to perform administrative duties and maintain information in China’s online system for each foreign registered facility producing certain categories of products.  These types of administrative functions are fundamentally the responsibility of the importing country, not foreign food safety regulators. GACC should ensure that all facilities are able to self-register without foreign competent authority involvement.The United States also remains concerned regarding GACC’s requests for additional detailed information from facilities and competent authorities, such as process-specific food safety plans and photographs on a facility-by-facility basis, as part of a pre-market registration process. These requirements have created a premarket approval regime with administrative burdens on foreign competent authorities and exporters that appear to be unnecessary and lack a risk or scientific justification. We look forward to China’s response to these specific requests and comments.
Summary: The United States reiterated its concern regarding China's lack of response to requests for scientific justification and sought clarification on how the measures established in Decrees 248 and 249 would address food safety and public health concerns. The United States urged China to provide the risk assessments that justified the identification of high-risk products and the application of the measures to low-risk products. The United States stressed the confusion and trade-disruption caused by the lack of guidance and the inconsistent implementation of measures. Noting that all facilities should be able to self-register, the United States noted that GACC was transferring to foreign competent authorities certain responsibilities of the importing country, and that the additional information requested as part of the pre-market registration process was unnecessarily burdensome. The United States submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2084.

StatementSubmitted: Australia respects the right of all WTO members to address the safety and quality of imported food products in accordance with the SPS Agreement and based on international standards and guidelines.Australia acknowledges China’s efforts in facilitating implementation of measures under its Regulation on Registration and Administration of Overseas Manufacturers of Imported Food (known as Decree 248). Further to previous statements, the requirements of Decree 248 duplicate effort when exporting country authorities have already certified to agreed conditions. Australia acknowledges that the implementation of CIFER has not been without disruption and that GACC has adjusted the program during the intervening period.Australia remains concerned about a number of issues and delays surrounding the registrations of new food businesses and the renewal of registrations of Australian food businesses. Issues experienced by Australia include:1.            The requirement for the complete updating of a registration and approval by GACC before an extension application can be submitted to ensure continued registration listing with China.2.            Lack of clarity on the documentation required to support an application, and on the process and timing for an assessment to be completed.3.            GACC’s slow response time to submissions of applications making it difficult for Australian businesses to make corrections and return applications for reconsideration ahead of GACC-imposed deadlines. 4.            Rejection of applications with insufficient information for food businesses to comprehend the reason for rejection and for the Australian competent authority to assist within the limited time available.More recently, a technical issue with CIFER prevented all Australian seafood establishments from accessing their registrations to update information during the limited period allowed to extend their registrations before expiration.Australia would like China to advise the length of time it will take GACC to approve new registrations and the inspection requirements required for new registrations to take effect. Australia has previously raised concerns over the number of applications for listing registration dating back to 2017, for which Australia has received no advice on how to proceed.Australia appreciates the recent assistance of GACC in accepting the 220 seafood applications and 5 infant formula applications submitted by food Australian businesses to update their records before they can extend their registration. The requirement to complete these by 30 September however was not achievable given the lack of clarity and instruction issues outlined above and Australia seeks assurances that China GACC will work closely with Australia to address these and other ongoing implementation issues to avoid disruption to trade.
Summary: Australia noted the duplication of efforts imposed by Decree 248, the disruptions experienced in the implementation of CIFER, and the adjustments to the programme made by GACC during the intervening period. Listing some of the issues experienced by food businesses, Australia requested China to advise the time needed for the approval of new registrations and the inspection requirements for new registrations to take effect. Regretting the absence of response on previous concerns raised and the inability to meet China's deadlines due to the lack of instructions, Australia sought assurance on the cooperation with GACC to address these ongoing issues.

StatementSubmitted: • Thank you, Chair.• Canada and other Members continue to raise significant concerns and challenges with China's administrative measures for the registration of overseas manufacturers of imported food.• I refer to Canada’s previous interventions on this item, which remain valid.• It remains unclear how China’s Decrees 248 and 249 will contribute to achieving China’s appropriate level of protection. Canada remains concerned that China’s Decrees and the implementation of the China Import Food Enterprise Registration (CIFER) system is negatively and unnecessarily impacting trade.• Canada notes that the implementation of the CIFER system is increasing the burden on the resources of foreign competent authorities and creating significant financial impacts and uncertainty for industry.• As an example, China’s registration and approval process in CIFER requires both the foreign competent authority and Customs China to manually review and approve the information submitted by companies in CIFER. This requires the allocation of significant resources by foreign competent authorities and causes delays in the registration update and renewal process for companies seeking to export to China.• The registration process in the CIFER system is confusing, substantially hindered by ongoing technical challenges, and lacks clear guidance and defined timelines for both competent authorities and industry.• Despite repeated requests from trading partners, there remains limited engagement or guidance from Customs China regarding the implementation of the CIFER system, which is resulting in continued uncertainty and concerns by trading partners.• Canada notes that after repeated attempts, none of the Canadian fish and seafood establishments, whose CIFER registrations will expire on December 31, 2022, have been able to successfully obtain approval from Customs China for their applications.• Canada strongly urges China to communicate all timelines and decisions related to its review and approval process in CIFER in a transparent manner. Canada urges China to develop clear guidance documents to address the questions and concerns from both industry and foreign competent authorities.• As many questions remain regarding the CIFER registration process, Canada calls on China to create separate contact points within Customs China for both industry and foreign competent authorities, or to work directly with companies for the completion and renewal of their registrations in CIFER.• Canada remains deeply concerned about the impact these measures are having on trade and recalls that in October 2021, China stated that Decrees 248 and 249 and CIFER would not impact trade. Therefore, Canada asks that China commit to improving the efficiency of its registration approval process in CIFER to ensure that trade is not disrupted.• In conclusion, Canada calls on China to provide Members with additional information, clarification and flexibility on the requirements under Decrees 248 and 249 and the CIFER system immediately to avoid further delays in the registration process for Canadian companies and prevent unnecessary trade disruptions.    • Thank you, Chair.
Summary: Referring to its previous statements on this issue, Canada reiterated its concern regarding China's administrative measures and the implementation of the CIFER system that were negatively impacting trade. Noting China's lack of engagement and guidance, Canada stressed that the registration process in CIFER system was confusing and experienced technical challenges. Canada called for transparency in the communication of decisions on the approval process in the CIFER system and for the development of clear guidance to address concerns of trading partners. Canada requested China to establish a contact point or to work directly with establishments for the completion of registrations; to provide clarifications and flexibilities on the requirements under Decrees 248 and 249 and the CIFER system; and to prevent unnecessary trade disruptions.

StatementSubmitted: The EU must raise this topic again to highlight remaining concerns about the implementation of Decree 248 of the General Administration of Customs of the People's Republic of China. The EU does not question the wish of China to ensure that imported food products come from legitimate sources. We overall share and support this objective.However, EU applicants are still facing many issues in the registration process, mostly due to the web-based registration system (CIFER), which still shows numerous technical problems, making the electronic submission of documents cumbersome, time consuming and uncertain.Adding to this difficulty, the Customs Administration informed recently EU Member States that certain product categories will be exempt from the registration procedure that had previously been included under Article 7 of Decree 248. But GACC does not clearly identify these products. Due to the unclear scope of the registration and the numerous technical issues with CIFER, EU Member State authorities are facing massive difficulty implementing Decree 248. Competent authorities and businesses must consult the CIFER data base almost permanently to follow individual registrations and react to unforeseen issues. To avoid food trade disruption, we must request that existing approvals remain valid until the renewal process under Decree 248 is soundly established. Under the current circumstances it appears impossible to complete the registration process under Article 7 by the deadline foreseen, which is June 2023.The EU urges China to:-Provide clear guidance and supporting materials on products falling under Article 7 of Decree 248 and on procedures applicable to products which are not covered. -Simplify the data entry and resolving the software problems with the CIFER system; -Facilitate amendments/corrections and follow up to ongoing registrations;-Extend the deadline of June 2023 given that it is very unlikely, given the technical problems relating to the registration system, that all establishments falling under Article 7 of Decree 248 can complete their registration in time.The EU would like to thank China for the dialogue so far which helped to address several technical questions related to Decree 248. However, important issues remain to be resolved. Thank you, Chair.
Summary: While sharing the wish to ensure that imported food products came from legitimate sources, the European Union raised concerns on the difficulties in registering business in the CIFER system. The European Union noted that GACC had not clearly identified the product categories previously subject to registration under Decree 248 that were to be exempt from the procedure. The European Union urged China to provide clear guidance on the implementation of Decree 248; to simplify data entry and solve technical problems in the CIFER system; to facilitate amendments and follow-up of ongoing registrations; and to extend the June 2023 deadline for registration.

StatementSubmitted: Australia respects the right of all WTO members to address the safety and quality of imported food products in accordance with the SPS Agreement and based on international standards and guidelines.Australia acknowledges the difficulties China has had in the implementation of the CIFER system as part of its roll out of the regulation known as Decree 248, and that GACC has adjusted the program since the regulation was first promulgated.Australia acknowledges and appreciates the cooperation between the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry and GACC to mitigate the risk of trade disruption throughout the process of establishment registration extensions. While we acknowledge that China has responded to Australia’s comments in both the WTO TBT and SPS Committees, it is often difficult to get clear direction and information to support our understanding of what is required to comply with China’s requirements.Australia remains concerned about timeframes, lack of clear advice from GACC, and delays in registration of new and existing Australian food businesses. Australia therefore encourages China to provide:Reasonable timeframes for:assessing, re-evaluating and adjusting applications in the CIFER system;notifying competent authorities of updates to the system.Clear and timely advice on:evidence required to support applications, and the acceptance of official verification of documentation for its intended purpose;changes to HS codes, including additions or removals of commodity lines, that need to comply with regulations.Appropriate guidance (including instructional material), assistance and resources to both individual enterprises and competent authorities in meeting China’s registration requirements.Continuity of trade for all registered food businesses until CIFER IT system issues are resolved. Equal opportunity for all food businesses registered in CIFER to access their accounts in CIFER and apply for modifications and registration extensions  For example, establishments registered in CIFER that are suspended from trade by GACC due to non-compliances, do not have the functionality in their profiles to submit applications for extension. Therefore, they are unable to apply to extend their registrations before they expire, effectively cancelling their trading registration.
Summary: Australia acknowledged the difficulties China had in the implementation of its CIFER system in the context of the implementation of China's Decree 248 and appreciated cooperation with the GACC to mitigate the risk of trade disruption throughout the process of establishment registration extensions. However, Australia remained concerned about timeframes, lack of clear and timely advice from the GACC, and delays in registration of new and existing Australian food businesses. Australia encouraged China to allow for reasonable timeframes for application submission and adjustment in the CIFER system, notify competent authorities of updates to the system, provide clear and timely advice on any changes to HS codes, provide appropriate guidance to all affected entities on meeting requirements, ensure continuity of trade until CIFER IT system issues are resolved, and provide equal opportunity for all food businesses registered in CIFER to access their accounts in CIFER and apply for modifications and registration extensions.

StatementSubmitted: Thank you, Chair.The EU must raise this topic again to highlight remaining concerns about the implementation of Decree 248 of the General Administration of Customs of the People's Republic of China (GACC). More than a year after its entry into force, the EU considers that the whole process of implementation of Decree 248 is still very burdensome and not transparent.As previously mentioned, EU applicants are still facing many issues in the registration process, mostly due to recurrent technical problems with the web-based registration system (CIFER), making the electronic submission of documents cumbersome, time consuming and uncertain, be it to apply for new registrations or to amend or correct existing registrations. In this context, EU applicants are concerned with the upcoming deadline of June 2023 to provide supplementary information for existing registrations. Due to recurrent technical problems with the CIFER system it is unlikely that all establishments will be able to complete their registration on time.  More recently EU applicants have also faced difficulties regarding the renewals of past registrations, with a burdensome procedure including first an application for “modification” followed by an application for “extension”.  In order to avoid food trade disruption, the EU urges China to:Resolve the technical software problems with the CIFER system; Facilitate the process to amend/correct existing registrations Extend the deadline of June 2023 to provide supplementary information on existing registrationsSimplify the renewal procedure for past registrations and allow that trade can continue until these establishments conclude the renewal The EU would like to thank China for the constructive dialogue which so far helped to address several questions related to implementation of Decree 248. Thank you, Chair.
Summary: The European Union expressed its continued concern regarding the process of implementation of China's Decree 248, which it considered to be burdensome and not transparent. The European Union noted applicants faced many issues during the registration process, and was concerned with the upcoming deadline of June 2023 for existing registrations. The European Union indicated that it was unlikely registrations would be completed for all establishments given technical issues and given recent issues faced regarding renewals, modification, and extension procedures. The European Union requested China to resolve these technical issues, facilitate amendment/correction of existing registrations, extend the June 2023 deadline for existing registrations, and simplify the renewal process.

StatementSubmitted: China Administrative Measures for Registration of Overseas Manufacturers of Imported Foods (26 November 2019) (STC 485)Statement by the United States  - March 2023 WTO SPS CommitteeThe United States remains deeply concerned with China’s lack of scientific justification or explanation of how Decrees 248 and 249 address food safety and public health concerns.In its response to the United States and other members during the November SPS 2022 Committee meeting, China did not respond to any of the substantive concerns raised and still has not provided the scientific basis or risk assessments that informed the development of these Decrees, which the United States and other members have repeatedly requested. The United States once again requests that China provide this vital information.In addition, we again note that China’s General Administration of Customs (GACC) appears to require foreign competent authorities to maintain information in China’s online system for each registered facility from their country producing certain categories of products.  Such a requirement creates tremendous administrative burdens on foreign competent authorities without a clear connection to food safety outcomes. GACC should ensure that all facilities are able to self-register without foreign competent authority involvement or unreasonable information requirements.Finally, we note that GACC’s deadline of June 30, 2023, for firms and competent authorities to complete the registration process is completely unrealistic.  The actions GACC appears to request would take years to complete, if they are even possible at all. We request that China indefinitely suspend this deadline to allow trade to continue while China addresses outstanding concerns with these requirements.We maintain our availability to work with China on this issue and look forward to receiving the information that we have requested.
Summary: The United States reiterated its concern regarding China's lack of response to requests for scientific justification and sought clarification on how the measures established in Decrees 248 and 249 would address food safety and public health concerns. The United States urged China to provide the risk assessments that informed the development of these Decrees. The United States stressed the confusion and trade disruption caused by the lack of guidance and the inconsistent implementation of measures and indicated that all facilities should be able to self-register. The United States considered the GACC's deadline of June 2023 for registration of all firms to be unrealistic, and requested suspension of this deadline until concerns were addressed. The United States submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2113.

StatementSubmitted: Once again, Japan would like to raise its concerns regarding China’s implementation of Decree 248, which involves administrative measures for registration of overseas manufacturers of imported food.  Japan remains concerned that the regulations lack transparency and impose a significant burden on foreign authorities and manufacturers, for the reasons Japan and other Members have expressed repeatedly at previous meetings of this Committee. In addition, while Japan appreciates the letter from China’s General Administration of Customs (GACC), dated 27 October 2022, explaining that overseas manufacturers of certain primary edible agricultural products need to be registered via letters/emails, instead of using the China Import Food Enterprise Registration (CIFER) system, the details of these alternative procedures have not been made clear. Moreover, the procedures are uncertain and lack predictability.Japan reiterates that one of the fundamental obligations under the SPS Agreement is the requirement that Members ensure their SPS measures are based on scientific principles and appropriate risk assessments, and are not more trade-restrictive than required to achieve an appropriate level of SPS protection. Therefore, Japan requests that China improve its registration procedures, and make the procedures appropriately transparent.Specifically, Japan requests that China: Explain the scientific justification for introduction of the regulations, including the results of the risk assessment on which China relied.Notify the Members promptly of any changes in the operation of its regulations or the CIFER system, including changes to product codes (HS?CIQ) used in the system, which will or might affect exports. Should any changes occur, we also ask that GACC provide a reasonable transition period.As an interim measure, permit facilities that were registered prior to introduction of the regulation to export all items, even when there are incorrect or incomplete product information, until 30 June 2023.Add all product codes (HS?CIQ) that are currently missing from the product code list shown on the system.Give an explanation, supported by sufficiently clear and detailed reasons, when an application is rejected.Establish an enquiry point for interested parties and competent authorities, and hold an information session in Geneva for concerned Members regarding implementation of the regulations, including an explanation of registration procedures for certain primary edible agricultural products.Respond to unanswered questions within a reasonable time.Japan also would like to echo the previous speakers, in stating that China should extend the June 2023 deadline for submission of additional relevant information for the validity of existing approvals of establishments falling within Article 7 of Decree 248.Japan thanks China for its prompt attention to resolving these issues in an appropriate and timely manner.
Summary: Japan echoed the concerns expressed by other Members on China's implementation of Decree 248 and its obligations under the SPS Agreement. Japan remained concerned regarding issues associated with the CIFER system, including the lack transparency, burdensome requirements, uncertain procedures, and lack of predictability. Japan requested China to provide a scientific justification of its new measures including the results of risk assessments, notify any change in the operation of the CIFER system with a reasonable transition period, allow previously registered facilities to export any items regardless of the registered product codes until 30 June 2023, add all missing product codes to the system, provide clear explanations as to when an application would be rejected; establish an enquiry point for interested parties, hold an information session in Geneva, and respond to unanswered questions within a reasonable time.

StatementSubmitted: Australia respects the right of all WTO members to address the safety and quality of imported food products in accordance with the SPS Agreement and based on international standards and guidelines.Australia welcomes the recent information session in Geneva and amendments to the CIFER system and hopes these changes deliver the desired outcome of a simplified registration process. Whilst we are yet to fully understand the impacts of these recent amendments, we believe the changes to allow suspended establishments to retain their registration and the ability for establishments to change details such as their address and legal representatives will result in a more efficient system.Australia acknowledges the difficulties China has had in the implementation of the CIFER system as part of its roll out of the regulation known as Decree 248, and that GACC has adjusted the program since the regulation was first started.Australia acknowledges and appreciates the cooperation of GACC officials to mitigate the risk of trade disruption throughout the process of establishment registration. While we acknowledge that China has responded to Australia’s comments in both the WTO TBT and SPS Committees, it has been difficult to get clear direction and consistent information to support our understanding of what is required to comply with China’s requirements.Australia remains concerned about timeframes, lack of clear advice from GACC, and delays in registration of new and existing Australian food businesses. Australia therefore encourages China to provide:Reasonable timeframes for:assessing, re-evaluating and adjusting applications in the CIFER system;notifying competent authorities of updates to the system.Clear and timely advice on:evidence required to support applications, and the acceptance of official verification of documentation for its intended purpose;changes to HS codes, including additions or removals of commodity lines, that need to comply with regulations.Appropriate guidance (including instructional material), assistance and resources to both individual enterprises and competent authorities in meeting China’s registration requirements.Continuity of trade for all food businesses with extension and/or modification applications submitted in the CIFER system. We look forward to continuing to work with China on these important matters.
Summary: Australia welcomed the recent information session in Geneva and amendments to the China Imported Food Enterprise Registration (CIFER) system and hoped these changes would deliver the desired outcome. In Australia's view, changes that allowed for suspended establishments to retain their registration and for the ability to change details such as their address and legal representatives would result in a more efficient system. Australia also acknowledged the difficulties China had in the implementation of its CIFER system and appreciated cooperation with the General Administration of Customs China (GACC) to mitigate the risk of trade disruption throughout the process of establishment registration extensions. However, Australia remained concerned about timeframes, lack of clear and timely advice from the GACC, and delays in registration of new and existing food businesses. Australia encouraged China to allow for reasonable timeframes for application submission and adjustment in the CIFER system, notify competent authorities of updates to the system, provide clear and timely advice on any changes to HS codes, provide appropriate guidance to all affected entities on meeting requirements, ensure continuity of trade until CIFER system issues were resolved, and allow for modifications of applications submitted in the CIFER system.

StatementSubmitted: Once again, Japan would like to raise its concerns regarding China’s implementation of Decree 248, which involves administrative measures for registration of overseas manufacturers of imported food.  Japan appreciates China’s willingness to address the concerns we have expressed in previous occasions, and also thanks China for its recent bilateral engagement with us. We especially welcome China’s explanation that?there will be no adverse impact on trade for the manufacturers having submitted additional documents to China by 30 June, even if the procedures by Chinese side to register these establishments have not completed by the end of June.Having said that, Japan remains concerned that the regulations lack transparency and impose a significant burden on foreign authorities and manufacturers, for the reasons Japan and other Members have expressed repeatedly at previous meetings of this Committee.Therefore, Japan requests that China improve its registration procedures, and make the procedures appropriately transparent.Specifically, Japan requests that China: Establish a standard processing period for applications made through the CIFER system (i.e., a standard timeline to be followed from application through registration), and make that processing period known to the Members and foreign manufacturers.Notify the Members promptly of any changes in the operation of its regulations or the CIFER system, including changes to product codes (HS?CIQ) used in the system, which will or might affect exports. Should any changes occur, we also ask that GACC provide a reasonable transition period.Correct any defects in the CIFER system as soon as possible, including: (a) the current, considerable delays in the registration process; (b)its inability to accept letters of proxy; and (c) the fact that some of the product codes (HS CIQ) are missing from the list shown on the system.Respond to unanswered questions within a reasonable time.Give sufficient explanation, for the reasons when an application is rejected through the CIFER system and ensure its consistency. Japan thanks China for its prompt attention to resolving these issues in an appropriate and timely manner.
Summary: Japan thanked China for its bilateral engagement and information on documents submitted by 30 June, but remained concerned that regulations lacked transparency and imposed a significant burden on foreign authorities and manufacturers. Japan requested China to establish a standard processing period for applications made through the CIFER system and clarify the processing period to the Members, notify changes in the operation of its regulations or the CIFER system with a reasonable transition period if changes were introduced, correct defects in the CIFER system as soon as possible, respond to unanswered questions within a reasonable time, provide explanations when an application was rejected through the CIFER system, and ensure consistency.

StatementSubmitted: CHINA’S ADMINISTRATIVE MEASURES FOR REGISTRATION OF OVERSEAS MANUFACTURERS OF IMPORTED FOOD (26 NOVEMBER 2019) – SPECIFIC TRADE CONCERN 485Statement by the United States of America - July 2023 SPS Committee:The United States remains deeply concerned with China’s lack of scientific justification or explanation of how Decrees 248 and 249 address food safety and public health concerns.In its response to the United States and other members following previous SPS Committee meetings, China noted that limited guidance had been provided on these measures and stated the numbers of facilities that appear to have successfully registered per these Decrees. However, China did not respond to any of the substantive concerns raised and has not provided the scientific basis or risk assessment that informed the development of these Decrees, which the United States and other members have repeatedly requested. The United States once again requests that China provide this vital information.In addition, we again note that China’s General Administration of Customs requires foreign competent authorities to maintain information in China’s online system for each registered facility from their country producing certain categories of products.  Such a requirement creates tremendous administrative burdens on foreign competent authorities without a clear connection to food safety outcomes. It remains unclear to the United States how China determined which products may self-register and which products require registration through a competent authority. GACC should ensure that all facilities subject to Decree 248 requirements are able to self-register without foreign competent authority involvement.We look forward to receiving the information that we have requested from China.Finally, we note that new requirements that came into effect after June 30, 2023 have caused significant confusion for U.S. exporters due to the lack of clear guidance.  We once again emphasize the importance of meaningful outreach to foreign governments and private exporters well in advance of significant changes to the implementation of these Decrees.
Summary: The United States reiterated its concern regarding China's lack of response to requests for scientific justification and sought clarification on how the measures established in Decrees 248 and 249 would address food safety and public health concerns. The United States urged China to provide the risk assessments that informed the development of these decrees. The United States stressed the large administrative burden on competent authorities and requested that all facilities should be able to self-register. The United States noted that the new requirements that came into effect after 30 June 203 had caused confusion due to lack of guidance and highlighted the importance of meaningful outreach ahead of implementation of these decrees. The United States submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2147.

StatementSubmitted: The EU reiterates its concerns about the implementation of “administrative measures for registration of overseas producers of imported foods” i.e. Decree 248 of the General Administration of Customs of the People's Republic of China (GACC). The EU concerns were most recently raised in May 2023 in a joint letter to the Permanent Mission of the People's Republic of China in Geneva that the EU co-signed with five other WTO members.In general, EU applicants have been facing many issues in the registration process, mostly due to recurrent technical problems with the online registration system (CIFER), making the electronic submission of documents cumbersome, time consuming and uncertain, be it to apply for new registrations and/or to amend or renew existing registrations.More specifically, over the last weeks, the EU expressed concerns with the deadline of 30 June 2023 to provide supplementary information for existing registrations. In the May 2023 joint letter, the EU called for a pragmatic approach in the implementation of Decree 248 that will allow establishments to continue exporting beyond the deadline of 30 June 2023. At this stage, it looks that the 30 June deadline did not lead to trade disruptions and we hope this will continue to be the case in the future.To avoid any food trade disruption due to Decree 248, the EU urges China to simplify and facilitate the process to apply for new registrations and/or to amend or renew existing registrations.The EU would finally like to thank again China for the constructive dialogues which has allowed to address several questions related to implementation of Decree 248 and which has so far helped to avoid major trade disruption.
Summary: The European Union reiterated its concern regarding the process of implementation of China's Decree 248, which it considered to be burdensome and not transparent. The European Union noted applicants faced many issues during the registration process and was concerned with the upcoming deadline of June 2023 for existing registrations. The European Union recalled a joint letter to China which had called for a pragmatic approach to implementation of Decree 248 and called for an extension of the deadline. While the 30 June deadline did not cause major trade disruptions, the European Union requested China to simplify and facilitate the process to apply for new registrations and to amend existing ones.

Brazil provided the following statement: Last February, Saudi authorities suddenly suspended imports from two Brazilian major poultry-producing plants. In that month, Brazil became aware of Letter No. 19672/E, through which the Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) informs about its decision to temporarily suspend imports from plants SIF 1985 and SIF 2518 (both from same company, BRF S/A). One of them was responsible for over 20% of our poultry exports to Saudi Arabia. No clear technical grounds were provided by Saudi authorities, except for media reports on an investigation conducted by Brazil's federal police that, in 2018, targeted an alleged fraud scheme in the production of animal feed. However, neither of the plants suspended last February were involved in said investigation. Brazil's Agriculture and Foreign Affairs authorities provided Saudi Arabia all the technical information necessary, but the issue remains open. As Members will recall, at the WTO SPS Committee 77th Regular Meeting, Saudi Arabia informed it would disclose said technical reasons, but failed to do so. It goes without saying that SPS measures without any scientific substance goes against the very core of SPS Agreement. We therefore urge Saudi Arabia to reconsider its restrictive measures as soon as possible.

StatementSubmitted:
Mr. Chair,

As we have previously stated here in the SPS Committee, Brazil was taken by surprise when it came to our knowledge, last February, that Saudi authorities had suspended imports from two major Brazilian poultry-producing plants. That month Brazil became aware of Letter No. 19672/E, through which the Saudi Food and Drug authority (SFDA) informs about its decision to temporarily suspend imports of products manufactured in establishments under SIF codes 1985 and 2518 (both belonging to the same company, BRF S/A). One of them was responsible for over 20% of our poultry exports to Saudi Arabia. No clear technical reasons were provided by the Saudi authorities. Saudi Arabia has claimed that the suspension of these two plants happened as a consequence of media reports on an investigation conducted by Brazil`s federal police that, in 2018, targeted an alleged fraud scheme in the production of animal feed. Neither of the plants suspended last February was involved in the investigation, though.

Brazil`s ministries of Agriculture and Foreign Affairs, through direct and diplomatic channels, have provided Saudi Arabia with all the technical information necessary, but have not received any response yet. Saudi Arabia has so far not given Brazil a technical reason for the suspension of the two establishments, most recently at this floor, during the WTO SPS Committee 77th Regular Meeting. It goes without saying that SPS measures without any scientific substance go against the very core of SPS Agreement.

We therefore urge Saudi Arabia to reconsider its restrictive measures.

Thank you.
Summary: Brazil reiterated its concern regarding the temporary suspension by Saudi Arabia of imports from two major Brazilian poultry-producing plants since February 2019, without providing clear technical reasons. Brazil noted Saudi Arabia's reference to media reports on an investigation conducted in Brazil regarding an alleged fraud scheme in the production of animal feed. Brazil indicated that neither of the plants affected by the suspension of imports was involved in this investigation and all necessary technical information had been provided to Saudi Arabia.

StatementSubmitted:
Brazil would like call all Members’ attention to this STC, since we believe Saudi Arabia`s policies to protect its market from imported poultry are systematically defying many rules of the multilateral
trading system, especially the SPS Agreement.

In recent years, Saudi Arabia has been increasingly adopting a series of tariff and non-tariff measures in order to restrict the access of imported poultry to its domestic market. These measures range from tariff rises and a new import licenses` system to regulatory changes in shelf-life periods, as well as the outright suspension of plants from exporting countries without scientific evidence, which is the object of this STC.

In what regards restrictive SPS measures without scientific evidence, Brazilian products, whose quality and safety have been recognized by sanitary authorities around the world, have been the main target of Saudi
authorities. As we have previously stated here in the SPS Committee, the Brazilian government was taken by surprise when it came to our knowledge, in February 2020, that Saudi authorities had suspended imports
from two major Brazilian poultry-producing plants.

 

That month, Brazil became aware of Letter No. 19672/E, through which the Saudi Food and Drug authority (SFDA) informs about its decision to temporarily suspend imports of products manufactured in establishments
under SIF codes 1985 and 2518 (both belonging to the same company. One of them was responsible for over 20% of our poultry exports to Saudi Arabia.
No technical reasons were provided then by the Saudi authorities. Saudi Arabia has claimed that the suspension of these two plants happened as a
consequence of media reports on an investigation conducted by Brazil`s federal police that, in 2018, targeted an alleged fraud scheme in the production of animal feed. Neither of the plants suspended that February was involved in the investigation. As Members will recall, on the WTO SPS Committee 77th Regular Meeting, Saudi Arabia informed it would disclose said technical reasons, but failed to do so.

More recently, another round of suspension of Brazilian poultry producing plants took place. On May 9th, Saudi Arabia, through a note verbale to our
Embassy in Riyadh, informed that 11 more plants were suspended. We should highlight that the official communication to our authorities came after it was published on the website of the Saudi Food and Drug Authority. In other words, the communication came only after the plants had been suspended, without any possibility of technical clarifications, which, may I stress, have not even been asked for.

The reasons given by Saudi Arabia were evasive, claiming that these 11 Brazilian plants did not comply with overall limits of microbiological patterns established by a domestic technical regulation. However, Saudi authorities did not specify any data regarding quantifications of the limits which were allegedly surpassed.

Brazil understands that such restrictions reinforced by Saudi Arabia`s attitude towards our exports of poultry conflict with the dispositions of SPS Agreement, especially article 2, 5, 8 and its Annex C.
 

We therefore urge Saudi Arabia to reconsider its restrictive measures as soon as possible.
Summary: Brazil drew Members' attention to the tariff and non-tariff measures imposed by Saudi Arabia restricting market access of poultry without scientific evidence. In 2020, Brazil became aware through Letter No. 19672/E that the Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) had temporarily suspended imports of products manufactured in two establishments, without providing technical reasons. Later on, another 11 plants were suspended without the possibility to provide technical clarifications. Brazil considered such restrictions to violate Articles 2, 5 and 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement and urged Saudi Arabia to reconsider its restrictive measures as soon as possible.

As Members will recall, at the WTO SPS Committee 77th Regular Meeting, Saudi Arabia informed it would disclose technical reasons, but it has failed to do so.

On May 9th, Saudi Arabia, through a "note verbale" to our Embassy in Riyadh, informed that 11 more plants were suspended. StatementSubmitted: Once again, Brazil would like to draw all Members' attention to this STC, as we believe that Saudi Arabia's policies restricting access to its market for imported poultry systematically clash with obligations established in the SPS Agreement.Since February 2020, Saudi Arabia has been suspending poultry-producing plants without any scientific justification. Saudi Arabia has failed to provide even a single laboratory report indicating any requirement violation. In one of the cases, Brazil was informed that a plant that was authorized to export was suspended for violation of the parameters; however, at that time, that specific plant was not even allowed to export to Saudi Arabia.During the last SPS Committee Meeting, Saudi Arabia responded that the measures imposed on Brazilian establishments were compliant with the provisions of the SPS Agreement. This is not the case: Saudi Arabia has still not provided specific scientific documents to base its restrictions, which constitutes a breach of article 2 of the Agreement. Furthermore, as its risk evaluation was not clearly presented, it is also not in accordance with article 5.Despite the suspensions in force, on January 27th, Saudi Arabia authorized the suspended plants to export poultry, even though the suspensions were not formally withdrawn yet. For Brazil, this position demonstrates that there is an unwarranted measure in force, not based on proper risk analysis that would aim at determining the appropriate level of sanitary protection.Therefore, Brazil would like to address a specific question to Saudi Arabia: what kind of sanitary concern regarding poultry can justify the suspension of Brazilian establishments, but still allow exports from them to Saudi Arabia? Brazil hopes Saudi Arabia can kindly provide us with the answer to this question during this session.
Summary: Brazil explained that since February 2020, Saudi Arabia had suspended exports from Brazilian poultry-producing plants without scientific justification. Brazil considered Saudi Arabia's policies to be at odds with Articles 2 and 5 of the SPS Agreement. Brazil informed Members that on 27 January 2022, Saudi Arabia had authorized the suspended plants to export poultry, although the suspensions had not been formally withdrawn. In Brazil's view, this demonstrated that the measures were neither justified nor based on a proper risk analysis. Brazil requested clarification on the sanitary concern which justified suspending Brazilian poultry establishments, while still allowing them to export to Saudi Arabia.

StatementSubmitted: For the 6th consecutive time, Brazil is presenting this STC regarding suspensions of Brazilian poultry meat establishments by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. As we have already stated in this committee, Saudi Arabia has suspended Brazilian establishments alleging sanitary problems, without presenting supporting documentation and, to this day, it still maintains the suspensions. In Brazil’s view, Saudi Arabia is not observing the provisions of the SPS Agreement on this topic, especially those in articles 2 and 5, due to the imposition of unjustified measures that lack a scientific basis, and due to the absence of proper risk analysis to establish an adequate level of protection. This year, surprisingly, Saudi Arabia authorized the resumption of imports from the same suspended establishments, according to its convenience - however, without withdrawing the suspension. I take this opportunity to bring back the same question that we raised during the March meeting, so that Brazil and this Committee can understand the reason for the suspension of these establishments. Hence, we pose this question: what is the sanitary problem with Brazilian poultry meat that is capable of motivating the suspension of establishments, but still allows export, entry, and consumption of this product in Saudi Arabia? Finally, if there are no sanitary problems, as previously claimed, we kindly request the prompt removal of these restrictive measures unfairly imposed on Brazilian products.
Summary: Brazil regretted that Saudi Arabia had not provided supporting documentations regarding the ongoing suspension of Brazilian exports alleging sanitary problems. In Brazil's view, Saudi Arabia was not respecting Articles 2 and 5 of the SPS Agreement. In 2022, Saudi Arabia's had authorized the resumption of imports from the suspended establishments, without the withdrawal of the suspension. Brazil asked Saudi Arabia to explain the sanitary reason for suspending the establishments while allowing exports, entry and consumption of Brazilian's poultry meat in the country. Brazil kindly requested Saudi Arabia to remove the restrictions if no sanitary problems were identified.In response to Saudi Arabia, Brazil reiterated its questions regarding the sanitary reason for suspending the establishments while allowing exports, entry and consumption of Brazilian's poultry meat in the country. In Brazil's view, the letter sent by Saudi Arabia with certificates of analysis of Brazilian products contained inconsistencies in the data presented, suggesting that there was no evidence to maintain the suspension for some of the Brazilian establishments.
