StatementSubmitted: For the 9th consecutive time, Brazil raises this STC regarding suspensions of Brazilian poultry establishments by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. We regret that Saudi Arabia has not yet provided documentation that can give adequate support to the continuous suspension of Brazilian exports under sanitary justifications.Saudi Arabia is not following the provisions of articles 2 and 5 of the SPS Agreement, considering the adoption of measures without any scientific justification,  although it has reported to this Committee that it is complying with it.In 2022, Saudi Arabia authorized the resumption of imports from 6 of the 13 suspended establishments, however, without formally withdrawing the suspensions. Currently, these 6 Brazilian establishments are considered "partially suspended" by Saudi authorities and the other 7 remain formally suspended as well.Brazil has sought an explanation from Saudi Arabia about its sanitary reasons to formally maintain the suspension of these 6 establishments while allowing exports, entry, and consumption of Brazilian poultry. We have still received no satisfactory response.Although  Arabia informed this committee that it had raised the suspension of some establishments,in fact they kept them "partially suspended" without any justification for this status that is unknown to international organizations.Brazil would like to raise again three questions: 1)what is the sanitary problem with Brazilian poultry that is capable of motivating the suspension of establishments, but allows imports and consumption of Brazilian poultry in Saudi Arabia 2) What is the legal basis or international guideline that gives support to classify an establishment as “partially suspended”? 3) What does a “partial suspension” mean? Finally, we would like to request once more the end of these unjustified suspensions of establishments.
Summary: Brazil regretted that Saudi Arabia had not provided supporting documentation regarding the ongoing suspension of Brazilian exports. In Brazil's view, Saudi Arabia was not respecting Articles 2 and 5 of the SPS Agreement. In 2022, Saudi Arabia had authorized the resumption of imports from 6 of 13 suspended establishments, but the suspensions had not been formally withdrawn. These Brazilian establishments remained "partially suspended" and other establishments formally suspended. Brazil requested Saudi Arabia to clarify what type of sanitary issue could motivate the suspension of establishments while allowing imports and consumption of Brazilian poultry in Saudi Arabia. Brazil further enquired what was the legal basis for and meaning of partial suspensions.

Canada emphasized the need for cooperation to meet the challenges that COVID-19 posed to health and economies, avoid unnecessary barriers to trade, and contribute to food security. Canada also emphasized the importance of basing COVID-19 related measures on sound scientific principles and a risk assessment. In the context of COVID-19, unjustified trade restrictions threatened the integrity of global food supply chains. The United States encouraged China to withdraw its measures and work to support the guidance of international organizations by building the body of scientific evidence on COVID-19. StatementSubmitted:
The European Union would like to recall that according to the assessment of the World Health Organisation, the Food and Agriculture Organisation, the International Commission on Microbiological Specifications of Food and other assessment bodies at international as well as at regional or national levels, there is no evidence that food and packaging may be a relevant source of transmission of the COVID-19 disease.
	There is wide scientific consensus that adherence to general hygiene measures along the food production and transport chain prevent the spreading of the virus through trade.
	The European Union regrets that the COVID-19 outbreak has led China to adopt trade restrictions in the form of tests, inspections, supplementary guarantees on agreed certificates or other attestations regarding imported food and other products. These measures cause uncertainty, delays and increase the costs of exports to China.
	Despite numerous requests, China has not provided scientific evidence to justify the measures. In the interest of all trading partners, the EU would like to invite the People's Republic of China to share its risk assessment, scientific proof and any valid data which justifies its measures on imported food products and to explain why these measures are considered necessary and proportionate. As long as the EU cannot verify the assessments of China, it has no choice but to consider the measures currently in place may be in breach of China’s obligations under the SPS Agreement.
	The European Union would like also to recall the G20 Leaders’ commitment at the Extraordinary G20 Leaders’ Summit on 26 March 2020 that “[e]mergency measures aimed at protecting health will be targeted, proportionate, transparent, and temporary."
	The European Union will continue to work together with trading partners to support global trade on the basis of internationally agreed standards and recommendations.
Summary: The European Union recalled that, according to several international, regional and national bodies, there was no evidence of transmission of COVID-19 through food and packaging. The European Union regretted that the restrictions imposed by China, without providing scientific evidence, caused uncertainty, delays and increased costs of exports to China. The European Union invited China to share its risk assessment or any scientific evidence which justified its measures and to explain why these measures were considered necessary and proportionate. The European Union would continue to work with trading partners to support global trade on the basis of internationally agreed standards and recommendations.

StatementSubmitted:
CHINA´S ACTIONS RELATED TO COVID-19 THAT AFFECT TRADE IN FOOD
AND AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS – CONCERNS OF THE USA (STC No. 487)
The Russian Federation notes that it closely follows the developments related to Chinese restrictions on the supply of food and agricultural products aimed at prevention of cross-border spread of COVID-19. 


Russia supports China's efforts to counter the spread of the new coronavirus infection and protect people's lives and health. At the same time, we are deeply concerned by the fact that Chinese measures have caused a significant reduction of Russian food and  agricultural cargo traffic to China and negatively affected bilateral trade.


The Russian Federation is concerned that Chinese measures in question are not transparent and are applied exclusively to foreign companies.


The Russian exporters are now facing significant difficulties and delays in gaining customs clearance for shipments to China. Russian exporters experience frequent delays at the Russian-Chinese border caused by Chinese side.


China examines incoming cargo for the presence of genetic material of the SARS-CoV-2 virus, the infectious agent of COVID-19. 


The Russian Federation notes that currently there is no scientific consensus on the possibility of transmission of COVID-19 through contaminated surfaces. Even international organizations recognize that there is an extremely low probability of human infection through contaminated surfaces. 


China also conducts examinations of crews of vehicles, including ships delivering cargo. Some detections of coronavirus infection in the crews of Russian ships have not been confirmed by Russian laboratories.

We believe that it necessary to avoid the use of non-transparent measures and measures that create unjustified trade barrier. The Russian Federation would like to emphasize that measures aimed at the prevention of spread of coronavirus infection should be based on available scientific data and corresponding risk assessment.

So far, Russia has not received any scientific justification confirming the risk of cross-border spread of COVID-19.

The Russian competent authorities have notified the Chinese partners about the measures taken by the Russian side to prevent the spread of a new coronavirus infection.

The Russian Federation expresses its readiness for comprehensive cooperation with China on COVID-19 issues related to trade in order to ensure food safety and resume previous trade volumes.
Summary: The Russian Federation was concerned by the reduction of Russian food and agricultural cargo traffic to China as a result of the imposed COVID-19 measures, which, in its view, were not transparent and applied exclusively to foreign companies. The Russian Federation noted the lack of scientific consensus on the transmission of COVID-19 through contaminated surfaces. The Russian competent authorities had informed China about the measures taken to prevent the spread of the virus, and had not received any scientific justification confirming the risk of cross border spread of COVID-19. The Russian Federation expressed its readiness to cooperate with China to ensure food safety and resume previous trade volumes.

StatementSubmitted:
Australia recognises the right of governments to take emergency measures necessary to protect public health, including measures at the border to prevent the introduction of pathogens injurious to human health.
	Australia notes that China has notified some emergency measures, through SPS notification G/SPS/N/CHN/1173, to prevent the risk of introducing COVID-19 via imported foods.
	
		These measures are described in General Administration of Customs of the People’s Republic of China (GACC) Announcement 103 of 2020.
	
	
	Under these measures, GACC will stop processing import declarations from a food businesses where there has been a positive detection of SARS-CoV-2 in imported cold chain products or their packaging
	
		the first two detections from the same overseas manufacturer results in suspension for a week that is automatically lifted; and
		any further detections from the same overseas manufacturer results in a suspension for four weeks that is again automatically lifted.
	
	
	In addition to the emergency measures outlined in GACC Announcement No.103 of 2020 and voluntary suspension of establishments, Australia understands that China has implemented additional measures to prevent the risk of introducing COVID-19 that have not been notified to the WTO, including:
	
		widespread testing and disinfection of imported products and packaging;
		requiring mandatory commercial declarations or variations to commercial contracts;
		requirements for virtual audits to maintain or regain market access; and
		requests for overseas food manufacturing establishments to voluntarily suspend exports to China following the detection of SARS-CoV-2 in onsite workers.
	
	
	In relation to the voluntary suspension of export establishments, Australia wishes to highlight the misalignment between establishments that have voluntarily suspended operations to China following COVID-19 cases in onsite workers and GACC’s Announcement 103.
	Establishments that have proactively voluntarily suspended trade to China and promptly notified GACC have been subject to unreasonable suspension periods.
	
		Noting that the longest suspension under Announcement 103 is four weeks, which is automatically lifted after the four weeks elapses
		Some establishment that have voluntarily suspended have been subject to longer suspension for over 8 months.
	
	
	We request GACC ensure establishments that have voluntarily suspended exports to China following the detection of SARS-CoV-2 in onsite workers are offered the same transparency and treatment as afforded under Announcement 103 and that suspensions are not unnecessarily prolonged.
	Australia remains concerned about the lack of reinstatement of three Australian establishments who voluntarily suspended exports to China in July and September 2020 due to the detection of SARS-CoV-2 in onsite workers. 
	
		These establishments acted in good faith and pursuant to the GACC’s commitment to trading partners that such establishments would have a clear and expedited pathway to lifting the suspension and reinstating trade following the resolution of COVID-19-related incidents. 
		For other trading partners, we are aware that suspensions have been lifted for a number of establishments.
	
	
	Australia also remains concerned that COVID-19 measures being implemented by China are disproportionate to risk and are being maintained without sufficient scientific evidence, as required under the SPS Agreement.
	Australia reminds members of the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) statement that, "[there] is no evidence to date of viruses that cause respiratory illnesses being transmitted via food or food packaging." This advice has not changed.
	Given the international guidance that SARS-COV-2 is not transmitted through food or food packaging
	
		we request China reconsider all measures and base any future COVID-19-related sanitary and phytosanitary measures on agreed scientific principles and evidence, and
		facilitate the resumption of exports from establishments that voluntarily suspended exports following the successful resolution of COVID-19 cases in on-site workers.
Summary: Australia stated that China's implementation of additional measures to prevent the risk of introducing COVID-19 had yet to be notified to the WTO. Australia expressed its concern regarding COVID-19 measures implemented by China without sufficient scientific evidence, as required under the SPS Agreement, and requested China to reconsider the measures and base future COVID-19 related SPS measures on agreed scientific principles.

StatementSubmitted:
Thank you Chair.
	As Canada has stated in previous Committee meetings, all WTO Members are trying to meet the challenges that COVID-19 poses to the health of our citizens and our economies, to avoid unnecessary barriers to trade and to contribute to food security. 
	It remains crucial that the Membership works together to meet these challenges and share the latest science on COVID-19 as we continue to learn more.
	It is also paramount that Members base any SPS measures taken to control COVID-19 on sound scientific principles and an assessment of risks, taking into account risk assessment techniques developed by the relevant international organizations, and that these SPS measures are not sustained without sufficient scientific evidence.
	Canada would like to draw attention to the document from the World Health Organization and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations  entitled COVID-19 and Food Safety: Guidance for Food Businesses, which was originally published in April 2020 and recently updated in August of this year.
	The revised WHO/FAO guidance document reconfirms that neither food nor food packaging is a pathway for the spread of viruses causing respiratory illnesses, including COVID-19.
	As well, the revised WHO/FAO guidance document continues to recommend that environmental sampling and testing for COVID-19 in food processing facilities or on food is not needed. This was borne out by the International Commission on Microbiological Specifications for Foods (ICMSF), which released an opinion on COVID-19 and its relationship to food safety in September 2020.
	Canada questions the scientific basis for China’s SPS measures relating to COVID-19 affecting trade in food and agricultural products, notified to the SPS Committee in G/SPS/N/CHN/1173 on September 21, 2020, as these measures continue to create unnecessary and unjust trade disruptions for Canadian industry.
	Canada urges China to remove their SPS measures related to COVID-19, since the scientific evidence is insufficient to support neither the adoption nor maintenance of COVID-19 related SPS measures.
	Canada would like to reiterate that the available scientific evidence indicates that there is no risk of transmission of COVID-19 through, food, food packaging or food handling.
	Canada is also concerned with the lack of clarity, transparency and predictability with these measures.
	In particular, the reinstatement process for establishments suspended due to China’s COVID-19 related SPS measures and China’s request to conduct audits on COVID-19 mitigation measures in establishments.
	Canada views these audits as unnecessary as COVID-19 does not present a food safety risk.
	With no scientific evidence to support these measures, the continued suspension can only be viewed now as a tool to block trade. We urge China to base its SPS measures on sound science and to take into account the updated FAO/WHO guidance.
	Canada urges China to reinstate the suspended Canadian meat establishments without undue delay.
	Canada notes that our technical experts are in contact with their Chinese counterparts and calls on China to maintain this technical dialogue to resolve our concerns with China’s COVID-19 related SPS measures.
	Canada welcomes the opportunity for continued collaboration with China – both bilaterally and multilaterally – towards our common objective of avoiding unnecessary barriers to trade and contributing to food security.
	Thank you Chair
Summary: Canada emphasized the importance of basing COVID-19 related measures on sound scientific principles and risk assessments, and drew the Committee's attention to the recently updated WHO/FAO guidance on COVID-19 and Food Safety. Canada questioned the scientific basis for China's measures relating to COVID-19 as notified in G/SPS/N/CHN/1173. Canada urged China to remove these measures, since the scientific evidence was insufficient to support their adoption or their maintenance. Canada expressed concerns as well on the lack of clarity, transparency and predictability of these measures taken, in particular, for the reinstatement of suspended establishments. Canada requested their reinstatement without undue delays and called on China to maintain the ongoing technical dialogue to resolve the concerns at issue.

Reiterating its concern on China's measures, the United States explained that China had not provided science-based justification or test results in support of maintaining the provisional measures notified in G/SPS/N/CHN/1173. The United States referred to the updated WHO/FAO guidance, and encouraged China to withdraw its measures and to support the guidance of international organizations by building the body of scientific evidence on COVID-19. The United States also encouraged China to share the process to reinstate establishments as eligible for export to China and to resume the exports from two poultry production facilities suspended on the basis of COVID-19 related concerns. The United States submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/1982.

StatementSubmitted:
The Russian Federation notes that it continues to closely follow the developments related to Chinese restrictions on the supply of food and agricultural products aimed at prevention of cross-border spread of COVID-19. On the pretext of preventing the risk of COVID-19 introduction with frozen and chilled food China implemented emergency preventive measures applied to foreign manufacturers of imported frozen foods including testing of product packages on the presence of a new coronavirus nucleic acid.

We are concerned by the fact that Chinese measures have caused a significant reduction of Russian fish exports to China and negatively affected bilateral trade. In 2020 exports of fish from Russia to China decreased by 69% in physical terms and about 35% in value terms.

The Russian Federation is also concerned that Chinese measures in question are not transparent. China justifies restrictive measures against Russian fish exports by several cases of the COVID-19 coronavirus particles detection on product packaging. Still, the vast part of the questions requiring clarification from China remain unanswered by China. Non-transparent actions of China still are fraught with grave consequences of complete disruption of fish exports from Russia to China, including exports via third countries.

Russian competent authorities undertake systemic actions to restore the volume of supplies fish, produced in Russia to the People's Republic of China. The ongoing work of Rosselkhoznadzor and Rospotrebnadzor is aimed at strengthening cooperation with the Chinese side in order to prevent the spread of coronavirus, including through additional disinfection of cargo packaging and conducting research. Other measures are being taken to prevent the spread of COVID-19 among personnel, including vaccination of fishing boat crews and employees of processing plants.

 

However, we note that despite the ongoing work, elaboration of control methods in accordance with the Chinese requirements and the provision of appropriate level of sanitary and epidemiological safety of goods exported to China, China has not yet eased the requirements.

 

China continues to insist on the high probability of transmission of coronavirus infection through the packaging of goods, in particular cold chain goods even when international organizations such as WHO, FAO, the International Commission on Microbiological Specifications for Foods recognized that there is an extremely low probability of human infection through contaminated surfaces.

We believe that it is necessary to avoid the use of non-transparent measures and measures that create unjustified trade barrier. The Russian Federation would like to emphasize that measures aimed at the prevention of spread of coronavirus infection should be based on available scientific data and corresponding risk assessment.

So far, Russia has not received any Chinese scientific justification confirming the risk of cross-border spread of COVID-19 and any information on methods of food packaging research.

Unfortunately, the Russian Federation has not succeeded to establish an open effective dialogue with China on SPS measures related to COVID-19 that affect trade in food and agricultural products. Russia seeks to resolve the current situation with fish exports and is ready to continue consultations with China on a bilateral basis. Russia expresses its readiness for comprehensive cooperation with China on COVID-19 issues related to trade in order to ensure food safety and resume previous trade volumes.

Russia encourages China to withdraw the abovementioned COVID-19 measures and work with its global partners to support the guidance of international organizations by building the body of scientific evidence on COVID-19. Collaborative engagement is essential as we collectively combat the pandemic, avoid unnecessary barriers to trade on food and agricultural products, and maintain food security for all.
Summary: The Russian Federation expressed its concern regarding China's emergency measures on imported frozen foods to prevent the risk of introduction of COVID-19, which, in its view, were not transparent. These restrictions had mainly affected Russian fish exports, on the basis of several cases of COVID-19 detected on product packaging. Regretting the lack of scientific justification provided by China confirming the risk of cross-border spread of COVID-19, the Russian Federation urged China to withdraw its COVID-19 measures and expressed its willingness to cooperate bilaterally to ensure food safety and resume previous trade volumes.

Australia reiterated its concerns that China's continued enforcement of emergency measures to prevent the risk of COVID-19 transmission via food products, such as those notified in G/SPS/N/CHN/1173, those outlined in GACC Announcement No. 103 of 2020, and its prevention measures released on 30 January 2022, were not based on scientific evidence and offered a less favourable treatment than that afforded to domestic goods. Australia questioned the consistency of China's measures with revised WHO/FAO guidance, requested an update on China's review of emergency measures for food businesses related to COVID-19 and the notification of China's additional measures related to COVID-19, and asked for an update on the timeframe for lifting suspensions applied to Australian export establishments. Australia was of the view that China's COVID-19 measures, including at borders, were increasingly discriminatory towards foreign imports. Australia indicated its willingness to work with China and other Members to ensure that measures to prevent the spread of COVID-19 were science- and risk-based, took account of the latest available pertinent information and minimized unnecessary impacts on trade.

relevant international organizations, and that these SPS measures are not sustained without sufficient scientific evidence. Canada once again emphasizes that the WHO and FAO guidance document entitled COVID-19 and Food Safety: Guidance for Food Businesses, which was updated in August 2021, reconfirms that neither food nor food packaging is a pathway for the spread of viruses causing respiratory illnesses, including COVID-19.  Canada notes that the revised WHO/FAO guidance document continues to recommend that environmental sampling and testing for COVID-19 in food processing facilities or on in September 2020. Canada therefore continues to question the scientific basis for China’s SPS measures relating to COVID-19 affecting trade in food and agricultural products, notified to the SPS Committee in G/SPS/N/CHN/1173 on September 21, 2020.  These measures continue to create unnecessary and unjustifiable trade disruptions for Canadian industry. Canada once again reiterates its request Summary: Canada emphasized the importance of basing COVID-19 related measures on sound scientific principles and risk assessments, and drew the Committee's attention to the recently updated WHO/FAO guidance on COVID-19 and Food Safety. Canada questioned the scientific basis for China's measures relating to COVID-19 as notified in G/SPS/N/CHN/1173 and expressed concerns on the lack of clarity, transparency and predictability of the measures, in particular regarding the reinstatement process for suspended establishments. Canada noted that multiple reinstatement packages had been submitted to China, and urged China to respond to its requests, reinstate all suspended establishments without undue delays, and base its SPS measures on sound scientific principles. Canada called on China to work more collaboratively with its trading partners to avoid unnecessary trade barriers.

StatementSubmitted: China’s COVID-19-Related Trade Actions against Food and Agricultural Products (STC 487)March 2022 WTO SPS Committee - Statement by the United States The United States would like to reiterate the concerns we have shared over the past year and a half regarding several measures China continues to implement, including testing requirements on imported foods, port-of-entry rejections of imported products when positive nucleic acid test results are reported, and suspension of imports from specific facilities.    As the United States and other Members have on numerous occasions reminded China, the most recent FAO guidance for preventing transmission of COVID-19 within food businesses states that “current data indicates that neither food nor food packaging is a pathway for the spread of viruses causing respiratory illnesses, including SARS-CoV-2. In other words, SARS-CoV-2 is not a direct food safety concern.” Through notification G/SPS/N/CHN/1173, China indicated that it is implementing these measures on an emergency basis.  China has had sufficient time to collect and present scientific evidence justifying these measures. To date, China has not provided any science-based justification or testing results to support the need for, or efficacy of, these measures, despite numerous requests by WTO Members.   As the world continues to reopen and rebuild, the unjustified trade restrictions adopted by China during the COVID-19 pandemic continue to increase food prices for consumers, threaten global food supply chains, slow global recovery efforts, and further challenge global food security. We again urge China to withdraw these measures and work with its global partners to support the guidance of international organizations, which is based on the body of scientific evidence on COVID-19.  Collaborative engagement is essential as we collectively seek to combat the pandemic, avoid unnecessary barriers to trade on food and agricultural products, and maintain food security for all.   Lastly, the United States notes that two U.S. poultry production facilities remain ineligible to export to China over a year after China suspended exports allegedly based on COVID-19-related concerns. These facilities have provided substantial information to China to support reinstatement, but China has not provided a clear process for trade to resume.  We encourage China to make public this process and promptly reinstate these facilities as eligible to export to China.
Summary: Reiterating its concern on China's measures, the United States explained that China had not provided scientific justification to support the need and effectiveness of the emergency measures notified in G/SPS/N/CHN/1173. The United States referred to the updated WHO/FAO guidance, and encouraged China to withdraw its measures and support the guidance of international organizations on COVID-19. The United States also encouraged China to share the process to reinstate establishments as eligible for export to China and to resume the exports from two poultry production facilities suspended on the basis of COVID-19 related concerns. The United States submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2005.

StatementSubmitted: China's actions related to COVID-19 affect trade in food and agricultural products (ID 487)  India expressed its concern regarding the suspension of export approvals by China, citing the detection of COVID-19 nucleic acid on seafood packaging. Many other members also have raised this concern. India reiterates its concern yet again. India considered China's measures to be inconsistent with Articles 2.2 and 5.1 of the SPS Agreement. Referring to the FAO/WHO document "COVID-19 and Food Safety: Guidance for Food Businesses", India highlighted the lack of evidence of COVID-19 transmission via food or food packaging. India requested China to share the test reports for the consignment on which COVID-19 nucleic material had been found and establish how the measure was necessary to protect human, animal or plant life or health. So far, China has not provided reports or procedures adopted to test for the presence of COVID-19 nucleic acid. Instead, the GACC (General Administration of Customs China)   is demanding for video inspection of the unit & following it up with indefinite suspension of the unit without specifying the regulation based on which they are initiating such an action. The GACC announcement No.103 (2020) dated 11.09.2020 does not indicate the need for virtual inspection or indefinite suspension. As on date, GACC has indefinitely suspended 51 Fish & Fishery Products establishments for export to China on detection of Covid-19 nucleic acid in inner/outer packages of frozen products. The relevant test reports, the sampling procedure, and the adopted testing protocols are not shared with the Export Inspection Council to undertake a detailed investigation in India. Indian exporters have implemented preventive controls as per guidelines of FAO & WHO to ascertain that processing workers are free from COVID-19. Contamination during processing, inventory and handling of packaging materials and loading of consignment are eliminated through stringent preventive controls at the establishment level. This is being monitored during official controls by EIC. Further, FAO's August 2, 2021 guidelines clearly state, “Current data indicates that neither food nor food packaging is a pathway for spreading viruses causing respiratory illnesses, including SARS-CoV-2. In other words, SARS-CoV-2 is not a direct food safety concern.” The report also pointedly states that COVID-19 is a risk for public health in general as well as an occupational safety risk for workers. However, SARS-CoV-2 itself is not viewed as a direct food safety hazard. there is currently no scientific evidence confirming that food or food packaging is associated with transmission of the COVID-19.” In view of the above, India requests China to share relevant test reports, the sampling procedure, and the testing protocols adopted or immediately allow exports from our delisted units.
Summary: India reiterated its concern regarding the indefinite suspension of exports from over 50 fish and fishery product establishments on the basis of presence of COVID-19 nucleic acid on the packaging of frozen products. China had not shared the relevant test reports, hindering detailed investigations in India. Following the WHO/FAO guidance, Indian exporters had implemented stringent preventive controls. India requested China to share the relevant reports that had led to the export restrictions or allow exports from the delisted units.

StatementSubmitted: Further to statements made in previous SPS Committee meetings, Australia remains concerned that China’s COVID-19 emergency measures are not based on internationally agreed scientific evidence and are unnecessarily trade restrictive, lack clear timeframes for the review of its emergency measures and do not follow a clear process for the reinstatement of trade from establishments suspended under these measures.  Australia notes that there are establishments that have been suspended and unable to export to China for almost two years due to China’s COVID-19 based suspensions. This is despite establishments demonstrating freedom from COVID-19, and continuing to maintain precautionary measures and controls. Australia requests that China provide guidance on how the suspensions applied to Australian export establishments can be lifted via remote inspection or other means.    Australia is willing to work with China, and other members, to ensure any measures to prevent the spread of COVID-19 are science and risk-based, take account of the latest available pertinent information and minimise any unnecessary impact on trade.
Summary: Australia reiterated its concerns that China's COVID-19 emergency measures were not based on scientific evidence, unnecessarily restricted trade, lacked clear timeframes for their review, and did not follow a clear process for the reinstatement of suspended establishments. Noting that certain export establishments had been suspended for close to two years, Australia requested China to provide guidance on lifting these suspensions including through remote inspection or other means. Australia indicated its willingness to work with China and other Members to ensure that measures to prevent the spread of COVID-19 were science- and risk-based, took account of the latest available pertinent information, and minimized unnecessary impacts on trade.

StatementSubmitted: Thank you Chair.Canada is disappointed to have to once again reiterate our concerns with China’s actions related to COVID-19, which have negatively and unnecessarily affected trade in food and agricultural products. As Canada has stated in previous Committee meetings, all WTO Members are trying to meet the challenges that COVID-19 poses to the health of our citizens and our economies, to avoid unnecessary barriers to trade and to contribute to food security. All of the points raised in Canada’s previous interventions on this item remain valid.The available scientific evidence and the guidance of the WHO and FAO indicates that there is no risk of transmission of COVID-19 through food, food packaging or food handling.Further, the WHO and FAO continue to recommend that environmental sampling and testing for COVID-19 in food processing facilities or on food is not needed.Canada therefore continues to question the scientific basis for China’s SPS measures relating to COVID-19 affecting trade in food and agricultural products, notified to the SPS Committee in G/SPS/N/CHN/1173 on September 21, 2020. Canada once again reiterates its request that China provide details on the assessment of risks that serves as the basis for their COVID-19 related SPS measures, including the suspension of establishments due to COVID-19.Canada strongly urges China to remove their COVID-19 related SPS measures, since – even after more than two years of diligent study of COVID-19 transmission – there is insufficient scientific evidence to support the adoption and maintenance of China’s measures. Additionally, Canada is deeply concerned with the lack of clarity, transparency and predictability with these unjustified measures, including the reinstatement process for establishments suspended due to COVID-19 and China’s request to conduct audits on COVID-19 mitigation measures in establishments. China has not even acknowledged receipt of the multiple reinstatement packages that have been submitted for Canadian establishments suspended by China as a result of its COVID-19 measures, nor indicated whether or not the applications are complete; nor provided any timeframes for decisions.Canada urges China to respond to Canada’s request for reinstatement of the suspended Canadian meat establishments without undue delay.With no sufficient scientific evidence to support these measures, Canada notes that these measures are inconsistent with the SPS Agreement obligations; therefore, the continued suspension can only be viewed now as a tool to block safe trade. Canada urges China to work collaboratively with its trading partners towards our common objective of avoiding unnecessary barriers to safe trade and contributing to food security. Thank you Chair.
Summary: Referring to its statements in previous meetings, Canada reiterated its concern regarding China's measures related to COVID-19, which it considered to negatively impact trade in food and agricultural products. Canada highlighted that the WHO/FAO guidance on COVID-19 indicated no risk of transmission of COVID-19 through food, food packaging or food handling. Canada questioned the scientific basis for China's measures relating to COVID-19 as notified in G/SPS/N/CHN/1173 and expressed concerns on the lack of clarity, transparency and predictability of the measures, in particular regarding the reinstatement process for suspended establishments. Canada noted that multiple reinstatement packages had been submitted to China, and urged China to respond to its requests without undue delays. Canada called on China to work collaboratively with its trading partners to avoid unnecessary trade barriers.

StatementSubmitted: China’s actions related to COVID-19 that affect trade in food and agricultural products (STC 487)June 2022 WTO SPS Committee - Statement by the United StatesThe United States again raises the concerns we have shared with this Committee for the past two years regarding the measures China continues to implement, including testing requirements on imported foods, port-of-entry rejections of imported products when positive nucleic acid test results are reported, and suspension of imports from specific facilities.   We and other Members again remind China of the most recent FAO guidance for preventing transmission of COVID-19 within food businesses, which states that “current data indicates that neither food nor food packaging is a pathway for the spread of viruses causing respiratory illnesses, including SARS-CoV-2. In other words, SARS-CoV-2 is not a direct food safety concern.”Increasingly, these measures appear to discriminate against imports while providing significantly more lenient pathways for the production, transportation, and sale of domestic food products.  SPS measures, including unjustified measures, should not operate as a discriminatory barrier to trade that unfairly advantages a Member’s domestic producers.As the world continues to reopen and rebuild, the unjustified trade restrictions adopted by China during the COVID-19 pandemic continue to increase food prices for consumers, threaten global food supply chains, slow global recovery efforts, unfairly disadvantage imported cold chain food products, and further challenge global food security.We urge China to immediately withdraw these measures and meaningfully engage with its global partners to support the guidance of international organizations, which is based on the body of scientific evidence on COVID-19.  Collaborative engagement is essential as we collectively seek to combat the pandemic, avoid unnecessary barriers to trade on food and agricultural products, and maintain food security for all.
Summary: Reiterating its concern regarding China's measures, the United States referred to recent FAO guidance, and encouraged China to withdraw its measures and to support the guidance of international organizations on COVID-19. The United States considered China's measures to be discriminatory, and underlined that SPS measures should not constitute a barrier to trade to the advantage of Members domestic producers. The United States submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2043.

StatementSubmitted: India reiterates its concern regarding the suspension of export approvals by China, citing the detection of COVID-19 nucleic acid on seafood packaging. Many other members also have raised this concern. India reiterates its concern yet again.India considered China's measures to be inconsistent with Articles 2.2 and 5.1 of the SPS Agreement. Referring to the FAO/WHO document "COVID-19 and Food Safety: Guidance for Food Businesses", India highlighted the lack of evidence of COVID-19 transmission via food or food packaging. India requested China to share the test reports for the consignment on which COVID-19 nucleic material had been found and establish how the measure was necessary to protect human, animal or plant life or health. So far, China has not provided reports or procedures adopted to test for the presence of COVID-19 nucleic acid. Instead, the GACC (General Administration of Customs China) is demanding for video inspection of the unit & following it up with indefinite suspension of the unit without specifying the regulation based on which they are initiating such an action. The GACC announcement No.103 (2020) dated 11.09.2020 does not indicate the need for virtual inspection or indefinite suspension.Indian seafood to China is facing unnecessary barriers on account of the detection of Covid-19 nucleic acid on the packaging, product and container wall of seafood consignments since November 2020. As on date, GACC has indefinitely suspended 101 Fish & Fishery Products establishments for export to China on detection of Covid-19 nucleic acid in inner/outer packages of frozen products. The relevant test reports, the sampling procedure, and the adopted testing protocols are not shared with the Export Inspection Council to undertake a detailed investigation in India. Indian exporters have implemented preventive controls as per guidelines of FAO & WHO to ascertain that processing workers are free from COVID-19. All the employees and staff of the fishery establishments are fully vaccinated against COVID-19. Contamination during processing, inventory and handling of packaging materials, loading of consignment and environment (processing/stuffing of containers) are eliminated through stringent preventive controls at the establishment level. This is being monitored during official controls by EIC.As of 6th June 2022, 77 fishery establishments are video inspected by GACC and in turn, corrective action measures taken by 44 establishments have been communicated to GACC. However, the suspension of 41 out of 44 units has not been revoked from indefinite suspension so far.Further, FAO's August 2, 2021 guidelines clearly state, “Current data indicates that neither food nor food packaging is a pathway for spreading viruses causing respiratory illnesses, including SARS-CoV-2. In other words, SARS-CoV-2 is not a direct food safety concern.” The report also pointedly states that COVID-19 is a risk for public health in general as well as an occupational safety risk for workers. However, SARS-CoV-2 itself is not viewed as a direct food safety hazard. there is currently no scientific evidence confirming that food or food packaging is associated with transmission of the COVID-19.”In view of the above, Exporters are losing confidence as the majority of the establishments despite taking corrective actions, are not re-listed. India requests China to share relevant test reports, the sampling procedure, and the testing protocols adopted and immediately permit exports of fishery products from Indian establishments submitted corrective action, against observation shared by GACC at the time of video inspection.
Summary: India reiterated its concern regarding the suspension of exports from over 101 fish and fishery product establishments on the basis of presence of COVID-19 nucleic acid on the packaging of frozen products. China had not shared the relevant test reports, hindering detailed investigations in India. India considered China's measures to be inconsistent with Articles 2.2 and 5.1 of the SPS Agreement. Following the WHO/FAO guidance, Indian exporters had implemented stringent preventive controls, and staff of fishery establishments were vaccinated against COVID-19. India noted that corrective measures had been taken by 44 of the 77 fishery establishments subject to video inspections by General Administration of Customs of China (GACC) in June 2022, but 41 of these establishments continued to be suspended. India requested China to share the relevant reports that had led to the export restrictions, and to allow exports from Indian establishments that had implemented corrective measures.

StatementSubmitted: November 2022 WTO SPS Committee Meeting - U.S. Statement on China’s actions related to COVID-19 that affect trade in food and agricultural products (STC ID 487)The United States is disappointed on the lack of engagement from China on this issue and again reiterates our concerns raised over the past three years with this Committee regarding the measures China continues to implement purportedly to mitigate the transmission of COVID-19.  These measures include declarations, testing requirements on imported foods, port-of-entry rejections of imported products when positive nucleic acid test results are reported, and suspension of imports from specific facilities.   We join other Members in reminding China of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) guidance for preventing transmission of COVID-19 within food businesses, which states that “current data indicates that neither food nor food packaging is a pathway for the spread of viruses causing respiratory illnesses, including SARS-CoV-2. In other words, SARS-CoV-2 is not a direct food safety concern.” (Note document available here: https://www.fao.org/3/cb6030en/cb6030en.pdf).These measures appear to discriminate against imports while providing significantly more lenient pathways for the production, transportation, and sale of domestic food products.  SPS measures, including unjustified measures, should not operate as a discriminatory barrier to trade that provides unfair advantages to a Member’s domestic producers. These unjustified trade restrictions adopted by China during the COVID-19 pandemic continue to increase food prices for consumers, threaten global food supply chains, slow global recovery efforts, unfairly disadvantage imported cold chain food products, and further challenge global food security.We again urge China to immediately withdraw these measures and meaningfully engage with its global partners to support the guidance of international organizations, which is based on the body of scientific evidence on COVID-19.  Collaborative engagement is essential as we collectively seek to respond to lasting impacts of the pandemic, avoid unnecessary barriers to trade on food and agricultural products, and maintain food security for all.
Summary: Disappointed with China's lack of engagement, the United States reiterated its concern on the measures implemented purportedly to mitigate the transmission of COVID-19. Referring to the WHO/FAO guidance on COVID-19 stating that SARS-CoV-2 was not a direct food safety concern, the United States considered China's measures provided an unfair advantage to domestic producers and further challenged global food security. The United States urged China to withdraw its measures and to support the guidance of international organizations on COVID-19. The United States submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2083.

StatementSubmitted: • Thank you Chair.• Canada is disappointed to have to once again, for the seventh time in this Committee, raise our concerns with China’s actions related to COVID-19, which have negatively and unnecessarily affected trade in food and agricultural products.• All of the points raised in Canada’s previous interventions on this item remain valid.• The available scientific evidence and the guidance of the WHO and FAO indicates that there is no risk of transmission of COVID-19 through food, food packaging or food handling.• Further, the WHO and FAO continue to recommend that environmental sampling and testing for COVID-19 in food processing facilities or on food is not needed.• Canada therefore continues to question the scientific basis for China’s SPS measures relating to COVID-19.• Canada once again reiterates its request that China provide details on the assessment of risks that serves as the basis for their COVID-19 related SPS measures, including inspection processes for establishments processing live aquatic animals for human consumption; and the suspension of meat establishments due to COVID-19. Without an assessment of risks, China’s measures unjustifiably restrict trade more than necessary.• Canada strongly urges China to remove their COVID-19 related SPS measures, since – after more than two years of diligent study of COVID-19 transmission – there is insufficient scientific evidence to support the adoption and maintenance of China’s measures.• Additionally, Canada is deeply concerned with the lack of clarity, transparency and predictability with these unjustified measures, including the reinstatement process for establishments suspended due to COVID-19 and China’s request to conduct audits on COVID-19 mitigation measures in establishments.• Canada acknowledges China’s reinstatement of 2 Canadian meat establishments in July 2022 that had been suspended due to China’s COVID-19 measures.• Canada urges China to immediately reinstate all the Canadian meat establishments that remain suspended from exporting to China without undue delays.  • Furthermore, Canada requests an explanation as to why these establishments remain suspended from exporting to China.• Canada once again notes that these measures appear inconsistent with the SPS Agreement obligations; therefore, China’s continued implementation of its COVID-19 measures and the suspension of Canadian establishments can only be viewed as a tool to block safe trade.• Canada urges China to work collaboratively with its trading partners towards our common objective of avoiding unnecessary barriers to safe trade and contributing to food security.• Thank you Chair.
Summary: Referring to its statements in previous meetings, Canada reiterated its concern regarding China's actions related to COVID-19, which negatively impacted trade in food and agricultural products. Canada highlighted that the WHO/FAO guidance indicated no risk of transmission of COVID-19 through food, food packaging or food handling. Canada questioned the scientific basis for China's measures and expressed concerns on the lack of clarity, transparency and predictability. Canada sought clarification on why only two meat establishments had been reinstated while others remained suspended, and asked China to reinstate all Canadian establishments without undue delay. Noting that the measures appeared inconsistent with the SPS Agreement, Canada called on China to provide the relevant risk assessment, to remove the measures and to work collaboratively to avoid unnecessary trade barriers and contribute to food security.

StatementSubmitted: Australia acknowledges the review by China of its management of COVID-19 in the cold chain and encourages China to continue with their reassessment of the current port of entry processes, especially in the risk assessment of findings and development of appropriate actions required to improve conditions for trade. Australia remains concerned at the disproportionate application of suspensions to food businesses where the establishment self-declared a small cluster of COVID-19 infections which has long since resolved. Of particular concern is the suspension of establishments that now have been unable to export to China for almost two years due to a self-declaration of an incident of COVID-19 within those establishments. Several establishments remain suspended that have not been offered a clear pathway to lift suspensions, especially in the cases of COVID detection in a staff member.Australia would be grateful for advice from China on when these suspensions might be lifted so that the establishments are able to re-continue trade. Australia remains committed to working with China bilaterally, and with other members, to ensure any measures to prevent the spread of COVID-19 are science and risk-based, take account of the latest available pertinent information and minimise any unnecessary impact on trade.
Summary: Australia encouraged China to continue with the reassessment of the processes at the port of entry regarding COVID-19 in the cold chain. Noting that certain export establishments had been suspended for almost two years following a self-declaration of COVID-19 infections, Australia requested China to provide guidance on the lifting of these suspensions. Australia reiterated its commitment to work bilaterally with China to ensure science- and risk-based measures.

StatementSubmitted: India expresses its disappointment in the lack of progress on this matter, despite several members raising the matter in a number of meetings in the last two years. All the points raised in India's previous statements remain valid. General Administration of Customs China (GACC) has been suspending Indian seafood export units (ranging from 1 week to an unspecified period) on account of the detection of Covid-19 nucleic acid in the packaging material of seafood consignments.This action has no scientific basis, and no market other than China, to which India exports seafood, is carrying out any such covid-19 testing.India urges China to provide the scientific basis on which nucleic acid tests are being carried out. China is requested to share any test results reports or scientific evidence to show that detecting positive nucleic acid from packaging can cause any health hazards. China is also requested to share the sampling procedure and the testing protocols adopted in this regard.  India considers China's measures to be inconsistent with Articles 2.2 and 5.1 of the SPS Agreement.It has also been reported that GACC is demanding a video inspection of the unit & following it up with indefinite suspension of the unit without specifying the regulation based on which they are initiating such an action. GACC announcement No.103 (2020) dated 11.09.2020 does not indicate the need for virtual inspection or indefinite suspension.So far, 95 Indian fishery establishments have been suspended by China due to the alleged presence of COVID-19 nucleic acid material. India requests China to share the relevant reports that have led to the export restrictions and to allow exports from Indian establishments that have implemented corrective measures.
Summary: Referring to its interventions in previous meetings, India expressed its disappointment with the lack of progress on this concern. In its view, the suspension by the General Administration of Customs of China (GACC) of Indian seafood export units on account of the detection of COVID-19 nucleic acid on the packaging material lacked scientific grounds. India noted that GACC had not specified the legal basis for demanding a virtual inspection or the indefinite suspension of units. India considered the measures to be inconsistent with Articles 2.2 and 5.1 of the SPS Agreement, and requested China to share the relevant reports that had led to the export restrictions as well as the sampling procedure and the testing protocols adopted in this regard, and to allow exports from Indian establishments that had implemented corrective measures.

StatementSubmitted: The Separate Customs Territory of Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen and Matsu would like to register our concern again regarding China’s suspension of the importation of our fresh or chilled silverfish and frozen Japanese jack mackerel in 2022 for the asserted positive reaction of COVID-19 virus on the packages. We continue to be disappointed and regret that China has implemented these trade restrictive measure without any scientific evidence. We urge China to resume the importation of the concerned fishery products in accordance with the SPS agreement and relevant international standards, guidelines, and recommendations as soon as possible. There is no scientific evidence showing that COVID-19 can be transferred to human beings through packaging. Also, our competent authority has taken the initiative to conduct random inspection on the processing factories involved in packaging the fish products in question to check whether there is any presence of the COVID-19 virus. The results of the testing on the packages of these fishery products have all been negative. The inspection report and our reinforcement measures have also been shared with China for reference. We urge China to review its measures based on scientific evidence, adopting reasonable practices in line with the least trade-restrictive principles to fulfill its WTO commitments. We also request China to engage in a scientific and technical dialogue with us to resolve this trade issue in a constructive manner.
Summary: Chinese Taipei regretted the lack of scientific evidence for the suspension of imports of fresh or chilled silverfish and frozen Japanese jack mackerel, and urged China to resume imports in accordance with the SPS Agreement and international guidance. Chinese Taipei called on China to review its measures on the basis of scientific principles, to adopt the least trade restrictive measures and to engage in a scientific and technical dialogue.

StatementSubmitted: Australia remains committed to working with China bilaterally, and with other members, to ensure any measures to prevent the spread of COVID-19 are science and risk-based and minimise any unnecessary impact on trade. Australia was grateful to receive advice from the General Administration of Customs China (GACC) on 17 February 2023 acknowledging the need to strengthen communication and cooperation around food safety and to reaffirm that China’s COVID-19 measures had been removed. Australia welcomes China’s removal of the requirements to test imported product and its packaging for COVID-19 genetic material and seeks clarification on when will China remove outstanding COVID-19 suspensions? Australia appreciates China’s February 2023 removal of the trade suspension imposed on Australian dairy establishment 1416—which had been in place since August 2020, due to a COVID-19 detection in on-site workers. However, despite the removal of all relevant COVID-19 policies in China and Australia providing corrective action responses, three Australian meat establishments remain suspended.The significant duration of these suspensions ranging from 12 months to 2.5 years is inappropriate, even more so now with the removal of all relevant COVID-19 policies.Australia is aware that China has reinstated trade for several meat establishments in other trading partner nations that had been suspended due to the detection of COVID-19. We seek similar consideration of our meat establishments and encourage China to provide advice on when these suspensions will be lifted, or to provide timely feedback on Australia’s corrective actions, so that the establishments are able to recommence trade.
Summary: Australia indicated that it was grateful to have received advice from the General Administration of Customs China (GACC) in February 2023, acknowledging the need to strengthen communication and cooperation around food safety and reaffirming that China's COVID-19 related measures had been removed. Australia welcomed China's removal of the requirements to test imported products and packaging for COVID-19 genetic material and sought clarification on when China would remove outstanding COVID-19 related suspensions. While Australia appreciated China's removal of the suspension imposed on an Australian dairy establishment, three Australian meat establishments remained suspended. Australia requested that these suspensions be lifted.

StatementSubmitted: Japan welcomes the fact that on January 8 of this year, China lifted the measures they had taken on imported cold-chain foods such as testing of COVID-19 and disinfection at the border as part of its preventive measures against COVID-19.However, Japan would like to continue to raise this issue in this Committee, because Japanese specific facilities whose imports were suspended in association with these measures still remain suspended.In December 2020, China conducted online audits on two Japanese seafood processing facilities to verify compliance with the FAO/WHO Guidance on COVID-19 and Food Safety. These audits were not due to the detection of COVID-19 in the export cargoes of these two facilities. As a result of the audits, deficiencies in the prevention and control of COVID-19 and food safety management at these facilities were pointed out, and their imports were suspended.In response, these two facilities had immediately undertaken corrective actions, and Japan has repeatedly requested China to lift the suspension of these facilities as they meet the China’s food safety requirements. However, the import suspension of these facilities has continued for two years without any scientific or risk-based justification from China.Now that China lifted the measures related to COVID-19, Japan urges China to remove without undue delay its unjustified trade restrictive measures on these facilities, where food safety problems do not exist. Japan also requests an explanation as to what food safety concern remains for the continued import suspension of these facilities.
Summary: Japan welcomed that measures had been lifted in January, but raised concerns on continued suspensions. Japan indicated that, in 2020, two facilities had their imports suspended due to online audits unrelated to the detection of COVID-19 in export cargoes. These two facilities had immediately undertaken corrective actions, but import suspensions had continued for two years without scientific or risk-based justification. Given that the measures had been lifted, Japan urged China to reinstate these facilities and requested clarification on the food safety concerns that justified the continued import suspensions.

StatementSubmitted: In past meetings, the EU, together with other Members, had asked China to lift its COVID-19 related import measures and refrain from adopting new and unjustified measures allegedly on COVID-19 grounds on imported food and other products.In this context, the EU welcomes the announcement No 131 from China made on 28 December 2022 which lead to the lifting of China’s COVID-19 related measures on food imports as of 8 January 2023. However the EU would like to note that there are still today export establishments that cannot export to Chia due to suspensions that were imposed due to COVID-19 related measures. We would urge China to lifts these suspensions immediately and that they are authorised again to export to China. The EU would also like to ask China to confirm whether future audits to EU export establishments will contain COVID-19 requirements.
Summary: The European Union welcomed the announcement made in December 2022, which had led to the lifting of China's COVID-19 related measures on food imports as of February 2023, but noted that there were still export establishments that could not export to China due to COVID-19 related ongoing suspensions. The European Union urged China to lift all suspensions immediately, and to clarify whether future audits to EU export establishments would contain COVID-19 requirements.

StatementSubmitted: Australia remains committed to working with China bilaterally, and with other members, to ensure any measures to prevent the spread of COVID-19 are science and risk-based and minimise any unnecessary impact on trade. Australia notes that China has rescinded the requirements to test imported product and its packaging for COVID-19 genetic material and seeks clarification on when will China remove the outstanding COVID-19-related suspensions on three Australian meat processing establishments that remain in place.The significant duration of these suspensions ranging from 18 months to 3 years is inappropriate, even more so now with the removal of all relevant COVID-19 policies.Australia seeks similar consideration given to other trading partner nations who have had their trade for meat establishments reinstated by China and encourage China to provide advice on when these suspensions will be lifted, or to provide timely feedback on Australia’s corrective actions, so that the establishments are able to recommence trade.
Summary: Australia noted China's removal of the requirements to test imported products and packaging for COVID-19 genetic material and sought clarification on when China would remove outstanding COVID-19 related suspensions. Australia sought clarification regarding three Australian meat establishments that remained suspended. Australia requested these suspensions be lifted, similar to other Members who had had their meat establishments reinstated, and timely feedback on Australia's corrective actions.

Summary: Japan raised concerns on continued suspensions, despite China's lifting of some measures earlier in 2023. Japan indicated that the two facilities whose imports had been suspended due to online audits in 2020 had immediately undertaken corrective actions but import suspensions had continued for two and a half years without scientific or risk-based justification. Given that the measures had been lifted, Japan urged China to reinstate these facilities and requested clarification on China's food safety concerns to justify the continued import suspensions.

StatementSubmitted: Australia remains committed to working with China bilaterally, and with other members, to ensure any measures to prevent the spread of COVID-19 are science and risk-based and minimise any unnecessary impact on trade. Australia notes that China rescinded the requirements to test imported product and its packaging for COVID-19 genetic material and once again seeks clarification on when will China remove the outstanding COVID-19 suspensions on three Australian meat processing establishments that remain in place.The significant duration of these suspensions ranging from 18 months to 3 years is inappropriate, even more so now with the removal of all relevant COVID-19 policies.Australia seeks similar consideration given to other trading partner nations who have had their COVID-19 related suspensions lifted by China, so that the establishments can recommence trade.
Summary: Noting that China had rescinded the requirements to test imported product and its packaging for COVID-19 genetic material, Australia sought clarification from China on the removal of the outstanding COVID-19 suspensions in place. Australia expressed concern on the significant duration of these suspensions, which it considered inappropriate. Australia requested similar consideration as granted to other trading partners and requested the lifting of the COVID-19 related suspensions so that trade could recommence.

Brazil informed the Committee that the Philippines had suspended the importation of poultry from Brazil, as notified in G/SPS/N/PHL/467, arguing the detection of SARS-CoV-2 in a surface sampling conducted in chicken meat imported from Brazil to China. Despite the information provided by Brazil, the Philippines ban had been lifted only partially. Brazil considered that the restrictions lacked clear scientific justification and were inconsistent with Articles 2.2-2.3 and 5.1-5.2 of the SPS Agreement.

Brazil reported that, in April 2019 and after 16 years of negotiations, its authorities had been informed of the negative result of the risk analysis regarding market access of Brazilian pork to Mexico. Despite the subsequent exchange of information and the recognition by the OIE of the state of Santa Catarina as free from foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) without vaccination, Mexico questioned the efficiency of risk mitigation strategies applied in that area. Brazil considered that this position was inconsistent with Article 6 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement. In July 2019, Brazil had proposed an international sanitary certificate model for pork meat for industrial processing and was now awaiting a response. Brazil reiterated that pork meat exported to Mexico came from a zone free from classical swine fever (CSF) and FMD, according to the OIE, and that pork imports were to be processed by Mexico's food industry.

StatementSubmitted:
Almost fifteen years have now passed since Brazil started to negotiate with Mexico the opening of its market to Brazilian "in natura" pork produced in the state of Santa Catarina. In April 2019, after a long exchange of documents, questionnaires and an audit, the Mexican government informed our authorities of the negative result of the risk analysis. After that, a thorough exchange of further information ensued.

Nevertheless, SENASICA continues to allege the information is insufficient and that it is not convinced of the efficiency of risk mitigation strategies in the Brazilian state of Santa Catarina, despite the OIE recognizing this area as free from foot-and-mouth disease without vaccination. The Mexican position goes against Article 6 of the SPS Agreement, as well as its Annex C.

When negotiations started, Brazil sent to Mexican authorities the same documents we used to receive OIE`s recognition of the state of Santa Catarina as a zone free of foot-and-mouth disease. We find it difficult to understand why the same zone, recognized by the OIE and all our other trading partners, does not seem to meet Mexican risk assessment standards. Furthermore, we recall Article 1.3.2.2 of OIE`s Terrestrial Code, which reads: "An importing country may decide to permit the importation using the appropriate sanitary standards recommended in the Terrestrial Code, thus eliminating the need for a risk assessment".

Brazil has a very strict National Program on Swine Health, which encompasses the whole national territory and ensures the containment of the diseases and the protection of the sanitary conditions. Brazil takes this very seriously. No wonder why we currently export pork to about 90 countries.

We would like to reiterate that the pork meat to be exported to Mexico presents no risk, since it comes from a zone which is, according to the OIE, free from Classic Swine Fever as well as foot-and-mouth disease. Nonetheless, these pork imports would be processed by Mexico`s food industry before they reach Mexican households. In July 2019, Brazil proposed to Mexico an International Sanitary Certificate model specifically on pork meat for industrial processing. So far, Mexican authorities have not responded.
Summary: Brazil noted that, in April 2019, its authorities had been informed of the negative result of the risk analysis concerning market access to Mexico of Brazilian pork produced in the state of Santa Catarina. Despite the OIE recognition of the state of Santa Catarina as free from FMD without vaccination, Mexico had continued to question the efficiency of its risk mitigation strategies. Brazil considered this position to be inconsistent with Article 6 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement. Brazil reiterated that pork meat exported to Mexico presented no risk as it came from a zone free from classic swine fever (CSF) and FMD, as recognized by the OIE, and that pork imports were to be processed by Mexico's food industry. In July 2019, Brazil had proposed an international sanitary certificate model for pork meat for industrial processing, and was waiting for Mexico's response.

We find it difficult to understand why the same zone, recognized by the OIE and all our other trading partners, does not seem to meet Mexican risk assessment standards.

Furthermore, we recall Article 1.3.2.2 of OIE`s Terrestrial Code, which reads: "An importing country
may decide to permit the importation using the appropriate sanitary standards recommended in the
Terrestrial Code, thus eliminating the need for a risk assessment".

Brazil has a very strict National Program on Swine Health, which encompasses the whole national territory and ensures the containment of the diseases and the protection of the sanitary conditions. Brazil takes this very seriously. No wonder why we currently export pork to about 90 countries.

from a zone which is, according to the OIE, free from Classic Swine Fever as well as foot-and-mouth disease. Nonetheless, these pork imports would be processed by Mexico`s food industry before they reach Mexican households. Meanwhile, the OIE has recently expanded the portion of Brazil’s territory free from foot-and-mouth disease.


We, therefore,  believe that Mexico’s restrictive policies towards our exports of pork are discriminatory and have no scientific basis.

Despite the OIE recognition of the state of Santa Catarina as free from FMD without vaccination, Mexico had continued to question the efficiency of its risk mitigation strategies. Brazil considered this position to be inconsistent with Article 6 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement, and recalled the provisions of article 1.3.2.2 of the OIE Terrestrial Code.
