Brazil considered Mexico's measures to be discriminatory and to lack scientific basis.

StatementSubmitted:
Almost fifteen years have now passed since Brazil started to negotiate with Mexico the opening of its market to Brazilian "in natura" pork produced in the state of Santa Catarina. We also recall that the first time we raised our concerns on Mexico`s restrictions on Brazilian pork meat exports was back in 2008, under STC ID 271.

First of all, it is important to mention that the state of Santa Catarina has been recognized by the OIE as free from FMD without vaccination for 13 years now. The last vaccination applied in this state was 21 years ago. The last occurrence of FMD happened 28 years ago.

Brazil has a very strict National Program on Swine Health, which encompasses the whole national territory and ensures the containment of the diseases and the protection of the sanitary conditions. Brazil takes this very seriously. No wonder why we currently export pork to about 90 countries.

We would like to reiterate that the pigmeat to be exported to Mexico presents no risk, since it comes from a zone which is, as attested by the OIE, free from Classic Swine Fever as well as foot-and-mouth disease. Nonetheless, these pork imports would be processed by Mexico`s food industry before they reach Mexican households. In July 2019, Brazil proposed to Mexico an International Sanitary Certificate model specifically for pigmeat for industrial processing. So far, Mexican authorities have not responded. 

In this regard, Mexico is not complying with the regionalization provision set forth in Article 6 and in the Decision G/SPS/48, when it does not consider Santa Catarina as a different zone, even though Mexico is also a large country, just like Brazil, with a vast territory and huge differences among its states. Neither does Mexico take into account the provision on harmonization, when it refuses to consider the OIE official status  recognition to Brazil in 2008.

Furthermore, Brazil understands that, by restricting our exports of pork, Mexico`s conduct also goes against the basic obligation of non-discrimination between Members where identical and similar conditions prevail. As is known, Mexico imports from another South American Member that is considered free from FMD with vaccination and, even so, refuses to accept pork meat imports from a Brazilian state free from FMD without vaccination since 2007.

It is important to emphasize, once again, that the product in question would be thermoprocessed in Mexico. This means it presents very low risk for the Mexican cattle. 

At the last SPS Committee Meeting, Mexico said Brazil had conflicting rules, citing Normative Instruction 52 and Santa Catarina State Law 17.826. As has already been explained to Mexico bilaterally, I would like to clarify that there is no contradiction. Both rules forbid the entry into Santa Catarina of cattle from other Brazilian states that are subject to vaccination, and both rules allow cattle from states that are free from FMD without vaccination, just as recommended by the OIE.

Another argument presented by the Mexican delegation was that Normative Instruction nº 52, issued in August 2020, allowed entry into the state of Santa Catarina of animals and products coming from Acre, Paraná, Rio Grande do Sul and Rondônia, as well as parts of Amazonas and Mato Grosso. According to Mexico, such animals and products would bear FMD risk. However, as Members will recall, the OIE recognized last May this whole area as free from FMD without vaccination.

Therefore, Brazil would like to address two specific questions to Mexico: Why does Mexico not accept OIE official recognition in the case of Brazil? Why does Mexico import from Members that are free from FMD with vaccination and does not import from a zone free from FMD without vaccination?
Summary: Brazil reiterated concerns regarding Mexico's restrictions on pork imports from Santa Catarina. According to Brazil, Santa Catarina had been recognized by the OIE as free from FMD without vaccination for the past 13 years, and FMD had last occurred 28 years ago. Underscoring the effectiveness of its National Program on Swine Health, Brazil considered that exports of pig meat to Mexico presented no risk since they came from a zone free from classic swine fever and FMD, as recognized by the OIE, and because pork imports would be thermo processed in Mexico before reaching households. Specifically, Brazil specified that there was no conflict between its Normative Instruction 52 and Santa Catarina State Law 17.826, as stated by Mexico, since both rules followed OIE's recommendations regarding the entry of cattle into FMD-free areas. Brazil was waiting for a response from Mexico on a proposed model international sanitary certificate for pig meat for industrial processing. Brazil argued that Mexico's restrictions were inconsistent with the principles of non-discrimination, harmonization and regionalization, and with Decision G/SPS/48.Brazil appreciated the information provided by Mexico on the consideration of OIE recognition, and referred to G/SPS/GEN/1932 outlining states and zones recognized by the OIE as FMD-free without vaccination. Regarding epidemiological calculations, Brazil argued that Mexico's approach was neither supported by the OIE Terrestrial Code nor by the available and relevant scientific evidence on the issue, and urged Mexico to revise its methods accordingly.

StatementSubmitted: Once again, Brazil would like to bring to the attention of this Committee the long-lasting restriction it has been facing to export pork to Mexico.More than fifteen years have passed since Brazil started to negotiate with Mexico the opening of its market to Brazilian "in natura" pork produced in the state of Santa Catarina. We also recall that the first time we raised our concern on Mexico's restrictions on Brazilian pork exports was in 2008, under STC ID 271.It is important to highlight that the state of Santa Catarina has been recognized by the OIE as free from FMD without vaccination for almost fifteen years now.The last vaccination applied in this state was 22 years ago, and the last case of the disease was reported in 1993, almost thirty years ago.During the last SPS Committee Meeting, Mexico affirmed that it still had concerns with the guarantees offered by Brazil on export safety and regionalization.However, Mexico imports pork from another South American member that offers guarantees as solid as those offered by Brazil. This conduct indicates that Mexico is going against the basic obligation of non-discrimination between members where identical or similar conditions prevail.First of all, Brazil has a very strict National Program on Swine Health, which encompasses the whole national territory and ensures the containment of diseases and the protection of sanitary conditions. As a result, Brazil has been able to export pork to about 90 countries. Secondly, as mentioned before, the OIE has recognized the Brazilian state of Santa Catarina as free from FMD since 2007. Mexico is not complying with the regionalization provision outlined in Article 6 and in Decision G/SPS/48, when it does not consider Santa Catarina as a different zone, even though Mexico is also a large country, just like Brazil, with a vast territory and differences among its states.Thirdly, in a bid to lower Mexico`s sanitary worries even further Brazil proposed in 2019 that future pork imports from Brazil would be exclusively for processing by Mexico's food industry before reaching Mexican households. Unfortunately, so far, Mexican authorities have not responded to this proposal. Besides stating that it would still be a matter of concern for Mexico, notwithstanding all the guarantees from Brazil, Mexico also alleged that there would be a conflict between Normative Instruction n. 52 and Santa Catarina State Law N. 17.829. However, we would like to ask Mexico to observe that, as Brazil stated during the last SPS Committee Meeting, both rules forbid the entry into Santa Catarina of cattle from other Brazilian states that are subject to vaccination, and both rules allow cattle from states that are free from FMD without vaccination, as recommended by the OIE. Hence, these rules are compatible and not conflicting.Therefore, Brazil would like to ask three specific questions to Mexico: 1) Does Mexico understand that Normative Instruction n. 52 and Santa Catarina State Law N. 17.829 only allow the entry of cattle from states free of FMD? 2) Could Mexico indicate what guarantees it requires from countries that are not FMD free to allow exports? Brazil hopes Mexico can kindly provide us with the answer to these questions during this session.
Summary: Brazil reiterated concerns regarding Mexico's restrictions on pork imports from Santa Catarina. Brazil explained that Santa Catarina had been recognized by the OIE as free from FMD without vaccination for almost 15 years, and FMD had last occurred almost 30 years ago. Referring to Mexico's concerns with the guarantees offered by Brazil on export safety and regionalization, Brazil noted that Mexico imported from another country which offered similar guarantees and considered that this was discriminatory. Underscoring the effectiveness of its National Program on Swine Health, Brazil considered that exports of pig meat to Mexico presented no risk since they came from a zone free from classic swine fever and FMD, as recognized by the OIE. Brazil also informed Members that it had not received a response on its proposal for future pork imports from Brazil to be processed by Mexico's food industry before reaching Mexican households. Regarding Normative Instruction No. 52 and Santa Catarina State Law No. 17.829, Brazil emphasized that there was no conflict as both rules did not allow the entry of cattle into Santa Catarina from other Brazilian states that were subject to vaccination, and both rules allowed cattle from states that were free from FMD without vaccination, as recommended by the OIE. Brazil asked Mexico to confirm that this information was clear, and also requested Mexico to indicate the guarantees it required from countries that were not FMD-free to export to Mexico. Brazil argued that Mexico's restrictions were inconsistent with the principles of non-discrimination, harmonization and regionalization, and with Decision G/SPS/48.

StatementSubmitted: For Brazil, the negotiation for the export of Brazilian pork to Mexico is one of the oldest negotiations in course, having reached 16 years since its beginning, and yet we still do not see any significant progress. As we have already affirmed in this committee, the issue concerns Mexico’s allegations regarding the status of Foot-and-Mouth Disease in Brazil. However, Brazil has already provided all the guarantees necessary to achieve the adequate level of protection required by Mexico to make progress in this negotiation. Despite the OIE’s recognition of a large region of Brazil as FMD-free, we are not even allowed to export to Mexico products from animals born and raised in the Brazilian state of Santa Catarina, the first FMD-free Brazilian state. Furthermore, Mexico only accepts pork destinated exclusively for industrial thermoprocessing in Mexico. The Mexican position on this issue has been continuously disregarding Articles 2, 5, 6, and Annex C of the SPS Agreement. As previously stated, Mexico usually brings to this committee a generic answer, mentioning that it has always favored dialogue and that it is open to continuing working with the Brazilian authorities. However, Mexico continues to affirm that it does not recognize what the OIE recognized more than 10 years ago, on the grounds that Brazil’s system for FMD vigilance would not be equivalent to its system.  Mexico has also been mentioning alleged conflicts in the Brazilian legislation that could create risk for products. Even though it has already been explained that there is no conflict between the legislations, Mexico insists that it needs to further analyze the Brazilian legislation, and that it is still evaluating the Brazilian request for a reassessment of epidemiological data carried out by Mexico, which presents a methodology that differs from that recommended by international guidelines. We reintroduce this STC to this committee in an attempt to obtain from Mexico concrete answers, that bring new elements that can generate effective progress on the topic.
Summary: Brazil noted that Mexico did not recognize its FMD status despite having received the guarantees necessary for the achievement of its appropriate level of protection (ALOP). In particular, Brazil regretted that it could not export animal products from Santa Catarina, despite WOAH recognition as FMD-free. Brazil further highlighted that Mexico only accepted pork destined exclusively for industrial thermoprocessing in Mexico. In Brazil's view, Mexico had continuously disregarded Articles 2, 5 and 6 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement, and did not accept the equivalence of Brazil's system for FMD vigilance. In response to Mexico's indication of the need to further analyze Brazilian legislation, based on the allegation that conflicts therein could create risk for products, Brazil reiterated that there was no conflict in its legislation. Brazil also noted that Mexico was still evaluating its request for a reassessment of epidemiological data, which had been carried out by Mexico following a methodology that differed from the one recommended by international guidelines.Reiterating its guarantees to export the product in question, Brazil emphasized that it had the capacity to inspect and trace animals born and raised in Santa Catarina, which was the first FMD-free state of Brazil. Brazil considered that some additional guarantees requested by Mexico were not justified under the SPS Agreement.

StatementSubmitted: Brazil would like to start by recognizing Mexico`s recent renewed engagement on the issue, with significant efforts made by Mexican authorities in the recent weeks to advance in the opening of its market for Brazilian pork exports.On October 25th, Mexico published the sanitary requirements for imports of Brazilian pork produced in the State of Santa Catarina to be thermically processed by Mexico`s food industry. Another important step was taken last Friday, November 4th, when Mexicoagreed to the sanitary certificate proposed by Brazil. Notwithstanding the recent progress, it is Brazil`s understanding that the effective opening of Mexico`s market will only take place when the list of Brazilianexporting establishments is published by Mexica sanitary authorities.However, we are confident that, given the current engagement, which includes technical dialogue between our capitals, Mexico will be able to conclude this process in the coming days.Brazil is hopeful that, at the next Committee meeting this long-standing STC can finally be withdrawn from the agenda.
Summary: Brazil announced that, following the publication in October 2022 of the requirements for imports of pork produced in Santa Catarina to be thermically processed by Mexico's food industry, Mexico had agreed to the sanitary certificate proposed by Brazil. It was Brazil's understanding that the effective opening of the market would take place after the publication of the list of Brazilian exporting establishments. Brazil expected the concern to be concluded in the coming days.

The European Union was concerned that bans on imports of beef from the European Union imposed by Korea in 2001, following cases of BSE, were still in place. The European Union had provided Korea with all necessary information on BSE-related control measures to guarantee safe trade. While acknowledging the re-opening in 2019 of the Korean beef market for two EU member States, which in the EU view demonstrated the trust of Korea in the EU food safety and animal health policy, the European Union regretted that the assessment of most EU applications had not been finalized, despite the satisfactory completion of all the technical and scientific work. The European Union stated that Korea was not complying with Article 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement and was discriminating against the European Union compared to other Members with a similar BSE risk status as the European Union. The European Union urged Korea to grant market access for beef from remaining interested EU member States.

StatementSubmitted:
The European Union regrets having to repeat this previously raised Specific Trade Concern on an import ban for bovine products maintained by Korea on many EU Member States due to Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE). 
	The European Union welcomes the earlier re-opening by Korea in 2019 for imports of bovine products from two Member States of the European Union. This clearly demonstrates the trust of the Republic of Korea in the EU policy on food safety and animal health, which is harmonised at EU level and implemented by all EU countries. The European Union would like to highlight that identical food safety and animal health control conditions prevail in all EU Member States. The EU would like to remind Korea to limit the information requirements to what is necessary as required under the WTO SPS Agreement.
	Moreover, the EU notes that the Republic of Korea has acted in a much more diligent manner on applications and re-opened its market to other WTO Members with a similar BSE risk status as in the EU, and thus seems to discriminate against EU applications.
	With regard to pending applications from European Union Member States, the EU considers that the further delays in the finalisation of the approval procedure by the Republic of Korea are not justified.
	The Republic of Korea is thus not complying with its commitments, in particular under Article 8 and Annex C (1) and Article 2 paragraph 3 of the WTO SPS Agreement.
	Against that background, the EU remains open to continue working with the Republic of Korea and urges the Republic of Korea to grant market access to all EU countries without further delay.
Summary: The European Union reiterated its STC regarding import bans for bovine products maintained by Korea due to BSE concerns. The European Union welcomed the re-opening of Korea's market in 2019 for imports from two EU member States, stressing that identical food safety and animal health control conditions prevailed in all its member States. The European Union reminded Korea to limit the information requirements to what was necessary under the SPS Agreement. In addition, Korea had been more diligent in re-opening its market to other Members with similar BSE status, and thus seemed to discriminate against EU applications. The European Union considered that delays in approval procedures were not justified and that Korea was not complying with its commitments, in particular under Articles 2.3 and 8, and Annex C.1 of the SPS Agreement. While open to continue working with Korea, the European Union urged Korea to grant market access to EU member States without further delay.

Summary: Referring to the re-opening by Korea in 2019 for imports of bovine products from two EU member States, the European Union noted that the EU policy on food safety and animal health was harmonized at EU level and, therefore, identical food safety and animal health control conditions prevailed in all EU member States. The European Union urged Korea to conclude the approval procedures for the pending applications.

StatementSubmitted: The European Union appreciates the close co-operation with Korea on SPS related issues. However, we regret having to repeat this particular Specific Trade Concern on unjustified delays in market access for bovine products from the European Union to Korea. The European Union welcomes the earlier re-opening by Korea in 2019 for imports of bovine products from two Member States of the European Union. This clearly demonstrates the trust of the Republic of Korea in the EU policy on food safety and animal health, which is harmonised at EU level and implemented by all EU countries. The European Union would like to highlight that identical food safety and animal health control conditions prevail in all EU Member States. Furthermore, the European Union would like to highlight that other WTO Members with the same BSE country-risk status have received market access for their beef already many years ago. In this regard, the EU would like to request Korea to respect the WTO SPS Agreement, in particular Article 3.2.Since all EU Member States have ‘negligible or controlled BSE risk’ status in accordance with the Terrestrial Code of the World Animal Health Organisation, the import health requirements previously agreed is applicable for any EU Member State. Hence, Korea’s remaining steps in its internal procedure can be swiftly concluded for all the pending requests. The EU expects Korea to finally solve this demand which is long overdue. As always, the EU remains open to continue working with the Republic of Korea.
Summary: The European Union informed the Committee that Korea had re-opened its markets for imports of bovine products from two EU member States in 2019. Noting that the EU policy on food safety and animal health was harmonized at EU level, the European Union emphasized that identical food safety and animal health control conditions prevailed in all EU member States. The European Union urged Korea to comply with Article 3.2 of the SPS Agreement and to conclude the remaining steps for the pending applications.

However, we regret having to repeat this particular Specific Trade Concern on unjustified delays in market access for bovine products from the European Union to Korea as no further progress has been seen since the last Committee meeting. The European Union welcomes the earlier re-opening by Korea in 2019 for imports of bovine products from two Member States of the European Union. This clearly demonstrates the trust of the Republic of Korea in the EU policy on food safety and animal health, which is harmonised at EU level and implemented by all EU countries. The European Union would like to highlight that identical food safety and animal health control conditions prevail in all EU Member States. Furthermore, the European Union would like to highlight that other WTO Members with the same BSE country-risk status have gained market access for their beef already many years ago. In this regard, the EU would like to request Korea to respect the WTO SPS Agreement, in particular Article 3.2..Ten EU Member States have applications for market access pending, several of them have been applied for already more than 15 years ago. The assessment procedure carried out by Korea for each of the applicant EU Member State is overly lengthy and burdensome. When the technical assessment is concluded satisfactorily, within the Korean procedure, the Korean National Assembly has to make a deliberation. The EU notes that such a deliberation is unnecessarily delayed whereby some EU Member States await their deliberation already for nearly 2 years. The EU expects Korea to finally solve this demand, which is long overdue. As always, the EU remains open to continue working constructively with the Republic of Korea on this important matter.
Summary: The European Union reiterated its concern relating to unjustified delays in market access for bovine products. The European Union urged Korea to comply with the SPS Agreement, in particular its Article 3.2, recalling that several EU member States had market access applications pending, some of which for more than 15 years. The European Union viewed Korea's assessment procedure as overly lengthy and burdensome, and hoped that Korea would solve this issue.

The Russian Federation expressed its concern with the lack of transparency and the delays of Malaysia's approval procedures for import of meat and dairy products. The Russian Federation had not received responses regarding the access of Russian products of animal origin to Malaysia, the invitation to inspect Russian establishments interested in exporting poultry meat, ready-to-eat dairy, and meat products into Malaysia, and the organization of bilateral meetings to discuss mutual market access. The Russian Federation considered this to be inconsistent with Article 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement and called upon Malaysia to implement transparency and prompt approval procedures and to provide the requested responses.

StatementSubmitted:
DELAYS IN MALAYSIA’S APPROVAL PROCEDURES FOR MEAT AND DIARY IMPORTS –
CONCERNS OF THE RUSSIAN FEDERATION (STC No. 491)
The Russian Federation reiterates its specific trade concern on the lack of transparency and unmotivated
delays in approval procedures for Russian dairy and meat products.
The Russian Federation notes that in accordance with WTO obligations a WTO member shall ensure that
its approval procedures are transparent and are undertaken and completed without undue delay.
From October 2019, the Russian Federation is waiting for veterinary certificates approval for products of
animal origin exported from Russia to Malaysia (pork, poultry, beef and dairy products).
Within a year (from March 2020.), the Russian Federation is waiting for provision by the Malaysian side
of veterinary and sanitary requirements on import of dairy products.
In December 2020, the Rosselkhoznadzor has submitted to the Malaysian side comprehensive materials
on measures undertaken by competent authorities for control of avian influenza and successful deliveries
of Russian poultry meat to the countries of the South Asian.
However, the Malaysian side has not shared its view regarding the issue of recognition of regionalization
of the Russian territory for avian influenza and access of safe Russian poultry products to the Malaysian
market.
Despite repeated attempts to organize bilateral negotiations and reminders of the requests and materials
sent, no responses has been received from the Malaysian side so far.
Even taking into account the possible difficulties in communication caused by the COVID-19 pandemic,
the Russian Federation is forced to consider the lack of substantive reaction of the Malaysian side on all
the above-mentioned issues as a deliberate delay in the prescribed procedures and a violation of the
obligations under Article 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement.
The Russian Federation requests Malaysia to comply with its WTO obligations regarding the application
of transparent and timely approval procedures.
Moreover, the Russian Federation urges Malaysia to accelerate the provision of responses to requests and
to resume effective cooperation with the Russian side.

The European Union raised a concern regarding the delay in the publication of the final rule "Importation of Sheep, Goats, and Certain Other Ruminants" by the United States, which was a necessary step in the approval procedures for exports of small ruminant meat. The relevant proposed rule had been published in the US Federal Register on 18 July 2016 and all technical and administrative work necessary to the publication of the final rule had been completed by August 2017. According to the European Union, the long delays were inconsistent with Article 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement. The European Union urged the United States to lift remaining restrictions related to transmissible spongiform encephalopathies (TSE) for all EU member States, and not to delay further the publication of the final rule. The European Union remained open to continue working constructively with the United States and all trading partners.

StatementSubmitted:
The EU reiterates its concerns about the unjustified and long delay in the publication by the US of the final rule “Importation of Sheep, Goats, and Certain Other Ruminants”. The EU is aware that this will be only the starting point to allow the EU and other WTO members to start the relevant procedure with the US competent authority to get approval for export of small ruminant meat.
	The relevant proposed rule was published in the US Federal Register on 18 July 2016 and all technical and administrative work necessary to the publication of the final rule was completed by August 2017, more than three years ago.
	This long awaited step would finally complete the much-extended process of alignment of the US animal health rules with the relevant international standards for BSE/TSE. The EU would like to stress here that a very fruitful EU/US joint effort in the multilateral arena, which started in 2006, fourteen years ago, upon request of the US to the EU, shaped the relevant OIE terrestrial animals manual Chapter to what it is today.
	The EU is of the opinion that, in this context it is not even anymore an issue of a Member ignoring existing and indisputable science; and the long delays that have accumulated in its procedure constitute a violation of Article 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement.
	The EU urges the US, to comply with its obligations under the WTO SPS Agreement and apply international standards to lift remaining TSE related restrictions for all EU Member States and not unjustifiably further delay the publication of the final rule.
	The EU notes that the discussion in the recent EU/US Animal Health Technical Working Group which took place on 3-4 March 2021 did not reveal any new substantial development.
	As always, the EU remains open to continue working constructively with the US and all trading partners but is calling them to respect their international obligations.

Ukraine updated the Committee on its latest case of avian influenza (H5N8), which had occurred in January 2020 and had been reported to the OIE and trading partners. In response to the highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) outbreak, a stamping policy out had been applied in the affected areas and zoning and surveillance had been carried out in accordance with the OIE Terrestrial Code. A rapid and effective disease control programme had been implemented to eradicate the virus and control the outbreak. Ukraine had also introduced a system of urgent notifications of quarantine restrictions, including the list of localities and establishments subject to such restrictions. Ukraine regretted that China, the European Union, and Kazakhstan continued to apply restrictions despite Ukraine having been recognized as free from HPAI since May 2020 and in disregard of international standards and their regionalization obligations. Ukraine urged Members to lift their restrictions without delay and indicated that it stood ready to work closely with Members to resolve this concern.

Costa Rica underscored that raising STCs should not be a mere formality and urged Members to maintain the dialogue and the search of solutions in the Committee.Costa Rica expressed its concern on the increasing number of import restrictions imposed by Panama and the negative effects on bilateral and regional agricultural trade, which were exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. Tomato, strawberry, banana, plantain and pineapple were some of the affected products. In Costa Rica's view, Panama was systemically opting for the most restrictive option and was not taking any measure to resume trade. Costa Rica additionally reported that, in June 2020, Panama had decided not to renew authorizations for exports from establishments of products of animal origin before physically inspecting the plants. This affected exports of dairy, pork, beef, processed poultry meat, sausages, and food for fish from Costa Rica and other trading partners. In Costa Rica's view, Panama's measures appeared to be inconsistent with Articles 2-3 and 5-8 of the SPS Agreement as well as with Articles I:1 and XI:1 of the GATT 1994.Costa Rica reiterated that there had been no change in its sanitary status that could affect the risk of products of animal origin and that the inability to conduct the physical inspection due to the pandemic had resulted in the sudden closure of trade of these products into Panama. Costa Rica regretted the lack of explanations provided by Panamanian authorities in bilateral meetings, where Panama had argued the non-compliance of the forms and times for applications for the renewal of plants and the need to narrow the trade balance with Costa Rica. Costa Rica additionally referred to Panama's intention to withdraw tariff quotas for liquid milk and evaporated milk, as communicated in G/SECRET/45. Costa Rica urged Panama to lift import bans and implement measures facilitating agricultural trade while waiting for the situation to return to normal.

Colombia asked the Panamanian authorities to organize an in-person or online visit so that dairy products, processed meat products, and foods ready for human consumption could again be exported to Panama. Colombia circulated document G/SPS/GEN/1852 on this issue

Ukraine expressed concerns regarding the lack of progress in Chinese Taipei's pest risk assessments (PRAs) concerning imports of onions and apples from Ukraine. Ukraine noted the bilateral exchanges held with Chinese Taipei. Ukraine had provided the requested priority ranking of products and asked Chinese Taipei to provide an update on the development of the PRAs and their results, including indicative timeframes for completing such assessments. In Ukraine's view, the lack of responses on the substance constituted undue delays and an unjustified barrier to trade, making export of certain of fresh vegetables and fruits to Chinese Taipei impossible. Ukraine requested Chinese Taipei to remedy the current situation.

StatementSubmitted:
Ukraine remains concerned by the lack of progress in conducting Pest Risk Assessments (PRAs) by Chinese Taipei regarding Ukraine’s exports of fresh vegetables and fruits.

We would like to thank Chinese Taipei for its communication on the matter raised after the SPS Committee meeting held in November 2020.

Along with this, we would like to note that no practical results have been achieved in resolving this issue.

We would like to stress that in accordance with the provisions of the WTO SPS Agreement WTO Member is obliged to ensure that transparent market access procedures are applied and completed without undue delay. The country requesting market access shall be informed of the processing period, its stages and the results of the procedure, with any delay being explained.

Ukraine is still awaiting substantial information on the progress and results of the PRAs on Ukraine's applications for imports of onions and apples to Chinese Taipei. As a kind reminder, respective applications were submitted back in 2017 and 2018.

Ukraine considers that further delays in the finalization of phytosanitary risk assessment procedures by Chinese Taipei create unjustified barriers to trade for Ukrainian products. In addition, the long-lasting period needed for risk assessment also cannot be justified from a scientific point of view.

Ukraine urges Chinese Taipei to follow its obligations under Article 8 and Annex C paras. 1. (a) and 1. (b), and finalise with no undue delay Ukraine’s applications in line with the WTO SPS Agreement.

Ukraine remains open to continue working with Chinese Taipei on the issue of granting market access for Ukrainian fresh vegetables and fruits.

Thank you Chair!
Summary: Ukraine remained concerned by Chinese Taipei's lack of progress in conducting PRAs regarding imports of fresh vegetables and fruits from Ukraine. Ukraine thanked Chinese Taipei for its communication following the November 2020 Committee meeting, but noted the lack of practical results as Ukraine was still awaiting substantial information on the PRAs for imports of onions and apples. Ukraine considered that further delays in the finalization of risk assessment procedures created unjustified barriers to trade and could not be justified from a scientific point of view. Ukraine urged Chinese Taipei to follow its obligations under Article 8 and Annex C.1(a)-(b) of the SPS Agreement and finalize with no undue delay Ukraine's applications. Ukraine added that it remained open to continue working with Chinese Taipei on this issue.

StatementSubmitted:
Ukraine reiterates its concern over the lack of progress in Chinese Taipei’s phytosanitary risk assessment procedure for imports of fresh vegetables and fruits from Ukraine.

Ukraine continues to experience significant undue delays in the completion of certain Pest Risk Assessments (PRAs) by Chinese Taipei and in spite of positive indications in the first half of the year, no progress has been achieved in the past couple of months. Even more, new request for information has been made after more than three years of the initial request on conducting Pest Risk Assessments for imports of onions and apples to Chinese Taipei.

With this in mind, we would like to draw the attention to the following.

During 2019 - 2021 capital-based authorities exchanged letters on the matter at issue and a few respective bilateral meetings were held on the margins of the SPS Committee.

At the request of the responsible authority of Chinese Taipei, Ukraine provided the priority ranking of products and therefore asked Chinese Taipei to inform on the developments of the PRAs and their results, including indicative timeframes for completing such assessments. So far, Ukraine has received broad answers without a deadline for the completion of the assessments.

The undue delay in carrying out necessary procedures of phytosanitary risk assessment for onions and apples exported from Ukraine leads to significant uncertainty, which makes it impractical to import these agricultural products to Chinese Taipei from Ukraine.

Ukraine is concerned with the lack of progress and reinstates its position that actions of Chinese Taipei go against the provisions of the SPS Agreement, namely Article 8 and Annex C para. 1. (a) and 1. (b), which require Members to ensure that the procedures are undertaken and completed without undue delay and the applicants are promptly informed of the duration of the procedure, its stages and results of the requested examination, with any delay being explained.

It is against this background that Ukrainian delegation strongly calls on Chinese Taipei to respect relevant obligations under the SPS Agreement by applying transparent and expeditious phytosanitary risk assessment procedures and to finalize consideration of Ukraine’s applications for Pest Risk Assessments without undue delay and to transmit the result in a precise and complete manner.
Summary: Ukraine regretted the lack of progress in the completion of pest risk assessments (PRAs) for imports of fresh vegetables and fruits from Ukraine. Following the bilateral meetings held and the provision of the priority ranking of products, Ukraine had received a new request for information. Ukraine lamented the undue delays in the procedures to conduct PRAs for onions and apples and considered Chinese Taipei's actions to be inconsistent with Article 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement. Ukraine urged Chinese Taipei to conduct transparent PRAs, to finalize Ukraine's applications and to transmit the results in a precise and complete manner.

Canada expressed concerns about the impact of India's trade restrictive measures on pulses, including mandatory fumigation requirements and new measures on weed seeds. Canada considered its science-based systems approach to pest management to be an effective and equivalent alternative to fumigation. While Canada had raised the recognition of its systems approach with India on numerous occasions and at various levels, a solution was yet to be found. Turning to India's new measures on weed seeds, Canada noted that India had added 26 new weed seeds species to its List of Quarantine Weed Seeds in October 2019. In Canada's view, these actions were inconsistent with the principles of transparency, predictability, and scientific basis for international rules-based trade. Specifically, Canada questioned India's technical justification as it did not appear to follow IPPC guidance. Canada hoped for an early and final resolution to these issues.

Canada reiterated its concern regarding India's trade-restrictive measures on pulses, including mandatory fumigation requirements and measures on weed seeds. Canada recalled that India had committed, at the November 2020 Committee meeting, to continue engaging on the issue of alternatives to India's fumigation requirements. However, there had been a lack of engagement since then and India had not yet responded to Canada's overtures of November 2020. Turning to India's measures on weed seeds, Canada noted that India had added 26 new weed seeds species to its List of Quarantine Weed Seeds in October 2019. In Canada's view, these actions were inconsistent with the principles of transparent and predicable international rules-based trade. Canada was troubled by the lack of transparency, predictability and scientific basis for these measures, as well as their non-conformity with relevant international standards. Canada urged India to continue engage with the aim of finding an early resolution of these issues.

StatementSubmitted:
Thank you Chair.

 As we stated at the June 2020, November 2020 and March 2021 WTO SPS Committee meetings, pulses have long been an important element of Canada’s bilateral trade relationship with India.

Canada therefore remains concerned about the impact of India’s trade restrictive measures on pulses. These include India’s mandatory fumigation requirements as well as measures imposed in October 2019 related to weed seeds.

Fumigation

Canada has raised the matter of India’s import fumigation requirements on several occasions with India, at every level, including bilaterally on the margins of previous meetings of this Committee and in formal interventions.

We note India’s recommitment at previous SPS Committee meetings to continue engaging with Canada with a view to finding a mutually acceptable solution at the earliest opportunity.

However, we are disappointed by the lack of engagement since and note that India still has not yet responded to Canada’s written correspondences of fall 2020. 

 Canada continues to be prepared to work with India to resolve this matter which is affecting the trade in pulses, and calls for India’s engagement and timely resolution of the issue. 

Weed Seeds

In October 2019, India published amendments to its List of Quarantine Weed Seeds, adding 26 new weed seed species.

Canada is concerned with the impact of India’s expanded regulation of weed seeds on trade in pulses, and has conveyed to India our view that these actions are inconsistent with the principles of transparent and predicable international rules-based trade.

These concerns remain despite the two sides having agreed to continue technical discussions, most recently through India’s commitment at the November 2020 and March 2021 SPS Committee meetings.

Canada urges India to undertake bilateral technical engagement with the aim of an early resolution to these outstanding issues.

Response to India’s remarks 

Canada thanks India for these comments. There does indeed appear to be some confusion regarding the sharing of information

Canada wishes to clarify that Canada has provided all requested information to India for both matters; there is nothing outstanding.

Canada looks forward to technical engagement to clarify these matters and move toward resolution.

StatementSubmitted: Thank you Chair.Canada has raised concerns about India’s import requirements for pulses at several past meetings of the Committee, including most recently at the March 2022 meeting.FumigationCanada welcomes India’s recent longer-term announcements on fumigation options for pulse shipments, as we continue to engage bilaterally on India’s import requirements. In this regard, Canada looks forward to having continued engagement with India in achieving a lasting solution on India’s import fumigation requirements for Canadian pulses.Weed SeedsWhile Canada is pleased with the progress on the fumigation issue, we do continue to have concerns with respect to India’s approach on weed seeds. As we have raised previously, in October 2019, India published amendments to its List of Quarantine Weed Seeds, adding 26 new weed seed species. Canada continues to be concerned that India’s actions are not aligned with principles of transparent, science-based and predicable international rules-based trade.  Canada is committed to working with India to achieve a lasting resolution to this issue.ConclusionIn conclusion, Canada appreciates the progress made since the March 2022 Committee meeting, and looks forward to working collaboratively with India on both these matters.  Thank you Chair.Responsive interventionCanada thanks India for its detailed response. While we acknowledge progress on India’s fumigation requirements, work still is needed to reach a lasting solution. Canada looks forward to continuing bilateral technical discussions on weed seeds and reaching a mutually agreed lasting solution on India’s fumigation requirements. Canada has a strong science-based, risk-based regulatory system in place, based on international standards, to protect plant health and mitigate the threat of plant pests.  Canada has provided detailed information to India regarding the measures in place as part of Canada’s system based pest management approach. Canada has also promptly provided all requested information to India, including submitting to India, earlier this month, a revised proposal for the pilot pest management systems approach for pulses, that India suggested was outstanding..  Canada looks forward to working collaboratively with India this issue.

Peru raised its concern regarding Ecuador's import restrictions on grapes and onions due to maximum levels of pesticides. Peru recognized the legitimate objective of health protection but considered Ecuador's actions to be more trade restrictive than necessary. Peru further indicated that it had provided and requested additional information on several occasions, but that no response had been received from Ecuador. In Peru's view, there was evidence of non-compliance with Article 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement. Peru regretted that, despite having complied with all the requirements requested by Ecuador to re-establish market access, restrictions remained in force without any technical justification. Emphasizing the significant loss to Peruvian exporters, Peru urged Ecuador to grant market access to grapes and onions from Peru.

Peru reiterated its concerns regarding Ecuador's restrictive measures on Peruvian grapes and onions. Ecuador had closed its market to grapes in 2015 and to onions in 2016, requesting Peru to develop an action plan to mitigate contamination risks. Peru was of the view that Ecuador's actions constituted a violation of the legislation in place in Ecuador, of Articles 5.4, 7 and 8, and Annexes B and C of the SPS Agreement, and of Codex Guidelines for the Exchange of Information Between Countries on Rejections of Imported Food (CAC/GL 25-1997). While the Technical Resolution DAJ 20133EC-0201.0096 had been notified in document G/SPS/N/ECU/132, Resolution 0064, from 2017, had not been notified and Members had not been able to submit comments, despite the impact of the regulation on trade. Peru regretted that, despite having answered all of Ecuador's requests, restrictions were still in place without a technical justification, contravening Articles 2.2 and 5.1 of the SPS Agreement, as well as the principle of non discrimination. Given the resulting economic losses, Peru requested Ecuador to avoid imposing measures that were against the provisions of the SPS Agreement and the basic principles of the WTO, not to disregard technical agreements previously developed, to notify its measures and provide opportunities for comments, and to reopen the market for grapes and onions.

StatementSubmitted:
Comité de Medidas Sanitarias y Fitosanitarias de la Organización Mundial del Comercio

RESTRICCIONES IMPUESTAS POR EL ECUADOR A LA IMPORTACIÓN DE UVAS Y CEBOLLAS (PCE N°498)

COMUNICACIÓN DEL PERÚ

El Perú presenta ante los Miembros de la OMC su preocupación comercial con relación a las medidas restrictivas aplicadas por Ecuador en la reapertura del acceso de la uva y cebolla procedentes del Perú.

El Perú reconoce el objetivo legítimo de protección a la salud establecido en el artículo 5 del Acuerdo MSF, sin embargo, considera que las acciones del Ecuador han sido desproporcionadas toda vez que, no se dio el seguimiento de acciones correctivas y el muestreo más estricto, a fin de salvaguardar la salud pública al momento del cierre del mercado de uvas y cebollas peruanas, contradiciendo incluso la propia normativa ecuatoriana vigente[1].

En el numeral 14.4.3 de la Resolución DAJ-20133EC-0201.0096[2], la legislación ecuatoriana establecía medidas previas antes de proceder a la suspensión de un país proveedor que no fueron aplicadas en el caso peruano. De esta forma, Ecuador contraviene el párrafo 4 del artículo 5 del Acuerdo MSF, dado que no se ha buscado reducir al mínimo los efectos negativos sobre el comercio.

Con relación a las declaraciones del Ecuador durante la reunión del Comité MSF del 25 y 26 de marzo de 2021, resulta oportuno señalar que el Código de Ética para el Comercio Internacional de Alimentos Incluyendo Transacciones en Condiciones de Favor y Ayuda Alimentaria (CAC/RCP/20-1979), no limita los derechos y obligaciones de los Acuerdos de la OMC, conforme se establece en el pie de página número 2 del artículo 4.2 del mencionado documento. En ese sentido, el artículo 3 del documento CAC/RCP/20-1979 tampoco representa un sustento técnico que justifique el cierre del mercado de uvas y cebollas del Perú, sin considerar el resto del contenido del documento CAC/RCP/20-1979, las disposiciones del Acuerdo MSF, en especial el artículo 5, y la propia normativa ecuatoriana.

Es necesario mencionar que la primera notificación recibida por AGROCALIDAD por la cebolla fue a través del Oficio Nro MAGAP-DE/AGROCALIDAD-2014-000600-OF. Dicho oficio fue remitido con fecha 25 de junio de 2014, transcurrido más de 7 meses desde la toma de muestras, la cual fue realizada con fecha 01 de octubre de 2013. Igualmente, AGROCALIDAD no indicó si este es un reporte o notificación de alerta sanitaria al Perú, ni informó sobre las acciones que implementaron con el alimento ingresado al Ecuador. Caso similar sucedió con la uva, ya que se remitió el Oficio Nro. MAGAP-CIA-AGROCALIDAD-2015-002045-OF con fecha 05 de junio de 2015, sin embargo, la muestra fue tomada con fecha 23 de febrero de 2015.  Incluso posterior al cierre del mercado, Ecuador remitió, dos (02) meses después, otras dos (02) notificaciones, por lo que consideramos que  la información no se ha transmitido de manera oportuna tal como establecen las Directrices para el intercambio de información entre los países sobre casos de rechazo de alimentos importados[3], aprobadas por el Codex Alimentarius, sobre todo en lo que se refiere a la identificación de los alimentos afectados, detalles de la importación, detalles de la decisión sobre el rechazo y sobre las medidas adoptadas.

Del mismo modo, y respecto a las declaraciones del Ecuador durante la reunión del Comité MSF del 25 y 26 de marzo de 2021, Ecuador confirmó que solicitó un plan de acción; sin embargo, la Resolución DAJ-20133EC-0201.0096 no establecía este requerimiento. Incluso, al no existir un modelo de plan de acción en la Resolución DAJ-20133EC-0201.0096, éste fue propuesto en repetidas ocasiones por el Perú, sin encontrar respuesta hasta la entrada en vigencia del Resolución 0064 de AGROCALIDAD.

A diferencia de la Resolución DAJ-20133EC-0201.0096 que fue notificada a este Comité mediante el documento G/SPS/N/ECU/132, la Resolución 0064 de AGROCALIDAD de 2017 no fue notificada, como lo establece el artículo 7 y, el Anexo B del Acuerdo MSF, a pesar de que esta medida demanda requisitos adicionales que tienen un impacto en el comercio de otros Miembros.  Por ello, el Perú lamenta que Ecuador no haya dado un plazo prudencial a los Miembros de este Comité para plantear sus observaciones y generar previsibilidad en el comercio. Del mismo modo, Ecuador ha incumplido las disposiciones del párrafo 6 del Anexo B y el artículo 7 del Acuerdo MSF, ya que el cierre del mercado debió ser también notificado a este Comité, como una medida de emergencia, siendo ésta provisional.

El Perú desea señalar que, conforme a las disposiciones del párrafo 1 del Anexo C y del Artículo 8 del Acuerdo MSF, los procedimientos de tipo sanitario o fitosanitario deben ser atendidos y concluidos sin demoras indebidas, facilitando información a la Parte interesada y con prescripciones que se limiten a lo que sea razonable y necesario. En ese sentido, se han sostenido reuniones y remitido reiteradas comunicaciones con las medidas correctivas solicitadas por Ecuador desde agosto del 2014 hasta noviembre del 2019[4], sin recibir respuesta a las acciones que como país aplicamos para buscar una solución técnica.  En este contexto, causa preocupación que, Ecuador afirme que el Perú dio respuesta en junio de 2018 al plan de acción requerido, toda vez que en línea con lo señalado, el Perú atendió de manera oportuna lo solicitado por las autoridades ecuatorianas, sin recibir respuesta[5].

Conforme la preocupación comercial presentada mediante el documento G/SPS/GEN/1907, el Perú señaló que es preocupante que el Ecuador desconozca de manera sistemática acuerdos técnicos previamente definidos entre autoridades sanitarias. En ese sentido, como parte de la reunión del 09 de marzo de 2021, se acordó que Ecuador remitiría una respuesta al plan de acción para la cebolla el 23 de marzo de 2021; sin embargo, esto no ha sido cumplido hasta la fecha.  Igualmente, mediante los mediante la CARTA-0090-2021-MIDAGRI-SENASA-DIAIA, del 30 de abril de 2021, la CARTA-0111-2021-MIDAGRI-SENASA-DIAIA del 24 de mayo de 2021, la Nota RE(DPE)N°6-12/42, del 10 de junio de 2021, y el OFICIO N° 068 - 2021 - MINCETUR/VMCE/DGPDCE/DRTCE, del 11 de junio de 2021, se ha reiterado a AGROCALIDAD, el Ministerio de Producción, Comercio Exterior, Inversiones y Pesca del Ecuador y la Embajada de Ecuador en el Perú, que remitan los requisitos y la fecha para la reapertura de las exportaciones de uva; sin embargo, no se tiene respuesta a la fecha.

El Perú lamenta que, a pesar de haber cumplido con todas las exigencias solicitadas por Ecuador para lograr reestablecer los accesos, las restricciones para el acceso a la cebolla y uva peruana al mercado ecuatoriano siguen en vigencia sin una justificación técnica y contraviniendo los artículos 2.2 y 5.1 del Acuerdo MSF.

El Perú debe resaltar que, las preocupaciones presentadas previamente mediante el documento G/SPS/GEN/1907 y en el Comité MSF OMC del 5, 6 y 13 de noviembre de 2020, son coordinadas multisectorialmente, y resaltan el interés peruano de retomar las exportaciones de cebolla y uvas. Las medidas aplicadas por Ecuador han significado un perjuicio para las exportaciones de uvas peruanas de alrededor de 6.6 millones de USD; así como de 500 mil USD en exportaciones de cebolla peruana. Es importante resaltar, que el comercio de uvas que Perú mantiene con el mundo alcanza los 1,030 millones USD, ingresando actualmente a 96 mercados, con un crecimiento promedio anual de 12.86% en los últimos cinco años. Mientras que, el comercio de cebollas con el mundo alcanza los 96 millones USD, ingresando actualmente a 27 mercados, con un crecimiento promedio anual de 8.7% en los últimos cinco años.

Considerando que las medidas aplicadas por el Ecuador son discriminatorias y contravienen las disposiciones de los artículos 2, 5, 7, 8, Anexo B y Anexo C del Acuerdo MSF, solicitamos al Ecuador:

Evitar proponer medidas que contravengan las disposiciones del Acuerdo MSF y los principios básicos de la OMC;

Evitar desconocer los acuerdos técnicos previamente desarrollados;

Notificar su medida y dar la oportunidad a los otros Miembros de la OMC para remitir comentarios;

Reaperturar el acceso a las uvas y cebollas del Perú al mercado ecuatoriano.

[1] Resolución DAJ-20133EC-0201.0096

[2] En el el numeral 14.4.3 citado por Ecuador se establecía de manera progresiva la aplicación de medidas más estrictas, conforme el siguiente detalle:

“En frontera siempre se aplica muestra de control (dirigido) que pueden variar de Control a través de muestreo reducido o de muestreo estricto.

En el caso de control con muestreo reducido, asumo que no tengo un historial negativo ni sospechas sobre el tipo de cultivo, origen (país y/o empacadora), ni sobre el importador.

Por lo tanto, todos los nuestros de frontera se inician como muestreo reducido y sin retención de producto.

Si un lote presenta un plaguicida que supera el LMR establecido, entonces se informa a través del SIAR y el origen (empresa y país) y el importador para ese producto pasan de muestreo reducido a muestreo estricto por cinco embarques consecutivos, con retención de mercadería. Si los 5 embarques consecutivos dan por debajo del LMR, entonces vuelve a muestreo reducido. Si alguno supera el LMR, entonces se rechaza el producto (destrucción), se informa al SIAR y se prosigue por 5 muestreos estricto más. Si vuelve a aparecer una muestra por encima del LMR se informa al SIAR y se define si se sigue autorizando las importaciones.

Las consecuencias podrían ir desde la suspensión de la habilitación de la empacadora para ese cultivo, hasta la suspensión de la habilitación del país proveedor.”

Summary: Peru reiterated its concern regarding Ecuador's restrictive measures on Peruvian grapes and onions. Peru was of the view that Ecuador's actions constituted a violation of the legislation in place in Ecuador, of Articles 2, 3, 4, 5, 7 and 8, as well as Annexes B and C of the SPS Agreement, and of Codex Guidelines for the Exchange of Information Between Countries on Rejections of Imported Food. While the Technical Resolution DAJ-20133EC-0201.0096 had been notified in document G/SPS/N/ECU/132, Resolution 0064, from 2017, had not been notified and Members had not been able to submit comments, despite the impact of the regulation on trade. Despite the exchanges held since 2014, Peru regretted that the answers received from Ecuador seemed to unnecessarily delay market access. Peru requested Ecuador to avoid proposing measures that violate the provisions of the SPS Agreement and the basic principles of the WTO; not to disregard the technical agreements previously developed; to notify its measure and provide opportunities for comments; and to reopen the market for grapes and onions. Peru submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/1975.

StatementSubmitted: 1.       El Perú vuelve a presentar su preocupación comercial ante los Miembros de la OMC con relación a las medidas restrictivas aplicadas por Ecuador en la reapertura del acceso de la uva y cebolla procedentes del Perú. 2.       En el caso de la uva, y de manera adicional a la información presentada en preocupaciones anteriores en este Comité[1], el Perú desea señalar que, conforme a las disposiciones del Artículo 8 y del Anexo C del Acuerdo MSF, los procedimientos de tipo sanitario o fitosanitario deben ser atendidos y concluidos sin demoras indebidas, facilitando información a la Parte interesada y con prescripciones que se limiten a lo que sea razonable y necesario. En ese sentido, se han sostenido reuniones y remitido reiteradas comunicaciones con las medidas correctivas solicitadas por Ecuador desde agosto del 2014 hasta la fecha, obteniendo respuestas que parecen dilatar la apertura más allá de lo necesario, por ejemplo: a.       Ecuador presentó de manera no programada una solicitud de visita de inspección para uvas, la cual fue realizada en febrero de 2020 y cuyo informe fue remitido a Perú después de siete meses. b.       Ecuador modificó de manera unilateral el plan de acción propuesto por el Perú para el acceso del mercado para las uvas. c.       Se propuso sin sustento técnico y desconociendo que el comercio histórico se da por vía terrestre, que la fruta de uva debía ingresar en barco únicamente por el Puerto Marítimo de Guayaquil. d.       Se ha propuesto el uso de transporte refrigerado en los envíos de uva, sin que este tratamiento se justifique con el riesgo de la presencia de plaguicidas o alguna plaga cuarentenaria para Ecuador asociada a la fruta de origen y procedencia del Perú. 3.       Con relación al transporte refrigerado, AGROCALIDAD[2]  señala que, de acuerdo con datos científicos disponibles al público, la refrigeración de frutas y hortalizas es el mejor sistema para mantener estos alimentos frescos y aumentar su vida útil comercial. En tal sentido, agrega que invertir en frío:a.       Retrasa la maduración y envejecimiento de las células de los tejidos.b.       Evita el ataque de microorganismos.c.       Minimiza las pérdidas cuantitativas y cualitativas globales de los productos. 4.       De lo expuesto, cabe resaltar que AGROCALIDAD se limitó a presentar información para evitar la presencia de microorganismos y la conservación óptima de las frutas y hortalizas; sin embargo, no se hace mención alguna sobre el tratamiento del transporte sanitario (frío) y la presencia de residuos de plaguicidas en la uva originaria de Perú, y si esta exigencia cumpliese con el objetivo último que es el de reducir el riesgo de contaminación. 5.       Asimismo, AGROCALIDAD se basa en el estudio “Aspectos técnicos para un adecuado transporte de uva de mesa en contenedores”, relacionado al transporte de uva desde que se produce hasta que llega a los mercados de destino en el exterior, donde el producto requiere mantener condiciones de refrigeración por un periodo largo durante el transporte del producto hasta llegar a su destino final (Estados Unidos, Unión Europea, entre otros). 6.       Por otro lado, Ecuador hace referencia al documento “Estudio de prefactibilidad para determinar la viabilidad de inversión de una planta de packing de uva en la empresa Asociación Agrícola Compositan Alto – La Libertad”, el cual señala que las uvas deben ser sometidas al tratamiento en frío, con la finalidad de matar, inactivar o eliminar plagas relacionadas a la mosca de fruta, lo cual no corresponde en el presente caso. 7.       Adicionalmente, es necesario resaltar que, a efectos del ingreso y la salida de la uva de otros países, AGROCALIDAD no contempla como exigencia el cumplimiento de condiciones relacionadas a la calidad de la fruta ni al transporte en frío. 8.       Con relación a las cebollas, la Resolución N° 2253 de la Comunidad Andina ha señalado que las medidas de Ecuador como resultado de la implementación del Plan Nacional de Vigilancia y Control de Residuos Contaminantes en la Producción Primaria son consideradas como medidas restrictivas al comercio intrasubregional y solicita a Ecuador retire las medidas identificadas como restricción[3]. Sin embargo, Ecuador plantea medidas para dilatar el proceso de acceso de la cebolla peruana, mediante el desarrollo de un nuevo análisis de riesgos de plagas[4]. Es necesario señalar que la suspensión del comercio no está prevista como una medida para la actualización del análisis de riesgos de plagas conforme a las Normas internacionales para medidas fitosanitarias de la Convención Internacional de Protección Fitosanitaria (CIPF), 9.       El Perú lamenta que, a pesar de haber cumplido con todas las exigencias solicitadas por Ecuador, las restricciones para el acceso a la uva y cebolla peruana al mercado ecuatoriano siguen en vigencia sin una justificación técnica y contraviniendo los artículos 2.2 y 5.1 del Acuerdo MSF[5]. 10.     Considerando que las medidas aplicadas por el Ecuador son discriminatorias y contravienen las disposiciones de los artículos 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, Anexo B y Anexo C del Acuerdo MSF, solicitamos al Ecuador: a.       Evitar proponer medidas que contravengan las disposiciones del Acuerdo MSF y los principios básicos de la OMC; b.       Evitar desconocer los acuerdos técnicos previamente desarrollados; c.       Notificar su medida y dar la oportunidad a los otros Miembros de la OMC para remitir comentarios; d.       Brindar acceso a las importaciones de uvas y cebollas peruanas.[1] Preocupaciones presentadas previamente mediante los documentos G/SPS/GEN/1937, G/SPS/GEN/1975; G/SPS/GEN/1907 y en el Comité MSF OMC del 5, 6 y 13 de noviembre de 2020.[2] Oficio N° AGR-AGROCALIDAD/DE-2021-001556-OF[3] Resolución disponible en: https://www.comunidadandina.org/DocOficialesFiles/Gacetas/Gaceta%204415.pdf [4] Mediante el Oficio Nro. AGR-AGROCALIDAD/DE-2022-000412-OF, supuestamente, AGROCALIDAD levanta las restricciones a la importación de cebolla peruana, pero mediante Oficio Nro. AGR-AGROCALIDAD/DE-2022-000425-OF, se solicita iniciar un análisis de riesgos de plagas para brindar acceso a la cebolla peruana.[5] Comunicaciones enviadas a AGROCALIDAD por el mantenimiento de las restricciones a las cebollas:-          CARTA-0047-2022-MIDAGRI-SENASA-DIAIA-          CARTA-0046-2022-MIDAGRI-SENASA-DIAIA
Summary: Peru referred to its full statement on eAgenda, and provided a brief statement orally. Drawing attention to some provisions of Annex C of the SPS Agreement, Peru acknowledged bilateral engagement with Ecuador regarding the latter's measures on grapes, but considered that the responses from Ecuador seemed to unnecessarily delay market access. Regarding onions, Peru noted that Ecuador's measures were restrictive in the context of intra-subregional trade as indicated in Resolution 2253 of the Andean Community. Furthermore, Peru noted that Ecuador's proposed measures included the development of a new PRA which would further delay market access for Peruvian onions, and stressed that the suspension of trade to update a PRA was inconsistent with ISPMs. Peru was of the view that Ecuador's actions constituted a violation of Articles 2, 3, 5, 7 and 8, as well as Annexes B and C of the SPS Agreement. Peru requested Ecuador to avoid proposing measures which were inconsistent with the SPS Agreement and the basic principles of the WTO; to respect previously developed technical agreements; to notify its measure and provide opportunities for comments; and to reopen the market for grapes and onions. Peru submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2012.

Peru expressed its concerns regarding Ecuador's trade restrictive measures on Peruvian grapes and onions. Regarding onions, Peru reported that a technical meeting had been held in April 2022 during which Ecuador had indicated that it would reopen its market for Peruvian onions in July 2022. Concerning grapes, Peru regretted that, despite its compliance with Ecuador's sanitary requirements, the restrictions on Peruvian grapes remained in force. Peru was of the view that Ecuador's actions constituted a violation of Articles 2, 3, 5, 7 and 8, as well as Annexes B and C of the SPS Agreement. Peru requested Ecuador to avoid proposing measures which were inconsistent with the SPS Agreement and the basic principles of the WTO, to respect previously developed technical agreements, and to reopen the market for Peruvian grapes and onions. Peru submitted its statement in G/SPS/GEN/2049.

Peru expressed its concerns regarding Ecuador's trade restrictive measures on Peruvian grapes and onions. Ecuador had not responded to the request for the establishment of the phytosanitary requirements for the opening of the onion market, despite having indicated it would reopen its market in July 2022. Peru also noted that Ecuador still required the refrigerated transport of grapes and that, despite its compliance with Ecuador's sanitary requirements, the restrictions on Peruvian grapes remained in force. Peru was of the view that Ecuador's actions constituted a violation of Articles 2, 3, 5, 7 and 8, as well as Annexes B and C of the SPS Agreement. Peru requested Ecuador to avoid proposing measures inconsistent with the SPS Agreement and the basic principles of the WTO, to respect previously developed technical agreements, and to reopen the market for Peruvian grapes and onions. Peru submitted its statement in G/SPS/GEN/2089.

Hoping to make progress bilaterally on onions, Peru raised concerns regarding the measures applied by Ecuador to the reopening of access for grapes. Peru had provided responses on the requirement for the refrigerated transport of grapes and hoped to agree on the import requirements and to conclude this process following the revision and analysis of the information provided. Peru submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2121.

Peru raised concerns regarding the measures applied by Ecuador to reopen access for onions and grapes. Regarding onions, Peru regretted the lack of information on the timeline to receive the phytosanitary requirements since the technical meeting held in April 2022, during which Ecuador had indicated that it would reopen its market in July 2022. Peru regretted that the market for grapes was also still closed, despite the answers provided on the refrigerated transport requirement proposed by Ecuador. Peru requested Ecuador to avoid proposing measures inconsistent with the SPS Agreement and the basic principles of the WTO and to reopen the market for Peruvian onions and grapes.
