StatementSubmitted:
Como lo indica la UE la Estrategia de la Granja a la Mesa no tiene valor jurídico, pero al final contemplará una combinación de medidas normativas y no normativas, con un efecto vinculante y de impacto para terceros países.

Y esta es la preocupación que deseamos resaltar en este tema, sobre el impacto que generará  a los terceros países exportadores de productos agrícolas.

Comprendemos que el objetivo de transformar un 25% de las tierras de producción agrícola en orgánica para el año 2030, es un reto. Sin embargo, es un objetivo interno de la Unión Europea, y el mismo no debe de trasladarse o generar impactos negativos en terceros países, en particular países en desarrollo.

Nos referimos a un comercio desbalanceado y distorsionado, debido a que para lograr ese objetivo del 25% y su conversión a una producción ecológica, reformarán la Política Agrícola Común para dar estímulos para esta producción.  Esto generará desventaja a los países en desarrollo, como Guatemala, que no tiene los recursos de dar apoyo interno a los productores para una reconversión ecológica.  Como se ha discutido en otros Comités en este foro multilateral.

Adicionalmente, la preocupación es el de imponer (de forma indirecta)  a los países tropicales, a una reconversión agrícola orgánica a las exportaciones hacia la Unión Europea. Debido a que se requiere como mínimo 5 años, en algunos casos más tiempo,  para que los productores terminen su transformación, únicamente si tienen recursos propios para este proceso. Es decir durante este tiempo los productores guatemaltecos, no tendrán ingreso porque se encuentran en proceso de reconversión a orgánico.  Es importante recalcar que solamente un porcentaje mínimo de productores podrán sobrevivir a esta etapa de recoversión.  Generando una pobreza en el área rural, desempleo, incremento del índice de hambruna y todo ello, porque la agricultura es el motor de las áreas rurales en los países en desarrollo. El objetivo de los acuerdos comerciales es que los productores puedan participar en el comercio internacional.

Entendemos que la UE no prohibirá el ingreso de estos productos, simplemente exigirá las mismas condiciones que tiene los productores europeos, pero lo preocupante es que las condiciones geográficas, climáticas y económicas no son las mismas.

Con relación a la respuesta de la UE en el documento G/SPS/GEN/1868, la UE  indica que  las evaluaciones de riesgo han identificado graves problemas ambientales a nivel mundial sobre el tiametoxam, (neonicotinoides). Sin embargo, después del cambio de los LMR en mayo 2018 de esta sustancia, la UE ha realizado 53 autorizaciones de urgencia a esta sustancia, beneficiando a los productores agrícolas de algunos países europeos. Condición que carecen los terceros países ante el uso de ciertas sustancias.

Adicionalmente, mencionan que una de las alternativas es negociar Acuerdos de Equivalencia, o tolerancias a la importación, cuando sabemos que estos acuerdos no son inmediatos y tienen su proceso de aprobación de mínimo de 2 años.  Ante ello Guatemala sigue manifestando preocupación de cómo las políticas europeas continuarán afectando la producción y exportación agrícola a partir del año 2022, con efectos negativos para el desarrollo rural.
Summary: Guatemala expressed its concern regarding the impact of the EU Farm to Fork Strategy on third country agricultural exporters as of 2022. In Guatemala's view, the internal EU objective to transform 25% of agricultural production land into organic by 2030 should not create negative impacts on third countries. Guatemala was concerned by the disadvantages that the reform of the EU Common Agricultural Policy to transit to organic production could have on developing countries, and by the indirect demand for tropical countries to convert to organic production of exports to the European Union. Guatemala deplored of the differential treatment granted to European producers concerning emergency authorizations for thiamethoxam, despite the environmental concerns indicated in G/SPS/GEN/1868. Finally, Guatemala stated that the negotiation of equivalence agreements, proposed as an alternative solution, would require at least two years before approval.Acknowledging an error in the statement uploaded in eAgenda, Guatemala reiterated the outstanding concern regarding the Strategy and its potential impact on trade, in spite of a virtual seminar that had taken place in October.

Australia looked forward to receiving formal answers from the European Union to comments provided in response to notification G/SPS/N/EU/401 regarding changes to export certificates for animal products and to an EU letter regarding requirements for the import of casings into the European Union. Australia considered that a separate residues plan for casings could not be justified as a risk management measure and that it would set a precedent for similar trade-limiting actions on other processed animal products. In Australia's view, the European Union had not provided the relevant scientific evidence and the measures were arbitrary and unjustified. Australia noted the lack of provisions for countries with EU approved residues monitoring plans for the species of animal from which the casings may be derived, the lack of justification for imposing the requirements on countries with controls over establishments preventing the use of antimicrobials in the production of casings, and the lack of relevance of the list of compounds proposed for testing to the concerns.

StatementSubmitted:
Australia reiterates our previous concerns regarding changes to the model health certificate for casings in EU regulation [Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/2235,  G/SPS/N/EU/401] which requires a separate residue monitoring plan for the production of animal casings exported to the EU.
	Australia notes that this significant requirement has not been notified to trading partners through a stand-alone SPS notification, but was rather referenced in notification notice G/SPS/N/EU/401 which outlined changes to all export certificates for animal products.
	As it stands, the European Union has not provided scientific evidence to support the proposed changes and Australia considers the measures arbitrary, unjustified and more trade restrictive than necessary.
	Australia is concerned this requirement sets a precedent for similar un-justified, trade-limiting actions on other processed animal products.
	Specifically, the concerns raised by the EU over the possible use of antimicrobial substances during the production of animal casings do not justify the imposition of an additional, separate residues testing system for casings.
	
		This is particularly true for countries such as Australia, which have controls over establishments that prevent the use of antimicrobials in the production of casings.
		The key substances of concern are prohibited from use on casings in Australia and Australia understands that they are not used in casings preservation anywhere in the world. The proposed requirement fails to recognise that low levels can occur naturally.
		Further, the measure also does not make any provision for countries that have EU-approved residues monitoring plans for each species of animal from which the casings may be derived.
		These plans are sufficient to monitor the risks of residues in the casings derived from those animals.
	
	
	Additionally, the list of compounds the EU has proposed for testing included some compounds that were not relevant to the concerns raised by the EU in its correspondence with Australia.
	While Australia welcomes ongoing bilateral engagement on this issue, we encourage the EU to separately notify the details of this requirement for residue testing for animal casings to the Committee, so that Members may have the opportunity to provide formal comments, and for comments to be considered prior to implementation.
Summary: Australia reiterated its concerns regarding changes to the model health certificate for casings set out in Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/2235, referenced in notification G/SPS/N/EU/401. Australia considered the measures to be arbitrary, unjustified and more trade restrictive than necessary, and that they would set a precedent for similar trade-limiting actions on other processed animal products. The EU concerns over the possible use of antimicrobial substances during the production of animal casings did not justify the imposition of a separate residues testing system for casings for countries such as Australia, where controls were in place to prevent establishments from using antimicrobials in the production of casings. The measures did not include any provision for countries with EU-approved residues monitoring plans for each species of animal from which the casings may be derived. Australia encouraged the European Union to notify the requirements, provide an opportunity for comments and take them into account before implementing the measure.

The United States expressed concerns about India's new measures requiring "non-GM (genetically modified) origin and GM-free certificates for certain agricultural imports, notified in G/TBT/N/IND/168, but not to the SPS Committee. India had not identified any specific food safety risk associated with the products at issue and the United States requested that India reconsider and delay implementation of its temporary measure. The United States provided its statement in G/SPS/GEN/1865.

StatementSubmitted:
India – “Non-GM/GM free” certificate requirement for imported food 

March 2021 WTO SPS Committee Meeting - United States' Intervention

The United States again raises serious concerns with India’s new measure mandating “non-GM (genetically modified) origin and GM free certificates” for certain agricultural imports into India, notified on September 2, 2020, as G/TBT/N/IND/168, with a proposed entry into force date of March 1, 2021.

The United States would like to remind India of our previous statement delivered at the November 2020 Committee meeting which details our concerns regarding India’s implementation of G/TBT/N/IND/168.

These concerns are documented in the Committee’s summary reports of the previous meeting and in G/SPS/GEN/1865.

The United States notes that, after numerous requests for India to revoke the order, on January 27, 2021, the U.S. Department of Agriculture proposed technical cooperation to develop alternatives to the non-GM origin and GM free certificate and we are optimistic that the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) will agree to this opportunity.

The United States requests that India withdraw this Order.

If India is unwilling to withdraw this Order, the United States requests that India delay implementation to January 2022 to allow for further technical engagement between the FSSAI and trade partners to develop less burdensome alternatives that could meet the Order’s stated food safety goals.

The United States also notes FSSAI’s “Clarification” published February 8, 2021 establishing a one percent tolerance for presence of GE in imported food consignments.  We request that India provide the scientific justification for establishing the tolerance at this level and provide any relevant risk assessments or international standards on which this tolerance is based.
Summary: The United States reiterated its concerns with India's new measure mandating non-GM (genetically modified) origin and GM-free certificates for certain agricultural imports into India, notified as G/TBT/N/IND/168, with a proposed entry into force date of 1 March 2021. The United States referred to the concerns expressed in the November 2020 Committee meeting and in document G/SPS/GEN/1865. The United States was optimistic that the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) would agree to the technical cooperation proposed by USDA to develop alternatives to the non-GM origin and GM-free certificates. The United States requested India to withdraw its measure or, alternatively, to delay its implementation to January 2022. The United States requested India to provide the scientific justification and any relevant risk assessments or international standards for establishing a one percent tolerance for presence of genetically engineered (GE) food in imported consignments. The US statement is contained in document G/SPS/GEN/1901.

StatementSubmitted:
China appreciates India’s fulfillment of its transparency obligations and also believes that India has the right to take SPS measures necessary to protect the life or health of humans, animals and plants. However, China also has some concerns on this requirement, especially on the scope the products which require non-GMO certificate.

According to the International Service for the Acquisition of Agri-biotech Application, there is no report on genetic modification of Phaseolus vulgaris, the common bean. At present, all the common bean exports to India from China are non-GMO and Chinese competent authority has never approved the cultivation of genetically modified Phaseolus vulgaris. In addition, the genetically modified sampling conducted by the Chinese Customs on Phaseolus vulgaris also confirmed that the products exported to India are free of genetically modified ingredients .

Therefore, China believes that India’s requirements of non-GMO certificate for 24 categories of agricultural products exported to India should be based on risk assessment and we hope India could publish the risk assessment and decision-making basis for implementing this measure. This measure taken by India has increased the compliance costs and burdens of enterprises in the food value chain?which has affected the stability of the supply chain and trade. According to Article 5.4 of the SPS Agreement, when determining the appropriate level of SPS protection, members should take into account the objective of minimizing negative trade effect. The products listed in Circular G/TBT/N/IND/168 shall be subject to classified managed. For products such as Phaseolus vulgaris exported to India from China, which have been tested by the competent authorities before exporting and has no record of genetically modified detection, this member and such products should not be included in the scope of the control of this measure.

The common bean from China has a large share in the Indian import market. According to statistics, China exported more than 500 batches of common bean in 2019, accounting for about 50% of India’s imports. Once the above measures are implemented, the cost of exporting enterprises will be added, which will ultimately harm the interests of both the Indian consumers and Chinese farmers.
Summary: China raised its concerns on the scope of the products which required a non-GMO (genetically modified organisms) certificate. The common bean exported to India from China was free of GM ingredients, as confirmed by the sampling conducted by the Chinese Customs, and should not be included in the scope of the control of this measure. China requested India to publish the risk assessment and decision-making basis for implementing these requirements of non-GMO certificates for 24 categories of agricultural products. While according to Article 5.4 of the SPS Agreement, Members should take into account the objective of minimizing negative trade effect when determining the ALOP, the measure had increased the compliance costs and burdens for enterprises in the food value chain. The common bean from China accounted for about 50% of India's imports and the implementation of the measures would add costs, harming the interests of Indian consumers and Chinese farmers.

StatementSubmitted:
China shares India’s concern on food safety. China controls the import, distribution and cultivation of genetically modified foods through safety assessments conducted in accordance with Chinese domestic regulations. Unapproved genetically modified varieties cannot be imported into China or distributed domestically, such as kidney beans and other agricultural products exported to India. However, India’s order to require non-GM cum GM-free certificate accompanied with imported food consignment will greatly increase the export cost of Chinese enterprises and seriously affect foreign trade.

In particular, the selection criteria for the 24 food crops listed in Annex 1 to the Order were unclear and the applicable members failed to discriminate. China suggests that India should publish the risk assessment and decision basis for implementing the measure. This measure has increased the compliance cost of the food value chain and the burden on enterprises, and has had an impact on the stability of the supply chain and trade.

Therefore, related products should be classified and managed on the basis of risk assessment. For products like kidney beans exported from China to India, there was no record of GM detection after pre-export regulatory inspection, China suggests that India will not include non-GMO products in the scope of this measure. In addition, we hope that India will provide alternative measures with fewer trade restrictions to those members who have not approved the release of any genetically modified crops into the environment.
Summary: Sharing India's concerns on food safety, China explained that unapproved genetically modified (GM) varieties could not be imported into China or distributed domestically and, as such, India's order would affect trade and increase the cost of Chinese exports of kidney beans and other agricultural products to India. China invited India to publish the risk assessment and decision basis for the selection of the 24 food crops listed in annex 1 to the Order. China suggested India not to include non-GM products in the scope of this measure and to provide alternative measures to Members who had not approved the release of GM crops into the environment.

The United States reiterated the concerns about India's measures, notified under G/TBT/N/IND/168, contained in documents G/SPS/GEN/1865 and G/SPS/GEN/1901. Likewise, the United States requested India to consider alternative approaches that could be implemented in a non-discriminatory manner and were not more trade-restrictive than necessary. The United States looked forward to the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India's (FSSAI) response to the proposed technical cooperation to develop alternatives to the non-GM origin and GM-free certificate. The full intervention is available in document G/SPS/GEN/1940.

StatementSubmitted:
November 2021 WTO SPS Committee Meeting - Statement by the United States  - (SPS STC 501)


	The United States once again reiterates its concerns with India’s measure mandating “non-GM (genetically modified) origin and GM free certificates” for certain agricultural imports into India, notified on September 2, 2020, as G/TBT/N/IND/168.
	The United States has previously raised this issue at the November 2020, March 2021, and July 2021 SPS Committee meetings as documented in G/SPS/GEN/1865, G/SPS/GEN/1901, and G/SPS/GEN/1940. 
	Also, since January 2021, the U.S. has sought technical cooperation with the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) and to date has not received a response.
	We once again ask that India consider withdrawing this measure or develop alternative approaches that are less trade restrictive.  India has not provided scientific justification nor a risk assessment supporting this measure despite numerous requests from multiple trading partners.
Summary: The United States reiterated its concerns with India's measure mandating non-GM (genetically modified) origin and GM-free certificates for certain agricultural imports into India, notified as G/TBT/N/IND/168. Noting that no scientific justification nor risk assessment for the measures had been provided, the United States continued to seek technical cooperation with the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, for which it had not received a response to date. The United States requested India to consider withdrawing its measure, or to develop alternative approaches that were less trade-restrictive. The United States submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/1985.

StatementSubmitted: India's requirement for certificate for non-GM origin and GM-free status (STC 501)March 2022 WTO SPS Committee Meeting - Statement by the United StatesThe United States once again calls attention to its previous concerns raised in the past four SPS Committee meetings as documented in G/SPS/1865, G/SPS/GEN/1901, G/SPS/GEN/1940, and G/SPS/GEN/1985. India’s measure notified in G/TBT/N/IND/168 stipulates that the “Order is applicable to only food products listed in Annex-I of its Order and does not apply to processed food products in general.”  Yet, since the measure went into effect in March 2021, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, or FSSAI, has used the regulation as a basis to limit trade of certain processed products, including milled rice, which is not a food product listed in Annex-I of the Order discussed in G/TBT/N/IND/168, and thus, the Order should have no bearing. Despite numerous requests from multiple trading partners, India has not provided scientific justification nor a risk assessment supporting this measure. The United States continues to seek technical cooperation with FSSAI and urges India to immediately withdraw this temporary measure and develop alternative approaches that are less trade-restrictive and more consistent with international best practices.
Summary: The United States reiterated its concerns with India's measure mandating non-GM (genetically modified) origin and GM-free certificates for certain agricultural imports into India, notified as G/TBT/N/IND/168. The United States noted that the regulation was used as a basis to limit the trade of certain processed products which had not been listed in the Order in the Annex of G/TBT/N/IND/168. The United States continued to seek technical cooperation with the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India and urged India to withdraw this measure and develop alternative approaches that were less trade-restrictive and more consistent with international best practices. The United States submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2008.

StatementSubmitted: India – “Non-GM/GM free” certificate requirement for imported food (STC 501)June 2022 WTO SPS Committee Meeting - Statement by United States The United States again raises its concerns regarding India's Order as previously documented in G/SPS/1865, G/SPS/GEN/1901, G/SPS/GEN/1940, G/SPS/GEN/1985, and G/SPS/GEN/2008.Despite numerous requests from the United States and multiple trading partners, India has provided neither scientific justification nor a risk assessment supporting this measure.The United States notes that India has previously asserted that the Order is not trade restrictive and cited both the compliance of various trading partners and the lack of approvals for GM- and GE-origin crop varieties by its Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee as evidence.The United States stresses that instances of compliance and a lack of GE approvals do not provide appropriate or adequate justification for the Order, but rather highlight the negative impacts on trade and inefficient biosafety regulation in India.The United States again reiterates its desire to engage in technical cooperation with FSSAI and urges India to immediately withdraw this temporary measure in favor of an alternative approach that is less trade-restrictive and more consistent with international best practices.
Summary: The United States regretted that, despite its numerous requests, India had provided neither scientific justification nor a risk assessment in support of this measure. In the view of the United States, India's assertion that the Order was not trade-restrictive was not justified. The United States reiterated its willingness for bilateral technical cooperation and urged India to withdraw this temporary measure and apply an alternative, less trade-restrictive approach. The United States submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2045.In response to India, the United States argued that trade had been affected, and reiterated its willingness to engage in technical dialogue on this issue.

StatementSubmitted: The United States has repeatedly raised its concerns regarding the Order in the past six SPS Committee meetings, most recently in June of this year, as documented in G/SPS/GEN/2045.            The United States notes that India still refuses to furnish an explanation of the scientific basis and risk assessment which justifies this non-GM certificate requirement on a consignment basis for the 24 crops listed in the Order.            India has stated that the requirement to regulate the import of “GM” food is not new, as outlined in the Environmental Protection Act (1986), and that the requirement has not caused trade disruptions.            The United States must stress that the requirement of a non-GM certificate on a consignment basis was first ordered in 2020, and since its entry into force the Order has caused trade disruptions for U.S. exports, most notably apples and rice.            The United States asserts that instances of compliance by other countries, and India’s own issuance of similar certificates, do not constitute sufficient justification for this Order, and furthermore the Order must be notified to the SPS Committee.             The United States once again reiterates its desire to engage in technical cooperation with FSSAI and urges India to immediately withdraw this measure.
Summary: The United States regretted that, despite its numerous requests, India had not provided a scientific justification nor a risk assessment in support of the non-GM certificate requirement on a consignment basis for the 24 crops listed in the Order. The United States affirmed that the requirements had first been ordered in 2020 and that, contrary to India's assertion, the Order had disrupted US exports. Requesting that the Order be notified to the SPS Committee, the United States reiterated its willingness for bilateral technical cooperation and urged India to withdraw this measure. The United States submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2085.

StatementSubmitted: Also the EU would like to raise its concerns regarding the Indian requirement for non-GMO certification: the EU submitted comments to the TBT notification asking for further clarification; they have not been replied to and the India Order entered already into force.The EU considers that the India requirements go beyond what is necessary to achieve the stated objective and put an additional burden and costs on EU exporters. The EU would invite India to explain why it considers necessary to impose such a burden on trading partners with a high prevalence of non-GM food on their domestic market and a robust regulatory regime governing the use of GMs. In addition to the fact that only a limited number of the food crops referred to in the Annexure are authorised to contain GMs, there are very strict traceability and labelling requirements applicable to food that contains GMOs. The EU would like to ask India to waive the requirement to attach the certificate for food items
Summary: The European Union reported that it was still awaiting a response to comments it had provided on the TBT notification of this measure. The European Union highlighted that the measure was costly and burdensome for trading partners who had a high prevalence of non-GM foods in their domestic market. The European Union also expressed concerns with the limited number of food crops authorized to contain GMOs under the measure, as well as the strict traceability and labelling requirements which would apply to food containing GMOs. In closing, the European Union asked India to waive the certificate requirement for food items.

StatementSubmitted: India Requirement for Certificate for Non-GM Origin and GM-Free Status (STC ID 501)United States Statement - March 2023 WTO SPS Committee Meeting The United States has repeatedly raised concerns with the Order requiring a “non-GM (genetically modified) origin and GM-free certificate” in the past seven SPS Committee meetings, most recently in November of 2022, as documented in G/SPS/GEN/2085. In floor statements during the previous SPS Committee meetings, India asserted that the certification requirement is an assurance from competent authorities that food crops exported to India are of non-GM origin and GM-free and cited several trade partners who are complying. The United States acknowledges India’s right to regulate products for food safety so long as those regulations are based on scientific evidence and risk principles; however, India has still not provided the scientific justification for requiring a GM-free certificate for the twenty-four agricultural products covered by the Order. The United States also notes that compliance with the GM-free certificate requirement is not evidence that the measure is consistent with the WTO SPS Agreement. The United States once again requests that India immediately revoke this trade restrictive measure and engage in further dialogue to find alternatives that address India’s legitimate SPS concerns and facilitate safe trade.
Summary: The United States acknowledged India's right to regulate products for food safety reasons but noted that India had not provided the scientific justification for its non-GM certificate requirement for the 24 crops listed in its order. The United States requested India to immediately revoke its measure and to engage to find alternatives that would address India's legitimate SPS concerns and facilitate safe trade. The United States submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2114.

StatementSubmitted: The European Union would also like to raise its concerns on this STC.The EU considers that the India requirements go beyond what is necessary to achieve the stated objective and put an additional burden and costs on EU exporters. The EU would invite India to explain why it considers necessary to impose such a burden on trading partners with a high prevalence of non-GM food on their domestic market and a robust regulatory regime governing the use of GMs as the EU. Furthermore, the Indian requirement that fresh fruit and vegetables are accompanied by a certificate attesting to the GM-free nature is a redundant obligation as no authorised GMOs exist in the EU fruit and veg. sector. The additional costs that the issuance of these certificates carries for exporters, particularly as there is a need for a certificate for each container in each consignment of exported fresh fruit and vegetables to India, are not negligible.According to the information provided by the industry, in 2022, the costs associated with GM-free certificates to export to India add up to more than €105,000. This cost is entirely unnecessary as no fruits or vegetables in the EU can be genetically modified under EU legislation. The EU would like to ask India to waive the requirement to attach the certificate for food items.
Summary: The European Union considered India's requirement to go beyond what was necessary to achieve its stated objective and to put an additional burden on and substantial costs for EU exporters. The European Union requested explanations as to why India considered it necessary to impose such a burden on trading partners with a high prevalence of non-GM food and have a robust regulatory regime covering the use of GM products. The European Union asked India to waive its requirement for food items.

StatementSubmitted: India's requirement for certificate for non-GM origin and GM-free status (ID 501)Statement by the United States of America - July 2023 SPS Committee:This marks the eighth SPS Committee meeting of the United States raising its concerns on India’s Order requiring a “non-GM (genetically modified) origin and GM-free certificate” for 24 commodities imported for human consumption.The United States acknowledges India’s right to regulate products for food safety, so long as those regulations are based on scientific evidence and risk principles; however, India has still not shared the requested scientific justification for requiring a GM-free certificate for the 24 products covered by the Order.In previous floor statements, India asserted that the certification requirement is an assurance from competent authorities that food crops exported to India for human consumption are of non-GM origin and GM-free and cited several trade partners who are complying.The United States has noted that compliance with the GM-free certificate requirement is not evidence that the measure is consistent with the WTO SPS Agreement.After numerous requests, India still has not provided a science- and risk-based justification for these requirements. India appears to be ignoring a decades-long track record of publicly available risk assessments conducted by competent authorities demonstrating that approved foods and feeds derived from modern biotechnology are safe for consumption. We also note that India recently approved domestically produced GM mustard for commercial use and that India’s farmers routinely cultivate GM cotton. The United States continues to request India immediately revoke this trade restrictive measure.  The United States remains available to engage in further dialogue to identify safe trade facilitative alternatives that address India’s legitimate SPS concerns.
Summary: The United States noted that India had not provided the scientific justification for its non-GM certificate requirement for the 24 crops listed in its order. To the United States, India appeared to ignore decades of risk assessments demonstrating that approved foods and feeds derived from modern biotechnology were safe for consumption. The United States requested India to revoke its measure and engage to find alternatives that would address India's legitimate SPS concerns and facilitate safe trade. The United States submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2148.

StatementSubmitted: The United States has raised concerns with the Order requiring a “non-GM (genetically modified) origin and GM-free certificate” in the past nine SPS Committee meetings, most recently in July of 2023. In floor statements during the November 2022 SPS Committee meetings, India asserted that the certification requirement is an assurance from competent authorities that food crops exported to India are of non-GM origin and GM-free and cited several trade partners who are complying. The United States acknowledges India’s right to regulate products for food safety, so long as those regulations are based on scientific evidence and risk principles; however, India has still not provided the scientific justification for requiring a GM-free certificate for the twenty-four agricultural products covered by the Order. The United States also notes that the willingness of certain trading partners to provide GM-free certificates is not evidence that the measure is based on science or risk. The United States once again requests that India immediately revoke this trade restrictive measure and engage in further dialogue to identify a legitimate SPS concern and, if necessary, find alternatives that facilitate trade in safe food and feed.
Summary: Acknowledging the right to regulate products for food safety, the United States reiterated its concern that India had not provided the scientific justification for requiring a GM-free certificate for the 24 agricultural products covered by the Order. The United States requested India to revoke its measure, and to engage in further dialogue to find less restrictive alternatives that facilitate trade of safe food and feed. The United States provided its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2182.

StatementSubmitted: The United States remains deeply concerned with India’s Order mandating “non-GM origin and GM free certificates” for certain agricultural imports into India, notified on September 2, 2020.      We are taking the floor for the tenth and likely final time in this Committee to share our concerns.  We are extremely disappointed that India maintains this measure, despite extensive efforts to engage constructively by the United States and the international community, including in SPS, TBT, and CTG meetings, in bilateral engagements, and through letters. India did not meet the repeated requests of trading partners to provide the rationale, or a scientific or risk basis, for requiring a non-GM certificate on a per-consignment basis for each of the 24 crops named in the Order. We ask once more that India meet its international and bilateral obligations.  The United States remains ready to engage in meaningful dialogue with India. The United Sates also remains ready to consider other forms of collaboration with WTO Members who have registered concerns similar to our own.
Summary: The United States reiterated its concern over India's requirement for non-GM origin and GM-free certificates for certain agricultural imports. The United States noted that India maintained the measure despite the efforts to engage constructively through various channels, without providing the rationale or scientific basis for this requirement. Expressing its willingness to collaborate with other concerned Members, the United States urged India to meet its international and bilateral obligations. The United States provided its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2219.

China expressed concerns regarding the different types of controls that chondroitin sulphate exported from China was subject to at different EU border control posts. China explained that, on the basis of risk and of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/626, chondroitin sulphate exported as food was permitted. However, only chondroitin sulphate considered as feed material was covered in the Annex to Decision 2002/994/EC concerning certain protective measures with regard to the products of animal origin imported from China, which stipulated that only imports of products of animal origin from China covered in Annex should be authorized. China requested the European Union to amend the Annex to Decision 2002/994/EC to include chondroitin sulphate in the list of food of animal origin authorized into the European Union from China, and to clarify whether the import of chondroitin sulphate derived from animals from China was authorized and provide reasons.

StatementSubmitted:
China appreciates the EU's positive response to out concern at last meeting. After the meeting, the experts of China Customs made a further study on the information provide by EU and found that the Decision 2002/994 has been amended and updated by series of Decisions including the Decision 2015/1068 and the latest consolidated version is published on 3rd July, 2015, but in the list of latest consolidated version of 2002/994, only chondroitin regarded as feed material was covered and not for human consumption.

Therefore, China kindly suggests EU to amend the part I annex to the Decision 2002/994/EC to include the chondroitin, hyaluronic acid and chitosan for human consumption which is made from the materials derived from ungulate, fishery products and poultry to the list of products of animal of origin intended for human consumption.

Meanwhile China government and industry are also looking forward to the response from EU to our concerns on the harmonization and consistence of enforcement, which we raised at last meeting.
Summary: China acknowledged that Decision 2002/994/EC had been amended and updated by a series of EU Decisions, including Decision 2015/1068. China regretted that the latest consolidated version of Decision 2002/994 only covered chondroitin regarded as feed material, and not for human consumption. China suggested that the European Union amend Decision 2002/994/EC to include chondroitin, hyaluronic acid and chitosan in the list of products of animal origin intended for human consumption. China also looked forward to the EU response on the harmonization and consistency of enforcement raised in the previous Committee meeting.

Peru raised its concern regarding Regulation (EU) 488/2014 and provided the statement circulated in G/SPS/GEN/1870. In Peru's view, the EU Regulation negatively impacted trade of cocoa beans and cocoa powder. Peru also reminded of the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives' (JECFA) opinion of 2013 and noted the economic damage resulting from the request by EU importers of analysis of cadmium in cocoa beans, despite the Regulation referring to chocolate and cocoa products.Peru stated that exports of cocoa beans to the European Union had decreased and, as a consequence, the price of beans had dropped. Peru complained that EU importers required analysis of cadmium for all exported batches, performed both in Peru and upon arrival, with applied levels between 0.7 ppm and 1.0 ppm depending on the destination. Exports of cocoa powder to the European Union had also dropped. In Peru's view, Regulation (EU) 488/2014 was inconsistent with the objective of protecting the final consumer and created unnecessary barriers to exports of this product. Peru asked the European Union to explain what actions had been or were to be taken to avoid importers misusing the standard. The commercial consequences were also visible from the reductions of exports of traditional cocoa to the EU market and an increase of exports to the Asian market at a reduced price.Peru also noted the development of the industrialization process for cocoa exports undertaken over the previous five years and regretted that the EU Regulation increased costs and reduced the industry's profitability. Peru stated that the implementation of Regulation (EU) 488/2014 would make it impossible to achieve results on the cooperation projects funded by the European Union, which required avoiding negative impacts in the price of cocoa. Peru requested the European Union to revoke Regulation (EU) 488/2014 which, in its view, was inconsistent with Articles 2 and 5 of the SPS Agreement and generated unnecessary barriers to trade.

StatementSubmitted: Comité de Medidas Sanitarias y Fitosanitarias de la OMC25 y 26 de marzo de 2021 EU restrictions on exports of chocolate and cocoa products due to the application of the Commission Regulation (EU) N° 488/2014 of 12 May 2014 Amending Regulation (EC) N° 1881/2006 as regards maximum levels of cadmium in foodstuff DECLARACIÓN DEL PERÚ El Perú presenta ante los Miembros de la OMC su preocupación comercial con relación al Reglamento (UE) N° 488/2014 de la Comisión, del 12 de mayo de 2014, que modifica el Reglamento (CE) N° 1881/2006 en relación al contenido máximo de cadmio en los productos alimenticios. Específicamente, la normativa europea establece niveles máximos de cadmio para el chocolate y otros productos derivados del cacao, que en la práctica tienen un impacto negativo en el comercio de grano de cacao y de polvo de cacao. En primer lugar, el Perú quisiera resaltar el desempeño comercial e importancia social de la cadena productiva del cacao: El Perú presenta ventajas comparativas en la producción y el comercio de la cadena productiva del cacao, especialmente respecto al cacao en grano, manteca de cacao, pasta de cacao y cacao en polvo. Las exportaciones de esta cadena superaron los 278 millones de USD en el 2020[1]. Si bien las exportaciones han decrecido en 5.6% respecto a 2019, se estima un potencial exportador de más de 165 millones de USD[2]. El Perú es el noveno productor mundial de cacao en grano. La actividad cacaotera tiene un impacto descentralizador e inclusivo en el Perú. Representa: 16 regiones productoras[3], 90 mil familias cacaoteras, 136 mil hectáreas de superficie cosechada y 108 mil toneladas de producción. Asimismo, se tiene una participación importante de mujeres en la producción agrícola del cacao, representando el 21.3% del total de productores[4]. El cacao es considerado el segundo principal producto alternativo a los cultivos ilícitos en el Perú, después del café[5]. En segundo lugar, el Perú considera que el Reglamento (UE) N° 488/2014 de la Comisión vulnera el artículo 2 del Acuerdo MSF, debido a que: No se basa en principios científicos, y tampoco en una norma internacional, al no encontrarse concluida ésta. Al respecto, durante la 77°sesión de 2013 del Comité Mixto FAO-OMS de Expertos en Aditivos Alimentarios (JECFA), se señaló que los niveles de cadmio en el cacao no son considerados como un riesgo para la salud pública, lo cual debió ser tomado en cuenta por la Unión Europea (UE), al momento de desarrollar su normativa. En este punto, es necesario recalcar que el sustento de la normativa europea considera informes previos del JECFA, mas no el Informe del año 2013[6]. Las declaraciones de la FAO, en representación de la Secretaría del JECFA en la 42° sesión de la Comisión del Codex Alimentarius de julio de 2019, señalan que la exposición dietética al cadmio en cacao es insignificante en comparación con la derivada de otras fuentes y no supone una preocupación de salud pública[7].  El documento JECFA/91/SC, del 05 de marzo de 2021, mediante el cual se indica que la contribución de cadmio por productos derivados del cacao sigue siendo poco significativa, incluso en países de alto consumo[8]. En tercer lugar, es necesario resaltar las consecuencias negativas de la normativa europea: Existe una complementariedad en el comercio peruano del cacao y sus productos derivados con la UE, lo que ha permitido que se puedan consolidar las ventajas comparativas del Perú en dicho mercado[9].  Sin embargo, desde la entrada en vigencia de la normativa europea en 2019, las exportaciones de cacao y sus productos derivados a la UE han disminuido y han tenido que colocarse en mercados asiáticos, en los cuales el valor de compra del cacao es menor hasta en un 30%.  En efecto, las exportaciones de cacao y derivados a la UE, en el año 2020, presentaron una disminución de 5.59% en comparación con las exportaciones del año 2019. Además, en los últimos 5 años, las exportaciones peruanas de cacao y productos derivados con destino a la UE han registrado un decrecimiento promedio anual del -10.79%[10]. Los importadores europeos exigen, sin sustento técnico o normativo, niveles máximos para el cacao en grano. Los niveles máximos que se exigen varían entre 0.7 a 0.8 ppm en el caso de compradores alemanes y hasta 1.0 ppm en el caso de importadores holandeses y franceses[11]. Asimismo, se presentan órdenes de compra de importadores españoles para cacao en grano que solicitan un “Certificado de cadmio”, a pesar de que éste no se encuentra regulado. Igualmente, los importadores europeos solicitan conocer los niveles de cadmio para el cacao en polvo, indicando que “debido al nuevo reglamento de la UE su polvo de cacao debe tener menos de 0.6 mg de Cd”[12], a pesar de que el cacao en polvo no se encuentra destinado al consumo final y, por lo tanto, no se encuentra regulado mediante el Reglamento (UE) N° 488/2014. En la práctica, la normativa europea es utilizada para todo cacao en polvo, indistintamente del riesgo que éste pueda representar. Esta situación se ve agravada mediante mensajes erróneos brindados por la misma UE que indican que para todo el cacao en polvo se aplicaría un nivel máximo de cadmio de 0.6 ppm[13], frente a los cuales el Perú ha solicitado bilateralmente una rectificación. En ese sentido, los niveles máximos se han convertido en una herramienta de negociación comercial, y no de protección a la salud humana, en contra de los productores. Sobre el particular, es preciso señalar que los productores consideran que uno de los factores de mayor importancia para continuar en el sector es que el cacao tenga un mercado seguro; así como un buen precio de venta y se adapte a las condiciones climáticas[14]; sin embargo, caídas de precio superiores al 10% afectan la estrategia de desarrollo alternativo basada en cacao, ya que la rentabilidad de éste deja de ser relevante frente a la de la coca[15]. Alrededor del 44% de los productores peruanos de cacao en grano, lo que significa más de 39,600 familias, se ha visto afectado por la norma de la UE, en especial los productores peruanos de las zonas de desarrollo alternativo, tales como San Martín, Huánuco, Ucayali y Junín, en donde se produce el 80% del cacao de Perú[16]. En cuarto lugar, el Perú quisiera volver a señalar el caso presentado en la reunión del Comité MSF OMC de noviembre de 2020[17]. Al respecto, se señaló que la empresa exportó 100 y 140 toneladas de cacao en polvo en 2017 y 2018, respectivamente. Sin embargo, debido a que, en la práctica, los importadores europeos solicitan un nivel máximo de 0.6 ppm (a pesar de que el cacao en polvo no es destinado al consumo final), en el año 2019, la empresa solo pudo exportar 40 toneladas y, en el año 2020, no pudo concretar ventas en octubre, noviembre y diciembre. Comité de Medidas Sanitarias y Fitosanitarias de la OMC

14, 15 y 16 de julio de 2021- Intervenciones del Perú

RESTRICCIONES IMPUESTAS POR LA UNIÓN EUROPEA A LAS EXPORTACIONES DE PRODUCTOS DE CHOCOLATE Y DE CACAO DEBIDO A LA APLICACIÓN DEL REGLAMENTO (UE) Nº 488/2014 DE LA COMISIÓN, DE 12 DE MAYO DE 2014, QUE MODIFICA EL REGLAMENTO (CE) Nº 1881/2006 POR LO QUE RESPECTA AL CONTENIDO MÁXIMO DE CADMIO EN LOS PRODUCTOS ALIMENTICIOS (Nº 503)

Preocupaciones comerciales específicas anteriormente planteadas – nº iii

INTERVENCIÓN DEL PERÚ

El Perú presenta ante los Miembros de la OMC su preocupación comercial con relación al Reglamento (UE) N° 488/2014 de la Comisión, del 12 de mayo de 2014, que modifica el Reglamento (CE) N° 1881/2006 en relación al contenido máximo de cadmio en los productos alimenticios. Específicamente, la normativa europea establece niveles máximos de cadmio para el chocolate y otros productos derivados del cacao, que en la práctica tienen un impacto negativo en el comercio de grano de cacao y de polvo de cacao.

En primer lugar, el Perú quisiera resaltar el desempeño comercial e importancia de la cadena productiva del cacao:

Las exportaciones peruanas del cacao y sus derivados han alcanzado los 64 millones de USD durante el periodo enero-marzo 2021, con un crecimiento del 15.62% respecto al mismo periodo del año 2020. De este total, aproximadamente el 39.2% se ha destinado a la UE[1].

Las exportaciones de cacao orgánico representan el 23% del total de exportaciones del cacao en grano.

El Perú es el octavo productor mundial de cacao en grano con un estimado de producción al 2021 de 150,000 toneladas. Las estrategias gubernamentales y privadas destinadas a fomentar y desarrollar el cultivo de cacao fino o de aroma han contribuido a la tendencia del alza de la producción[2].

El Perú estima que para el año 2030 se tendrá una producción de alrededor de 250,000 toneladas, lo que representará un crecimiento de alrededor del 65% en comparación con el año 2020[3].

El Perú, en conjunto con otros Miembros, lidera el desarrollo del Código de prácticas para la prevención y reducción de la contaminación por cadmio en granos de cacao en el marco del Comité del Codex sobre Contaminantes de los Alimentos.

El Perú ha liderado la creación del grupo de trabajo sobre cadmio en el marco de la Organización Internacional del Cacao (ICCO).

El cacao es considerado el principal producto alternativo a los cultivos ilícitos en el Perú, después del café.

El Perú considera que el Reglamento (UE) N° 488/2014 de la Comisión vulnera el artículo 2 del Acuerdo MSF, debido a que las medidas sanitarias solo deben aplicarse en cuanto sean necesarias, entre otras para la protección a salud y vida de las personas; sin embargo, el documento JECFA/91/SC, del 05 de marzo de 2021, indica que la contribución de cadmio por productos derivados del cacao sigue siendo poco significativa, incluso en países de alto consumo[4]. Con este documento se presenta una evidencia adicional respecto a que la presencia de cadmio en chocolate y derivados del cacao no constituye una preocupación para la salud pública y que la aplicación de niveles máximos de cadmio en chocolate y derivados del cacao no tiene un beneficio significativo en la reducción de la exposición alimentaria al cadmio.

Igualmente es preciso resaltar que, si bien en el documento JECFA/91/SC se indica un supuesto en el que no se descartaría un problema de salud pública con niños europeos que solo consumiesen productos del cacao procedentes de América Latina, dicho supuesto no se cumple en la realidad. Incluso si todas las exportaciones de cacao en grano de América Latina y el Caribe se enviaran a la Unión Europea, éstas solo han representado en promedio el 20.8% del total de importaciones del mercado europeo durante el periodo 2016-2020[5].

Adicionalmente, la ingesta de chocolate representa una fracción muy pequeña de la canasta total de alimentos del poblador europeo, y bastante menor en el resto del mundo. La mayor cantidad de cadmio se ingiere a través de cereales, frutas, verduras, pescados y mariscos[6]. Un incremento pequeño en los niveles máximos de cadmio en cualquiera de estos grupos de alimentos tendría un efecto más importante que el que se puede lograr con los niveles máximos en cualquiera de los tipos de chocolate.  Por tanto, la disminución de la ingesta de cadmio en los alimentos mediante la reducción de cadmio en los distintos tipos de chocolates no contribuye de manera significativa a disminuir la ingesta total de cadmio, inclusive en la población infantil.

La Unión Europea ha establecido niveles máximos de cadmio en los distintos tipos chocolate, sobre la base de una Ingesta Máxima Tolerable Posible de 2,5 µg/Kg p.c. semana (microgramos por kilo de peso corporal a la semana) [7], en tanto que el valor utilizado por JECFA es de 5,8 µg/Kg p.c (microgramos por kilo de peso corporal a la semana). semana. En ese sentido, el valor establecido por EFSA es menos de la mitad (43,1%) del establecido por JECFA, lo cual lleva a disminuir los niveles máximos en su normativa regional.  Al respecto, solicitamos a la Unión Europea que comparta la evidencia científica por la cual que sustente que los ciudadanos de la Unión Europea son 232% más sensibles al cadmio que los ciudadanos del resto del mundo.

Por otro lado, el Perú mantiene su preocupación respecto a que los niveles máximos de cadmio en chocolate y derivados del cacao continúen siendo utilizados como una herramienta de negociación frente a los productores, quienes han visto disminuidos sus ingresos por niveles máximos exigidos de entre 0.7 y 0.8 ppm por parte de compradores alemanes y hasta 1 ppm por compradores franceses y holandeses en el grano de cacao[8].

Conforme lo hemos expuesto previamente, la normativa europea es utilizada para todo cacao en polvo, indistintamente del riesgo que éste pueda representar. Esta situación se ve agravada mediante mensajes erróneos brindados por la misma Unión Europea que indican que para todo el cacao en polvo se aplicaría un nivel máximo de cadmio de 0.6 ppm[9].

Los niveles máximos de cadmio en los distintos tipos de chocolate, tal como los define el Reglamento (UE) N° 488/2014, no contribuyen a resolver de manera significativa, el problema de salud pública que puede significar el cadmio en los alimentos. Los niveles máximos de cadmio establecidos por la Unión Europea tampoco generan condiciones de comercio equitativas, ya que perjudica a los productores de cacao principalmente de una sola región del mundo. Esta medida genera un escenario de sobrecostos para productores y sus familias del Perú, así como de otros países de la Latinoamérica, que en conjunto representan el 18% de la producción mundial aproximadamente.

Por lo anteriormente expuesto, el Perú solicita a la UE dejar sin efecto el Reglamento (UE) N° 488/2014 de la Comisión, con respecto al chocolate y otros productos derivados del cacao, en vista de que no se encuentra en concordancia con el Acuerdo MSF OMC y genera barreras innecesarias al comercio.

Australia expressed concerns about the potential negative impact that the EU proposed changes relating to shelf-stable composite products under Regulation (EU) 2019/625, notified in G/SPS/N/EU/401, might have on trade in shelf-stable composite products. Products previously excluded from the original EU Regulation of 2007 would now be captured in the proposed requirements for food manufacturers of shelf-stable composite products to attest the sourcing of animal origin ingredients (dairy, fishery, or egg origin) from EU approved establishments either in EU member States or in authorized third countries. Australia considered that these requirements were not justified and would not lead to significant improvements in safety or a higher quality of products, and asked the European Union to explain how the proposed regulatory requirements were in line with the SPS Agreement and Codex international standards.Australia requested the European Union to recognize equivalence of third countries already implementing a sufficient level of sanitary regulation for low-risk shelf-stable composite products, as established in Article 4 of the SPS Agreement. It also requested the European Union to indicate how the proposed changes corresponded with the level of risk posed by the presence of low levels of animal origin ingredients contained within shelf-stable composite products, as required under Article 5 of the SPS Agreement. Australia looked forward to receiving the EU views on the precedent that this regulation would set for international trade in shelf-stable foods, and requested the European Union to reconsider the implementation of this regulation as currently drafted, including product coverage and thresholds.

StatementSubmitted:
Australia welcomes the opportunity to discuss it’s concerns about the EU’s notification (G/SPS/N/EU/401) regarding the proposed changes relating to shelf-stable composite products under EU Regulation 2019/625.
	Under this proposed new system, food manufacturers of shelf stable composite products that contain any dairy, fishery or egg origin ingredients would need to attest to sourcing these animal origin ingredients from EU-approved establishments either in EU Member States or in authorised third countries.
	Australia understands this requirement would capture products previously excluded from the EU’s original regulation of 2007, including products such as biscuits, bread, cakes, chocolate and confectionary, pasta and noodles.
	For example, under existing EU regulations, some shelf stable composite products containing less than half of their weight or volume of either dairy ingredients, fish ingredients or egg ingredients are not required to be sourced from EU approved establishments either in EU Member States or in authorised third countries. (Note: this cut off varies depending upon specific product, with some as low as 20%, others are at 50% content – refer Annex 2 of EU Regulation 2016/1196/NC).
	Australia believes the EU’s proposed new rules on composite products (G/SPS/N/EU/401) will restrict trade in shelf-stable composite products (defined by the EU as foodstuffs intended for human consumption that contain both processed products of animal origin and products of plant origin).
	Australia maintains that the sourcing of animal-origin ingredients from EU-listed establishments for all composite products, irrespective of the percentage of animal ingredient in the product, is not justified as the consumer exposure to contaminants would be negligible and will not lead to significant improvements in safety for EU consumers.
	Further, as set out in Article’s 4 and 5 of the SPS Agreement, Australia requests that the EU recognise the equivalence of third countries, where those countries already implement a sufficient level of sanitary regulation for low-risk shelf-stable composite products, and that the sanitary measures are commensurate with the level of risk. 
	In summary, Australia requests the EU’s reconsideration of the implementation of this regulation as currently drafted, including the product coverage and thresholds. Australia requests that animal ingredients that make up a low percentage of a composite product not be subject to the proposed regulation and that the EU recognise Australia as having equivalence, since we already implement a sufficient level of sanitary regulation.
	We would welcome the EU’s response on these issues.

StatementSubmitted:
The Separate Customs Territory of Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen and Matsu would like to express once again our concerns about the EU’s proposed new rules on composite products.

We are pleased to learn that the EU is consulting its stakeholders to both extend the current list of composite products to be exempted from controls due to their lower risk, and change the certification requirements. In this regard, we particularly urge the EU to reconsider the necessity of requiring minor or trace ingredients of animal origin in composite products to be produced in establishments approved by the EU. For examples, seasonings or extracts are highly processed or denatured and in our view are at a level of extremely low risk considering their limited amount compared to other ingredients of animal origin. To require that such minor or trace ingredients of animal origin be sourced from EU approved establishments has been and will continue to impose a disproportionate burden on business operators as it does not contribute substantially to food safety considering the limited amount existing in composite products. We are concerned that the requirement is likely to discriminate composite products of specific cultural characteristics. Access to EU’s market is tantamount to a factual denial because an approved establishment producing such special ingredients simply does not exist.

The EU has mentioned that it is not a new rule that any processed product of animal origin contained in the composite product must come from an EU approved establishment. The rule’s preexistence does not automatically justify the necessity of requiring minor or trace ingredients of animal origin in composite products to be produced in establishments approved by the EU due to the reasons mentioned earlier. Most importantly the requirement applies to all ingredients of animal origin regardless of the risks associated or scientific evidence. The EU requirement applies without consideration of the risks paramount to the amount of presence of ingredients of animal origin.

We thank the EU for taking our concerns into account and look forward to actions taken by the EU towards implementing SPS measures consistent with its WTO commitments. A written response from the EU is greatly appreciated.
Summary: Chinese Taipei reiterated its concerns about the EU proposed new rules on composite products. Chinese Taipei urged the European Union to reconsider the necessity of requiring minor or trace ingredients of animal origin in composite products to be produced in establishments approved by the European Union, which, in its view, imposed a disproportionate burden on business operators and was likely to discriminate composite products of specific cultural characteristics. Chinese Taipei thanked the European Union for taking their concerns into account and looked forward to a written response by the European Union.

StatementSubmitted:
On 12 June 2020, the EU issued Circular G/SPS/GEN/1786 to revise the rules applicable to the entry of composite products into the EU as of 21 April 2021. The main revised contents include: definition of composite products, special requirements applicable to the processed products of animal origin contained in the composite products, risk-based categories of products, category-based requirements for certification and attestation guarantees, and controls at entry into the union.

China is of the view that the following four aspects of the new rules will have a great impact on trade: 1) The new requirements on the entry of composite products into the EU is that any processed products of animal origin contained in the composite product must be produced in EU approved establishments located either in the EU member states or in third countries authorized for the entry into the European Union of those processed products of animal origin. 2) The exporting country shall carry out an approved residue monitoring plan for each of the ingredients of animal origin in the same way as for products of animal origin. 3) Processed products that contained meat, fishery products, dairy products (lactoprotein) and eggs should be authorized for entry into the EU in advance. 4) The competent authorities of the exporting country need to source the ingredients of animal origin contained in the composite product and ensure that they meet the requirements of EU regulations.

The implementation of the rule will bring the following two impacts on the export of processed products:

1.It will increase the cost of manufacturers. Previously, the EU set a certain content level for different ingredients of animal origin in the processed foods, such as meat, aquatic products, dairy products and egg products. If the content of animal origin ingredients is lower than a certain level, the corresponding control measures for the products of animal origin will be exempted. There are many kinds of processed products that contained animal origin ingredients, such as cakes, biscuits, protein drinks, candy and instant noodles, the food manufacturers would be forced to change their raw material supply chain and management system due to the implementation of the new regulations, the consequent rising costs of compliance would dampen the enthusiasm of exporting to EU and result in a sharp decline of processed food exporting to EU.

2.It will increase the cost of supervision. The administrative costs could be very large to source and monitor each ingredient of animal origin in the processed products exported to the EU. As the quarantine risk of most processed products has been fully eliminated during processing, the benefit in improving food safety by sourcing and monitoring animal origin ingredients would be negligible, especially for members who have already implemented relatively sound regulation of agricultural inputs such as pesticides and veterinary drugs.
    Therefore, in order to ensure the unimpeded and convenient trade of composite products, we would like to make two proposals.

1.In view of the fact that the processing technique of processed products has made the food safety risks much lower than those of animal origin products, the EU Commission could formulate a list of low-risk products which should be exempted from the new rules, so as to avoid significant impact on trade.

2. Adopt the principle of equivalence. Third countries with a relatively well-established regulatory system should be recognized to meet the requirements of the EU’s regulations, and the composite products under the supervision of their competent authorities should also be accepted by the EU.
Summary: China was of the view that the implementation of the new EU rules would have a great impact on the exportation of processed products, namely increases in the costs for manufacturers and of supervision. As such, China proposed the formulation by the EU Commission of a list of low risk products to be exempted from the new rules, and the adoption of the principle of equivalence so that Members with a relatively well-established regulatory system be recognized to meet the requirements of the EU regulations, and the composite products under the supervision of their competent authorities be accepted by the European Union.

StatementSubmitted:
NEW EU RULES ON COMPOSITE PRODUCTS – CONCERNS OF AUSTRALIA
(STC No. 504)
The Russian Federation supports this Australian concern regarding new EU requirements
for the import of composite products, which come into effect on April 21, 2021.
The Russian Federation is of the view that new EU rules for composite products will
significantly affect trade of the WTO Member States.
An analysis of new European requirements for shelf-stable composite products indicates
that they are excessive and restrict trade more than it is necessary to achieve an
appropriate level of sanitary and phytosanitary protection.
In particular, goods that previously did not fall under the requirements for composite
products will be covered by the new measures.
And since April 21, 2021 low-risk shelf-stable composite products, which include raw
materials that have undergone a deep heat treatment, must meet the same high
requirements for the control of raw materials as higher-risk composite products.
The Russian Federation notes that a deep heat treatment guarantees safety of composite
products in veterinary terms.
The Russian Federation urges the EU to provide sufficient scientific evidence and risk
assessment supporting the requirement of production in establishments authorized by the
EU for minor or trace ingredients of animal origin in the composite products, especially
the highly processed or denatured.
It is already clear that the new EU requirements are not feasible to the majority of Russian
confectioneries exporters, as well as for a number of widely known international
companies, including European, since Russian producers of milk powder and milk whey
do not currently have access to the EU market.
We shall also mention that the European Union refused to inspect such Russian enterprises
in 2021 on the pretext of COVID-19 related measures.
It is unclear for the Russian Federation when such an audit can take place.
The Russian Federation notes that Article 2.2 of the SPS Agreement obliges WTO
Members to apply SPS measures only to the extent necessary to protect human, animal or
plant life or health.
Given the circumstances, the Russian Federation proposes first of all, to include producers
of raw materials for composite products in the registers of the European Union under the
guarantees of the competent authorities of the exporting countries.
Secondly, the Russian Federation is of the view that the EU requirements for mandatory
certification of manufacturers of raw materials of animal origin used for production of

composite products that fall into the list of exceptions from the EU border control posts, in
other words of no or low veterinary risk, are excessive and therefore could be eliminated.
Third, the EU could provide for a transition period for the application of a new form of
veterinary certificate for products of short-term storage containing less than 50% of animal
origin, and a special certificate for non-perishable food products.
The Russian Federation believes that the EU's measures should be not more trade-
restrictive than necessary to achieve appropriate level of SPS protection as it is provided
for in the WTO SPS Agreement.
Summary: The Russian Federation considered that new EU rules for composite products, entering into force on 21 April 2021, were excessive and more trade-restrictive than necessary. The new rules now covered goods that did not previously fall under the requirements, such as raw materials that had undergone a deep heat treatment. The Russian Federation urged the European Union to provide sufficient scientific evidence and a risk assessment supporting the requirements established, which were not feasible for a number of companies worldwide. The Russian Federation proposed the inclusion of producers of raw materials for composite products in the registers of the European Union under the guarantees of the competent authorities of the exporting countries. The Russian Federation was of the view that the EU requirements for mandatory certification of manufacturers of products of no or low veterinary risk were excessive and could be eliminated. Finally, the Russian Federation requested the European Union to provide a transition period for the application of a new form of veterinary certificate for products of short-term storage containing less than 50% of animal origin, and a special certificate for non-perishable food products.

StatementSubmitted:

StatementSubmitted:
The Separate Customs Territory of Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen and Matsu would like to once again express our concerns about the EU’s new regulations on composite products.

We appreciate the EU updating the Q&A document about the import requirements of composite products on DG SANTE’s website on June 11, 2021, which helps Members to understand the requirements for exporting composite products to the EU.

Based on the Q&A document, any ingredients of processed products of animal origin in composite products must be from EU-approved establishments, regardless of the ingredients being highly processed extracts or food additives, or being only for flavoring and seasoning or trace additives.

Article 12 of the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/625, which entered into force on April 21, 2021, establishes that composite products are classified into three categories based on their risks and requirements such as their shelf-stability and ingredients of animal origin. Official health certificates or private attestation are required depending on the categories. However, the EU has not made any clear correlation between the requirements for ingredients of animal origin to be produced by EU-approved establishments, and shelf-stability, food safety as well as risks to public or animal health.

In particular, we would like to highlight the conclusion on microbiological hazard assessment of composite products released by the EFSA in its Journal 2012; 10(5):2662 entitled “Scientific Opinion on Public Health Risks Represented by Certain Composite Products Containing Food of Animal Origin” which was referenced by the new Regulation (EU) 2019/625 as evidence of its risk assessment. The report pointed out that the risk of microbiological hazard is lower for soups, flavorings, meat extracts or concentrates, heat-treated foods, and food supplements. The HACCP system, which is widely adopted in the food manufacturing processes, further ensures control of potential hazards such as microorganisms, chemicals, and physical properties. The logic or reasoning is not present for requiring ingredients of processed products of animal origin used in trace amounts, such as seasoning or flavoring, to be produced by EU-approved establishments when alternative approaches exist to achieve the same health protection level.

We would like to give two examples. The first one is a frozen kelp (the main ingredient or raw material) product that has a small amount of bonito stock added for flavoring. Although bonito stock is highly refined and of low-risk, and is a trace component for flavoring, it is classified as a non-shelf-stable composite product according to EU regulations. The EU requires that it must be obtained in an EU-approved establishment, from an EU-approved third country, and accompanied by an official health certificate (COMP). The second example is a squid shredded snack product that has a small amount of lactose to enhance the flavoring, and it is classified as shelf-stable. Because it is a fishery product, the EU requires an official certificate and the lactose to be obtained in an EU-approved establishment, from an EU-approved third country for exporting dairy products to the EU.

We would like to ask the EU to justify and provide us with the logic and reason on the safety concerns presented by bonito stock and lactose with the purpose of flavoring in the minute quantities requiring their use to be sourced from EU-approved establishments.

Although the EU said that this requirement is not new, it is still subject to the provisions of Article 5 of the SPS Agreement. We urge the EU to review this requirement and to set a threshold level of ingredients of animal origin to be sourced from EU-approved establishments based on their risks to ensure that it does not create unnecessary barriers to trade in composite products.

We look forward to the EU’s positive responses on the issues mentioned above.
Summary: Thanking the European Union for the updated information provided on DG SANTE's website, Chinese Taipei regretted the lack of a clear correlation between the requirements for ingredients of animal origin to be produced by EU-approved establishments, and shelf-stability, food safety and risks to public or animal health. Chinese Taipei considered there was no reasoning for requiring ingredients of processed products of animal origin used in trace amounts to be produced by EU-approved establishments when alternative approaches existed to achieve the same health protection level. Chinese Taipei urged the European Union to review the requirement, that was subject to Article 5 of the SPS Agreement, and to set a threshold level of ingredients of animal origin to be sourced from EU-approved establishments based on their risks to avoid unnecessary barriers to trade.

Australia was still concerned about the new EU rules for shelf-stable composite products under Regulations (EU) No 2019/625 and (EU) No 2020/2235. For Australia, these new rules were not commensurate with risk and had already restricted trade in shelf-stable composite products. The requirement that animal origin ingredients be sourced from EU-listed establishments for all composite products was unjustified. Australia considered that the private attestation requirement, which added transaction costs and brought no food safety benefits, could be eliminated without any impact on food safety. Referring to Articles 4 and 5 of the SPS Agreement, Australia requested the European Union to recognize equivalence of third countries and to establish measures commensurate with the level of risk, and asked for information on the process for consideration of alternative equivalent measures. Australia asked the European Union to reconsider the implementation of this regulation.
