Firstly, the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/625, which entered into force on 21 April 2021, does not illustrate a strong correlation for requiring ingredients of processed products of animal origin (PPAO) in shelf-stabled composite products to be produced by EU-approved establishments and food safety risks to public or animal health. Secondly, the conclusion on microbiological hazard assessment of composite products released by the EFSA in its Journal 2012; 10(5):2662, referenced by the new Regulation (EU) 2019/625 as evidence of its risk assessment, did not present sufficient scientific evidence to support that the requirement for ingredients of PPAO used in trace amounts, such as seasoning or flavoring, to be produced by EU-approved establishments.

Thirdly, this requirement, even it is not new as the EU stated, is still subject to the provisions of Article 5 of the SPS Agreement. We urge again that the EU reviews this requirement and sets a threshold level of ingredients of PPAO to be sourced from EU-approved establishments based on their risks to ensure that it does not result in discrimination or a disguised restriction on international trade.

We look forward to EU’s response to the specific concerns we have expressed, including the rationale and risk assessment relevant to the control measures on composite products.
Summary: Chinese Taipei reiterated its concern and noted the lack of strong correlation between the requirement for ingredients of processed products of animal origin in shelf-stable composite products to be produced by EU-approved establishments, and food safety risks to public or animal health. Chinese Taipei considered that there was insufficient scientific evidence to support the requirement for ingredients of processed products of animal origin used in trace amounts to be produced by EU-approved establishments. Chinese Taipei urged the European Union to review the requirement and to set a threshold level for ingredients of animal origin to be sourced from EU approved establishments based on risks to avoid unnecessary barriers to trade. Chinese Taipei looked forward to a response by the European Union on this matter.

Australia reiterated its concerns about the new EU rules for shelf-stable composite products under Regulations (EU) No 2019/625 and (EU) No 2020/2235. For Australia, the new rules were not commensurate with risk and had already restricted trade in shelf-stable composite products and caused delays in border clearance for Australian exporters. In Australia's view, the requirement to source animal origin ingredients from EU-listed establishments for all composite products, irrespective of the percentage of animal ingredient in the product, was unjustified and unnecessarily trade restrictive. Australia also considered that the private attestation requirement could be eliminated without any impact on food safety. Referring to Articles 4 and 5 of the SPS Agreement, Australia asked the European Union to recognize the equivalence of third countries and to establish measures commensurate with the level of risk, and requested information on the process for consideration of alternative equivalent measures. Australia urged the European Union to reconsider the implementation of this regulation, including its provisions related to the product coverage and thresholds.

StatementSubmitted: The Separate Customs Territory of Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen and Matsu have been following closely these regulations since the 77th SPS committee meeting. We still have the following concerns, which have not been answered by the EU.The EU has been mentioning that according to Article 6(4) of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 of EU, ingredients of processed products of animal origin (PPAO) in composite products are requested to be produced by EU-approved establishments. A threshold of 50% had been applied to composite products with processed meat and PPAO for at least 15 years from 2006 to 2021 indicating that the effectiveness of the practice had been approved over a long period of time. This practice was supported by Commission Decision 2007/275/EC for the official control of composite products from third countries, which classified composite products into 2 categories based on the percentage of PPAO, one with PPAO above 50% and the other with PPAO under 50%. It was clear that the control was risk-based.  However, the new measure has removed the threshold of 50% and treated all composite products with processed meat and PPAO on the same level of risk, even when some ingredients can be barely traced; Moreover, this decision was made based on a study (EFSA Journal 2012;10(5):2662) 10 years ago without taking into account the development of scientific and risk assessment techniques. We hope to seek further clarification from the EU of the following: 1. Except the 2012 research, what is the scientific evidence supporting the EU’s new rules on requiring all composite products with ingredients of PPAO to be produced by EU-approved establishments? Does the EU consider the nature of their risks? How were relevant international standards on risk assessment considered, such as those developed by CODEX or OIE?2. What are the practical cases of hazards caused by composite products with only trace amounts of PPAO (such as seasoning or flavoring) when they are not produced in EU-approved establishments? What has made the EU determined that the practice, operated for 16 years, was unable to achieve the “appropriate level of protection”? What is the rationale for adopting a control measure that is more than necessary and disproportional to the minimal hazards posed by such composite products?We would be grateful if the above?mentioned comments could be taken into account and look forward to a written response.
Summary: Chinese Taipei reiterated its concern and noted that the decision to treat all composite products with processed products of animal origin (PPAO) on the same level of risk was based on 2012 EFSA research, and did not take account of developments in scientific and risk assessment techniques. Chinese Taipei sought clarification of the scientific evidence supporting the new rules for all composite products with PPAO ingredients to be produced by EU approved establishments. Chinese Taipei also requested information on the practical cases of hazards caused by composite products with only trace amounts of PPAO when they were not produced in EU approved establishments, and questioned how the European Union determined that prior practice would no longer achieve the ALOP. Finally, Chinese Taipei considered the measure to be disproportional to the level of hazard, and asked the European Union to explain the rationale for adopting the measure.

StatementSubmitted: Australia reiterates its concerns about the EU’s new rules for shelf-stable composite products under EU Regulations 2019/625 and 2020/2235.  In particular, the private attestation requirement, which requires operators to list all EU approved establishments in which the animal ingredients in the product are sourced from, imposes a heavy burden for operators. It also imposes a competitive disadvantage on small and medium size companies which may not have the market power to gather the required information from food manufacturers.  In Australia’s case, the new rules have already restricted trade in shelf-stable composite products. And in some cases, trade has ceased, negatively impacting Australian businesses. Operators are notably experiencing difficulties at Border Control Points in the EU as businesses and Port authorities adjust to the new private attestation requirement.  We remain concerned that the private attestation, required for shelf stable composite products not containing meat, adds cost and complexity for traders, and is a disincentive to trade and is not commensurate with the risk of the product. Australia considers that the sourcing of animal-origin ingredients from EU-listed establishments for all composite products, irrespective of the percentage of animal ingredient in the product is not justified and unnecessarily restricts trade by applying stringent measures to low safety risk foods.  Australia requests the EU to reconsider the private attestation requirements and expand the list of low-risk shelf stable foods which do not require checks at the border.  Australia appreciates the bilateral discussions it has had with the EU on this topic and requests further discussions to explore these issues in more detail.
Summary: Australia reiterated its concerns about the new EU rules for shelf-stable composite products in Regulations (EU) No 2019/625 and (EU) No 2020/2235. Specifically, Australia considered that the private attestation requirements for shelf-stable composite products not containing meat added cost and complexity for traders, particularly for SMEs, was a disincentive to trade, and was not commensurate with the risk of the product. In Australia's view, the requirement to source animal origin ingredients from EU-listed establishments for all composite products, irrespective of the percentage of animal ingredient in the product, was unjustified and unnecessarily trade-restrictive. Australia urged the European Union to reconsider the private attestation requirements and to expand the list of low-risk shelf-stable foods which would not require checks at borders.

StatementSubmitted: The Separate Customs Territory of Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen and Matsu have repeatedly expressed concerns in the past six meetings about the new EU rules for composite products. EU’s responses did not reflect  our concerns positively about the risk assessment or scientific evidence. Although we understood the EU have already announced a new delegated regulation recently to amend some requirements for composite products exempted from official controls at border control posts and will be in force at the end of this month, however, the new requirements still did not address our concerns. We reiterate the following concerns and expect that the EU will respond.The only scientific evidence provided by the EU to support the new rules was a 2012 European Food Safety Authority's research (EFSA Journal 2012; 10(5): 2662), which was done a decade ago and was not able to take into account the advances in food processing technology. We are particularly concerned about the requirements for each processed product of animal origin (PPAO), even in extremely trace amounts or being highly refined, to come from an EU-approved establishment. We support the EU’s policy that regulatory intervention shall be risk-based and not more trade-restrictive than necessary. We regret to see that the EU has not been able to address our concerns that have been raised six times over the past one and a half years. We urge the EU to clarify the following points:1. What are the hazards caused by PPAO, even in trace or refined existed in composite products (such as lactose or fish extract as seasoning) and stored under controlled temperatures, that justify the requirements for them to be from EU-approved establishments? Please provide practical cases illustrating such hazards.2. How international standards (such as Codex, OIE, etc.) are used in terms of the risk assessment of composite products with PPAO? Is there other scientific evidence from the last 5 years other than the 2012 research? We continue to look forward to the EU’s response to the concerns we have expressed, including the rationale and risk assessment relevant to the control measures on composite products.
Summary: Chinese Taipei was of the view that recent amendments to the EU regulation did not address its concerns. Chinese Taipei considered that the 2012 EFSA research underpinning the decision to treat all composite products with processed products of animal origin on the same level of risk did not take account of advances in food processing technology. In particular, Chinese Taipei had concerns with the requirements that each processed product of animal origin with only trace amounts had to come from EU-approved establishments, and requested practical illustration of the related hazards. Chinese Taipei also sought clarification on the use of international standards for risk assessments of composite products with processed products of animal origin, and whether there was any recent scientific evidence supporting the measure.

Australia appreciated China's assurance that Phase One of the Economic and Trade Agreement between the United States and China (Phase One Agreement) regarding technical SPS measures would be implemented in a WTO consistent manner, in alignment with international standard-setting practices, and following a science- and risk-based approach. As such, Australia requested that all Members receive the same treatment granted to the United States with respect to streamlining of regulatory processes and equitable application of import conditions.Australia had longstanding concerns regarding the significant delays in obtaining Chinese government approval for export establishments for Australian agricultural commodities. Australia sought China's commitment to apply to other countries the same assessment timeframes outlined in the Phase One Agreement for relevant commodities. Australia also requested the prompt amendment of relevant Chinese regulations, where required, for the equitable application of other agreed changes to Chinese import requirements. Given China's commitments under the Phase One Agreement, it was Australia's understanding that highly processed products containing poultry material would be eligible for import into China regardless of a country's avian influenza status, on the basis of Chapter 10.4 of the OIE Terrestrial Code. Australia requested China to extend to all trading partners the same opportunities provided to the United States under these commitments.

StatementSubmitted: New Format of Health Certificates proposed by China for import of Shrimp from India • India is concerned about the new format of health certificate proposed by China for Shrimp imports from India. • The proposed certificate requires every Shrimp consignment to be tested for OIE-listed pathogens, including WSSV (White spot Syndrome virus) and IHHNV (Infectious hypodermal and Hematopoietic Necrosis virus).  • This requirement is highly restrictive and makes it extremely difficult for Indian exporters to comply. In this regard, the following points are presented. o Indian waters are not free from the above viruses; issuing health certificates in the revised format will be extremely difficult and will make most of India’s consignments unfit for export to China.o As per the scientific evidence, both the referred viruses are prevalent in the Chinese territory too.o Other Shimp exporting nations to China, especially from South East Asia, are also infected with the WSSVo The presence of these viruses poses no threat to human health. o If every shrimp consignment to China shall be tested for OIE listed pathogens, including WSSV and IHHNV, it will cause delays and  heavy expenditure  • Hence China asking for a health certificate for a prevalent pathogen in shrimps, including its own waters, is not justified.   • As per Article 2.3 of the SPS Agreement: Members shall ensure that their sanitary and phytosanitary measures do not arbitrarily or unjustifiably discriminate between Members where identical or similar conditions prevail, including between their own territory and that of other Members. Sanitary and phytosanitary measures shall not be applied in a manner that would constitute a disguised restriction on international trade.   • Given Indian and Chinese conditions are similar to the prevalence of WSSV and IHHNV, China is requested to share the objective behind enforcing the new health certificate. • As per Article 3.1 of the SPS Agreement, Members shall base their sanitary or phytosanitary measures on international standards, guidelines, or recommendations, where they exist (except as provided in Article 3 of the SPS Agreement).  • To conform with the requirements of Article 3, the Chinese measures will have to comply with the relevant international standards, i.e., the OIE Aquatic Animal Code. The relevant section 5.1.2.2 of the Aquatic animal health code of OIE states that: The international aquatic animal health certificate should not include requirements for the exclusion of pathogenic agents or aquatic animal diseases that are present in the importing country and are not subject to any official control programme, except when the strain of the pathogenic agent in the exporting country is of significantly higher pathogenicity and/or has a larger host range. The measures imposed on imports to manage the risks posed by a pathogenic agent or aquatic animal disease should not require a higher level of protection than that provided by measures applied as part of the official control programme operating within the importing country • As stated above, Article 5.1.2.2. of the Aquatic Code provides that an importing country should not include requirements on excluding certain pathogens or animal diseases in the veterinary certificate, in case these are present in its own territory and are not subject to any official control programme. • It is seen, from the documents available in the public domain, there is no official control programme in China regarding WSSV and IHHNV to be a deviation from the relevant international standards and hence a violation of Article 3.1 of the SPS Agreement.  • In the absence of any official control programme as required by the OIE,  China would have to justify its health certificate requirements based on a risk assessment, as per Article 3.3 of the SPS Agreement. In view of this,  China is requested to share the details of its official control programme on WSSV and IHHNV. If there is no official control programme, it may share the risk assessment for enforcing a new health certificate.     • To conclude, given the above analysis,  China is requested to share the risk assessment carried out and what less trade-restrictive measures it considered before proposing the new format of health certificate
Summary: India raised its concern about China's proposed new health certificate format for shrimp imports, requiring every shrimp consignment to be tested for OIE-listed pathogens, including the White Spot Syndrome (WSS) and the Infectious Hypodermal and Hematopoietic Necrosis (IHHN) viruses. India observed that (i) requiring health certificates in the revised format would make most of India's shrimp consignments unfit for export to China; (ii) the viruses were prevalent in China and the WSS virus was also present in other countries that export shrimps to China; and (iii) the presence of these viruses posed no threat to human health. Referring to Article 2.3 of the SPS Agreement, India considered the conditions in China and India to be similar regarding the prevalence of the WSS and IHHN viruses and requested China to share the objective behind enforcing the new health certificate. India also pointed to Article 3 of the SPS Agreement and section 5.1.2.2 of the OIE Aquatic Animal Health Code, which did not allow requirements for the exclusion of certain pathogens or animal diseases that were present in the importing territory and were not subject to any official control programme. India requested China to share the details of its official control programmes on WSS and IHHN or, in the absence thereof, to share its risk assessment and indicate the less trade-restrictive measures it had considered.

StatementSubmitted: CHINA- NEW FORMAT OF HEALTH CERTIFICATES FOR IMPORT OF SHRIMP FROM INDIA SUMMARY OF CONCERNS RAISED:China proposed a new health certificate format for shrimp imports, requiring every shrimp consignment to be tested for OIE-listed pathogens, including the White Spot Syndrome (WSS) and the Infectious Hypodermal and Hematopoietic Necrosis (IHHN) viruses.India observed that (i) requiring health certificates in the revised format would make most of India's shrimp consignments unfit for export to China; (ii) the viruses were prevalent in China and the WSS virus was also present in other countries that export shrimps to China; and (Article 2.3) (iii) the presence of these viruses posed no threat to human health.Stating Article 3 of the SPS Agreement and 5.1.2.2 of the OIE Aquatic Animal Health Code, India requested China to share the details of its official control programmes on WSS and IHHN or, to share its risk assessment and indicate the less trade restrictive measures it had considered.i.                 CHINAS RESPONSE:China responded that the new certificate format detailed information of overseas fishing vessels, transport vessels, processing vessels, refrigerators and processing enterprises, and added the requirements of implementing FAO/WHO guidelines. In December 2020, China had informed India that Indian certificates were missing important information on fishing boats and refrigerators. China stressed that the information at issue was not a new requirement, but was listed as a special item in the certificate to avoid omissions. China added that from November 2020 to March 2021, China had detected COVID-19 five times on the packaging of aquatic products from India, indicating problems in the implementation of FAO/WHO guidelines in the Indian food safety management system. China hoped that India would adopt the new certificate format as soon as possible.ii.                COMMENT:  Reply submitted by China does not address concerns raised by India. It does not provide any risk assessment or indicate the less trade restrictive measures it had considered as requested by India. India request China to address the above concerns.
Summary: India raised its concerning regarding China's proposed new health certificate format, that would make most of India's shrimp consignments unfit for export to China. The health certificate format required that shrimp consignment be tested for OIE-listed pathogens, including the white spot syndrome and the infectious hypodermal and hematopoietic necrosis viruses, which were also prevalent in China and did not pose a threat to human health. In India's views, the responses provided by China in the March 2021 Committee meeting did not address its concerns. India requested China to provide a risk assessment or indicate the less trade-restrictive measures it had taken into consideration.

StatementSubmitted: India refers to its detailed statements in the previous SPS meetings on its concern regarding China's proposed new health certificate format, making most of India's shrimp consignments unfit for export to China.  India thanks  China for its response in the last SPS meeting.  In India's view, the responses provided by China did not address its concerns. India had requested China to provide a risk assessment or indicate the less trade-restrictive measures it had considered.  From the response, India noted China adopted this measure as a temporary emergency preventive, protective measure to suspend the import of related products in line with the SPS Agreement and OIE standards.  To this effect, India wishes to know when this emergency measure ends. In the meantime, China is requested to provide the risk assessment carried out before imposing this measure.
Summary: India raised its concerns regarding China's proposed new health certificate format that would make most of India's shrimp consignments unfit for export to China. Referring to its statements in previous Committee meetings, India considered that the responses provided by China in the July 2021 Committee meeting did not address its concerns. India requested China to provide a risk assessment or indicate the less trade-restrictive measures it had taken into consideration, and enquired when the temporary preventive measure would be suspended.

The proposed certificate requires every Shrimp consignment to be tested for OIE-listed pathogens, including WSSV (White Spot Syndrome Virus) and IHHNV (Infectious Hypodermal and Hematopoietic Necrosis Virus). Summary: India raised its concerns with the new health certificate format proposed by China for shrimp imports from India, which required every consignment to be tested for WOAH-listed pathogens, including White Spot Syndrome Virus (WSSV) and Infectious Hypodermal and Hematopoietic Necrosis Virus (IHHNV). StatementSubmitted: India expresses its disappointment in the lack of progress on this matter, despite raising it in every SPS Committee in the last two years. All the points raised in India's previous statements remain valid.India is concerned about the new format of health certificate proposed by China for Shrimp imports from India. The proposed certification requires every Shrimp consignment to be tested for OIE-listed pathogens, including WSSV (White Spot Syndrome Virus) and IHHNV (Infectious Hypodermal and Hematopoietic Necrosis Virus). This requirement is highly restrictive and makes it extremely difficult for Indian exporters to comply. 15 Indian seafood units have been suspended by GACC on account of WSSV, from November 2019 to till date. Total 16 consignments were rejected. The outcomes of the investigation of 12 complaints (out of 15) were shared with GACC by the competent authority, EIC. However, to date, these establishments cannot export aquaculture products to China. Further, GACC has not notified EIC about the requirement/commencement of checking for shrimp pathogens in advance. It may be noted that China is also not free from WSSV; hence, the action of GACC regarding the suspension of the units on account of WSSV cannot be considered justified. China is requested to share the scientific objective behind enforcing the additional conditions in the new health certificate.
Summary: Referring to its previous interventions, India expressed its disappointment with the lack of progress on this matter. India reiterated its concerns with the new health certificate format proposed by China for shrimp imports, which required every consignment to be tested for WOAH-listed pathogens, including White Spot Syndrome Virus (WSSV) and Infectious Hypodermal and Hematopoietic Necrosis Virus (IHHNV), and for which the commencement had not been notified in advance. India regretted that, despite having shared with GACC the outcomes of the investigations of 12 out of 15 complaints, the establishments could still not export aquaculture products to China. India noted that WSSV was also present in China, and asked China to share the scientific objective of the proposed certificate.

StatementSubmitted: China's proposed new health certificate format for shrimp imports (STC ID 506)India thanks China for its response.India reiterates its concerns with the new health certificate format proposed by China for shrimp imports, which requires every consignment to be tested for WOAH-listed pathogens, including White Spot Syndrome Virus (WSSV) and Infectious Hypodermal and Hematopoietic Necrosis Virus (IHHNV), and for which the commencement had not been notified in advance.India initiated Phase II of the National Surveillance Programme on Aquatic Animal Diseases (NSPAAD) in March 2023, which is an active surveillance programme involving 32 participating organisations. StatementSubmitted:
Since 2013, Mexico has suspended the import of shrimp products from China on the grounds of preventing the introduction of Acute Hepatopancreas Necrosis. Thereafter both sides have conducted a number of technical exchanges, and  China has provided technical data for many times in accordance with the requirements of Mexico. During the 77th session of the WTO/SPS Committee in June 2020, China raised specific trade concerns on resuming the export of frozen shrimp products to Mexico, and Mexico responded in August. In September 2020,  the two sides held a bilateral meeting. During the 78th session in November 2020, China reiterated its concerns to Mexico once again.

Chapter 2.2.1, Article 2.1.3 of the “Manual of Diagnostic Tests for Aquatic Animals” by the World Organization for Animal Health (OIE) clearly states that the source of Acute Hepatopancreatic Necrosis disease (AHPND) will not be transmitted by frozen shrimp. Article 3.1 of the SPS agreement indicates: “To harmonize sanitary and phytosanitary measures on as wide as a basis as possible, Members shall base their sanitary or phytosanitary measures on international standards, guidelines or recommendations.” Therefore, China believes that Mexico's import suspension of shrimp products from China on the ground of preventing the introduction of Acute Hepatopancreatic Necrosis is inconsistent with the relevant provisions of SPS Agreement and GATT 1994.

“Aquatic Animal Health Code” of OIE emphasizes that shrimp products for different purposes should meet the corresponding requirements of importing countries, and Article 9.1.12 stipulates?Competent Authorities should not require any conditions related to AHPND, regardless of the AHPND status of the exporting country, zone, or compartment, when authorizing the importation(or transit) of peeled frozen shrimp(shell off, head off) that have been prepared and packaged for retail trade and comply with Article 5.4.2.

Article 5.6 of the SPS Agreement states that when establishing or maintaining sanitary and phytosanitary measures to achieve the appropriate level of sanitary and phytosanitary protection, Members shall ensure that such measures are not more trade-restrictive than required to achieve their appropriate level of sanitary and phytosanitary protection, taking into account their technical and economic feasibility. Mexico has obviously put forward an excessively high level of protection for the prevention and control of the disease.

China and Mexico are important trading partners in aquatic products. We hope Mexico will resume importing frozen shrimp from China as soon as possible based on scientific and objective principles, so as to promote the healthy development of our aquatic products trade.
Summary: China expressed its concern regarding Mexico's suspension of imports of shrimp products from China on the grounds of preventing the introduction of the Acute Hepatopancreatic Necrosis disease (AHPND). China referred to Chapter 2.2.1, Article 2.1.3 of the OIE Manual of Diagnostic Tests for Aquatic Animals, according to which the source of AHPND was not transmitted by frozen shrimp. In light of Article 3.1 of the SPS Agreement, China considered Mexico's measure to be inconsistent with the SPS Agreement and the GATT 1994. China also pointed to Article 9.1.12 of the OIE Aquatic Animal Health Code, pursuant to which authorities should not add any conditions related to AHPND when authorizing the importation or transit of peeled frozen shrimp that were prepared and packaged for retail trade and complied with Article 5.4.2. Considering Article 5.6 of the SPS Agreement, China believed that Mexico put forward an excessively high level of protection. China hoped that Mexico would resume importing frozen shrimp from China as soon as possible.

China expressed its concern regarding Mexico's suspension of imports of shrimp products from China on the grounds of preventing the introduction of the Acute Hepatopancreatic Necrosis disease (AHPND). In May 2021 China had received Mexico's sanitary requirements for imported frozen shrimp. China appreciated Mexico's cooperation and bilateral engagement in this regard. Nonetheless, China considered that Articles 3, 4 and 5 of Mexico's sanitary requirements set an excessively high level of protection for the control of the disease, and contradicted the OIE Aquatic Code. In addition, China considered Mexico's measure to be inconsistent with the SPS Agreement and the GATT 1994. China hoped that Mexico would comply with the relevant standards, scientifically formulate its import requirements for Chinese frozen shrimps and resume importing frozen shrimp from China as soon as possible.

StatementSubmitted: RUSSIA Fish and Fishery Products India is deeply concerned with the restrictive trade measures used by Russia in respect of fish and fishery product exports to the Eurasian Customs Union (CU) These measures may be violative of Article 5 of the SPS Agreement, and the MoU between the Export Inspection Council (EIC) India and Federal services of veterinary and phytosanitary surveillance (FSVPS) Russia signed a Memorandum on 28th July 2009 to facilitate the trade of fish and fishery products. The EIC has been sharing a list with FSVPS of approved Indian fish & fishery products processing establishments as per the said Memorandum provisions. However,  FSVPS does not regularly update the list of fishery establishments, due to which newly approved establishments are not able to export to CU. This may be because FSVPS is insistent that these establishments are to be subjected to verification by them.  Verification of establishments already approved by FSVPS would only add cost and delay.  Second, this defeats the objective of signing the MoU with CU as the stated objective of signing the MoU was to facilitate the trade of fish and fishery products. As part of the signed MoU, EIC shares the list of establishments only after strict examination and after the units have met all CU requirements in this regard.  This issue has been raised several times in bilateral meetings, but no resolution has been reached. In a bilateral meeting, the Russian authorities had stated that 80 units were already listed on the FSVPS website, which is sufficient to cater to the Russian market. Thus, by limiting approval of new facilities, the Russian authorities seem to have imposed a non-tariff barrier.  This measure of Russia appears to violate Article 2.3 of the SPS agreement, which states that sanitary and phytosanitary measures shall not be applied in a manner that would constitute a disguised restriction on international trade. It is to be noted that out of 80 listed facilities, 16 are facing temporary suspension, and only six facilities are added by Russia to the existing list of approved facilities in 2020. Under the SPS Agreement, Article 5 details the assessment of risk and determination of an Appropriate Level of sanitary or phytosanitary Protection (ALOP). When alternative measures that provide the same safety level as the proposed measure exist, governments should choose the least restrictive available measure. In this case, as per MoU, EIC is finalizing the list of establishments eligible for export to Russia based on their compliance with the Russian requirements.  This shows that there are less trade-restrictive alternative measures available for export to Russia. However, Russian authorities' insistence on verification by them is not justified as it creates an unnecessary trade barrier. Additionally, equivalence provisions within the WTO SPS Agreement encourage members to enter into multilateral agreements to recognize equivalence for specified sanitary measures. India has signed an MoU with Russia to facilitate the trade of fish and fishery products. To Conclude, the Russian authorities are requested to share the risk assessment done for insisting on the inspections to be done by the Russian authorities
Summary: India raised its concern regarding measures imposed in respect of fish and fish product exports to the Eurasian Customs Union (ECU). India stated that it had been sharing a list of approved Indian processing establishments in accordance with a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between India and Russia to facilitate trade in fish and fish products. However, the register of approved enterprises had not been updated by the Russian Federation, and newly approved enterprises had not been able to export to the ECU. India considered that, by not including new facilities in its register and requiring verifications by Russian authorities, the Russian Federation seemed to have imposed a non-tariff barrier and to be in violation of the MoU and Articles 2.3 and 5 of the SPS Agreement, in particular the obligation to adopt the least-trade restrictive measure. India also referred to the equivalence principle in the SPS Agreement. India requested the Russian Federation to share its risk assessment in support of insisting on inspections by Russian authorities.

StatementSubmitted: RUSSIA - PROCEDURES FOR AUTHORIZING UNITS ELIGIBLE FOR EXPORT OF FISH AND FISH PRODUCTS TO EURASIAN CUSTOMS UNION  SUMMARY OF CONCERNS RAISED: In March 2021, India raised its concern regarding measures imposed in respect of fish and fish product exports to the Eurasian Customs Union (ECU). India stated that it had been sharing a list of approved Indian processing establishments in accordance with a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between India and Russia [2009] to facilitate trade in fish and fish products. However, the register of approved enterprises had not been updated by the Russian Federation, and newly approved enterprises had not been able to export to the ECU [defeats the objective of signing the MOU with CU]. India considered that, by not including new facilities in its register and requiring verifications by Russian authorities, the Russian Federation seemed to have imposed a non-tariff barrier and to be in violation of the MoU and Articles 2.3 and 5 of the SPS Agreement, in particular the obligation to adopt the least-trade restrictive measure. India also referred to the equivalence principle in the SPS Agreement. India requested the Russian Federation to share its risk assessment in support of insisting on inspections by Russian authorities. RUSSIAS RESPONSE: The Russian Federation responded that there were no quantitative restrictions on Indian fish products. The ECU requirements for conducting inspections prior to expanding the list of exporting enterprises that could supply fish and seafood aimed to ensure the safety of imported products and were applied to all Members. The Russian Federation pointed to Eurasian Economic Council Commission Decision No. 94 as supporting its inspection of foreign enterprises. The Russian Federation also stated that, in February 2020, it had proposed inspections, but no response had been received thus far. In addition, the Russian Federation took issue with delays in India in the process of approving export certificates for Russian products. In conclusion, the Russian Federation expressed its readiness to include new Indian exporting fish and fish products enterprises in its register after the implementation of existing requirements and agreements.   The Reply submitted by Russia does not address India’s concerns. Russian authorities are requested to share the risk assessment done for insisting on the inspections to be done by Russian authorities.
Summary: India complained that the Russian Federation had not updated its register of approved enterprises and newly approved enterprises had not been able to export to the Eurasian Customs Union, despite the list of approved processing establishments provided by India in accordance with a bilateral MoU. In India's view, this was in violation of the MoU and Articles 2.3, 4 and 5 of the SPS Agreement. India requested the Russian Federation to share its risk assessment in support of insisting on inspections by Russian authorities. India considered that the responses provided by the Russian Federation did not address its concerns and reiterated the request that the risk assessment be shared.

StatementSubmitted: Russian Federation - Procedures for authorising units eligible for export of fish and fish products to Eurasian Customs Union (ID 508) In the previous SPS committee meeting, India raised this concern. India had complained that the Russian Federation had not updated its register of approved enterprises. Therefore, newly approved enterprises are not able to export to the Eurasian Customs Union. This is despite India's list of approved processing establishments being in accordance with the bilateral MoU.  In India's view, this violated the MoU and Articles 2.3, 4 and 5 of the SPS Agreement. India also requested the Russian Federation to share its risk assessment in support of insisting on inspections by Russian authorities. India considered that the responses provided by the Russian Federation did not address its concerns and reiterated them at the subsequent meetings.  Currently, the FSVPS (Federal Service for Veterinary and Phytosanitary Surveillance) has informed that they would like to come to India for verification and then listing will be done. It is relevant to mention here that Russia has signed an MOU with EIC and recognised the audit system of EIC. As per the provisions of the said Memorandum, EIC is forwarding the list of approved fish & fishery products processing establishments intended to export to the Russian Federation for registering the names with FSVPS regularly. This is done after ensuring the said establishments meet the requirements of the Customs Union for the export of fish & fishery products.  Therefore, verification of establishment should not be a barrier for listing approved establishments. FSVPS can inspect approved establishments at any time as per clause 11 of the MoU. However, making it a pre-condition is a possible violation of the MoU and a trade barrier. Therefore Russian is requested to register  India's EIC approved enterprises with the FSVPS.
Summary: India expressed concerns that the Russian Federation had not updated its register of approved enterprises, and that newly approved enterprises had not been able to export to the Eurasian Customs Union, despite the list of approved processing establishments provided by India in accordance with a bilateral MoU. In India's view, this was in violation of the MoU and Articles 2.3, 4 and 5 of the SPS Agreement. India requested the Russian Federation to share its risk assessment to support the inspections by Russian authorities. India considered that the responses provided by the Russian Federation did not address its concerns. According to India, the Russian Federation's authority under clause 11 of the MoU to inspect approved Indian establishments was not a prerequisite for listing approved Indian establishments. Given the MoU's recognition of India's audit system, India requested that the Russian Federation register approved Indian establishments.

StatementSubmitted: Russian Federation - Procedures for authorising units eligible for export of fish and fish products to Eurasian Customs Union (ID 508)Non-listing of Indian Processing units by FSVPS is a major trade barrier being faced by Indian seafood exporters. Indian seafood processing units, qualified for approval as per the Russian standards by the Assessment Penal of Experts (APE) and recommended by EIC to the Russian side, are yet to be listed by FSVPS, due to which these units are not in a position to commence export to Russia. As of now, 96 establishments are listed on the FSVPS website; the request for the listing of 44 fishery establishments is still pending. Summary: India indicated that its seafood exporters could not export to the Russian Federation due to the non-listing of Indian processing units by the Federal Service for Veterinary and Phytosanitary Supervision (FSVPS). India informed the Committee that 96 establishments were listed on the FSVPS' website and that the request for the listing of 44 fishery establishments were still pending and urged the Russian Federation to list the units urgently. StatementSubmitted: India would like to reiterate its concern about the Non-listing of Indian processing establishments by FSVPS which is a major trade barrier faced by India to export of fish and fish products to Russia. India signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the Federal Services of Veterinary and Phytosanitary Surveillance (FSVPS) of Russia on 28th July 2009 in order to facilitate the smooth trade of fish & fishery products from India to the Customs Union (CU). As per the provisions of the said Memorandum, the Indian competent authority forwards the list of approved fish & fishery products processing establishments intended to export to CU for registering the names on the official websiteof FSVPS on a regular basis, after ensuring that the said establishments are meeting the requirements of Customs Union for export of fish & fishery products. Currently, 51 new fishery establishments are pending for listing by CU. These measures violate Article 5 of the SPS Agreement. This may be because FSVPS is insistent that these establishments are to be subjected to inspection by them. Verification of establishments by FSVPS, already approved by EIC, would only add cost and delay. This stand defeats the objective of signing the MoU with CU, as the stated objective of signing the MoU was to facilitate thetrade of fish and fishery products. Presently, in the month of October 2023, FSVPS has delisted the 12 fishery establishments from the existing list. Thus, the Russian authorities have imposed a non-tariff barrier by delisting the establishment and limiting the approval of new facilities. This measure of Russia violates Article 2.3 of the SPS agreement.India once again requests the Russian authority to share its risk assessment in support of insisting on the inspections by the Russian authorities for approval of the Indian processing establishments.
Summary: India was of the view that the non-listing of processing establishments by the Federal Services of Veterinary and Phytosanitary Surveillance (FSVPS) were a trade barrier to export fish and fish products to the Russian Federation. Despite the Memorandum of Understanding signed in 2009, FSVPS insisted on inspecting the establishments included in India's list of approved fish and fishery products processing establishments intended to export to the Customs Union. India informed the Committee that 51 new fishery establishments were still pending for listing by the FSVPS, and 12 fishery establishments had been delisted earlier in 2023. India stated that this situation violated Articles 2.3 and 5 of the SPS Agreement and urged the Russian Federation to share the risk assessment in support of the inspections.

StatementSubmitted: India would like to reiterate its concerns about the Non-listing of Indian processing establishments by FSVPS, which is a major trade barrier faced by India to export fish and fish products to the Russia. India and Russia had signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the federal Services of Veterinary and Phytosanitary Surveillance (FSVPS) of Russia to facilitate the smooth trade in fish & fishery products from India to the Customs Union (CU). As per the provisions of the said Memorandum, the Indian competent authority forwards the list of approved fish & fishery products processing establishments intended to export to CU for registering the names on the official website of FSVPS on regular basis, after ensuring that the said establishments are meeting the requirements of Customs Union for export of fish & fishery products. However, FSVPS has listed three establishments in the year 2023, only one in 2024, as of now 66 are still awaited. This may be because FSVPS is insistent that these establishments are to be subjected to inspection by them. Verification of establishments by FSVPS, already approved by EIC would only add cost and delay for Indian exports. This stand defeats the objective of signing the MoU with CU as the stated objective of signing the MoU was to facilitate the trade of fish and fishery products. As part of the signed MoU, Indian competent authority shares the list of establishments only after strict examination and after the establishments have met all CU requirements. In the month of October 2023, FSVPS has delisted the 12 fishery establishments from the existing list of 97 establishments; however, no new establishments are listed in place of the delisted establishments. Thus, by delisting the establishment and limiting approval of new facilities, the Russian authorities seem to have imposed a nontariff barrier. FSVPS had requested the Indian side to offer fishery establishments for inspection by them vide letter dated 22.02.2024, to which the Indian competent authority agreed for the inspection by the FSVPS vide letter dated 01.03.2024. However, till now, there are still 66 new fishery establishments pending for listing by the CU. India once again requests the Russian authority to list the establishments and also share its risk assessment in support of insisting on inspection by Russian Authorities.
Summary: India reiterated its concerns regarding the non-listing of Indian processing establishments to export fish and fish products. A Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) had been signed to facilitate the smooth trading of fish and fish products to the Eurasian Customs Union. The MoU foresaw that India send a list of approved processing establishments for registration after ensuring that these establishments met the export requirements of the Eurasian Customs Union. India regretted that only three Indian establishments had obtained the necessary authorization in 2023 and only one in 2024, with 66 establishments remaining non-listed. In addition, 12 establishments had been delisted in October 2023 and no other establishments had been listed to replace them. In India's view, delisting establishments and limiting new approvals amounted to a non-tariff barrier. India requested the Russian Federation to list establishments and share its risk assessment in support of requiring certain inspections, which India considered would add cost, lead to delays, and defeat the purpose of the MoU.

StatementSubmitted: Comité de Medidas Sanitarias y Fitosanitarias de la OMC25 y 26 de marzo de 2021- Intervenciones del Perú Panama's undue delays in the renewal of authorizations for plants of Peruvian fishery and livestock enterprises El Perú presenta ante los Miembros de la OMC su preocupación comercial con relación a las demoras indebidas para la renovación de habilitaciones de las plantas de empresas pesqueras y pecuarias peruanas por parte de Panamá. El artículo 8 y, a los párrafos 1.a) y 1.c) del Anexo C del Acuerdo MSF señalan que los procedimientos para verificar el cumplimiento de una medida sanitaria que se inicien deben ser finalizados sin demoras indebidas y sin exigir más información de la necesaria a efectos de los mencionados procedimientos, lo que se ha visto vulnerado por Panamá dado que no se ha recibido respuesta ni se ha procedido con la habilitación de las empresas pesqueras y pecuarias pendientes solicitadas por Perú. Asimismo, Panamá recientemente solicitó actualizar información que fue debidamente enviada en su momento por la autoridad sanitaria peruana competente. El Perú desea destacar que, a pesar de las reuniones y gestiones bilaterales sostenidas, Panamá no ha comunicado el periodo de tramitación previsto y no se tiene certeza sobre cuál es el plazo que se les daría a las empresas peruanas en caso se logre la renovación, contraviniendo el artículo 8 y el párrafo 1.b) del Anexo C del Acuerdo MSF. Actualmente, son veintidós (22) empresas peruanas exportadoras de productos hidrobiológicos que se encuentran en rojo y, por ende, vencidas en la Lista Oficial de la autoridad sanitaria panameña, ello a pesar de que el Perú ha brindado toda la información sanitaria requerida desde mayo de 2020[1] y, a solicitud de Panamá, la ha vuelto a remitir en marzo de 2021[2], sin que se hayan presentado razones sanitarias para generar este segundo envío de información. Del mismo modo, existen cuatro (04) empresas pecuarias peruanas pendientes de renovación de habilitación por parte de Panamá. Al respecto, el Perú ha remitido, durante el 2020, cinco (05) comunicaciones oficiales[3], con la información necesaria, las cuales no han sido respondidas a la fecha. A esto se adiciona una comunicación enviada en enero de 2021, la cual, de la misma forma no ha sido atendida conforme lo estipula el Anexo C del Acuerdo MSF de la OMC[4]. Adicionalmente, el Perú desea recordar que, conforme al artículos 2.2 y 5.1 del Acuerdo MSF de la OMC, las medidas sanitarias de los Miembros deben ser aplicadas solo cuando sean necesarias para proteger la salud y la vida de las personas y de los animales o para preservar los vegetales y éstas deben estar basadas en una evaluación de riegos. DEMORAS INDEBIDAS DE PANAMÁ EN LA RENOVACIÓN DE LAS AUTORIZACIONES PARA LAS PLANTAS DE LAS EMPRESAS PESQUERAS Y PECUARIAS PERUANAS (PCE N° 509)             

Preocupaciones comerciales específicas anteriormente planteadas – nº xxiv

INTERVENCIÓN DEL PERÚ

El Perú presenta ante los Miembros de la OMC su preocupación comercial con relación a las demoras indebidas para la renovación de habilitaciones de las plantas de empresas pesqueras y pecuarias peruanas por parte de Panamá.

El artículo 8 y los párrafos 1.a) y 1.c) del Anexo C del Acuerdo MSF establecen que los procedimientos para verificar el cumplimiento de una medida sanitaria que se inicien deben ser finalizados sin demoras indebidas y sin exigir más información de la necesaria a efectos de los mencionados procedimientos, lo que se ha visto vulnerado por Panamá dado que no se han habilitado o renovado habilitaciones de empresas peruanas a pesar de las reiteraciones enviadas por el Perú y sin un debido sustento técnico.

El Perú desea destacar que, a pesar de las reuniones y gestiones bilaterales sostenidas, Panamá no ha comunicado el periodo de tramitación previsto para renovar las habilitaciones o incluir nuevas empresas habilitadas; así mismo no se tiene certeza sobre cuál es el plazo que se les daría a las empresas peruanas en caso se logre la renovación o una nueva habilitación, contraviniendo el artículo 8 y el párrafo 1.b) del Anexo C del Acuerdo MSF, que indica que previa petición los Miembros deben comunicar el periodo previsto de tramitación de un procedimiento de aprobación. Asimismo, Perú desconoce las razones por las cuales se otorga a algunas empresas mayor plazo en la renovación de sus habilitaciones y a otras un periodo más corto.

Actualmente, son dos (02)[1] empresas peruanas exportadoras de productos hidrobiológicos que se encuentran en rojo (con habilitación vencida), sin un sustento técnico. Igualmente se tienen sin atención por parte de Panamá, otras 47 empresas para las cuales se ha solicitado su inclusión en la Lista Oficial de la autoridad panameña, ello a pesar de que el Perú ha brindado toda la información sanitaria requerida desde del año 2019[2].Al respecto es necesario mencionar que el Perú tiene un potencial de exportación de productos hidrobiológicos de 1.4 millones de USD[3].

Del mismo modo, existen tres (03)[4] empresas pecuarias peruanas pendientes de renovación de habilitación y una (01)[5] empresa con una nueva solicitud de habilitación por parte de Panamá. Al respecto, el Perú ha remitido comunicaciones desde octubre de 2020, las cuales no han sido atendidas conforme lo estipula el Anexo C del Acuerdo MSF de la OMC. Las exportaciones de estas empresas a Panamá alcanzaron los 323 miles USD en el 2020 y, además, el Perú tiene un potencial de exportación de carne de pavo congelado y pavo sin trocear en Panamá de aproximadamente 138.9 miles de USD y 338 miles USD, respectivamente[6].

Igualmente, se mantiene sin renovación una (01)[7] empresa peruana exportadora de productos lácteos procesados, para lo que se ha remitido las comunicaciones y reiteraciones pertinentes[8]. Las exportaciones de lácteos a Panamá de la empresa en mención alcanzaron los 697 miles USD en el 2020. Cabe indicar que el Perú tiene un potencial de exportación de productos lácteos (leche/crema concentrada) en Panamá de hasta 1.5 millones de USD[9].

Adicionalmente, el Perú desea recordar que, conforme al artículos 2.2 y 5.1 del Acuerdo MSF de la OMC, las medidas sanitarias de los Miembros deben ser aplicadas solo cuando sean necesarias para proteger la salud y la vida de las personas y de los animales o para preservar los vegetales y éstas deben estar basadas en una evaluación de riegos. Lamentablemente, Panamá sigue sin señalar ninguna razón sanitaria para no renovar las habilitaciones o brindar nuevas habilitaciones a las empresas peruanas.

Por lo anteriormente expuesto, y en aras de evitar una continua vulneración de los artículos 2.2, 5.1, 8 y los párrafos 1.a), 1.b) y 1.c) del Anexo C del Acuerdo MSF de la OMC, el Perú solicita a Panamá que se renueven las habilitaciones de las plantas exportadoras peruanas, se brinden nuevas habilitaciones y se eviten mayores demoras que no tienen un sustento técnico y que en la práctica representan barreras innecesarias al comercio.

StatementSubmitted: El Perú desea presentar su preocupación comercial específica por las demoras indebidas en la renovación de habilitaciones para las plantas de empresas pesqueras y, pecuarias peruanas por parte de Panamá. Sobre el particular, en el caso de las plantas peruanas de productos hidrobiológicos y, lácteos, Perú señala que el artículo 8 y los párrafos 1.a) y 1.c) del Anexo C del Acuerdo MSF estipulan que los procedimientos para verificar el cumplimiento de una medida sanitaria deben completarse sin demoras indebidas y, sin exigir información adicional innecesaria. No obstante, Panamá ha incumplido estos requisitos al continuar sin renovar las habilitaciones de las empresas peruanas, lo cual se realizó sin justificación técnica y, a pesar de las reiteradas solicitudes tanto a nivel bilateral como en este Comité.Adicional a ello y, a pesar de las gestiones bilaterales y, multilaterales sostenidas, Panamá continúa sin comunicar el plazo previsto para concluir con la renovación de las habilitaciones. En ese sentido, a la fecha aún no es posible conocer el plazo que tomaría Panamá en otorgar la renovación a las empresas peruanas.Con relación al procedimiento que se viene realizando entre el Perú y Panamá, deseamos destacar que, durante la última semana de mayo del 2024 se realizó una visita de inspección a establecimientos pesqueros peruanos; sin embargo, a la fecha el Perú aún se mantiene a la espera de recibir el reporte final de dicha visita por parte de Panamá.Deseamos precisar que, el próximo 24 de julio del 2024 vence la habilitación de la última planta peruana que cuenta con su habilitación vigente y, posterior a ello serían más de 31 plantas de empresas pesqueras y, pecuarias que no obtuvieron respuesta, ni renovación de su habilitación.Por lo anteriormente expuesto, solicitamos a Panamá 1) el envío del Reporte Final de la visita de inspección realizada en mayo; 2) la renovación de las empresas hidrobiológicas y, pecuarias peruanas; 3) el envío de las normas correspondientes donde se establece el procedimiento y, plazos para concluir este tipo de gestiones. Por último, el Perú desea expresar su disposición de sostener reuniones del Comité de Medidas Sanitarias y Fitosanitarias establecido en el artículo 6.11 de nuestro Acuerdo Comercial bilateral vigente.

StatementSubmitted: Market Access of Bovine Meat to ChinaIndia is seriously concerned about China not allowing Indian bovine meat exports because India is not an FMD free country (FMD- Foot and Mouth Decease). This is discriminatory and violative of the SPS agreement. China continues to impose this restriction despite;India raising three STCs at the WTO.An MoU between the two countries, signed in 2013.China clearing 14 centres in 2017 for the export of bovine meat from India.China itself is not an FMD free country, and it has an O strain of FMD, the same as in India. China is at the same level of compliance as India. China also imports from Namibia, which is on OIE Members' list, with an endorsed official control programme for FMD similar to India. The World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE) does not prohibit the export of meat from FMD affected countries to FMD free counties, provided they follow Article 8.8.22 of Terrestrial Animals Health Code for terrestrial animals. I.e., animals are procured from within ten kilometers of the meat plant.  Indian meat exporters follow Article 8.2.22 of OIE, ensuring that no FMD virus transmission occurs by the export of deboned, deglanded frozen buffalo meat. Article 8.8.22 explicitly lists the conditions required for the safe importation of fresh meat of bovines from FMD infected counties or zones where an official control programme exists.  As provided in the Article, the carcasses are chilled at a temperature of 2-40C  for a minimum of 24 hours, bringing down the pH value below 6.0. There is absolutely no chance for the FMD virus to pass through deboned and deglanded meat with a pH value below 6.0, a scientific fact.   Hence, Indian buffalo meat is safe and risk-free. India has been exporting frozen buffalo meat since 1969 to over 70 countries, including FMD free countries. All export-oriented abattoirs are the most modern, state of the art integrated meat plants certified for Quality Management (ISO 9001:2008) and Food Safety Management System (FSSC 22000:2011). There has not been any instance of FMD transmission from India to any importing countries as India strictly follows Article 8.8.22 of the Animal Health Code for terrestrial animals. The SPS Agreement recognizes Members' right to develop and apply measures to protect their animal/plant/human health and life. However, such measures should not more trade-restrictive than required and comply with the fundamental WTO principle of non-discrimination.  First, China's measure is discriminatory and violative of Article 2.3 of the SPS agreement. It allows bovine meat imports from Namibia but not from India, despite both Namibia and India featuring in OIE Members' list with the endorsed official control programme for FMD.   Second, a member's SPS measures must be based on scientific principles and must not be maintained without sufficient scientific evidence (Article 2.2. of the SPS agreement). Further, a member is permitted to introduce an SPS measure that results in a higher protection level than the international standards, only if such a measure is backed by scientific risk assessment. (Article 3.3, read with Article 5.1 of the SPS agreement).  China's requirement is not scientifically justifiable and is not based on international standards/recommendations. Despite OIE's requirements, China's refusal to accept India's exports may be inconsistent with the SPS agreement's requirements if adequate scientific justification or risk assessment is not shared.  Third, India raised as an STC in the SPS Committee in 2015 and 2016. In response to that STC, in 2016, China stated as follows: "China's field investigation on Indian FMD prevention and control systems had concluded that FMD still existed in India and had pointed to inefficiencies present in the system. China further explained that according to Chinese experts, India did not meet the requirements of OIE recognized FMD free status. Therefore, China notified the result of the assessment to India on 12 January 2016 and suggested that India carry out regionalization management in accordance with OIE standards. China invited India to re-apply after obtaining OIE recognition."With respect to FMD-free status, the OIE under its Terrestrial Code does not require countries to be FMD-free before undertaking bovine meat export. India, similar to China, has a recognised official control program for FMD.  Since China is imposing a higher than prescribed international standard to provide market access to bovine meat, it is requested to show the scientific justification. Further, explain why the level of level of protection offered by the international standard does not result in the protection that China deems appropriate. Given the above, China is requested to share its scientific justification and risk assessment to impose a higher standard of disease-free status than what is required by the OIE.
Summary: India raised its concern regarding China's import restrictions on bovine meat based on India's foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) status. India noted that China continued to impose restrictions despite previously raised STCs, a MoU signed between the two countries in 2013, the clearing by China in 2017 of 14 centres for the export of bovine meat from India, and China's FMD status. India recalled that the OIE did not prohibit exports of meat from FMD-affected countries to FMD-free countries, provided there was compliance with Article 8.8.22 of the OIE Terrestrial Code. India highlighted that it had a recognized official FMD control programme similar to Namibia, from which China allowed bovine meat imports. India considered China's measures to be inconsistent with Articles 2.2, 2.3, 3.3 and 5.1 of the SPS Agreement. India requested China to share its scientific justification and the risk assessment undertaken to impose a higher standard of disease-free status than that required by the OIE.

StatementSubmitted: CHINA- RESTRICTION ON BOVINE MEAT IMPORTS SUMMARY OF CONCERNS RAISED: In March 2021, India raised its concern regarding China's import restrictions on bovine meat based on India's foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) status. India noted that China continued to impose restrictions despite previously raised STCs, a MoU signed between the two countries in 2013, the clearing by China in 2017 of 14 centres for the export of bovine meat from India, and China's FMD status. India recalled that the OIE did not prohibit exports of meat from FMD-affected countries to FMD-free countries, provided there was compliance with Article 8.8.22 of the OIE Terrestrial Code. India has been exporting meat to FMD free countries like Philippines and Indonesia and there has not been any instance of FMD transmission from India to any of the importing countries as India strictly follow Article 8.8.22 of Animal Health Code for terrestrial animals.  India highlighted that it had a recognized official FMD control programme similar to Namibia, from which China allowed bovine meat imports. On November 1, 2020 Saudi Arabia informed us that beef and products, sheep meat and products, white meat and products, fisheries and aquaculture products, foods that are alternative to milk and breast milk, eggs and products, honey and products exported from Turkey have been temporarily suspended as of 15 November 2020.

In their communication to Turkey, Saudi Arabia stated that the questions submitted on November 2018 were not answered and the requests to conduct an on-site inspection were not responded by Turkey.

Actually, the questions were answered by Turkey in 2019, but no reply has been received from Saudi Arabia. Saudi Food and Drug Authority - SFDA already paid a visit to Turkey in August 2016. After the visit, the additional information requested by Saudi Arabia regarding the enterprises deemed suitable to export to Saudi Arabia was also provided in 2017.

Same year, in 2017, a second invitation was officially sent to SA officials for on-site inspection. However, no response was received.

Again, additional specific information for each meat and poultry meat and products, honey and honey products, milk and dairy products, and aquaculture establishments was submitted through numerous official letters in 2018, 2019 and 2020. The aforementioned letters were conveyed once again with our official letter on November 2020. In addition, the veterinary health certificate models requested by Saudi Arabia last month were also sent to Saudi Arabia in early March.

In 2019, 3 bilateral meetings were held with Saudi Arabian officials on the occasion of the SPS Committee. During these meetings, the questions and issues related to Turkey’s fishery and aquaculture exports as well as trade issues regarding plant products were discussed. In those meetings, it has been confirmed by the Saudi authorities that right steps have been taken by Turkey for the initiation of exports.

After the written communication, we also requested to hold an inter-ministerial video conference and it has not been answered until now.

Turkey and Saudi Arabia, with close economic relations and cooperation, have been important trade partners for each other for many years, and our bilateral trade volume has exceeded 6 billion US dollars in 2019. As such, we would have expected Saudi Arabia to consult with Turkey and act in cooperation to take the necessary steps, before suspending the import of animal products with a Note Verbal.

We think that the suspension of trade of animal products through a single and sudden official Note is not consistent with SPS Agreement, specifically with the


	Article 2.2. which states that the SPS measure is applied only to the extent necessary to protect human, animal or plant life or health and;
	Article 5.4. which states that when determining the SPS measures of the countries, the principle of least restrictive trade effects should be considered.


We would also like to emphasize that the prohibitive import policies of Saudi Arabia are not only harmful to bilateral trade, but also have disruptive effects on global value chains where Turkey has an active role as a strategic agricultural production and logistics hub, and hence these practices have systemic effects on the overall world trade.

In addition, delays at Saudi customs of up to 7 days due to burdensome control procedures especially for plant products with a short shelf life, cause significant problems in agricultural trade.

Finally, Turkey invites Saudi Arabia to repeal the import restriction in order to ensure sustainable smooth trade flow.

We once again would like to state that Turkey is ready to work in collaboration with Saudi Arabia’s authorities in order to overcome the existing problems.
Summary: Turkey expressed concerns regarding Saudi Arabia's import restrictions on agricultural products. Turkey indicated that it had been informed by Saudi Arabia on November 2020 of the temporary suspension of imports of beef and its products, sheep meat and its products, white meat and its products, fisheries and aquaculture products, foods alternative to milk and breast milk, eggs and egg products and honey and honey products. In a communication to Turkey, Saudi Arabia had stated that the request to conduct on-site inspections and questions submitted to Turkey in November 2018 had not been answered. Turkey clarified that these questions had been answered in 2019 and that no reply had been received from Saudi Arabia. Turkey stressed that it had submitted additional information to Saudi Arabia concerning these agricultural products through official letters in 2018, 2019 and 2020. Turkey considered Saudi Arabia's measure to be inconsistent with Articles 2.2 and 5.4 of the SPS Agreement and invited Saudi Arabia to lift the import restrictions. Turkey expressed its willingness to work in close collaboration with Saudi Arabia on this matter.

StatementSubmitted: Comité de Medidas Sanitarias y Fitosanitarias de la OMC25 y 26 de marzo de 2021- Intervenciones del Perú Panama's restrictions regarding the procedure to regain access for Peruvian potatoes and onions El Perú presenta ante los Miembros de la OMC su preocupación comercial con relación al cierre de las importaciones de cebolla y papa para consumo desde Perú por parte de Panamá y demoras indebidas en las gestiones fitosanitarias para el restablecimiento del comercio de los citados productos. Con relación al comercio de cebolla peruana, Panamá suspendió su importación desde el año 2016, motivado por la ejecución de un análisis de riesgo de plagas (ARP) con fines de actualizar los requisitos fitosanitarios de importación. Al respecto, Perú observó que dicha actualización no justificaba la suspensión de la importación en un producto cuyo comercio histórico desde el año 2003 registra más de 19,000 TM, sin reportes de interceptación de plagas por la autoridad panameña. No obstante, a lo indicado, durante el 2016, Perú remitió comentarios al ARP desarrollado por Panamá que a la fecha no han sido atendidas. Por otro lado, y en lo relativo al comercio de tubérculos de papa para consumo, la importación de este producto se encuentra suspendida por Panamá desde el año 2009, motivado por la interceptación de una plaga en destino en un envío. La autoridad fitosanitaria del Perú, en mayo de 2010, remitió a Panamá una propuesta de protocolo fitosanitario para la exportación de papa, previo intercambio de comentarios con su contraparte. Sin embargo, a la fecha no se ha tenido respuesta oficial. En estos casos, el Perú considera que Panamá ha contravenido a los artículos 2.2 y 5 del Acuerdo MSF de la OMC, ya que los Miembros deben establecer medidas sanitarias y fitosanitarias solo cuando sean aplicables, entre otros, para preservar los vegetales y dichas medidas deben estar basadas en una evaluación de riesgos. Igualmente, en el artículo 5.4 se detalla que los Miembros deben tener en cuenta el objetivo de reducir al mínimo los efectos negativos sobre el comercio, el cual tampoco ha sido tomado en cuenta en ninguno de los dos (02) casos mencionados previamente. Del mismo modo, conforme el artículo 8 y el Anexo C, los procedimientos de tipo sanitario o fitosanitario, entre otros, deben ser atendidos y concluidos sin demoras indebidas, facilitando información a la Parte interesada y con prescripciones que se limiten a lo que sea razonable y necesario. Lamentablemente, el Perú ha remitido de manera constante, información técnica referida al análisis de riesgos de plagas para lograr la reapertura del mercado panameño para la papa y la cebolla, sin obtener respuestas por parte de la autoridad sanitaria de Panamá respecto a los resultados de su análisis de riesgos. Sobre el particular, es necesario enfatizar que Panamá ha solicitado continuamente la misma información remitida oportunamente por nuestra autoridad sanitaria, lo cual ha originado que el proceso se prolongue de manera innecesaria e injustificada. Por lo anteriormente expuesto, el Perú considera que Panamá ha generado demoras indebidas en el establecimiento de los requisitos fitosanitarios de importación que permitan reiniciar la importación de cebolla y papa peruana. Las medidas aplicadas por Panamá han significado un perjuicio para las exportaciones de papa y cebolla peruana. El último año que se registraron cifras de exportación de papa a Panamá, tanto en términos de volumen y valor fue el año 2009. El año 2008 fue el mejor año de exportación de papa peruana con destino Panamá debido a que se envió más de 604 toneladas valorizadas en 249 miles de USD. Sin embargo, para el año 2009, disminuyeron las exportaciones de papa peruana a Panamá en hasta -69%. Asimismo, en el 2017, las exportaciones peruanas de cebolla fresca a Panamá se contrajeron sustancialmente tanto en términos de valor y volumen. Para finales dicho año, se registró que las exportaciones del producto cayeron hasta por un -98.04% frente al 2016 y debido a ello, el crecimiento promedio anual, comprendido en el periodo 2012-2017, se vio afectado en un -53.17%. a pesar de que este sector tiene un potencial exportador de 2.3 millones de USD[1]. Por lo anteriormente expuesto y en aras de evitar una vulneración de los artículos 2, 5, 8 y, el Anexo C del Acuerdo MSF, el Perú solicita a Panamá la reapertura del mercado a las exportaciones peruanas de cebolla y papa; así como evitar cualquier otra acción que prolongue innecesariamente dicho proceso, generando barreras innecesarias e injustificadas en el comercio. Página 1 de 2[1] Información en base al Export Potential Map del ITC para la partida arancelaria 070310.
Summary: Peru raised concerns regarding Panama's import restrictions for Peruvian onions and potatoes and undue delays in the phytosanitary procedures to regain market access. Peru noted that Panama had suspended onion imports from Peru in 2016 following a pest risk analysis (PRA) undertaken to update its phytosanitary import requirements. Concerning trade in potatoes, Peru indicated imports had been suspended by Panama since 2009 due to the detection of a pest. Peru had shared in 2010 a phytosanitary protocol proposal with Panama, on which no response had been provided. Peru considered Panama's measures to be inconsistent with Articles 2.2, 5, 5.4 and 8, and Annex C of the SPS Agreement. Peru emphasized that Panama had continuously requested information which had been previously sent by Peru in a timely manner, causing unnecessary delays. Peru requested Panama to reopen the market for Peruvian onion and potato exports and avoid unjustified barriers to trade.
