Comité de Medidas Sanitarias y Fitosanitarias de la Organización Mundial del Comercio

RESTRICCIONES APLICADAS POR PANAMÁ RESPECTO DEL PROCEDIMIENTO QUE PERMITE RESTABLECER EL ACCESO DE LAS PAPAS Y LAS CEBOLLAS PERUANAS AL MERCADO (PCE N° 512)

Preocupaciones Comerciales Específicas anteriormente planteadas nº xxxiv

INTERVENCIÓN DEL PERÚ

El Perú presenta ante los Miembros de la OMC su preocupación comercial con relación al cierre de las importaciones de cebolla y papa para consumo desde Perú por parte de Panamá, así como demoras indebidas en las gestiones fitosanitarias para el restablecimiento del comercio de los mencionados productos.

El Perú desea recordar que, los artículos 2.2 y 5 del Acuerdo MSF de la OMC indican que los Miembros deben establecer medidas sanitarias y fitosanitarias solo cuando sean aplicables, entre otros, para preservar los vegetales y dichas medidas deben estar basadas en una evaluación de riesgos. Igualmente, en el artículo 5.4 se detalla que los Miembros deben tener en cuenta el objetivo de reducir al mínimo los efectos negativos sobre el comercio. Sin embargo, lamentamos que Panamá no ha considerado estas disposiciones y por el contrario ha aplicado medidas restrictivas e injustificadas en el comercio de papas y cebollas.

Con relación al comercio de cebolla peruana, no se ha tomado en consideración que el comercio histórico de cebollas representaba desde el año 2003 más de 19,000 TM, los cuales no presentaron reportes de interceptación de plagas desde dicha fecha. Al respecto, Panamá suspende la importación de este producto en el año 2016. Dicha suspensión se basó, únicamente, en la actualización de un análisis de riesgos de plagas (ARP) y sin una razón técnica, conforme lo establece el artículo 5 del Acuerdo MSF, para interrumpir el comercio entre ambas Partes. Es necesario precisar que el ARP permite establecer requisitos fitosanitarios para la importación de nuevos productos a nuestros países y/o actualizar requisitos de importación vigentes sin paralizar el flujo comercial existente, y cuyos resultados pueden ser igual, más exigente o menos exigentes, incluyendo el dejar sin efecto las normas vigentes.

Por otro lado, y en lo relativo al comercio de tubérculos de papa para consumo, la importación de este producto se encuentra suspendida por Panamá desde el año 2009, debido a la interceptación de una plaga en destino en un envío. La autoridad fitosanitaria del Perú, en mayo de 2010, remitió a Panamá una propuesta de protocolo fitosanitario para la exportación de papa, previo intercambio de comentarios con su contraparte, la cual a la fecha no tiene respuesta.

En ese mismo sentido, conforme el artículo 8 y el Anexo C, los procedimientos de tipo sanitario o fitosanitario, entre otros, deben ser atendidos y concluidos sin demoras indebidas, facilitando información a la Parte interesada y con prescripciones que se limiten a lo que sea razonable y necesario. Ante esta situación, el Perú ha remitido de manera constante, información técnica referida al análisis de riesgos de plagas para lograr la reapertura del mercado panameño para la papa y la cebolla, sin obtener respuestas por parte de la autoridad sanitaria de Panamá respecto a los resultados de su análisis de riesgos y se nos ha solicitado continuamente la misma información remitida oportunamente por nuestra autoridad sanitaria, lo cual ha originado que el proceso se prolongue de manera innecesaria e injustificada.

Igualmente, y a pesar de que durante la reunión del Comité MSF del 25 al 26 de marzo de 2021, el Perú presentó el documento G/SPS/GEN/1905, con esta preocupación, a la fecha Panamá mantiene el cierre del mercado para las papas y cebollas, sin dar respuesta a las comunicaciones de Perú.

Por lo anteriormente expuesto, el Perú considera que Panamá continúa generando demoras indebidas en el establecimiento de los requisitos fitosanitarios de importación que permitan reiniciar la importación de cebolla y papa peruana.

Las medidas aplicadas por Panamá han perjudicado las exportaciones de papa y cebolla peruana. El último año que se registraron cifras de exportación de papa a Panamá, tanto en términos de volumen y valor fue el año 2009. El año 2008 fue el mejor año de exportación de papa peruana con destino Panamá debido a que se envió más de 604 toneladas valorizadas en 249 miles de USD. Sin embargo, para el año 2009, disminuyeron las exportaciones de papa peruana a Panamá en hasta -69%.

Asimismo, en el 2017, las exportaciones peruanas de cebolla fresca a Panamá se contrajeron sustancialmente tanto en términos de valor y volumen. Para finales dicho año, se registró que las exportaciones del producto cayeron hasta por un -98.04% frente al 2016 y debido a ello, el crecimiento promedio anual, comprendido en el periodo 2012-2017, se vio afectado en un -53.17%. a pesar de que este sector tiene un potencial exportador de 2.3 millones de USD[1].

Por lo anteriormente expuesto y en aras de evitar una vulneración de los artículos 2, 5, 8 y, el Anexo C del Acuerdo MSF, el Perú solicita a Panamá la reapertura del mercado a las exportaciones peruanas de cebolla y papa; así como evitar cualquier otra acción que prolongue innecesariamente dicho proceso, generando barreras innecesarias e injustificadas en el comercio.

[1] Información en base al Export Potential Map del ITC para la partida arancelaria 070310.
Summary: Peru raised concerns about Panama's restrictions and undue delays in granting access to Peruvian potatoes and onions. In Peru's view, Panama's measures were in violation of Articles 2.2, 5, 5.4 and 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement. Peru indicated that Panama had suspended the importation of onions in 2016 on the basis of an updated pest risk analysis (PRA). Trade in potatoes had been suspended in 2009 following the interception of a pest in a consignment at destination; Peru regretted the lack of response at the phytosanitary protocol for the exportation proposed in 2010. Panama's market was kept closed for potatoes and onions, and no response was provided to Peru's information and communications, including G/SPS/GEN/1905. Peru requested Panama to reopen the market to Peruvian potato and onion exports and to avoid unnecessary and unjustified barriers to trade. More information is available in document G/SPS/GEN/1938.

Esta gestión es además contraria al principio de “justificación técnica” de la Convención Internacional de Protección Fitosanitaria (CIPF), que indica que las Partes deberán justificar técnicamente las medidas fitosanitarias sobre la base de conclusiones alcanzadas mediante un apropiado análisis de riesgo de plagas o, cuando proceda, otro examen y evaluación comparable de la información científica disponible. 4.       Por otro lado, y en lo relativo al comercio de tubérculos de papa para consumo, la importación de este producto se encuentra suspendida por Panamá desde el año 2009, debido a la interceptación de una plaga en destino en un envío. La autoridad fitosanitaria del Perú, en mayo de 2010, remitió a Panamá una propuesta de protocolo fitosanitario para la exportación de papa, previo intercambio de comentarios con su contraparte, la cual a la fecha no tiene respuesta. En este contexto, no se tiene sustento técnico que imposibilite la reapertura del mercado panameño. 5.       En ese mismo sentido, conforme el artículo 8 y el Anexo C, los procedimientos de tipo sanitario o fitosanitario, entre otros, deben ser atendidos y concluidos sin demoras indebidas, facilitando información a la Parte interesada y con prescripciones que se limiten a lo que sea razonable y necesario. Ante esta situación, el Perú ha remitido de manera constante, información técnica referida al análisis de riesgos de plagas para lograr la reapertura del mercado panameño para la papa y la cebolla, sin obtener respuestas por parte de la autoridad sanitaria de Panamá respecto a los resultados de su análisis de riesgos y se nos ha solicitado continuamente la misma información remitida oportunamente por nuestra autoridad sanitaria, lo cual ha originado que el proceso se prolongue de manera innecesaria e injustificada. 6.       Igualmente, y a pesar de las constantes preocupaciones comerciales presentadas en este Comité, a la fecha Panamá mantiene el cierre del mercado para las papas y cebollas, sin dar respuesta a las comunicaciones de Perú.  7.       Por lo anteriormente expuesto, el Perú considera que Panamá continúa generando demoras indebidas en el establecimiento de los requisitos fitosanitarios de importación que permitan reiniciar la importación de cebolla y papa peruana. 8.       Las medidas aplicadas por Panamá han perjudicado las exportaciones de papa y cebolla peruana. El último año que se registraron cifras de exportación de papa a Panamá, tanto en términos de volumen y valor fue el año 2009. El año 2008 fue el mejor año de exportación de papa peruana con destino Panamá debido a que se envió más de 604 toneladas valorizadas en 249 miles de USD. Sin embargo, para el año 2009, disminuyeron las exportaciones de papa peruana a Panamá en hasta -69%. 9.       Asimismo, en el 2017, las exportaciones peruanas de cebolla fresca a Panamá se contrajeron sustancialmente tanto en términos de valor y volumen. Para finales dicho año, se registró que las exportaciones del producto cayeron hasta por un -98.04% frente al 2016 y debido a ello, el crecimiento promedio anual, comprendido en el periodo 2012-2017, se vio afectado en un -53.17%. a pesar de que este sector tiene un potencial exportador de 2.3 millones de USD[1]. 10.   Por lo anteriormente expuesto y en aras de evitar una vulneración de los artículos 2, 5, 8 y, el Anexo C del Acuerdo MSF, el Perú solicita a Panamá la reapertura del mercado a las exportaciones peruanas de cebolla y papa; así como evitar cualquier otra acción que prolongue innecesariamente dicho proceso, generando barreras innecesarias e injustificadas en el comercio. 11.   Finalmente, el Perú reitera las siguientes consultas que fueron realizadas durante el Examen de Política Comercial de Panamá, llevado a cabo en febrero del presente año. Se agradecerá que Panamá pueda brindar respuesta por escrito a estas preguntas. a.       Considerando que el párrafo 1b del Anexo C del Acuerdo MSF establece que previa petición, se comunique al solicitante sobre el período de tramitación previsto y se informe al solicitante de la fase en que se encuentra el procedimiento, explicándole los eventuales retrasos:-          ¿en qué etapa del análisis de riesgos de plagas se encuentra Panamá con relación a la reapertura de la cebolla peruana?-          ¿cuáles son los motivos que Panamá ha encontrado para no brindar acceso al mercado para la cebolla peruana desde el año 2016?-          ¿cuál es el plazo previsto por Panamá para brindar acceso su mercado para la cebolla peruana?-          ¿por qué Panamá no ha respondido a la propuesta de protocolo fitosanitario enviado por el Perú en mayo de 2010 para la reapertura de la papa peruana?-          ¿cuál es el plazo previsto por Panamá para brindar acceso a su mercado para la papa peruana? b.       En base a los artículos 2 y 5 del Acuerdo MSF de la OMC; así como el numeral 1.1.3 de la NIMF N°02 que establece que cuando ya exista comercio, no deberían aplicarse nuevas medidas hasta que el examen o el nuevo análisis de riesgos de plagas se hayan completado, a menos que lo justifiquen situaciones fitosanitarias nuevas o inesperadas que puedan exigir medidas de emergencia, ¿cuáles son las razones técnicas por las cuales Panamá suspendió las importaciones de la cebolla peruana? ¿De qué forma Panamá considera que con la suspensión a las importaciones de cebolla peruana ha dado cumplimiento a las disposiciones antes señaladas? c.       Si Panamá suspendió la importación de papa peruana por la interceptación de una plaga en destino, ¿cuáles son las razones técnicas para no considerar alguna medida menos restrictiva que la suspensión conforme al artículo 5.4 del Acuerdo MSF? d.       Si Panamá consideró el cierre de su mercado aplicando una medida de emergencia por la presencia de una plaga en un envío de papa peruana, ¿por qué Panamá no notificó dicha suspensión al Comité MSF OMC conforme al párrafo 6 del Anexo B del Acuerdo MSF? e.       Considerando el numeral 3.155 del documento G/SPS/R/104, ¿cuáles son las razones técnicas por las cuales Panamá considera que esta preocupación debe ser discutida en el Comité de Obstáculos Técnicos al Comercio de la OMC?[1] Información en base al Export Potential Map del ITC para la partida arancelaria 070310.
Summary: Peru referred to its full statement on eAgenda, and provided a brief statement orally. Peru expressed its concerns regarding Panama's suspension of imports of onions and potatoes from Peru, and the related undue delays to restore trade. Highlighting the negative impact of the measures on its onion and potato exports, Peru requested Panama to allow market access for these products to prevent violation of Articles 2, 5 and 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement, as well as unnecessary and unjustified barriers to trade. Peru's full statement was circulated in G/SPS/GEN/2051.

Peru expressed its concerns regarding Panama's suspension of imports of onions and potatoes from Peru, and the related undue delays in restoring trade. Peru recalled that Panama had suspended imports of Peruvian onions in 2016 based on an updated pest risk analysis (PRA), which was contrary to the SPS Agreement and the principle of "technical justification" under the International Plant Protection Convention. Peru also reported on the lack of response to the proposed phytosanitary protocol for the exportation of potatoes to Panama, following an exchange of comments in 2010. Peru requested Panama to allow market access for these products to prevent violations of Articles 2, 5 and 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement and to avoid unnecessary and unjustified barriers to trade. Peru submitted its statement in G/SPS/GEN/2088.

Temporarily putting aside its concerns regarding potatoes, Peru expressed its concerns regarding Panama's suspension of imports of onions from Peru and the related undue delays in restoring trade. Peru recalled that Panama had suspended imports of Peruvian onions in 2016 based on an updated pest risk analysis, which was contrary to the SPS Agreement and the IPPC principle of "technical justification". Peru also reported on the lack of response regarding the results of Panama's risk analysis and complained about reiterated requests for information that had been previously submitted. Peru requested Panama to allow market access for Peruvian onions to prevent violations of Articles 2, 5 and 8 and Annex C to the SPS Agreement and to avoid unnecessary and unjustified barriers to trade. StatementSubmitted:
China appreciates Korea's fulfillment of its transparency obligations and providing an almost two-year transition period. But it should be considered that China exports more than two hundred thousand tons of Kimchi to Korea every year which occupied 99% imported kimchi market share of Korea. The implement of the measure will be a disguised restriction for Chinese exporting Kimchi, which would directly increase the Chinese Kimchi manufacturers' cost and harm their market competitiveness.

China signed a cooperation agreement with the world's largest non-governmental food safety organization-Global Food Safety Initiative (GFSI) on Nov 2, 2015. GFSI officially recognized the China Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point  (CHINA-HACCP) accreditation system, which means that food companies that have obtained China’s HACCP certification will be exempted from the purchaser’s verify or foreign certification when they enter the supply chain of GFSI members, thereby reducing trade costs. GFSI has continued its recognization of China-HACCP on Oct 16 2019. Korea is working on the way of being a member of GFSI in the future. 

Till now, most of the Chinese Kimchi manufacturers have obtained the CHINA-HACCP, which complies with "Korea Kimchi Manufacture HACCP Management Standard Guideline" and "Korea Kimchi Manufacture Prerequisite Management Standard". Meanwhile, the China Customs conduct supervision to ensure the export kimchi manufacturers meet importing countries’ food safety requirements. However, according to Korea’s notification, these manufactures need to get Korean certification.

Therefore, China suggests Korea follow the SPS agreement principles of minimum trade impact and equivalence, withdraw the measure of designating kimchi as a product under mandatory HACCP application or recognize the equivalence of the Chinese food safety supervision system with Korea, fulfilling SPS agreement obligations of maximally reducing the burden of China exporters.
Summary: China raised its concern regarding Korea's mandatory Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) certification for imported kimchi. While appreciating Korea's fulfilment of its transparency obligations, China stated that the implementation of the measure would constitute a restriction for Chinese kimchi exports. China noted it had signed a cooperation agreement on November 2015 with the Global Food Safety Initiative (GFSI), which recognized the China-HACCP accreditation system. In addition, China indicated that most of its kimchi manufacturers had obtained China-HACCP certification, complying with the "Korea Kimchi Manufacture HACCP Management Standard Guideline" and the "Korea Kimchi Manufacture Prerequisite Management Standard". Notwithstanding, China noted that, under Korea's notification, manufacturers needed to obtain a Korean certification. China urged Korea to withdraw the measure designating kimchi as a product under mandatory HACCP application or recognize the equivalence of the Chinese food safety supervision system.

StatementSubmitted:
On 20 April 2021, Korea notified the WTO of its regulation on the Standard Operating Procedures for Imported Food Safety Management Certification?G/SPS/N/KOR/714?. On 17 May 2021, Korea notified the WTO of its supplementary opinions on the revised draft of the Imported Food Safety Management Special Act?G/SPS/N/KOR/702/Add.1??which stipulates that cabbage kimchee is identified as a mandatory HACCP product.

The average annual export volume of Chinese kimchee exported to Korea is close to 300,000 tons, and the value of the goods is nearly 2 billion RMB, accounting for more than 99% of the total imported kimchee from Korea. If HACCP certification is implemented, Chinese kimchee exporting companies will be greatly affected. At the 79th meeting of the SPS Committee, the Chinese side expressed STC on this measure. The Korean side stated that when implementing HACCP on imported foods, it can negotiate and adjust with the exporting members. The Chinese side hereby expresses our welcome.

It is well-known that the current production process of Chinese kimchee exported to Korea is completely the same as that of local Korean kimchee. Besides, most Chinese factories have stationed or regular Korean technicians to guide the production. Meanwhile, both China and Korea are members of the International Accreditation Forum?IAF?. The China National Accreditation Service for Conformity Assessment ?CNAS?implements accreditation activities based on standards, guidelines and other normative documents issued by IAF, which means that the certificate obtained by CNAS is equivalent to the certificate recognized by Korea.

Therefore, China suggests that the Korean side amend the draft measures to“certificates issued by the Korea Food Safety Management Certification Institute or an accreditation body (such as CNAS) recognized by signatories of the mutual recognition agreement among IAF member states”. China also recommends that both sides conduct discussions on the Imported Food Safety Management Certification Standard Operating Procedures and certification standards. We would like the Korean side can facilitate the recognition of the results of the conformity assessment made by the Chinese side, adopt the list of companies recommended by the Chinese competent authority or accept the certificate issued by China’s HACCP certification body.
Summary: China reiterated its concern regarding Korea's mandatory Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) certification for imported kimchi, the implementation of which would negatively impact Chinese kimchi exports. China noted that the Chinese National Accreditation Service for Conformity Assessment (CNAS) employed the standards and guidelines issued by the "International Accreditation Forum", of which Korea was a member. China considered the certification obtained by CNAS to be equivalent to the certification recognized by Korea. China urged Korea to recognize China's conformity assessment, adopt the list of companies recommended by China or recognize the certificate issued by China's certification bodies.

StatementSubmitted: Mexico Restrictions on Chilli India has a significant concern about the series of measures Mexico adopted regarding imports of dry chilli from Indian since 2017. First: In the year 2017, Mexico suspended imports of dried chilli from India, citing interception of the Khapra Beetle. Second, based on Mexico's response, the DA&FW (Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare) formulated a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for exports of dried chilli to ensure pest-free exports and shared it with the Mexican side.  But Mexico insisted on deputing Mexican inspectors to verify all the warehouses and treatment facilities. Third: India further requested a one-time joint inspection before recommencement of export of dry chilli to Mexico. The assignment of a Mexican inspector at each time adds delay and cost for chilli exports. However, Mexico did not agree to India's request. These artificial barriers created by Mexico have resulted in a drastic reduction of dry chilli exports to Mexico. In the year 2016-17, India exported 12112 Metric Tonns of dry chilli worth USD 28 million. This was reduced to zero in 2018-19 due to the restrictions imposed by Mexico.  Export of Chilli Whole (09042110) from India to MexicoYear Quantity (MT)Value (in Lakhs)Value (in USD Mn)2016-17121121877727.992017-1828313596.375.582018-19NIL  2019-203558.950.082020-21 (Apr-Oct)222437.260.58 India recognizes Mexico has the right to regulate sanitary requirements for imports.  However, Article 5 of the SPS Agreement details the risk assessment and the appropriate level of sanitary or phytosanitary protection (ALOP). When alternative measures that provide the same safety level as the proposed measure exist, governments should choose the significantly least trade-restrictive measures. Further, Article 5.6 of the SPS Agreement requires members to ensure that "measures are not more trade-restrictive than required to achieve their appropriate level of sanitary or phytosanitary protection." To be considered a valid alternative measure, it must be reasonably available, taking into account technical and economic feasibility; it must achieve the same ALOP. It must be significantly less restrictive to trade. India already follows a Standard Operating Procedure for Export of Dried Chilli, prepared by the Directorate of Plant Protection, Quarantine and Storage, and the NPPO ( National Plant Protection Organisation). This SoP provides a system for the export of pest-free dried chilli, explicitly focusing on pests, including the khapra beetle. It requires registration of warehouses, joint inspections, certificates of origin for each consignment, and exporters' declarations. Additionally, the inspection, certification, and sampling regime are in place to ensure freedom from pests of concern to the importing country, including Khapra beetle and other storage pests. Permitting Indian authorities to conduct required inspections and issue certificates following the existing SoP is a valid alternative measure in line with Article 5.6 of the SPS agreement.  In view of the above, Mexico is requested  1)                to respond why a one-time joint inspection, or monitoring and inspections by Indian authorities alone, is insufficient to meet their desired level of protection?2)                to share the risk assessment done for arriving at the present regime of inspection of all consignments of chilli by Mexican inspectors.3)                to share what other less trade-restrictive measures Mexico considered before arriving at the current regime of inspection of all consignments by Mexican inspectors.
Summary: India raised concerns on the measures adopted by Mexico regarding imports of dried chili from India. India noted that Mexico had suspended imports of dried chili in 2017 citing the interception of the khapra beetle, following which a standard operating procedure for the export of pest-free dried chili had been formulated and shared with Mexico. India remarked that Mexico had insisted on sending Mexican inspectors to verify warehouses and treatment facilities, which had added delays and costs for chili exports. Recalling Articles 5 and 5.6 of the SPS Agreement, India requested Mexico to respond why it considered a one-time joint inspection, or monitoring and inspections performed by Indian authorities, to be insufficient to meet its appropriate level of protection (ALOP); share the risk assessment for arriving at the present regime of inspection; and share other less trade-restrictive measures that had been considered.

StatementSubmitted:
La delegación de México presenta esta preocupación comercial específica debido a la demora en las gestiones por parte de la Autoridad Panameña de Seguridad de Alimentos (AUPSA), con relación a la renovación de autorizaciones a establecimientos mexicanos exportadores de productos y subproductos de la especie bovina.

Cabe mencionar que el extrañamiento que nuestra Delegación presenta, obedece a demoras en la atención de comunicaciones por parte de la autoridad de Panamá, lo cual ha impactado en el vencimiento de autorizaciones de establecimientos que habían estado exportando sin problema alguno.

Previo al vencimiento de la autorización de 4 establecimientos, en septiembre de 2020, México envió comunicaciones en julio y agosto del mismo año, solicitando información sobre el procedimiento a seguir para la renovación de las actualizaciones.

En octubre, noviembre y diciembre de 2020 se enviaron nuevas comunicaciones reiterando la solicitud de atención a la renovación de establecimientos, cuya autorización ya había vencido en septiembre de 2020.

Siendo hasta diciembre de 2020, que la autoridad de Panamá solicitó información con respecto al estatus sanitario de la especie bovina en México, misma que fue remitida por la autoridad sanitaria de México en febrero de 2021.

Asimismo, en febrero de 2021, el tema fue abordado en un encuentro bilateral, en el que la autoridad de Panamá indicó que para renovar las autorizaciones, requiere desarrollar un procedimiento para la elegibilidad de los países que desean exportar dichos productos a Panamá, además de la evaluación de los servicios veterinarios de México, siendo que existía un comercio abierto y no se presentó algún cambio en el estatus sanitario de México.

En la perspectiva de México, las autoridades panameñas han mostrado demoras indebidas en las gestiones, ya que, aun considerando las condiciones generadas por la actual contingencia sanitaria, México ha otorgado prórrogas a establecimientos panameños que exportan a México.

La delegación de México desea hacer referencia a los derechos y obligaciones de los Miembros ante el Acuerdo de Medidas Sanitarias y Fitosanitarias de esta Organización, particularmente a los principios de basar las medidas en sustento científico y en una evaluación adecuada a las circunstancias de los riesgos existentes para la vida y la salud de las personas y de los animales, así como al Anexo C de dicho Acuerdo, en lo que se refiere a la obligación de que los procedimientos para verificar y asegurar el cumplimiento de MSF se inicien y ultimen sin demoras indebidas. 

La delegación de México agradece a la delegación de Panamá por la atención a esta declaración y reitera su disposición de mantener una comunicación abierta entre autoridades.
Summary: Mexico expressed concerns regarding delays in Panama's procedures for the renewal of authorizations for establishments that exported bovine products and by-products. Mexico noted that the delays in responses to the correspondence sent to Panama had prompted the expiration of authorizations in several establishments. Mexico mentioned a bilateral meeting held in February 2021 in which Panama had explained that, for the renewal of authorizations and in addition to the evaluations of veterinary services, a procedure needed to be developed for the eligibility of countries wishing to export bovine products and by-products. Mexico recalled the provisions of the SPS Agreement to base measures on science and highlighted the provisions of Annex C.

Mexico reiterated its concerns on the undue delays by Panamanian Food Safety Authority (AUPSA) in the renewal of authorization of Mexican establishments exporting products and by-products of bovine animals. Despite Mexico's repeated requests for renewals, AUPSA had indicated the need to develop a procedure for the eligibility of countries exporting to Panama and an assessment of Mexico's veterinary services, even though trade was ongoing and Mexico maintained the same sanitary status. Mexico recalled that SPS measures had to be based on science and appropriate to the circumstances, as well as the obligations under Annex C of the SPS Agreement. Reiterating its willingness to cooperate with Panama, Mexico hoped to reach an agreement in the bilateral meeting of the SPS committee of the Free Trade Agreement to be held later in July.

StatementSubmitted:
Australia recognises the right of governments to take appropriate sanitary and phytosanitary measures consistent with their WTO obligations under the SPS Agreement.
	Australia has concerns with the undue delays in China’s approval procedures for a range of products and establishments, the disproportionate actions taken by China in response to minor or technical breaches, and China’s lack of transparency in its approval procedures.
	Australia has longstanding requests for Chinese government approval of food export establishments and products which have not progressed.
	
		This has led to Australian products receiving less favourable treatment than China’s domestic goods and establishments, and those of other trading partners.
	
	
	Some Australian meat establishments have been waiting for over a decade for listing approval following successful audit findings by Chinese regulators.
	
		Further delays of up to two years have also been faced for Australian infant formula brand registrations and four or more years for new approvals of Australian seafood species.
	
	
	Over 20 export establishment and eligible products lists are required to support trade in Australian agricultural goods to China.
	
		These lists need to be regularly updated to reflect changes to business names or locations, new establishments to be added, or for amendments to the types of eligible products to be exported.
		For some commodities, establishment registrations have a period of validity which need to be renewed on a periodic basis.
	
	
	Australia has faced significant delays in China accepting and publishing our list requests, as well as requests for renewal of registrations prior to expiry.
	Delays in updating of lists can have significant commercial consequences
	
		This can lead to increased clearance times at the border that result in increased storage costs and reduced product shelf life.
		It also creates uncertainty and frustration for exporters and their Chinese customers.
	
	
	Australia reminds China that it must ensure that such procedures are undertaken without undue delay as required in Annex C of the SPS Agreement.
	Worryingly, given our existing concerns, there has also been a recent trend in China to expand the scope of commodities requiring establishment registration.
	
		This includes recent proposed changes to regulations for the registration of overseas producers of imported foods to include a range of 'low risk' foods.
		Australia urges China to apply consistent criteria and transparent timeframes on a non-discriminatory basis for a range of approval procedures
		including the procedures for assessment and approval of commodity registrations, establishment listings and lifting restrictions on suspended establishments.
	
	
	Australia is also concerned with China’s apparent deviation from internationally recognised scientific principles, and its failure to take a risk-based and proportionate approach when applying measures on imported goods.
	
		For example, measures to withdraw establishment approvals for non-compliances that do not pose a significant food safety risk.
	
	
	Australia requests China remain committed to and apply a risk-based and proportionate approach when implementing measures on imported food for all trading partners
	
		This includes applying consistent, non-discriminatory, and transparent approaches in lifting suspensions following the submission of evidence that appropriate corrective actions have been implemented by affected establishments.
	
	
	Australia considers China’s approach, including to the approval of commodity registrations, establishment listings and lifting of restrictions on suspended establishments, is inconsistent with its WTO obligations under the SPS Agreement
	
		including Annex B on Transparency and Annex C on Control, Inspection and Approval Procedures.
	
	
	Australia would welcome bilateral engagement on any of these matters and requests China to ensure it is meeting its obligations under the Agreement by ensuring SPS measures are science and risk-based, are not more trade restrictive than necessary, and through improved transparency.


Australia’s Response to China 


	Australia stands by our high standards of our systems and safety and quality of our product which is recognised internationally. Australia has worked in good faith with China to progress our technical market access requests and to comply with Chinese import requirements.
	We have provided all requested information and undertaken any corrective actions resulting from audits and inspection. This has been done in a timely and transparent manner. We have also reached out to China to find ways to address our issues through consultation and it is disappointing that we have not had such engagement.
	We remain concerned that the lack of response on our requests and the lengthy timeframes we have outlined are clearly inconsistent with China’s WTO obligations. We now look forward to these issues being addressed in a timely and transparent way.
Summary: Australia raised its concern regarding undue delays and lack of transparency in China's approval procedures for a range of products and establishments. Australia urged China to apply consistent criteria and transparent timeframes on a non-discriminatory basis for approval procedures including the procedures for approval of commodity registrations, establishment listing and lifting of restrictions on suspended establishments. Australia requested China to apply a risk?based approach when implementing measures on imported food. In addition, Australia considered China's approach to be inconsistent with Annexes B and C of the SPS Agreement. Australia welcomed bilateral engagement on the matter.In response to China, Australia clarified that its concern preceded the incidents China referred to. Australia indicated it had provided all requested information and undertaken corrective actions following audits and inspections in a timely and transparent manner. In addition, Australia noted that it had attempted to engage in bilateral consultations with China to address this matter and remained concerned by the lack of engagement.

Australia was concerned with the long delays and lack of transparency in China's approval and administrative update process, as well as with the lack of risk and/or evidence basis of China's approach. Noting longstanding requests for approval of food export establishments, Australia requested China to avoid discrimination of Australian products, in accordance with Article 2.3 of the SPS Agreement. China was requested to apply SPS measures that were science-based, proportionate to the risk and not more trade-restrictive than necessary. Australia was waiting for China to approve establishment registrations and update administrative listings changes, and to accept and publish the product listing requests and requests for renewal of registrations prior to expiry. Australia reminded China of the obligations established in Annex C of the SPS Agreement and urged China to apply consistent criteria and transparent timeframes on a non-discriminatory basis for approval procedures.Australia responded to China by underscoring the high standards of its food system and the quality of its agricultural products. Australia regretted that China had not honoured commitments made during bilateral negotiations, that no progress had been made on market access requests, and that no response had been received to the requests for engagement. Noting that other trading partners had also raised concerns on delays and lack of transparency, Australia believed that China's actions were inconsistent with WTO obligations.

Canada was disappointed at the undue delays in China's approval procedures for the import of food products and of foreign establishments. These delays and the lack of transparency and of a rationale of approval procedures for foreign export establishments resulted in uncertainty and trade disruptions. Recalling the obligations established under Annex C of the SPS Agreement, Canada urged China: to finalize and publish the lists of Canadian products await registration; to provide timelines for acceptance; to transmit the result of the approval procedures; to explain the undue delays; to provide the reason why Canadian products or establishments had not been approved; to limit information requirements to what was necessary; and to ensure transparent and predictable approval procedures.In response to China, Canada emphasized the adherence of all Canadian federally licensed establishments to internationally accepted standards and food safety. Both countries shared a long history of safe trade. While Canada had provided all the detailed information required, China had not responded to approve and publish the eligibility for exporting establishments.

Australia remained concerned with the long delays and lack of transparency in China's approval and administrative update process for agricultural and seafood establishments and products. Noting a lack of improvement since first raising the concern, Australia waited for China to approve establishment registrations and to update administrative listing changes. Australia requested China to fulfil its obligation under Article 2.3 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement, and to provide details regarding the assessment and approval of products and establishments, updating administrative lists and lifting restrictions on suspended establishments.Australia responded to China by underscoring the high standards of its food system and the quality of its agricultural products. Australia regretted that China had not honoured their bilateral commitments, the lack of progress on market access requests, and the unresponsiveness to the requests for engagement. Australia highlighted that it had responded to all requests for information from China and had undertaken corrective actions in a timely and transparent manner. Noting that other trading partners had also raised concerns on delays and lack of transparency, Australia believed that China's actions were inconsistent with WTO obligations.

Thank you, Chair.
	Canada and other Members continue to experience significant undue delays in China’s approval procedures for food products and of foreign establishments seeking to export to China.
	Canada continues to wait for China to update over ten separate lists of approved Canadian products and facilities eligible to export to China, including:
	Canadian companies exporting grains and oilseeds, which has not been updated since March 2019;
	Canadian cherry and blueberries exporters, which has not been updated since 2020; and
	Canadian fish and seafood facilities and approved species, which has not been updated since 2018.
	As well, there is also a number of Canadian meat and dairy establishments that are still waiting for approval from China to be added to the list of establishments eligible to export to China. Some of these establishments submitted their applications to China in 2017 following audits conducted by China and have yet to receive a response.
	These undue delays have resulted in unjustified barriers to trade and  administrative burdens for Canadian industry.
	The concerns that were just highlighted, illustrate how China’s implementation of eligibility lists continues to create trade disruptions and barriers for Canadian industry resulting from the continued lack of predictability, transparency, and rationale for China’s approval procedures for foreign export establishments.
	The inaction, excessive delays, and lack of information provided by Chinese officials relating to China’s approval procedures for maintaining and providing new market access for Canadian products and establishments has created  significant uncertainty for Canadian industry and impacted their ability to export  Canadian agriculture, agri-food, and fish and seafood products to China.
	The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) verifies that Canadian establishments recommended for export to China comply with Canada's food safety requirements under Canadian legislation as well as China’s import requirements. 
	Canada recalls that Annex C(1)(a) of the SPS Agreement states that: 
	
	Members shall ensure… that [approval] procedures are undertaken and completed without undue delay and in no less favourable manner for imported products than for like domestic products.
	
	Canada urges China to update and publish the many lists of Canadian products and establishments that continue to await registration to the Chinese market without any further undue delay.
	Furthermore, Canada recalls that Annex C(1)(b) states that:
	
		
		Members shall ensure… that the standard processing period of each procedure is published or that the anticipated processing period is communicated to the applicant upon request...   
		
	
	
	Although Canada has repeatedly requested further information related to the eligibility and registration of Canadian establishments and of food and food products China has continually not provided defined timelines and has not provided a reason or a rationale why Canadian establishments have not been approved.
	Canada urges China to respect its obligations under the WTO SPS Agreement and provide timelines for the acceptance of all Canadian food products and establishments awaiting approval by China and transmit the result of the approval procedures as soon as possible in a precise and complete manner. 
	Per Annex C(1)(b) of the SPS Agreement, China must communicate any deficiencies in applications in a precise and complete manner; process applications that have deficiencies as far as practicable; and provide information on the stage of the approval and an explanation of any delays.
	Canada urges China to immediately provide reasons or other information as to why Canadian products and establishments have not been approved, and provide a clear explanation of the undue delays in the approval of the products and establishments. 
	Moreover, Canada recalls that Annex C(1)(c) of the SPS Agreement states that:
	
		
		Members shall ensure… that information requirements are limited to what is necessary for appropriate control, inspection and approval procedures.
		
	
	
	Canada urges China to limit information requirements to what is necessary and ensure that their approval procedures are transparent and predictable. Canada considers some requirements requested by China to be restrictive and not necessary to undertake approval procedures necessary for China’s appropriate level of sanitary or phytosanitary protection.
	Over the years, Canada and China have implemented many bilateral arrangements that have successfully reinforced and provided food safety assurances and protections for consumers in our respective nations. 
	Canada is ready to continue supplying safe, high-quality products to Chinese consumers.
	In conclusion, Canada calls on China to implement transparent and predictable approval procedures for foreign export establishments that are undertaken and completed without undue delay to meet our common objective of avoiding unnecessary barriers to trade and ensuring trade is maintained based on science and risk. 
	Thank you, Chair.
Summary: Canada continued to experience undue delays in China's approval procedures for the import of food products and of foreign establishments, and was waiting for China to provide updated information over 10 lists of approved Canadian products and facilities eligible to export. These delays and the lack of transparency and of a rationale of approval procedures for foreign establishments had resulted in unjustified barriers to trade, administrative burdens, and trade disruptions. Recalling the obligations in Annex C of the SPS Agreement, Canada urged China to update and publish the lists of Canadian products and establishments awaiting registration; to provide timelines for acceptance; to transmit the result of the approval procedures; to provide the reason why Canadian products and establishments had not been approved; to explain any delays; to limit information requirements to what was necessary; and to ensure transparent and predictable approval procedures.In response to China, Canada emphasized the adherence of all Canadian federally licensed establishments to internationally accepted standards and food safety requirements. In case of any potential food safety risks, appropriate actions were taken immediately by Canada to prevent contaminated foods from entering the domestic and international food supply. Despite the fulfilment of all the requests, including audits on Canadian establishments, China had not responded to approve and publish the eligibility for exporting establishments.

Australia reiterated its concerns with the long delays and lack of transparency in China's approval and administrative process for agriculture and fisheries exports. Australia noted that it was waiting for China to approve establishment registrations, and to update administrative listing changes. Australia requested China to provide information on the assessment and approval of products as well as the lifting of restrictions on suspended establishments. Australia reminded China of the obligations of Article 2.3 of the SPS Agreement, and welcomed engagement to discuss these issues.In response to China, Australia underscored the high standards of its food system and the quality of its agricultural products. Australia regretted that China had not honoured its WTO commitments, the lack of progress on market access requests, and the unresponsiveness to the requests for engagement. Australia highlighted that it had responded to all requests for information from China and had undertaken corrective actions in a timely and transparent manner. Noting that other trading partners had also raised concerns on delays and lack of transparency, Australia believed that China's actions were inconsistent with WTO obligations.

StatementSubmitted: Australia recognises the right of Members to take appropriate sanitary and phytosanitary measures consistent with their obligations under the SPS Agreement.  Australia is a responsible and reliable trading partner with safe and wholesome food production systems that are respected globally. Not only does Australia self-review, but also provides clear assessments and timely responses to trading partners to support a transparent, stable and thriving trade system. We have a similar expectation of our trade partners.  Australia remains concerned with the long delays and lack of transparency in China’s processes for approval and updating administrative lists for Australian agricultural and fisheries exports. Despite multiple requests to approve, amend or publish the listing of Australian food businesses which have been audited to show they meet requirements for trade with China, these requests remain unfulfilled or unanswered.  Australia has meat establishments that have been audited by China but are still awaiting listing since 2010, dairy establishments awaiting listing since 2018 and seafood establishments awaiting listing since 2020. Similarly, there are a number establishments suspended by China that have been offered no clear pathway to lift the suspension, especially in the case of a COVID detection in a staff member.  Australia reminds China that control, inspection and approval activities under the SPS Agreement are to be undertaken without undue delay in a manner that is no less favourable than those undertaken for domestic products. Australia requests that China provide full details of its processes and procedures, including timeframes, for assessment and approval of products and establishments, updating administrative lists and lifting restrictions on suspended establishments.  Australia reiterates that we welcome engagement with China to discuss these issues and ensure that trade is not unnecessarily disrupted.

StatementSubmitted: The European Union shares the concerns expressed by Australia and Canada. In this Committee, China has mentioned the occurrence of SPS non-compliances in imported products. However, despite several requests, China has not yet established transparent, predictable and swift procedures for the approval of products and the listing or re-listing of establishments in-line with agreed international standards – including the expeditious management of non-compliances. In particular, the EU would like to reiterate its concerns regarding the focus on COVID control measures when auditing establishments for the opening of the export session, instead of focusing on the compliance with sanitary and phytosanitary conditions. Furthermore, China announces audits at very short notice - in some cases, few days in advance only, which makes the preparation and logistics very difficult. In many cases, operators and the competent authority have not received a report of the result of the audit, so there is no clarity on the necessary remedial actions. In the interest of China and all trading partners, the EU would like to invite China again to remove these unnecessary additional barriers to trade and to ensure the application of SPS measures in a non-discriminatory, transparent and predictable manner.Clear rules and predictable import assessment procedures, including audits, with reasonable timelines are indispensable for business operators to invest in trade, which contributes to global prosperity.
Summary: The European Union supported the concern and called for transparent, predictable and swift approval procedures and for the listing or re-listing of establishments in line with agreed international standards, including the management of non-compliances. The European Union was concerned about the focus on COVID-19 control measures in establishment audits, as well as the short notice of the announcement of these audits. The European Union requested China to ensure the application of SPS measures in a non-discriminatory, transparent and predictable manner, and to remove unnecessary barriers to trade.

StatementSubmitted: Australia recognises the right of Members to take appropriate sanitary and phytosanitary measures consistent with their obligations under the SPS Agreement. Australia acknowledges the sizeable task in the implementation of the China Imported Food Enterprise Registration (CIFER) system and has been working diligently with China (GACC) and Australian food businesses to assist where possible with updating existing registrations. Members should undertake control, inspection and approval activities under the SPS Agreement in a timely manner that is no less favourable than those undertaken for domestic products. Australia respectfully requests China provides timeframes and pathways, for the assessment and approval of products and establishments, the updating of administrative lists and the lifting of restrictions on suspended establishments. Under the agreed terms of the protocol of phytosanitary requirements for the export of wheat and barley from Australia to China, Australia has provided the updated lists of Australian businesses exporting wheat and barley; and lists of Australian registered establishments where wheat and barley is prepared to China on 7 July 2022. Since mid-2020, these lists have not been updated, in contravention of the agreed protocol.Australia restates its disappointment in the failure to include Australian establishments that were notified as eligible for registration prior to the implementation of CIFER and seeks an explanation from China as to why these businesses have not been included when some applications were assessed as compliant with Chinese importing authority requirements in 2017.Australia’s horticulture lists have not been updated for several consecutive years, with some published lists (i.e., citrus, cherries and apples) last updated in 2019.Updated lists continue to be provided to China on a regular basis, most recently Australia submitted the lists of orchards, packhouses and treatment facilities for mangoes, summer fruit and cherries on 13 September 2022, in accordance with their respective protocols. Prior to this was citrus fruit, which was submitted on 12 April 2022. Australia reiterates that we welcome bilateral engagement with China to discuss these issues and ensure that trade is permitted and afforded to these Australian businesses, and that existing trade is not unnecessarily disrupted because of the implementation of this additional registration requirement.
Summary: Noting the complexity of implementing the CIFER system, Australia underscored that control, inspection and approval activities should be undertaken in a timely manner that was no less favourable than those undertaken for domestic products. Australia requested China to provide information regarding the assessment and approval of products and establishments, the updating of administrative lists and the lifting of restrictions on suspended establishments. Australia regretted that the failure to update the list of businesses that had been provided to China violated the agreed terms of the protocol of phytosanitary requirements for exports of these products, and sought clarification on the issue. Australia would welcome bilateral engagement with China to ensure that the registration requirements did not unnecessarily disrupt trade.In response to China, Australia underscored the high standards of its food system and the safety and quality of its agricultural products. Australia regretted that China had not honoured its WTO commitments, the lack of progress on market access requests, and the unresponsiveness to the requests for engagement. Australia highlighted that it had responded to all requests for information from China and had undertaken corrective actions in a timely and transparent manner. Noting that other trading partners had also raised concerns on delays and lack of transparency, Australia looked forward to a resolution of the issue in a timely and transparent manner.

StatementSubmitted: Australia recognises the right of Members to take appropriate sanitary and phytosanitary measures consistent with their rights and obligations under the SPS Agreement. SPS control, inspection and approval activities implemented under the SPS Agreement should be timely and no less favourable than those undertaken for domestic circumstances. Australia requests China to provide timeframes and pathways for: the assessment and approval of establishment registrations and their products;the updating of administrative listings;and the removal of restrictions and suspensions on establishments and products.Examples of China’s non-adherence with the agreed practices under the SPS Agreement include:Timely updating of administrative listing. Australia’s horticulture lists have not been updated for several consecutive years, with some published lists not updated since 2019 (including: citrus, cherries, table grapes, Tasmanian apples, mangoes and summer fruit). Australia continues to provide updated listings to China on a regular basis in adherence with agreed protocol arrangements.Most recently, Australia submitted lists, in accordance with their respective protocol for Tasmanian apples in December 2022.Immediately prior to this, Australia submitted lists for mangoes, summer fruit and cherries (September 2022) and table grapes (October 2022).China has not provided Australia any reason why the lists have not been updated, nor have any concerns been raised in relation to any of the facilities.Timely finalisation of establishment approval. There are 15 Australian meat establishments that were audited and notified they were eligible for registration by China in 2017. Despite this, none of these establishments have been added to lists on the GACC websites nor in the CIFER system.The facilities have not been contacted by China to alter the approval determination and Australia has not been contacted or given any reason for the delay.Timely updating of eligible product lists.  Seafood exporters have been waiting over four years for China to consider their comprehensive submissions to list new live Australian seafood species for export to China.  China has not provided Australia any reason why the list has not been updated, nor asked for any additional information or clarification to facilitate the finalisation of the listing process.Australia reiterates that we welcome open bilateral engagement with China to resolve these issues. We seek agreement from China that existing trade should not be unnecessarily disrupted and that the registration of businesses and products (in CIFER and through the lists provided) are not delayed.
Summary: Recalling that SPS control, inspection and approval activities should be timely and no less favourable than those undertaken for domestic circumstances, Australia requested China to provide timeframes and pathways for the assessment and approval of establishment registrations and their products, the updating of administrative listings, and the removal of restrictions and suspensions on establishments and products. StatementSubmitted: Australia recognises the right of Members to take appropriate sanitary and phytosanitary measures consistent with their rights and obligations under the SPS Agreement. SPS control, inspection and approval activities implemented under the SPS Agreement should be timely and no less favourable than those undertaken for domestic circumstances. Australia requests China to provide timeframes and pathways for: The removal of restrictions and suspensions of Australian establishments and products. Australia has provided extensive investigation and rectification reports to support reinstatement of trade for 11 Australian export meat establishments currently suspended from the China market. These establishments have been waiting several years to re-establish trade. Australia requests China’s urgent attention to lift suspensions or provide information on the pathway to reinstate trade for these affected establishments that considers existing technical submissions.   Timely assessment and approval of establishments and other lists:Registration for Australian germplasm collection centres lapsed across 2020 and 2022. Despite providing extensive documentation to support the renewal of their accreditation, Australia is yet to receive a response from China.Timely updating of eligible product lists for non-viable seafood. Seafood exporters have been waiting for several years for China to consider their comprehensive submissions to list additional non-viable Australian seafood species as eligible for import into China. Several new species have been added outside of these submissions. However, an official application process is yet to be clarified by GACC.Infant formula exporters (via Chinese business partners) have submitted to China’s domestic focussed State Administration of Market Regulation their comprehensive submissions for brand registration approval in 2022. 12 months later Australian exporters are awaiting formal confirmation from the State Administration of Market Regulation confirming their status and upcoming audits for brand approval.Australia welcomes open technical engagement with China to resolve these issues.
Summary: Recalling that under the SPS Agreement, SPS control, inspection and approval activities should be timely and no less favourable than those undertaken for domestic circumstances, Australia requested China to provide timeframes and pathways for the removal of restrictions and suspensions of Australian establishments and products, and assess and approve establishments and other lists as well as eligible product lists for non-viable seafood in timely manner. Australia welcomed bilateral engagement with China to resolve these issues.

StatementSubmitted: Thank you Chair. I refer to Canada’s previous interventions on this item, which remain valid.Similar to other Members, Canada continues to experience significant undue delays in China’s approval process for market access requests and establishments seeking to export to China, many of which date from 2018. Canada also continues to experience delays in China reinstating suspended Canadian meat establishments and one pet food establishment, despite the fact that Canada has provided all the information requested by China to facilitate their reinstatement.  As expressed in the November 2023 WTO TBT Committee, while Canada appreciates efforts to facilitate the registration and renewal process in the China Import Food Enterprise Registration (CIFER) system; greater consistency and reduced administrative burden would ensure CIFER does not cause delays.  Canada is ready to continue supplying safe, high-quality products to Chinese consumers and facilitating the timely approval of Canadian food products and establishments would contribute to China’s food security objectives.
Summary: Referring to its interventions at previous Committee meetings, Canada stated that it continued to experience undue delays in China's approval procedures for market access requests and establishments seeking to export to China and for the reinstating of suspended Canadian establishments. While appreciating China's efforts to facilitate the registration and renewal process in the CIFER system, Canada reiterated its request for greater consistency and a reduced administrative burden to avoid delays. Canada underscored that the approval of Canadian food products and establishments would contribute to China's food security objectives.

StatementSubmitted: Japan, like other Members, would like to raise its concerns again regarding the implementation of Decree 248 by China concerning administrative measures for registration of overseas manufacturers of imported food. Japan appreciates China’s flexibility to address the difficulties Japanese manufacturers faced in renewal of registrations. Having said so, Japan is still concerned that the procedures are not based on scientific principles and lack predictability and transparency.Japan requests China to improve the operation of the CIFER system, and to ensure that the procedures related to the Decree 248 are undertaken and completed without undue delay and in a transparent manner.Japan would also like to ask China the followings:To establish a standard processing period for applications made through the CIFER system (i.e., a standard timeline to be followed from application through registration), and make that processing period known to the Members and foreign manufacturers.To give sufficient explanation for the reasons when application is rejected through the CIFER system, and ensure its consistency.To notify the Members promptly of any changes in the operation of the regulations or the CIFER system, including changes to product codes (HS CIQ) used in the system, which will or might affect exports. Should any changes occur, we also ask that the GACC provide a reasonable transitional period.To correct any defects in the CIFER system as soon as possible, including: (a) the loss of the past input data when the GACC or competent authorities of exporting countries refuses an application from a manufacturer and the manufacturer needs to input data from the scratch; (b) the current, considerable delays in the registration process; (c)its inability to accept letters of proxy; and (d) the fact that some of the product codes (HS CIQ) are missing from the list shown on the system.To proceed in a timely manner with review of additional information submitted by registered manufacturers. Even now there are manufacturers who have not received any response from the GACC, that is 145 out of 899 manufacturers for products designated in Article 7 of Decree248.To respond to unanswered questions within a reasonable time.Japan would like to communicate closely with China to address our concerns in a corporative manner.
Summary: Whereas Japan appreciated China's flexibility to address the difficulties faced by manufacturers in the renewal of registrations, Japan remained concerned that the procedures were not based on scientific principles and lacked predictability and transparency. Japan requested China to improve the operation of the CIFER system and to ensure that the procedures related to Decree 248 were undertaken without undue delay and in a transparent manner. Japan asked China to establish a standard processing period for applications made through the CIFER system and make that processing period known to Members and foreign manufacturers, to provide sufficient explanations in case of rejections, to promptly notify any changes in the operation of the regulations or in the CIFER system, to correct any defects in the CIFER system as soon as possible, to proceed in a timely manner with review of additional information submitted by registered manufacturers, and to respond to unanswered questions within a reasonable time. Japan expressed its desire to communicate closely with China to address concerns in a cooperative manner.

StatementSubmitted: The United States is disappointed China has not published all requested new U.S. seafood establishments and some existing dairy establishments in over a year, despite repeated U.S. requests for these modifications.  We request that China publish immediately the list of dairy and seafood establishments provided by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and we look forward to receiving confirmation of the prompt registration of eligible U.S. dairy and seafood establishments.  Further, the United States remains disappointed that China has not relisted meat facilities that are awaiting action from China’s General Administration of Customs, or GACC, before being able to resume shipments, nor has GACC outlined a process for relisting suspended facilities in general.   In addition, the United States is concerned that China is testing for animal diseases in products that are deemed “safe to trade” by the World Organization for Animal Health, or WOAH, and pose no risk to human health and present no food safety concerns.  The United States is frustrated that China is suspending establishments on the basis of such animal diseases and other purported infractions after individual detections, particularly in cases where some common tests are known to result in false positives in vaccinated animals.   We request that China accept the provided corrective actions and preventive measures taken by all affected establishments and verified by FSIS, immediately relist the suspended establishments, and outline a process for relisting suspended facilities in the future.
Summary: The United States requested China to publish the list of dairy and seafood establishments provided by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The United States expressed its disappointment that GACC had not relisted meat facilities nor had outlined a process for relisting suspended facilities in general. In addition, the United States was concerned that GACC was testing for animal diseases in products that were deemed "safe to trade" by WOAH and suspending establishments on the basis of such animal diseases. The United States requested China to accept the provided corrective actions and preventive measures taken by all affected establishments, to relist the suspended establishments, and to outline a process for relisting suspended facilities in the future. The United States provided its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2181.
