StatementSubmitted: The United States appreciates the positive development of the reinstatement of one U.S. meat establishment in December 2023.  However, the United States remains deeply concerned with the significant delays of the General Administration of Customs of the People’s Republic of China (GACC) to reinstate several other delisted facilities.  Specifically, the United States remains disappointed that GACC has yet to relist the four remaining U.S. meat facilities that were determined to be non-compliant with Chinese food safety standards concerns despite being provided with corrective actions. In addition, the United States is concerned that GACC is testing for animal diseases in products that are deemed “safe to trade” by the World Organization for Animal Health and pose no risk to human health and present no food safety concerns. The United States is frustrated that GACC is suspending establishments after one violation and we request that GACC accept the provided corrective actions and preventive measures taken by all affected establishments and verified by FSIS and immediately relist the suspended establishments.
Summary: The United States acknowledged the reinstatement of one of its meat establishments in December 2023 by the General Administration of Customs of the People’s Republic of China (GACC). However, the United States reiterated its concern regarding the significant delays in relisting several other delisted facilities despite the corrective actions provided. The United States was also concerned by GACC's testing for animal diseases in products deemed safe by WOAH. The United States requested acceptance of the provided corrective actions verified by the Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) and the immediate relisting of suspended establishments. The United States provided its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2218.

StatementSubmitted: Australia recognises the right of Members to take appropriate sanitary and phytosanitary measures consistent with their rights and obligations under the SPS Agreement. SPS control, inspection and approval activities implemented under the SPS Agreement should be timely and no less favourable than those undertaken for domestic circumstances. Australia requests China to provide clear and reasonable timeframes and pathways for: • the assessment and approval of establishment registrations and their products; • the updating of administrative listings;• and the removal of restrictions and suspensions on establishments and products. Examples of China’s non-adherence with the agreed practices under the SPS Agreement include: • Assessment and removal of suspensions for eight Australian meat establishments. Whilst Australia appreciates China’s decision in December 2023 to lift suspensions on three export meat establishments, there are still eight Australian meat establishments that remain suspended. Australia has provided extensive investigation and rectification reports to support reinstatement of trade for these establishments. China made repeated commitments that formal feedback on these suspensions would be provided ‘shortly’. However, these establishments are still prevented from trading and there is no clear pathway forward to remove their suspensions. Australia requests that China prioritises the work needed to resolve these suspensions. • Timely and streamlined updating of eligible product lists for non-viable seafood. Seafood exporters have been waiting for several years for China to consider their comprehensive submissions to list additional non-viable Australian seafood species as eligible for import into China. • Australia acknowledges China’s recent proposal for a draft protocol for aquatic products to formalise trade, including the updating of the species list. Australia notes that this may be a long and complex process. • Australian seafood exporters have been waiting since 2020 for GACC to consider a submission, demonstrating the safety of live Australian lobsters exported to China, specifically on cadmium levels. An additional submission was delivered to GACC in January 2024. • To date GACC has not formally responded to either submission and Australian live lobster exporters remain unable to access the market as importers cannot obtain necessary import permits for these products. Australia welcomes open bilateral engagement with China to resolve these issues.
Summary: Emphasizing the importance of timely and equitable SPS control, inspection, and approval activities, Australia requested that China provide clear timeframes and pathways for assessing and approving establishment registrations and their products. Additionally, Australia urged China to expedite updating administrative listings and removing restrictions and suspensions on establishments and products. Noting the lifting of suspensions on three Australian meat establishments in December 2023, Australia urged China to resolve the suspension of the eight remaining establishments promptly. Australia also cited delays in considering submissions for listing additional Australian seafood species. Australia acknowledged China's recent proposal for a draft protocol for aquatic products, recognizing that this process might be lengthy and complex. Australia called for bilateral engagement with China to address these issues and to ensure fair and efficient trade relations.

StatementSubmitted: Australia recognises the right of Members to take appropriate sanitary and phytosanitary measures consistent with their rights and obligations under the SPS Agreement. SPS control, inspection and approval activities implemented under the SPS Agreement should be timely, transparent and no less favourable than those undertaken for domestic circumstances. Australia welcomed productive technical discussions with China in Beijing in early June 2024 as a return to regular dialogue between competent authorities and we look forward to continued and consistent engagement to progress mutually beneficial trade. This is in line with the strategic direction agreed at the Australia-China Annual Leaders’ Meeting on 17 June 2024, which put engagement and dialogue at the centre of our bilateral relationship. We encourage China to support the continued and consistent engagement required to progress mutually beneficial trade, including recent commitments from the ChAFTA Joint Commission meeting to step up engagement under ChAFTA subsidiary committees.Australia notes that there are still outstanding delays to the following three things:assessment and approval of establishment registrations and their products,updating of administrative listings,and the removal of suspensions and restrictions on certain establishments and products.Examples of these include:Assessment and removal of outstanding suspensions for Australian meat establishments.Australia welcomed China’s decision in May 2024 to lift suspensions on five meat establishments and in December 2023 to lift suspensions on three export meat establishments. However, as Prime Minister Albanese raised directly with Premier Li during his visit to Australia last week, there are still two Australian meat establishments that remain suspended since 2020 and 2021. Australia has provided extensive investigation and rectification reports to support reinstatement of trade for these establishments. In recent technical discussions in Beijing last month, Australia again provided a detailed technical case and sought the removal of suspensions as a matter of priority. It is important that both sides maintain the momentum to resolve these long-standing matters. Reissuing of import permits for Australian live rock lobsters. As raised in recent bilateral discussions, Australian seafood exporters have been waiting since 2020 for GACC to re-issue import permits to Chinese businesses for Australian live rock lobsters exported to China. DAFF has provided comprehensive and consistent evidence to demonstrate Australia’s strong export controls for seafood products, compliance with China’s importing country requirements and robust monitoring and surveillance systems. China has committed to expedite its assessment of Australia’s submissions in support of reinstating trade.Timely and streamlined updating of eligible product lists for non-viable seafood. Australia acknowledges China’s recent proposal for a draft protocol for aquatic products to formalise trade, including the updating of the species list. Australia notes that this may be a long and complex process. Seafood exporters have been waiting since 2020 for China to consider their comprehensive submissions to list additional non-viable Australian seafood species as eligible for import into China.Reaccreditation of animal germplasm facilities. Accreditation for all Australian germplasm collection centres has not been renewed since 2020 and the impacted establishments are not able to trade. Building on the multiple submissions provided to China to support re-accreditation, Australia welcomes China’s commitment at recent technical meetings to conduct audits and reminds China this process should be timely and transparent.Compliance with due process for updates to Australian horticulture lists. Australia reminds China that updates to horticulture list are a routine action that should be applied to all commodities consistently. In conclusion, Australia welcomes open direct engagement with China to resolve these issues. Our leaders also committed to supporting a fair, open and non-discriminatory business environment and maintaining the WTO-centred and multilateral rules-based trading system. We look forward to working with China to give effect to these commitments and support non-restrictive trade in the interests of both countries.Rebuttal:We understand that several commitments have been made at high level meetings over the last month – it is now time that we move those conversations toward action. We look forward to working together to resolve outstanding issues and to move toward a more predictable and reliable trading environment between our two countries.
Summary: In expressing its concerns, Australia recalled that SPS control, inspection, and approval activities needed to be timely, transparent, and no less favourable than those for domestic circumstances. Australia informed the Committee about productive technical discussions with China in June 2024, which had marked a return to a regular dialogue. Australia noted outstanding delays concerning the assessment and approval of establishment registrations and their products, updating administrative listings, and removing suspensions on certain establishments and products. Australia specifically referred to: the removal of suspensions for Australian meat establishments, with two establishments suspended since 2020 and 2021; the re-issuing of import permits for Australian live rock lobsters that had been delayed since 2020; updates of eligible product lists for non-viable seafood, with exporters awaiting consideration of their submissions since 2020; the reaccreditation of animal germplasm facilities that had not been renewed since 2020, and due process concerns for updates of horticulture lists. Australia concluded that it welcomed open direct engagement with China and reaffirmed its commitment to a fair, open, and non-discriminatory, WTO-centred rules-based trading system.Australia took the floor again to concur with the previous intervention from the United States. Australia believed China's response had not adequately addressed the questions raised by Members. Australia stated that it understood several commitments had been made at high-level meetings and it was now time to move those conversations towards action. Australia looked forward to working with China to resolve outstanding issues and have a more reliable trading environment.

StatementSubmitted:
Gracias señor Presidente, Paraguay quisiera introducir su preocupación por la no renovación de esta sustancia, notificada en el documento   G / TBT / N / EU / 770.

La sustancia alfa-cipermetrina se encuentra debidamente registrada en mi país ante la autoridad competente, el Servicio Nacional de Calidad y Sanidad Vegetal y de Semillas (SENAVE); como insecticida sistémico, y es utilizada para controlar plagas que atacan a rubros de gran relevancia económica. Entre ellas, se mencionan algunas sujetas al control de la sustancia afectada: la Spodoptera frugiperda en cultivo de maíz y soja; Anticarsia gemmatalis(oruga de las leguminosas), Loxostege bifidales (orugita verde), Epinotia aporema (barrenador de brote) en cultivo de soja; Horcia novilellus (chinche rayada), Alabama orgillacea (oruga de la hoja), Porosagrotis gypaetina (gusano cortador pardo) entre otros lepidópteros, hemípteros e insectos que atacan a cultivos como el algodón, maíz y girasol. En este sentido, estos insectos constituyen un verdadero problema para el desarrollo de varios cultivos, por lo que es importante contar con sustancias, debidamente controladas, autorizadas, que cumplen con las exigencias técnico científicas para su uso, y que actualmente han demostrado eficacia en el control de estas plagas, siendo  indispensables para la rotación de ingredientes activos evitando la resistencia en insectos en el marco del manejo integrado de plagas.

Paraguay considera la no renovación por parte de la Unión Europea, podría generar al productor local una gran limitación en cuanto a las sustancias tecnológicas disponibles para un buen manejo de su cultivo impactando directamente en la economía nacional, pues como es practica consuetudinaria en la UE hace unos años, seguirán próximamente las reducciones de los LMRs de esta sustancia.

Nuestra preocupación responde a los impactos negativos que generaría dicha medida en los productores paraguayos, teniendo en cuenta la importancia de los cultivos que utilizan alfa-cipermetrina y su implicancia en las exportaciones de productos nacionales en los cuales es utilizado. 

Paraguay insiste en que la falta de valoración de riesgos continúa restringiendo cada vez más el uso de productos de protección de planta y reduciendo los LMR a niveles que restringen el comercio, utilizando como argumento la imposibilidad de determinar la seguridad del uso de numerosas sustancias.

Si bien se reconoce que reconoce que los Miembros tienen derecho a determinar el nivel apropiado de protección sanitaria o fitosanitaria necesaria para proteger la vida o la salud de las personas, los animales o los vegetales, se resalta la importancia de adoptar un enfoque científico y basado en el riesgo para reglamentar los productos fitosanitarios, por lo que consideramos que el criterio adoptado por la Unión Europea para limitar el uso de plaguicidas restringe el comercio más de lo necesario para alcanzar sus objetivos legítimos, de conformidad con sus obligaciones en esta cosa contraídas en vigor  de los acuerdos MSF y OTC.

Muchas gracias.
Summary: Paraguay expressed concerns on the non-renewal of alpha-cypermethrin, as had been notified in G/TBT/N/EU/770. The substance was registered by the National Plant and Seed Quality and Health Service (SENAVE) as a systemic insecticide to control pests that attack crops of great economic importance. It was essential to have authorized substances that fulfilled the scientific and technical needs, that had proven to be effective to control these pests and that were necessary to ensure the rotation of active ingredients and avoid resistance within an integrated pest management. Assuming that maximum residue limits (MRLs) would subsequently be reduced, the non-renewal of alpha-cypermethrin by the European Union would limit the substances and technologies available for producers, affecting national economy. While recognizing Members' right to determine their appropriate level or protection, Paraguay reiterated the importance of a risk-based scientific approach to regulate phytosanitary products. In its view, the EU criteria restricted trade more than necessary and violated the obligations under the SPS and TBT Agreements.

StatementSubmitted: EUROPEAN UNION - CLASSIFICATION OF 'ANTHRAQUINONE' AS A PESTICIDE AND MRL LEVEL OF 0.02 MG/KG FOR IMPORTED TEA CONCERNS: Due to the anthraquinone detection in tea, European Union through Commission Regulation (EU) No 1146/2014[2] , has classified anthraquinone as a pesticide and has set a maximum reside limit of 0.02 mg/kg for tea. In case of India, Anthraquinone is not a registered pesticide and no pesticide formulation of Anthraquinone is available. Further, there is no standard in India at present as per the Food Safety and Standards (Contaminants Toxins and Residues) Regulation, 2011 and neither is there any CODEX limit for anthraquinone in Tea. Various importers of tea from EU have conducted tests across tea plantations in India and it has been established that ‘Anthraquinone’ is a naturally occurring pollutant/ hydrocarbon and not a pesticide. Hence, the MRL level of 0.02 mg/kg in EU is too low for anthraquinone which is naturally occurring. This strict testing of Anthraquinone has been greatly affecting Indian tea exports to EU. In view of the above, India requests European Union to establish how classification of Anthraquinone as a pesticide falls under the ambit of Annex A, 1(c) – to protect human life or health within the territory of the Member from risks arising from diseases carried by animals, plants or products thereof, or from entry, establishment or spread of pests. Article 2.2 of SPS agreement lays down two basic requirements for SPS measures, namely that: (1) they are applied only to the extent necessary to protect human, animal or plant life or health; and (2) they have a basis in scientific evidence, except as provided in Article 5.7(which deals with cases where there is insufficient scientific evidence). The study of European Food Safety Authority’s reasoned opinion on the review of existing MRLs for anthraquinone[3] concludes that  “Residues of anthraquinone are not expected to occur in any plant commodity or in any animal product because the pesticide use of anthraquinone is no longer authorized within the EU, no CXLs are available for this active substance and no uses authorized in third countries were notified to the RMS. A risk assessment is therefore in principle not required. Due to the lack of data regarding mammalian toxicology, plant and livestock metabolism and analytical methods of enforcement of residues, EFSA is however not in a position to recommend any enforcement measure for the potential illegal use of anthraquinone.” Based on the above, it can be gathered that the scientific evidence does not offer any conclusions with respect to the MRLs of 0.02 mg/kg on tea, hence, in this regard, India seeks information from EU on the study, scientific evidence based on which the MRL have been set at 0.02mg/kg for tea and how classification of Anthraquinone is necessary to protect human, animal or plant life. CONCLUSION: In view of the above, India requests EU to  share the scientific basis for setting up the MRLs at 0.02 MG/KG.share information on EU’s sampling and testing methodology for tea and international standards on which it is based.If the residue released on infusion is substantially limited, how does EU justify its measure with the specified MRLs on tea.***

StatementSubmitted: India reiterates its concern raised in the previous meeting on the basis for classifying anthraquinone as a pesticide is unknown and setting a maximum residue limit of 0.02 mg/kg for tea, mainly when it is a naturally occurring hydrocarbon and not an applied pesticide. The MRL of 0.02 mg/kg is too low and has greatly affected Indian tea exports to the European Union.The Working Group of the FAO-IGG on MRLs, in the Inter-Sessional Meeting of the Group at Sochi in May 2019 has shown utmost concern on the decisions by regulatory bodies regarding anthropogenic contamination like Anthraquinone that is not under the control of the Tea Industry and has felt the need for a global air transport study to investigate the possible sources of Anthraquinone contamination in tea. Accordingly, the Secretariat of FAO-IGG on Tea contracted the Max-Planck Institute für Meteorologie in order to study the effects of Anthraquinone contamination on tea production systems. Specifically, the Max-Planck team was tasked to look at the possible contamination of tea leaves resulting from the deposition of atmospheric Anthraquinone using a global chemical transport model that accounts for the emission, atmospheric transport, chemical transformation, and deposition of Anthraquinone on the surface. The results of this study were recently presented in a Webinar organized by FAO on March 31, 2022. The study has confirmed the atmospheric deposits as the major source of contamination of teas with Anthraquinone. Burning of fossil fuel and bio-wastes leads to the formation of Anthracene, a poly-aromatic hydrocarbon which is oxidized to Anthraquinone in the atmosphere and is deposited to the ground and foliage. Long-distance air transport of Anthraquinone mostly in a particulate state has also been clearly indicated in the study. For example, higher Anthraquinone concentration measured during winter in China could be explained by more coal and wood-burning for heating.One major conclusion from this study is that Anthraquinone deposit on tea leaves from atmospheric contamination is likely to cause a residue value higher than the EU MRL in certain tea-producing areas in the range of simulation parameters adopted in the work.Hence, in view of the above facts, the EU is requested to put on hold their proposed downward revision of the MRI- of Anthraquinone in tea.

StatementSubmitted:
Thank you, Chair.



	Canada agrees with the European Union that there are a number of naturally-occurring metals and other contaminants that may be of concern to human health when a certain level of exposure is reached.



	 The European Union’s implementation of hazard-based regulatory decision-making requirements under Regulation (EC) 1881/2006 concerning the maximum levels for certain contaminants in foodstuffs is leading to the revision of maximum levels (MLs) for contaminants found in many food products.
	Canada is concerned that the EU’s approach of lowering MLs does not appear to take into account consumption patterns and levels of dietary risk. 
	As a major agricultural producing nation, Canada is concerned that these new lower MLs will negatively impact trade for many products that Canadian producers currently export to the EU.  Or that the EU imports from Canada.



	 Canada is particularly concerned with the trade implications of the EU’s approach to the regulation of maximum levels of cadmium in cereals and pulses and oilseeds, ergot and ergot alkaloids in cereals, and hydrocyanic acid in linseed (flax).



	Firstly, regarding the EU’s proposed MLs for cadmium:



	Canada notes that the EU’s MLs for cadmium in certain foodstuffs do not align with the MLs established by the Codex Alimentarius Commission.



	Canada is concerned that these new requirements will have a negative impact on trade. Canada is a major exporter of cereals, pulses, flaxseed, mustard seed and canola and the EU is a major importer of these commodities.



	The immediate implementation of the lower MLs creates significant uncertainty for major grain suppliers and exporters serving the EU market and could affect market availability.



	Mitigation measures could include significantly higher levels of testing activities specifically for cadmium, in addition to segregation in the supply chain, raising the cost of grains destined for the EU.



	Canada requests that the EU extend the transition period until June 2022 to allow trading partners the necessary time to adjust and adapt - as feasible, recognizing that the majority of the determinants of cadmium levels are beyond the control of farmers.



	Canada has provided a detailed account of its concerns to the EU in a comment letter addressed to the EU WTO Enquiry Point, sent on May 14, 2021. Canada looks forward a response.



	Secondly, regarding the EU’s proposed MLs for ergot and ergot alkaloids: 



	Canada notes that the EU’s MLs for ergot in certain foodstuffs are half of the MLs established by Codex.



	Canada is concerned that the new MLs for ergot and ergot alkaloids found in cereals will have a negative impact on trade. 



	The EU is a major importer of the Canadian cereal products including barley, wheat, rye and oats that would be impacted by these new MLs. The immediate implementation of such MLs could affect market availability and prices of these commodities.
	 
	Canada requests further information from the EU on the scientific basis of the EU’s proposed MLs for ergot and ergot alkaloid as requested in our letter addressed to the EU WTO Enquiry Point, sent on June 11, 2021.



	To date, Codex has not set in place MLs for ergot alkaloids. Canada encourages the EU to delay the adoption of MLs for ergot alkaloids until the full report of the 91st meeting of Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA) is released. This will allow the EU to take into account the scientific information and assessment from the JECFA.



	Canada also notes that weather plays a significant role in the presence of ergot. Despite good agricultural practices, ergot and ergot alkaloids are found at detectable levels in nearly all export shipments of cereals.



	There will be substantial challenges with testing grain for ergot alkaloids if the ML is applied to exported raw grains and implemented as scheduled.



	Canada would like to emphasize that there are no commercially available simple tests for use in rapid screening of grain to help with ergot alkaloid management in the grain handling chain that have undergone inter-laboratory validation.



	Moreover, Canada highlights the need for a systematic and accurate sampling scheme for the assessment of ergot and ergot alkaloids in whole grain.



	Canada notes that the absence of appropriate sampling guidance increases the chance of creating a biased sample, and test results that do not represent the cargo.



	We would appreciate additional information on how the EU intends to apply a sampling scheme for ergot and ergot alkaloids, specifically in bulk grain shipments.



	Mitigation measures that will be required by industry could include significantly higher levels of testing activities specifically for ergot and ergot alkaloids, in addition to segregation in the supply chain, raising the cost of grains destined for the EU.



	Canada requests that the EU extend the transition period until September 2023 to allow trading partners the necessary time to review EU’s risk assessment and mitigation strategy and to adapt testing methodologies, if needed.



	Canada would like to once again stress that the majority of the determinants of ergot and ergot alkaloid levels are beyond the control of the farmer.



	Finally, regarding the EU’s proposed MLs for hydrocyanic acid:



	Canada’s understanding is that following an inconclusive study conducted by the European Food Safety Authority, the European Commission has convened a working group to set MLs for hydrocyanic acid in certain foodstuffs, however the decision has not been finalized.



	Canada requests an update concerning the EU’s deliberations on proposed MLs for hydrocyanic acid and when WTO Members will have an opportunity to provide comment, with a view of allowing the EU to take into accounts these comments.



	As the EU moves forward in discussing the MLs for hydrocyanic acid in flaxseed, Canada urges the EU take into account dietary risks and consumption patterns.



	 Canada also requests a response to the letter and scientific dossier regarding hydrocyanic acid in certain foodstuffs dated March 12, 2021. Canada hopes the EU will take into account the risks associated with hydrocyanic acid released from linseed.


 


	 In conclusion, Canada once again recalls that these substances are naturally occurring and that mitigation of MLs are extremely difficult, if not impossible to control.


 


	The immediate implementation of new and lower MLs creates significant uncertainty for major grain suppliers and exporters serving the EU market and could affect market availability and prices of these commodities. 


 


	Canada would like to underline the importance of providing significant advance notice between the adoption of regulations and entry into force, to enable industry sufficient time to adapt to any legislative and regulatory changes.


 


	Thank you, Chair.

In particular, Canada has requested that the European Union delay the entry into force of this measure, which will provide time for the European Union to consider the scientific review performed by Health Canada.Canada is optimistic that the current dialogue with the EU will continue to be productive and the EU will consider adjusting or removing the ML for hydrocyanic acid in food grade linseed (flaxseed) until further evidence is gathered.Finally, Canada stresses that transition periods for changes to MLs should be lengthened to two years at minimum to enable industry sufficient time to adapt to the changes.This will help to reduce the significant uncertainty for major grain suppliers and exporters serving the EU market and impacts on market availability created by the implementation of new and lower MLs.In the current global context where food security is of the utmost importance, Canada urges the EU to ensure that measures do not inadvertently restrict trade or impact supply chains for key staple commodities.We trust these comments will be taken into account in order to facilitate safe trade, and will welcome further technical discussion with the EU on this matter.Thank you, Chair.
Summary: Canada considered that the EU implementation of the precautionary-based regulatory decision-making requirements under Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006 was leading to the lowering of MLs for contaminants in many food products. Canada reiterated that the MLs did not align with international standards and would negatively impact trade for many products exported to the European Union. In particular, Canada was concerned with the negative trade implications of the EU approach to the regulation of MLs of cadmium in cereals, pulses and oilseeds; ergot and ergot alkaloids in cereals; ochratoxin A in cereals; and cyanogenic glycosides in linseed. Canada indicated that it had provided comments and a scientific review on a draft EU regulation notified to the WTO that cited new and lower MLs for hydrocyanic acid for certain food stuffs. Canada had requested the delay of the entry into force of the EU measure, and was optimistic that the European Union would consider adjusting or removing the MLs for hydrocyanic acid in food grade linseed until further evidence was available. Canada stressed that the transition periods for changes to MLs should be of a minimum of two years, to allow sufficient time for adaptation and reduce uncertainty amongst exporters. Canada welcomed further technical discussions with the European Union on this matter.

StatementSubmitted:
On March 5, 2020, EU notified the WTO of its proposal to amend the Regulation (EU) No 10/2011 on plastic materials and articles intended to come into contact with food?notification number: G/SPS/N/EU/372?. EU is the main export destination of China’s food contact products, and this regulation has had a great impact on China’s exporters. In order to meet the requirements, some Chinese enterprises reported that material costs of food contact products exported to EU increased by 20-35%, but quoted prices of the products only increased by 7%-10%, compared to the same period of 2020. Some companies abandon orders due to no profit or even loss. We understand the original intention of the EU to amend the regulation to protect consumer health. However, in accordance with the SPS Agreement, we have the following comments on this updated regulation:

1. Among ten newly added metals that have restrictions in Annex II of the regulation, lanthanum (La), europium (Eu), gadolinium (Gd) and terbium (Tb) are rare earth elements, the harm of which to the human body is only at the preliminary research stage. Based on the literature review, no report shows that the four elements (La, Eu, Gd, Tb) cause serious harm to the human body. Besides, primary aromatic amines that are listed in REACH should not be detected above 0.002 mg/kg and the total migration of ones that are not listed should be limited to a maximum of 0.01 mg/kg.

What is the basis for setting a total limit of 0.05mg/kg for europium, yttrium, lanthanum and terbium? Is the assessment of these four elements harmful to the human body adequate? What is the basis for setting a limit of primary aromatic amines to 0.002 mg/kg or 0.01mg/kg?

2. Compliance of migration from repeated use articles or materials in Annex V is debatable. Safety of food contact materials is mainly based on whether migration of harmful substances meets requirements of regulations and standards. It is inappropriate to regard certain repeated use articles or materials as non-compliance if the second and third migration test results of the articles or materials increase or fluctuate, even though all the results do not exceed the limit. Although the three migration test results are all below the limit, the product is deemed non-compliant for the results do not display a decreasing trend, regardless of effects from the material itself or the test method. It substantially restricts the placing of such products into the EU market.

What is the basis for verifying compliance according to the stability of the material or article from the first to the third migration test? Is it assessed sufficiently? It is suggested to take materials or articles with fluctuant migration test results into consideration and set allowable fluctuation range.

3. As lots of items are amended, like newly adding migration limit of ten mental elements, lowering the migration limit of primary aromatic amines by 5 times and specifying migration conditions and compliance of repeated use articles or materials, updating and testing products has produced massive expenses. Therefore, the price of products placed on the EU market increases, and consumers finally bear the extra costs. In addition, companies in various countries are currently severely affected by COVID-19 and large numbers of companies, especially MSMEs have operational difficulties. It is hoped that the EU will give a scientific and reasonable response to the above-mentioned comments put forward by China. Meanwhile, considering the great impacts of COVID-19, it is suggested that the EU assesses the effects of the amended regulation on production and trade and extend the transitional period.
Summary: China highlighted the large impact on its exporters of a proposal to amend the Regulation (EU) No 10/2011 on plastic materials and articles intended to come into contact with food, notified as G/SPS/N/EU/372. Firstly, China argued that the preliminary research on the four rare earth elements (lanthanum, europium, gadolinium and terbium) restricted in annex II of the Regulation had not reported serious harm to the human body, and questioned the basis for setting a total limit of 0.05 mg/kg for these elements. China also asked about the basis for setting a limit of primary aromatic amines that are listed in the REACH Regulation at 0.002 mg/kg, or for setting the total migration of ones at a maximum of 0.01 mg/kg.Secondly, China queried about the basis of verifying compliance of migration from repeated use articles or materials in annex V according to the stability of the material or article from the first to the third migration test, and whether it was suggested to take materials or articles with fluctuant migration test results into consideration and set allowable fluctuation range. Finally, China complained that the amendment of numerous items had led to large expenses due to updating and testing of products, ultimately borne by consumers. Numerous companies, especially MSMEs, were having operational difficulties due to COVID-19. China hoped that the European Union would provide a scientific and reasonable response to the above-mentioned comments and suggested that the European Union extend the transitional period of this regulation.

StatementSubmitted:
Brazil would like to bring to the attention of the SPS Committee the restriction it has been facing to export poultry to Chinese Taipei. Brazil believes that the Chinese Taipei's approach goes against the provisions of Article 5 of the SPS Agreement, as well as its Annex C.

It is our understanding that there has been undue delay by Chinese Taipei on performing the risk analysis for Brazilian poultry exports.

Let me start by mentioning that this sanitary negotiation has been going on for many years, and has intensified since 2016. However, it is still in its initial steps. The Chinese Taipei's risk analysis successively requires the exporter to provide answers to animal and public health questionnaires. Brazil has already provided these answers, however, repeated questions keep being asked to the Brazilian authorities, either about animal health (Newcastle disease) or about food safety.

Every time Brazil answers a question, Chinese Taipei takes several months to analyze and ends up coming back with further questions that could have been raised in the first round of questionnaires. This kind of action affects predictability and transparency. Therefore, Brazil would be thankful if Chinese Taipei could present a short timeframe for the next step to be taken.

We have been trying to engage bilaterally with Chinese Taipei authorities, both through our capitals and at the margins of the SPS Committee, but these talks have not helped to accelerate the process. Despite all the information shared and our technical experts´ openness to engage fruitfully with Chinese Taipei`s authorities, there is no sign of predictability as to when this first stage of the negotiations will be concluded.
Summary: Brazil brought to the Committee's attention the restrictions faced by its poultry exports to Chinese Taipei which, in its view, constituted a violation of Article 5 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement. Brazil considered that there had been undue delays in Chinese Taipei's risk analysis for Brazilian poultry exports and noted that sanitary negotiations had been ongoing for many years. Despite answers provided by Brazil on several occasions, Chinese Taipei continued to ask questions about animal health of food safety, which affected predictability and transparency. Brazil requested Chinese Taipei to present a short timeframe for the next step. Brazil regretted that bilateral engagement had failed to accelerate negotiations and the lack of predictability as to when this first stage of the negotiations would be concluded.

StatementSubmitted:
As previously stated, Brazil would like to bring to the attention of the SPS Committee the restrictions it has been facing to export poultry and beef to Chinese Taipei. Brazil believes that their approach goes against the provisions of Article 5 of the SPS Agreement, as well as its Annex C.

As we will further develop in this intervention, it is our understanding that there has been undue delay by Chinese Taipei on performing the risk analysis for Brazilian poultry exports.

Let me start by recalling that this sanitary negotiation has been going on for many years, and has intensified since 2016. However, the procedures are still on their initial steps. The Chinese Taipei risk analysis requires the exporter to provide answers to animal and public health questionnaires. Brazil has already provided these answers; however, repeated questions are still being asked to the Brazilian authorities, either in relation to animal health (Newcastle disease) or in relation to food security.

Our previous Committee Meeting, in July, we also brought to Members` attention that, in addition to poultry, Chinese Taipei`s procedures have also been restricting access to our beef exports. In both cases, there is a pattern of systematic undue delays, keeping the market closed, without scientific justification.

We have been trying to engage bilaterally with Chinese Taipei authorities, both through our capitals and on the margins of the SPS Committee, but these talks have not helped to accelerate the process. In spite of all the information shared and our technical experts' openness to engage fruitfully with Chinese Taipei's authorities, there is no sign of predictability as to when this first stage of the negotiations will effectively be concluded.
Summary: Brazil considered restrictions on poultry and beef imports to Chinese Taipei to be at odds with Article 5 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement. Brazil lamented of undue delays in the risk analysis process for poultry, despite having provided the necessary information. In its view, beef exports were also facing undue delays and market access restrictions, without scientific justification. Brazil urged Chinese Taipei to be more transparent and predictable in its approval procedures and indicated its openness to providing any information scientifically necessary to accelerate the risk analysis process.

StatementSubmitted:
Brazil would like to bring to the attention of the SPS Committee the restrictions it has been facing to export bovine meat, pet food and other by-products of animal origin to South Africa.

Regarding bovine meat with bone and offal, Brazil has requested that South Africa lift its restrictions to our exports. In October 2020 the South African authorities demanded that Brazil presented further information in order to perform a risk assessment on foot-and-mouth disease. Although the Brazilian authorities have already provided all the required information, no reaction has been received.

As for by-products of animal origin, in July 2017, Brazil proposed a model of International Sanitary Certificate to South African authorities. So far, our authorities have not received any reply whatsoever.
The same has happened to our request on pet food, for which we have presented an updated proposal of International Sanitary Certificate in August 2019. Yet again, there was no reaction by South African
authorities.

It is also worth noting that Brazil has repeatedly tried to engage bilaterally with South Africa on these issues, without any progress or sign of predictability.

Brazil understands that such restrictions reinforced by South Africa`s attitude towards our exports of bovine meat, pet food and other by-products of animal origin are in conflict with the dispositions of SPS
Agreement, especially article 2, 5, 8 and its Annex C.
Summary: Brazil informed the Committee of the import restrictions imposed by South Africa on several products. Concerning bovine meat with bone and offal, no response had been received after Brazil had provided information requested by South Africa to perform a risk assessment on foot-and-mouth disease (FMD). Concerning by-products of animal origin and pet food, Brazil was still waiting for a response to the models of international sanitary certificate that it had proposed in 2017 and 2019, respectively. In Brazil's view, South Africa's unresponsiveness was in violation of Articles 2, 5, 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement.

StatementSubmitted:
Brazil would like to bring to the attention of the SPS Committee the restriction it has been facing to export several products to Nigeria, which range from meat, pork and poultry to genetic material. To be more
specific, Nigerian authorities have not provided any response at all to Brazil´s proposals of sanitary and zoosanitary certifications.

There is a list of sanitary certification proposals that have not been answered.
In August 2016 and August 2017, we proposed to Nigerian authorities models of sanitary certifications for live bubaline and bovine;
In March 2018 we proposed to Nigerian authorities models of sanitary certifications for genetic material for bovine and bubaline.
In June 2018, we proposed to Nigerian authorities models of sanitary certifications for beef, pork and poultry.
In July 2019 we proposed to Nigerian authorities models of sanitary certifications for hatching eggs and day old poultry;
In September 2019, we proposed to Nigerian authorities models of sanitary certifications for milk and dairy products; and
In January 2020, we proposed to Nigerian authorities models of sanitary certifications for dried bovine skin.
 

Since our first proposal of sanitary certification, in 2016, Brazil has been trying to engage bilaterally with Nigeria both through our capital, as well as on the margins of the SPS Committee. Despite these attempts, Nigeria has turned out to be unresponsive.

Brazil understands that such an attitude by Nigerian authorities is clearly in conflict with the principles of SPS Agreement, especially articles 2, 5, 8 and its Annex C.
Summary: Brazil referred to import restrictions imposed by Nigeria on several products and regretted the lack of response to its proposals of sanitary certifications for live bubaline and bovine; genetic material for bovine and bubaline; beef, pork and poultry; hatching eggs and day-old poultry; milk and dairy products; and dried bovine skin. In Brazil's view, Nigeria's unresponsiveness was in violation of Articles 2, 5 and 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement.Brazil clarified that this STC related to the negotiation of sanitary certificates and the undue delays in approval procedures, which was an SPS issue.

StatementSubmitted: Once again, Brazil raises this STC about Nigeria's lack of response to Brazilian proposals for sanitary certifications for buffaloes and live cattle; genetic material for cattle and buffaloes; beef, pork, and poultry meat; hatching eggs and day-old chickens; milk and dairy products, and also lack of information regarding the requirements for exporting dry bovine skin. As you can see, this STC is uncommon, since it involves many different products, which seems to indicate there is a systemic, procedural issue with Nigeria’s treatment of SPS requests. We raised this STC for the first time during the 80th Regular Meeting of this Committee. Unfortunately, a satisfactory resolution within the scope of the SPS Committee remains pending.  Despite several attempts to obtain reaction to Brazilian proposals, including a bilateral meeting in March 2021, the filing of this STC in July 2021, and addressing this same topic in other fora at the WTO, it was not possible to move forward with the procedural issues that led to the re-submission of this STC at this meeting.  Brazil was surprised by the Nigerian statement in response to this STC in its last presentation, when Nigeria reported that the issues raised by Brazil would not be within the scope of the SPS Committee. Furthermore, Nigeria added that it would have no obligation to negotiate sanitary certificate proposals sent by a member of this Organization. However, it is clearly an obligation, set forth on the principle of non-discrimination. In Brazil's view, Nigeria's lack of response to the Brazilian proposals disregards Articles 2, 5, and 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement. Since the Nigerian response to the last submission of this STC, we now understand there is also lack of compliance with Article 7, concerning transparency and exchange of information between Members.  In this sense, with this further attempt, Brazil expects to receive responses from Nigeria regarding pending proposals for sanitary certificates, as well as information on health requirements for the export of dry bovine skin.
Summary: Brazil regretted the lack of responses and information by Nigeria regarding this STC affecting many different products, which had been raised in several WTO fora. Brazil disagreed with Nigeria's previous indications that the issue was not within the scope of the SPS Committee and that it would have no obligation to negotiate sanitary certificate proposals sent by a WTO Member, since it believed this was an obligation set forth on the principle of non-discrimination. In Brazil's view, Nigeria's lack of response disregarded Articles 2, 5, 7 and 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement. Brazil hoped to receive responses from Nigeria regarding pending proposals for sanitary certificates, as well as information on health requirements for the export of dry bovine skin.Brazil considered that the SPS Committee was the appropriate forum to address Nigeria's lack of response on its proposals for buffalo, live cattle, genetic material, beef, pork, poultry meat, hatching eggs and day-old chickens. Brazil would continue to try to engage bilaterally with Nigeria and would continue raising this concern with a view to finding a solution on this issue.

StatementSubmitted: For the 4th time, Brazil raises this STC about Nigeria's lack of response to Brazilian proposals for sanitary certifications for beef, pork, and poultry; buffaloes and live cattle; genetic material for cattle, poultry, and buffaloes; hatching eggs and day-old chickens; milk and dairy products; and also lack of information regarding the requirements for exporting dry bovine skin. Brazil submitted proposals more than two years agoBrazil took note of Nigeria's statement mentioning that it is restricting imports of some goods, due to economic restrictions. Among other reasons, Nigeria has mentioned that it is imposing restrictions to safeguard its balance of payments, an issue that is out of the scope of this Committee. However, we need to reiterate that Brazil's request concerns the lack of responses to sanitary certificate proposals and, therefore, falls within the scope of the SPS Committee. Nigeria has recognized that its sanitary authorities are analyzing these proposals, so it has already acknowledged that this STC was raised in the correct forum.Despite several attempts to obtain a reaction to Brazilian proposals, both in Abuja as in Geneva, in the SPS Committee, as well as in the Council for Trade in Goods (CTG), it was not possible to move forward with the procedural issues that led to the re-submission of this STC at this meeting.With this further attempt, Brazil expects to receive responses from Nigeria regarding pending proposals for sanitary certificates for the aforementioned products, as well as information on health requirements for the export of dry bovine skin.
Summary: Brazil regretted the lack of responses from Nigeria regarding proposals for sanitary certifications for certain products and lack of information regarding requirements for exporting dry bovine skin. Noting Nigeria's statement in a previous Committee meeting that import restrictions were due to economic reasons, Brazil emphasized that its request concerned lack of responses to sanitary certificate proposals and, therefore, fell within the scope of the SPS Committee. Brazil submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2116.Brazil took note that Nigerian authorities were analysing its proposals for sanitary certificates, which Brazil reiterated were issues within the scope of the SPS Committee. Brazil also emphasized that it was raising concerns about transparency, avoiding undue delays, and the timely analysis of proposals, all of which related to SPS approval procedures. Brazil stood ready to continue the bilateral dialogue with Nigeria.

StatementSubmitted: For the fifth time, Brazil raises this STC about Nigeria's lack of response to Brazilian proposals for sanitary certifications for beef, pork, and poultry; buffaloes and live cattle; genetic material for cattle, poultry, and buffaloes; hatching eggs and day-old chickens; milk and dairy products; and lack of information regarding the requirements for exporting dry bovine skin.Brazil has taken note of Nigeria's statement during the 85th regular meeting of this committee. On that occasion, Nigeria mentioned that there could be no violation of articles 2, 5, 7, and 8, as well as Annex C of the SPS Agreement. We would like to clarify this issue, as we believe that Nigeria is not complying with these articles.First, we would like to reiterate that Brazil's request concerns the lack of responses to sanitary certificate proposals and, therefore, falls within the scope of the SPS Committee, according to Article 2.2 of the SPS Agreement. Nigeria has recognized that its sanitary authorities are analyzing these proposals, so it has already acknowledged that this STC was raised in the correct forum. When Nigeria takes an unreasonable time to analyze these proposals without proper scientific basis, it is not complying with the SPS Agreement.Second, we would like to highlight that, by not giving Brazil any information about the completeness of the sanitary certificate proposals sent, Nigeria does not comply with Article 8 and Annex C, article 1, points (a) and (b) of the Agreement. We have continuously been asking for reactions from Nigeria both through our Embassy in Abuja and here in Geneva, and we are still hopeful we can make progress with this issue. However, the continuous lack of response indicates that Nigeria is not complying with Article 7 and Annex B, article 3, point (c)of the Agreement, which state that members must be transparent about the application of its internal regulations and be open to answering questions about how it is determining its appropriate level of sanitary protection (ALOP).Third, as we have mentioned the ALOP, we also would like to know if there is any scientific reason for the delay in analyzing our proposals. If there is none, we believe that Nigeria is also not complying with Article 5 of the Agreement, as it is restricting trade with a partner without relevant scientific justification, taking into account risk assessment techniques.To conclude, Brazil still expects Nigeria can send responses regarding pending proposals for sanitary certificates for the aforementioned products, as well as information on sanitary requirements for the export of dry bovine skin.We also remain open to engaging with Nigeria in a fruitful bilateral dialogue so we can make progress in this issue, in a transparent manner, by harmonizing the need for compliance with the SPS Agreement with any difficulties that Nigeria may be facing.
Summary: Brazil regretted the lack of responses from Nigeria regarding proposals for sanitary certifications for certain products and the lack of information regarding requirements for exporting dry bovine skin. Brazil was of the view that Nigeria's requirements were in violation of Articles 2, 5, 7, and 8, as well as Annexes B and C to the SPS Agreement, and sought clarification on Nigeria's statement in a previous Committee meeting. Brazil asked Nigeria to provide answers regarding the pending proposals as well as information on sanitary requirements for the export of dry bovine skin. Brazil remained open to bilateral discussions with Nigeria.

Australia recognises and respects China’s right to undertake import checks at the border to ensure imports meet biosecurity and food safety conditions, and to take reasonable action where there is a necessity to protect human, animal or plant life health.

However, such arrangements including inspection and border clearance procedures should be consistent with Members’ SPS Agreement obligations, including that they are risk based and not more trade restrictive than necessary. Members also have obligations to be transparent about the measures they are imposing, and – except in urgent circumstances – to allow a reasonable interval between their publication and their entry into force so that Members can become acquainted with them.

Australia considers that China’s increased import check are constraining its exports and requests that China explain the reasons for these measures as required under Article 5.8.

Over the past 12 months Australia has seen an increased amount of import clearance interventions on Australian agricultural products by China that appears targeted at product of Australian origin, without any prior notification and justification. It has also not occurred in a way that would have prevented loss of shipments due to lack of ability to manage holding conditions (such as temperature control for perishable goods).

Further, on advising Australia of detected non-compliances, China has not provided full detail on their findings, such as testing regime and methodologies.  Australia also considers China’s response on non-compliances have not been proportionate to the potential risks posed. China has not responded to Australia’s proposals for enhanced measures or corrective actions to be taken and China has not considered valid alternative approaches to ensure their import conditions have been met.

 For example:


	China introduced new inspection and testing requirements for Australian live rock lobster without any prior notification, preventing exporters from making arrangements to avoid spoilage and severe losses from lengthy holding periods while testing and border clearance was completed
	
		China has also not responded to Australia’s investigation report or proposals for alternative approaches to border testing such as pre-export testing and monitoring that would remove the need for lengthy delays on arrival in China.
	
	


  


	China has not responded to Australia’s investigation findings and proposal for enhanced measures following China’s suspension of timber log imports from all Australian states
	
		China has not provided sufficient evidence to justify the suspension as proportionate to the risk
		While Australia has formally responded to China, proposing stronger fumigation processes and closer technical engagement, China has not engaged with Australia on the non-compliances or on a way forward.
		 
	
	
	China has increased inspection rates, testing and document verification for Australian wheat, barley, canola and oats without prior notice and justification. Inspection rates have increased from a low level, random monitoring to a very high level with no reasonable justification for the increased import checks  
	
		Australia requested China provide information on their sampling, inspection procedures and identification methodologies. No response has been received.
		Australian considers these grains shipments were compliant with thresholds set out in the Australian Grain Industry Management Plan agreed with China and or import permits. 
	
	


 


	China has reportedly increased inspection rates on shipments of several Australian horticulture products including table grapes, leading to clearance delays at some ports in China. China has not provided any official notification of changes to import conditions.
	 



	Finally, China has without prior notice, increased inspection and laboratory testing of imports of Australian bottled wine, bulk wine and sparkling wine, leading to significant delays to the border clearance of these products.
	
		Typical food additives or MRL testing should take approximately 2 weeks to report whereas Australian wine has taken in some cases up to 6 weeks or more to clear the border and without clear reasons for the delays. There has been no reasonable explanation provided by Chinese authorities for the necessity for increased inspection, testing and border delays despite our ongoing efforts to engage Chinese authorities.
	
	


Australia takes all detections of non-compliance seriously and initiates investigations into their cause.  Australia has strong biosecurity and food safety systems and the compliance and safety of our products are recognised internationally. Australia is concerned the cumulative impact of these measures, their sudden increase in intensity over the past 18 months, the disproportionate impact of these measures on Australia, the lack of transparency and justification on the introduction of these measures and China’s public statements linking trade with unrelated issues in our relationship give rise to concerns about China’s adherence to the letter and spirit of its international trade obligations.

Australia continues to treat these issues on their technical merits. We have sought to address them bilaterally with relevant Chinese authorities.  Australia has made a number of technical submissions to China seeking to address China’s concerns, including provision of investigation reports for all alleged non-compliances and proposing enhanced measures to address reported non-compliances to ensure our trade meets China’s import requirements. However, many of these submissions have gone unanswered and we are disappointed with China’s lack of response to our efforts to re-instate trade.

We once again ask China to:


	respond to the submission of non-compliance investigation reports;
	respond to Australia’s reasonable requests for information on China’s inspection and testing requirements; and
	implement changes to inspection and testing requirements in a timely, transparent, non-discriminatory and predictable manner, consistent with China’s WTO obligations.


 Australia would welcome bilateral engagement on these matters by China.
Summary: Australia stated that China's arrangements to undertake import checks at the border, including inspection and border clearance procedures, should be risk-based, not more trade-restrictive than necessary, transparent and allow a reasonable interval between their publication and entry into force. Australia complained about the increased amount of import clearance interventions targeted at Australian agricultural products, without prior notification. China had not provided detailed information on detections of non-compliances in Australian products and had not considered proposed valid alternative approaches to ensure compliance. Australia presented several examples of increased requirements and lack of responses by China that had led to delays and losses. Australia asked China to respond to its requests for information and implement changes to inspection and testing requirements in a timely, transparent, non-discriminatory and predictable manner. Australia said that it would welcome bilateral engagement on these matters.

Australia stated that China's increased inspections and testing measures at the border had constrained trade of several agricultural commodities including rock lobster, wine, wheat, barley, oats, canola, logs and table grapes. Australia stressed that the measures had been initiated without prior notice, were arbitrary and did not appear to be based on scientific evidence. China had not provided detailed information on detections of non-compliances in Australian products and had not engaged with Australia on proposed corrective approaches to ensure compliance. Australia would welcome bilateral engagement on these matters, and asked China to respond to its requests for information, to provide details for its inspection and testing measures, and to engage with Australia on its proposals.Australia clarified it had provided information outlining its food safety and biosecurity system and was awaiting a response from China on investigations following non-compliance reports.

Recalling the obligations in Article 5.8 of the SPS Agreement, Australia remained concerned with China's increased inspections and testing measures at the border which had been initiated without prior notice, did not appear to be based on scientific evidence and had led to trade constraints across a range of agricultural products. Australia would welcome bilateral engagement on these matters, and urged China to respond to its requests for information, provide details of its inspection and testing measure and engage with Australia on its proposals.Australia clarified it had provided information outlining its food safety and biosecurity system and was awaiting a response from China on investigations following non-compliance reports. Australia regretted that China had not engaged with Australia on these investigations, and that technical submissions had not yet been answered.

StatementSubmitted: Further to previous statements made in the SPS Committee on this issue.  Australia remains deeply concerned over the increased intervention on imported products at China’s border that has been initiated without warning or communication and without science-based consideration of SPS risks associated with the product. The lack of notice of China’s actions at the border has prevented exporters from making necessary holding arrangements, which are particularly important for perishable goods. China’s actions have also led to delays and significantly constrained trade across a range of agricultural commodities.   Despite repeated requests, China still has not provided evidence to support these actions. Australia requests that agricultural imports into China continue in a predictable and transparent manner, without undue delays in inspection procedures and that import controls and measures are applied in a way proportionate to the risk, consistent with Members’ obligations.  Australia requests that when China makes substantive changes to its regulations – including when regulations are extended to cover new products, or where domestic standards are applied instead of previously applied import standards – that it makes these changes transparent by notifying this Committee.  Australia again repeats its call for China to:  respond to Australia’s requests for information on China’s import inspection and testing requirements;   provide Australia with details of its inspection and testing measures and explain to Australia its reasons for imposing each measure; and  engage with Australia on our proposals—including responding to our submissions and investigation reports addressing China’s concerns. As we have said previously, Australia would welcome bilateral engagement on these matters, including the exchange of information between our regulators. Australia stands ready to work collaboratively with China to resolve problems or misunderstandings so that trade can promptly resume.
Summary: Australia remained concerned with China's increased intervention on imported products at the border without prior notice, which did not appear to be based on scientific evidence and had led to trade constraints across a range of agricultural products. Australia requested China to ensure that agricultural imports continued in a transparent manner and without undue delays in inspection procedures and to notify changes to its measures, which should be applied in a manner proportionate to the risk. Australia would welcome bilateral engagement on these matters, and urged China to respond to its requests for information, to provide details of its inspection and testing measure, and to engage with Australia on its proposals.In response to China, Australia clarified it was awaiting an answer from China on investigations following non-compliance reports. Australia was looking forward to continuing bilateral dialogue and emphasized the absence of feedback from China.

StatementSubmitted: Further to previous statements made in the SPS Committee on this issue. Australia remains concerned over the inconsistent intervention on imported products at China’s border that continue without science-based consideration of the associated SPS risks. China’s actions have led to delays and constrained trade across a range of important – and sometimes perishable – agricultural commodities. Australia requests that agricultural imports into China continue in a predictable and transparent manner, without undue delays in inspection procedures and that import controls and other measures are applied in a way proportionate to the risk, consistent with Members’ obligations commensurate with the risk. As we have stated on four occasions previously, Australia would welcome bilateral engagement on these matters.Australia stands ready to work collaboratively and constructively with China to resolve problems or misunderstandings so that normal trade can resume promptly.
Summary: Australia remained concerned with China's increased intervention on imported products at the border, which appeared to lack science-based consideration of the associated SPS risks and had led to trade constraints across a range of agricultural products. Australia requested China to ensure that agricultural imports continued in a predictable and transparent manner and without undue delays, and to apply measures in a manner proportionate to the risk. Australia would welcome bilateral engagement on these matters, and stood ready to collaborate with China towards resumption of trade.In response to China, Australia underlined its strong food safety and biosecurity systems and clarified it was awaiting an answer from China on investigations following non-compliance reports. Australia was looking forward to continuing bilateral dialogue and regretted the absence of feedback from China.

India expressed its concern regarding the Russian Federation's classification of tea as fruits and vegetables, which had resulted in requirements of higher levels of mould parameters (103 KOE per gram). India considered this measure to be inconsistent with international standards, as these did not apply mould parameters to bulk tea and tea products. India recalled the provisions of Articles 3.3 and 5.6 of the SPS Agreement and highlighted the need for a scientific justification or a risk assessment for SPS measures deviating from international standards. India requested the Russian Federation to provide the scientific justification for the classification of tea as fruits and vegetables, and the risk assessment done to define higher standards of mould parameters. India considered the measure to be more trade-restrictive than necessary to achieve the appropriate level of protection (ALOP).India looked forward to engaging further with the Russian Federation on this matter.

StatementSubmitted: The Russian Federation's classification of tea as "fruits and vegetables" (ID 525)In the previous SPS meetings, India raised the concern of the Russian Federations' classification of tea as "fruits and vegetables", resulting in requirements of higher levels of mould parameters (103 KOE per gram). We thank Russia for their interim reply and await a complete response to the concern raised.India's concern also referred to Articles 3.3 and 5.6 of the SPS Agreement and highlighted the need for a scientific justification or a risk assessment for SPS measures deviating from international standards. India requested the Russian Federation to provide the scientific rationale for classifying tea as fruits and vegetables and the risk assessment to define higher mould parameters standards. India considered the measure to be more trade-restrictive than necessary to achieve the appropriate level of protection (ALOP).India reiterates its concern.It is scientifically proven that mould is not dangerous to human health per se, but the possibility of certain mycotoxins being produced in certain conditions matters. One such important product is "Aflatoxin B1".   While stringent control measures relating to  direct safety criteria  of the Aflatoxin B1 are in  place in Russia, the same stringent measures are imposed on the indirect agent, i.e. "Mould."Such a practice seriously affects tea exports from India to Russia since some of the teas accepted as entirely safe for the rest of the world become prohibitive for Russia. India considers the measure to be more trade-restrictive than necessary to achieve the appropriate level of protection (ALOP). Hence, India yet again requests Russia to either share the risk assessment done to define higher standards of mould parameters or withdraw the measure.
Summary: India raised its concern regarding the Russian Federation's classification of tea as "fruits and vegetables", which had resulted in higher levels of mould parameters. Referring to Articles 3.3 and 5.6 of the SPS Agreement, India highlighted the need for a scientific justification or a risk assessment for SPS measures deviating from international standards, and asked the Russian Federation to provide the scientific rationale for classifying tea as fruits and vegetables and the risk assessment to define higher mould parameters standards. India also considered the measure to be more trade-restrictive than necessary to achieve the ALOP. India thanked the Russian Federation for its interim reply and looked forward to a complete response on the concern raised.

StatementSubmitted: India reiterates its concern raised in the previous meetings and the statements made. India  acknowledges the documents presented by the Russian Federation bilaterally regarding this concern, particularly the scientific justification for imposing such a measure. However, India notes these documents are in the Russian language; hence the Russian Federation is requested to provide an English version of the document for examination.
Summary: India indicated that it had received documents in Russian, which were under examination in its capital.India looked forward to receiving the English version of the documents.

StatementSubmitted: In response to India's request, Russia shared the translated version of the study it referred to in its reply to India STC raised previously in the SPS committee. India thanks Russia for sharing this translated version of the study.  It is observed that the sample size in the Russian study is very small to arrive at any scientific conclusion. Since Tea is not consumed directly but rather taken after brewing in hot water, the chances of such contamination in the end product are apparently much less.  Hence, India reiterates its concern about Tea not being a perishable commodity like fruits and vegetables. Russia has classified it under the category of "Fruits & Vegetables" with the application of a higher level of mould parameters (103 KOE/gm). Such strict control on mycotoxins, namely 'Aflotoxin B1', forces to subject Tea through extra layers of control, resulting in increased cost of exports. The mould parameters are not only included in the norms but also kept at much higher levels than the EU levels. It's a well-established matter that many countries don't apply mould parameters to bulk teas and tea products. In light of this understanding, Russia is requested to remove the classification of Tea from being under 'fruits and vegetables and consequentially prevent the application of higher levels of mould parameters.
Summary: Thanking Russia for sharing the translated version of the documentation requested, India observed that the sample size used in the study was too small to allow for scientific conclusions. Since tea was brewed in hot water, the contamination in the end product would apparently be lower than in products consumed directly. India noted that the classification of tea as fruits and vegetables, with the application of higher levels of mould parameters, led to stricter controls on mycotoxins, namely aflatoxin B1, that resulted in increased export costs. India asked Russia to remove tea from the classification as fruits and vegetables, and consequentially prevent the application of higher levels of mould parameters.

The Korean government would like to raise a concern over the delayed progress in import approval of Samgyetang, Korean ginseng chicken soup, for entry into the EU market.

Since 1996, Korea has taken required steps for market access of heat-treated poultry meat products. But, despite the 25 years of efforts, the EU has not completed the import approval process.

Korea has provided data in response to the four-times of EU’s correction requests on the National Residue Program (NRP) report following on-site inspection conducted by the EU. And in April 2020, the EU notified that it would proceed with the next steps for gaining market access as all of the EU recommendations on residue control of Samgyetang have been satisfactorily addressed. However, to date, it has not approved the import.

Moreover, regarding the eight Korean establishments which were listed on the European Union website in October 2020 as third country establishments, EU unilaterally notified in June 2021 that the listing was an administrative error. And to date, the EU has not provided time frame of the Member States’ voting procedure, the information which Korea requested various times in bilateral meetings including the one held during the last WTO SPS Committee meeting.

We believe that this undue delay would constitute a violation of Article 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement, which are about control, inspection and approval procedures.

Korea is highly concerned about this unnecessary delay in import approval, and urges the EU, once again, to swiftly take up the remaining procedure of the import approval and to inform the Korean government of the time frame.
Summary: Korea expressed concerns on import approval delays imposed by the European Union regarding Korean chicken soup Samgyetang. According to Korea, the European Union had conducted an onsite inspection and had subsequently received all the data requested on the National Residue Programme report. Despite the indications by the European Union that it would proceed with the next steps for granting market access for Samgyetang, and the listing of eight Korean establishments as third country establishments, no information had been provided on timeframes of the EU member States' voting procedure. In Korea's views, the EU delays in import approvals were a violation of Article 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement. Korea urged the European Union to complete the procedure and to provide information on the timeframes.
