StatementSubmitted: ? Korea reiterates our concern over the delayed import authorization of Samgyetang to the European Union. ? Since 1996, the Korean government has taken numerous actions to comply with the EU’s requests, such as receiving approval of Korea’s National Residue Program (NRP) from the EU, coordinating on-site inspections, and submitting supplementary documents to gain Samgyetang’s approval into the EU market. Finally, in April 2020, the EU announced its plan to carry out follow-up procedures for import authorization after receiving the risk assessment results. However, import authorization of Samgyetang is still not approved.? This undue delay in import authorization of Samgyetang constitutes a violation of Article 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement (Control, Inspection, and Approval Procedures).? Korea had previously raised this issue through bilateral channels such as FTA and WTO SPS Committee meetings. Though the EU stated that it would extensively discuss this matter with Korea bilaterally at the previous meeting in March, we still have not received any updates on the progress or schedule concerning the import approval process of Samgyetang.? Korea is highly concerned about this unnecessary delay in import approval and urges the EU, once again, to swiftly take up the remaining procedure of the import approval and to inform the Korean government of the time frame.
Summary: Korea expressed concerns on import approval delays imposed by the European Union on Korean chicken soup Samgyetang. Korea regretted that, despite the numerous actions it had taken to comply with EU requests, it had still not received approval for imports. In Korea's views, the EU delays in import approvals were a violation of Article 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement. Korea urged the European Union to complete the procedure and to provide information on the timeframes.

StatementSubmitted: ? 26 years have passed since Korea requested the European Union’s import authorization of Samgyetang, and to this end, Korea reiterates our concerns over the European Union’s delayed authorization.? Since 1996, the Korean government has strived to comply with the EU’s requests, such as receiving approval of Korea’s National Residue Program (NRP) from the EU, coordinating on-site inspections, and submitting supplementary documents. Moreover, Korea has been providing the results of our residue monitoring plan of the previous year and also the plans for the current years to the EU, including this year’s. Korea has been sharing such information every year despite lack of progress in the EU’s import authorization for Samgyetang.? At the 10th EU-Korea FTA Committee on Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures held on November 25, 2021, the EU provided a response to Korea that they do not have additional requests to make considering the on-site inspection results conducted in 2018 and that the EU is consulting with Member States about listing Korean establishments approved for export? However, Korea is yet to receive specific information such as progress being made within the EU and future timelines.? This undue delay in import authorization of Samgyetang is a practice that is not aligned with Article 8 and Annex C (Control, Inspection, and Approval Procedures) of the WTO SPS Agreement.? Korea is highly concerned about this unnecessary delay and urges the EU, once again, to swiftly proceed with the remaining import approval procedures and to inform the Korean government of the time frame so as to promote mutual benefit.
Summary: Korea expressed concerns about import approval delays imposed by the European Union on Korean chicken soup Samgyetang. Despite the numerous actions taken to comply with EU requests, Korea had still not received approval for imports. In its view, the EU delays in import approvals were a violation of Article 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement. Korea urged the European Union to complete the procedure and to provide information on the timeframes.

StatementSubmitted: ? The Republic of Korea reiterates our concerns over the fact that the import authorization procedure of Samgyetang to the EU has been stalled for 27 years. ? Since 1996, the Korean government has put efforts into this import authorization procedure by coordinating on-site inspections for the approval of Korea’s National Residue Program (NRP) and submitting supporting documents as per the EU’s requests. Even though, any notable progress in Samgyetang import authorization procedure has not been made, Korea has continued to submit the NRP results of the previous year and plan for the current year to the EU, and as usual, Korea will submit this year’s NRP to the EU. ? StatementSubmitted:
The European Union raises its concerns about Qatar's new import rules for dairy products for the first time in this Committee.
	The European Union refers to the Qatar’s Ministry of Public Health Circular of 30 May 2019 establishing new import requirements for UHT milk and white cheese that entered into force the following day, on 1 June 2019. The EU raised Specific Trade Concerns against Qatar on this measure already in the TBT Committee at several occasions.
	More recently, Qatar’s Council of Ministers instructions were issued on 22 August 2021 affecting imports of dairy products. These instructions expanded further the scope of dairy products covered under the Circular issued in 2019 and the trade restrictive measures cover now nearly all dairy products.
	The EU regrets that Qatar did NOT notify any of these measures to the WTO, under neither the TBT nor the SPS Agreements.
	The EU would like to recall that the measure of 2019 is now in place for over 2 years without any clarity provided by Qatar on when this measure will be lifted. Furthermore, the new measures issued since August 2021 creates additional barriers to a wider range of dairy products impacting thus even more negatively on EU exported dairy products to Qatar.
	Therefore, the implementation of these rules are considered more trade disruptive than necessary, as compliance with these requirements is not feasible for a wide range of cheeses and milk products exported from the EU to Qatar.
	The EU is particularly concerned about the stringent restrictions on the shelf life that disadvantage imported products in comparison to local products, but also about certain product characteristics for milk products and cheeses, in particular the obligatory addition of vitamins to milk and low-fat-only requirements for certain cheeses.
	These requirements are not in line with CODEX Alimentarius relevant international standards, are not science-based and are not required to guarantee the safety of imported products. The measures therefore appear to be more trade restrictive than necessary to fulfil the legitimate objective of public health protection. In this context, the EU would like in particular to refer to Articles 2.2, 2.3, 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 5.4 and 5.6 of the WTO SPS Agreement.
	The EU urges Qatar to suspend the application of both measures without further delay, align it to the WTO rules and comply with its notification obligations.
	The EU would like to thank Qatar for bilateral exchanges during the past months, which unfortunately have not yet resulted in an effective solution. The EU is prepared to continue work constructively with Qatar to resolve this important issue.
Summary: The European Union expressed its concerns regarding Qatar's new trade-restrictive import rules for dairy products, previously raised in the TBT Committee. Qatar's Ministry of Public Health Circular established new import requirements for UHT milk and white cheese, and the instructions issued by Qatar's Council of Ministers expanded the range of dairy products covered under the Circular, creating additional barriers to EU products. The European Union noted that none of the measures had been notified under SPS nor the TBT Agreements. In particular, the European Union was concerned by the stringent restrictions on the shelf-life, as well as about certain product characteristics for milk products and cheeses, which it considered to be more trade-restrictive than necessary, not based on science, not in line with Codex international standards and not required to guarantee the safety of imported products. In the EU view, Qatar's measures violated several provisions in Articles 2 and 5 of the SPS Agreement. The European Union urged Qatar to suspend the application of both measures and to comply with its WTO notification obligations. The European Union thanked Qatar for the bilateral exchanges and expressed intention to continue the constructive dialogue.

StatementSubmitted: ·    The European Union would like to refer to the Qatar’s Ministry of Public Health Circular of 30 May 2019 establishing new import requirements for UHT milk and white cheese that entered into force already in 2019. StatementSubmitted: The European Union would like to reiterate its concern on the import conditions for dairy products issued by Qatar’s Ministry of Public Health that entered into force already in 2019. The scope of these measures was further expanded with Qatar’s Council of Ministers instructions issued in August 2021 and in May 2022. Regrettably, these measures affected several dairy products exported from the EU to Qatar.Qatar did not notify these new import conditions for dairy products to WTO Members as required under the WTO SPS Agreement. One of the main concerns of these import conditions is the short shelf-life  imposed for several dairy products which are not based on science nor on international standards. In practice, it is impossible for EU exporters to continue to ship some dairy products to Qatar. At the same time, domestic dairy product producers in Qatar are favored as these companies do not have to take into account the long transport time that foreign exporters need for shipping their dairy products to Qatar. The EU is grateful for the continued dialogue with Qatar on this longstanding concern and would like to urge Qatar to withdraw the current trade restrictions and to adopt a permanent solution, which should be first notified at a draft stage to this committee. The European Union would like to thank Qatar for the constructive bilateral exchanges over the past months and remain available to continue to work constructively with Qatar.
Summary: The European Union remained concerned at Qatar's Ministry of Public Health Circular establishing new import requirements for dairy products, which had entered into force in 2019 and had been further expanded in 2021 and 2022, without being notified to the WTO. The European Union's main concern related to the short shelf life imposed for several dairy products, which were not based on science nor on international standards. These requirements hindered exports to Qatar and favoured domestic producers who did not have to ship their products. Grateful for the constructive bilateral dialogue, the European Union urged Qatar to withdraw the current trade restrictions and to adopt a permanent solution, which would be notified at a draft stage to the SPS Committee.

StatementSubmitted: Comité de Medidas Sanitarias y Fitosanitarias de la Organización Mundial del ComercioRESTRICCIONES IMPUESTAS POR BOLIVIA A LAS EXPORTACIONES AGROPECUARIAS DEL PERÚINTERVENCIÓN DEL PERÚEl Perú presenta ante los Miembros de la OMC su preocupación comercial específica con relación a la práctica adoptada por el Gobierno de Bolivia que se materializa a través de diversas medidas restrictivas aplicadas a las exportaciones peruanas de productos agropecuarios, las cuales vienen siendo recurrentes en los últimos tres años, aduciendo diferentes razones que, en la práctica, impiden el ingreso de principales productos originarios del Perú al mercado boliviano, tales como la papa y cebolla.  Al respecto, es importante hacer notar que el Perú ha buscado constantemente una solución amistosa y bilateral a esta problemática solicitando reuniones e información respecto a la justificación técnica de las medidas aplicadas por Bolivia[1].  En esa línea, el 10 de setiembre de 2021 las autoridades sanitarias, de comercio y de aduanas de Perú y Bolivia, se reunieron en las instalaciones del Centro Binacional de Atención en Frontera (CEBAF)-Desaguadero[2], donde los Viceministros de Comercio Exterior de ambos países suscribieron un Acta en el que alcanzaron distintos compromisos, entre los cuales se encuentra la de resolver a partir de esa fecha cualquier tipo de afectación al comercio bilateral de los productos agropecuarios, garantizando la expedición de permisos fitosanitarios y la realización de las inspecciones fitosanitarias en frontera. Sin perjuicio de ello, los problemas de ingreso de productos peruanos a Bolivia subsisten.  Asimismo, y como parte de los continuos esfuerzos del Gobierno peruano para privilegiar una solución bilateral, quisiera informar de los acuerdos adoptados por ambos países en la reunión del Gabinete Binacional Perú-Bolivia, liderados por los señores Presidentes de ambos países, el pasado 30 de octubre, en la que se acordó continuar desarrollando acciones para garantizar y mejorar la fluidez, así como agilizar los procedimientos en materia sanitaria y fitosanitaria entre ambos países. De manera más específica y como parte de los compromisos adoptados en el Plan de La Paz, el Perú quisiera hacer referencia al compromiso de “Promover el comercio bilateral de productos agropecuarios, hidrobiológicos y pecuarios procesados garantizando a su vez el libre flujo de los mismos, conforme a la regulación sanitaria vigente en ambos países, acordando mantener reuniones bimestrales entre las autoridades sanitarias y comerciales para evaluar el desarrollo comercial entre las Partes”. El Perú confía que esta aproximación bilateral permita una solución satisfactoria y permanente a esta problemática que afrontan nuestros empresarios en la zona de frontera, así como las pequeñas empresas y agricultores. Así, esperamos que las reuniones bimestrales que se realicen entre las autoridades sanitarias y comerciales de ambos países permitan establecer un libre flujo comercial entre ambos países, caracterizado fundamentalmente por el respeto, la complementariedad, la voluntad de integración y los profundos lazos de hermandad histórica y solidaridad que rigen entre nuestros pueblos y Gobiernos, con el objetivo de establecer una agenda de desarrollo y cooperación conjunta.  El Perú quisiera reiterar su compromiso por la estricta defensa de sus intereses económicos-comerciales en todos los foros, así como su plena disposición a dialogar con sus socios para solucionar cualquier inconveniente en beneficio mutuo. StatementSubmitted: 1.       El Perú presenta ante los Miembros de la OMC su preocupación comercial con relación a diversas medidas restrictivas aplicadas por el Gobierno de Bolivia a las exportaciones peruanas de productos agropecuarios, durante los últimos 3 años, las cuales establecen bloqueos (de facto), al ingreso de principales productos originarios del Perú al mercado boliviano, tales como la papa y cebolla. Igualmente, se presentan medidas restrictivas a la exportación de trucha entera, las cuales carecerían de sustento técnico. 2.       Al respecto, es necesario mencionar que el 21 de julio de 2021, las autoridades del gobierno boliviano representadas por el Ministerio de Desarrollo Rural y Tierras, el Viceministerio de Lucha Contra el Contrabando, la Dirección General de Lucha Contra el Contrabando, la Dirección Nacional del Servicio Nacional de Sanidad Agropecuaria e Inocuidad Alimentaria (SENASAG), la Gerencia Regional de Aduana de Cochabamba, en conjunto con la Federación de Productores Agropecuarios del Valle Bajo y la Federación de Horticultores Municipio Paria y Soracachi del Departamento de Oruro, suscribieron un Acta de Entendimiento, en la cual se asumieron compromisos de corto, mediano y largo plazo dirigidos, entre otros, a controlar y restringir el acceso de los productos agrícolas al mercado boliviano incrementando los aranceles e imponiendo medidas restrictivas no arancelarias tal como la aplicación de contingentes. 3.       Los compromisos establecidos en la mencionada acta de entendimiento contravienen las disposiciones del artículo XI del GATT de 1994, relacionado a la eliminación general de las restricciones cuantitativas, considerando que ningún Miembro impondrá ni mantendrá -aparte de los derechos de aduana, impuestos u otras cargas- prohibiciones ni restricciones a la importación de un producto del territorio de otro Miembro, ya sean aplicadas mediante contingentes, licencias o por medio de otras medidas[1]. 4.       Asimismo, como parte de las restricciones sanitarias y fitosanitarias impuestas por el Gobierno de Bolivia, se presentan los siguientes hechos: a.       No otorgamiento del permiso fitosanitario por SENASAG desde julio 2021 para la importación de productos agrícolas peruanos como la papa y cebolla.b.       No realización del procedimiento de inspección fitosanitaria por parte del SENASAG de Bolivia en el Centro Binacional de Atención en Frontera (CEBAF) Desaguadero[2] a los productos agrícolas perecibles originarios de Perú.c.       El rechazo de la importación de envíos de papa certificados por el SENASA (noviembre 2021) motivado por la detección de una larva en el tubérculo sin evidenciar que corresponda a una plaga cuarentenaria o exótica para Bolivia, que justifique la prohibición como una medida de emergencia. 5.       Con relación al no otorgamiento del permiso fitosanitario de importación, el SENASAG ha dejado de otorgar dichos permisos para la importación de papa y cebolla  desde julio de 2021 a la fecha, sin expresar las causas ni observar lo establecido en las normas internacionales para medidas fitosanitarias ni en el AcuerdoMSF de la OMC que pudieran justificar tal medida, limitándose a señalar que los sistemas no se encontraban habilitados para registrar el trámite o que no tenían autorización para realizar dicha función, lo cual no permitió la importación de productos perecibles peruanos. Esta situación de suspender periódicamente la emisión de permisos fitosanitarios de importación viene ocurriendo desde el 2018, contraviniendo las disposiciones del Acuerdo MSF e incluso su propia normativa nacional, en particular, lo establecido en la Resolución Administrativa N° 085/2016 del 6 de junio del 2016, que aprueba el "Manual de Procedimiento Fitosanitario de Importación", en la cual se indica que la emisión de permisos fitosanitarios en papel y en forma electrónica tienen un plazo de dos (02) días hábiles o un día (01) hábil respectivamente. 6.       Con relación a las inspecciones fitosanitarias, el SENASAG debe realizar las mismas previo a la nacionalización del producto, así como realizar las pruebas de verificación que fueren pertinentes, de conformidad con los requisitos establecidos en el procedimiento correspondiente. De acuerdo a los resultados, el SENASAG podrá autorizar la nacionalización del producto, cuando éste se sujete al cumplimiento de los requisitos establecidos en el correspondiente permiso fitosanitario de importación. 7.       No obstante, el SENASAG no viene realizando el procedimiento de inspección fitosanitaria a las importaciones de productos perecibles provenientes del Perú, (papa, cebolla, frutas, entre otros) en las instalaciones del CEBAF-Desaguadero; limitándose a señalar que los inspectores  no se encuentran autorizados para tal efecto, o que sus sistemas no se encuentran habilitados para registrar el trámite de inspección de dichos productos, lo cual impide que las exportaciones de productos perecibles de pequeños empresarios sean efectuadas. Asimismo, cuando se permiten las inspecciones, Bolivia presenta demoras y barreras injustificadas al comercio. 8.       El no otorgamiento del permiso fitosanitario de importación y la no realización del procedimiento de inspección fitosanitaria de productos vulneran las disposiciones de los artículos 2, 8 y el Anexo C del Acuerdo MSF, ya que las MSF no deben ser aplicadas de manera que constituyan una restricción encubierta del comercio internacional; asimismo, los procedimientos de inspección y control deben iniciarse y concluirse sin demoras indebidas y de manera que no sea menos favorable para los productos importados que para los productos nacionales similares. 9.       Por otro lado, con relación al rechazo de la importación de envíos de papa motivado por la detección de una larva en el tubérculo, el Perú no ha recibido ninguna notificación de no cumplimiento por parte de Bolivia que justifique tal medida, a fin de que se puedan tomar las acciones correctivas correspondientes y se continúe con el comercio de este producto. Al respecto, el Perú ha solicitado conocer la identificación taxonómica y condición en Bolivia de la plaga interceptada, así como el reporte del laboratorio oficial, sin tener una respuesta a la fecha. 10.   Este accionar por parte de Bolivia, contraviene el principio básico de “necesidad” y “justificación técnica” para la protección de las plantas y aplicación de medidas fitosanitarias en el comercio internacional de la CIPF, que indica que las Partes pueden aplicar medidas fitosanitarias solamente cuando tales medidas sean necesarias para prevenir la introducción y/o dispersión de plagas cuarentenarias  y deberán justificar técnicamente las medidas fitosanitarias sobre la base de conclusiones alcanzadas mediante un apropiado análisis de riesgo de plagas o, cuando proceda, otro examen y evaluación comparable de la información científica disponible. Igualmente, Bolivia como país importador no ha remitido a Perú las notificaciones correspondientes identificando la plaga interceptada en los envíos de papa con fines de investigar y realizar correcciones necesarias por parte del Perú como país exportador, contraviniendo la NIMF N°13 de la CIPF, directrices para la notificación del incumplimiento y acción de emergencia. 11.   En este sentido, consideramos que se ha vulnerado el artículo 3 del Acuerdo MSF sobre armonización en el que se indica que los Miembros basarán sus medidas en las normas, directrices o recomendaciones internacionales. Adicionalmente, se contravendrían las disposiciones de los artículos 2 y 5, ya que las medidas fitosanitarias deben ser aplicadas cuando sean necesarias, entre otros, para la preservación de los vegetales y estar basadas en principios científicos, teniendo en cuenta el objetivo de reducir al mínimo los efectos negativos sobre el comercio. 12.   Asimismo, consideramos que se han vulnerado las disposiciones del artículo 7 y el Anexo B del Acuerdo MSF, los cuales establecen, entre otros, que si a un Miembro se le planteasen o amenazaran planteársele problemas urgentes de protección fitosanitaria, dicho Miembro debe notificar inmediatamente a los demás Miembros, por conducto de la Secretaría, la reglamentación y los productos de que se trate, indicando brevemente el objetivo y la razón de ser de la reglamentación, así como la naturaleza del problema o problemas urgentes; y brindar la posibilidad a otros Miembros para formular observaciones y mantener conversaciones respecto a la medida urgente. Sin embargo, Bolivia no ha presentado ninguna notificación de urgencia al Comité MSF OMC respecto a las medidas aplicadas a la papa del Perú. 13.   Asimismo, el 10 de setiembre de 2021, las autoridades sanitarias, de comercio y de aduanas de Perú y Bolivia, se reunieron en las instalaciones del CEBAF-Desaguadero, donde los Viceministros de Comercio Exterior de ambos países suscribieron un Acta en el que alcanzaron distintos compromisos, entre los cuales se encuentra la de resolver a partir de esa fecha cualquier tipo de afectación al comercio bilateral de los productos agropecuarios, garantizando la expedición de permisos fitosanitarios y la realización de las inspecciones fitosanitarias en frontera. Estos compromisos también han sido desconocidos por Bolivia, manteniendo a la fecha el bloqueo a las exportaciones de productos agrícolas antes mencionadas. 14.   La papa y cebolla son los casos más relevantes que mantienen hasta la fecha problemas para el ingreso que consiste en que la autoridad boliviana no otorga los permisos fitosanitarios de importación y la realización del procedimiento de inspección que permitan al importador boliviano completar el proceso de nacionalización de estos productos. Esto se puede observar en la evolución de las exportaciones de hortalizas, siendo Bolivia a nivel de los socios andinos el segundo destino más importante para dichas exportaciones. Las exportaciones de Perú a Bolivia de papas correspondiente al periodo enero-junio 2021 ascendió a US$ 263 mil equivalentes a 2,381 toneladas, mientras que a partir de julio 2021 a diciembre, las exportaciones peruanas han sido nulas. Un caso similar, ocurre con las cebollas, donde las exportaciones peruanas a Bolivia para el periodo enero-julio 2021 alcanzaron un total de US$ 1,034 miles, equivalentes a 9,067 toneladas, mientras que, a partir del mes de agosto 2021 en adelante, las exportaciones han sido nulas. 15.   Con relación a la trucha, SENASAG comunicó oficialmente la aprobación del certificado sanitario armonizado para la exportación de trucha fresca – refrigerada / entera-granel en el año 2017[3] 16.   En este contexto, a lo largo de los años 2019, 2020 y 2021. el Organismo Nacional de Sanidad Pesquera del Perú (SANIPES) en aras de dar cumplimiento a los compromisos binacionales, ha realizado actividades que permitan la comercialización de trucha en frontera garantizando un producto sano e inocuo[4]. Igualmente, durante julio de 2020 y marzo de 2021, se llevaron a cabo reuniones entre Altos Directivos de SANIPES y SENASAG en las que ambas autoridades sanitarias asumieron compromisos que coadyuvarían a la formalización de la exportación de trucha entera-granel / fresca-refrigerada con destino a Bolivia. 17.   A pesar de los acuerdos entre ambas Partes, SENASAG no ha dado cumplimiento, entre otros, a los siguientes compromisos que permitan exportar trucha entera a dicho país: a.       Se desconoce si Bolivia ha establecido mecanismos de mejora en el transporte, cadena de frío y prácticas de eviscerados.b.       SENASAG no se presentó a la visita técnica de campo dirigida a establecimientos acuícolas[5].c.       SENASAG no ha cumplido con incorporar 20 empresas o personas autorizadas en su registro de importadores a diciembre de 2021. 18.   Es aún más preocupante que en enero de 2022, SENASAG ha indicado que bajo su regulación solo se puede comercializar animales eviscerados y debido a su marco regulatorio no podrían aceptar otro tipo de productos. Es decir, después de 5 años de haber aprobado un certificado sanitario para exportar trucha entera, SENASAG restringe su acceso injustificadamente. 19.   De la revisión de la normativa boliviana, la cual no ha sido notificada previamente al Comité MSF OMC conforme al artículo 7 y el Anexo B del Acuerdo MSF, no se evidencia ninguna razón técnica ni legal que impidan las exportaciones peruanas de trucha entera. 20.   Esta prohibición no solo carecería de sustento desde el Acuerdo MSF, sino que también sería contraria a las disposiciones del artículo XI del GATT de 1994 relacionado a la eliminación general de las restricciones cuantitativas. 21.   Por lo anteriormente expuesto, Bolivia habría contravenido las disposiciones del artículo XI del GATT de 1994; así como de los artículos 2, 3, 5, 7, 8 y los Anexos B y C del Acuerdo MSF. Summary: Peru expressed concerns over various restrictive measures applied by Bolivia on Peruvian exports of agricultural products, such as potatoes and onions. In Peru's view, these measures were inconsistent with Article XI of the GATT 1994 and Articles 2, 3, 5, 7, 8 as well as Annexes B and C of the SPS Agreement. Peru urged Bolivia to lift the restrictions on Peruvian exports of perishable goods as well as trout. Peru submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2009.

Peru stated that Bolivia's measures blocked access to the Bolivian market for Peruvian exports such as potatoes, onions and black trout. Peru requested Bolivia to comply with the provisions of Resolution No 2264 on the investigation procedure presented by Peru to Bolivia, issued by the General Secretariat of the Andean Community. Peru also noted that, despite the approval of the harmonized health certificate in 2017, Bolivia had not complied with the corresponding commitments for the exportation of trout. Peru considered that Bolivia was breaching provisions of Article XI of the GATT 1994, as well as Articles 2, 3, 5, 7 and 8, as well as Annexes B and C of the SPS Agreement, and asked Bolivia to rescind restrictions in place on Peruvian exports. Peru submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2048.

Peru stated that Bolivia's measures blocked market access for Peruvian exports of whole trout without scientific justification. Despite the approval of the harmonized health certificate in 2017, Bolivia had not yet complied with the corresponding commitments to allow the imports. In January 2022, Bolivia's National Agricultural Health and Food Safety Service (SENASAG) had indicated that its current regulations allowed for the marketing only of eviscerated animals. Peru was still awaiting a response to the requests for information submitted, as well as an official invitation for an in-person meeting to resolve the issue. In Peru's view, Bolivia's measures contravened the provisions of Article XI of the GATT 1994, as well as Articles 2, 3, 5, 7 and 8 and Annexes B and C of the SPS Agreement. Peru asked Bolivia to rescind restrictions in place on Peruvian exports. Peru submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2087.

Peru stated that Bolivia's measures blocked market access for Peruvian exports of whole trout without scientific justification. Despite the approval of the health certificate in 2017, Bolivia had not yet complied with the corresponding commitments to allow imports. In January 2022, Bolivia had indicated that its current regulations allowed for the marketing of eviscerated animals only. Peru was still awaiting a response to the requests for information submitted as well as an official invitation for an in-person meeting to resolve the issue. In Peru's view, Bolivia's measures contravened the provisions of Article XI of the GATT 1994, as well as Articles 2-3, 5, and 7-8 and Annexes B and C to the SPS Agreement. Peru asked Bolivia to lift its restrictions. Peru submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2119.

Peru stated that Bolivia's measures blocked market access for Peruvian exports of whole trout. Despite the approval of the health certificate in 2017, Bolivia had not yet complied with the corresponding commitments to allow imports. Peru also complained that Bolivia had not notified its national legislation. Peru was still awaiting a response to the requests for the technical justification and the risk assessment carried out for the inclusion of fresh chilled or frozen (eviscerated) fish in health risk category 1 of Annex 1 to Administrative Resolution SENASAG No. 078/2022. Peru asked Bolivia to lift its restrictions. Peru provided its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2152.

Peru stated that Bolivia's measures blocked market access for Peruvian exports of whole trout. Despite the approval of the health certificate in 2017, Bolivia had not yet complied with the corresponding commitments to allow imports. Peru also indicated that Bolivia had not notified its national legislation. Peru asked Bolivia to lift its restrictions. Peru provided its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2185.

Peru stated that Bolivia's measures blocked market access for Peruvian exports of whole trout. Despite the approval of the health certificate in 2017, Bolivia had not yet complied with the corresponding commitments to allow imports. Peru was of the view that Bolivia disregarded its international commitments under the SPS Agreement. Peru asked Bolivia to allow the imports of whole trout and reiterated its willingness to hold bilateral consultations.

StatementSubmitted: El Perú desea presentar ante los Miembros de la OMC su preocupación comercial específica con relación a diversas medidas restrictivas que, desde el año 2017, vienen evitando el ingreso de las exportaciones peruanas de trucha entera fresca y, refrigerada a Bolivia. Cabe destacar que, han pasado casi siete años desde que la autoridad sanitaria boliviana informó oficialmente al Perú sobre la aprobación del certificado sanitario para la exportación de trucha fresca – refrigerada / entera-granel, comprometiéndose a permitir la exportación de trucha entera a su país. Sin embardo, Bolivia no ha realizado las gestiones administrativas internas necesarias para lograr que el Perú inicie sus exportaciones a dicho mercado.El Perú ha venido manifestando su profunda preocupación en este Comité por el desconocimiento de los compromisos internacionales asumidos a nivel bilateral como en el marco del Acuerdo MSF de la OMC, ya que Bolivia ha desconocido la aprobación del mencionado certificado sanitario y, a la vez ha desarrollado, publicado y, tiene vigentes normas internas en esta materia que no se han notificado a los Miembros de la OMC, y mucho menos, se ha otorgado un plazo de 60 días para comentarios de los Miembros.   Deseamos precisar que, en el marco de anteriores Comités, Bolivia ha comunicado su voluntad por mantener un diálogo abierto y transparente con el Perú. No obstante, a la fecha, no hemos recibido pronunciación y/o respuesta a nuestras solicitudes por entablar una reunión técnico-bilateral en aras de buscar una solución que satisfaga a ambas partes. Por lo anteriormente expuesto, solicitamos a Bolivia 1) sostener una reunión técnica- bilateral entre nuestras autoridades sanitarias competentes 2) nos explique las razones del desconocimiento de un certificado sanitario negociado y, aprobado por ambas Partes 3) se nos envíe las disposiciones normativas vigentes para la no autorización de este tipo de productos a Bolivia 4) autorizar el ingreso de trucha fresca entera y, refrigerada peruana.Finalmente, el Perú desea expresar, nuevamente, su total disposición de trabajar de manera conjunta con Bolivia, en aras de lograr una solución a este asunto.
Summary: Peru reiterated its concerns regarding Bolivia's trade restrictions, which had affected exports of fresh and chilled whole trout from Peru since 2017. Despite the approval of a health certificate, Bolivia had not yet concluded its internal administrative steps to allow market access. Peru was of the view that Bolivia disregarded its international commitments and the SPS Agreement. Peru also regretted that Bolivia had applied SPS requirements without notifying them and without providing a 60-day comment period. While Bolivia had indicated, in pervious Committee meetings, its readiness to have a dialogue with Peru, Peru had not received any statement or answer from Bolivia concerning the holding of a bilateral meeting. Peru therefore asked Bolivia to: hold a bilateral technical meeting; explain the reasons for not recognizing health certificates; provide a list of relevant applicable SPS requirements; and allow the imports of whole trout from Peru.

México desea expresar su preocupación respecto de las gestiones para la exportación de productos de la pesca, vivos y procesados de México a la República Popular de China, misma que ha sido objeto de discusión técnica en diversos foros como el Grupo de Alto Nivel entre México y China y reuniones bilaterales en el marco de este Comité. 

El tema es de máxima importancia y relevancia para México y ha involucrado a diversas autoridades de nuestro Gobierno que han intentado mejorar los canales de comunicación con la Administración General de Aduanas (AGA) de China, a fin de tratar de resolver esta situación que ha afectado las exportaciones de este importante sector productivo en México.

México desea manifestar que, desde 2019, empresas mexicanas han enfrentado diversos obstáculos en cuanto al proceso de autorización de establecimientos mexicanos para exportar productos de la pesca-vivos y procesados- a la República Popular de China, debido a constantes, abruptos y excesivamente detallados requerimientos de información por parte de la AGA.

Cabe mencionar que, la Comisión Federal para la Protección contra Riesgos Sanitarios (COFEPRIS), autoridad sanitaria responsable en México, ha enviado la información de las empresas mexicanas interesadas en exportar, las cuales han sido suspendidas de manera unilateral, y condicionadas a video inspecciones por parte de la autoridad china. Asimismo, es importante señalar que además del requisito de las video inspecciones, se han recibido notificaciones  con pocos días de anticipación para realizar dichas video inspecciones a algunos establecimientos, así como la cancelación de exportaciones a establecimientos, sin argumentos contundentes para la decisión y sin posibilidad de establecer contacto para resolver y aclarar dudas, lo que ha generado incertidumbre para la industria pesquera de nuestro país, pérdidas de empleo e impactos en la producción de comunidades que dependen de esta actividad.

 

México ha solicitado a las autoridades chinas, avanzar en los procedimientos de autorización de establecimientos y especies en diversas ocasiones, destacando que nuestro Gobierno siempre ha favorecido el diálogo técnico entre autoridades, sin embargo, estos esfuerzos no han dado resultados favorables y la respuesta por parte de China ha sido dilatoria. 

 

A la luz de lo anterior, se considera que al amparo del Acuerdo sobre la Aplicación de Medidas Sanitarias y Fitosanitarias (Acuerdo MSF) de la Organización Mundial del Comercio, China ha recurrido a demoras indebidas e injustificadas, incurriendo en incumplimientos a principios básicos del Acuerdo MSF, tales como los referidos en los artículos 2.2, 2.3 y 5.4 del Acuerdo MSF.

 

Con base en lo anterior, la delegación de México solicita amablemente a la delegación de China, lo siguiente: 

 


	Proporcionar de manera oportuna y clara, los procedimientos e información que permitan el registro de los establecimientos mexicanos interesados en exportar, así como cualquier información de actualización o seguimiento sobre los requisitos necesarios solicitados por la AGA.
	Actualizaciones de los listados de establecimientos mexicanos autorizados para exportar producto a China en un plazo razonable.
	Autorización de las especies que se capturan en las costas mexicanas sin restricciones injustificadas, salvo el cumplimiento de los requisitos de sanidad acuícola establecidos por la OMC o con un sólido fundamento científico y técnico basado en riesgo.
	Apertura por parte de la AGA para establecer comunicación directa, que permita obtener una evaluación de equivalencia de la legislación sanitaria de ambos países, buscando como resultado el reconocimiento del sistema de vigilancia sanitaria aplicado por México, con la finalidad de agilizar los procesos correspondientes.


Finalmente, reiteramos nuestro interés y apertura a continuar un diálogo cordial entre ambos Gobiernos, a fin de atender esta preocupación lo más pronto posible y de conformidad con los compromisos asumidos por China ante esta Organización. 

La delegación de México agradece a la delegación de China por la atención a esta declaración y las solicitudes en ella expuestas.
Summary: Mexico expressed its concern regarding on the exportation of live and processed fishery products to China. Mexico highlighted the barriers to authorization faced by Mexican establishments since 2019 due to the excessive requirements for information of the General Administration of Customs of the People's Republic of China (GACC). Mexico regretted the uncertainty, the loss of employments and the impacts on production resulting from China's suspension of Mexican establishments; the short-notice requirements to undertake remote inspections; and the lack of response by China, despite having provided all the requested information on establishments interested in exporting to China. In Mexico's view, China was incurring in undue and unjustified delays, and was breaching Articles 2.2, 2.3 and 5.4 of the SPS Agreement. Mexico asked China: 1) to share the procedures for the registration of Mexican establishments, as well any additional requirement by the GACC; 2) to provide an updated record of Mexican establishments authorized to export to China; 3) to authorize species captured in Mexico without unjustified restrictions; and 4) to open communication with the GACC in order to establish the equivalence of sanitary legislation between both countries. Mexico reiterated its willingness to continue the dialogue with China.

Thank you, Chair.

Let me first join other Members in congratulating you on your appointment as the chair for this Committee.

The Separate Customs Territory of Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen and Matsu raises its concerns about China’s suspension of the importation of our fresh fruits of pineapple, sugar apple and wax apple.

We request China to resume its imports of the aforementioned three fresh fruits from our side without delay in accordance with the SPS Agreement and relevant international standards, guidelines and recommendations.

At the outset, we must emphasize that for pineapple, sugar apple and wax apple exported to China, we attached great importance to China’s non-compliance notifications. After receiving respective notifications from China, we immediately implemented the following relevant enhanced pest-control measures:

Regarding our pineapple, after receiving the non-compliance notifications from China during March to April in 2020, we traced the origin back to the orchards, and have adopted additional measures to strengthen pest-control and prevention. In addition, we have also strengthened our source management in orchards and in packing houses, and have regularly conducted quarantine inspections prior to the fruit’s exportation to China since 19 October 2020. Our farmers fully cooperated with the competent authority to comply with the enhanced measures and all exported fruits are in full compliance with China’s quarantine requirements. The full compliance of our fruits with China’s quarantine requirements can be proven by the fact that we had not received any non-compliance notifications ever since we adopted our tightened pest-control and prevention measure.

Unfortunately and unexpectedly, the General Administration of Customs of China (the GACC) notified us on 25 February 2021 that China would suspend the import of our pineapples from 1 March 2021 (that was as short as 4 days from its notification) due to the “alleged” interception of “scale insects” (Planococcus minor) on the pineapple.

Regarding our sugar apple and wax apple, after receiving the non-compliance notifications from China during March to June in 2021, we not only continued to trace the origin back to the orchards, adopted additional measures to strengthen pest-control and prevention measures, but also intensified systematic management from the fruits’ production to their exportation since 7 July 2021. As a result, since 28 June 2021, we have not received any notification of non-compliance from China concerning our exported sugar apple and wax apple. This also demonstrates that our strengthened pest-control and export quarantine measures are effective. However, on 19 September 2021, due to the “alleged” interception of “scale insects” (Planococcus minor) on the sugar apple and wax apple, China unexpectedly notified its suspension of the importation of our sugar apple and wax apple effective as of 20 September 2021.

Again, we would like to emphasize that after receiving the non-compliance notifications from China, we have been responsive in taking enhanced measures, including tracing back to the origin of orchards and strengthening pest-control and prevention measures. We have also notified China about the aforementioned two stages of concrete strengthening measures on 25 February and 10 September 2021 respectively. We also provided China with our draft “Requirements for the Inspection and Quarantine of Fresh Fruits of Pineapple, Sugar Apple and Wax Apple Exported to China” on 29 September 2021 for comments and urged that both sides should convene technical discussions to address queries or questions or to resolve any concern. But we receive no response from China.

In addition to what I have explained above, there are many reasons to prove that it is apparently not necessary for China to suspend its import of our fruits:

First, our efforts of pest-control have been effective. In fact, starting from 2020, the non-compliance rate of aforementioned fruits exported to China is far less than 1%.

This is an undeniable fact to prove the high effectiveness of our pest-control management measure in place.

Second, from a research report conducted in China that we collected, the “scale insects” also occur in quite a number of regions in China. This shows that taking an extreme measure of suspending importation by China due to a minimal percentage of “scale insects” (Planococcus minor) being found in the fruits is excessive and unnecessary.

Third, the widely accepted international practices, as adopted by other Members is that if this insect is found during import inspection, the usual/common way of addressing the problem is to have the consignment subject to quarantine treatment, such as the commonly used fumigation. We are yet to find any other Member taking an extreme measure of totally suspending the importation of such products merely because of less than one percent of imports being found of having “scale insects” (Planococcus minor).

From any perspective, there is no need for China to take measures to suspend imports, not to mention that China’s suspension of imports is in breach of its obligations under the SPS Agreement and the GATT.

Since China suspended the importation of our pineapples to China on 1 March 2021, we have requested China to conduct scientific and technical dialogues on such cases through the bilateral channel for a total of 10 times, but China has not responded. We have also made our request through the SPS Enquiry Point, but are yet to receive any reply.

We hereby take this opportunity before the Committee to request China to review its measures, to meet the requirement of least trade restrictive effective, to withdraw the suspension of import of our fruits without delay in order to bring its measures in line with Articles 2, 3 and 5 of the SPS Agreement and to be in conformity with China’s WTO commitments. We also urge China to agree on conducting bilateral scientific and technical dialogue to resolve the trade issue of our pineapple, sugar apple and wax apple exported to China as soon as possible. We also request China to share with us its risk assessment and supporting scientific evidence that can justify its suspension of import, if there is any.
Summary: Chinese Taipei raised concerns about China's suspension of the importation of pineapples, sugar apples and wax apples, and requested China to resume imports without delay. Following notifications of non-compliance from China, Chinese Taipei had adopted measures to strengthen pest-control and prevention. Although no additional notifications had been received, the GACC had suspended imports of these fruits, arguing interception of scale insects (Planococcus minor). Chinese Taipei emphasized that the low rate of non-compliance, below 1%, proved the effectiveness of the pest-control management measure in place. Chinese Taipei noted that scale insects were also detected in some Chinese regions and that quarantine and fumigation of consignments were accepted international practices, less restrictive than import suspension. Chinese Taipei urged China to bring its measures in conformity with Articles 2, 3 and 5 of the SPS Agreement, to conduct bilateral scientific and technical dialogue, and to share the relevant risk assessment and supporting scientific evidence.In response to China, Chinese Taipei highlighted that China had provided no scientific evidence to support the import suspension, and underscored that pest rates in consignments detected from 2020 to 2021 were extremely low (0.29% rate of inconsistency for pineapple, 0.23% for sugar apple and 0.16% for wax apple). Chinese Taipei reiterated that no additional notification of non-compliance had been received after the enhancement of the two-stage pest control mechanism.

StatementSubmitted: The Separate Customs Territory of Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen, and Matsu would like to raise the STC regarding China’s importation suspension against our pineapple, sugar apple and wax apple again in this committee. We request China to resume the trade of these three fruits in accordance with the SPS Agreement and relevant international standards, guidelines and recommendations.We have attached great importance to the non-compliance notifications from China. Since receiving these notifications in 2020 and 2021, we have adopted effective improvement measures. Moreover, on 29 September 2021, we provided China with our draft “Requirements for the Inspection and Quarantine of Fresh Fruits of Pineapple, Sugar Apple and Wax Apple Exported to China” for comments and urged that both sides should convene technical discussions to solve any queries or questions on this issue. We requested China to provide detailed identification reports, its “Appropriate Level of Protection”, and Risk Analysis reports to us, so that we can have a better understanding on China’s measures.The “scale insect” (Planococcus minor) occurs throughout many regions in China. The widely accepted international practice for this insect, if found during import inspection, as adopted by other countries, is that the consignment is subject to quarantine treatment. The conventional way of addressing this insect in quarantine treatment is fumigation. On the contrary, adopting an extreme measure of suspending importation by China due to a minimal percentage being found in the fruits appears excessive and unnecessary.We contacted China through the SPS inquiry point on 16 October 2021, and kept on providing information, explaining the above-mentioned draft. We have requested China to conduct scientific and technical dialogues on these issues through the bilateral channel. However, we have not received any reply from China. We urge China again to provide detailed identification reports, its “Appropriate Level of Protection”, and Risk Analysis report for our further study.In conclusion, China suspended the importation of our pineapples on 1st March 2021. We contacted China through the SPS inquiry point on 16 October 2021, requested 14 times to conduct scientific and technical dialogues on these issues through the bilateral channel, and raised the first STC in previous SPS Committee meeting. Yet, no progress has occurred despite our utmost communication efforts. We hereby take this opportunity in the Committee once again to request China to review its measures, to meet the requirement of least trade restrictive principle, and to withdraw the suspension of importation of our fruits in order to bring its measures in line with Articles 2, 3 and 5 of the SPS Agreement and to be in consistence with China’s WTO commitments. We also urge China to agree on conducting bilateral scientific and technical dialogue to resolve the trade issue of our pineapple, sugar apple and wax apple as soon as possible.

StatementSubmitted: EU: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/2246 of 15 December 2021 amending Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1793 on the temporary increase of official controls and emergency measures governing the entry into the Union of certain goods from certain third countries implementing Regulations (EU) 2017/625 and (EC) No 178/2002 of the European Parliament and of the Council (Text with EEA relevance) on the presence of ETO in spicesDetails: European Commission has implemented Regulation (EU) 2021/2246 dated 15 December 2021, which took effect on 6 January 2022, wherein the official controls governing the entry into the EU of spices have been increased. As per the regulation, consignments of spices from India should be accompanied by an Official Certificate (Health Certificate), stating compliance with maximum residue levels of ETO [Ethylene oxide expressed as a sum of ethylene oxide and 2-chloro-ethanol]. The regulation is applicable to all products that fall under the CN Codes from 0904 to 0910 and 2103, thereby covering all spices and most of the spice products.Fixing the limit of ETO at default level: It is noted that the EU has set the regulatory limit for ETO at the default level, which is lower than what is being used by other countries. EU is requested to share the risk assessment or scientific basis for re-setting the ETO limit to default.  The regulatory limit in the EU for ETO is 0.02 ppm for chilli and ginger and 0.1 ppm for all other spices. This is drastically stringent when compared with the maximum limits of other countries (e.g., USA has a limit of 947 ppm for ETO + ECH).  Industry sources have pointed to the possibility of Ethylene being generated naturally in the growing environment, which can get converted to Ethylene Oxide. This could fail consignments intended to EU as the EU MRLs have been fixed at trace level.The EU is requested to share the scientific basis for measure and the alternative measures considered before finalising the measure.  No comment period is provided: The said regulation was notified to WTO SPS website only on 14 January 2022, as a regular notification, after eight days from the date of taking effect, that too with NIL provision for comments.  EU is requested to share the reasons as to why the notification was not notified through WTO at the draft stage so that comments can be provided. This approach is inconsistent with SPs agreement. Secondly, if the measure is an emergency, then why is the notification not notified under the relevant provisions. Increased cost of inspection and increased clearance time: Many of the consignments of spices that have been exported from India to the EU since December are stranded at various EU ports as the Port Health authorities are demanding 100% testing for ETO (in case of consignments shipped before 6 January, 2022) and official certificate issued by India (in the case of consignments shipped on or after 6 January 2022). There is no prior information before the said notification came into effect. Nor any transition time is allowed for in-transit consignment.
Summary: India informed the Committee that through Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/2246, the European Union had increased official controls for the entry of spices and spice products by setting the limit of ethylene oxide at the default level, which was 0.02 ppm for chilli and ginger, and 0.1 ppm for all other spices. India urged the European Union to share the risk assessment for establishing the limit at the default level. India further noted that the regulation had been notified to the WTO eight days after entry into force, which did not allow time for comments.

StatementSubmitted: India thanks the EU for its response to the Indian concern on the European Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/2246 of 15 December 2021.  However, India's concerns remain unanswered. Inadequate Scientific Basis: The European Union has stated that in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 1272/2008, Ethylene oxide (EtO) is classified as a mutagen, category 1B, a carcinogen, category 1B, and a reproductive toxicant, category 1B. Currently, the EU considers ethylene oxide (EtO) and its metabolite 2-chloroethanol or ethylene chlorhydrin (ECH) together, reported as ethylene oxide, in compliance assessments. Two studies from the EU have reported the following: (i) In 2021, a report issued by German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment (BfR) states that from recent studies in sesame seeds tested positive for ethylene oxide (EtO+ECH), it was found that ethylene oxide was seen to be almost completely converted to 2-chloroethanol. (ii) The European Food Safety Authority (ESFA), in a 2022 study, states that there is not sufficient data to prove the carcinogenicity of 2-chloroethanol, and states that "Further notice pending, it is hence recommended to evaluate the genotoxicity and carcinogenicity of the metabolite 2-chloroethanol in line with that of ethylene oxide". Given that EtO is converted almost completely to ECH and that there is no sufficient safety data for ECH, it could be seen that the extremely strict Maximum Residue Limits (MRL) of 0.02 mg/kg for Chilli & Ginger and 0.1 mg/kg for other spices, fixed for EtO+ECH by EU, is based on insufficient safety evaluation data without adequate scientific basis. Hence, the claim of the EU such as no safe level of exposure for consumers can be defined and any level consumers may be exposed to, presents a potential risk to their health, needs to be explored scientifically.Possible Natural Occurrence of EtO in trace level, above the EU MRL: Literature indicates the possibility of the natural occurrence of EtO. Ethylene oxide is produced from a few natural sources. In certain plants, ethylene (a natural plant growth regulator) is degraded to ethylene oxide (Abeles & Dunn, 1985). It is also a product of ethylene catabolism in certain microorganisms (De Bont & Albers, 1976). Ethylene oxide can be generated from water-logged soil (Smith & Jackson, 1974; Jackson et al., 1978), manure, and sewage sludge (Wong et al., 1983). Evidence of ethylene metabolism is reflected in studies which show that a portion of the ethylene is oxidized to EtO (Jerie and Hall, 1978; Dodds et al., 1979; Smith et al., 1985). The findings in the studies, listed above points to the possibility of the natural occurrence of EtO in plant products and thus having a NIL tolerance approach for EtO and fixing EtO limits at the level of quantification by the EU, presents a trade barrier. No comment Period & inadequate transitional period: India would like to note that the regular notification (G/SPS/N/EU/538) for the special conditions with regard to EtO under the SPS agreement, was made only on 14 January 2022 as a regular notification, after eight days from the date of taking effect (6 January 2022), that too with NIL provision for comments. Further, India would like to note the information provided by the EU that, the EU had circulated the document (G/SPS/GEN/1968) regarding the increase of official controls and emergency measures governing the entry into the Union of certain goods from certain non-EU countries, in November 2021.  However, India would like to remind the EU that, G/SPS/GEN/1968  provided only the process, including framework, controls etc., that too in a broader perspective, without any specific information about the increase of official controls for the export of spices from India to the EU, due to the EtO concern. Hence, notification of G/SPS/GEN/1968 cannot be construed to absolve the EU of the commitment under the SPS agreement for prior notification of a regular measure. The transitional period provided by the EU, up to 17th  February 2022, only for the consignments shipped to the EU before 6th January 2022, is inadequate and was further subject to the condition of 100% testing of such consignments at the EU ports, which has caused the significant additional cost to the exporters, thereby making exports uncompetitive. Also, some of the consignments, which were shipped from India in November 2021, much before the publishing of the regulation on 15th December 2021, have been kept on hold by the EU port health authorities, for want of an Official Certificate on EtO, citing that the consignment has reached the EU port after 17th February 2022. Lack of Harmonization & Rationale in fixing EtO MRLs: The MRL fixed by the EU for EtO residues for Spices is drastically stringent when compared to other major countries. For example, USA & Canada have a limit of 947 mg/kg (EtO 7 + ECH 940) for Ethylene Oxide + 2-chloro ethanol. Moreover, for dried/dehydrated chilli & ginger EU has fixed a much more stringent limit of 0.02 mg/kg, when compared to other spices which have a limit of 0.1 mg/kg. The consumption patterns of chilli and ginger are not different from other spices. However, the maximum limits of 0.02 mg/kg in chilli and ginger are much more stringent when compared to the maximum limit of 0.1 mg/kg in other spices.The consumption data from WHO Global Environment Monitoring System (GEMS) / Food Cluster Diets (representative Cluster chosen: G08 - Austria, Germany, Poland, Spain) shows that the category ‘ Herbs, Spices, Condiments & Sauces’ is consumed at 4.79 grams/day, whereas categories such as  ‘Milk & Diary Products’, ‘Grains & Grain-based products’, ‘Vegetable and vegetable products’ etc are consumed in the range of 260.45 - 286.61 grams/day. This highlights the irrationality in fixing of EtO MRLs for Chilli & Ginger at 0.02 by the EU, at par with the MRL for milk, grains, vegetables etc.  Hence the MRL for all spices, including chilli & ginger, may be unified at 0.1 mg/kg.Imposition of increased official controls on spices which do not have a history of EtO concern: India would like to note the information from the EU that the increase in official controls for the export of spices from India to the EU is the consequence of the  RASFF (Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed) notifications concerning India, which showed contamination with ethylene oxide in spices. India would like to remind the EU that, many of the spice items such as Mint Products, Fennel, Fenugreek, Garlic, Tamarind, Nutmeg & Mace etc, which have been brought under increased official control do not have any history of RASFF alerts for EtO during the entire financial year 2021-22 (April- March).  This underlies that the blanket imposition of increased official controls for EtO on all spices exported from India to the EU is a specific trade barrier.
Summary: India was of the view that the MRL of 0.02 mg/kg for chilli and ginger and 0.1 mg/kg for other spices, fixed for ethylene oxide (EtO) and its metabolite 2-chloroethanol or ethylene chlorhydrin (ECH) together, lacked sufficient scientific basis. India stated that, given the possibility of the natural occurrence of EtO, establishing an MRL for EtO at the level of quantification constituted a trade barrier. India regretted that the notification G/SPS/N/EU/538 had not provided the possibility for comments and that the information circulated by the European Union in document G/SPS/GEN/1968 provided only the process from a broad perspective, without specific information about the increase of official controls. Likewise, the transitional period provided by the European Union was inadequate and was subject to the condition of 100% testing of such consignments at EU ports, which had caused the significant additional cost to the exporters.India also noted that the EU MRL for EtO residues was more stringent that the limits in other countries, and considered that MRLs for all spices, including chilli and ginger (which presented similar consumption patterns as other species), might be unified at 0.1 mg/kg. StatementSubmitted: India thanks the EU for its response. India would like to maintain the view that the MRL of 0.02 mg/kg for chilli and ginger and 0.1 mg/kg for other spices, fixed for ethylene oxide (EtO) and its metabolite 2-chloroethane or ethylene chlorohydrin (ECH) together, has been set on a HAZARD basis by the EU and it is lacking the sufficient risk assessment and scientific basis.Inadequate Scientific Basis:The European Union has stated that in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 1272/2008, Ethylene oxide (EtO) is classified as a mutagen, category 1B, a carcinogen, category 1B, and a reproductive toxicant, category 1B. Currently, the EU considers ethylene oxide (EtO) and its metabolite 2-chloroethanol or ethylene chlorohydrin (ECH) together, reported as ethylene oxide, in compliance assessments. The studies from the EU have reported the following:(i) The European Food Safety Authority (ESFA), in a 2022 study (https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2022.7147), states that there is no sufficient data to prove the carcinogenicity of 2-chloroethanol, and says that "Further notice pending, it is hence recommended to evaluate the genotoxicity and carcinogenicity of the metabolite 2-chloroethanol in line with that of ethylene oxide".Given that EtO is converted almost completely to ECH and that there is no sufficient safety data for ECH, it could be seen that the extremely stringent Maximum Residue Limits (MRL) of 0.02 mg/kg for Chilli & Ginger and 0.1 mg/kg for other spices, fixed for EtO+ECH by EU, is based on insufficient safety evaluation data without adequate scientific basis.(ii) Concise International Chemical Assessment Document 54 (WHO) 2003(https://www.inchem.org/documents/cicads/cicads/cicad54.htm ), states that ‘Ethylene oxide is produced from a few natural sources. In certain plants, ethylene (a natural plant growth regulator) is degraded to ethylene oxide (Abeles & Dunn, 1985). It is also a product of ethylene catabolism in certain microorganisms (De Bont & Albers, 1976). Ethylene oxide can be generated from waterlogged soil (Smith & Jackson, 1974; Jackson et al., 1978), manure, and sewage sludge (Wong et al., 1983). Quantitative estimates of production from these natural sources are not available, but emissions are expected to be negligible’, which points to the natural occurrence of EtO at trace level.The findings in the studies listed above point to the possibility of the natural occurrence of EtO in plant products. Thus, having an approach of very minimal tolerance for EtO and fixing extremely stringent EtO limits for spice by the EU, presents a trade barrier.Accordingly, as per Article 5 of the SPS agreement, the EU may consider providing the risk assessment and scientific basis for fixing the ETO MRLs in the Spices to trace level, which is a repeated request from India that the EU has not considered.Lack of Harmonization & Rationale in fixing EtO MRLs:Within the spices group, the EU has fixed extremely stringent MRL for EtO for ginger and chillies without risk assessment and scientific basis. The consumption patterns of chilli and ginger are not different from other spices. However, the maximum limits of 0.02 mg/kg for EtO in chilli and ginger are much more stringent when compared to the maximum limit of 0.1 mg/kg in other spices.The consumption data from WHO Global Environment Monitoring System (GEMS) / Food Cluster Diets (representative Cluster chosen: G08 - Austria, Germany, Poland, Spain) shows that the category ‘Herbs, Spices, Condiments & Sauces’ is consumed at 4.79 grams/day, whereas categories such as ‘Milk & Dairy Products’, ‘Grains & Grain-based products’, ‘Vegetable and vegetable products’ etc are consumed in the range of 260.45 - 286.61 grams/day. This highlights the irrationality in fixing EtO MRLs for Chilli and ginger at 0.02 by the EU, at par with the MRL for milk, grains, vegetables etc. The MRL set by the EU for EtO residues for Spices is drastically stringent when compared to other countries like the USA & Canada, which have a limit of 947 mg/kg (EtO 7 + ECH 940) for Ethylene Oxide + 2-chloro ethanol. A uniform ETO MRL of 0.1 mg/kg for all spices would have been trade facilitative and not restrictive as in the present case of a drastically stringent MRL of 0.02 mg/kg for Chilli and Ginger without risk assessment / scientific. Hence the EU may either consider providing specific scientific evidence for fixing higher MRL for EtO for chilli and ginger or may consider harmonizing the MRL for all spices, including chilli & ginger, at 0.1 mg/kg.Non-uniform, arbitrary and unjustifiable decisions with regard to re-dispatch of the rejected consignment to the source country: Article 66(b) of EU Regulation 2017/625 provides for re-dispatch of a non-compliant consignment outside the Union in accordance with Article 72 (1) and (2) of the same regulation, whereas Article 67 of EU Regulation 2017/625 stipulates destruction of the consignment if it presents a risk to human, animal or plant health, animal welfare etc.The EU member countries interpret the same concern (non-compliance with EtO MRL) non-uniformly under Article 66 or Article 67 of Regulation 2017/625. Some EU member countries have carried out mandatory destruction of the spice consignments that have not been permitted entry into the EU due to the presence of EtO exceeding the EU MRL, by considering EtO as a ‘risk’. It may be noted that countries like the USA & Canada etc, which are significant buyers of Indian spices have a limit of 947 mg/kg (EtO 7 + ECH 940) for Ethylene Oxide + 2-chloro ethanol and such mandatory destruction by the EU authorities results in the exporter losing the opportunity of exporting the same consignment to a country with higher MRL for EtO. It is also noteworthy that such mandatory destruction has been carried out by the EU Member States, despite the competent authority in India informing the Member State concerned that, if the consignment is re-dispatched to India, necessary steps will be taken to ensure that the goods will not further be exported to the EU. The non-uniform, arbitrary and unjustifiable decisions taken by EU Member States, with regard to re- dispatch of rejected consignment are trade-restrictive and acts as a significant trade barrier. The EU may consider permitting re-dispatch of the non-compliant consignments/ consignments which are deemed to possess a risk as per the EU regulation, considering that the applicable standards/regulations of various importing countries permit entry and use of such consignments in their countries.India requests the EU to:(i)Provide the risk assessment and scientific evidence for fixing higher MRL for EtO for chilli and ginger or harmonize the MRL for all spices, including chilli & ginger, at 0.1 mg/kg.(ii)Permit the re-dispatch of the non-compliant consignments/ consignments which are deemed to possess a risk as per the EU regulation
Summary: India was of the view that the MRLs of 0.02 mg/kg for chilli and ginger and 0.1 mg/kg for other spices, fixed for ethylene oxide (EtO) and its metabolite 2-chloroethanol or ethylene chlorhydrin (ECH) together, were set on a hazard basis, lacked sufficient scientific basis, and were more stringent than the limits in other countries. Noting that the consumption patterns of chilli and ginger were not different from other spices, India urged the European Union to provide the risk assessment and scientific evidence for fixing higher MRLs for EtO for chilli and ginger or to harmonize MRLs for all spices at 0.1 mg/kg. Australia raised its concerns on the European Union's plan to reduce neonicotinoid MRLs to default values and set import MRLs taking into account environmental impacts in the exporting country, without any justified risks identified for consumers. StatementSubmitted: Australia reiterates its concern about the EU’s plan to take into account environmental impacts in exporting countries when setting import MRLS and assessing requests for import tolerances.   Australia considers that decisions regarding import MRLs should only be assessed in light of food safety risks. In Australia’s view, using food MRLs as a proxy to pursue environmental standards outside EU’s borders is incompatible with international standards and guidelines, and poses a threat to third countries’ ability to apply their own environmental policies, in contradiction with WTO rules.  Australia does not consider that MRLs are an appropriate nor efficient tool to achieve environmental outcomes. Third country national authorities are indeed the best decision maker to ensure that pesticide application is undertaken in a responsible and sustainable manner in each country, and in accordance with their unique environment.   Australia notes the EU’s response at the March 2022 meeting of this committee and asks the EU to clarify to which Committee within the WTO it will notify this measure, and when it intends to notify the draft Regulation.   We look forward to continuing to engage with the EU on this important topic.

Summary: Referring to the new STC raised by India (ID 549), Australia questioned the design of the EU draft regulation on the neonicotinoid insecticides clothianidin and thiamethoxam. StatementSubmitted: China appreciates the opportunity to comment on the TBT Notification G/TBT/N/EU/908. China notices the importance to protect pollinators including bees. However, China would like to encourage the EU to consider the concerns of members and make the measure more appropriate. Firstly, China noticed that the EU normally notifies the regulations related to substance registration to WTO members through both committees on TBT and SPS, and indicates in its TBT notification its intention to notify MRL modification to WTO members through the SPS Committee. Considering MRL modification is internationally recognized as an SPS measure, the EU is advised to notify its proposed MRL development or amendment through the SPS Committee as per its usual practice instead of merely through the TBT Committee, or the proposed measures should be discussed within the SPS Committee to avoid unnecessary confusion. Secondly, China, along with the international community is in agreement that MRLs shall be set or amended to protect consumer health and facilitate fair trade of food. The environmental problems such as the decline in bee colonies can be addressed through MRL measures and are supported by neither adequate scientific evidence nor international consensus. The scientific basis for the EU to revoke and lower the MRLs of clothianidin and thiamethoxam due to the risk to bees is not sufficient. There is still a matter of academic debate about whether neonicotinoid pesticides are the main cause of the decline in bee colonies. Some studies have concluded that the combination of parasites, pesticides, pollen deficiency, and climate change is the real reason for the decline in honey bee colonies. China recommends the EU provide data and reports on the risk assessment of neonicotinoid pesticides on bees in order to confirm the scientific validity and completeness of the assessment.Thirdly, as per Article 2.2 of the TBT Agreement, members shall ensure that technical regulations are not prepared, adopted, or applied with a view to or with the effect of creating unnecessary obstacles to international trade. Revoking or lowering MRLs for clothianidin and thiamethoxam won’t affect the EU’s agricultural production since their approvals expired earlier. However, the proposed EU regulation will create unnecessary obstacles to international trade as it will be a de facto trade barrier that has major consequences on WTO members that export foods to the EU although they approve the use of the two substances, which no concern was raised after science-based risk assessment.Fourthly, as per Article 5.1 of the SPS Agreement, China believes it would be better if the EU could take full account of the differences in different pesticide products, application periods, and treated crops when conducting risk assessments of neonicotinoid pesticides on bees. Clothianidin and thiamethoxam can also be applied to non-nectar or flowering crops (no exposure to bees). In particular, the limit of crops such as crops harvested before flowering or cultivated indoors should not be revoked, and a full and reasonable risk assessment should be considered. Obviously, the EU's measures expand the scope beyond the purpose of protecting bees and create unnecessary trade barriers for other members, especially for developing members. Therefore, China suggests that the EU should formulate MRLs reasonably or in line with CAC while effectively safeguarding the safety of bees and other non-target organisms.
Summary: China referred to its statement under STC ID 549. China had also raised this concern in the TBT Committee and looked forward to bilateral engagement.
