StatementSubmitted: El Ecuador agradece a los demás Miembros que han levantado esta preocupación y a quienes la apoyan.  Al Ecuador le  inquieta respecto a los principios que guían esta categoría de decisiones de la Unión Europea. Invitamos a la a notificar estas medias en este comité sin perjuicio de la como  notificación en el Comité OTC el 6 de julio de 2022 (G/TBT/N/EU/908). Nuevamente el Ecuador quisiera señala que la propuesta de la Unión Europea de utilizar barreras no arancelarias al comercio para proteger el ambiente, desconoce y descalifica la idoneidad de las políticas regulatorias de los demás países, los cuales soberanamente establecen las condiciones de producción de alimentos y la actividad agrícola en sus jurisdicciones. Estos objetivos extraterritoriales de la UE no siempre parecen ajustarse a las Reglas de la OMC, sin tomarse en cuenta las condiciones climáticas y el desarrollo de sus distintos socios comerciales. Entendemos que la UE siendo pionera de estas medidas y con el fin de cumplir con los objetivos propuestos en el Pacto Verde se ha apartado de obligaciones contenidas del Acuerdo sobre Medidas Sanitarias y Fitosanitarias -MSF- de la OMC, en los que se requiere conocer si se ha establecido un análisis de riesgo concluyente respecto a la afectación de la salud humana y de los polinizadores. Sin embargo, la UE sin contar con un análisis concluyente está estableciendo los límites más bajos posibles para sectores como las frutas tropicales, el café y el cacao, principales productos de exportaciones al mercado europeo. La no renovación en el uso de una sustancia activa o la consecuente fijación de un límite máximo de residuos (LMR) a niveles mínimos de detección analítica, se traduce en un cierre de facto. Adicionalmente, se requiere conocer en qué normativas u organismo internacional se está basando para establecer los LMR para los neonicoticoides (clotianidina y tiametoxam). Para el caso del banano, el tiametoxam es efectivo contra los nemátodos y el pulgón negro, mientras que para el caso de las flores tiene efectividad en lo thrips y el pulgón. Igualmente, la cantidad de residuos que deja en el ambiente es significativamente menor y con una descomposición mucho más rápida que otros productos. En virtud de lo expuesto las disposiciones que está tomando la UE estarían contraponiéndose al AMSF – OMC en cuanto a los principios de no discriminación contra los productos importados (artículo 2.3), la transparencia (artículo 7 y Anexo B), la necesidad de justificación científica y la utilización de normas internacionales (artículos 2, 3 y 5) y procedimientos de control, inspección y aprobación que facilitan el comercio (Anexo C). Finalmente, estas medidas afectan negativamente a los pequeños productores. Se invita a la UE a continuar con los diálogos respecto a las medidas que se encuentran planteando, y que estas sean consideradas en el marco del Acuerdo MSF cuyo objeto es proteger la salud del consumidor y evitar al mismo tiempo obstáculos injustificados al comercio.
Summary: Ecuador shared the concern regarding the EU's extraterritorial objectives, which did not seem to follow WTO rules. The EU proposal to use non-tariff trade barriers for environmental protection disqualified the legislation of trading partners. Asking about the regulatory basis for the decision, Ecuador observed that the non-renewal of a substance or the lowering of MRLs without conclusive risk analyses regarding the effects of neonicotinoids on human health and pollinators was leading to a de facto market closure, affecting small producers. Ecuador invited the European Union to notify the measure to the SPS Committee and continue the dialogue to avoid unnecessary trade barriers.

StatementSubmitted: China appreciates the opportunity to comment on the TBT Notification G/TBT/N/EU/908. To avoid causing unnecessary confusion, China advises the EU to notify its proposed MRL development or amendment through the SPS Committee as per its usual practice.The environmental problems such as the decline in bee colonies can be addressed through MRL measures supported by neither adequate scientific evidence nor international consensus. The scientific basis for the EU to revoke and lower the MRLs of clothianidin and thiamethoxam due to the risk to bees is not sufficient. There is still a matter of academic debate about whether neonicotinoid pesticides are the main cause of the decline in bee colonies. Some studies have concluded that the combination of parasites, pesticides, pollen deficiency, and climate change is the real reason for the decline in honey bee colonies. In the face of increasing restrictions on various active compounds, which may be the basis of agricultural production, the proposed EU regulation would create an unnecessary barrier to international trade as it would have a significant impact on WTO members. China recommends the EU provide data and reports on the risk assessment of neonicotinoid pesticides on bees in order to confirm the scientific validity and completeness of the assessment.
Summary: China appreciated the opportunity to comment on the notification G/TBT/N/EU/908 and invited the European Union to notify the proposed MRL developments to the SPS Committee. China was of the view that the scientific basis underpinning the revoking and lowering of MRLs for clothianidin and thiamethoxam due to the risk to bees was not sufficient. China noted the lack of scientific consensus on the reason for the decline in honeybee colonies, while the combination of parasites, pesticides, pollen deficiency, and climate change might be the reason for the decline in honey bee colonies. China recommended that the European Union provide the relevant data and risk assessment report in order to confirm the validity and completeness of the risk assessment of neonicotinoid pesticides on bees.

StatementSubmitted: Australia would again like to raise its concerns with the EU’s Regulation on the neonicotinoid insecticides clothianidin and thiamethoxam for environmental purposes and the lack of response from the EU to reconsider its approach despite the widespread concerns expressed by third countries within the SPS Committee and other forums.  Australia considers there is a lack of scientific evidence to support a link between a lowering of the MRLs and pollinator health. Like other Members, Australia considers that import MRLs are not an appropriate nor an efficient tool to pursue environmental outcomes. This stems from the design of MRL settings whose objective is to ensure food safety and facilitate trade of safe agri-food products. MRLs are not designed to measure environmental health in third countries. The Codex Committee on Pesticide Residues recently confirmed that consideration of environmental issues of global concern was outside the scope of its mandate.Using food MRLs as a proxy to pursue environmental standards outside EU’s borders is incompatible with international standards and guidelines, and poses a threat to third countries’ ability to apply their own environmental policies consistent with their unique environmental circumstances, and of course, in contradiction with WTO rules. Such a misapplication of the MRL instrument, may undermine current MRL setting principles and efforts toward harmonisation among Members.Australia therefore calls on the EU to find a less restrictive alternative that meets the objective of protection of pollinators’ health, while preserving trade and third countries’ sovereign rights to conduct their own unique risk assessments. We consider that such an alternative approach should be discussed with third countries in the relevant multilateral forums. Australia would be pleased to work with the EU and other Members at these forums on this important topic.
Summary: Australia questioned the design of the EU regulation on the neonicotinoid insecticides clothianidin and thiamethoxam and lack of response from the European Union to reconsider its approach despite the widespread concerns expressed by third countries within the SPS Committee and other forums. Australia was of the view that only food safety risks should drive decisions regarding import MRLs and that MRLs were not an appropriate nor an efficient tool to pursue environmental outcomes. Australia considered that using food MRLs as a proxy to pursue environmental standards outside EU borders was incompatible with international standards and guidelines and threatened Members' ability to apply their own environmental policies, in contradiction with WTO rules. Australia called on the European Union to find a less restrictive alternative that would meet its objective while preserving trade and third countries' sovereignty. Australia also requested the European Union to provide robust scientific evidence in support of the link between the lowering of MRLs to the limit of determination and pollinator health.

StatementSubmitted: EU import tolerances for certain pesticides to achieve environmental outcomes in third countries (ID 534)India share concerns raised by other members on the EU approach to import tolerances to achieve environmental outcomes in third countries. Summary: India shared the concerns regarding the extraterritorial application of domestic laws and reiterated its request that the European Union delay the implementation of the regulation's amendments and engage with Members to find a viable solution.

StatementSubmitted: EUROPEAN UNION IMPORT TOLERANCES FOR CERTAIN PESTICIDES TO ACHIEVE ENVIRONMENTAL OUTCOMES IN THIRD COUNTRIES – SPECIFIC TRADE CONCERN 534Statement by the United States of America - July 2023 SPS Committee:The United States notes that the high volume of concern from WTO members representing a broad swathe of agricultural producers around the world highlights the diversity and extent of multilateral opposition to the EU’s approach of integrating environmental concerns into the use of pesticide MRLs and the establishment of import tolerance.The United States shares the European Commission’s goals for the continued transition to more sustainable food systems. We recognize the importance of tailoring measures that take into account the economic, social, and environmental dimensions of sustainability that are unique to each Member. We also note that Members’ sustainability actions must be consistent with their obligations under relevant WTO Agreements.The United States reiterates its concerns with the application of EU domestic environmental policies to food and agricultural products imported from third countries. We echo the comments of the many WTO Members who rightly understand that countries require the use of diverse approaches, tools, and technologies to meet their sustainability objectives. We can all agree that pest control and crop protection needs vary by crop and by country and region.  National competent authorities must remain empowered to establish the measures necessary for the protection of human, animal, or plant life or health within their own territories. However, the regulation published in the Official Journal of the European Union on February 15, 2023, is a de facto extension of the EU’s production requirements to farming communities outside the EU because it requires third country imports to satisfy the EU’s environmental policy preferences and comply with pesticide MRLs that appear to have been reduced without scientific justification.Pesticide MRLs are not an appropriate tool for achieving the EU’s domestic environmental objectives. International consensus-based pesticide MRLs reflect the highest level of pesticide residue that is legally tolerated in or on food or feed in consideration of consumer exposure and possible health risks; pesticide MRLs are not an appropriate or efficient indicator of environmental outcomes because MRLs are not developed to address this objective. We note that in the most recent European Food Safety Authority, or EFSA, opinion, the European competent authority on MRLs determined that existing EU MRLs did not pose a food safety risk for consumers.  The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and Codex also completed science-based human health risk assessments confirming that existing MRLs above the limit of determination for clothianidin and thiamethoxam do not pose a food safety risk for consumers. WTO Members rely on pesticide MRLs, including MRLs established by Codex, to ensure food safety for consumers and to facilitate trade in agricultural products. The United States reminds the EU that the Codex Committee on Pesticide Residues, or CCPR, confirmed in 2022 that consideration of environmental issues of global concern is not within its mandate and that environmental issues are not included in CCPR risk management principles. The United States shares the EU’s concerns about pollinator health and is actively working to protect bees and other pollinators in the United States.  We note the widely shared scientific understanding that complex interactions among multiple factors affect bee colony and wild pollinator health, including the presence of pests, pathogens, and diseases; pesticide use; poor nutrition due to loss of foraging habitats and monoculture; bee management practices; and lack of genetic diversity. The United States would again reiterate our concerns with the paucity of scientific evidence that the EU has provided thus far to demonstrate the relationship between the new regulation and the stated objective of protecting animal or plant life or health and protection of the environment in a manner that is no more trade restrictive than necessary.  The EU has not provided data demonstrating that the use of these substances at current MRL levels poses an actual risk to pollinators, either in the EU or globally. The studies cited only evaluate European production systems and a limited number of pollinators found in Europe and do not take into account regional conditions, practices, and fauna in other parts of the world.We therefore repeat our request that the EU provide robust scientific evidence and scientific justification that demonstrates how the reduction of these two pesticide MRLs contributes to protecting global pollinator health, the stated objective of the EU’s measure. Regardless of the transition period provided by the EU, measures that are not technically justified should not be implemented by Members.   Global challenges require collaboration across the global community; unilateral approaches based on questionable and incomplete science may complicate or further delay meaningful progress on these pressing issues while unnecessarily affecting agricultural production and trade. In place of the EU’s regulation, the United States continues to welcome a collaborative approach to protecting pollinators and the opportunity to exchange resources, scientific expertise, and new ideas.
Summary: The United States recalled that Members' actions to pursue shared sustainability goals should be consistent with WTO rules, and echoed concerns regarding the extraterritorial application of EU environmental domestic policies. The United States reinforced the need for diverse approaches in different regions and noted the unclear link between the stated objective of protecting global pollinator health and the EU requirement that imported food and agricultural products meet the reduced MRLs for clothianidin and thiamethoxam. In the US view, pesticide MRLs were not the appropriate tool to address environmental health objectives and the EU measure restricted trade more than necessary, given a shared scientific understanding that pollinator health was affected by complex interactions among multiple factors. The United States submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2146.

StatementSubmitted: The United States reiterates its concerns with the European Union’s Commission Regulation 2023/334 regarding the reduction of maximum residue levels (MRLs) for clothianidin and thiamethoxam, notified to the TBT Committee as G/TBT/N/EU/908 on June 6, 2022, through which the EU appears to be applying domestic environmental policies to food and agricultural products imported from third countries.   The United States is disappointed that the EU has not provided a substantive response to the legitimate concerns raised by multiple Members in this Committee. This lack of response is particularly troubling considering recent farmer protests in EU member states that would suggest that agricultural producers within the EU are aligned with concerns previously raised by Members regarding the detrimental effects of these measures.  Given the critical importance of pesticides such as clothianidin and thiamethoxam to produce crops that are exported to the EU from the United States and other WTO Members, we are concerned that the reduction of these MRLs to the limit of quantification, or LOQ, poses a significant barrier to trade.  As the EU has previously recognized, global environmental challenges cannot be achieved by prescriptive, one-size-fits-all approaches that are narrowly tailored to the conditions in one country or region.  The United States urges the EU to refrain from using pesticide MRLs outside of their intended purpose, which is to allow regulators to monitor the lawful applications of pesticides and to ensure consumer food safety.  WTO Members rely on pesticide MRLs, including MRLs established by Codex, to ensure food safety for consumers and to facilitate trade in agricultural products. International consensus-based pesticide MRLs reflect the highest level of pesticide residue that is acceptable in or on food or feed in consideration of consumer exposure and possible health risks; pesticide MRLs are not an appropriate or efficient indicator of environmental outcomes because MRLs are not developed to address this objective.  The United States recalls that the European Food Safety Authority’s (EFSA) review of clothianidin and thiamethoxam recommended MRLs that were safe for consumers.  We, therefore, reiterate our request for the EU to share the scientific and technical information that demonstrates how the reduction of these MRLs to the LOQ for products produced outside of the EU protects pollinators, including bees. In the absence of scientific or technical information indicating how the reduction of MRLs to the LOQ for products produced outside of the EU contributes to the objective of protection of pollinators, including bees, the United States requests that the EU refrain from additional attempts to achieve global environmental outcomes through pesticide MRLs and to restore prior MRLs for clothianidin and thiamethoxam.
Summary: The United States reiterated its concerns regarding the Regulation (EU) 2023/334 lowering MRLs for clothianidin and thiamethoxam, notified as G/TBT/N/EU/908, through which the European Union appeared to be extending its domestic environmental policies to imported food and agricultural products from third countries. The United States emphasized that reducing MRLs for these critical pesticides posed a significant barrier to trade, underscoring the need for diverse approaches in different regions. Noting the unclear link between the stated objective of protecting global pollinator health and the EU requirement that imported food and agricultural products met the reduced MRLs for clothianidin and thiamethoxam, the United States insisted that MRLs were not the appropriate tool to address environmental health objectives. The United States urged the European Union to provide scientific evidence on how the reduction of MRLs contributed to the protection of pollinators and, in the absence of such evidence, to restore the previous MRLs. The United States provided its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2216.

Summary: The United States reiterated its concerns regarding the lowering of MRLs for clothianidin and thiamethoxam, through which the European Union appeared to be extending its domestic environmental policies to imported products from third countries. In the absence of scientific justification indicating how the reduction of MRLs to the limit of quantification (LOQ) for products produced outside of the European Union contributed to consumer health, the United States requested the European Union to restore previous MRLs. The United States submitted its statement in document G/SPS/GEN/2242.

StatementSubmitted: Tolerancias de importación de la UE para ciertos pesticidas para lograr resultados ambientales en terceros países (ID 534)Colombia expresa su preocupación respecto a tolerancias de importación de la UE para ciertos pesticidas para lograr resultados ambientales en terceros países. Es por ello, que quisiera que se registrara que Colombia apoya la preocupación que India presentó ayer sobre esta sustancia thiacloprid, un neocotinoide. En el caso de Clothianidin y Thiamethoxam, la UE ha rechazado tolerancias de importación a pesar de contar con suficiente evidencia científica, violando el Acuerdo MSF. También solicitamos una actualización sobre el número de autorizaciones de emergencia y tolerancias de importación solicitadas y rechazadas, así como el tiempo promedio de procesamiento de estas solicitudes, como se mencionó en el documento G/SPS/GEN/2038. Quisiera incorporar las declarations de Colombia en los comites aneteriores.Preocupaciones sobre ThiaclopridTriacloprid es un neocotinoide Cloronicotinilo con actividad insecticida (MoA IRAC Grupo 4A), por vía sistémica y residual; actúa por contacto e ingestión sobre insectos (chupadores y masticadores). Actúa como agonístico sobre el receptor nicotínico de la acetilcolina del sistema central, primero estimulando las membranas postsinápticas y después paralizando la conducción nerviosa. Sus propiedades insecticidas se basan en la activación y siguiente bloqueo de los impulsos nerviosos en los receptores acetilcolínicos postsinápticos lo que produce la muerte de los insectos. Es transportado por la savia bruta y distribuido por las hojas conforme va desarrollándose la planta.Colombia utiliza el pesticida en varias pacifloras como la grandilla. Basado en una evaluación científica profunda realizada por la EFSA, en mayo de 2023, la Comisión Europea propuso mantener la mayoría de los LMR existentes para thiacloprid, especialmente aquellos basados en los LMR del Codex Alimentarius (CXL) y las Tolerancias de Importación.En septiembre y diciembre de 2023, los Estados miembros de la UE votaron sobre la propuesta a nivel técnico y político. No hubo mayoría calificada en apoyo a la propuesta. Varios Estados miembros se opusieron a establecer LMR para sustancias que cumplen con los criterios de “eliminación” de la UE, citando la “competencia desleal” para los agricultores de la UE como una razón.El 17 de enero de 2024, el Parlamento Europeo se opuso a la propuesta de la Comisión Europea de mantener la mayoría de los LMR de thiacloprid a pesar de la evaluación científica favorable reciente de la EFSA. El Parlamento solicitó a la Comisión preparar un nuevo borrador de reglamento que reduzca todos los LMR de thiacloprid al límite de detección (LOD).El 1 de febrero, el Primer Ministro francés, en respuesta a las protestas de los agricultores franceses, declaró que se tomarían medidas para “proteger contra la competencia desleal” y que Francia implementaría una cláusula de salvaguardia respecto al thiacloprid.El 23 de febrero de 2024, Francia suspendió la introducción, importación y comercialización de frutas y verduras frescas de países no pertenecientes a la UE tratadas con thiacloprid y que contengan residuos cuantificables (por encima de 0,01 mg/kg), citando serias preocupaciones de salud humana.El 5 de marzo, durante una reunión del SCoPAFF para discutir la medida francesa:La Comisión consideró que no había un riesgo inmediato y serio para la salud que justificara una medida a nivel de toda la UE para reducir todos los LMR de thiacloprid. Una posible solución podría ser trabajar prioritariamente en una medida regular que aborde las preocupaciones de los Estados miembros, basada en indicaciones de que el thiacloprid es un posible disruptor endocrino (ED), como identificó la EFSA en 2019.El 22 de abril, la Comisión de la UE propuso provisionalmente reducir todos los LMR de thiacloprid al LOD, citando un enfoque precautorio hacia la protección del consumidor, a la espera de evaluaciones adicionales de la EFSA sobre sus propiedades ED y la toxicidad para las abejas.El 8 de mayo, la UE notificó al Comité MSF de la OMC (G/SPS/N/EU/763), iniciando un período de comentarios de 60 días que finaliza el 7 de julio.La próxima discusión sobre los LMR de la UE podría ocurrir en la reunión del SCoPAFF de septiembre, con el objetivo de adopción en otoño y entrada en vigor el 31 de diciembre de 2024. Se permitiría un período de transición de seis meses para que las partes interesadas cumplan con los nuevos requisitos.PreocupacionesLa medida propuesta genera preocupaciones sobre la previsibilidad del proceso de establecimiento de TI de la UE, potencialmente cargando a los productores y exportadores fuera de la UE, dada la incertidumbre sobre el período de revisión para obtener la información adicional necesaria para las evaluaciones de riesgo.Incertidumbres y Preguntas¿Por qué la evaluación de riesgo de la EFSA, basada en información científica reciente y utilizada como base para la propuesta inicial de la Comisión de la UE, ahora se considera insuficiente?Si la EFSA concluyó en 2023 que no hay riesgo para la salud del consumidor, ¿qué nueva información requiere ahora reducir provisionalmente todos los LMR de thiacloprid al LOD?El Acuerdo MSF permite medidas SPS provisionales basadas en la información disponible, pero requiere obtener información adicional para una evaluación de riesgo más objetiva y revisar las medidas dentro de un tiempo razonable. ¿Cuándo espera la UE completar su evaluación de riesgo?¿Por qué la UE se desvía de las prácticas pasadas al reducir los LMR al LOD cuando la EFSA y la Comisión no solicitan nuevos estudios?Reducir las ITs requiere ajustes complejos para los agricultores y otras partes interesadas, especialmente para productos de larga vida útil. El período de transición propuesto impondrá una carga indebida a los productores y exportadores en los Miembros exportadores.Finalmente, la decisión unilateral de Francia de suspender la importación de frutas y verduras frescas tratadas con thiacloprid es preocupante, especialmente cuando la Comisión de la UE afirmó que no había un riesgo inmediato y serio para la salud que justificara una medida a nivel de toda la UE. Estas medidas unilaterales se impusieron sin previo aviso a los socios comerciales.Colombia amablemente solicita a la Unión Europea considerar nuestra consulta sobre la revisión de estas regulaciones y la alineación con las normas internacionales para evitar medidas que puedan percibirse como proteccionistas y que afectan negativamente el comercio.
Summary: Referring to its full statement on eAgenda, Colombia reiterated its concerns regarding the EU import tolerances for certain pesticides and expressed support for STC ID 585. Colombia regretted that the European Union had lowered the MRL for thiacloprid to the LOD despite a favourable evaluation by EFSA in 2023 and that France had unilaterally suspended imports of produce treated with thiacloprid. Colombia requested the European Union to revise its regulation and align with international standards.

StatementSubmitted: India would like to reiterate its concerns regarding application by the EU of domestic environmental policies to food and agricultural products imported from third countries. Concerns on the EU setting import tolerances to achieve environmental outcomes in third countries has been raised by various Member States but the EU has been unable to provide satisfactory justification. The EU’s assertion of MC12 SPS Declaration Work Programme and the important role of the SPS Committee in the transition towards sustainable food systems is without prejudice to its obligations under the Agreement on Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures (SPS Agreement). India expresses its deep concern regarding the reduction of MRLs citing global environmental concerns. India urges the EU for giving positive consideration to the diverse agricultural practices, soil compositions, and climatic variations present in different Member States and not adopt a one-size-fits-all approach to import tolerances. In addition, setting of MRLs and related import tolerances for reasons unrelated to food safety and health risks is against the scope and objective of the SPS Agreement and creates trade restrictions which cannot be justified without presenting scientific evidence. India calls the EU to revise their MRLs and import tolerances on the basis of objective scientific justification and assessment of risk.
Summary: India reiterated its concerns about the European Union applying domestic environmental policies to imported products. To India, the EU reference to the MC12 SPS Declaration Work Programme and the Committee's role in the transition to sustainable food systems did not absolve the European Union of its obligations under the SPS Agreement. India added that the setting of MRLs and import tolerances for reasons unrelated to food safety and health risks was against the scope and objective of the SPS Agreement and created unjustified trade restrictions. India called on the European Union to revise its MRLs and import tolerances based on objective scientific justification and risk assessment.

StatementSubmitted: According to COMMISSION IMPLEMENTING REGULATION (EU) 2021/405 laying down the lists of third countries or regions thereof authorized for the entry into the Union of certain animals and goods intended for human consumption in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2017/625 of the European Parliament and of the Council, China is included in the list of third countries authorized for the entry of collagen into the EU in ANNEX IX, ANNEX XII and ANNEX XIII.We request that the EU implement the above regulation and remove the warning on the registration page 'Collagen is not listed in the Annex to Commission Decision 2002/994/EC'. According to Article 2 of the same Decision, collagen originating from China is not authorized to be imported into EU’.
Summary: China informed the Committee that pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2017/625, Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/405 authorized collagen from China in accordance with its Annexes IX, XII, and XIII. China regretted that the European Union intended to use the previous Commission Decision 2002/994/EC which prohibited the import of collagen from China, and stated that it had raised the same concern in the TBT Committee. China urged the European Union to implement the more recent EU regulation.

StatementSubmitted: China raised the concerns once again on the EU’s restrictions of the importation of collagen for human consumption. In 2002, the EU issued Commission Decision 2002/994/EC, restricting the importation of collagen and other products of animal origin. Since then, the above-mentioned Commission Decision has been revised several times, and the EU has successively issued relevant regulations. Thanks to the joint efforts of both sides, the EU approved the registration of Chinese collagen production enterprises in 2016. The official website of the EU has published the lists of the registered Chinese enterprises and the corresponding export products as collagen. However, since 2018, the EU has placed a warning on the registration website stating that collagen from China is not authorized to be imported into the EU. After many times of coordination, the EU canceled the warning in August 2021, and the exportation resumed. However, recently the EU displays the warning “China collagen is not listed in the Annex to Commission Decision 2002/994/EC” on the website again. Chinese collagen is blocked from customs clearance. We believe that the EU should make timely adjustments to this Commission Decision, especially its Annex, adding China’s collagen in the Annex, so as to ensure the consistency of the Commission Decision and its Annex with the subsequent amendments, and the accuracy of information disclosure of EU competent authorities and the consistency of enforcement at the customs. China hopes that the EU could resume the exportation from registered Chinese enterprises as soon as possible.
Summary: China reiterated its concern regarding EU Commission Decision 2002/994/EC restricting imports of collagen and other products of animal origin into the European Union. The Commission Decision had been revised and successive regulations had been issued. The European Union had approved the registration of Chinese collagen production enterprises in 2016, with an official website listing the registered Chinese enterprises and export products. China underlined that the European Union had blocked Chinese collagen from customs clearance, and that the official website displayed a warning of Chinese collagen not being listed in the Annex to Commission Decision 2002/994/EC. China asked the European Union to add Chinese collagen to the Annex of its Decision to ensure their consistency with subsequent amendments.

StatementSubmitted: In December 2021, EU reported that it amended regulation (EU) No. 2019 / 1793, temporarily increased official control and emergency measures, listed Chinese xanthan gum in Annex II, and increased the detection frequency of 2-ethylene oxide and its reactant chloroethanol by 20%. The manufacturer is also required to attach a statement of all product sampling and analysis results in accordance with EU regulation No. 396 / 2005 and (EU) 2019 / 1793 on the maximum residue of ethylene oxide. In our opinion, the above-mentioned measures of the European side have the following problems:Firstly, the EU ethylene oxide (EO) limit standard is not scientific: At present, most countries do not have the limit requirements for ethylene oxide and 2-chloroethanol in food, and the settings in a few regions are also carried out separately.Secondly, insufficient evidence to initiate relevant measures. EU informed that the measure was taken because it received a warning notice from RASFF about xanthan gum produced in China. Xanthan gum produced in China is sold well in many countries or regions around the world. The main reason for frequent setbacks in the EU region is that the EU tacitly believes that xanthan gum for different purposes is an additive for food and feed, so it limits the same strict standards.  In fact, xanthan gum has the effects of anti-oxidation and preventing skin aging.Therefore, xanthan gum is regarded as its main functional component in many cosmetics factories in Europe. The practice of covering all relevant production enterprises in the industry did not give Chinese products an appropriate adaptation period, which seriously affected the normal production of enterprises.Thirdly,  it should be noted that the occurrence probability of ethylene oxide in xanthan gum is very low. Ethylene oxide (EO) may come from fumigation disinfection or packaging contact materials.Lastly, the Chinese side was notified that the residues of ethylene oxide and 2-chloroethanol in the products were very low. According to statistics in 2021, the EU RASFF system reported that 19 batches of Chinese exported food(including the food additives) exceeded the standard due to ethylene oxide and 2-chloroethanol. The lowest detectable value of ethylene oxide residue in the notification was 0.068mg/kg, the lowest detection value of 2-chloroethanol residue is 0.29mg/kg.Therefore, China hopes that the EU will consider the scientific basis and necessity of the (EU) 2019/1793 requirements for EO residue of xanthan gum and other food exported to EU , adjust the restrictions or delimit the residue range according to the way of use based on the principle of minimizing trade restrictions. If there are corresponding restrictions on xanthan gum, it is suggested to consider canceling or reducing the detection frequency of ethylene oxide and 2-chloroethanol imported from China based on the manufacturing and packaging characteristics of xanthan gum.
Summary: Referring to its full statement available on eAgenda, China emphasized that the EU ethylene oxide limit was not science-based, and that only a few countries imposed limits on ethylene oxide and chloroethanol in food, and that these limits varied according to food category. China also highlighted that the occurrence probability of ethylene oxide in xanthan gum was very low, and could come from fumigation disinfection or packaging contact materials. China urged the European Union to consider the scientific basis and necessity of the requirements of Regulation (EU) 2019/1793 for ethylene oxide residues of xanthan gum, and adjust the residue limit, using a less trade-restrictive approach.

StatementSubmitted: The arsenic limit in the draft regulation notified by the Indonesian FDA is 0.15 mg/kg, which is in conflict with the limit of 2.0mg/kg stipulated in the Dry Baking Yeast Standard, (SNI 01-2982-1992), issued by BSN.At present, the arsenic limit of yeast stipulated by the regulations and standards of international organizations and most WTO members is 1.5-5mg/kg, and the arsenic limit of different types of yeast is different. According to the classification of dry yeast, fresh yeast and liquid yeast, their corresponding arsenic limits are reduced successively.The arsenic limit in the notification is too strict, which is quite different from the international practice, and there are no different arsenic limit standards formulated for different yeast categories. The arsenic limit is too strict, lacking a scientific basis, which has a negative impact on international trade. It is suggested that the regulation on the limit of arsenic in yeast be adjusted to 1.5mg/kg-5.0mg/kg according to different types of yeasts.
Summary: China expressed its concerns about the arsenic limit of 0.15 mg/kg in the draft regulation notified by Indonesia, which was at odds with the 2.0 mg/kg limit stipulated in the dry baking yeast standard, issued by the National Standardization Agency of Indonesia. China stated that the internationally recognized arsenic limit for yeast was 1.5-5 mg/kg, while the arsenic limit for different types of yeast varied. In China's view, the arsenic limit in Indonesia's draft regulation was excessive, lacked scientific basis, and had a negative impact on international trade. China proposed adjusting the arsenic limit to 1.5 mg/kg-5.0 mg/kg based on the type of yeast.

StatementSubmitted: China once again raised concerns on Indonesia’s draft regulation on heavy metals contaminants in processed food. Based on arsenic standards of yeast from international organizations and Codex members and the test data of commercial dried yeast in various countries, which has been provided to Indonesia before this meeting, China believes that the arsenic limit of 0.15 milligram per kilogram in yeast is too strict and substantially different from the international common practice, and no different arsenic limit is set for different yeast types. Therefore, China requests Indonesia to explain and clarify the reason that arsenic limits for different yeast types are not specified, and strongly suggests that the draft regulation be formulated for different yeast types and in line with international standards or common practice. Thanks very much.
Summary: China reiterated its concerns regarding Indonesia's draft regulation on heavy metals contaminants in processed food. China underlined that the arsenic limit of 0.15 mg/kg in yeast was too strict, substantially different from international common practice, and that no different arsenic limit was set for different yeast types. China requested Indonesia to clarify the reason for not specifying arsenic limits for different yeast types, and suggested that the draft regulation be formulated for different yeast types and in line with international standards or common practice.

The European Union expressed its concerns with Chinese Taipei's new procedure, notified in document G/SPS/N/TPKM/543, which required third countries to submit detailed dossiers on animal disease status, to allow for a subsequent risk assessment to be conducted by Chinese Taipei. The European Union stated that the animal disease status of its relevant products was verified by the European Commission and notified to the OIE. The European Union expressed regret that, despite its comments, the procedure had entered into force in Chinese Taipei in December 2021. In the view of the European Union, the new procedure was burdensome and inconsistent with Article 5.6 of the SPS Agreement.

StatementSubmitted: The European Union regrets to reiterate its concerns on the procedure of Chinese Taipei concerning the recognition of infectious animal disease-free status of a foreign country. (Notification G/SPS/N/TPKM/543)This procedure requiring third countries to submit detailed dossiers on their animal health disease status and the subsequent risk assessment to be conducted by the authorities of Chinese Taipei is an unnecessarily burdensome and redundant procedure.The animal disease status of the EU Member States is verified by the European Commission and is notified to the OIE.In addition, a Member-State-by-Member-State and disease-by-disease recognition process is not in line with Article 5.6 of the WTO SPS Agreement, as it is clearly not the least trade restrictive option to confirm disease freedom.Despite the detailed comments of the EU on this matter transmitted to Chinese Taipei on several occasions, the concerns of the EU have not been taken into consideration in the final text of the regulation, which eventually entered into force in December 2021.The EU considers it is not scientifically justified to require the recognition of disease-free status of e.g.: classical swine fever (CSF), risk status of BSE for the reason that Chinese Taipei has been recently recognized by the OIE as free from peste des petits ruminants (PPR) and African horse sickness (AHS).The EU calls on Chinese Taipei to resolve this issue by relying on the status notified to the OIE.
Summary: The European Union expressed its concerns with Chinese Taipei's new procedure for the recognition of infectious animal disease-free status of a foreign country, notified in document G/SPS/N/TPKM/543, which required third countries to submit detailed dossiers on animal disease status, to allow for a subsequent risk assessment to be conducted by Chinese Taipei. The European Union stated that the animal disease status of its relevant products was verified by the European Commission and notified to WOAH. The European Union expressed regret that, despite its comments, the new procedure had entered into force in December 2021. In the view of the European Union, the procedure was burdensome and inconsistent with Article 5.6 of the SPS Agreement.

StatementSubmitted: The European Union regrets to reiterate its concerns on the procedure of Chinese Taipei concerning the recognition of infectious animal disease-free status of a foreign country. (Notification G/SPS/N/TPKM/543)This procedure requiring third countries to submit detailed dossiers on their animal health disease status and the subsequent risk assessment to be conducted by the authorities of Chinese Taipei is an unnecessarily burdensome and redundant procedure.The animal disease status of the EU Member States is verified by the European Commission and is notified to the WOAH.In addition, a Member-State-by-Member-State and disease-by-disease recognition process is not in line with Article 5.6 of the WTO SPS Agreement, as it is clearly not the least trade restrictive option to confirm disease freedom.Despite the detailed comments of the EU on this matter transmitted to Chinese Taipei on several occasions, the concerns of the EU have not been taken into consideration in the final text of the regulation, which eventually entered into force in December 2021.The EU calls on Chinese Taipei to resolve this issue by relying on the status notified to the WOAH.
Summary: The European Union was of the view that the procedure applied by Chinese Taipei to recognize the infectious animal disease-free status of foreign countries, notified in G/SPS/N/TPKM/543, was unnecessarily burdensome and redundant. The European Union regretted that the regulation had entered into force in December 2021 without taking into account the EU concerns. The European Union was of the view that the procedure was not in line with Article 5.6 of the SPS Agreement, and requested Chinese Taipei to resolve this issue by relying on the animal disease status verified by the European Commission and notified to WOAH.

StatementSubmitted: Brazil would like to bring to the attention of this Committee an issue it has been facing to export wet blue leather to Thailand. Brazil understands that Thailand should not require an international health certificate for allowing exports of this category of products.Wet blue leather is a processed product that does not pose risks to animal or human health of an importing country. Since 2019, Brazil made extensive efforts toprovide technical information on the topic to the Department of Livestock Development (DLD). After a series of bilateral contacts without any progress, in 2021, Thailand refused a proposal of a bilateral meeting with Brazil on the margins of the 81st SPS Committee Regular Meeting. Thailand argued that there would be no additional issue to address and affirmed that Brazil should held negotiations directly with the DLD. Brazil regrets this lack of disposition to address the issue bilaterally, the reason why we are proposing this STC. Thailand affirms that its Animal Epidemics Act B.E 2558 definition of "carcass" encompasses leather products, therefore requiring a health certificate to support imports. However, the OIE Terrestrial Code mentions in article 8.8.27 that national authorities should authorize, without requiring additional certification, imports of wet blue leather. Therefore, Brazil would like to address the following four questions:1) Is the 2015 Animal Epidemics Act B.E 2558 based on any international standard or guideline? 2) What was the scientific justification used by the DLD for the definition of "carcass" and for the inclusion of "finished artificial items made from carcasses asprescribed in the Notifications by the Minister"? 3) What official publication states that wet blue leather should be considered carcass? 4) Brazil has failed to locate Thailand`s WTO notification for the 2015 Animal Epidemics Act B.E 2558 and its following modifications. We would like to know if there was any notification for this legislation, and if so, if Thailand could kindly provide it.Brazil kindly expects Thailand`s answers and hopes that Thailand will withdraw the requirement of a health certificate for wet blue leather within a reasonable period of time.
Summary: Brazil raised its concerns about the export of wet blue leather to Thailand, which was subject to a health certificate requirement. Brazil noted that Thailand's 2015 Animal Epidemics Act B.E 2558 included wet blue leather under the definition of "carcass" and considered this to be at odds with Article 8.8.27 of the OIE Terrestrial Code. Brazil requested clarification on whether Act B.E 2558 was based on an international standard or guideline, the scientific basis on which "carcass" was defined, and whether the legislation had been notified.

StatementSubmitted: Once again, Brazil would like to bring to the attention of this Committee an issue it has been facing to export wet blue leather to Thailand. In Brazil’s view, Thailand should not require an international health certificate for allowing exports of this category of products, as recognized by the OIE itself. We thank Thailand for mentioning during the last meeting of this Committee, in March, that it is considering amending its Animal Epidemics Act BE 2558 (2015) to correct this, but we still expect that further progress can be made on this issue before we could be able to cease raising this STC. As we stated in March, wet blue leather is a processed product that does not pose risks to animal or human health of an importing country, as the leather undergoes a process of industrial tanning by which collagen from the skin is transformed into rot-resistant fibers. This makes the development and survival of etiological agents of diseases that affect animals not viable. Since 2019, Brazil made extensive efforts to provide technical information on the topic to the Department of Livestock Development (DLD). Brazil regrets the initial lack of disposition from Thailand to address the issue bilaterally. Thailand affirms that its Animal Epidemics Act B.E 2558 definition of “carcass” encompasses leather products, therefore requiring a health certificate to support imports. However, the OIE Terrestrial Code mentions in article 8.8.27 that national authorities should authorize, without requiring additional certification, imports of wet blue leather. We understand that Thai legislation provides for the requirement of certification for other types of leather; however, taking into account the characteristics of wet blue leather, Brazil believes that such legislation is not applicable to this product, therefore it should be no obstacle to observing the guideline given by the OIE for the product. If all these arguments would not suffice, we also highlight that last May, after direct consultation by Brazil to the OIE Secretariat, the organization affirmed that they agree with the interpretation of the Terrestrial Code that clarifies that wet blue leather is a product whose imports should be authorized without any restriction. Hence, we would like to restate some questions that we have made during the last Committee meeting:  1) Is the 2015 Animal Epidemics Act B.E 2558 based on any international standard or guideline? 2) What was the scientific justification used by the DLD for the definition of “carcass” and for the inclusion of “finished artificial items made from carcasses as prescribed in the Notifications by the Minister”? 3) Which official publication states that wet blue leather should be considered carcass? 4) Brazil has failed to locate Thailand’s WTO notification for the 2015 Animal Epidemics Act B.E 2558 and its following modifications. We would like to know if there was any notification for this legislation, and if so, if Thailand could kindly provide it. Once again, Brazil kindly expects Thailand’s answers and hopes that Thailand will withdraw the measure requesting a health certificate for wet blue leather without undue delay.
Summary: Brazil acknowledged Thailand's indication in the March 2022 Committee meeting that it was considering amending its Animal Epidemics Act B.E. 2558 (2015), which restricted imports of wet blue leather, to correct the requirement of an international health certificate for allowing imports of this category of products. Brazil referred to article 8.8.27 of WOAH Terrestrial Code regarding the authorization, without requiring additional certification, of imports of wet blue leather, and stated that the Thai legislation provided no obstacle to consider WOAH guidelines for wet blue. Brazil asked whether the Animal Epidemics Act B.E. 2558 (2015) was based on any international standard or guideline, and about the scientific justification used by the Department of Livestock Development (DLD) for the definition of "carcass" and for the inclusion of "finished artificial items made from carcasses as prescribed in the Notifications by the Minister"? Brazil also asked which official publication stated that wet blue leather should be considered as carcass, and requested clarification regarding the notification of the legislation. Brazil expected Thailand to provide answers to these questions and to withdraw the measure without undue delay.

StatementSubmitted: For the 4th time, Brazil would like to bring to the attention of this Committee an issue it has been facing to export wet blue leather to Thailand. This time, we would like to bring a proposal that could avoid the adoption of unnecessary requirements, while respecting Thai national legislation and the SPS Agreement. Brazil reinforces and clarifies that wet blue leather is not like raw, dried, or salted leather, products that require sanitary certification. It is known that the transformation of collagen into rot-proof fibers prevents the development and survival of etiologic agents of diseases that affect animals or humans, as already recognized by Thailand.Thailand has mentioned that it needs to make amendments to Normative Act B.E. 25558, in order to stop requiring sanitary certificates to import wet blue leather, as this act considers leather as “carcass”. However, as we have a well-established international standard recognized by the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH) on this issue, we would like to ask Thailand to consider the possibility of evoking this international reference, article 8.8.27 of the Terrestrial Animal Health Code, in order to to remove the unjustified sanitary requirement without the need of further amendments on its internal legislation.By doing so, Thailand would be in compliance with the SPS Agreement, in particular with regard to the principle of harmonization, without breaching its own legislation. Brazil would like to pose some questions for reflection and as a means to help resolving this STC: 1) As Wet Blue leather is a product totally different from the types of leather addressed in the Thai Regulation, would it still be necessary to amend or revise its legislation? 2) Could Thai authorities consider that it already recognizes that there is no need for a sanitary certificate for this product and that there is a specific international guideline on this issue as a means to authorize Brazilian exports with a less bureaucratical procedure? 3) How much time does Thailand expect to conclude its approval procedure?We expect that further progress can be made on this issue so that we can cease raising this STC.
Summary: Reiterating its concern regarding the export of wet blue leather to Thailand, Brazil indicated that it was putting forward a proposal to avoid the adoption of unnecessary requirements while respecting Thai domestic legislation and the SPS Agreement. Wet blue leather was not like raw, dried, or salted leather since the transformation of collagen into rot-proof fibres prevented the development and survival of etiologic agents of diseases affecting animals or humans. Brazil suggested that Thailand consider the possibility of relying on Article 8.8.27 of the WOAH Terrestrial Code to remove its requirement without the need of further amendments of its domestic legislation. In this context, Brazil asked Thailand to consider if amending its legislation was necessary given that wet blue leather was different from the types of leather addressed in its domestic regulation; if it could be deemed that no sanitary certificate was in fact required for this product, and that there was an international standard, as a means to authorize Brazilian exports; and how much time would be needed to conclude its approval procedure.

StatementSubmitted: Brazil presents this issue to the Committee for the 5th time to, once again, try to reconcile the need to avoid unnecessary sanitary requirements while maintaining compliance with local legislation and the SPS Agreement.In this sense, Brazil reinforces and clarifies that wet blue leather is not raw, dried, or salted leather, products that require sanitary certification. It is a differentiated product that undergoes a chemical treatment which makes it different from any product of animal origin.It is important to affirm that the relevant Thai legislation is from 1956, and the technology to produce and treat the leather to become wet blue leather is from the 90s, so Thai legislation precedes the invention of this product. That is why we understand that this legislation does not consider wet blue leather within its scope.It is globally known that the transformation of collagen into rot-proof fibers prevents the development and survival of etiologic agents of diseases that affect animals or humans. This is the reason why it is not necessary to have a sanitary certificate for leather shoes or leather jackets. The same logic applies to the trade of wet blue leather, which is confirmed by the fact that Thailand is one of the very few countries that still require sanitary certificates for this product.It follows that, when a country requires a sanitary certificate for this kind of product, it is inherently incapable of demonstrating it is following the principle of determining its appropriate level of sanitary protection, as it is imposing a sanitary restriction higher than needed, an action that goes against Articles 2 and 5 of the SPS Agreement.Considering this situation and that the Normative Act B.E. 2558 of 2015 should not comprise wet blue leather, Brazil requests Thailand to consider the subject absent in its legislation and evoke the international reference that deals specifically with wet blue leather. Hence, we evoke article 8.8.27 of the World Organization of Animal Health (WOAH) Terrestrial Animal Health Code, which affirms that national authorities should authorize the transit of wet blue leather without any restrictions.We already know that Thailand does not consider the sanitary certificate requirement as a restriction; however, we understand that any unneeded sanitary document that brings difficulties to the export process, adding another layer of bureaucracy, is a restriction. Furthermore, this kind of procedure makes the product costlier and turns into an unnecessary barrier.During the last SPS committee meeting, Thailand suggested a technical meeting to try to reach a solution to this situation, and we thank them for maintaining this technical engagement. This meeting took place virtually on 20th June, and, unfortunately, we have not yet been able to solve this issue, as Thailand insists that they have to revise their internal legislation and that this review is difficult to take place. However difficult, there was a legislative amendment in 2015 on other issues, indicating that it is feasible.As an alternative to address this problem, we kindly suggest that maybe there is no need for Thailand to review its legislation, provided that it considers wet blue a different product from unprocessed hides and skins.For this situation, I also remember that Thailand has another form of legal norm that could be used to avoid the need for a new act: the Notification of the Ministry of Agriculture and Cooperatives, mentioned, for instance, in Section 4 (3) of the Animal Epidemics Act (B.E 2558 - 2015). By using this instrument, Thailand could differentiate wet blue leather from other products and accept it without sanitary certification.Based on these facts, Brazil requests Thailand once more to remove the unjustified sanitary requirement imposed on wet blue leather, not only to comply with the SPS Agreement, but also to follow the guidelines of the international reference on the subject.We are sure that Thailand could comply with the SPS Agreement, in particular with regard to harmonization, without transgressing its internal legislation.Brazil leaves here some questions for reflection and assistance in resolving this Specific Trade Concern:- What are the sanitary problems that could be related to wet blue leather?- What was the scientific basis used by the DLD for the definition of "carcass" and the inclusion of finished artificial items(s), such as the wet blue leather, in it?- In Thailand's technical view, what are the etiological agents of diseases that could be still viable after the treatment that wet blue leather undergoes? Does Thailand have scientific evidence regarding this specific product?- Does the Thai regulation provide any sanitary action or obligation for chemically treated leather before wet blue enters the country?As an alternative, could this product be considered as not encompassed by the legislation, so the sanitary authorities consider another act or orientation based on the international guideline provided by WOAH that deals with the subject, and remove this requirement?

StatementSubmitted: Each time Brazil raises this STC new evidence seems to strengthen our case. We have been continuously informing Thailand that unlike raw, dried, or salted leather, wet blue leather does not require sanitary certification. Wet blue leather is a differentiated kind of product, as it undergoes a chemical treatment that makes it different from any regular product of animal origin.In different sessions in this Committee, Thailand has mentioned that, in order to lift its restrictions, it was expecting WOAH`s review of the Terrestrial Animal Health Code to include wet blue leather on the list of safe commodities under Chapter 8.8. Last May, during WOAH`s World Assembly, delegates decided to include "semi-processed leathers" on the list of safe commodities of article 8.8.27 of the Terrestrial Code. This article explicitly mentions that veterinary authorities should authorize imports of wet blue without restrictions.It is scientifically known that the transformation of collagen into rot-proof fibers prevents the development and survival of etiologic agents of diseases that affect animals or humans. This is the reason why a sanitary certificate for leather shoes or leather jackets is not necessary. The same logic applies to the trade of wet blue leather. Nevertheless, Thailand remains as one of the very few countries that still require sanitary certificates for this product.Any unnecessary sanitary document brings difficulties and adds another layer of bureaucracy, thus working as a restriction to export.Therefore, Brazil requests Thailand to remove the unjustified sanitary requirement imposed on wet blue leather and to bring Thai legislation into compliance with the SPS Agreement and the last revision of WOAH`s terrestrial code.We remain open to discuss this issue bilaterally, in the hope that, as soon as possible, this concern will be solved in a mutually satisfactory manner.
Summary: Reiterating this concern, Brazil indicated that wet blue leather was not like raw, dried, or salted leather since the transformation of collagen into rot-proof fibres prevented the development and survival of etiologic agents of diseases affecting animals or humans. For this reason, a sanitary certificate was not required. Brazil reminded of previous interventions in the Committee where Thailand had indicated that it was expecting a review of the WOAH relevant list of safe commodifies to lift its restrictions. In this context, Brazil reported that, in May 2024, "semi-processed leathers" had been included on the list of safe commodities of Article 8.8.27 of the WOAH Terrestrial Code. Brazil requested that Thailand remove the sanitary requirement imposed on wet blue leather to comply with the SPS Agreement and follow this latest revision of WOAH guidelines. Brazil expressed its willingness to discuss the issue bilaterally and hoped for a prompt resolution of the issue.

StatementSubmitted: Russian Federation:  WTO SPS Notification No. G/SPS/N/RUS/241 issued by Russian Federation pertaining to Quarantine pests-reg.Russian Federation has issued Notification No. G/SPS/N/RUS/241 dated 2nd December 2021 pertaining to all trading partners, thereby providing inclusion to the Common List of Quarantine Pests of the Eurasian Economic Union, 11 new quarantine pests.According to the SPS agreement of WTO and IPPC guidelines, the ‘quarantine pest’ is a pest of potential economic importance to the area endangered thereby and not yet present there, or present but not widely distributed and being officially controlled. According to available information, out of 11 listed pests in the above-said Notification, the following two pests are American dagger nematode (Xiphinema americanum sensustricto Cobb) and Californian dagger nematode (Xiphinema californicum Lamberti & Bleve Zacheo), are also present in Russia. Hence, these two pests are not quarantined pests in Russia.  Secondly, out of the eleven notified pests, the  following nine pests are not known to occur in India:                (i)    Natal fruit fly (Ceratitis rosa Karsch),               (ii)   Cucurbit beetle (Diabrotica speciosa Germar),               (iii)  Western potato flea beetle (Epitrix subcrinita LeConte),               (iv)  Emarginate ips (Ips emarginatus LeConte),               (v)   Monterey pine engraver (Pseudips mexicanus Hopkins),               (vi)  Western cherry ftuit fly (Rhagoletis indfferens Curran),               (vii) African armyworm (Spodoptera exempta Walker),               (viii) Sunflower fruit fly (Strauzia longipennis Wiedemann) and               (ix)   Bricolense dagger nematode (Xiphinema bricolense Ebsary, Vrain & Graham) Based on Articles 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3 of the SPS Agreement and IPPC guideline ISMP-11, none of these pests pose any quarantine threat to Russia as mentioned in this Notification. We, therefore, request  Russia to issue suitable amendments and/ or suitable advisories to its entry points that consignments from India are not detained as the above notified nine pests are not known to occur in India.
Summary: India expressed concerns regarding notification G/SPS/N/RUS/241, which added 11 new quarantine pests to the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) Common List of Quarantine Pests. India noted that two of the listed quarantine pests, namely American dagger nematode (Xiphinema americanum sensustricto Cobb) and Californian dagger nematode (Xiphinema californicum Lamberti & Bleve Zacheo), were also present in the Russian Federation. Additionally, India informed the Committee that nine out of the eleven notified pests were not known to occur in India and considered that these pests posed no threat to the Russian Federation, referring to Articles 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3 of the SPS Agreement and ISPM 11. India requested the Russian Federation to issue appropriate amendments or advisories to its entry points to ensure that consignments from India would not be detained.

StatementSubmitted: Russian Federation: Requirement of an additional declaration by Russia in the Phytosanitary certificate for Groundnut and Sesame Seed Eurasian Economic Union has introduced the requirement of additional declaration (stating that Peanuts and Sesame seed are produced in a region free from Striga spp., Callosobruchus spp, Caulophilus latinasus, Trogoderma granarium) in the phytosanitary certificate (PSC)  for export to Eurasian Economic Union.The industry has informed that as the seeds of Striga are very tiny (dust-like) and can spread readily via wind and water and in soil via animal vectors, it is technically not possible to issue a declaration stating that the consignments of Groundnut/Sesame Seed shipped from India were produced in ‘areas’ which is free from Striga, Callosobruchus spp, Caulophilus latinasus, Trogoderma granarium.   Rather, a declaration in the Phytosanitary Certificate that the “Consignment” is free from Striga spp., Callosobruchus spp, Caulophilus latinasus, Trogoderma granarium strigga would be a technically and practically feasible proposition. Due to the imposition of this requirement, exports of oilseeds to Russia have virtually come to a halt.We, therefore, request that the Russia/ Eurasian Economic Council may kindly accept the declaration that the goods being shipped are free from Striga and other related organisms.
Summary: India expressed its concerns regarding a new EAEU requirement to include a declaration in phytosanitary certificates stating that exported peanuts and sesame were produced in areas free of Striga spp., Callosobruchus spp., Caulophilus latinasus, Trogoderma granarium. India noted that this was not technically possible due to the small size of Striga seeds, which could easily spread. India suggested that a more feasible alternative would be to declare that the consignment was free from the above-mentioned pests. India expressed regret that this requirement had hindered its oilseed exports to the Russian Federation, and urged the Russian Federation to accept its declaration that the goods shipped from India were free from Striga and other related organisms.

StatementSubmitted: Brazil would like to express its concerns related to U.S. undue delay in opening its citrus market. Negotiations around the opening of this market have lasted more than twenty years. Since 2020, however, Brazilian concerns have grown, as U.S. authoritieshave still not opened the public consultation prescribed in its Pest Risk Analysis (PRA) process.In May 2019, in a bid to overcome the delay in this analysis, the Brazilian Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock and Supply offered to break down the PRA, focusing on opening the U.S. market for Brazilian lime, without prejudice to the original PRA that had been analyzing risks related to all Citrus genus. In that same year, the U.S. agreed to the Brazilian proposal and informed that there would be no need for starting a new PRA, as it could consider pieces of information from the original PRA.In August 2020, the US Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) informed Brazil that they would send within a month a schedule for the final steps to conclude the Brazilian lime PRA. The U.S. authorities also informed Brazil that after that conclusion, there would be an internal public consultation process of 30 days, which also still did not occur.Subsequently, in June 2021, the APHIS informed Brazil that the PRA was complete. However, so far, it has not been formally published. In the meantime, the U.S. market was opened for other countries that started negotiations after Brazil,Brazil considers that having a PRA ready and not publishing it constitutes an undue delay. Therefore, Brazil asks the U.S. to kindly publish the PRA as soon as possible.
Summary: Brazil raised its concerns on the United States' undue delay in opening its citrus market despite more than twenty years of negotiations. Brazil explained that in an effort to avoid delays, it had proposed to break down the PRA related to all Citrus genera, to focus on market access for Brazilian lime. Brazil stated that the United States had agreed with its proposal, informing Brazil that a new PRA would not be necessary. Brazil had been informed by the US Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) that an internal public consultation would take place after conclusion of the Brazilian lime PRA; however, the consultation still had not been opened. Brazil was also informed by APHIS that the PRA was complete but not formally published, and expressed its concern that other countries had access to the US market despite having started negotiations after Brazil. Considering that the decision not to publish an available PRA constituted an undue delay, Brazil called on the United States to publish the PRA as soon as possible.

StatementSubmitted: Once again, Brazil would like to express its concerns related to undue delay by the United States in opening its citrus market, a remarkably long-standing issue between our countries. Our concerns have grown, as U.S. authorities have still not opened the public consultation prescribed in its Pest Risk Analysis (PRA) process. We thank the US for keeping the discussion of this issue with us during a bilateral meeting last March, but we still hope further progress could be achieved more quickly. In August 2020, the U.S. Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) informed Brazil that they would send within a month a schedule for the final steps to conclude the Brazilian lime PRA. The U.S. authorities also informed Brazil that, after that conclusion, there would be an internal public consultation process of 30 days, which still did not occur. Subsequently, in June 2021, the APHIS informed Brazil that the PRA was complete. However, a year later, it has not been formally published. In the meantime, the U.S. market for products within the Citrus genus was opened for other countries that started negotiations after Brazil, without proper scientific justification for this kind of different treatment. During the last meeting of this Committee, in March, to our surprise, the US affirmed that publishing a PRA that is already finished for more than a year would not be a simple procedure. The US stated that “there are several steps needed” before APHIS can publish the PRA.  Brazil considers that having a PRA ready and not publishing it constitutes an undue delay. Therefore, Brazil kindly asks the US two questions: 1) what “several steps” are needed before publishing the PRA for Brazilian lime? 2) What is preventing the US from making progress on this issue? One last observation: since the last SPS Committee meeting, we have tried to reach the APHIS for technical meetings or updates on the issue, but, even after three months, we could not get a response.
Summary: Acknowledging their bilateral exchanges, Brazil pointed out that the US Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) had not opened the public consultation prescribed in the PRA process, despite the procedural details provided in August 2020. In June 2021, APHIS had reported that the PRA was complete, and Brazil considered that the lack of publication constituted an undue delay. Noting that, in the meantime, the US market had been open for other products in the Citrus genus, Brazil queried what were the steps needed before publishing the PRA for Brazilian lime and what was preventing progress on this issue. Finally, Brazil regretted the failure to obtain a response from APHIS to their requests for technical meetings and hoped to hear from the United States to progress towards the resolution of the issue.
