StatementSubmitted: Once again, Brazil would like to express its concerns related to the United States` undue delays in opening its citrus market. It has been more than twenty years since Brazil informed the U.S. about its interest to export lime. As you are aware, due to the delay in the U.S. Pest Risk Analysis (PRA) on citrus, in May 2019, Brazil asked the U.S to split the PRA to consider a new analysis aimed at opening the U.S. market for Brazilian lime, without prejudice to the original PRA aimed at analyzing risks related to all Citrus genus. In the same year, the U.S. agreed to the Brazilian proposal and informed that there would be no need to start a new PRA, as it could consider pieces of information from the original PRA.In November 2022, the U.S. finally published the PRA along with the results of its public consultation. We acknowledged that this was an important step and hoped that further progress would be achieved, so we did not raise this STC for more than a year. However, the subsequent lack of progress made us resume raising this STC in November 2023. Brazil has already participated in numerous technical and high-level bilateral meetings in Washington, in addition to the constant bilateral meetings held on the sidelines of this committee, and at all meetings the US made it clear that there were no technical or sanitary issues to be resolved, only bureaucratic issues. No progress has been achieved, unfortunately. We acknowledge that other members from this Committee are also concerned with undue delays for the approval of their fruit exports to the U.S. Chile has raised a STC on U.S. undue delays in the publication of import requirements for table grapes and Argentina has raised a STC on U.S delays in the authorization of sweet citrus fruits. We are supporting these STCs during this session and we would like to know what are the reasons these delays. During this session, we would like to request the U.S. an explanation for the lack of progress on this process, since more than one year has passed since the publication of the PRA. It would be useful and helpful if the US could provide further clarificaton on the next steps and of a reasonable timeframe for the conclusion of this negotiation, in order to finally enable Brazil`s exports of limes to the U.S.
Summary: Brazil reiterated its concerns regarding US undue delays in opening its citrus market. In 2019, Brazil had requested that the United States split the PRA for lime from other citrus genus, following which the United States had indicated that no new PRA would be needed as it could consider pieces of information from the original PRA. In 2022, the United States had published the PRA and the results of the public consultations, but subsequently, no further progress had been made despite bilateral discussions. Referring to two other STCs (STC ID 569 and STC ID 570), Brazil highlighted that other Members shared similar concerns and there was a systemic problem affecting US approval procedures. Brazil requested an explanation for the lack of progress as almost two years had passed since the publication of the PRA. Brazil also requested clarification on the next steps and a reasonable timeframe for the conclusion of the process.

StatementSubmitted: México desea hacer referencia a la solicitud que se ha presentado a la Unión Europea desde el año 2017 con respecto al reconocimiento como país con riesgo insignificante de Encefalopatía Espongiforme Bovina (EEB), otorgado por la Organización Mundial de Sanidad Animal desde el año 2016. México ha solicitado reiteradamente a la UE ser listado como país de riesgo insignificante en el Anexo de la Decisión 2007/453/CE del 29 de junio del 2007, lo cual no ha sido atendido y hemos observado en las actualizaciones más recientes del dicho instrumento, que otros países fueron listados aproximadamente seis meses después de haber obtenido el reconocimiento ante la Organización Mundial de Sanidad Animal a pesar de que esos países obtuvieron dicho reconocimiento en años posteriores a México. Es la primera vez que manifestamos esta preocupación en este foro, debido a que no hemos logrado obtener una respuesta oficial que brinde certeza de que la Unión Europea está dando atención a la solicitud de México. En el Comité Especial de Medidas Sanitarias y Fitosanitarias del Tratado de Libre Comercio entre México y la Unión Europea, éste ha sido un tema recurrente en la agenda y la respuesta de manera verbal por parte de la Unión Europea ha sido que se sigue revisando internamente el tema, sin que a la fecha se haya recibido una respuesta oficial a las comunicaciones enviadas por México en diversas ocasiones. Desde 2018, México ha presentado 10 solicitudes formales para dar seguimiento al reconocimiento de su condición sanitaria respecto a EEB, por parte de la Unión Europea. Cabe señalar, que México acepta el estatus sanitario que los Estados Miembros han alcanzado ante la Organización Mundial de Sanidad Animal, situación que se ha reiterado a la UE, tanto de manera verbal durante las citadas reuniones, como en las solicitudes formales de reconocimiento mutuo.  Desde nuestra perspectiva, no hay justificación científica para tal retraso, situación que está ocasionando la restricción de la comercialización de productos de interés, por tanto, México solicita a la UE incluir a México en la lista de la Decisión 2007/453/CE, de conformidad con las disposiciones del Acuerdo MSF de la OMC. La delegación de México agradece la atención de la Delegación de la Unión Europea y, deseando avanzar a una solución de manera cordial en este asunto, solicitamos se brinde una respuesta oficial por escrito a las comunicaciones enviadas por México en 2017, 2018, y la más reciente el 22 de marzo de 2022.
Summary: Mexico complaint that the European Union had not accommodated its repeated request to recognize the negligible risk status with regard to bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), granted by WOAH in 2016. Mexico had failed to obtain an official response from the European Union regarding this issue, despite the frequent discussions in the context of the Mexico - European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA). Mexico noted it accepted the sanitary status granted by WOAH to EU member States, and objected there was no scientific justification for this delay, which was restringing trade in products of interest. Mexico requested to be included in EU Decision 2007/453/EC and asked for an official response to the communications sent since 2017.

StatementSubmitted: México desea hacer referencia nuevamente a la solicitud que se ha presentado a la Unión Europea desde el año 2017 con respecto al reconocimiento como país con riesgo insignificante de Encefalopatía Espongiforme Bovina (EEB), otorgado por la Organización Mundial de Sanidad Animal desde el año 2016. México ha solicitado reiteradamente a la UE ser enlistado como país de riesgo insignificante en el Anexo de la Decisión 2007/453/CE del 29 de junio del 2007, lo cual no ha sido atendido y hemos observado en las actualizaciones más recientes del dicho instrumento, que otros países fueron listados en menos de seis meses, después de haber obtenido el reconocimiento ante la Organización Mundial de Sanidad Animal (OMSA), a pesar de que esos países obtuvieron dicho reconocimiento en años posteriores a México. En la reunión previa de este Comité, cuando México planteó por primera vez esta preocupación, la Unión Europea indicó que emitiría una respuesta en el Comité Especial de Medidas Sanitarias y Fitosanitarias del Tratado de Libre Comercio entre México y la Unión Europea, donde éste ha sido un tema recurrente en la agenda. La respuesta por parte de la Unión Europea, en la más reciente reunión de dicho Comité bilateral, celebrada en octubre de 2022, fue reenviar un oficio emitido desde julio de 2022, en el que se condicionó el avance de la negociación, a realizar un análisis de los requisitos específicos de México para la importación de carne de origen bovino, en relación a Encefalopatía Espongiforme Bovina, proponiendo que una vez concluida dicha evaluación, se celebre una reunión técnica. Lo anterior, bajo el argumento de que existen dificultades expresadas por Estados Miembros, para exportar estas mercancías a México. La Delegación Mexicana manifestó no estar de acuerdo con esta propuesta, considerando que dicho procedimiento no se aplicó a otros países listados en la Decisión 2007/453/CE, ni fue comunicado desde 2017, cuando se presentó por primera vez la petición por escrito. Aunado a ello, y pese a que se trata de temas completamente independientes, no se identifican gestiones bilaterales en curso con los Estados Miembros, en que se hayan manifestado tales dificultades, México considera que realizar dicho análisis implica que la UE no reconoce el estatus sanitario alcanzado por México ante la OMSA, desde 2016, como país de riesgo insignificante respecto a EEB.Cabe señalar que, México acepta el estatus sanitario que los Estados Miembros han alcanzado ante la Organización Mundial de Sanidad Animal, situación que se ha reiterado a la UE, tanto de manera verbal durante las citadas reuniones, como en las solicitudes formales de reconocimiento mutuo. Desde nuestra perspectiva, no hay justificación técnico-científica para tal retraso, situación que está ocasionando la restricción de la comercialización de productos de interés, que no implican un riesgo zoosanitario respecto a EBB, como los dispositivos pericárdicos de origen bovino, para su uso en la salud pública, por tanto, México solicita a la UE, conocer el procedimiento que cualquier socio comercial de la UE debe cumplir, para que su condición sanitaria respecto a EEB, sea actualizada en la lista de la Decisión 2007/453/CE, de conformidad con las disposiciones del Acuerdo MSF de la OMC. La delegación de México agradece la atención de la Delegación de la Unión Europea y, deseando avanzar a una solución de manera cordial en este asunto, solicitamos se brinde una respuesta oficial por escrito a las comunicaciones enviadas por México en 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021 y la más reciente, en octubre de 2022.
Summary: Mexico regretted that the European Union had not accommodated its repeated request to recognize the negligible risk status with regard to BSE, granted by WOAH in 2016. Mexico noted that other Members who had obtained the recognition from WOAH later than Mexico had already been included in EU Decision 2007/453/CE. Noting that it accepted the sanitary status granted by WOAH to EU member States, Mexico objected that there was no scientific justification for the EU delay, which was restringing trade in products of interest. Mexico requested to be included in EU Decision 2007/453/EC and asked for an official response to the communications sent since 2017.

StatementSubmitted: México desea hacer referencia nuevamente a la solicitud que se ha presentado a la Unión Europea desde el año 2017 con respecto al reconocimiento como país con riesgo insignificante de Encefalopatía Espongiforme Bovina (EEB), otorgado por la Organización Mundial de Sanidad Animal (OMSA) desde el año 2016. México ha solicitado reiteradamente ser listado como país de riesgo insignificante en el Anexo de la Decisión 2007/453/CE del 29 de junio del 2007, lo cual no ha sido atendido y hemos observado en las actualizaciones más recientes de dicho instrumento, que otros países fueron listados en menos de seis meses, después de haber obtenido el reconocimiento ante la OMSA, a pesar de que esos países obtuvieron dicho reconocimiento en años posteriores a México. Hace un par de reuniones de este Comité, cuando México planteó por primera vez esta preocupación, la Unión Europea indicó que emitiría una respuesta en el Comité Especial de Medidas Sanitarias y Fitosanitarias del Tratado de Libre Comercio entre México y la Unión Europea, foro en el que éste ha sido un tema recurrente en la agenda. La respuesta por parte de la Unión Europea, en dicho Comité bilateral, consistió en el reenvío de un oficio emitido desde julio de 2022, en el que se condicionó el avance de la negociación, a realizar un análisis de los requisitos específicos de México para la importación de carne de origen bovino, en relación a Encefalopatía Espongiforme Bovina, proponiendo que una vez concluida dicha evaluación, se celebre una reunión técnica. Lo anterior, bajo el argumento de que existen dificultades expresadas por Estados Miembros, para exportar estas mercancías a México. México manifestó no estar de acuerdo con esta propuesta, considerando que dicho procedimiento no se aplicó a otros países listados en la Decisión 2007/453/CE, ni fue comunicado desde 2017, cuando se presentó por primera vez la petición por escrito. Aunado a ello, y pese a que se trata de temas completamente independientes, no se identifican gestiones bilaterales en curso con los Estados Miembros, en que se hayan manifestado tales dificultades, México considera que realizar dicho análisis implica que la UE no reconoce el estatus sanitario alcanzado por México ante la OMSA, desde 2016, como país de riesgo insignificante respecto a EEB.  Cabe señalar que, México acepta el estatus sanitario que los Estados Miembros han alcanzado ante la OMSA, situación que se ha reiterado a la UE, tanto de manera verbal durante las citadas reuniones, como en las solicitudes formales de reconocimiento mutuo.  México considera que no existe justificación técnico-científica para tal retraso, o al menos, la UE no la ha argumentado, situación que está ocasionando la restricción de la comercialización de productos de interés, que no implican un riesgo zoosanitario respecto a EBB, por tanto, México solicita a la UE, conocer el procedimiento que cualquier socio comercial de la UE debe cumplir, para que su condición sanitaria respecto a EEB, sea actualizada  en la lista de la Decisión 2007/453/CE, de conformidad con las disposiciones del Acuerdo MSF de la OMC. En la reunión previa de este Comité, al plantear nuestra declaración, la Unión Europea, en respuesta, informó al Comité que ha tomado nota del estatus de México e indicó que en de manera bilateral se ha atendido el tema y se ha dado respuesta. No obstante, el tema no ha sido resuelto ni atendido por la Unión Europea, ya que México sigue sin estar listado en el Anexo correspondiente y no se ha reconocido el estatus de México otorgado por la OMSA. La Delegación de México agradece la atención de la Delegación de la Unión Europea y, deseando avanzar a una solución de manera cordial en este asunto, solicitamos se considere esta declaración como una solicitud formal de contar con una respuesta de manera oficial por escrito a las comunicaciones enviadas por México desde 2017 con reiteradas solicitudes en 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021y 2022.
Summary: Mexico regretted that the European Union had not accommodated its repeated request to recognize its BSE negligible risk status, granted by WOAH in 2016. Mexico noted that other Members who had obtained the recognition from WOAH subsequent to Mexico had already been included in EU Decision 2007/453/CE. Mexico expressed its disagreement with the request made by the European Union to undertake analysis of Mexico's specific requirements to import beef with regards to BSE, to be followed by a technical meeting on the basis that EU member States experienced difficulties to export such goods to Mexico. In Mexico's view, this analysis implied that the European Union did not recognize the sanitary status granted by WOAH. Noting that it accepted the sanitary status granted by WOAH to EU member States, Mexico objected that there was no scientific justification for the EU delay, which was restricting trade in products of interest. Mexico requested to be included in EU Decision 2007/453/EC and asked for an official response to the communications sent since 2017.

StatementSubmitted: La delegación de México desea expresar nuevamente la preocupación en relación con la solicitud que se ha reiterado a la Unión Europea para que se reconozca el estatus de país con riesgo insignificante respecto a Encefalopatía Espongiforme Bovina (EEB).  Respetuosamente, hemos planteado nuestra preocupación en este foro en diversas ocasiones, por primera vez en junio de 2022, y reiterándola en noviembre de 2022, y en marzo de 2023. En 2016, la Organización Mundial de Sanidad Animal (OMSA), reconoció a México como país con riesgo insignificante respecto a Encefalopatía Espongiforme bovina (EEB). Asimismo, consideramos relevante hacer notar que podría considerarse discriminatorio que otros Miembros que han obtenido el reconocimiento ante la OMSA después que México, ya han sido incluidos en la Decisión 2007/453/CE de la UE, donde se les da el estatus como países de riesgo insignificante respecto a Encefalopatía Espongiforme Bovina (EEB). Deseamos resaltar en esta ocasión que, la demora en la falta de este reconocimiento a nuestro país representa un gran impacto negativo en la comercialización de los dispositivos médicos derivados de pericardio de origen bovino mexicano, obstaculizando innecesariamente el comercio hacia la Unión Europea e impidiendo la expansión del producto hacia nuevos mercados, lo que genera un riesgo en los siguientes sectores: Salud púbica: Anualmente, se estima la producción e implementación de 19,500 válvulas bioprótesis quirúrgicas, las cuales contribuyen a restaurar la salud de miles de personas en el mundo. Es preciso señalar, que el 50% de la materia prima empleada para la elaboración de dichas prótesis, es pericardio bovino de origen mexicano. Empleos: Las estimaciones de crecimiento para la bioprótesis Avalus y otros productos en fase de diseño, pueden alcanzar más de 800 empleos directos en México. Además, la adquisición de materia prima de otros países, generaría un incremento de los costos de producción y, en consecuencia, la pérdida de empleos directos e indirectos en México, lo que afectará tanto el desarrollo de las economías locales como regionales. Todo lo anterior, sin que exista un sustento técnico científico, que justifique la implicación de un riesgo zoosanitario respecto a EEB, derivado de la importación de las referidas bioptrótesis cardiacas de origen mexicano. La delegación de México desea hacer referencia a los derechos y obligaciones de los Miembros ante el Acuerdo MSF, particularmente a los principios de basar las medidas en sustento científico y en una evaluación adecuada a las circunstancias de los riesgos existentes para la vida y la salud de las personas y de los animales, así como al Artículo 6, en lo que se refiere a evaluar las características sanitarias o fitosanitarias de una región, los Miembros tendrán en cuenta, entre otras cosas, el nivel de prevalencia de enfermedades o plagas concretas, la existencia de programas de erradicación o de control, y los criterios o directrices adecuados que puedan elaborar las organizaciones internacionales competente, así como al Anexo C del Acuerdo, en lo que se refiere a la obligación de que los procedimientos para verificar y asegurar el cumplimiento de medidas se inicien y ultimen sin demoras indebidas. En virtud de lo anterior, México reitera la solicitud de ser incluido en la Decisión 2007/453/CE de la Unión Europea o se proporcione el fundamento técnico científico que sustente la negativa de reconocer el estatus de México, alcanzado ante la OMSA. La delegación de México agradece a la delegación de la Unión Europea por la atención a esta declaración y los comentarios que tenga al respecto.
Summary: Mexico regretted that the European Union had not accommodated its repeated request to recognize its negligible BSE risk status, granted by WOAH in 2016. Mexico noted that other Members who had obtained the recognition from WOAH subsequent to Mexico had already been included in EU Decision 2007/453/CE. Mexico detailed that the delay in this recognition affected the marketing of medical devices derived from bovine animals, affecting the public health and employment sectors. Referring to Articles 2 and 6 and to Annex C of the SPS Agreement, Mexico objected that there was no scientific justification for the EU delay, and requested to be included in EU Decision 2007/453/EC and to receive the scientific justification for the non-recognition of the status granted by WOAH.

Summary: Mexico regretted that the European Union had not accommodated its repeated request to recognize its negligible BSE risk status granted by WOAH in 2016. Mexico noted that other Members who had obtained WOAH's status recognition after Mexico had already been included in EU Decision 2007/453/CE. Mexico detailed that the delay in this recognition concerned the marketing of medical devices derived from bovine animals, affecting the public health and employment sectors. Mexico also requested an indication of the expected timeline for consulting EU member States on recognizing Mexico's negligible BSE risk status.

StatementSubmitted: The European Union raises this concern about Peru’s import restrictions due to African swine fever for the first time in this Committee. The European Union is concerned by the countrywide import bans that Peru maintains on pork products from EU Member States that reported outbreaks of African swine fever.The EU requests Peru to respect its obligations, in accordance with the WTO SPS Agreement and the relevant OIE standards, and allow trade from disease free areas. The EU urges Peru to identify their procedures, counterparts and information requirements to engage in meaningful, solution-oriented exchanges.
Summary: The European Union expressed concerns on Peru's country-wide import bans imposed on EU pork products from member States that reported outbreaks of African swine fever (ASF). The European Union urged Peru to respect its international obligations and allow trade from disease-free areas, and to engage in solution-oriented exchanges.

StatementSubmitted: The European Union raises this concern about Peru’s import restrictions due to African swine fever for the second time in this Committee. The European Union is very concerned by the countrywide import bans that Peru maintains on pork products from EU Member States that reported outbreaks of African swine fever.The EU has requested Peru several times by letter and in meetings, most recently at the EU-Andean community SPS subcommittee on October 2022, to apply the regionalisation concept to the porcine meat imported from the EU, without any success yet.The disease-free areas are established according to WOAH standards in the EU Members States and the competent authority in the exporting EU Member State is responsible for issuing export certificates only for products from these areas. The EU requests again Peru to comply with its obligations, in accordance with the WTO SPS Agreement and the relevant WOAH standards, and allow trade from disease free areas. The EU urges Peru to review its procedures for alignment with WTO SPS Agreement and to engage in meaningful, solution-oriented exchanges.

Summary: The European Union expressed concerns regarding Peru's country-wide import bans imposed on EU pork products from EU member States that reported outbreaks of ASF. Despite repeated requests, most recently at the EU-Andean Community SPS subcommittee, the European Union regretted that Peru did not apply the principle of regionalization for pork meat nor accepted the WOAH ASF-free self-declarations, as in the case of Belgium. The European Union urged Peru to respect its international obligations and to allow trade from disease-free areas, to review its procedures, and to engage in solution-oriented exchanges.

StatementSubmitted: The European Union is very concerned by the countrywide import bans that Peru maintains on pork and pork products from EU Member States that have reported outbreaks of African swine fever in the past or currently.The EU has requested Peru several times by letter and in meetings, most recently at the EU-Andean community SPS subcommittee on November 2023, to apply both the regionalisation concept to pork meat imported from the EU and accept WOAH self-declarations of freedom from ASF, as in the case of Belgium, which is free from ASF since December 2020. Unfortunately, no progress has been made until now.The disease-free areas are established according to WOAH standards in the EU Members States and the competent authority in the exporting EU Member State is responsible for issuing export certificates only for products originating from these areas. The EU reminds Peru of its obligation to accept pork safe commodities which have been treated in line with the methods foreseen in Article 15.1.23 of WOAH terrestrial code. The EU requests again Peru to comply with its obligations, in accordance with the WTO SPS Agreement and the relevant WOAH standards and allow trade from disease free areas.
Summary: The European Union reiterated its concerns regarding Peru's country-wide import bans imposed on pork products from EU member States that reported outbreaks of ASF. Despite repeated requests, most recently at the EU-Andean Community SPS subcommittee, the European Union regretted that Peru did not apply the principle of regionalization for pork meat nor accepted the WOAH ASF-free self-declarations, as in the case of Belgium. The European Union urged Peru to respect its international obligations, allow trade from disease-free areas, review its procedures, and engage in solution-oriented exchanges.

StatementSubmitted: The European Union is very concerned by the countrywide import bans that Peru maintains on pork and pork products from EU Member States that have reported outbreaks of African swine fever in the past or currently.The EU has requested Peru several times by letter and in meetings, most recently in a meeting between the Peruvian competent authorities and the  EU held in Lima on 30 May, to apply the regionalisation concept to pork meat imported from the EU,  accept WOAH self-declarations of freedom from ASF, and to lift the ban of safe commodities from MS with ASF outbreaks in line with the methods foreseen in Article 15.1.23 of WOAH terrestrial code. Unfortunately, no progress has been made until now.The disease-free areas are established according to WOAH standards in the EU Members States and the competent authority in the exporting EU Member State is responsible for issuing export certificates only for products originating from these areas.  The EU requests again Peru to comply with its obligations, in accordance with the WTO SPS Agreement and the relevant WOAH standards and allow trade from disease free areas.
Summary: The European Union expressed its concerns regarding Peru's country-wide import ban on pork and pork products from EU member States that had reported ASF outbreaks. Despite repeated requests, including at a recent meeting in Lima at the end of May, the European Union regretted that Peru had failed to apply the principle of regionalization, accept the WOAH ASF-free self-declarations, and lift the ban for safe commodities from EU member States with ASF outbreaks in line with the methods foreseen in the WOAH Terrestrial Code. The European Union reiterated its request for Peru to comply with its obligations under the SPS Agreement and the relevant WOAH standards and allow trade from disease-free areas.

StatementSubmitted: For a long time, China has been issuing an English version of the health certificates for food products exported to the EU in accordance with the Regulations (EU) No. 2020/2235 and other relevant regulations. The certificate samples have been confirmed by the EU side, and the bilateral trade has also remained stable and smooth. In April this year, some Chinese food companies reported that some EU member states (currently involving France, Spain, and Italy) declared through their importers that from 1 May 2022, they will no longer accept import health certificates for products of animal origin issued in English only, but require the use of member states’ languages, or English and member states’ languages together (such as French, Spanish, Italian, etc.) As far as we know, neither the EU nor its member states have ever notified the above-mentioned requirements to WTO, which do not comply with WTO rules and will seriously hinder food trade.China has repeatedly tried to verify the above-mentioned requirements with the EU side but has not received any official reply. On May 10, 2022, China sent a letter to the EU to draw attention to this issue and requested the EU to clarify the relevant requirements for the issuance of the version of the health certificate as soon as possible. If it is really necessary to add the language of member states, please provide the relevant basis, formally notify the WTO and give a 6-month transition period. Unfortunately, as of May 16, 2022, no reply has been received from the EU on this issue.China hopes that before the two sides reach an agreement on this issue, the EU will coordinate with the member states to ensure that China's food trade with the EU will not be affected.
Summary: China complaint that some EU member States had declared that, from 1 May 2022, they would no longer accept only the English version of the health certificates for food products of animal origin exported to the European Union, as had been the practice for a long time in accordance with the Regulation (EU) No 2020/2235 and other relevant regulations. Certificates in the member States' languages, or English and member States' languages together, would now be required. China was not aware of the notification of those requirements to the WTO which, in China's view, did not comply with WTO rules and restricted food trade. Regretting the lack of official response to the letter sent on 10 May, China asked the European Union to clarify the relevant requirements, to formally notify the WTO and to give a six-month transition period. China hoped to reach an agreement on this issue to avoid disruptions of China's food trade.

StatementSubmitted: According to EU Commission Decision 2002/994/EC, the Veterinary Health Certificate together with an additional statement shall be issued to prove the veterinary drug residue in the products of animal origin exported from China. There are many kinds and quantities of egg and milk products exported to Europe, and the numbers of laboratory tests continue increasing, leading to the extension of the supervision period before export, affecting the scheduled shipping, extending the delivery period, and having a great impact on the exporting business.EU Resolution 2002/994/EC was issued 20 years ago, while China's food safety system has undergone great changes. In 2012, the former General Administration of Quality Supervision, Inspection, and Quarantine of the People's Republic of China (AQSIQ) issued Announcement No. 149, which clarified the list of raw materials for export food subject to filing management, and stipulated that poultry meat, eggs, pork, rabbit meat, bee products, aquatic products and other raw materials of animal origin used for export food must be filed by the General Administration of Customs. During the process of assessment, veterinary drug residues should be tested according to the requirements of the destination country. From January 1st, 2022, the Customs system implemented the new version of the Measure of the People's Republic of China for the Administration of Import and Export Food Safety, and incorporate the above requirements for the record-keeping of farms into the management system. Therefore, China hopes that the EU side could cancel the requirement of issuing the additional statement.
Summary: China noted the impact of the requirements in Commission Decision 2002/994/EC on exporting businesses, namely regarding the additional statement on veterinary drug residues in the exported products of animal origin that had to accompany the veterinary health certificate. China emphasized that its food system had undergone great changes since the issuance of the Commission Decision and informed the Committee that, since 2022, GACC implemented the new version of the measures for the Administration of Import and Export Food Safety incorporating the requirement to test for veterinary drug residues according to the country of destination. China requested the European Union to remove the requirement to issue an additional statement accompanying the veterinary health certificate.

StatementSubmitted: The matrine and oxymatrine in the Chinese honey( mainly acacia honey ) are derived from the nectar of Sephora vicifolia Hence-a plant flowering at the same time as acacia, not caused by artificial addition or contamination. In addition, there is no evidence to prove that matrine and oxymatrine in honey may cause food safety risks. However, the EU conducted the test on the honey imported from China with a strict residue limit of 0.01 mg/kg according to the REGULATION (EC) NO 396/2005. China believes that there are several questions to be discussed in the following aspects: First, the scope of application. Matrine and oxymatrine in Chinese honey (acacia honey, jujube honey, etc.) are not pesticide residues, it should not be regulated by REGULATION (EC) NO 396/2005. Second, application of the limit. A comprehensive risk assessment should be carried out for the edible safety of the honey exported from China to the EU, rather than using a temporary limit level of 0.01mg/kg directly. Third, the notification procedure. Unilateral action against the honey exported to Europe from China without a clear legal basis and notification through the RASFF system will not only affect the normal trade, but also have a negative impact on Chinese bee products. China suggests that the Eu side could notify the trading authorities to clarify the concerns before notifying through RASFF. Fourth, scientific rationality. Sephora vicifolia Hence is an endemic nectar plant in China. The detection of matrine and oxymatrine in honey exported to the EU from China actually exaggerated the food safety risks. China hopes that the EU side could provide a reasonable scientific basis.China hopes that the EU will take into account China’s explanation and clarification on the natural content of matrine, oxymatrine and other alkaloids in the honey and refer to the relevant scientific research achievements of China and other members, and no longer detect matrine, oxymatrine in the honey exported from China.
Summary: China raised questions regarding the tests conducted by the European Union on honey imported from China with a residue limit of 0.01 mg/kg according to the Regulation (EC) No 396/2005. China explained that Chinese honey was mainly acacia honey and that the matrine and oxymatrine were derived from the nectar of Sephora vicifoliai Hence, a plant flowering at the same time as acacia, and not by artificial addition or contamination. China further indicated that there was no evidence that matrine and oxymatrine in honey might cause food safety risks. China questioned the scope and limit of application, the notification procedure and the scientific rationality of the measure, and hoped that the European Union took into account the clarifications provided.

StatementSubmitted: China is extremely concerned about the resumption of normal trade of robinia honey between China and Europe, and highly appreciates the EU’s contribution and active technical consultations to maintain the stability of the trade supply chain of honey products between China and Europe.China conducted a general survey on the content levels and sources of matrine and oxymatrine in honey (including robinia honey) produced in China for three consecutive years from 2021 to 2023, confirming that:Firstly, the matrine and oxymatrine in Chinese honey are derived from the nectar of Sephora vicifolia Hence (a plant that blooms at the same time as robinia), and are not artificially added or contaminated. Sephora vicifolia Hence is a unique deciduous shrub of Sophora (Leguminosae) in China. It is widely distributed in the low mountainous areas of the southern Taihang Mountains in northwestern Henan, southeastern Shandong, southwestern Hebei, as well as in the Loess Plateau of northern Shaanxi and east Gansu, as well as the northern slope of the Qinling Mountains, Yunnan Plateau, and Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. It is a traditional nectariferous plant. The stems, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds of Sephora vicifolia Hence contain various alkaloids such as matrine, oxymatrine and oxysophocarpine, etc. These alkaloids have anti-inflammatory, anti arrhythmia, liver protection, anti-liver fibrosis, anti-tumor, and immune regulation effects, and are important raw materials for drugs, detergents, and biocides/insecticides. According to the distribution of nectariferous plants in North and Northwest China, there is a large amount of mixed growth of Sephora vicifolia Hence and other nectariferous plants such as Robinia pseudoacacia L. and jujube tree, etc., with highly overlapping flowering periods. Some apiaries also choose mixed growth sites of Sephora vicifolia Hence and Robinia pseudoacacia L. to compensate for the shortage of Robinia pseudoacacia pollen and extend the honey collection period. Robinia pseudoacacia L. is the nectariferous plant of robinia honey. It is not necessary to use matrine and oxymatrine as pest control, and it has never been reported. It is also not possible to use such pesticides in beekeeping. The test results of the China Chamber of Commerce of Import & Export of Foodstuffs, Native Produce & Animal By-Products (CFNA) also prove that there is a significant correlation between the content of matrine and oxymatrine in robinia honey and the region (distribution of Sephora vicifolia Hence).Firstly, the matrine and oxymatrine in Chinese honey are derived from the nectar of Sephora vicifolia Hence (a plant that blooms at the same time as robinia), and are not artificially added or contaminated. Robinia pseudoacacia L. is the nectariferous plant of robinia honey. It is not necessary to use matrine and oxymatrine as pest control, and it has never been reported. It is also not possible to use such pesticides in beekeeping. The test results of the China Chamber of Commerce of Import & Export of Foodstuffs, Native Produce & Animal By-Products (CFNA) also prove that there is a significant correlation between the content of matrine and oxymatrine in robinia honey and the region (distribution of Sephora vicifolia Hence).Thirdly, the EU did not provide scientific basis for the limit requirements of matrine and oxymatrine, which greatly affected normal trade. In addition to more than 20 batches of products notified by the European Union, the situation is even more serious when the EU importer returns the products due to the detection of matrine or oxymatrine, or domestic production enterprises are unable to fulfill the contract. According to statistics, the export of robinia honey in northwest China accounts for over 80% of the total export volume of robinia honey in China. Among them, the export volume of single robinia honey to Europe is about 8000 tons, and the export volume of mixed robinia honey is about 15000 tons. Based on this estimation, it is estimated that the economic losses (including goods and related testing, transportation, and other related links) of robinia honey exported from China to Europe are nearly 70 million US dollars due to the impact of matrine problems.Sephora vicifolia Hence is a unique nectariferous plant in China, and the matrine in robinia honey in northwest China is brought in by the honey of Sephora vicifolia Hence in mixed growth, which is difficult to avoid. According to the research conducted by China Customs on enterprises, Chinese enterprises' export of robinia honey to EU requires waiting for relevant testing at the port, resulting in long detention time and a significant increase in trade costs. If EU cannot adjust the testing measures for alkaloids such as matrine and oxymatrine, etc. in honey, it will directly lead to the inability of Chinese honey to be exported to the European market normally. China conducted friendly consultations with the EU on the 86th WTO/SPS meeting and forwarded the food source assessment reports of matrine and oxymatrine in robinia honey of China. As of October 23, EU has not responded. China hopes to conduct relevant technical consultations with EU to promote the normalization of the export of robinia honey to Europe.China hopes to coordinate with the EU in the following aspects:The first is the scope of application. Matrine and oxymatrine in Chinese honey are not pesticide residues and shall not fall within the scope of the EU pesticide residue limit regulations (REGULATION (EC) NO 396/2005).The second is the limit value. A comprehensive risk assessment shall be conducted on the edible safety of matrine and oxymatrine in honey exported from China to EU, rather than directly using a temporary limit level of 0.01 mg/kg. Referring to the “Technical guidelines for determining the magnitude of pesticide residues in honey and setting Maximum Residue Levels in honey” (2018 Edition), China proposes to set a temporary limit of 0.05 mg/kg.Thirdly, it is recommended to coordinate the establishment of a consistency evaluation mechanism for the test methods of matrine and oxymatrine in honey by the Chinese and European laboratories.The fourth is to coordinate and solve the problems of long detention periods and significant increases in trade costs caused by high sampling rates and long inspection times at the port of entry for the honey exported from China to Europe.Moreover, China has conducted a food borne safety risk assessment of matrine and oxymatrine in Chinese robinia honey for three consecutive years from 2021 to 2023, and has formed an assessment report, which we have forwarded again. Based on this report, we suggest that the EU fully consider and adopt the trade demand for a temporary limit of oxymatrine in Chinese robinia honey, and carry out further technical consultations in this regard.
Summary: Appreciating the ongoing technical consultation, China maintained its concerns about the resumption of normal trade of robinia honey. China had shared with the European Union the report of a foodborne safety risk assessment of matrine and oxymatrine in robinia honey, which confirmed that the matrine and oxymatrine in Chinese honey were derived from the nectar of Sephora vicifolia Hence, a plant flowering at the same time as acacia, and not by artificial addition or contamination. China further indicated that there was no evidence that matrine and oxymatrine in honey might cause food safety risks, and regretted that the European Union had not provided the scientific evidence for the established limits. China expressed its willingness to hold technical discussions on the scope of the application and on the limit value. Additionally, China recommended the establishment of a bilateral consistency evaluation mechanism for the test methods of matrine and oxymatrine in honey, and the resolution of the issues associated to long detention periods and significant increases in trade costs caused by high sampling rates and long inspection times at the port of entry for the exported honey.

StatementSubmitted: The European Union raises its concerns about Egypt’s Customs Circular Decision No. 4060 on radioactivity checks on imported food for the first time in this Committee. Egypt has recently issued an internal Customs Circular (Decision no. 4060) that orders all food products imported into Egypt and originating from 30 countries (including 11 EU Member States) to undergo radioactivity checks in order to verify whether their radioactivity levels are in line with limits set by the Egyptian Nuclear and Radiological Regulatory Authority (ENRRA) in its Board Decision no. 2 of 2014. ENRRA claims that products not listed in their Board Decision are not permitted to have any level of radioactivity. However, the text of the indicated Board Decision does not include such zero-radioactivity requirement. This requirement does not exist in writing and was not notified to WTO. However, already a number of EU shipments have been suffering import blockages in Egypt due to this zero-radioactivity requirement. The EU is deeply concerned about this new requirement as there is no legal certainty about the permitted radioactivity levels. The EU would therefore like to ask Egypt to provide further information on the legal framework setting out the permitted radioactivity requirement for food products and to notify it to WTO SPS Committee. That would allow the EU and other interested trading partners to assess the measure, which, on the basis of the available information, does not seem to be in line with the relevant international standards or based on additional risk assessments as required under the WTO SPS Agreement. Furthermore, the measure also seems to be more trade restrictive than necessary.The EU would also like to invite the Egyptian authorities to suspend the applied zero-radioactivity requirement until notifying the requested regulation.
Summary: The European Union raised its concerns regarding Egypt's Customs Circular Decision No. 4060, which introduced radioactivity checks on imported products based on radioactivity limits set by the 2014 Board Decision No. 2 of the Egyptian Nuclear and Radioactive Regulatory Authority (ENRRA). The European Union noted that, despite the absence of a zero-radioactivity requirement in its Board Decision, Egypt claimed that non-listed products could not contain any level of radioactivity. The European Union stressed that this requirement resulted in import blockages of EU shipments in Egypt and was more trade restrictive than necessary, not in accordance with the relevant international standards, and not based on a risk assessment. The European Union urged Egypt to provide information on setting radioactivity requirements for food products, to notify this measure and to suspend the zero-radioactivity requirement until notifying its measure.

StatementSubmitted: The European Union would like to raise its concerns about Morocco’s measures on plant products in the fight against the spreading of Xylella fastidiosa disease, which includes a ban on ornamental plants.The first measure, notified to the WTO SPS Committee on 07th October 2021, as MAR/67 Add. 1, introduced major barriers for EU plant products.The EU has issued SPS comments on this measure which unfortunately have not been taken into account. In its comments, the EU asked Morocco to incorporate the list of host plants in the draft decision itself, to ensure transparency and legal certainty, and to specify further which requirements applied to which part of the list of the host plants.The EU, except for certain Demarcated Areas, is free of Xylella fastidiosa or has it under official control. Therefore, in the European Union, the import from the pest free zone should be without the prior condition of listing the plant nurseries, contrary to what is required by the notified measure.The EU has asked Morocco to consider removing the obligation to indicate in the accompanying phytosanitary certificate, among others, that the plant was officially tested and found free from Xylella fastidiosa, as the information on the Xylella free zones are provided to Morocco by the national plant health organisations. Regarding ornamental plants which are not host plants of Xylella fastidiosa, the draft requires a phytosanitary risk analysis when they originate from a country where the bacteria is present. The EU considers that this requirements is not proportionate and not technically justifiable for these kind of plants. The EU would therefore like to invite Morocco to consider the possibility of other alternatives.In case of Ornamental plants which are host of Xylella fastidiosa the notified text proposes an import ban from countries that are infected by this bacteria. In respect of the last point, the EU has learnt that the Moroccan authorities have already enforced this import ban as of  10th March 2022 for  all ornamental plants from countries where the Xylella fastidiosa disease is present by a ‘note de service’ of the Moroccan national plant health organisation. The EU considers these measures, especially a full ban, disproportionate and unjustified under the WTO SPS Agreement and urges Morocco to comply with the principles of the Agreement. The EU is available to discuss further these issues with Morocco.
Summary: The European Union raised its concerns on Morocco's measures against the spreading of Xylella fastidiosa disease in plants, as notified in document G/SPS/N/MAR/67/Add.1. The European Union regretted that its comments on this measure had not been taken into account, and emphasized that imports from EU pest-free zones should not be contingent on the prior condition of listing of plant nurseries. The European Union requested that Morocco considered removing the phytosanitary certificate requirement, taking into account that the information on Xylella-free zones was provided by its NPPOs. The European Union emphasized that the phytosanitary risk analysis requirements for ornamental plants which were not host of X. fastidiosa and the total import ban of ornamental plants host of X. fastidiosa from countries infected by this bacteria were disproportionate and unjustified under the SPS Agreement.

StatementSubmitted: Thank you Chair.The European Union continues to be concerned about Morocco’s measures intended to fight against the spread of the Xylella fastidiosa disease.Morocco has considered various measures in this respect in the last years.The measure, notified to the WTO SPS Committee on 7 October 2021, as MAR/67 Add. 1, introduced major barriers for EU plant products. The EU has issued SPS comments on this measure and received the written replies of Morocco. The matter was also raised as an STC during the June 2022 meeting of the WTO SPS Committee. The EU had also noted that Morocco notified on 10 March 2023 to the WTO a final, adopted text under the reference MAR/67 Add. 2. The measure seemed to be adopted on 25 August 2022, with an entry into force on 16 September 2023. The EU has several questions and concerns related to this recently notified, final measure. Some of these were already raised in the past, while others emerge now, after the analysis of final, notified text. Does the notified measure replace the version which was notified under MAR/67 Add. 1?  Does it also replace the non-notified circular of the Moroccan Plant Health Authority, which introduced a general ban on ornamental plants in March 2022. If this is the case, the EU would ask, that due to the substantial changes in the text, compared to the earlier notification, Morocco re-notifies this measure in a draft version, which would allow for further exchanges. Regarding the content of the notified measure, the EU have the following detailed questions:The EU has major concerns about the proportionality of the measure given that it imposes a general ban of plants and plant products originating from countries where the Xylella fastidiosa is present, The measure does not seem to fully take into account the principle of regionalisation as defined in the WTO SPS Agreement. In this respect, the EU would like to receive further information from Morocco on the risk assessment carried out. The EU noted that the only exemption from the ban from countries where the disease is present, applies to fruit plants. In these cases, the concept of pest free areas is applied under certain conditions. The EU welcomes the reference to the relevant international standard in the text. However, in this respect, the EU would seek further clarifications, whether Morocco would be accepting the EU demarcated areas or are those to be defined by the Moroccan National Plant Health Authority. The EU would urge Morocco to accept the concept as defined in the EU, which provides the necessary control and prevention while ensuring trade, defined in line with the WTO SPS Agreement and the relevant international standards. After the earlier comments of the EU, in the version notified as MAR/67 Add. 1, Morocco incorporated the list of host plants by referring to the list as defined by the European Food Safety Agency. This reference does not seem to be included in the final version. Could Morocco provide further clarifications for this? The EU would like to receive further information on how the host plants are to be defined. The EU would also like to receive further clarifications on the rules applicable to ornamental plants, that were in the scope of the draft notified under MAR/67 Add. 1.Finally, the EU would also urge Morocco to reconsider the burdensome and duplicative requirements on certificates, which seem to apply even in case of plants and plant products originating from a country free of the disease. Besides these issues, the EU operators face uncertainty and lack of transparency with the often-changing requirements in this field. The EU considers these measures, especially a full ban and lack of full implementation of the regionalisation principle, disproportionate and unjustified under the WTO SPS Agreement and urges Morocco to comply with the principles of the Agreement. Taking the urgency and the complexity of these issues into account, the EU repeatedly proposed bilateral meetings to further discuss these issues, without success. The EU would urge Morocco to engage in discussing further these issues bilaterally in the very near future.Thank you, Chair.
Summary: Referring to its full intervention in eAgenda, the European Union reiterated its concern about Morocco's measures intended to fight against the spread of the Xylella fastidiosa disease. The European Union noted that a measure introducing major barriers for EU plant products had been notified by Morocco in October 2021 (G/SPS/N/MAR/67/Add.1), and another adopted measure in March 2023 (G/SPS/N/MAR/67/Add.2). The European Union enquired whether the latter measure replaced the previously notified measure as well as the (non-notified) circular imposing a general ban on ornamental plants. Should this be the case, the European Union requested Morocco to renotify its measure and allow for a period of time given the substantial changes that had been introduced. On substance, the European Union considered that the measure lacked proportionality, did not seem to fully take into account the principle of regionalization, imposed burdensome and duplicative requirements, and was disproportionate and unjustified. The European Union urged Morocco to comply with the SPS Agreement and engage in bilateral discussions in the very near future.

StatementSubmitted: First of all, the EU would like to thank Morocco for the bilateral meeting on this issue held on 4 July 2023, devoted to the measures introduced by Morocco in their fight against the spreading of Xylella fastidiosa in the country. This meeting provided the opportunity to have a useful technical exchange. As a follow-up, the EU would like to raise the following comments and concerns today.The EU appreciates the clarification that the measure does not restrict the import of plant and plant products from EU Member States which are free from Xylella fastidiosa. When it comes to the EU MS where the disease is present, fruit plants might be imported according to the requirements set out in the measure. However, there is a full ban for ornamental plants from these countries. In the view of the EU, taking into account the risks associated, the requirement applicable to fruit plants could be extended to the ornamental plants as well, instead of the current full ban. Furthermore, the EU is of the view, that regardless of the type of plant, be it ornamental or fruit, as long as they originate from a disease-free area, they should be treated as safe and there should not be a reason to differentiate between them. The EU looks forward to continue the technical exchanges on these matters with Morocco.
Summary: The European Union reported on a bilateral technical meeting with Morocco held in July 2023 regarding Morocco's measure to fight against the spread of Xylella fastidiosa. The European Union appreciated the clarification that the measure did not restrict the import of plants and plant products from EU member States which were free from the disease. For imports from member States where the disease was present, fruit plants could be imported according to the requirements set out in the measure. In the view of the European Union, instead of the current full ban, these requirements could be extended to ornamental plants. Moreover, as long as fruit and ornamental plants originated from a disease-free area, there should not be a reason to differentiate between them. The European Union expressed it is willingness to continue technical exchanges.

StatementSubmitted: First of all, the EU would like to thank Morocco for the continuous bilateral exchanges on this issue, including the latest written exchanges.The EU’s concerns relate both to the requirements and to the implementation. of the measures introduced by Morocco in their fight against the spreading of Xylella fastidiosa in the countryEU Member States where the disease is present, have provided information to Morocco in line with the requirements set out in the measure. However, these EU Member States have not yet received any official reply from Morocco explaining how trade could resume in line with the new requirements. Therefore, the EU would ask Morocco to provide written replies to the EU and the concerned EU Member States, applying the regionalisation rules foreseen in the measure for fruit trees. While the EU thanks Morocco for the additional details provided for ornamental plants, the EU would like to reiterate its request that  the requirements applicable to fruit plants could be extended to the ornamental plants as well, instead of the current full ban. The EU is of the view, that regardless of the type of plant, be it ornamental or fruit, as long as they originate from a disease-free area, they should be treated as safe and there should not be a reason to differentiate between them. The EU looks forward to continuing the technical exchanges on these matters with Morocco.
Summary: The European Union acknowledged the ongoing bilateral meeting regarding Morocco's requirements and implementation of measures to fight against the spread of X. fastidiosa. Despite having provided the information required, the EU member States where the disease was present had not received an official reply about the resumption of trade. In the view of the European Union, instead of the current full ban, the regionalization requirements set out for fruit plants could be extended to ornamental plants. Moreover, as long as fruit and ornamental plants originated from a disease-free area, they should be treated as safe and there should not be a reason to differentiate between them. The European Union expressed its willingness to continue technical exchanges.

StatementSubmitted: First of all, the EU would like to thank Morocco for the continuous bilateral exchanges on this issue, including the written reply of Morocco received on 15 March 2024.The EU would like to reiterate its concerns relating to the implementation of the measure introduced by Morocco in their fight against the introduction and spread of Xylella fastidiosa in the country.The EU Member States where the disease is present have provided information to Morocco in line with the requirements set out in the measure, so that trade can continue from those parts of their territories which are free from the disease.However, these EU Member States have not yet received any official reply from Morocco explaining how trade could resume in line with the new requirements. The EU thanks the recent written explanations provided by Morocco on certain provisions of the measure, such as the definition of host plants and the listing of production sites. The EU will further analyse these aspects of the reply.The EU would ask Morocco to provide follow-up to those EU Member States, where in some areas the disease is present. The EU looks forward to continuing the technical exchanges on these matters with Morocco.
Summary: Referring to its complete statement in eAgenda, the European Union acknowledged the ongoing bilateral meeting regarding Morocco's implementation of measures to fight against the spread of Xylella fastidiosa. Although EU member States where the disease was present had provided all the requested guarantees so that trade could resume from the parts of their territories free from the disease, the concerned member States had not received an official reply about the resumption of trade. Noting it would analyse the answers provided by Morocco on specific provisions of the measure, the European Union asked Morocco to follow up with the EU member States where the disease was present in some areas and looked forward to continuing technical exchanges.

StatementSubmitted: First of all, the EU would like to thank Morocco for the bilateral exchanges on this issue, including a very useful discussion this morning before the committee meeting.Once more, the EU would like to reiterate its concerns relating to the implementation of the measure introduced by Morocco in their fight against the introduction and spread of Xylella fastidiosa in the country, in particular the ban on the import of ornamental plants.The EU Member States where the disease is present have provided information to Morocco in line with the requirements set out in the measure, but have not yet received yet an official, reply from Morocco explaining how trade could resume in line with the new requirements. This morning we agreed with Morocco that a technical meeting will be organised before the November SPS committee, to discuss with the experts of the EU and Member States how we can facilitate trade in ornamental plants, while ensuring a high level of plant health. The EU looks forward to forthcoming technical meeting with Morocco.
Summary: Reiterating its concern regarding Morocco's measures against Xylella fastidiosa, particularly the ban on importing ornamental plants, the European Union thanked Morocco for bilateral exchanges, including a useful discussion they had prior to this Committee meeting. The European Union noted that EU member States affected by the disease had submitted required information, but Morocco had not yet provided an official response on resuming trade under the new rules. The European Union mentioned an upcoming technical meeting with Morocco before the November Committee, where EU member States experts would discuss facilitating ornamental plant trade while ensuring plant health.

StatementSubmitted: EU Regulation No 396/2005 setting pesticide MRLs in food and feed of plant and animal origin  India expresses severe concern regarding the EU's plan to reduce MRLs for Clothianidin and Thiamethoxam in certain products. EU's plan to lower the MRL of neonicotinoid for imported agricultural products will not ensure the sustainability of the global food system. India notes that with the proposed new Notification G/TBT/N/EU/908, the EU is proposing to fix the MRL for Clothianidin and Thiamethoxam at the Level of Determination citing reasons that food produced outside the EU with the use of these chemicals is not imported into EU.  This new Notification is based on the assumption that these neonicotinoids (clothianidin and thiamethoxam) are harmful to bees even at the level determined by Codex. However, the impact of field-level neonicotinoid exposure on honeybee health and survival has been less decisive than assumed by the proposed EU notification. Based on this understanding, India requests the EU to share the risk assessment done to fix the MRL of these neonicotinoids at the Level of Determination. Secondly, the EU is also requested to share the other measures considered before choosing this measure of fixing neonicotinoid at the level of determination. Neonicotinoid pesticides (Clothianidin and Thiamethoxam) have become the most widely used class of insecticides worldwide, since their discovery in the late 1980s, with large-scale applications ranging from - plant protection (crops, vegetables, fruits), veterinary products, biocides to invertebrate pest control in fish farming, etc. Therefore, the proposed EU measure will severely limit the choice of available plant protection measures. Therefore, India strongly encourages the EU to consider postponing the implementation of the proposed Notification till new alternative plant protection choices are readily commercially available. India also requests the EU to provide a detailed justification concerning the link between the new MRL limit set for clothianidin and thiamethoxam and its correlation with the objective sought to be achieved by the EU under the WTO covered agreements. Furthermore, India urges the EU to notify this measure to the SPS committee as well.
Summary: India expressed its concern regarding the reduction to the level of determination of MRLs for the neonicotinoids clothianidin and thiamethoxam for imported agricultural products, notified in document G/TBT/N/EU/908. India requested the European Union to share the risk assessment used as a basis for this decision, as well as to indicate the alternative measures that had been considered. Given the widespread use and the large-scale applications of neonicotinoids, the EU decision would severely impact the choice of available plant protection measures. India urged the European Union to postpone the implementation of the proposed regulation; to justify the link between the new MRLs and the objective to be achieved; and to notify the measure to the SPS Committee.

StatementSubmitted: China and the international community agreed that reasonable MRLs should be formulated to protect consumer health and promote fair trade in food. As per Article 2.2 of the TBT Agreement, members shall ensure that technical regulations are not prepared, adopted, or applied with a view to or with the effect of creating unnecessary obstacles to international trade. Revoking or lowering MRLs for clothianidin and thiamethoxam won’t affect the EU’s agricultural production since their approvals expired earlier. However, the proposed EU regulation will create unnecessary obstacles to international trade as it will be a de facto trade barrier that has major consequences on WTO members that export foods to the EU although they approve the use of the two substances, which no concern was raised after science-based risk assessment.As per Article 5.1 of the SPS Agreement, China believes it would be better if the EU could take full account of the differences in different pesticide products, application periods, and treated crops when conducting risk assessments of neonicotinoid pesticides on bees. Clothianidin and thiamethoxam can also be applied to non-nectar or flowering crops (no exposure to bees). In particular, the limit of crops such as crops harvested before flowering or cultivated indoors should not be revoked, and a full and reasonable risk assessment should be considered. Obviously, the EU's measures expand the scope beyond the purpose of protecting bees and create unnecessary trade barriers for other members, especially for developing members. Therefore, China suggests that the EU should formulate MRLs reasonably or in line with CAC while effectively safeguarding the safety of bees and other non-target organisms.
Summary: China considered that the proposed EU regulation would create an unnecessary de facto barrier to international trade with major consequences on WTO Members, especially developing countries exporting food to the European Union. Referring to Article 5.1 of the SPS Agreement, China indicated that a full risk assessment should be considered, taking into account differences in pesticide products, application periods, and treated crops. China complained the measure expanded beyond the scope of protecting bees and suggested adopting MRLs in line with Codex.

StatementSubmitted: STC ID 549 EU Regulation No 396/2005 setting pesticide MRLs in food and feed of plant and animal origin  India notes European Union’s response to SPS STC 549. In light of the responses from WTO Members in both SPS STC 534 and SPS STC 549, India requests European Union reconsider its approach to setting MRLs. In this regard,  India invites European Union to review the regulation taking into account  WTO rules and Codex recommendations.  As indicated in the previous statement, India requests the EU to share the detailed risk assessment underlying the ‘current knowledge’ as specified in response to SPS STC 534, as well as the details of the alternative measures that were considered in arriving at the conclusion of selecting reduction of MRLs. Further, India requests European Union to grant an opportunity to the WTO Members to examine the risk assessment and share their comments. Meanwhile, European Union is requested to delay the implementation of amendments to the regulation.
Summary: India requested the European Union to delay the implementation of the regulation's amendments . Specifically, India asked the European Union to reconsider its approach to setting MRLs, review the regulation taking into account WTO rules and Codex recommendations, share the detailed risk assessment and the alternative measures considered, and grant an opportunity to Members to examine the risk assessment and share their comments.

StatementSubmitted: EU Regulation No 396/2005 setting pesticide MRLs in food and feed of plant and animal origin (STC ID 549)India thanks the EU for its response. India would like to reiterate its earlier comments on the measures adopted by the EU. EU has not shared relevant scientific studies showing the risk assessment demonstrating the need to fix the MRL of these two pesticides at the level determined by the EU and its assessment vis-à-vis other approaches considered in arriving at the conclusion that this is the least trade-restrictive approach possible. The lowering of Maximum Residue Levels (MRLs) is a regulatory tool for ensuring food safety standards, not for environmental protection. India requests European Union to engage with other Members in exploring and arriving at a viable solution. Meanwhile, European Union is requested to delay the implementation of amendments to the regulation.
Summary: India drew Members' attention to its statement uploaded in eAgenda.

StatementSubmitted: India would like to reiterate its earlier concerns about the MRL measures adopted by the EU.India considers that imposing stringent MRLs on pesticide residuals is not an appropriatemeasure to pursue environmental outcomes. The objective of setting MRLs is to ensurefood safety and facilitate the trade of safe agri-food products. It is not to protect theenvironment in third countries. The Codex Committee on Pesticide Residues confirmedlast year that consideration of environmental issues of global concern was outside thescope of its mandate. In the previous statements, India requested the EU to share adetailed risk assessment and scientific studies illustrating the need to fix the MRLs of thetwo neonicotinoid substances, clothianidin and thiamethoxam, at the level determined bythe EU. The EU has not provided any data demonstrating that the use of these twosubstances at current MRL levels poses a real risk to pollinators, either in the EU orglobally. India is concerned about the EU’s measures expanding beyond the scope ofprotecting bees and creating unnecessary trade barriers for third countries. India onceagain requests the EU to engage with other members to come to a harmonized solution.Till then, the EU is requested to delay implementation of the amendments to the regulation.
Summary: India reiterated its concerns about the EU MRL approach as a tool to pursue environmental outcomes in third countries. India observed that the European Union had not shared information about the risk assessment and scientific studies that support the establishment of EU MRLs for clothianidin and thiamethoxam and the correlation of this measure with the risk to pollinators. India requested the European Union to engage with Members towards a harmonized solution and to delay the implementation of the amendments to the regulation.

StatementSubmitted: India would like to reiterate its earlier concerns regarding the reduction to the Level of Determination of MRLs for the neonicotinoids, clothianidin and thiamethoxam for imported agricultural products. The objective of setting MRL is to ensure food safety and facilitate the trade of safe agrifood products. It is not to protect the environment in the third countries. The Codex Committee on Pesticide Residues has confirmed that consideration of environmental issues of global concern is outside the scope of its mandate. Further the MRL of active substances, which has been revised by the EU exceeds the International standards set by the Codex. India is concerned that the EU is adopting protection levels that exceed the levels required to meet its legitimate objectives.India highlights that the EU’s ban on the imports of seeds treated with clothianidin and thiamethoxam is based on a study conducted by the EFSA which concludes that there are different levels of risks associated with different crops types and has not examined the impact of the use of these two substances on crops which are not attractive to bees. There are several crops grown in India – such as wheat, rice, potatoes, oats, tomatoes, etc. which are either non attractive to bees or have very low attractiveness as per the study conducted by the US Department of Agriculture. Therefore, EU may consider granting exemptions to the use of these active substances on crops that are not attractive to bees.India takes note that the EU has not granted exemption to those countries where the use of clothianidin and thiamethoxam cannot be avoided due to (i) different soil and other production conditions and including pest pressures and environmental conditions, and (ii) nonavailability of efficacious alternative pest control products. The EU's regulation enforces a complete prohibition on importing products treated with clothianidin and thiamethoxam. EU is yet to provide any data demonstrating that the use of these two substances at current MRL levels poses a real risk to pollinators, either in the EU or globally.India once again urges the EU to justify the link between the new MRLs and the objective to be achieved, develop a methodology whereby difference in the conditions of the production and pest pressures is taken into account and review the regulation considering WTO rules and Codex recommendations. India requests the EU to consider the concerns expressed by India and make appropriate amendments to its relevant regulations.
Summary: Referring to its complete statement in eAgenda, India reiterated its concerns about the reduction to the level of determination of MRLs for the neonicotinoids clothianidin and thiamethoxam for imported agricultural products. Underscoring that the objective of setting MRLs was to ensure food safety and facilitate the trade of safe agrifood products, and not to protect the environment in third countries, India urged the European Union to justify the link between the new MRLs and the objective to be achieved, to take into account the different conditions of the production and pest pressures, to review the regulation considering WTO rules and Codex recommendations, and to make appropriate amendments to its relevant regulations.

StatementSubmitted: India would like to reiterate its earlier concerns regarding the reduction of the MRLs to the Level of Determination (LOD) for the two neonicotinoids, clothianidin and thiamethoxam for imported agricultural products. India would like to mention that the lowering of the Maximum Residual limits (MRLs) is a regulatory tool used to ensure food safety standards and not for environmental protection in third countries. The Codex Committee on Pesticide Residues has also confirmed that consideration of environmental issues of global concern is outside the scope of its mandate. The EU has not even shared the risk assessment and scientific studies illustrating the need to fix the MRLs of the two neonicotinoid substances, clothianidin and thiamethoxam, at the level determined by the EU. No data has been provided by the EU, which demonstrates that the use of the two neonicotinoids pose a risk to pollinators in the EU or globally. India is concerned about the EU’s measures expanding beyond the scope of protecting bees and creating unnecessary trade barriers for third countries. India once again requests the EU review its regulation considering WTO rules and Codex recommendations and engage with other members to come to a harmonized solution.
Summary: India reiterated its concerns about the reduction of MRLs to the LOD for the neonicotinoids clothianidin and thiamethoxam in imported agricultural products. India underscored that setting MRLs was a regulatory tool to ensure food safety, not protect the environment in third countries. India noted that the CCPR had confirmed that consideration of environmental issues of global concerns were outside of its scope. India worried that the EU measure extended beyond the objective of protecting bees and requested the European Union to review its regulation considering WTO rules and Codex recommendations and engage with Members to find a harmonized solution.

StatementSubmitted: EU Commission proposal for reduction of the current MRL for 'nicotine' for imported Tea from India (G/SPS/N/EU/581)  At the outset, India would like to thank European Union (EU) for the reply furnished in response to the comments submitted by India in the context of Notification G/SPS/N/EU/581. However, India remains deeply concerned about the reduction of  MRL of Nicotine in Tea from the current level of 0.6 mg/kg to 0.5 mg/kg. India notes that the EU has relied on a study by EFSA recommending a revised threshold for the MRL of nicotine in Tea. India feels that the conclusions of this study by EFSA cannot be considered fairly representative of the EU population. Further, the decision to decrease the MRL of Nicotine in Tea is based on tests data collected based on a sampling of tea consignments received from various countries; and is not based on any toxicological analysis or field trials (as is the norm). Article 2.2 of the SPS Agreement states that SPS measures shall be based on scientific principles and are not to be maintained without sufficient scientific evidence. EU is requested to share the scientific risk assessment done in this regard. Nicotine is produced naturally by some of the alkaloid plants belonging to the Solanaceae family. It is also reported in non-quantifiable levels in some of the vegetables (cauliflower, broccoli), fruits (apple) and mushrooms.A research article (entitled "Quantitative Validation of Nicotine production in Tea (Camellia sinensis L.)" published by the Institute of Fruit & Tea Science, Kagoshima, Japan (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0195422) reported that endogenous nicotine is present in tea plant. All the analysed samples (collected from six Asian countries, including India) contained nicotine ranging from 0.011 to 0.694 mg/kg of dry weight.
