Nicotine contents remained constant during the manufacturing of green, oolong and black teas, implying that nicotine is stable against heating, drying, enzymatic oxidation and mechanical damage during processing.The decision to lower the MRL of Nicotine in Tea should not be taken based on the monitoring data only but with scientific data on the proper risk assessment. Until it is proven that the present level of 0.6 mg/Kg nicotine in Tea bears potential risk to EU consumers, the status quo should be maintained.
Summary: India thanked the European Union for its reply in the context of notification G/SPS/N/EU/581 and raised its concerns on the reduction of the MRL for nicotine in tea from 0.6 mg/kg to 0.5 mg/kg. India was of the view that the study on which the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) had based the lowering of this MRL was not representative of the EU population. Noting that SPS measures should be based on scientific principles, as established in Article 2.2 of the Agreement, India requested the European Union to share its scientific risk assessment. India further explained that some plants naturally produced nicotine, and that recent studies had shown that the content of endogenous nicotine present in tea plants remained constant during manufacturing of green, oolong and black teas. India urged the European Union to maintain the current limit of nicotine in tea in the absence of scientific data and a proper risk assessment.

StatementSubmitted: STC ID 550: EU Commission proposal for reduction of the current MRL for "nicotine" for imported tea from India (G/SPS/N/EU/581) India thanks European Union for its response. In furtherance of the same, India requests the EU to reconsider its acute risk exposure calculations, especially in light of the fact that the methodology used has assumed Nicotine is a pesticide which it is not. Secondly, the sample selections for calculating the exposure risks for ‘Unprocessed tea (dried tea leaves)’ and ‘Processed tea (tea infusions)’ do not seem to be sufficiently representative. For a further comprehensive analysis, India requests the EU to share the detailed methodology for arriving at the threshold residual concentration level of 0.52 mg/kg for Nicotine in tea. Lastly, the risk exposure calculations have assumed a 100% transfer of nicotine residues from dry tea leaves to their infusion as a default, which may be erroneous due to insufficiency in supporting data.With all these discrepancies in sight, India requests the EU to withdraw its MRL revision and ensure compliance with the principles of the SPS Agreement.
Summary: India requested the European Union to reconsider its acute risk exposure calculations given that the methodology used had wrongly assumed nicotine to be a pesticide. India noted that the sample selections for calculating exposure risks for unprocessed tea (dried tea leaves) and processed tea (tea infusions) did not seem to be sufficiently representative, and requested the European Union to share the detailed methodology for determining the threshold residual concentration level of 0.52 mg/kg for nicotine in tea. India further explained that the risk exposure calculations had assumed a 100% transfer of nicotine residues from dry tea leaves to their infusion as a default, which might be erroneous due to insufficiency of supporting data. India requested the European Union to withdraw its MRL revision and comply with the SPS Agreement.

StatementSubmitted: EU Commission proposal for reduction of the current MRL for "nicotine" forimported tea from India (STC ID 550)India thanks European Union for its response. Tea plants contain Nicotine that is not derived from exogenous sources. In addition, Nicotine contents in tea leaves change seasonally and differ among the cultivars. Furthermore, the difference in Nicotine contents is also observed among tea-growing regions.To determine whether endogenous Nicotine is present in tea, a study was conducted by the Faculty of Agriculture, Japan, where they measured Nicotine contents of several types of tea from Japan and five Other Asian countries, including India (Quantitative Validation of Nicotine Production in Tea — by Ikka T., Yamashita H., Kurita L, Tanaka Y., Taniguchi F., Ogino A., et al., 2018). The results show that the presence of Nicotine in black tea ranged between 00.02 mg/kg to 00.69 mg/kg higher than in green and oolong tea, which comes naturally in tea.Further, Nicotine is not a pesticide; instead, tea absorbs Nicotine naturally, and due to its extremely low levels and slow absorption rate, the Nicotine in tea is not addictive. India requests the EU to withdraw its MRL revision and ensure compliance with the principles of the SPS Agreement.
Summary: Reiterating its concern regarding the EU proposed reduction of the MRL for nicotine for imported tea, India noted that the nicotine present in tea plants was not derived from exogenous sources and that its content varied throughout the seasons and among different cultivars and tea-growing regions. India further indicated that nicotine was not a pesticide and that it was not addictive given its natural, slow absorption and the low level in tea. India requested the European Union to withdraw its MRL revision and to ensure compliance with the principles of the SPS Agreement.

StatementSubmitted: India would like to reiterate its previously raised concerns about the EU’s classification of Nicotine as a pesticide and reduction of the MRL for Nicotine in tea from 0.6 mg/kg to 0.5 mg/kg.Tea plants contain nicotine that is not derived from exogenous sources. Research says that despite being present in tea, it is absorbed differently than the Nicotine in cigarettes and poses very little risk to human health. Due to its extremely low levels and slow absorption rate, the nicotine in tea is not addictive. It does not cause nicotine cravings or trigger ‘Nicotine Addiction’, nor will it cause any side effects.To determine whether endogenous Nicotine is present in tea, a study was conducted by the Faculty of Agriculture, Japan, where they measured the Nicotine contents of several types of tea from Japan and five other Asian countries, including India. (c.f. ‘Quantitative Validation of Nicotine Production in Tea’ by Ikka T., Yamashita H., Kurita I., Tanaka Y., Taniguchi F. Ogino A. (2018).Results show that the presence of Nicotine in teas ranges between 00.02 to 00.69 mg/kg.In fact, the European Food Safety Authority first proposed an MRL for tea at 00.60 mg/kg, which was then established by the European Commission in 2011. Moreover, Nicotine has no Codex MRL, which proves that it is not harmful to food. Also, Nicotine is not a pesticide; rather, tea absorbs nicotine naturally and due to its extremely low levels and slow absorption rate, the Nicotine in tea is not addictive.The EFSA Study (Statement on the revised targeted risk assessment for certain maximum residue levels for Nicotine, dated February 07, 2023) which states that: “EFSA very recently received new information indicating that some of the consumption data based on which it had identified unacceptable risks for consumers with the existing MRL for Nicotine in teas of 00.60 mg/kg may not accurately reflect exposure of the population and would lead to an overestimation of the risk. Therefore, EFSA performed a new acute dietary risk assessment for nicotine in teas, excluding the controversial consumption data, and concluded that the current MRL for Nicotine in teas is safe for consumers”.In view of the foregoing, India requests the EU to withdraw its MRL revision and ensure compliance with the principles of the SPS Agreement.
Summary: India expressed its concerns about the EU proposal to reduce the MRL for nicotine for tea from 0.6 mg/kg to 0.5 mg/kg. India stated that the nicotine present in tea plants was not derived from exogenous sources and that it was absorbed differently than nicotine in cigarettes, posed little risk to human health and was not addictive given its slow absorption and the low level in tea. In India's view, nicotine was not a pesticide, and the fact that there was no Codex MRL established for nicotine proved that it was not harmful to food. India requested the European Union to withdraw its MRL revision and to ensure compliance with the principles of the SPS Agreement.

StatementSubmitted: India thanks the EU for its response. However, India remains deeply concerned about the EU’s continued classification of Nicotine as a pesticide and reduction of the MRL for Nicotine in tea from 0.6 mg/kg to 0.5 mg/kg. In India, it is observed that Nicotine found in tea plants originates internally, rather than from external sources. Moreover, the Nicotine levels in tea leaves fluctuate seasonally and vary among different varieties of tea plants and its content are also evident across various regions where tea is cultivated. The recent study has also shown that the content of endogenous nicotine present in tea plants remained constant during manufacturing of green, oolong and black teas.As per Tea and Herbal Infusions Europe (THIE), the EU health safety authority has clearly stated that there is no health risk arising from the existing MRL of 0.6mg/kg of Nicotine in Tea. Nicotine is not a pesticide in Indian tea cultivation and doesn’t have any label claim for use in tea from various competent authorities of India. EU’s decision for lowering the MRL of Nicotine in tea should not be based on the monitoring data only, but also with scientific data on the proper risk assessment as being done by the EFSA on potential consumer risk with the existing MRL.We understand that both India and the EU are in the process of collating and generating systematic data on Nicotine occurrence in tea. Both the data sets will be available for scientific scrutiny in some time and a fresh round of risk assessment can be undertaken. India urges the EU withdraw its MRL revision. India recalls that EU has also mentioned “MRLs should be set as low as reasonably achievable” it would be helpful if EU could elaborate on reasonably achievable parts. India seeks clarification from EU as to whether it is achievable through the analytical method (LOQ) or achievable through monitoring data of traded samples?In view of the foregoing, India requests the EU to withdraw its MRL revision and ensure compliance with the principles of the SPS Agreement.
Summary: India expressed its concerns about the EU reduction of the MRL for nicotine for tea from 0.6 mg/kg to 0.5 mg/kg. India stated that the nicotine present in tea plants was not derived from exogenous sources, that levels fluctuated seasonally and varied among varieties, and that the content of endogenous nicotine present in tea plants remained constant during the manufacturing of different teas. In India's view, nicotine was not a pesticide and, therefore, the EU decision to lower the MRL of nicotine in tea should not be based on the monitoring data only, but also on scientific data on the assessment of potential consumer risk with the existing MRL. India requested the European Union to withdraw its MRL revision until systematic data on nicotine occurrence in tea were available, to clarify the concept of "reasonably achievable" MRLs, and to ensure compliance with the principles of the SPS Agreement.

StatementSubmitted: India would like to reiterate its previously raised concerns about the EU’s continued classification of Nicotine as a pesticide and reduction of the MRL for Nicotine in tea from 0.6 mg/kg to 0.5 mg/kg. The MRL of Nicotine in tea was temporarily set by the EU Commission Regulation (EU) No. 812/2011 at 00.60 mg/kg which was reduced vide the aforesaid notification to 00.40 mg/kg which has now again recommended at 00.52 mg/kg. India would like to highlight that the Tea plants contain Nicotine which is not derived from exogenous sources. The Nicotine contents in tea leaves change seasonally and differ among the cultivars. Difference in the nicotine contents has also been observed among different tea-growing regions. In 2018, to determine whether endogenous nicotine is present in tea, a study was conducted in Japan where they measured nicotine contents of several types of tea from Japan and five other Asian countries including India (cf. “Quantitative validation of Nicotine production in tea” by Ikka et al). The results of the study indicated that the presence of nicotine in black tea ranges between 0.02 mg/kg to 0.69 mg/kg. In India, Nicotine is not a pesticide in tea cultivation and doesn’t have any label claim for use in tea from various competent authorities of India.EU’s decision for lowering the MRL of Nicotine in tea should be based on scientific data on the proper risk assessment and not only on monitoring data as being done by the EFSA on potential consumer risk with the existing MRL Additionally, the sample selection for calculating the exposure risk “Unprocessed Tea (dried tea leaves)” and “Processed Tea leaves (Tea infusions)” do not seem to be sufficiently representative. For a further comprehensive analysis, India requests the EU to share the detailed methodology for arriving at the threshold residue concentration level of 0.52 mg/kg for Nicotine. India would like to state that Nicotine is not a pesticide, instead tea leaves absorb nicotine naturally and due to its extremely low levels and slow absorption rates, Nicotine in tea is not addictive. Thus, India requests the EU to withdraw its MRL revision and ensure compliance with the principles of the SPS Agreement.
Summary: India reiterated its concerns about the EU classification of nicotine as a pesticide and the EU reduction of the MRL for nicotine for tea from 0.6 mg/kg to 0.5 mg/kg. India stated that the nicotine present in tea plants was not derived from exogenous sources, levels fluctuated seasonally and varied among varieties, and the content of endogenous nicotine present in tea plants remained constant during the manufacturing of different teas. Therefore, India argued that the EU decision to lower the MRL of nicotine in tea should not have been based solely on monitoring data from EFSA but should also have considered scientific data assessing the potential consumer risk associated with the existing MRL. Emphasizing that nicotine was not a pesticide, India requested the European Union to withdraw its MRL revision and ensure compliance with the principles of the SPS Agreement.

StatementSubmitted: In 2021, it is reported by certain establishments that the export of vitamin D3 from China was banned by the entry point of the Netherlands with the excuse that vitamin D3 is a product of animal origin and should be approved for market access according to Article 25 of (EU)2021/405. Since the transitional measures laid down in Commission Regulation (EU) 2017/185, which stipulated in article 4 that chapter III of Regulation 854/2004/EC shall not apply to imports of products of animal origin for which no harmonized public health import requirements have been established, the export of Vitamin D3 from China to EU keep normal before 2021. However, as the transitional regulations expired on December 31, 2020, the Netherlands refused to continue to import Chinese products on this ground.On 28th Mar. 2022, the (EU) 2022/887 was adopted by the EU which mentioned the fact that there is no public health concern related to the importation of vitamin D3 due to the robust process by which it is obtained from lanolin, so the importation of vitamin D3 referred to by the HS codes under heading 2936 and derived from lanolin should be authorized again. On 3rd May 2022, EU requested the comments on the amending 853/2004/EC which intend to put the vitamin D3 on the list of highly refined products.Before the new regulations come into force, the Netherlands immediately prohibited the import of related products from China, which caused serious obstacles to trade. According to 7 paragraph of Article 5 in the SPS Agreement, the member that provisionally adopted SPS measures shall seek to obtain the additional information necessary for a more objective assessment of risk and review the measure accordingly within a reasonable period of time, so the EU side may review it and adopt new measures within a reasonable period of time. Meanwhile, China highly appreciates the suggestion provided by the EU side to put vitamin D3 on the list of highly refined product and earnestly request the EU side to amend the relevant regulation and put it into effect soon to restore the import of vitamin D3 from China.
Summary: China noted that the Netherlands had banned the entry of exports of vitamin D3 on grounds of its classification as a product of animal origin, and therefore subject to approval for market access. The bans had taken effect in 2021, after the expiry of the established transitional periods. China regretted that the bans had been applied prior to the entry into force of the EU Regulations, and reminded Members of the obligations to seek additional information and to review provisional measures in accordance with Article 5.7 of the SPS Agreement. China appreciated the EU suggestion to put vitamin D3 on the list of highly refined products, and requested the European Union to restore the imports from China.

StatementSubmitted: Since last year, it has been repeatedly reported by China’s establishments that their shipments of lanolin-derived vitamin D3 for feed additives use exported to the EU have been blocked at the border of Belgium and Germany. The explanation we received is that the lanolin-derived vitamin D3 for feed use is considered to be animal origin, which doesn’t conform to the import conditions stipulated in Article 2 of Commission Decision of 2002/994/EC. In fact, it has been 20 years since the enactment of 2002/994/EC, during which the EU has kept importing lanolin-derived vitamin D3 for feed use originating from China normally. In addition, the EU adopted the regulation of (EU) 2022/887 on 28th Mar. 2022, which made very clear that “Due to the robust process by which vitamin D3 is obtained from lanolin, there is no public health concern related to the importation of such product. Importation of vitamin D3 derived from lanolin should therefore be authorised again”.Therefore, China requests the EU side to take appropriate measures to resume normal trade of vitamin D3 between China and the EU as soon as possible, based on the assessment and according to the scientific basis of the SPS Agreement.
Summary: China reported that, since 2002, shipments of lanolin-derived vitamin D3 for feed additives use exported to the European Union had been blocked at the border of Belgium and Germany on the ground that it was considered to be of animal origin, not compliant with Commission Decision 2002/994/EC. Yet, in the last 20 years since the enactment of that Commission Decision, the European Union had imported lanolin-derived vitamin D3 for feed use originating from China. China further referred to Regulation (EU) No 2022/887, which made clear that there was no public health concern related to the importation of such product. China requested the European Union to take appropriate measures to resume trade of vitamin D3 with China as soon as possible.

StatementSubmitted: EU increased sampling frequency for inspection of farmed shrimps and newly listed fishery establishments not permitted to export aquaculture products EU has drastically increased the sampling frequency for antibiotic residues in farmed shrimp from the existing levels of 10% to 50%, since October 2016.  The higher rate of the sampling frequency of 50% is acting as an implicit non-tariff barrier for the export of farmed shrimps from India as it adds to the cost of assessing the EU market.India has taken a number of corrective steps to ensure compliance with the EU's regulatory requirements. As a result, the number of rejections due to antibiotic detection has declined from 15 in 2017 to just 3 in 2021. India, therefore, urges the EU  to reduce the sampling frequency for testing antibiotic residue in farmed shrimp consignments from 50% to 10%, as was prevalent earlier.India would like to thank the EU for agreeing to India's request to permit new units to export sea-caught items. It is further requested that all newly enlisted units be permitted to export aquacultured products, as these units have no history of rejection in the EU market.  Further, the EU delisted 14 aquaculture units in 2016 and 2017. To date, only 5 units have been relisted for export of wild-caught items. India urges the EU to relist all the delisted units to export both wild caught and aquacultured products.
Summary: In India's view, the EU increased sampling frequency for antibiotic residues in farmed shrimp from 10% to 50% imposed a non-tariff barrier to trade. India requested the European Union to revert to the previous sampling frequency as a result of the corrective actions taken and the reduction in the number of rejections due to antibiotic detection. Expressing gratitude for the enlisting of new units to export sea-caught items, India further requested that newly enlisted units be permitted to export aquaculture products. Regretting that only five of the 14 aquaculture units delisted in 2016 and 2017 had been relisted for export of wild-caught items, India urged the European Union to relist the remaining units to export both wild-caught and aquaculture products.

StatementSubmitted: STC ID 552 – EU increased sampling frequency for inspection of farmed shrimps and newly listed fishery establishments not permitted to export aquaculture products India remains concerned about the increased level of sampling and testing implemented on imports for farm shrimps as India has successfully demonstrated a remarkable reduction in antibiotic rejections in farmed shrimps exported to the EU, with just only one rejection during previous year and NIL rejections as of now during the current year. EU is therefore requested to bring down the sampling and testing frequency to the previous level of 10%.  Considerable efforts have been taken by India to eliminate antibiotic rejections in Indian-origin-farmed shrimps. Finally, we also request the EU to list all the delisted units and permit newly listed units to export farmed shrimps.
Summary: India reiterated its concerns about the increased level of sampling and testing on imports for farmed shrimps despite India's remarkable reduction in antibiotic rejections in farmed shrimps exported to the European Union (one rejection in 2022 and no rejection in 2023 thus far). India requested the European Union to bring down the sampling and testing frequency to the previous level of 10% and to list all the delisted units and permit newly listed units to export farmed shrimps to the European Union.

StatementSubmitted: EU increased sampling frequency for inspection of farmed shrimps and newly listed fishery establishments not permitted to export aquaculture products (STC ID 552)India thanks the EU for its response. However, India remains concerned about the increased level of sampling and testing implemented on imports for farm shrimps. By corrective action, India has successfully demonstrated a remarkable reduction in antibiotic rejections in farmed shrimps exported to the EU. India urges the EU to provide equivalence in sampling frequency at par with other supplying countries considering the reduction in the number of rejections due to antibiotic residues and on the basis of corrective actions initiated based on the EU audit findings. Further, India requests the EU to list all the delisted units and permit newly listed units to export farmed shrimps.
Summary: India reiterated its concerns about the increased level of sampling and testing on imports for farmed shrimps despite India's remarkable reduction in antibiotic rejections in farmed shrimps exported to the European Union. India requested that the European Union provide equivalence in sampling with other supplying countries, to list all the delisted units and to permit newly listed units to export farmed shrimps to the European Union.

StatementSubmitted: India would like to reiterate its concern about the increased level of sampling and testing the EU implemented on imports for farm shrimps. By corrective action, India has successfully demonstrated a remarkable reduction in antibiotic rejections in farmed shrimps exported to the EU. India urges the EU to provide equivalence in sampling frequency at par with other supplying countries in considering the reduction in the number of rejections due to antibiotic residues and on the basis of corrective actions initiated based on the EU audit findings. The EU may lower the sampling frequency of aquaculture consignments from 50% to 10%. Secondly, the DG (SANTE) Mission visited India in September 2022 to audit the control of residues and contaminants in live animals and animal products, including controls on veterinary medicinal products. There were two recommendations raised related to aquaculture. India has taken action on the recommendations, even submitting supporting documents to the EU vide an EIC letter dated. 07.02.2023, 06.07.2023 and email dated 25.08.2023. Accordingly, both the recommendations raised w.r.t aquaculture have been satisfactorily closed by the EU on 23.10.2023. In view of the above, India requests the EU to expedite the following:- (i) Listing of all 36 new aquaculture establishments for which application has been submitted in TRACES.(ii) Re-listing of 8 delisted establishments for which application has been submitted in TRACES.(iii) Lower the sampling frequency of aquaculture consignments from 50% to 10%
Summary: India reiterated its concerns about the increased level of sampling and testing on farmed shrimps exported to the European Union, despite the reduction of antibiotic rejections and the fulfilment of the two recommendations raised following an EU mission to audit the control of residues and contaminants in live animals and animal products. India requested the European Union to provide equivalence in sampling with other supplying countries; to list all the 36 new aquaculture establishments and to re-list the eight delisted establishments for which applications had been submitted in TRACES; and to lower the sampling frequency of aquaculture consignments.

StatementSubmitted: India would like to reiterate its previously raised concerns regarding the increased level of sampling and testing implemented by the EU on the imports for farm shrimps. By corrective action, India has successfully demonstrated a significant reduction in antibiotic rejections in farmed shrimps exported to the EU.DG(SANTE) Mission during its visit has also observed the reduction in the number of rejections and the efficacy with which India has implemented its inspection programs and tests. India urges the EU to provide equivalence in sampling frequency at par with other supplying countries. Considering the reduction in the number of rejections due to antibiotic residues and on the basis of corrective actions initiated based on the EU audit findings, the EU may lower the sampling frequency of aquaculture consignments from 50% to 10%. Secondly, the applications of 19 sea caught establishments and 42 aquaculture establishments are yet to be considered by EU on TRACES. The listing of new fishery establishments on TRACES is not done expeditiously and on regular basis as and when India submits application for listing on website of TRACES by the EU. Thirdly, five of de-listed establishments are re-listed in TRACES. However, Indian exporters are unable to export aquaculture products, as these establishments are listed for ‘sea-caught’ category only. In view of the above, India requests the EU to expedite the following:(i) Listing of the new aquaculture establishments for which application has been submitted in TRACES. (ii) Re-listing of 8 de-listed establishments for which application has been submitted in TRACES. (iii) Lower the sampling frequency of aquaculture consignments from 50% to 10%.
Summary: India reiterated its concerns about the increased level of sampling and testing on farmed shrimps exported to the European Union, despite the reduction of antibiotic rejections and corrective actions initiated based on EU audit findings. India requested the European Union to: provide equivalence in inspection programme and test and in sampling frequency with other supplying countries; expedite the listing new aquaculture establishments and re-list eight delisted establishments for which applications had been submitted in the EU online platform for animal and plant health certification "TRACES"; and lower the sampling frequency of aquaculture consignments from 50 to 10 percent.

StatementSubmitted: The EU would like to refer to the Order issued on 10 October 2022 by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) covering five categories of products for which the registration of foreign food manufacturing facilities will become mandatory.This Order was notified to the TBT committee in November 2020 under G/TBT/N/IND/180. Unfortunately the Order was adopted without the EU receiving a reply to the comments submitted in February 2021. The EU has discussed this measure in the TBT committee but given that it contains SPS elements too we have decided to bring it also to this committee. The EU would like to thank India for clarifying:- The scope of products/food categories subject to the registration of foreign food facilities, even if only in general terms; -That the new requirements measures enter into force on 1 February 2023.However, given the: (1) risk of trade disruption associated to the new registration of facilities (2) the generic nature of the list of products/food categories; (3) the absence of any criteria to define the risks associated to the mentioned list; (4) and the number of unanswered questions by India; the EU would like to ask India to:- Further postpone the date of entering into force for, at least, 12 months so that the competent authorities and companies in the exporting countries to have enough time to adapt,- Provide a list of the HS product codes at least at 4 digit level of the commodities that need to be registered, and to indicate the risks associated to each of the products/food categories;-Make easily accessible the import sanitary measures of India (Regulations), which are applicable to each of the products/food categories subject to the registration of facilities;-Clarify the modalities related to inspections (and audits) of the facilities by India and by the competent authorities of the exporting countries;-Notify the measures related to the registration of establishments also to the WTO SPS Committee; Lastly we kindly invite India to reply in writing to the comments sent to the TBT notification and to a letter sent on 12 September 2022. We would also welcome the opportunity to meet bilaterally to discuss all these matters.
Summary: The European Union regretted that the Indian Order requiring the registration of foreign facilities manufacturing five product categories, issued by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) and notified as G/TBT/N/IND/180, had been adopted without a response to EU comments. The European Union requested India to clarify the scope of products subject to registration; to postpone the entry into force of new requirements for 12 months; to provide four-digit level HS codes for products subject to registration, with the indication of associated risks; to make Indian import sanitary measures easily accessible; to clarify the facility inspection modalities; to notify the measure at issue to the SPS Committee; and to respond to the comments submitted by the European Union. The European Union would welcome the opportunity to engage in bilateral discussions with Indian authorities.

StatementSubmitted: The European Union would like to refer to its previous statements on the India's import requirements related to the registration foreign food manufacturing facilities.Referring, we would like to thank India for clarifying our questions regarding the FSSAI Order of 10 October 2022 (including the scope of products/food categories subject to the registration), and for postponing the entering into force of the new requirements to 1 February 2023. However, we note that several food manufacturing facilities have not yet been registered in the new India’s ReFoM online system, and recall that we did not receive a formal written reply to the comments we sent to India in February 2021 to the notification G/TBT/N/IND/180.The EU is concerned about the absence of any specific criteria to define the risks associated to the listing or delisting of facilities, which may go beyond the India legislation; and that there are different authorities in India regulating imports of the same products,  resulting in unnecessary duplication and confusion for operators.The EU would like to ask India to:Clarify the modalities related to audits to the exporting countries, inspections of facilities, border checks and health certificates associated to the registration of foreign food manufacturing facilities, if and when these requirements will be made obligatory by any of the India authorities;Provide written guidance to the exporting countries and companies on how they should register the facilities and send the lists of facilities to India, and to maintain the guidance updated;Clarify to which India legislation the registration of food facilities relates to; andAvoid a duplication of certificates for the same productFinally, the EU would like to:Repeat its request for India to notify new measures related to the registration of food manufacturing facilities to both the WTO SPS and TBT Committees, and Reiterate its availability to cooperate with the different competent authorities of India to enhance mutual understanding and avoid unnecessary and unjustified disruptions to trade. *   *  *
Summary: Referring to its previous statements regarding India's import requirements related to the registration of foreign food manufacturing facilities, the European Union thanked India for clarifying its questions regarding the Order of October 2022 of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) and for postponing the entry into force of the new requirements to February 2023. However, the European Union noted that several food manufacturing facilities had not been registered in the online system, with no written reply from India to inquiries. The European Union expressed concerns regarding the listing or delisting of facilities and different authorities regulating imports of the same products. Among others, the European Union requested India to clarify the modalities related to audits and inspections of facilities, border checks and health certificates, provide written and update guidance to the exporting countries and companies on how they should register facilities, and avoid a duplication of certificates for the same product. The European Union also repeated its request for this measure to be notified in both the SPS and TBT Committees.

StatementSubmitted: The European Union would like to refer to India's import requirements relating to the registration of foreign food manufacturing facilities.The EU would like to thank India for clarifying our questions regarding the FSSAI Order of 10 October 2022, and in particular for having clarified that imports into India will not stop if establishments are not listed. However, the EU remains concerned about the possible trade disruptions that may occur in the future because of the absence of any specific criteria to define the risks associated to the listing or delisting of facilities, and that there are different authorities in India regulating imports of the same products, resulting in unnecessary duplication and confusion for operators.The EU would like to ask India to:clarify the modalities related to audits to the exporting countries, inspections of facilities, border checks and health certificates associated to the registration of foreign food manufacturing facilities, if and when these requirements will be made obligatory by any of the India authorities;provide written guidance to the exporting countries and companies on how they should register clarify to which Indian legislation the registration of food facilities relates to; andavoid a duplication of certificates for the same productFinally, the EU would like to:reiterate its request that India notifies new measures related to the registration of food manufacturing facilities to both the WTO SPS and TBT Committees, and reiterate our availability to cooperate with the different competent authorities of India to enhance mutual understanding and avoid unnecessary and unjustified disruptions to trade.
Summary: Referring to its statements in previous Committee meetings regarding India's import requirements related to the registration of foreign food manufacturing facilities, the European Union thanked India for responding to its questions regarding the Order of October 2022 of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) and postponing the entry into force of the new requirements to February 2023. However, several food manufacturing facilities had not been registered in the online system, with no written reply from India to inquiries. The European Union expressed concerns regarding the listing or delisting of facilities and different authorities regulating imports of the same products. Among others, the European Union requested India to clarify the modalities related to audits and inspections of facilities, border checks and health certificates, provide written and updated guidance to the exporting countries and companies on how they should register facilities, and avoid duplication of certificates. The European Union also reiterated its request for this measure to be notified to both the SPS and TBT Committees.

StatementSubmitted: The European Union would like to refer to the concerns raised at previous meetings regarding the registration of establishments and thank India for the guidance provided so far on how facilities should be registered. Even if no trade disruption has occurred until now, the EU remains concerned about the possible disruption to trade in the future associated to delays in listing registered facilities; given the absence of any specific criteria to define the risks associated to the listing or delisting of facilities.The EU would like to ask India to please:Provide written guidance on how to maintain the list of facilities updated;Provide details about the risk assessment India performed to base the requirements about the registration of facilities;Clarify the modalities related to audits to the exporting countries, inspections of facilities, border checks and health certificates associated to the registration of foreign food manufacturing facilities;Consider a long transition period before restricting imports based on the registration of facilities, and avoid that facilities that have not yet been registered in the India’s Registration of Foreign Manufacturers (ReFoM online system) due to administrative errors cannot export;Consider avoiding that the competent authorities of the export countries sign more than one certificate with regard to the same sanitary measure; andNotify to both the WTO TBT and SPS Committees the above-mentioned modalities and guidance, to ensure full transparency and timely follow-up by all the competent authorities, producers and exporters.
Summary: The European Union reiterated its concern about the possible disruption to trade associated with delays in listing registered foreign food manufacturing facilities. The European Union sought clarification on the risk assessment performed to establish the requirements for the registration of facilities; how to maintain the list of facilities updated; and the modalities related to audits to the exporting countries, inspections of facilities, border checks and health certificates. The European Union further requested India to consider a longer transition period before restricting imports based on the registration of facilities; to avoid suspending facilities that had yet been unable to register; and to avoid duplication in the signing of certificates. The European Union invited India to notify the measure to both the SPS and TBT Committees.

StatementSubmitted: The European Union would like to thank India for the guidance provided so far on how facilities should be registered. However, the EU would still refer to its previous statements on this measure and reiterate some of the concerns raised at previous meetings. The EU acknowledges that no trade disruption has occurred until now. However, the EU remains concerned about the possible disruption to trade in the future associated to lack of clarity and delays in listing registered facilities. The EU is particularly worried about the absence of specific criteria related: (1) to the inspections and audits to exporting countries; and (2) to the definition of the risks associated to the listing or delisting of facilities. Therefore, the EU would like to kindly ask India to provide guidance on these elements, as well as to clarify the procedure to follow to maintain the list of facilities updated.The EU would like to invite India to provide a sufficiently long transition period before restricting imports based on the registration of facilities, and avoid that facilities that have not yet been registered in the India’s Registration of Foreign Manufacturers (ReFoM online system) due to administrative errors, cannot export;The EU would like to repeat its request to India to notify these amendments and future measures related to the registration of food manufacturing facilities to the WTO SPS Committee.
Summary: Acknowledging India's guidance on facility registration, the European Union reiterated its concerns regarding the lack of clarity and the delays in listing registered facilities, which could potentially disrupt future trade. Specifically, the European Union sought further clarity on the criteria related to inspections, audits, and the definition of associated risks, as well as clarification on updating facility lists. The European Union urged India to consider a longer transition period to avoid suspending facilities that had yet to register and to prevent duplication in the issuance of certificates. The European Union reiterated its call for India to notify these amendments and future measures related to facility registration to the SPS Committee.

StatementSubmitted: The European Union would like to again thank India for the guidance provided so far on how facilities should be registered under the notified measure. However, the EU would still refer to its previous statements on this measure and reiterate some of the concerns raised at previous meetings. The EU acknowledges that no trade disruption has occurred until now. However, the EU remains concerned about the possible disruption to trade in the future associated to lack of clarity and delays in listing registered facilities. The EU is particularly worried about the absence of specific criteria related: (1) to the inspections and audits to exporting countries; and (2) to the definition of the risks associated to the listing or delisting of facilities.Therefore, the EU would like to kindly ask India to provide guidance on these elements, as well as to clarify the procedure to follow to maintain the list of facilities updated.The EU would like to invite India to provide a sufficiently long transition period before restricting imports based on the registration of facilities, and avoid that facilities that have not yet been registered yet in the India’s Registration of Foreign Manufacturers online system due to administrative errors, cannot export.The EU would like to repeat its request to India to notify these amendments and future measures related to the registration of food manufacturing facilities to the WTO SPS Committee.
Summary: Acknowledging India's guidance on facility registration, the European Union reiterated some of its concerns regarding the lack of clarity and the delays in listing registered facilities, which could potentially disrupt future trade. Specifically, the European Union sought further clarity on the criteria related to inspections, audits, and the definition of risks associated to the listing or delisting of facilities, as well as on the procedure to follow to maintain the list of facilities updated. StatementSubmitted: The EU would like to refer to the Order issued on 3 August 2022 by  the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) which provides for three new health certificates to accompany every imported consignment of three categories of products ? milk, pork, fish and their products. This Order was notified to the WTO TBT Committee in August with a date of entering into force on 1st November. On 27 October India informed about the postponement of the entry into force until 1 January 2023. The three model certificates refer to FSSAI Regulations, as well as to “guidelines” and “inspection/monitoring of checks criteria” specified from time to time by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India.The EU considers that the notified Order may seriously overcomplicate and disrupt EU imports into India. While we welcome the postponement of the entry into force by two months, we remain concerned that this period is too short to allow exporters and competent authorities to prepare themselves for its implementation.  The EU would like to point out that imports into India of the products covered by the certificates are already regulated by other competent authorities in India. There is thus a duplication of sanitary requirements and approval procedures.  The EU would like to ask India to: - postpone the entry into force of the notified Order by one year to give exporters and competent authorities sufficient time to comply with the new certificates and related import procedures. - provide clarification on the modalities related to “regular inspections/monitoring of checks” which is mentioned in the three certificates;- consider avoiding the duplication of sanitary measures in the different certificates by for instance merging the requirements relating to food safety and to animal health into one single model of import approval procedures. - notify, well in advance, its measures related to the new health certificates also to the WTO SPS Committee; - reply in written to the EU comments to the mentioned TBT notification and letter sent to the FSSAI on 12 September 2022. We would also welcome the opportunity to discuss this matter bilaterally. Thank you Chair
Summary: The European Union raised its concerns regarding an FSSAI Order introducing three new health certificates for milk, pork, fish and related products. While appreciating the two-month delay in the implementation of the Order notified to the TBT Committee, the European Union remained concerned that exporters and competent authorities would require extra time to prepare for its implementation. The European Union pointed to the duplication of sanitary requirements and approval procedures between different competent authorities in India, and requested India to postpone the Order's entry into force for one year; to provide clarifications on certificates modalities; to consider duplication avoidance in the different certificates; to notify this measure to the SPS Committee; and to provide written replies to EU comments. The European Union welcomed bilateral discussions on this matter.

StatementSubmitted: The EU would like to refer to India’s order covering health certificates for imported milk, pork, fish and related products. This measure was notified to the TBT committee.  The EU would like to thank India for the clarifications provided during an online information session and for providing the list of HS product codes associated to products covered by the new certificates. We would also like to thank India for recently announcing the postponement of the entry into force of the three health certificates, until further notice.We also acknowledge the new certificate for imports of milk and milk products that was merged by two competent authorities of India, in March 2023. We note however that pork and food products are still subject to two certificates requested by different authorities. Given the importance that the competent authorities and companies in the exporting countries  have sufficient time to adapt to new measures, the EU would like to ask India to:Avoid the duplication of sanitary measures associated to the different certificates for the import of the same products, which are required by different competent authorities of India;Notify to both the WTO TBT and SPS Committees the above-mentioned modalities and all future health certificates well in advance Finally, the EU reiterates its availability to cooperate with the competent authorities of India, to enhance mutual understanding and avoid unnecessary and unjustified disruptions to trade.
Summary: The European Union raised its concerns regarding an order issued by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) covering health certificates for imported milk, pork, fish, and related products, notified to the TBT Committee. The European Union thanked India for a recent information session and for providing the list of HS codes associated with the products covered by the health certificates. The European Union further welcomed the recently announced postponement of the entry into force of the health certificates until further notice. While the new health certificates for milk and milk products had been merged in March 2023, pork and fish products were still subject to two certificates issued by different authorities. The European Union requested India to avoid the duplication of SPS measures and notify any modalities relating to the application of the health certificates to the SPS and TBT Committees.

StatementSubmitted: The EU would like to refer to India’s health certificates for imported milk, pork, fish, and related products. This trade concern has been raised in the TBT committee too. The EU would like to thank India for the clarifications provided during online information sessions and meetings. We would also like to thank India for having postponed the entry into force of the health certificates for the import of pork and fish, until further notice, and of the merged certificate for import of milk and milk products until the end of this year.Given the importance that the competent authorities and companies in the exporting countries have sufficient time to adapt to new measures, the EU would like to ask India to:avoid the duplication of sanitary measures associated to the different certificates for the import of the same products, notify to both the WTO TBT and SPS Committees the model health certificates well in advance; take into consideration the comments that the EU has already shared, namely on the differences between the Indian import conditions and international standards; andensure that consignments of dairy products are not blocked whenever they arrive with the right model certificate – either the new merged certificate or the old certificate.Finally, the EU reiterates its availability to cooperate with the competent authorities of India, to enhance mutual understanding and avoid unnecessary and unjustified disruptions to trade.
Summary: The European Union raised its concerns regarding India's health certificates for imported milk, pork, fish, and related products, which had been notified to the TBT Committee. The European Union thanked India for a recent information session and the postponement of the entry into force of the health certificates until further notice. The European Union requested India to avoid the duplication of SPS measures and take into consideration comments provided, namely, on the differences between the Indian import conditions and international standards and to ensure that consignments with the correct model certificate were not blocked. The European Union also requested India to notify any modalities relating to the application of the health certificates to the SPS Committee well in advance.

StatementSubmitted: The EU would like to thank India for postponing until 1 January 2024 the entry  into force of the certificate for the import milk and milk products and for putting on hold until further notice the two certificates for the imports of pork, fish and their products.In relation to the animal health and food safety (integrated) certificate for import of milk and milk products, the EU would like to ask India to:Remove from the certificate all the requirements that are not covered by the Codex Alimentarius, such as those related to pesticides, several antibiotics and other drugs, or provide a scientific justification to maintain those requirements;In relation to the integrated certificates for import into India of pork and fishery products, the EU would like to ask India to:Clarify the state of play of the two integrated certificates;Confirm that the existing animal health certificates are the only certificates required; Confirm that the food safety certificates were withdrawn;In relation to the certificates used to import the three types of products (milk, pork, fishery products), the EU would like to ask India to:Remove from all certificates the non-animal health and non-food safety elements and requirements, such as invoice numbers or limitation of certain milk coagulating enzymes.Clarify the modalities related to audits to the exporting countries, inspections of facilities, questionnaires, regionalization, border checks and listing of establishments associated to all the certificatesNotify to both the WTO TBT and SPS Committees the above-mentioned modalities and all future certificates well in advance of the date of their entry into forceTake into consideration the comments that the EU has sent  Finally, the EU reiterates its availability to cooperate with the competent authorities of India, to enhance mutual understanding and avoid unnecessary and unjustified disruptions to trade.
Summary: The European Union thanked India for postponing until 1 January 2024 the entry into force of the certificate for the importation milk and milk products, and for putting on hold until further notice the two certificates for imports of pork, fish, and their products. The European Union asked India to remove the requirements that were not covered by Codex for imports of milk and milk products or provide a scientific justification for maintaining them. In addition, the European Union sought confirmation on the state of play and on the required certificates for pork and fishery products, and asked India to remove from all certificates the non-animal health and non-food safety elements and requirements. The European Union also requested India to clarify and notify to the SPS and TBT Committees the modalities relating to audits of exporting countries as well as future certificates well in advance. The European Union expressed its availability to cooperate towards an enhanced mutual understanding.

StatementSubmitted: The EU would like to thank India for putting on hold until further notice the two integrated certificates (animal health and food safety) for the imports of pork & pork products and fish & fish products.The EU would also like to thank India for postponing until mid-2024 the entry into force of the integrated certificate for the imports of milk and dairy products.Today, the EU would like to reiterate its concerns because the date of entry force of the milk/dairy certificate approaches quickly and India did not yet consider the EU comments and requests. In relation to the certificate for import of milk/dairy products, the EU would like to ask India to quickly remove from the certificate all the requirements which do not conform with the Codex Alimentarius, such as those related to pesticides, several antibiotics and other drugs, or to provide a scientific justification to maintain those requirements. In relation to the integrated certificates for import into India of pork and pork products & fish and fish products, the EU would like to ask India to confirm:the state of play of these two integrated certificates; that no additional animal health certificates are required;  and that the food safety certificates were withdrawn.In relation to the certificates used to import the three types of products (milk, pork, fish, and their respective products), the EU would like to ask India to:- Remove from all certificates the non-animal health and non-food safety elements and requirements, such as invoice numbers, limitation of certain milk coagulating enzymes, etc.; - Clarify the modalities related to audits to the exporting countries, inspections of facilities, questionnaires, regionalization, border checks and listing of establishments associated to all the certificates, if and when these requirements will be made obligatory by any of the authorities of India; - Notify to both the WTO TBT and SPS Committees the above-mentioned modalities and all future certificates – including integrated certificates – well in advance of the date of their entering into force, to ensure full transparency and timely follow-up by all the competent authorities, producers and exporters;- Take into consideration the comments that the EU has sent or may still send to India in relation to the certificates and provide in writing the scientific justifications for not taking those comments into account; - Avoid the duplication of sanitary measures in and associated to the different certificates, which are required by different competent authorities of India;Finally, the EU reiterates its availability to cooperate with the competent authorities of India, to enhance mutual understanding and avoid unnecessary and unjustified disruptions to trade.Thank you Chair
Summary: Referring to its complete intervention in eAgenda, the European Union thanked India for temporarily suspending the implementation of two integrated certificates (animal health and food safety) for importing pork, pork products, fish, and fish products. The European Union also appreciated India's decision to postpone the entry into force of the integrated certificate for the imports of milk and dairy products until mid-2024. However, the European Union noted the lack of response to EU comments and requests regarding the implementation of the milk and dairy certificates. Specifically, the European Union urged India to remove any requirements that were not covered by Codex or to provide scientific justification for maintaining them. The European Union sought confirmation on the status of the integrated certificates for importing pork, pork products, fish, and fish products; assurance that no additional animal health certificates were necessary; and clarification that the food safety certificates had been withdrawn. The European Union reaffirmed its willingness to collaborate with India's competent authorities to enhance mutual understanding and prevent unnecessary trade disruptions.

StatementSubmitted: The EU would like to reiterate its concerns about the certificate for import into India of milk and dairy products, which enters into force on 1st July 2024, and about the certificates to import pork and fishery products.As India discontinued the integrated pork and fish certificate, the EU’s biggest concern relates to the dairy certificate and in particular to the fact that India did not consider the EU comments to WTO notifications and requests of information. In this regard, the EU provided India with a detailed comparison between the Indian and international standards on pesticides, several antibiotics, and other drugs. The EU asked India to provide a scientific justification to maintain the deviating standards, which, as far as the EU is aware, are not related to any new or emerging risk. India only replied that its legislation is not new and would remain unchanged because, according to India, India’s trading partners have transparently been given the chance to comment India’s WTO notifications. In our opinion, this is not compatible with India’s WTO obligations because it ignores all the other obligations under the WTO SPS Agreement, including the obligation to ensure that any SPS measure: (1) is applied only to the extent necessary to protect human, animal or plant life or health; (2) is based on scientific principles, and (3) is not maintained without sufficient scientific evidence.Given that the date of entering into force of the certificate is approaching rapidly, the EU would like to again ask India to quickly remove from the certificate all the requirements which do not conform with the Codex Alimentarius, or to provide a scientific justification to maintain the diverging requirements. In relation to integrated certificates that India may decide in the future to put in place for the import into India of pork and pork products and fish and fishery products, the EU would like to ask India to please provide sufficient time before implementing them and to ensure that they do not contain any standard that are nor aligned with international standards or based on publicly available scientific justifications.Therefore, the EU urges all the India authorities to:Engage with the EU and comply with its WTO SPS obligations; Ensure transparent implementation of its import legislation; Work expeditiously and avoid undue delays; andAlign its standards with international standards or share the science that reportedly underpins India’s standards. In relation to the certificates used to import the three types of products (milk, pork, fish, and their respective products), the EU would like to ask India to:Remove from all certificates the non-animal health and non-food safety elements and requirements, such as invoice numbers, limitation of certain milk coagulating enzymes, etc.; Clarify the modalities related to audits to the exporting countries, inspections of facilities, questionnaires, regionalization, border checks and listing of establishments associated to all the certificates, if and when these requirements will be made obligatory by any of the authorities of India; Notify to both the WTO TBT and SPS Committees the above-mentioned modalities and all future certificates – including integrated certificates – well in advance of the date of their entering into force, to ensure full transparency and timely follow-up by all the competent authorities, producers and exporters;Take into consideration the comments that the EU has sent or may still send to India in relation to the certificates and provide in writing the scientific justifications for not taking those comments into account; and   In the future, avoid the duplication of sanitary measures in and associated to the different certificates, which are required by different competent authorities of India.Finally, the EU reiterates its availability to cooperate with the competent authorities of India, to enhance mutual understanding and avoid unnecessary and unjustified disruptions to trade.
Summary: The European Union expressed concerns about India's certificates for milk and dairy products, effective on 1 July 2024, and certificates for pork and fishery products. The European Union regretted India's disregard for comments on its WTO notifications and for information requests. The European Union asked India to remove certificate requirements that did not conform with Codex standards or provide the scientific justification for diverging from international standards. For future certificates, the European Union requested sufficient implementation time and alignment with international standards, urging India to ensure transparency and avoid delays. Referring to its full statement on eAgenda, the European Union reiterated its availability to cooperate with India to enhance mutual understanding and avoid unnecessary disruption to trade.

StatementSubmitted: STC New. Namibia’s approval procedures for beef and meat of small ruminants.The Russian Federation would like to draw attention of the Namibiandelegation to its specific trade concern on the lack of progress in Namibia´sapproval of veterinary certificates for imports of beef and meat of small ruminants fromRussia.For more than five years Namibia has been conducting a risk assessmentof the Russian system of veterinary control: precisely, the risk assessment of foot-and-mouth disease control system.Based on the results of the bilateral Intergovernmental Commission in Namibia in November 2017, the Namibian side announced that work on veterinary certificates will continue in parallel with the assessment of the Russian veterinarysupervision system and measures to control FMD in Russia. In December 2017 Russian competent authority submitted to Namibia relevant materials that were also sent to the OIE for restoration of the status of Russia as a country with “foot-and-mouth disease free zones without vaccination”. However, there was noresponse from the Namibian side and no other communication on this issue.We would like to highlight that World Organisation for Animal Health,which has a mandate from the WTO to officially recognize animal health status ofcountries for trade purposes, has acknowledged Russia as a state with zones freefrom foot-and-moth disease with or without vaccination. The only FMDoutbreak that occurred in the year 2021 was immediately notified andextinguished. Russian competent authority took all necessary measures for itselimination.At the same time, starting from 2017, Rosselkhoznadzor officially invitedNamibian specialists to visit the Russian Federation in order to review theveterinary supervision system, as well as to visit Russian enterprises interested insupplying their products to the Namibian market. Unfortunately, the visit ofspecialists did not take place in 2019 and was postponed to 2020, while a secondinvitation was sent in February 2020. No response from the Namibian side to theseinvitations has been received so far.Since 2017 and up to now, proposed drafts of certificates for the import ofdairy products, honey, finished meat products, fish and seafood products are alsopending approval.We urge Namibia to follow its WTO obligations under Articles 5 and 8 ofthe SPS Agreement in order to finalize its risk assessment without undue delay andto allow imports of Russian beef, meat of cattle and small ruminants.The Russian Federation would like to confirm itsreadiness for comprehensive bilateral cooperation with Namibia on this issue.
Summary: The Russian Federation raised its concern on the lack of progress in Namibia's approval of veterinary certificates for imports of Russian beef and meat of small ruminants. Although the Russian Federation had been recognized by WOAH as a country with zones free from foot and mouth disease (FMD) with or without vaccination, and all relevant documentation had been shared with Namibia, the risk assessment of the Russian FMD control system had been ongoing for more than five years without any response. The Russian Federation also regretted the postponement, without further confirmation, of an invitation for Namibian experts to review and visit the Russian veterinary supervision system and exporting enterprises. Emphasizing the pending approval of proposed drafts of certificates for the import of dairy products, honey, finished meat products, fish and seafood products, the Russian Federation urged Namibia to respect its obligations under Articles 5 and 8 of the SPS Agreement and to allow imports of beef, meat of cattle and small ruminants.

StatementSubmitted: Japan’s approval procedures for poultry products.The Russian Federation is concerned with delays in approval of veterinary certificate for imports of Russian poultry to Japan.In accordance to the Article 6.2 of the SPS Agreement a Member shall recognize the concept of disease free areas or areas of low disease prevalence. Russian competent veterinary and phytosanitary authority, Rosselkhoznadzor, submitted all relevant evidence-based materials, confirming regionalization of the territory of the Russian Federation with regard to highly pathogenic avian influenza. We highly appreciate Japan’s positive reaction to the Russian regionalization with respect to this disease.In March 2017, representatives of Japan’s competent authorities visited the Russian Federation to assess the risk in order to provide the access of poultry meat from Russia to Japan. Then in May 2019 Japan Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries positively considered the conclusion on the access of Russian poultry products to Japan. However, no access for the Russian poultry products has been granted yet due to the long period of approval of the certificate for poultry meat from the Russian Federation.In July 2021 Rosselkhoznadzor accepted the comments of Japan to the veterinary requirements and the certificate for poultry. The same month, Russian competent authority sent an initialed certificate and a proposal for negotiations. Unfortunately, no answer has been received so far on this issue despite repeated reminders.Moreover, Rosselkhoznadzor is still expecting to receive the questionnaires for enterprises wishing to export poultry meat from the Bryansk and Tula regions development of which was several times confirmed by Japan in April and July. In 2020 and in 2021 Rosselkhoznadzor repeatedly invited Japanese colleagues to inspect Russian enterprises in video format. However, no response has been received yet.Unfortunately, despite a positive dynamics expressed in Japan’s recognition of Russian regions’ epizootic well-being the Russian Federation notes the fact of undue delay in approval of veterinary certificate for imports of Russian poultry, difficulties in communication and unpredictability in further work.The Russian Federation urges Japan to speed up the procedure of veterinary certificate approval in order to prevent undue delay in approval procedures for imports of Russian animal products. The Russian Federation would like to confirm its readiness for comprehensive bilateral cooperation with Japan on this issue.
Summary: The Russian Federation expressed its concerns with delays in Japan's approval of veterinary certificates for Russian poultry. Referring to Article 6.2 of the SPS Agreement, the Russian Federation informed the Committee that it had submitted all appropriate materials confirming the regionalization of Russian territory in terms of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI). The Russian Federation was disappointed that, despite Japan's visit in 2017 and the positive consideration of Russian poultry products in 2019, no market access had been granted. The Russian Federation also noted the lack of progress in the approval of veterinary certificates, regretted it had not received the questionnaires for Russian poultry meat exporters, and that Japan had not responded to the invitations to conduct video inspections. The Russian Federation welcomed bilateral discussions and urged Japan to prevent undue delay in its approval procedures.

StatementSubmitted: Korea's requirement of a health certificate with a declaration of aquatic disease statusKorean Authorities insist that the export of Chilled, Frozen and Live aquatic animals, including ornamental fish, must accompany a health certificate and a declaration related to Aquatic disease status.Frozen shrimp is a major item of export to South Korea.  For export of frozen Head on shrimp (both wild and Aquaculture source) require health certificate along with the declaration on aquatic disease status.   As per regulation, for export of frozen shrimp (except for heated or peeled and beheaded), the product intended for export to South Korea shall also be tested for IHHN, WSD, TSV, IMNV from the EIC-approved laboratories.In this regard, India has concerns regarding the rationale for this requirement, its burdensome nature and potential duplicity. India would appreciate it if South Korea could restrict the certification requirement to only those considered necessary and prevent trade disruption in safe products.
Summary: India raised its concerns regarding Korea's requirement for a health certification and disease status declaration for aquatic animal exports. Highlighting the duplication and the burden of testing exported frozen shrimp for four diseases in accredited laboratories, India encouraged Korea to limit certification requirements to those considered necessary and to prevent trade disruption of safe products.

StatementSubmitted: STC ID 557 – Korea’s Requirement of Health Certificate with the declaration of aquatic disease status India thanks Korea for corporative engagement on the issue.  India takes note that as per the quarterly Aquatic Animal Disease Report (QAADR) publications for Asia and Pacific region, Korea has not officially submitted QAADR in the last few years (that is, after 2015) to World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH) and therefore urges Korea to provide a relevant update.  India also notes that there are reported instances of WASSV and IHHNV as per the earlier QAADR reports furnished by WOAH. In this regard, India would like to highlight Article 5.1.2.2 of the Aquatic Animal Health Code on Responsibilities of the importing country, which states that - “The international aquatic animal health certificate should not include requirements for the exclusion of pathogenic agents or aquatic animal diseases that are present in the importing country and are not subject to any official control programme. The measures imposed on imports to manage the risks posed by a pathogenic agent or aquatic animal disease should not be more stringent than those applied as part of the official control programme operating within the importing country”. Additionally, consignment-wise testing does not improve regulatory outcomes. India, therefore requests Korea to limit the certification requirements to those considered necessary, preventing disruption to trade in safe products and overall ensuring compliance with the SPS Agreement.
Summary: India urged Korea to provide an update for the purpose of the WOAH quarterly Aquatic Animal Disease Report publications for Asia and Pacific region, something Korea had failed to do since 2015. Referring to WOAH's Aquatic Code, India recalled that health certificates should not include requirements for the exclusion of pathogenic agents or aquatic animal diseases if they were present in the importing country and not subject to any official control programme. In addition, measures imposed on imports to manage the risks posed by a pathogenic agent or aquatic animal disease should not be more stringent than those applied domestically. India requested Korea to limit the certification requirements to what was necessary, preventing disruption to trade and ensuring compliance with the SPS Agreement.

StatementSubmitted: Statement for Korea's requirement of a health certificate with a declaration of aquatic disease status (STC ID 557)India thanks Korea for its response. The capacity building on biosecurity protocols and implementation of biosecurity at the field level to prevent cross-contamination have also been initiated. Further, the checks and controls are in place through the Aquatic Quarantine Facility,, which screens the import of Brood stock for all WOAH listed pathogens.In view of the above India find the certification requirement cumbersome and burdensome especially for pathogens not reported in India, and urged Korea to limit the certification requirements to those considered necessary.
Summary: India informed the Committee of the initiation of phase II of its National Surveillance Programme on Aquatic Animal Diseases in March 2023 and of the capacity building on biosecurity protocols and implementation of biosecurity at the field level to prevent cross-contamination, as well as of the checks and controls in place through the Aquatic Quarantine Facility.
