StatementSubmitted: Australia – G/SPS/N/Aus/555 – MRLs stricter than codes in the products which are of trade interest to India and share risk assessments India notes Australia's notification G/SPS/N/AUS/555 through which the MRLs for Glufosinate and Glufosinate-ammonium and Glyphosate have been made sticker than Codex.India is the largest producer of Non-GM soybeans and has export potential to Australia. The proposed stringent MRLs will act as a barrier to trade for Indian nonGMO soybean crops. India requests that Australia consider WTO obligations under Article 2, paragraph 2; Article 3, paragraph 1; Article 5, paragraphs 2 and 3 of the SPS Agreement. India also requested the following concerns and requested the member country to provide the supporting data supporting the regulation changes that are of trade concern to India.1. Could Australia define and identify the appropriate level of protection it seeks by modifying the MRLs for these substances?2. Does Australia consider that there is enough relevant scientific evidence to support the modification of the MRLs for these substances? If yes, please share the same. 3. In many products, the MRLs are aligned with Codex norms, but in other products where Codex is a sprint, the norms are stricter than similar crops. According to Basic Rights and Obligations Article 2.2, Members shall ensure that any sanitary or phytosanitary measure is applied only to the extent necessary to protect human, animal or plant life or health, is based on scientific principles and is not maintained without sufficient scientific evidence, except as provided for in paragraph 7 of Article 5. Please share the reasons and the risk assessment reports with the justification for this deviation. 4. How do the measures adopted by the Member Country to modify MRLs reconcile with its obligation under Article 3.1 of the SPS Agreement, which provides that to harmonise sanitary and phytosanitary measures on as wide a basis as possible, Members shall base their sanitary or phytosanitary measures on international standards, guidelines or recommendations, where they exist, except as otherwise provided for in this Agreement?5. Would Australia please provide a definition and comprehensive list of what it regards as "other legitimate factors" to be taken into account in establishing and granting import tolerances?6. According to the Agreement Assessment of Risk and Determination of the Appropriate Level of Sanitary or Phytosanitary Protection, Article 5.1, Members shall ensure that their sanitary or phytosanitary measures are based on an assessment, as appropriate to the circumstances, of the risks to human, animal or plant life or health, taking into account risk assessment techniques developed by the relevant international organisations. Could the member Country provide a complete list of the substances and MRLs that have already been reviewed and updated and a complete list of substances and MRLs currently in the evaluation phase?
Summary: India expressed concerns regarding Australia's reduction of the level of MRLs to stricter than Codex standards for glufosinate and glufosinate-ammonium and glyphosate. India was the largest producer of non-genetically modified (GM) soybeans and had export potential to Australia. According to India, the MRLs would act as a barrier to trade for Indian non-GM soybean crops. India also requested responses to a number of inquiries, which included clarification on the appropriate level of protection (ALOP), scientific evidence used for the modification of MRLs, harmonization obligations under the SPS Agreement, sharing of risk assessment results, other legitimate factors taken into account when establishing and granting import tolerances, the list of the substances and MRLs that had already been updated, and a list of substances and MRLs currently in the evaluation phase.

StatementSubmitted: Thank you Chair.Canada would like to note its concerns with China’s complete and long-term suspension of beef imports from Canada based on a single case of atypical bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE). In accordance with the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH) guidelines, the detection and reporting of this atypical BSE case did not affect Canada's WOAH negligible risk status and should not have affected trade.Nevertheless, at the request of Chinese authorities, Canada suspended exports of Canadian beef to China in December 2021, following Canada's notification of a single case of atypical BSE.Canadian officials have continuously engaged with Chinese authorities and have fully responded to all of their requests for technical information, yet we are still awaiting a timeline for the restoration of trade. Canadian beef has been locked out of the Chinese market for over a year now.China has previously allowed the resumption of beef exports from trading partners that have reported atypical BSE cases in a far more expeditious manner. It is important for all WTO members to avoid discrimination between Members where identical or similar conditions prevail, as per article 2.3 of the SPS Agreement.It is equally important for all WTO members to base their measures on international standards, guidelines, or recommendations, including those established by the WOAH, as per article 3 of the SPS Agreement. Canada urges China to remove its BSE-related restrictions on Canadian beef and restore trade without further delay.  Canada urges China to work collaboratively with Canada to resolve this issue, and to regularly work bilaterally and multilaterally towards achieving our common objective of avoiding unnecessary barriers to trade and contributing to food security.Thank you Chair.
Summary: Canada noted its concerns with China's complete and long-term suspension of beef imports from Canada based on a single case of atypical BSE, which did not affect Canada's WOAH BSE negligible risk status. Canada had continuously engaged with and responded to all requests from China, but were still waiting for restoration of trade for over a year now. China had previously allowed the resumption of beef exports from trading partners that had reported atypical BSE cases quickly, and Canada requested similar treatment. Canada urged China to work collaboratively to resolve this issue and to achieve their common objective of avoiding unnecessary barriers to trade and contributing to food security.

StatementSubmitted: • Thank you Chair. • Canada notes its continuing concerns with China’s complete and long-term prohibition of beef imports from Canada following a case of atypical bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE). • • In accordance with the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH) guidelines,  the detection and reporting of this atypical BSE case did not affect Canada's WOAH negligible risk status for BSE and should not have affected trade. • Moreover, revised WOAH standards on atypical BSE adopted in May 2023 reaffirm that atypical BSE detections do not affect the BSE risk status of a country or zone. • Nevertheless, China required the suspension of exports of Canadian beef to China in December 2021, following Canada's notification of a case of atypical BSE. • Canadian officials have continuously tried to engage with Chinese authorities and have fully responded to all the requests for technical information, yet China has not provided any timeframes for the restoration of trade. Canadian beef has been locked out of the Chinese market for a year and a half now. • Canada is concerned with the arbitrary and discriminatory treatment by China of Canadian beef compared to other WTO Members that have reported cases of atypical BSE.   • That is, China has previously allowed the resumption of beef imports from trading partners that have reported atypical BSE cases in a far more expeditious manner, yet Canadian beef remains shut out of the Chinese market. Moreover, in other instances, China has introduced no import prohibitions whatsoever following the detection of atypical BSE in other Members supplying beef to China. • It is important for all WTO members to avoid discrimination between Members where identical or similar conditions prevail, as per article 2.3 of the SPS Agreement.• • Moreover, it is equally important for all WTO members to base their measures on international standards, guidelines, or recommendations, including those established by the WOAH, as per article 3 of the SPS Agreement.  • China has provided no scientific justification for its ongoing atypical BSE-related trade prohibition on Canadian beef, which continues to unnecessarily disrupt trade and significantly impact Canadian industry.  • Canada urges China to remove its trade prohibition and restore market access for Canadian beef without further delays.  • Canada urges China to work more collaboratively with Canada to resolve this important issue, and to work bilaterally and multilaterally towards achieving our common objective of avoiding unnecessary barriers to trade and contributing to food security. • Thank you Chair.
Summary: Canada raised concerns regarding China's suspension of Canadian beef imports based on a single case of atypical BSE, which Canada stated did not affect its WOAH BSE negligible risk status. Canada informed the Committee that it had continuously tried to engage with and responded to all requests from China but was still waiting for trade to be restored for a year and a half. Canada indicated that China had previously allowed beef exports from trading partners that had reported atypical BSE cases to resume quickly and in other instances, no import prohibitions were introduced following the detection of atypical BSE in other Members supplying beef to China. Canada also noted that no scientific justification had been provided for the atypical BSE-related trade prohibition on Canadian beef and urged China to work collaboratively to resolve this issue. Canada indicated that its full intervention would be uploaded to eAgenda.

StatementSubmitted: I refer to Canada’s previous interventions on this item, which remain valid.  Canada would like to note its continuing concerns with China’s complete and long-term prohibition of beef imports from Canada following a case of atypical bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), which according to WOAH guidelines, does not affect Canada's WOAH negligible risk status for BSE and should not have affected trade. Canadian officials have continuously tried to engage with Chinese authorities and have fully responded to all requests for technical information, yet China has not provided any scientific justification for its suspension nor timeframes for the restoration of trade. StatementSubmitted: Thank you Chair. I continue to refer to Canada’s previous interventions on this item, which remain valid and our full statement will be uploaded.  As Canada has raised this issue a number of times, I would like to highlight the following. Canada continues to raise its concerns with China’s complete and long-term prohibition of beef imports from Canada following a case of atypical bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) in 2021. Canadian beef has been locked out of the Chinese market for over two years now, significantly impacting Canadian industry.  Canadian officials have continuously tried to engage with Chinese authorities and have fully responded to all requests for technical information, yet China has not provided any scientific justification for its suspension, should it have any, nor timeframes for the restoration of trade.  We once again note that in accordance with the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH) guidelines, the detection and reporting of this atypical BSE case did not affect Canada's WOAH negligible risk status for BSE and should not have affected trade. As Members are fully aware, revised WOAH standards on atypical BSE adopted in May 2023 reaffirm that atypical BSE detections do not affect the BSE risk status of a country or zone. China’s measures can only be seen as arbitrary and discriminatory, when compared to the actions China has taken when other countries have experienced cases of atypical BSE. StatementSubmitted: Thank you Chair.Canada is disappointed to have to raise its concerns regarding China’s trade restrictions on exports of Canadian heat-treated pet food containing poultry ingredients. Following confirmation of HPAI in Canada in February 2022, China halted Canadian exports of heat-treated pet food containing poultry ingredients while accepting the same products from other HPAI affected Members. The World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH)’s Terrestrial Animal Health Code identifies extruded dry pet food as safe regardless of the HPAI status of the exporting country or zone because the product is heat treated sufficiently to inactivate HPAI pathogens.Pet food products from Canada are processed and heat-treated at a temperature that inactivates HPAI pathogens and that exceeds WOAH recommendations as per article 10.4.24 of the Terrestrial Animal Health Code.Canada therefore continues to question the scientific basis for China’s SPS measures relating to its restrictions on Canadian heat-treated pet food and is seeking resolution as soon as possible. It is important for all WTO members to base their measures on international standards, guidelines, or recommendations, including those established by the WOAH, as per Article 3 of the SPS Agreement. It is also important for all WTO members to avoid discrimination between Members where identical or similar conditions prevail, as per Article 2.3 of the SPS Agreement.Canada urges China to remove its HPAI restrictions on heat-treated pet food containing poultry ingredients and allow exports to resume without further delays as per WOAH guidelines.Thank you Chair.
Summary: Canada raised its concerns regarding China's trade restrictions on exports of Canadian heat-treated pet food containing poultry ingredients. Following confirmation of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in Canada, China had halted Canadian exports of heat-treated pet food containing poultry ingredients while accepting these products from other HPAI affected Members. Canada reminded that WOAH had identified extruded dry pet food as safe regardless of HPAI status because the product was heat-treated sufficiently to inactivate HPAI pathogens, and Canadian pet food products were treated at a temperature that exceeded WOAH recommendations. Canada noted that SPS measures should be based on international standards, guidelines, or recommendations, and not discriminate between Members. Canada urged China to remove its restrictions as per WOAH guidelines.

StatementSubmitted: • Thank you Chair.• Canada is disappointed to have to again raise its concerns regarding China’s ongoing trade prohibition on Canadian exports of heat-treated pet food containing poultry ingredients. •  I refer to Canada’s previous intervention on this item, which remains valid and note our full statement will be uploaded on the eAgenda. • Following confirmation of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) in Canada in February 2022, China halted imports of Canadian heat-treated pet food containing poultry ingredients while continuing to accept the same products from other HPAI affected Members. • Canada continues to be concerned with the arbitrary and discriminatory treatment by China of Canadian pet food exports compared to other Members that have experienced cases of HPAI. Summary: Canada reiterated concerns with China's arbitrary and discriminatory treatment of Canadian pet food exports. StatementSubmitted: I refer to Canada's previous interventions on this item, which remain valid. Canada is disappointed to have to once again raise its concerns regarding China’s ongoing trade prohibition on Canadian exports of heat-treated pet food containing poultry ingredients.Canada is concerned with China’s arbitrary and discriminatory treatment  of Canadian pet food exports compared to other countries that have also experienced cases of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) yet have faced no such prohibition.   Canada once again notes that Canadian pet food products are processed and heat-treated at a temperature that inactivates HPAI pathogens and which exceeds WOAH recommendations as per article 10.4.24 of the Terrestrial Animal Health Code.Moreover, Canada strictly follows all the import requirements that China agreed to when the existing export certificate was established in December 2013. Canada therefore continues to question the scientific basis for China’s prohibition on Canadian heat-treated pet food containing poultry ingredients and we would highlight that to date China has not provided Canada with any evidence that this ban does, in fact, have a scientific basis. It is important for all WTO members to base their measures on international standards, guidelines, or recommendations, including those established by the WOAH, as per Article 3 of the SPS Agreement. It is also important for all WTO members to avoid discrimination between Members where identical or similar conditions prevail, as per Article 2.3 of the SPS Agreement.Canada urges China to respect WOAH guidelines, to remove its HPAI prohibitions, and to allow exports to resume without further delays.
Summary: Referring to its interventions at previous Committee meetings, Canada reiterated concerns with China's arbitrary and discriminatory treatment of Canadian pet food exports, and questioned the scientific basis for China's prohibition on Canadian heat-treated pet food containing poultry ingredients. Canada further indicated that pet food products were processed and heat-treated at a temperature exceeding WOAH recommendations, which inactivated HPAI pathogens, and that it strictly followed the import requirements bilaterally agreed in 2013. Referring to Articles 2.3 and 3 of the SPS Agreement, Canada urged China to respect WOAH guidelines, to remove its HPAI-related prohibitions, and to allow exports to resume without further delays.

StatementSubmitted: Thank you Chair. I continue to refer to Canada's previous interventions on this item, which remain valid and will upload our full statement shortly. Given we have now raised this issue on numerous occasions, Canada would like to highlight the following: Canada remains disappointed to have to once again raise its concerns regarding China’s ongoing trade prohibition on Canadian exports of heat-treated pet food containing poultry ingredients. Canada notes once again China’s arbitrary and discriminatory treatment of Canadian pet food exports compared to other Members that have also experienced cases of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) yet have faced no such trade prohibitions from China.  This treatment is not consistent with the guidelines of the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) nor with the principles of the SPS Agreement and the WTO writ large.    As previously noted, Canadian pet food products are processed and heat-treated at a temperature that inactivates HPAI pathogens and which exceeds WOAH recommendations as per article 10.4.24 of the Terrestrial Animal Health Code. Moreover, Canada strictly follows all the import requirements that China agreed to in the existing export certificate. Canada therefore continues to question the scientific basis for China’s prohibition on Canadian heat-treated pet food containing poultry ingredients. We once again request that China provide Canada with scientific justification for its trade prohibition. WTO Members must respect their trade obligations. It is important for all Members to base their measures on international standards, guidelines, or recommendations, including those established by the WOAH, as per article 3 of the SPS Agreement.  It is also important for all WTO Members to avoid discrimination between Members where identical or similar conditions prevail, as per article 2.3 of the SPS Agreement. Canada urges China to respect WOAH guidelines, to remove its HPAI-related prohibitions, and to allow exports of affected Canadian pet food to resume without further delays.  Thank you Chair.
Summary: Referring to its previous statements and its complete intervention in eAgenda, Canada reiterated concerns with China's arbitrary and discriminatory treatment of Canadian pet food exports. It questioned the scientific basis for China's prohibition on Canadian heat-treated pet food containing poultry ingredients. Canada further indicated that pet food products were processed and heat-treated at a temperature exceeding WOAH recommendations, which inactivated HPAI pathogens, and that it strictly followed the import requirements bilaterally agreed in the existing export certificate. Canada urged China to provide the scientific justification for its measure, respect WOAH guidelines, remove HPAI-related prohibitions, and allow exports to resume without further delays.

StatementSubmitted: Thank you Chair.I continue to refer to Canada's previous interventions on this item, which remain valid and will upload our full statement shortly. Given we have now raised this issue on numerous occasions, Canada would like to highlight the following:Canada remains disappointed to have to once again raise its concerns regarding China’s ongoing trade prohibition on Canadian exports of heat-treated pet food containing poultry ingredients, which have been shut out of the Chinese market for over two years now. Canada notes once again China’s arbitrary and discriminatory treatment of Canadian pet food exports compared to other countries that have also experienced cases of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI), but did not face similar trade prohibitions from China. This treatment is not consistent with the guidelines of the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), the SPS Agreement or the WTO’s principles for rules-based trade writ large.   As previously noted, Canadian pet food products are processed and heat-treated at a temperature that inactivates HPAI pathogens and which exceeds WOAH recommendations as per article 10.4.24 of the Terrestrial Animal Health Code.Moreover, Canada strictly follows all the import requirements that China agreed to in our existing and valid bilateral export certificate.Canada therefore continues to question the scientific basis for China’s prohibition on Canadian heat-treated pet food containing poultry ingredients. We once again request that China provide Canada with scientific justification for its trade prohibition. WTO Members must respect their trade obligations. It is important for all Members to base their measures on international standards, guidelines, or recommendations, including those established by the WOAH, as per Article 3 of the SPS Agreement. It is also important for all WTO Members to avoid discrimination between Members where identical or similar conditions prevail, as stipulated in Article 2.3 of the SPS Agreement.Canada urges China to respect WOAH guidelines, to remove its HPAI-related prohibitions, and to allow exports of affected Canadian pet food to resume without further delays. Canada insists that this matter be resolved without further undue delay, in a manner consistent with China’s WTO obligations. Canada is considering all options to restore trade for pet food as engagement efforts at the bilateral level have thus far not achieved resolution.Thank you Chair.
Summary: Referring to its interventions in previous Committee meetings, Canada reiterated concerns with China's trade prohibitions of Canadian heat-treated pet food containing poultry ingredients, applied for the past two years. Canada considered China's measure to be arbitrary and discriminatory and questioned the scientific basis for the measure. Canada indicated that pet food products were being processed and heat-treated at a temperature that inactivated HPAI pathogens and exceeded WOAH recommendation, and that it strictly followed the import requirements bilaterally agreed in the existing export certificate. Canada urged China to provide the scientific justification for its measure, respect WOAH guidelines, remove HPAI-related prohibitions, and allow exports to resume without further delays. Canada added that it was considering all options to restore trade for pet food as engagement efforts at the bilateral level had thus far not achieved resolution.

StatementSubmitted: The European Union would like to raise a new trade concern relating the lack of application of the regionalisation principle by Mexico.The European Union is very concerned by the countrywide import bans that Mexico maintains on pork products from EU Member States. Mexico imposes import suspensions to Member States that reported outbreaks of African swine fever,  even if cases are limited to feral pigs. The EU requests Mexico to respect its obligations, in accordance with the WTO SPS Agreement and the relevant WOAH standards, and allow trade from disease free areas. The EU has requested Mexico several times by letter and in meetings, most recently at the EU-Mexico SPS subcommittee on October 2022, to apply the regionalisation concept to pork meat imported from the EU, without any success yet.The EU would like to reiterate its availability to engage in bilateral technical discussions to solve this matter .
Summary: The European Union expressed concerns regarding country-wide import suspensions imposed by Mexico on pork products from EU member States that had reported ASF outbreaks. The European Union regretted the lack of progress despite repeated requests for Mexico to respect its obligations, apply regionalization to pork meat imported from the European Union, and allow trade from disease-free areas, most recently raised at a EU-Mexico SPS subcommittee meeting in October 2022. The European Union reiterated its availability to engage bilaterally to solve this matter.

StatementSubmitted: The European Union would like to raise for the second time in this committee a trade concern on the lack of implementation of the regionalization principle by Mexico in relation to pork products.The European Union is very concerned by the countrywide import bans that Mexico maintains on pork from EU Member States. Mexico imposes import suspensions to Member States that reported outbreaks of African swine fever, even if cases are limited to feral pigs. The EU requests Mexico to respect its obligations, in accordance with the WTO SPS Agreement and the relevant WOAH standards, and allow trade from disease free areas as other many important trading partners are doing already, without reporting any problem.The EU has requested Mexico several times in writing and during meetings, including at the EU-Mexico SPS subcommittee in October 2022, to apply the principle of regionalization to pork imported from the EU.The continued trade flow from disease free areas in the EU to important trading partners all over the world demonstrates the reliable, effective, and science-based measures in place against ASF in the EU. As indicated in a recent meeting with SENASICA, the EU would like to reiterate its availability to engage in bilateral technical discussions to demonstrate the effectiveness and reliability of its control measures against the spread of ASF.
Summary: The European Union reiterated its concerns regarding country-wide import suspensions imposed by Mexico on pork products from EU member States that had reported ASF outbreaks. The European Union regretted the lack of progress despite repeated requests for Mexico to respect its obligations, apply regionalization to pork meat imported from the European Union, and allow trade from disease-free areas, most recently raised at an EU-Mexico SPS subcommittee meeting in October 2022. The European Union requested bilateral technical discussions to solve these concerns.

StatementSubmitted: The European Union would like to raise this trade concern which relates to the lack of implementation of the regionalization principle by Mexico in relation to pork products.The European Union is concerned by the countrywide import bans that Mexico maintains on pork from several EU Member States. This matter has been raised several times in writing and during bilateral meetings.The EU requests Mexico to respect its obligations, in accordance with the WTO SPS Agreement, the relevant WOAH standards and the health certificate for exporting pig meat to Mexico which was agreed in 2017, and allow trade from disease free areas as other many important trading partners are doing already, without reporting any problem.The EU would like to reiterate its availability to engage in bilateral technical discussions to demonstrate the effectiveness and reliability of its control measures against the spread of ASF. At a recent regional seminar held in Chile, representatives of MEX had the opportunity to get better acquainted with the EU’s regionalisation system and control measures against ASF. We look forward to making progress on this matter during the forthcoming EU-MEX SPS committee meeting in mid-April.
Summary: The European Union reiterated its concerns regarding country-wide import suspensions imposed by Mexico on pork products from EU member States that had reported ASF outbreaks. Despite numerous bilateral meetings, the European Union expressed disappointment at the lack of progress on this issue. Emphasizing its readiness to engage in bilateral technical discussions, the European Union shared its optimism about advancing discussions during the forthcoming EU-Mexico SPS committee meeting in mid-April and remained committed to resolving the matter.

StatementSubmitted: The European Union would like to raise this trade concern which relates to the lack of implementation of the regionalization principle by Mexico in relation to pork products.The European Union is very concerned by the countrywide import bans that Mexico maintains on pork from several EU Member States which have or have had outbreaks of ASF. This matter has been raised several times in writing and during bilateral meetings, most recently at the EU-Mexico SPS subcommittee on 9 April 2024The EU requests Mexico to respect its obligations, in accordance with the WTO SPS Agreement, the relevant WOAH standards and the health certificate for exporting pig meat to Mexico, which was agreed in 2017, and allow trade from disease free areas as other many important trading partners are doing already, without reporting any problem.The EU reminds Mexico of its obligation to accept pork safe commodities which have been treated in line with the methods foreseen in Article 15.1.23 of WOAH terrestrial code, from EU MS which have suffered outbreaks of ASF. The EU would like to reiterate its availability to engage in bilateral technical discussions to demonstrate the effectiveness and reliability of its control measures against the spread of ASF. At a recent regional seminar held in Chile, representatives of MEX had the opportunity to get better acquainted with the EU’s regionalisation system and control measures against ASF. We look forward to making progress on this matter and remain available to continue the bilateral exchanges.
Summary: The European Union reiterated its concerns regarding Mexico's country-wide import bans on pork from several EU member States that had ASF outbreaks, despite several engagements, including a recent bilateral meeting of April 2024. The European Union requested Mexico to respect its obligations under the SPS Agreement and relevant WOAH standards, as well as the health certificate agreed in 2017 and allow trade from disease-free areas as other partners had done without reporting any problems. The European Union further reminded Mexico of its obligation to accept pork safe commodities which had been treated in line with the methods foreseen in the WOAH Terrestrial Code. The European Union emphasized its willingness to engage in bilateral technical discussions to demonstrate the effectiveness and reliability of its ASF control measures.

StatementSubmitted: The Russian Federation would like to raise a specific trade concern regarding the delays in gaining access for the Russian livestock products to the market of South Africa.Russian competent authority requests South African counterparts to accelerate the process of reviewing answers on questionnaires regarding risk analysis for imports of beef, poultry and pork to South Africa, as well as a questionnaire on bovine spongiform encephalopathy which were sent to South Africa in 2018.We note that the Russian Federation has WOAH status as a country with zones free from foot-and-mouth disease. In May 2022, the Russian Federation was recognized by WOAH as a country free from bovine spongiform encephalopathy.With this statement we take an opportunity to confirm our readiness to invite specialists from South Africa to inspect Russian livestock enterprises, as well as to develop bilateral scientific and technical cooperation in the field of food and biological safety.Still we urge South Africa to comply with its WTO obligations under Article 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement so that the approval procedures for Russian animal products are being undertaken and completed without undue delay. Finally, we would like to confirm Russia’s readiness for comprehensive bilateral cooperation with South Africa on this issue.
Summary: The Russian Federation raised concerns regarding South Africa's delays in granting market access for Russian livestock products. The Russian competent authority had requested South Africa to accelerate the process of reviewing answers on questionnaires regarding risk analysis for imports of beef, poultry and pork, as well as a questionnaire on BSE. The Russian Federation reminded of its WOAH status as a country with zones free from FMD and country free from BSE. The Russian Federation invited South Africa to inspect Russian livestock enterprises and to develop bilateral scientific and technical cooperation in the field of food and biological safety. Expressing its readiness for bilateral cooperation, the Russian Federation reiterated that approval procedures needed to be undertaken and completed without undue delay.

StatementSubmitted: The Russian Federation reiterates is specific trade concern regarding lack of progress in granting SPS access for Russian poultry, beef, pork, fish and seafood to the South African market.Russian competent authority – the Rosselkhoznadzor - requests South African colleagues to expedite the process of consideration of submitted replies to the questionnaires on risk assessment of beef, pork and poultry imports. We also would like to receive feedback on the provided answers to the questionnaire on bovine spongiform encephalopathy - BSE.Russia would like to underscore that it has WOAH status as a country with zones free from FMD. In May 2022 we have received a country free from BSE status.We urge South Africa to comply with its WTO obligations under Article 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement so that the approval procedures for Russian animal products are being undertaken and completed without undue delay.Finally, we would like to confirm Russia’s readiness for comprehensive bilateral cooperation with South Africa on these issues. We also take an opportunity to invite South African SPS experts to inspect Russian livestock enterprises and to develop bilateral scientific and technical cooperation in the field of food and biological safety.
Summary: The Russian Federation reiterated its concern regarding the lack of progress in granting SPS access for Russian poultry, beef, pork, fish, and seafood to the South African market. The Russian Federation asked South Africa to expedite the process to consider submitted responses to questionnaires on risk assessment and to provide answers to the questionnaire on BSE. The Russian Federation recalled its WOAH status as a country with FMD-free zones and as a BSE-free country. Urging South Africa to respect its international obligations so that approval procedures could be completed without undue delay and emphasizing its readiness to engage in bilateral discussions, the Russian Federation invited South Africa to inspect Russian livestock enterprises.

StatementSubmitted: The EU would like to raise a new trade concern relating to the Indian approval procedures for plants, animals and their products.Over the years, the European Union and the different competent authorities of India have had several meetings and exchanged plenty of information about market access applications submitted by the EU to India. While these exchanges have been positive, allowing some progress, overall we find that India’s approval procedures for imports of plants, animals and their products remain unclear and often very slow.Despite our repeated requests, the standard processing period of the approval procedures and the anticipated processing period are not known. For the approval of new exports from the EU, India has not shared information with the EU about the stage of the assessment procedure and what information may be missing or deficiencies may have been found to complete India’s assessment of the applications we submitted. This prevents us from putting in place the necessary corrective actions and start exports.In the case of existing exports from the EU, often India provides no details about the specific non-conformities, which prevent us from putting in place the necessary corrective actions and resume exports.The EU is growingly concerned by the persistent lack of progress with many applications and the persistent lack of response from India to the EU requests. Delays persist, sometimes for many years, and the EU is not informed about the reasons for such delays. In this respect, based on the information we have shared with the India authorities, we note that unfortunately there are 13 pending applications related to the EU exports of animals and animal products, and 18 pending applications related to the EU exports of plants and plant products. Some of these applications were submitted to India almost 10 years ago with no progress being achived so far. Therefore, the EU urges India to comply with its WTO SPS obligations, by ensuring transparency of its import legislation and approval procedures, to reply to the EU requests for clarification, and to finalize the pending EU market access applications without undue delays. The EU looks forward to discussing these issues with India, and to be informed also bilaterally soon, about state of play of these applications.
Summary: The European Union regretted that India's approval procedures were unclear and slow and that the standard and anticipated processing periods had not been communicated. India had not provided information on the stages of the assessment procedure and what information might be missing or deficiencies might have been found for the approval of new exports. India had also not provided information on the specific non conformities for existing exports, which prevented the European Union from implementing corrective actions. The European Union reminded that there were a number of pending applications. Some of them had been pending for almost 10 years with no progress being achieved so far. The European Union urged India to comply with its WTO SPS obligations by ensuring transparency of its import legislation and approval procedures, and to provide requested clarifications to allow the finalization of the pending market applications without undue delay.

StatementSubmitted: The EU would like to raise again a trade concern relating to the Indian approval procedures for plants, animals, and their products.Despite exchanges in previous years, in recent years the different competent authorities of India have had refused to engage in technical meetings with the European Union about market access applications submitted by the EU to India and progress in approving applications has been extremely slow. In addition, several legislations, approval procedures for imports of plants, animals and their products remain unclear.Despite our repeated requests, the standard processing period of the approval procedures and the anticipated processing period are not known. For the approval of new exports from the EU, India has not shared information with the EU about the stage of the assessment procedure and what information may be missing or deficiencies may have been found to complete India’s assessment of the applications we submitted. This prevents us from putting in place the necessary corrective actions and start exports.In the case of existing exports from the EU, often India provides no details about the specific non-conformities, which prevent us from putting in place the necessary corrective actions and resume exports.The EU is growingly concerned by the persistent lack of progress with many applications and the persistent lack of response from India to the EU requests. Delays persist, sometimes for many years, and the EU is not informed about the reasons for such delays. In this respect, based on the information we have shared with the India authorities, we note that unfortunately there are 13 pending applications related to the EU exports of animals and animal products, and 18 pending applications related to the EU exports of plants and plant products. Some of these applications were submitted to India almost 10 years ago. To progress, all these applications require an action by India. These figures didn’t change since we raise this STC for the first time, last March.Therefore, the EU urges India to comply with its WTO SPS obligations, by ensuring transparency of its import legislation and approval procedures, to reply to the EU requests for clarification, and to finalize the pending EU market access applications without undue delays. The EU looks forward to discussing these issues with India, and to be informed also bilaterally ? soon, in detail and regularly.
Summary: The European Union regretted that India's approval procedures were unclear and slow, and that the standard and anticipated processing periods had not been communicated. The European Union noted that India had not provided information on the stage of the assessment procedure for the approval of new exports, nor the specific non-conformities for existing exports, and this prevented the implementation of corrective actions. The European Union recalled that there were a number of pending applications, and some of them had been pending for almost 10 years. The European Union urged India to comply with its WTO SPS obligations by ensuring transparency of its import legislation and approval procedures and provide requested clarifications to allow the finalization of the pending market applications without undue delay.

StatementSubmitted: The EU would like to refer to the Indian approval procedures for plants, animals, and their products. At the last meeting, the EU pointed that the approval procedures were extremely low and a number of applications were pending since years.Since the last WTO SPS committee meeting, the EU and India have held two technical meetings to discuss the state of play of pending market access applications submitted by the EU. During these meetings, the EU invited India to provide a standard processing period for the approval procedures and the anticipated processing period For the approval of new exports from the EU, we invite India to inform about  what information may be missing or deficiencies may have been found to complete India’s assessment of the applications we submitted. In the case of existing exports from the EU, often India provides no details about the specific non-conformities, which prevent us from putting in place the necessary corrective actions and resume exports. Even if some progress was recently observed, the EU remains concerned by the lack of progress with many applications and the persistent lack of response from India to the EU requests. Delays persist, sometimes for many years, and the EU is not informed about the reasons for such delays.Based on the information we have shared with the India authorities, we note that unfortunately there are still too many pending applications related to the EU exports of plants, animals and their productsTherefore, the EU urges India to comply with its WTO SPS obligations, by ensuring transparency and avoid undue delays.  The EU looks forward to continue  discussing these issues with India,
Summary: The European Union regretted that India's approval procedures were unclear and slow and that the processing periods had not been communicated. The European Union noted that India had not provided details on the missing information to complete the assessment procedure for the approval of new exports and had not indicated the specific non-conformities for existing exports, which prevented the implementation of corrective actions. Despite some recent progress, the European Union regretted that there were a number of pending market applications, some for many years. The European Union urged India to comply with its WTO SPS obligations by ensuring transparency of its import legislation and approval procedures, and provide the requested clarifications to allow the finalization of the pending applications without undue delay. The European Union looked forward to discussions with India on this issue.

StatementSubmitted: The EU would like to refer again to the lack of transparency and predictability, as well as to the long and unjustified delays related to India’s import approval procedures for plants, animals, and their products. In previous technical meetings, the EU and India discussed the state of play of pending market access applications submitted by the EU. During these meetings, the EU invited India to provide a standard processing period for the approval procedures and the anticipated processing period. In other cases, certain competent authorities of India simply refuse to meet or to provide any information about the state of play of the EU files, including the deficiencies or non-conformities reportedly identified by India. Therefore, market access applications remain blocked for many years. Delays persist and the EU is not informed about the reasons for the delays.Even if some progress was recently observed, the EU remains concerned by the lack of progress with many applications that are pending, and the persistent lack of engagement and responses from India to the EU requests. Therefore, the EU urges India to:Engage with the EU and comply with its WTO SPS obligations,ensure transparency of its import legislation and import approval procedures, and work expeditiously and avoid undue delays. The EU looks forward to deepening the technical discussions with India to avoid unnecessary and unjustified disruptions to trade.
Summary: The European Union expressed concerns about the lack of transparency and predictability, and the unjustified delays in India's import approval procedures for plants, animals, and their products. Despite some recent progress, the European Union remained concerned about the overall lack of advancement and India's insufficient engagement and responses, which resulted in prolonged delays. Referring to the bilateral technical meetings to discuss the status of pending market access applications, the European Union urged India to establish a standard processing period for approval procedures and to specify the anticipated processing timeframes. The European Union urged India to strengthen engagement, adhere to its obligations under the SPS Agreement, ensure transparency in import legislation and approval procedures, and expedite the process to avoid undue delays.In response, the European Union emphasized that undue delays were pertinent to the SPS Committee, extending beyond market access concerns.

StatementSubmitted: The EU would like to refer again to the lack of predictability, as well as to the long and unjustified delays related to India’s import approval procedures for plants, animals, and their products, with a particular concern on the latter. In previous technical meetings, the EU and India discussed the state of play of pending market access applications submitted by the EU. We are happy to report some progress in relation to the EU exports of plants and plant products. The EU thanks the competent authority of India responsible for imports of plants and plant products for their engagement and invites this authority to continue to progress to quickly eliminate the backlog of pending market access applications. Unfortunately, the situation differs considerably regarding animal products. Regrettably, India has not provided any information in the last two years in relation to the EU exports of animals and products, and furthermore, one of the  competent authorities responsible for imports of animals has refused to meet with the EU or to provide information on the state of play of the market access applications of Member States.In fact, the Indian authorities have been putting import legislation in place that does not comply with the transparency provisions of the WTO SPS Agreement nor the disciplines regarding the avoidance of undue delays. Market access applications are delayed and remain blocked for many years, without any justification by India. Therefore, the EU urges all the India authorities to:Engage with the EU and comply with its WTO SPS obligations; Ensure transparent implementation of its import legislation; Work expeditiously and avoid undue delays.The EU looks forward to deepening the technical discussions with India to avoid unnecessary and unjustified disruptions to trade.
Summary: The European Union expressed concerns about the lack of predictability and unjustified delays in India's import approval procedures for plants, animals, and their products. Despite some recent progress in relation to market application for plants and plant products, the European Union remained concerned about the overall lack of advancement and India's insufficient engagement and responses, which resulted in prolonged delays for animal products. The European Union considered India's import legislations not to comply with the transparency requirement in the SPS Agreement nor the disciplines regarding undue delays. The European Union urged India to strengthen engagement, adhere to its obligations under the SPS Agreement, ensure transparency in import legislation and approval procedures, and expedite the process to avoid undue delays.

StatementSubmitted: ? For the export of the 12 species of Korean fresh mushrooms to India, the Korean government has been conducting a pest risk analysis with India since 2015. ? India informed us of the import requirements for 12 species of Korean fresh mushrooms through the WTO notification (G/SPS/N/IND/131) in February 2016, and the two countries finally reached an agreement on the import requirements for the 12 Korean fresh mushrooms in December 2016 after collecting opinions from the Korean side, but though 6 years have passed since then, India has not allowed the import of 12 Korean fresh mushrooms.? Nevertheless, in the Korea-India CEPA SPS Joint Working Group Meeting held in November 2022, India proposed to re-initiate PRA for the 3 species of Korean fresh mushrooms, instead of publishing a notice of the import approval for 12 species of Korean fresh mushrooms in the gazette? After that, Korea raised a concern that India’s proposal is not consistent with ISPM 2 (Framework for Pest Risk Analysis) and ISPM 11 (Pest Risk Analysis for Quarantine Pests) via bilateral channels and Embassy of India in Korea, but India is still not allowing the import of 12 species of Korean fresh mushrooms. ? Though the two countries already reached an agreement on the import requirements of India for 12 species of Korean fresh mushrooms through PRA.? The Korean government would express its grave concern about India’s proposal for re-initiation of PRA from the beginning only for the 3 species of Korean fresh mushrooms.? And Korea urges India to comply with Article.8 and Annex C of the WTO SPS Agreement and without undue delay allow the import of 12 species of Korean fresh mushrooms for which all risk assessment processes have already been concluded
Summary: Korea raised concerns that six years had passed since an agreement had been reached on the import requirements for 12 Korean fresh mushrooms (G/SPS/N/IND/131), but yet India had not allowed the import of these 12 Korean fresh mushrooms. In the context of a Korea-India Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement SPS Joint Working Group Meeting of November 2022, India had proposed to re-initiate a pest risk assessment for three species of Korean fresh mushrooms, although a pest risk assessment had been previously completed for all 12 species. Korea considered that India's proposal was not consistent with IPPC standards (ISPMs 2 and 11). Korea urged India to allow the import of all 12 species of Korean fresh mushrooms.

StatementSubmitted: ? The Korean government requested import approval for 12 types of Korean fresh mushrooms to India, and the two countries finally reached an agreement on the import requirements for the 12 Korean mushrooms in December 2016 after conducting a pest risk analysis with India.  - About 7 years have passed since then, but India has not allowed the import of 12 Korean mushrooms.? Despite our continued request for the initiation of the remaining import approval process, India have not provided any explanations regarding the delay in import approval.   - Rather, India proposed to re-initiate PRA for the 3 types of Korean mushrooms, instead of publishing a notice of the import approval for 12 types of Korean mushrooms in the gazette, whose assessment has already been completed.? In this regard, the Korean government raised a new specific trade concern (STC) and asked for a faithful response and follow-up measures from the Indian side.  - But, India only responded that this is a matter of market access.? However, we firmly believe that this matter shall be considered as an SPS issue. Despite the completion of PRA, India is unduly delaying the import approval process for Korean mushrooms without any scientific evidence or explanation.  - Against this background, we urge India to approve import of the 12 types of Korean mushrooms whose PRA was already completed without undue delay, in accordance with its obligations prescribed in Article 8 and Annex C of the WTO SPS Agreement.
Summary: Korea raised concerns that seven years had passed since an agreement had been reached on the import requirements for 12 fresh mushrooms, yet India had not allowed imports of these products. Korea regretted the lack of explanations regarding the delay in import approval and complained that India had proposed to re-initiate a pest risk assessment for three types of Korean mushrooms, instead of publishing a notice of the import approval for 12 types of Korean mushrooms, for which the risk assessment was completed. Korea urged India to allow the import of the 12 fresh mushrooms without undue delay in accordance with Article 8 of and Annex C to the SPS Agreement.

StatementSubmitted: ? Since 2015, Korea and India have been conducting a pest risk analysis (PRA) on the 12 types of Korean fresh mushrooms for their import into India.    - India notified the draft import requirements for the 12 types of Korean mushrooms via the WTO in February 2016, and the two countries finally reached an agreement on the import requirements for the 12 types of Korean mushrooms in December 2016 after the opinion-gathering process.   - However, about 6 years have passed since then, but India has yet allowed the import of the 12 Korean mushrooms.? At the Korea-India CEPA SPS Joint Working Group Meeting held in November 2022, India proposed to re-initiate PRA for the 3 types of Korean mushrooms, instead of the import approval for the 12 types of Korean mushrooms published in the official gazette as a follow-up measure, even though the two countries already agreed to proceed to the pest risk management.   - Korea raised a question via the bilateral communication channels and Indian Embassy in Korea that the above-mentioned proposal from India is inconsistent with the ISPM 2 (Framework for pest risk analysis) and ISPM 11 (Pest risk analysis for quarantine pests), but India have yet approved the import of the 12 types of Korean mushrooms.? In March and July, 2023, Korea raised this as a new specific trade concern (STC) via the WTO SPS Committee, and India answered that the issues related to market access are not subject to discussion at the WTO SPS committee and requested to have a bilateral discussion on this matter. But, we firmly believe that the matter of delayed approval  needs to be under discussion at the WTO SPS Committee.   - Korea sent an official letter to India via diplomatic channels, proposing a bilateral discussion between the competent authorities of the two countries in May and November 2023, but still we have yet received any response from the Indian side.? Through the official PRA, the two countries reached a final agreement on the import requirements for the 12 types of Korean mushrooms proposed by India. But, India proposed to re-initiated the PRA for the three types of Korean mushrooms. The Korean government expresses its deep concern over India’s proposal.   - Against this background, we urge India to approve import of the 12 types of Korean mushrooms without undue delay, whose PRA has already been completed in accordance with its obligations prescribed in Article 8 of the WTO SPS Agreement.
Summary: Korea shared its concern that seven years had passed since the agreement reached on the import requirements for 12 fresh mushrooms, yet India had not allowed imports of these products. Korea regretted the lack of explanations regarding the delay in import approval, and noted that India had proposed to re-initiate a PRA for three types of Korean mushrooms, instead of publishing a notice of the import approval for 12 types of Korean mushrooms for which the risk assessment was completed. Korea urged India to allow the importation of the 12 fresh mushrooms without undue delay in accordance with Article 8 and Annex C to the SPS Agreement.

StatementSubmitted: Thank you Chair.The EU would like to raise a new trade concern regarding Japan’s approval procedures for plant products.Besides the commitments spelled out in the WTO SPS Agreement, the European Union and Japan also signed a Free Trade Agreement, which entered into force in 2019. It includes provisions on SPS issues.With the aim to fully implement the SPS commitments of both agreements, over the years, the European Union and Japan had many exchanges and meetings concerning the approval procedures for plant products in Japan. However, even after these exchanges, only very limited progress has been achieved in this domain. Due to the lengthy, burdensome and unpredictable approval procedures, EU plant product producers face serious difficulties to gain market access to their products in Japan. This is despite the substantial commitment on the EU side to provide all the necessary information requested by Japan under these procedures. Substantial and very often unjustifiable delays occur and applicants are often confronted  with new requirements during the processing of their applications. Some market access applications date back more than 20 years, which raises the question if these assessments are carried out purely under scientific grounds.The EU is equally concerned about the policy of Japan, which requires the choice of a single plant product per country for assessment, while suspending any other plant product application from that country. This approach is not in line with the FTA agreement and artificially limits the possibility of putting forward and progressing with multiple applications.Overall, the EU considers that these practices do not seem to provide sufficient transparency in these procedures and result in undue delays.  The EU considers that these procedures are not in line with the relevant provisions of the WTO SPS Agreement.The EU looks forward to continuing its cooperation with Japan on these issues and to find solutions that would simplify and speed up the treatment of the plant product applications. Thank you Chair.
Summary: The European Union expressed concerns regarding Japan's lengthy, burdensome, and unpredictable approval procedures for plant products. The European Union noted that, despite many meetings and the provision of all the necessary information, EU plant producers faced difficulties to gain market access, there were unjustifiable delays (some dating more than 20 years), and there were new requirements introduced during the approval process. The European Union also expressed concerns about Japan's choice of a single plant product per country for assessment while suspending any other plant product application from that country. The European Union considered Japan's approach not to be in line with the EU-Japan Free Trade Agreement or the SPS Agreement as it artificially limited the possibility of progressing multiple applications, lacked transparency and resulted in undue delays. The European Union looked forward to continuing cooperation with Japan on these issues.The European Union noted it was aware of the state of play of all the pending applications. Some delays that Japan attributed to an EU member State were due to the burdensome requirements, which discouraged EU member States from completing the procedure.

StatementSubmitted: First of all, the EU would like to thank Japan for its bilateral engagement on this issue.Since the last WTO SPS Committee meeting, the EU and Japan had three bilateral meetings concerning Japan’s SPS approval procedures for plants and plant products.The EU also appreciates the explanation provided by Japan on their revised “Standard Procedure for Lifting a Ban on Importation of Plants into Japan”, notified to the WTO SPS committee on 11 May 2023 under notification JPN/1201.However, the EU remains concerned about the lengthy and burdensome approval procedures, which result in that the EU plant product producers face serious difficulties to gain market access to their products in Japan.The EU also remains equally concerned about the policy of Japan, which requires the choice of a single plant product per country for assessment, while suspending any other plant product application from that country.The EU looks forward to continuing its cooperation and bilateral exchanges with Japan on these issues and to find solutions that would simplify and speed up the treatment of the plant product applications in line with the WTO SPS Agreement and the EU-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement.
Summary: The European Union thanked Japan for the recent bilateral engagement and the explanation provided on the revised Standard Procedure for Lifting a Ban on Importation of Plants into Japan (G/SPS/N/JPN/1201). The European Union expressed concerns regarding Japan's lengthy and burdensome approval procedures for plant products and noted the difficulties faced by EU plant producers to gain market access. The European Union also expressed concerns about Japan's choice of a single plant product per country for assessment while suspending any other plant product application from that country. The European Union looked forward to continuing cooperation with Japan on these issues to find solutions in line with the SPS Agreement and the EU-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement.

StatementSubmitted: In 2020, Brazil completed the process of expanding its free zoning without vaccination for Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD) for new areas. This successful expansion was recognized by the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH), in May 2021.Brazil is aware of the Canadian protocol to recognize an FMD-free zone without vaccination, since Canada has already carried out these procedures and recognized the Brazilian state of Santa Catarina as FMD-free without vaccination, enabling Brazilian establishments from that state to export pork to Canada.Taking into account the previous knowledge of the Canadian procedures for recognizing FMD-free areas without vaccination, in 2021, we requested Canada to take the relevant steps to recognize our updated sanitary status.Unfortunately, Canada informed us that it would only carry out a new evaluation when the entire Brazilian territory is free of FMD without vaccination, failing to take into account the regionalization principle envisaged in the SPS Agreement, as well as WOAH recommendations.While recognizing Canada as an outstanding supporter of the principles of the SPS Agreement, and taking into account that Canada itself has already carried out the recognition of the state of Santa Catarina, Brazil tried to clarify this issue by holding bilateral meetings with Canada to try to achieve a positive outcome.Two bilateral meetings have already been held on the sidelines of the SPS Committee's 84th and 85th regular meetings. Furthermore, a technical meeting was held in June with capital experts, but we have not yet been able to resolve this issue. During the technical meeting, Canada reaffirmed its understanding that would only carry out a new evaluation to import pork when the entire Brazilian territory is free of FMD without vaccination.Brazil has been trying to resolve this issue bilaterally, as we consider that it is important to keep an open dialogue about it. However, we could not agree with Canada's view on this subject, as it is contrary to articles 3, 5, and 6 of the SPS Agreement.Brazil also believes that Canada is not following the principle of harmonization, as it is not making the necessary efforts to harmonize its internal sanitary measures to WOAH's decision to recognize the Brazilian current status for FMD.We believe that Canada`s measure, in this case, is inconsistent with the concept of appropriate level of sanitary or phytosanitary protection, since the new free areas have the same sanitary status of the one already recognized by Canada.We kindly ask Canada to review its decision of not starting the relevant procedures to recognize Brazilian areas free from FMD already recognized by WOAH since 2021. Brazil remains open to further discuss this issue bilaterally, and based on scientific evidence.
Summary: Brazil expressed its concern that Canada did not recognize new areas free from foot and mouth disease (FMD) without vaccination, which had been recognized by WOAH in May 2021. Canada had recognized Santa Catarina as FMD free without vaccination for pork based on its procedure to recognize FMD free zones. In Brazil's view, the lack of recognition of its updated status for new zones was contrary to Articles 3, 5, and 6 of the SPS Agreement as well as the principle of harmonization and the concept of appropriate level of protection. Acknowledging ongoing bilateral efforts, Brazil asked Canada to review its decision of carrying out a new evaluation only when the entire Brazilian territory would be free of FMD without vaccination.Brazil clarified that, while at the time that Santa Catarina was evaluated, it was the only state that had been recognized by WOAH as FMD free, this status had now been expanded to six other states by WOAH. Brazil had circulated additional information under document G/SPS/GEN/1932.

Brazil expressed its concern that Canada did not recognize new areas free from foot and mouth disease (FMD) without vaccination, which had been recognized by WOAH in May 2021. Canada had recognized Santa Catarina as FMD free without vaccination for pork based on its procedure to recognize FMD free zones. In Brazil's view, the lack of recognition of its updated status for new zones was contrary to Articles 3, 5, and 6 of the SPS Agreement. Acknowledging ongoing bilateral efforts, Brazil asked Canada to review its decision of carrying out a new evaluation only when the entire Brazilian territory would be free of FMD without vaccination, and express its willingness for further bilateral discussions.

StatementSubmitted: Once more, Brazil would like to raise its concern on Canada`s lack of recognition of Brazilian FMD-free zones without vaccination for swines, as it is not in line with the SPS Agreement, and has been preventing some Brazilian states from exporting pork to Canada.In 2020, Brazil completed the process of expanding its free zoning without vaccination for Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD) for new areas. This successful expansion was recognized by the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH), in May 2022, more than two years ago. Brazil is aware of the Canadian protocol to recognize a FMD-free zone without vaccination. By means of that protocol, Canada has already carried out the procedures that led to the recognition of the Brazilian state of Santa Catarina as FMD-free without vaccination, enabling Brazilian establishments from that state to export pork to Canada. We are willing to work with Canada to fulfill its national regulations on the matter of recognition.Based on our previous knowledge of the Canadian procedures for recognizing FMD-free areas without vaccination, in 2021, when Brazil suspended the vaccination, we requested Canada to take the relevant steps to recognize our updated sanitary status, whichvencompasses the states of Rio Grande do Sul andvParaná. After the recognition by WOAH, in 2022, Brazilvrequested an update for the recognition of six other Brazilian states besides Santa Catarina.Unfortunately, Canada has informed us that it wouldvonly carry out a new evaluation when the entirevBrazilian territory is free of FMD withoutvvaccination, disregarding the regionalizationvprinciple envisaged in the SPS Agreement, as well as recommendations provided by WOAH. For Brazil, there is a clear logic contradiction here, as Canada itself has already carried out the recognition of a single state in Brazil, the state of Santa Catarina. Unfortunately, during the technical meetings on this matter, Canada has reaffirmed its position that it would only carry out a new evaluation to import pork when the entire Brazilian territory is free of FMD without vaccination.  Brazil does not agree with Canada's view on this subject, as it disrespects articles 3, 5, and 6 of the SPS agreement. Brazil also believes that Canada is not following the principle of harmonization, since it is not making the necessary efforts to harmonize its internal sanitary measures to WOAH's decision to recognize the Brazilian current status for FMD.  The success of Brazil`s decades-old National Program for Foot and Mouth Disease (PNEFA) should be a determining factor for Canada towards expanding its recognition of Brazilian FMD-free areas, in the same manner as it has supported Canada`s decision to recognize the area of the Southern state of Santa Catarina.We believe that Canada`s measure, in this case, is inconsistent in the application of the concept of appropriate level of sanitary or phytosanitary protection, since the new free areas have the same sanitary status of the one already recognized by Canada. We would also like to reiterate that, by not recognizing the sanitary status of the Brazilian states free from FMD without vaccination, Canada is not observing the principle of regionalization.The fact that Canada has already recognized our updated status for FMD in relation to beef exports also highlights the contradiction of its position against recognizing the updated Brazilian status for FMD in relation to Brazilian pork exports. In this scenario, Canada`s refusal to at least start the recognition process for our pork exports from areas besides the state of Santa Catarina characterizes undue delay.Considering our interest to export pork to Canada from states besides Santa Catarina, we would be thankful if Canada could give a response to this following proposal: could Canada consider first recognizing Rio Grande do Sul and Paraná, whose statuses as FMD-free were recognized by WOAH since 2022? Their territories are contiguous with the state Santa Catarina. If not, what would be the scientific reasons?We thank Canada for the bilateral engagement both in Geneva and in Ottawa and we hope that further progress can be achieved on this matter in the future. We remain open to further bilateral discussions, based on scientific evidence. Brazil remains to be convinced of Canada`s position as scientifically sound and compliant with the SPS Agreement.
Summary: Brazil reiterated its concern on Canada's lack of recognition of Brazilian FMD-free zones without vaccination for swine. Brazil had completed the process of expanding its free zoning without vaccination for FMD for new areas in 2020, which expansion had been recognized by WOAH in 2022. While Canada had recognized Santa Catarina as FMD-free without vaccination, Brazil regretted that Canada continued to prevent some other Brazilian states form exporting pork and that it would only carry out a new evaluation when the entire Brazilian territory would be free of FMD without vaccination. To Brazil, this approach disregarded the regionalization and harmonization principles as well as WOAH recommendations and showed an inconsistent application of the ALOP. Brazil thus considered Canada's measures to be inconsistent with Articles 3, 5, and 6 of the SPS Agreement. Brazil also took the view that Canada's refusal to start the recognition process from areas other than Santa Catarina characterized undue delay. Brazil enquired whether Canada could consider first recognizing the states of Rio Grande do Sul and Paraná, whose statuses as FMD-free had been recognized by WOAH in 2022 and wondered about the scientific reasons for recognizing these states. Brazil remained ready to continue bilateral discussions based on scientific evidence.

StatementSubmitted: La Argentina desea aprovechar esta oportunidad para plantear su preocupación por la falta de avance en el proceso de apertura del mercado de los Estados Unidos a nuestros cítricos dulces, situación que claramente configura una demora indebida en los términos del Acuerdo MSF.Lamentamos tener que realizar esta presentación, ya que ambos países coincidimos en todos los foros internacionales (especialmente en la OMC) en la importancia de adoptar medidas sanitarias y fitosanitarias basadas en la ciencia, evitar demoras indebidas en los procesos de apertura y no usar esta clase de medidas como para-arancelarias. Sin embargo, tal como se detallará a continuación, no tuvimos otra alternativa que plantear esta preocupación para instar a los Estados Unidos a acelerar el proceso. En agosto de 2019, una misión técnica del Servicio de Inspección de Sanidad Animal y Vegetal de los Estados Unidos (APHIS) auditó el sistema de producción y control de cítricos de exportación en nuestro país a los fines de llevar adelante el Análisis de Riesgos de Plagas.  Un año después, el equipo de gestión de riesgo del APHIS envió un documento borrador al Servicio Nacional de Sanidad y Calidad Agroalimentaria (SENASA), máxima autoridad sanitaria argentina, con la propuesta de medidas de mitigación de riesgo de plagas identificadas. Es decir que han transcurrido más de cuatro años desde la visita de inspección por parte de APHIS, y más de tres años del intercambio sobre las medidas de mitigación de riesgo, un tiempo más que suficiente y razonable para poder avanzar con la publicación del Análisis de Riesgo de Plagas (ARP) para comentarios públicos, paso indispensable para poder concluir con el proceso de apertura. Esta demora manifiestamente indebida es la que nos motiva a realizar la presentación de esta preocupación comercial en el Comité SPS.Argentina ha presentado en numerosas ocasiones y diversos ámbitos a nivel bilateral su gran interés en avanzar la apertura del mercado, siendo la exportación de cítricos dulces la máxima prioridad en nuestra agenda bilateral de negociaciones sanitarias y fitosanitarias. Estas presentaciones incluyeron notas de los sucesivos Ministros y Secretarios de Agricultura de Argentina antes las autoridades del Departamento de Agricultura de los Estados Unidos (USDA), así como también ante la Oficina del Representante de Comercio Exterior (USTR). Asimismo, el tema fue planteado en numerosas reuniones de autoridades del Ministerio de Relaciones Exteriores y la Embajada Argentina en Washington, ante el USDA, el USTR y el Departamento de Estado, destacándose su inclusión en la agenda de la II y III Reunión del Consejo de Alto Nivel del Acuerdo Marco en Materia de Comercio e Inversiones (AMCI/TIFA) en 2018 y 2022, respectivamente. Dicha reunión constituye el mecanismo de diálogo bilateral económico de mayor relevancia entre ambos países, en el cual se abordan los principales temas bilaterales de comercio e inversión, incluidas las preocupaciones comerciales de cada parte, acordándose los pasos a seguir para su resolución con el fin de mejorar y profundizar la relación económica y comercial entre ambos países. A pesar de todas estas gestiones y pedidos no se ha logrado alcanzar aún la apertura del mercado de cítricos dulces.  Frente a los numerosos requerimientos de Argentina, la respuesta recurrente del USDA ha sido señalar que el proceso está en curso y que su resolución lleva tiempo, sin poder estimar plazos.Entendemos que esta falta de avance en el proceso resulta inconsistente con el Acuerdo sobre la Aplicación de Medidas Sanitarias y Fitosanitarias, en particular con sus artículos 2.2; 5 y 8 así como su Anexo C.  Adicionalmente, debemos destacar que esta demora injustificada en la reapertura del mercado afecta seriamente a una economía regional. Enfatizamos que nuestro país ha dado todas las garantías sanitarias, como siempre lo hacemos con nuestros socios comerciales.  Por todo ello solicitamos a los Estados Unidos que proceda, sin mayor demora, a publicar el Análisis de Riesgos de Plagas al efecto de recibir comentarios, y concluir rápidamente el proceso de apertura del mercado de cítricos dulces, sobre base científica. Una vez más, la Argentina expresa su vocación de continuar trabajando bilateralmente con los Estados Unidos de forma constructiva para poder encontrar una pronta solución al tema.
Summary: Argentina raised its concerns about the lack of progress towards the opening of the US market to its sweet citrus fruits. In 2019, the US Animal and Plant Health and Inspection Service (APHIS) had audited Argentina's citrus production and control system to undertake a pest risk analysis (PRA) and in 2020, it had submitted a draft document with proposals of risk mitigation measures for the pests identified. Argentina regretted that the United States had not yet published the PRA for public comments, which was a necessary step to finalize the process of opening markets. Noting that exports of sweet citrus fruits constituted a priority in their bilateral SPS negotiations, and underscoring the numerous attempts to place this topic on the agenda for bilateral discussions, Argentina noted that the United States had not indicated a possible timeline for the resolution of the process. In Argentina's view, this delay was a violation of Articles 2.2, 5 and 8, as well as Annex C of the SPS Agreement. Argentina urged the United States to publish without delay the PRA for public comments and to promptly conclude the market opening for sweet citrus fruits. Argentina reiterated its availability for bilateral collaboration towards a prompt resolution of this issue.
