StatementSubmitted: La Delegación de Chile presenta ante los Miembros de la OMC su preocupación comercial con relación a las demoras indebidas por parte de los Estados Unidos en la publicación en el Registro Federal de la notificación que autoriza el ingreso de las uvas de mesa chilenas bajo el enfoque de sistemas (o systems approach), como alternativa a la fumigación con bromuro de metilo.La demora en esta publicación tiene gran impacto para toda nuestra cadena de producción y exportación, ya que el 40% de las importaciones de uva de Estados Unidos proviene de Chile.  El año 2022 se exportaron más de 240 mil toneladas, con un valor estimado de US$ 444 millones.La no materialización de este protocolo tendrá un fuerte impacto en la actividad económica de las 3 principales regiones productoras del centro norte del país que representan más del 60% del total de uvas enviadas a Estados Unidos, donde existen 10 mil hectáreas productivas de uvas de mesa, más de 1.500 pequeños y medianos productores, y 50 mil empleos asociados. Actualmente están en curso inversiones privadas para la construcción y habilitación de 2 sitios de inspección en las zonas productoras, por un monto total aproximado 5 millones de dólares, las cuales están en riesgo debido a esta demora. El Anexo C del Acuerdo MSF, en su artículo 8, párrafos 1.a) y 1.c) establece que los procedimientos para verificar el cumplimiento de una medida sanitaria se deben iniciar y ultimar sin demoras indebidas y sin exigir más información de la necesaria a efectos de los procedimientos de control, inspección y aprobación apropiados. Consideramos que estas disposiciones han sido vulneradas por los Estados Unidos, ya que según lo informado por APHIS la autorización está lista para su publicación desde mayo de 2023. No obstante, hasta la fecha y pese a reiteradas consultas por parte de las autoridades chilenas, Estados Unidos no ha entregado una justificación clara de los motivos de la demora en la publicación, lo que causará cuantiosas pérdidas económicas a los productores chilenos en la próxima temporada de uva de mesa que se inicia en el mes de noviembre.Por otro lado, tal como lo establece el Acuerdo MSF en su Artículo 4 Equivalencia y el Artículo 5 Evaluación de riesgos y determinación del nivel adecuado de protección sanitaria o fitosanitaria, los Miembros aceptarán como equivalente las medidas, si el Miembro exportador demuestra objetivamente que cumple con el nivel adecuado de protección fitosanitaria del importador, con miras a evitar una restricción encubierta al comercio internacional. Respecto a esto último, Chile ha esperado concretar la exportación de uva de mesa bajo el enfoque de sistemas desde el año 2000, y en esta línea, la tramitación de la autorización ha pasado distintas etapas de revisión técnica y 2 procesos de consulta pública, uno conducido por el Departamento de Agricultura  el 2022, y un segundo proceso en el Registro Federal de Estados Unidos el 2023. El resultado de los análisis publicados evidenció que:no existe riesgo de introducción de plagas cuarentenarias, no habría efectos económicos negativos para el país importador,sólo los productores que cumplieran determinadas condiciones podrían exportar bajo este sistema, y que;el consumidor contaría con una fruta de mejor calidad.En mayo de 2023 durante una reunión técnica entre el Servicio Agrícola y Ganadero y APHIS/USDA, se anunció que se había finalizado el proceso de análisis para la autorización del enfoque de sistemas para uva de mesa y que la norma estaba lista para la publicación.Cabe destacar que con la entrada en vigor del enfoque de sistemas para uva de mesa, se revitalizaría la industria exportadora nacional, ofreciendo a los consumidores estadounidenses uvas de mesa de mejor calidad, ya que la vida de postcosecha se acorta drásticamente en uva tratada con el fumigante bromuro de metilo. Adicionalmente, la exportación bajo el enfoque de sistemas constituye una práctica ambientalmente sustentable, ya que evita la fumigación con bromuro de metilo, tanto en los Estados Unidos como en Chile.Considerando los antecedentes precedentes, y que el enfoque de sistemas en Chile ya está funcionando con éxito para otras frutas exportadas a los Estados Unidos, solicitamos respetuosamente la publicación Final en el Registro Federal lo antes posible.La delegación de Chile agradece a la delegación de los Estados Unidos por la atención a esta preocupación y reitera su disposición de mantener una comunicación abierta entre autoridades para buscar una solución al problema.
Summary: Chile raised its concerns regarding the US undue delays in the publication of import requirements for table grapes under a systems approach, as an alternative to fumigation with methyl bromide. The delay was affecting the national production and export chain in the three main producing regions. In Chile's view, the United States was violating Articles 4, 5 and 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement. Following the confirmation received in May 2023 that the analysis for the authorization of the systems approach for table grapes had been finalized and that the measure was ready for publication, Chile requested its prompt publication in the Federal Register and reiterated its availability for an open communication towards the resolution of the issue.

StatementSubmitted: Chile expresa su preocupación por las demoras indebidas de Estados Unidos en la publicación de la autorización para la importación de uvas de mesa bajo enfoque de sistemas, lo que afecta significativamente a la cadena de producción y exportación de uva del país.En mayo de 2023 durante una reunión técnica entre el Servicio Agrícola y Ganadero de Chile y APHIS/USDA, se anunció que se había finalizado el proceso de análisis para la autorización del enfoque de sistemas en uva de mesa y que la norma estaba pronto a ser publicada. Posterior a esto, no ha habido avance significativo en las conversaciones bilaterales con Estados Unidos, aduciendo éste último razones para la demora que no se relacionan con riesgos fitosanitarios o falta de información técnica para la toma de decisiones, sino más bien a temas comerciales de otra índole.Esta demora impacta año a año en el comercio de este producto con el mercado estadounidense, que llega a los US$ 450 millones anuales y pone en riesgo más de 50 mil empleos, afectando principalmente a pequeños y medianos productores.Se solicita respetuosamente que se concrete la publicación por parte de EE. UU. lo antes posible y destacamos que hay un historial de intercambio comercial confiable y seguro en productos agrícolas entre Chile y Estados Unidos, toda vez que, el enfoque de sistemas ya está funcionando con éxito para otras frutas exportadas a los Estados Unidos. Por otra parte, evitar el uso del Bromuro de Metilo favorece la sustentabilidad del comercio del producto y alarga la vida post cosecha.
Summary: Chile reiterated its concerns regarding US undue delays in the publication of authorization of imports of table grapes under a systems approach as an alternative to fumigation with methyl bromide. The delay affected national production, mainly small and medium-sized producers. Chile regretted the lack of significant progress following the confirmation received in May 2023 that the analysis for the authorization of the systems approach for table grapes had been finalized and that the measure was ready for publication. Chile requested the prompt publication of the authorizations and highlighted the longstanding history of trade between the two countries, which successfully worked under a systems approach for other agricultural products.

StatementSubmitted: En relación con esta preocupación de Chile por las demoras indebidas de Estados Unidos en la publicación de la autorización para la importación de uva de mesa bajo enfoque de sistemas, quisiéramos informar que, si bien aún no se ha concretado la publicación por parte de EE. UU, el Ministerio de Agricultura de Chile y la Secretaría de Agricultura de Estados Unidos han retomado las conversaciones durante las últimas semanas para resolver este asunto lo antes posible.Agradecemos a los Estados Unidos la disposición para buscar vías efectivas de avance para concretar lo antes posible la autorización del Systems Approach, el cual lleva más de 20 años en agenda.Manifestamos nuestro interés en seguir avanzando en los recientes acuerdos y confiamos en que este asunto esté resuelto antes de la próxima temporada de producción en Chile que se inicia en el tercer trimestre del año
Summary: Regarding its concern about US undue delays in publishing the authorization for the import of table grapes under a systems approach, Chile informed the Committee that while the publication had not yet been finalized, the Ministries of Agriculture from both countries had recently resumed talks to resolve the issue as quickly as possible. Chile thanked the United States for its willingness to find effective solutions to finalize the authorization promptly. Chile expressed its interest in continuing progress on the recent agreements and trusted that the issue would be resolved before the next production season in Chile in the third quarter of this year.

South Africa raised its concern over Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1201 regarding measures to prevent the introduction into and the spread within the European Union of Xylella fastidiosa. South Africa questioned the need for X. fastidiosa-free countries to undertake risk-based surveys to trade with the European Union, where the pest had been recorded. Noting the high cost and resources involved in the surveys, South Africa was of the view that third countries should have the option to simply declare their pest freedom on a phytosanitary certificate. South Africa had strict import requirements against X. fastidiosa, which was a quarantine pest in the country.

StatementSubmitted: Before 2017, the export of Chinese agricultural products such as apple, pear, and marigold seeds to India had been progressing successfully. On June 1, 2017, the Indian side suspended the import of the above-mentioned agricultural products due to the interception of individual pests. The Chinese side has held technical consultations with the Indian side on many occasions and provided relevant technical materials at the request of the Indian side. In September 2019, the Chinese side invited Indian experts to China for field assessment and provided draft phytosanitary requirements for Chinese fruit exports to India, but there has been no feedback from the Indian side. We hope that the Indian side will give us feedback as soon as possible so that the two sides can negotiate to resume the export of Chinese apples, pears, and marigold seeds to India at an early date.
Summary: China indicated that, in 2017, India had suspended imports of apples, pears and marigold seeds from China in response to the identification of certain pests. China regretted the lack of feedback received after the bilateral technical consultations held, the provision of the requested technical materials and the field assessment undertaken in 2019. China looked forward to India's feedback in order to continue the negotiations to resume the exports.

StatementSubmitted: On June 1, 2017, the Indian side suspended the import of apple, pear, and marigold seeds due to the interception of individual pests. The Chinese side has held technical consultations with the Indian side on many occasions and provided relevant technical materials at the request of the Indian side. In September 2019, the Chinese side invited Indian experts to China for field assessment and provided draft phytosanitary requirements for Chinese fruit exports to India, but there has been no feedback from the Indian side. India's measures have had a great impact on the export of related products to China. To maintain normal trade between the two countries, it is recommended that India lift the import restrictions on Chinese apple, pear, and marigold seeds as soon as possible.
Summary: China indicated that, in 2017, India had suspended imports of apples, pears, and marigold seeds from China in response to the identification of certain pests. China regretted the lack of feedback after the bilateral technical consultations, the provision of the requested technical materials, and the field assessment undertaken in 2019. China asked India to lift the import restrictions on Chinese apple, pear, and marigold seeds as soon as possible.

StatementSubmitted: Since June 1, 2017, India has completely suspended the import of apple, pear and marigold seeds from China because India claimed that Pseudococcus comstocki Kuwana and Fusarium oxysporum were detected in pears and apples imported from China. Fusarium oxysporum, Fusarium oxysporum sp. Callistephi was detected in marigold seeds.Therefore, the Chinese side has held technical consultations with the Indian side on many occasions and provided relevant technical materials at the request of the Indian side. In September 2019, the Chinese side invited Indian experts to China for field assessment and provided draft phytosanitary requirements for Chinese fruit exported to India. In the last meeting, the Indian side pointed out that the relevant report had been shared with GACC. But so far, the Chinese side has not yet received the report. In this regard, China suggests that the Indian side send the report via the e-mail provided by GACC, which is pgdgacc@126.com, or via the e-mail of the Indian Embassy in China. China will respond based on the report provided by India.As we mentioned, India’s measures have had a great impact on the export of related products in China. In order to maintain normal trade between the two countries, it is recommended that India lift the import restrictions on Chinese apple, pear and marigold seeds as soon as possible.
Summary: China indicated that, since 2017, India had suspended import of Chinese apples, pears, and marigold seeds due to detected pests. China had engaged in technical consultations, had invited Indian experts for a field assessment in September 2019, and had shared draft phytosanitary requirements. However, China noted that, despite India claiming to have sent a relevant report to China Customs, it had not been received. China emphasized the significant impact on Chinese exports and recommended India to lift the import restrictions as soon as possible.China took the floor again to suggest that India send the relevant report via e-mail to the address provided by Chinese Customs or through the Indian embassy in China and assured that it would respond based on the report provided.

Brazil raised its concerns about the suspensions of transit of its poultry through Thailand's territory, which it considered to be a violation of Article 3 of the SPS Agreement and of WOAH guidelines. Brazil stated that there was no proper justification to extend the initial 90-day suspension. Underscoring that cases of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in Brazil did not occur in commercial poultry, which should thus not change the recognition of the country as a HPAI-free, Brazil hoped that Thailand would lift the suspension to be in line with the SPS Agreement and the relevant international references.

Brazil viewed Thailand's suspension of transit for Brazilian poultry as a breach of both the SPS Agreement and WOAH guidelines, and asserted that the extension of the initial 90-day suspension lacked proper justification. Brazil underscored that HPAI did not occur in commercial poultry, which should thus not change the country's recognition as HPAI-free. Highlighting recent progress in bilateral discussions where Thailand had confirmed the lifting of the suspension after the 90-day period, Brazil urged Thailand to formally notify the relevant authorities of the expiration of the temporary measures.

StatementSubmitted: Since the discharge of Advanced Liquid Processing System, or so-called ALPS, treated water started on 24 August 2023, the Government of Japan and Tokyo Electric Power Company Holdings, or otherwise called TEPCO, with the continued involvement of the IAEA, have been conducting monitoring of (i) concentration of radionuclides in ALPS treated water in tanks before discharge, (ii) tritium concentration after dilution, water flow rate, and gamma radiation level immediately before discharge, and (iii) concentration of tritium and other radionuclides in sea water, seabed sediments and fishery products after the discharge.ALPS treated water is sufficiently purified until the concentration of radionuclides other than tritium is below the regulatory standard[1] and it is diluted by seawater before being discharged. As for tritium, after the dilution, the concentration level will be less than 1,500 Bq/L, that is 1/7 of the WHO drinking water standard. The monitoring results also clearly show that the tritium concentration level at various monitoring points in the sea area is substantially lower than the operational standards. As part of Japan’s continued efforts to ensure transparency, all monitoring results are made available on the websites of the Government of Japan and TEPCO. They also demonstrate that the discharge has been conducted as planned and no anomalies have been detected to date. Japan is committed to taking appropriate measures, including suspension of the discharge, if any event occurs, such as detection of radionuclides exceeding the discharge suspension level, through the monitoring of the concentration levels. As for tritium, numerous nuclear facilities in operation around the world, including nuclear reactors in China, discharge more tritium on an annual basis than the tritium contained in ALPS treated water from Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station. For instance, the amount of tritium to be released annually from Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station is approximately1/10 (one-tenth) of the amount of tritium released from Qinshan Nuclear Power Plant in China. Nevertheless, since 24 August 2023, China; Hong Kong, China; Macao, China and the Russian Federation have taken further measures to restrict imports of Japanese fishery products and other products in response to Japan's discharge of ALPS treated water. China notified to suspend import of all aquatic products originating in Japan. Hong Kong, China notified an import prohibition of all aquatic products originating from 10 metropolis/prefectures (Fukushima, Miyagi, Ibaraki, Tochigi, Gunma, Saitama, Chiba, Tokyo, Nagano, and Niigata) in Japan. Macao, China notified an import suspension of a range of foodstuffs, including not only fishery products but other products such as fresh vegetables and fruit, dairy produce, meat, originating from the same ten metropolis/prefectures in Japan. And the Russian Federation introduced on 16 October 2023 a temporary restriction on imports of all aquatic products originating in Japan.The measures taken by China; Hong Kong, China; Macao, China and the Russian Federation are inconsistent with the SPS Agreement since they are not based on the scientific principles nor substantiated by scientific evidence that the agreement requires. These measures are completely unacceptable for Japan and we strongly urge these countries and regions to immediately repeal these measures.Japan submitted its comments to the notifications made by China; Hong Kong, China; Macao, China and Russian Federation requesting them to hold discussions with Japan in accordance with Annex B, paragraph 6 (c) of the SPS Agreement. Japan once again calls on China; Hong Kong, China; Macao, China and the Russian Federation to respond to the request of holding discussions with Japan immediately.[1] The regulatory standards are the standards that must be complied with under the Japanese law such as Act on the Regulation of Nuclear Source Material, Nuclear Fuel Material and Reactors. (Japan’s response to the statements from China; Hong Kong, China and Russian Federation)While we don’t intend to repeat the explanations which we have already don in the information sharing session, we would like to additionally provide the following comments briefly. Japan has been sharing information in detail on the safety of the discharge of the ALPS treated water, including the IAEA's comprehensive report, which concludes that the discharge of ALPS treated water is in accordance with the international safety standards. As a result, a wide range of countries and regions have expressed their understanding and support for the efforts of the Japan and IAEA. While it is true that the contaminated water that cooled the fuel rods in the accident reactor contains certain radioactive materials that are not contained in wastewater from ordinary nuclear power plants, ALPS can remove such radioactive materials to the below the regulatory standards. In the IAEA safety standards, the method for evaluating the safety of wastewater is the same for both accident reactors or not and the safety of Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station is also evaluated based on the international concepts. Japan will continue to take all possible measures to ensure the safety of the discharge into the sea in accordance with international law and international practice and will never allow any discharge that would adversely affect human health or environment of Japanese citizens or those of neighboring countries and regions. Even after the start of the discharge, Japan will continue to undergo IAEA reviews and will continue to disseminate information in a highly transparent manner, including promptly disseminating the information on sea area monitoring. ALPS technology has been approved by the NRA, which is an independent agency. Since 2019, it has functioned stably and sufficiently to purify the water. The effectiveness of ALPS has been confirmed through the analyses by the IAEA, third-country institutions and multiple third-party organizations. This shows that the effectiveness of the ALPS treatment and the safety of ALPS treated water have been repeatedly verified, and all results are disclosed to the public in a transparent manner.The assessment of radiological environmental impacts was carefully conducted in line with international standards and guidelines, taking into account ocean dispersion, the effect of bioaccumulation and long-term accumulation. Having considered these elements, TEPCO’s assessment concluded that the impact on humans and the environment would be negligible. The IAEA Comprehensive Report has likewise concluded that the radiological impact on humans and the environment will be negligible.In addition, China explained in its previous statement that its measure is with "precautionary" and "emergency" nature, which is a bit unclear and needs to be clarified in light of the framework of the SPS Agreement. Under the SPS Agreement, the "emergency" nature does not justify any SPS measures being imposed without scientific principles and risk assessment. Only an exception is that in the case of insufficiency of the relevant scientific evidence, a Member is allowed to conduct an provisional measure, under Article 5.7 of the SPS Agreement. However, it should not be the case here, since, as explained, Japanese government and TEPCO have disclosed the relevant information. China needs to clarify its position in this regard.In October, a dialogue between Japanese and Russian ministries and agencies was held, and, in response to the request form Russia, additional information has been provided to the Russian side.
Summary: Japan regretted that China; Hong Kong, China; Macao, China and the Russian Federation had taken measures to restrict imports of Japanese fishery products and other products in response to the discharge of ALPS treated water. With the involvement of the IAEA, Japan had been monitoring the concentration of radionuclides including tritium since the beginning of the discharge in August 2023. Japan insisted that ALPS treated water was sufficiently purified until the concentration of radionuclides other than tritium was below the regulatory standard and it was diluted by seawater before being discharged. As for tritium, after the dilution, the concentration level would be less than 1,500 Bq/L, that was 1/7 of the WHO drinking water standard. All monitoring results were publicly available and clearly showed that the tritium concentration level at various monitoring points in the sea area was substantially lower than the operational standards, and Japan was committed to taking the appropriate measures if radionuclides exceeding the discharge suspension level were detected. Arguing that the restrictions were not based on scientific principles nor substantiated by scientific evidence, and were thus inconsistent with the SPS Agreement, Japan urged China; Hong Kong, China; Macao, China and the Russian Federation to immediately repeal their restrictions. Japan had submitted comments to the corresponding notifications of the measures requesting them to hold discussions with Japan in accordance with paragraph 6c of Annex B of the SPS Agreement, and called on those Members to respond to the request of holding bilateral discussions.Regarding the discharged ALPS treated water into the sea, Japan noted it would not repeat the explanations which had already been provided in the previous agenda item and yet added that it had provided explanations on its efforts to ensure safety, including the conclusions of the IAEA's comprehensive report that the discharge was consistent with relevant international standards. As a result of Japan's outreach activities to ensure transparency, a wide range of countries and regions had expressed their support for the efforts undertaken. Japan insisted that ALPS could remove such radionuclides which the accident reactor contained to levels below the regulatory standards, that in the IAEA safety standards, the method for evaluating the safety of wastewater was the same for both accident reactors or not, and that the safety of Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station was also evaluated based on the international concepts. Japan sought further clarification on the emergency precautionary character of China's measures, since it believed that sufficient scientific evidence had been provided on the matter and, as such, Article 5.7 of the SPS Agreement was not relevant. Japan further clarified that it had provided the Russian Federation with the additional information it had requested in their bilateral dialogue.

StatementSubmitted: Water containing radioactive materials is stored and managed after the accident in 2011 at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station of the Tokyo Electric Power Company, or otherwise called TEPCO. Advanced Liquid Processing System, or so-called ALPS, treated water is water sufficiently purified until the concentration of radioactive materials other than tritium is below the regulatory standard based on international safety standards. It is, then, diluted by seawater before being discharged. As for tritium, after the dilution, the concentration will be less than 1/40 (one-fortieth) of the regulatory standard, or 1/7 (one-seventh) of the WHO standards for drinking water.By way of comparison, the amount of tritium to be released annually from Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station is approximately 1/9 (one-ninth) of the amount of tritium released from Qinshan Nuclear Power Plant in China.The impacts on human health resulting from the discharge of ALPS treated water into the sea were evaluated based on an internationally validated methodology. The evaluation results confirmed that the impacts are minimal, with the ratio ranging from 1/1,000,000 (one-millionth) to 1/70,000 (one-seventy thousandth) of the impacts from natural radiation that we receive every day. This means that there is no problem with respect to the safety of fish caught in the nearby waters.Japan would like to reemphasize that after two years of rigorous review, the International Atomic Energy Agency, IAEA concluded in its Comprehensive Report of July 2023 that the discharge of ALPS treated water into the sea is consistent with relevant international safety standards, and that the discharge will have a negligible radiological impact on people and the environment. The Report determined that radioactivity concentrations in international waters will not be influenced by the discharge of ALPS treated water into the sea and the transboundary impacts are therefore negligible.Since the discharge of ALPS treated water began in August last year, the discharge has been carried out safely as planned, in full compliance with international standards. Multi-layered monitoring activities by Japan with the involvement of the IAEA have found no anomalies. The level of radioactive nuclides, including tritium, in the discharged water have been far below the regulatory standards. The results of all these monitoring activities have been made available to the public. Additionally, in October last year, the IAEA Task Force, comprised of the IAEA and international experts from various countries including China and Russia, visited Fukushima to conduct its first review mission after the discharge of the ALPS treated water into the sea. In January this year, IAEA report summarizing its review was published. The report concluded that the Task Force did not identify anything that is inconsistent with the requirements in the relevant international safety standards, and that the IAEA can reaffirm the fundamental conclusions of its safety review as outlined in the Comprehensive Report.Nevertheless, since 24 August 2023, China; Hong Kong, China; Macao, China, and since 16 October 2023, the Russian Federation have adopted and still maintain additional measures to restrict imports of Japanese fishery products and other products in response to Japan's discharge of ALPS treated water. In this regard, the measures taken by China; Hong Kong, China; Macao, China and the Russian Federation are not based on the scientific principles nor substantiated by the scientific evidence that the SPS Agreement requires, and are completely unacceptable. Japan strongly urges these countries and regions to immediately repeal these measures.Some of those Members claimed that Japan had forced the discharge into the sea without adequate explanation to the countries concerned. However, the Government of Japan has provided explanation regarding the safety of discharging ALPS treated water into the sea on numerous occasions. Japan's efforts to ensure safety have been explained at international conferences and bilateral meetings in a sincere manner, including on the conclusions of the IAEA Comprehensive Report that the discharge of ALPS treated water into the sea is consistent with relevant international safety standards.Japan has submitted its comments to China; Hong Kong, China; Macao, China and the Russian Federation, and requesting to hold discussions in accordance with Annex B6(c) of the SPS Agreement, but no substantial bilateral discussion has been held yet. Japan continues to call on China; Hong Kong, China; Macao, China and the Russian Federation to hold the discussions with Japan without further delay. (Japan’s response to the statements from China; Hong Kong, China and Russian Federation)Regarding comments from some countries, we would like to provide additional our comments briefly. The water being discharged is not "nuclear contaminated water". It will be discharged after sufficient purification and dilution and will have no impact on humans or the environment.Japan has been addressing in good faith China’s and some other countries’ and regions’ concerns expressed in various forms at various levels on various occasions, including the three joint questionnaires China and Russia sent to Japan so far. Therefore, China's claim that Japan forced the discharge of ALPS treated water without sufficient explanation is not true.While it is true that the contaminated water that cooled the fuel rods in the accident reactor contains cesium, strontium, and other radioactive materials that are not contained in wastewater from ordinary nuclear power plants (but are contained in wastewater from reprocessing plants), ALPS can remove radioactive materials other than tritium, removed to below the regulatory standards.In the IAEA safety standards, which were developed through consultation with all IAEA Member States, the method for evaluating the safety of wastewater is the same for both accident reactors or not and the safety of the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station is also evaluated based on the international concepts.The ALPS treated water has been discharged into the sea with the involvement of the IAEA, in accordance with international standards and practices, and taking all possible safety measures in place. The IAEA has been providing monitoring data in addition to the presence of IAEA officials at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station since the start of the ocean discharge. With the IAEA's involvement, Japan will continue to disseminate the data that can be used by the international community. The IAEA will also continue to review Japan's monitoring activities.Under the framework of the IAEA review, the IAEA and several third-country analytical and research institutes selected by the IAEA have conducted interlaboratory comparison regarding monitoring of ALPS treated water.Japan would like to make it clear that the incident mentioned by China is not related to the discharge of the ALPS treated water. The issue of October last year was an incident in which cleaning water splashed onto workers during the cleaning of pipes used to transfer contaminated water undergoing purification treatment at ALPS, which was stopped for routine inspection. The incident of October last year was not a leak of contaminated water during the ALPS treatment process, nor was it directly related to the purification function of ALPS.The ALPS treated water discharge facility into the sea has equipment and multi-layered systems to prevent human error. In addition, there is a mechanism in place for third-parties including the IAEA to thoroughly check the safety of the water to be discharged after ALPS treatment.We are further supplementing some comments on the interventions by China, Hongkong, Russia. First, China mentioned that Japan’s decision to discharge the treated water to the sea “unilaterally”, and Hongkong described that Japan “persisted in” the discharge. Japan strongly disagree with those descriptions. Japan has been sharing information on the safety of ALPS treated water with the international community including China and Russia, in a transparent manner.  And Japan has provided individual briefing sessions to countries and regions which have expressed particularly keen interest.  As a result, a wide range of countries and regions, have expressed their understanding and support for efforts of Japan and the IAEA. These factual circumstances cannot be described as “unilateral” decisions. Second, China mentioned that its measures are “emergency” and “preventive” measure, but this reference reminds us that the nature of these relevant measures under the SPS Agreement has remained unclear. In particular, we wonder if these measures are “provisional” measures pursuant to Article 5.7 of the SPS Agreement. If these are provisional measures, then the imposing countries have to conduct periodic review to analyze the collected information. Japan awaits the opportunity of such periodic review, where it can be confirmed there is much information disclosed by Japanese government and TEPCO with respect to the safety of ALPS treated water and Japan’s compliance with the international standards. It can be confirmed that the prerequisite of the provisional measures – “scientific evidence is insufficient” cannot be met in this matter. On the other hand, if the measures are not provisional, then they must be based on the risk assessment and scientific principle, which Japan believes is lacking in this case. The measure should be then repealed immediately. Third, Hongkong colleagues mentioned that the discharge is “unprecedented”. It is true that the Great East Japan Earthquake was unprecedented, but as my colleague clarified, the practice and safety standard of discharging water is the same with respect to either accident reactors or normal reactors. Therefore, the “unprecedented” nature of the factual background cannot justify the discriminatory measures against products from Japan. Lastly, about the response by Russia, currently, Japan is sincerely preparing to respond to the Russian request for additional questions on this matter. Japan expects a sincere response from the Russian Federation to Japan’s request as well.
Summary: Japan provided a comprehensive overview of the management and discharge of water containing radioactive materials from the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station, overseen by Tokyo Electric Power Company (TEPCO) since the 2011 accident. Japan reminded Members that Advanced Liquid Processing System (ALPS) treated water was sufficiently purified until the concentration of radionuclides other than tritium was below the regulatory standard and was diluted by seawater before being discharged. As for tritium, after the dilution, the concentration level would be less than 1/40 of the regulatory standard, which was 1/7 of the WHO drinking water standard. Japan insisted that the impacts on human health resulting from the discharge of ALPS treated water into the sea were evaluated based on an internationally validated methodology, which confirmed that the impacts were minimal and, therefore, did not represent a problem with respect to the safety of fish caught in the nearby waters. Japan reemphasized that the IAEA Comprehensive Report, published in January 2024, had concluded that the discharge of ALPS treated water into the sea was consistent with relevant international safety standards and that the discharge would have a negligible radiological impact on people and the environment.Since August 2023, the discharge had been carried out safely as planned, in compliance with international standards, and no anomalies had been found in the multi-layered monitoring activities, whose results had been made available to the public. Nonetheless, China; Hong Kong, China; Macao, China and the Russian Federation had adopted and maintained additional measures to restrict imports of Japanese fishery products and other products. Japan believed that these measures were not based on scientific principles nor substantiated by scientific evidence and urged these Members to repeal the measures. Japan underscored its transparent approach towards water discharge bilaterally and at international conferences. Japan called on Members to respond to the call for bilateral discussions in accordance with Annex B of the SPS Agreement.In response, Japan reiterated that the ALPS treated water was not nuclear-contaminated since it was discharged after sufficient purification and dilution, and there were thus no potential risks to human health and the environment. Japan underscored that all safety measures were aligned with regulatory standards established through consultations among IAEA member states, adhering to global norms and practices. Japan further noted that, due its transparent outreach activities, a wide range of countries and regions had expressed their support for the efforts undertaken. Addressing China's concerns, Japan clarified that the incident cited was unrelated to the ALPS water plant. Japan sought further clarification on the emergency provisional measures adopted by China, as it believed Article 5.7 of the SPS Agreement was not relevant since sufficient scientific evidence had been provided. Japan also indicated readiness to furnish additional information concerning queries raised by the Russian Federation.

StatementSubmitted: With regard to Japan’s discharge of water treated by the Advanced Liquid Processing System, or so-called ALPS treated water, the International Atomic Energy Agency concluded in its Comprehensive Report of July 2023 that the discharge of ALPS treated water into the sea is consistent with relevant international safety standards, and that the discharge will have a negligible radiological impact on people and the environment. The Report determined that radioactivity concentrations in international waters will not be influenced by the discharge of ALPS treated water into the sea and the transboundary impacts are therefore negligible. The Government of Japan has explained the safety of discharging ALPS treated water into the sea on numerous occasions.Since the discharge of ALPS treated water began in August last year, multi-layered monitoring activities by Japan with the involvement of the IAEA have found no anomalies. The level of radioactive nuclides, including tritium, in the discharged water have been far below the regulatory standards. Additionally, from October 24th to 27th last year, the IAEA Task Force, comprised of the IAEA and international experts from various countries, visited Fukushima to continue its review mission, the first such mission after the start of the discharge in August last year. The IAEA report summarizing its review concluded that the Task Force did not identify anything inconsistent with the requirements in the relevant international safety standards, and that the IAEA can reaffirm the fundamental conclusions of its safety review as outlined in the Comprehensive Report. Additionally, in April, the IAEA Task Force conducted the second review mission and confirmed that the discharge of ALPS treated water is progressing in accordance with the implementation plan.Nevertheless, China; Hong Kong, China; Macao, China, and the Russian Federation have adopted and still maintain additional measures restricting imports of Japanese fishery and other products in response to Japan's discharge of ALPS treated water. Those measures are not based on the scientific principles nor substantiated by the scientific evidence that the SPS Agreement requires, and are completely unacceptable. Japan strongly urges those countries and regions to immediately repeal those measures.Japan has submitted its comments to those Members and requested to hold discussions in accordance with Annex B6(c) of the SPS Agreement. However, no substantial bilateral discussion has been held yet. Japan continues to call on them to hold the discussions with Japan without further delay. (Japan’s response to the statements from China; Hong Kong, China and Russian Federation)Japan will respond to the comments raised by some members countries. Japan reiterate that the water being discharged is not "nuclear contaminated water". It will be discharged after sufficient purification and dilution and will have no impact on humans or the environment. The IAEA's comprehensive report concludes that the discharge of ALPS treated water will have negligible radiological impacts on humans and the environment.Japan strongly disagrees with the expression that Japan's decision to discharge the ALPS treated water was "unilateral" or Japan takes "irresponsible" behavior, which are clearly against the fact. Japan has been sharing information on the safety of ALPS treated water with the international community including in a transparent manner. And Japan has provided individual briefing sessions to countries and regions which have expressed particularly keen interest. As a result, a wide range of countries and regions, have expressed their understanding and support for efforts of Japan and the IAEA. Japan is prepared to continue to provide explanations and information sharing in good faith and with a highly transparent manner so as to dispel concerns.While it is true that the contaminated water that cooled the fuel rods in the accident reactor contains cesium, strontium, and other radioactive materials that are not contained in wastewater from ordinary nuclear power plants, ALPS can remove radioactive materials other than tritium, removed to below the regulatory standards. In the IAEA safety standards, which were developed through consultation with all IAEA Member States, the method for evaluating the safety of wastewater is the same for both accident reactors or not and the safety of the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station is also evaluated based on the international concepts.The ALPS treated water has been discharged into the sea with the involvement of the IAEA, in accordance with international standards and practices, and taking all possible safety measures in place. The IAEA has been providing real-time monitoring data in addition to the presence of IAEA officials at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station since the start of the ocean discharge. With the IAEA's involvement, Japan will continue to disseminate the data that can be used by the international community. The IAEA will also continue to review Japan's monitoring activities. Under the framework of the IAEA review, the IAEA and several third-country analytical and research institutes selected by the IAEA have conducted interlaboratory comparison regarding monitoring of ALPS treated water.Japan would like to make it clear that the incidents stated by Hong Kong are not related to the discharge of the ALPS treated water. The ALPS treated water discharge facility into the sea has equipment and multi-layered systems to prevent human error. In addition, there is a mechanism in place for third-parties including the IAEA to thoroughly check the safety of the water to be discharged after ALPS treatment.As for comments by Russian Federation, Japan explained about the safety of Japanese aquatic products based on scientific evidence in the online dialogue with the Russian Federation on October last year, in response to the request by Russia. Japan also provided additional materials by October 15. Since then, Japan has been providing relevant materials based on the request from Russia. Most recently, this month June, Japan also responded to inquiries from Russian in February. Therefore, the Russian Federation's point that about Japan not providing sufficient information is completely incorrect. Japan believes that it has provided sufficient relevant information to demonstrate that the safety of Japanese marine products has been proven.
Summary: In raising this concern, Japan reiterated that, as per the IAEA, the discharge of ALPS treated water into the sea was consistent with relevant international safety standards and the discharge would have a negligible radiological impact on people and the environment. Japan insisted that the IAEA had concluded that radioactivity concentrations in international waters would not be influenced by the discharge of ALPS treated water into the sea. Since August 2023, when the discharge of ALPS treated water had begun, no anomalies had been found in the multi-layered monitoring activities conducted by Japan with the involvement of the IAEA. The level of radionuclides, including tritium, had been far below the regulatory standards. China; Hong Kong, China; Macao, China; and the Russian Federation nonetheless maintained measures to restrict imports of Japanese fishery products and other products. Considered that these measures were not based on science, Japan urged them to repeal the measures and respond to the call for bilateral discussions in light of Annex B of the SPS Agreement.Japan responded that the ALPS treated water was not nuclear-contaminated and there were no potential risks to human health and the environment. Japan added that, due its transparent outreach activities, a wide range of countries and regions had expressed their support for the efforts undertaken. While, as Japan agreed, contaminated water that cooled the fuel rods in the accident reactor contained cesium, strontium, and other radioactive materials that were not contained in wastewater from ordinary nuclear power plants, ALPS could remove radioactive materials other than tritium to below the regulatory standards.

StatementSubmitted: La delegación de México presenta esta preocupación comercial específica debido a la demora en las gestiones que se llevan a cabo ante el Departamento de Salud Animal del Ministerio de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural de Vietnam (MARD), con relación al establecimiento de requisitos sanitarios para importar a Vietnam carne de bovino de origen mexicano.  En el transcurso de diciembre de 2015 a agosto de 2022, el Servicio Nacional de Sanidad, Inocuidad y Calidad Agroalimentaria (SENASICA) ha intercambiado información técnica solicitada por el MARD en nueve ocasiones, sin que exista avance en la gestión para el establecimiento de requisitos sanitarios para importar a Vietnam este producto mexicano.  En octubre y diciembre de 2022, México solicitó a las autoridades vietnamitas el resultado del análisis de riesgo de este producto, con la finalidad de avanzar en la programación de la visita de inspección in situ a los establecimientos TIF interesados en exportar al mercado vietnamita. En febrero de 2023, el MARD confirmó la recepción de la información enviada por el SENASICA en agosto de 2022 y solicitaron nuevamente información técnica adicional, misma que fue remitida por el SENASICA en marzo de 2023, siendo esta ocasión, la 10ª en la que México envía información técnica requerida por Vietnam. En mayo y julio de 2023, se solicitó nuevamente a las autoridades vietnamitas el resultado del análisis de riesgo del análisis de la información remitida en marzo de 2023. En agosto de 2023, las autoridades vietnamitas confirmaron la recepción de la información remitida por el SENASICA en marzo de 2023 y solicitaron nuevamente información técnica adicional. En el mismo mes, se solicitó llevar a cabo una reunión virtual con las autoridades vietnamitas, para conocer cuál es el motivo del excesivo retraso de esta gestión. La delegación de México desea hacer referencia a los derechos y obligaciones de los Miembros bajo el Acuerdo MSF, particularmente a el Anexo C, en su artículo 8, párrafos 1a) y 1c) donde se establece que los procedimientos para verificar el cumplimiento de una medida sanitaria se deben iniciar y ultimar sin demoras indebidas y sin exigir más información de la necesaria a efectos de los procedimientos de control, inspección y aprobación apropiados. En virtud de que México ha proporcionado la información requerida, se solicita a Vietnam el estatus del análisis de riesgo, así como avanzar con la programación de la visita de inspección para continuar con la gestión de la apertura de mercado de este producto La delegación de México agradece a la delegación de Vietnam por la atención a esta declaración y reitera su disposición de mantener una comunicación abierta y cordial entre autoridades.
Summary: Mexico raised its concern regarding lack of progress on the establishment of sanitary requirements for the authorization of its beef imports into Viet Nam. Mexico had provided all the information requested by Viet Nam's Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (MARD), and had requested the results of the risk analysis with a view to organizing in situ inspections to the Federal Inspection Type establishments wishing to export to Viet Nam. Stating that these delays were a violation of Article 8 and Annex C of the SPS Agreement, Mexico asked Viet Nam to provide information on the status of the risk analysis and to move forward in programming the in situ inspections. Mexico reiterated its willingness to maintain the open bilateral communication to progress towards the opening of the market for beef.

StatementSubmitted: ? A new measure has been implemented in Qatar, imposing new obligations for all processed food products exported from Korea and the Philippines to attach Certificates of Conformity (CoC) per every shipment.? The Korean government and the exporters need to be aware of the necessity of this measure and be given the opportunity to provide opinions in prior to the implementation, but it is regrettable that the process has not been carried out formally and transparently.? Moreover, due to the new obligations imposed by Qatar, Korean exporters are spending a great amount of time and money for the issuance of CoC upon every shipment, and there are concerns that this may consequently become a trade barrier.? On February 21, 2024, the Korean government officially requested the Qatari government for a bilateral consultation to discuss on this matter. We wish to have a constructive discussion as soon as possible to come up with reasonable solutions.
Summary: Korea raised concerns on the new obligations imposed by Qatar to attach certificates of conformity to every shipment of processed food products exported from Korea and the Philippines. Korea regretted the lack of transparency and of an opportunity to provide comments prior to the implementation of the measure, which increased costs for Korean exporters and could become a trade barrier. Following the request for bilateral consultations, Korea expressed its willingness to hold constructive discussions to reach a reasonable solution.

StatementSubmitted: El Ecuador presenta ante los Miembros de la OMC su preocupación comercial con relación a las demoras de publicación de requisitos aplicadas por México en la reapertura del acceso de camarón congelado crudo procedentes de Ecuador.En el 2014 México, con la intención de proteger la industria camaronera nacional en contra la introducción de enfermedades no existentes ordenó la suspensión temporal de importaciones de camarón procedentes de algunos países.México, mediante Oficio B00.02.04.0392-2015 2563 del 14 de abril de 2015, suspendió las autorizaciones de importación del Ecuador por detectar enfermedades declaradas en el 2012 como exóticas.En la revisión documental enviada a mediante MAGAP-INP-2015-0676-OF, de 16 junio de 2015, el Ecuador informa que es nula la presencia de las enfermedades señaladas por la autoridad sanitaria mexicana:  virus del Taura (TSV), virus de la Cabeza amarilla (YHV) y mionecrosis infecciosa (IMNV), solicitando se revea la medida aplicada a las importaciones ecuatorianas.Dentro del proceso para retomar la habilitación del camarón en julio de 2015, las Partes acordaron también evaluar la equivalencia entre Servicio Nacional de Sanidad, Inocuidad y Calidad (SENASICA) y el Instituto Nacional de Pesca (INP) para lo cual, en noviembre de 2015, realizaron visitas técnicas para evaluar el cumplimiento de las medidas sanitarias correspondientes.El Ecuador en el 2016 remitió el plan epidemiológico y cronograma a ejecutarse conforme a los compromisos adquiridos. Y, posteriormente en el 2017 se envió el programa de vigilancia epidemiológica y sanidad acuícola en el Ecuador, cronograma del plan de sanidad animal y esquema del plan de sanidad animal.En febrero de 2018, el SENASICA indicó que requería de evidencia documental para solventar las no conformidades, lo cual permitiría programar una visita de constatación del estatus en sanidad acuícola. El Ecuador remitió los documentos y se planificó la visita.El 5 marzo de 2019, mediante OFICIO B00.02.04.0156/2019 1403, SENASICA remitió el informe de auditoría realizada en noviembre de 2018, concluyendo que, “no se encontró evidencia de la circulación de YHV y IMNV y se verificó la solventación y las acciones correctivas”. También se comprobó la implementación del programa oficial de vigilancia epidemiológica activa y pasiva, mediante muestreos presentando resultados negativos para YHV y IMNV, puesto que se llevan a cabo acciones de prevención, vigilancia, diagnóstico, bioseguridad, trazabilidad, BPA, BPM y HACCP.En mayo de 2019, mediante Oficio B00.02.04.0423 3554 SENASICA remitió la propuesta de hoja de requisitos de sanidad acuícola para la importación de camarón congelado proveniente de Ecuador. Posteriormente, se realizaron intercambios de información y observaciones a las consultas del formato del certificado sanitario en donde se incluyeron los atestados requeridos por SENASICA.El 13 de febrero de 2020, mediante Oficio Nro. MPCEIP-SN-2020-0184-O, Ecuador emitió su conformidad con la hoja de requisitos propuestos por México mediante Oficio B00.02.04.-0037.-0107-2020, e insiste en el interés de la apertura del mercado mediante la publicación de los requisitos ante la OMC para observaciones y comentarios de los Miembros, así como, en el Módulo del SENASICA. Así mismo, se solicitó el reconocimiento de la equivalencia de ambos sistemas sanitarios de control.México no ha emitido respuesta a las solicitudes del Ecuador mediante Oficio Nro. MPCEIP-SCI-2023-0010-EQ, de 26 de abril de 2024, y Oficio Nro. MPCEIP-SN-2020-0498-O, de 15 de junio de 2020, respecto a la publicación de requisitos y, por el contrario, ha solicitado información adicional, posterior al establecimiento de requisitos, los cuáles siempre fueron atendidos.El 16 de agosto 2023, mediante Oficio B00.02.04.1753, México, solicitó a Ecuador completar un cuestionario para conocer la situación sanitaria del Síndrome de Taura y un cuestionario para la actualización de la situación sanitaria de los establecimientos exportadores de crustáceos, sin embargo, esta información ya fue atendida por el Ecuador en la etapa de establecimiento de requisitos la cual concluyó en el 2020. A pesar de ello, se atendió el requerimiento en noviembre 2023, mediante Oficio Nro. MPCEIP-SCI-2023-0296-O.El Ecuador ha respondido las consultas planteadas en noviembre de 2023. Sin embargo, en febrero de 2024, nuevamente, México ha solicitado información complementaria.De conformidad en la normativa mexicana referente al “Acuerdo por el que se establece el módulo de requisitos en materia de sanidad para la importación de especies acuáticas, sus productos y subproductos, así como de los productos biológicos, químicos, farmacéuticos o alimenticios para el uso o consumo de dichas especies” publicado en el Diario Oficial de la Federación de México el 25 de mayo de 2012, en el que se expresa en su art. 9 “Una vez emitido el resultado del análisis de riesgo, el SENASICA dentro de los noventa días naturales posteriores, procederá a emitir, vía el Módulo, la resolución correspondiente (…)”Ante lo expuesto, el Ecuador solicita a México dar cumplimiento a los compromisos asumidos de conformidad con las disposiciones del artículo 2.3 del AMSF en el cual se especifica que, “Los Miembros se asegurarán de que sus medidas sanitarias y fitosanitarias no discriminen de manera arbitraria o injustificable entre Miembros en que prevalezcan condiciones idénticas o similares, ni entre su propio territorio y el de otros Miembros. Las medidas sanitarias y fitosanitarias no se aplicarán de manera que constituyan una restricción encubierta del comercio internacional”.El Ecuador hace referencia al artículo 5.6 del Acuerdo MSF “Sin perjuicio de lo dispuesto en el párrafo 2 del artículo 3, cuando se establezcan o mantengan medidas sanitarias o fitosanitarias para lograr el nivel adecuado de protección sanitaria o fitosanitaria, los Miembros se asegurarán de que tales medidas no entrañen un grado de restricción del comercio mayor del requerido para lograr su nivel adecuado de protección sanitaria o fitosanitaria, teniendo en cuenta su viabilidad técnica y económica”, por lo que, Ecuador considera que la negociación de requisitos lleva alrededor de 9 años, siendo la información adicional requerida por México posterior al establecimiento de requisitos estaría restringiendo el comercio más de lo necesario sin justificación técnica - científica.Se evidencia el incumplimiento del artículo 8 y el Anexo C del Acuerdo MSF que indica “Con respecto a todos los procedimientos para verificar y asegurar el cumplimiento de las medidas sanitarias y fitosanitarias, los Miembros se asegurarán: de que esos procedimientos se inicien y ultimen sin demoras indebidas y de manera que no sea menos favorable para los productos importados que para los productos nacionales similares (…)” a pesar que, el Ecuador ha remitido y aceptado la información y requisitos, respectivamente, solicitados por México, todavía no se finaliza el proceso de reapertura del camarón.En este sentido, el Ecuador insta a México que, a pesar de haber cumplido con todas las exigencias solicitadas para el cumplimiento de sus requisitos sanitarios para lograr reestablecer el acceso, estas restricciones continúan en vigencia sin una justificación técnica y contraviniendo el Acuerdo MSF.Ante lo expuesto, el Ecuador solicita la pronta publicación de requisitos tanto en la OMC como en el Módulo del SENASICA para la reapertura del mercado a las exportaciones ecuatorianas de camarón congelado.
Summary: Referring to its complete statement in eAgenda, Ecuador raised its concern about the undue delays in the publication of Mexico's requirements for reopening the market for raw frozen shrimp. Following the temporary suspension of imports in 2014, Ecuador had provided information on the Taura virus, the yellow head virus, and the infectious myonecrosis virus and had requested a review of the import restrictions. After the submission of epidemiological planning and surveillance programmes, as well as the technical visits undertaken, Mexico had proposed sanitary requirements for frozen shrimp. Ecuador had accepted the requirements and had requested that Mexico publish them and recognize the equivalence of their sanitary systems. Ecuador noted the lack of response and stated that there was no technical or scientific justification for the delay in publishing the requirements. Ecuador urged Mexico to comply with its obligations under the SPS Agreement and publish the requirements to facilitate the reopening of the market.

StatementSubmitted: Gracias, señora presidenta:Ecuador ha planteado nuevamente esta PCE, que atañe a la demora de publicación de los requisitos aplicados por México para la reapertura del acceso de camarón congelado crudo, procedente del Ecuador. Esta situación continúa sin ser resuelta desde nueve años atrás, como recordarán los miembros del Comité. Me permito hacer a continuación un recuento de los factores que motivan esta PCE y que se han sucedido a través de un lapso extremadamente largo.En 2014, México, con el propósito de proteger la industria camaronera nacional en contra de la introducción de enfermedades no existentes en ese país, ordenó la suspensión temporal de importaciones de camarón procedentes de varios países. Mediante Oficio Nro. B00.02.04.0392-2015 2563 de 14 de abril de 2015, México suspendió las autorizaciones de importación del Ecuador por supuestamente haber detectado enfermedades que, en 2012, habían sido declaradas como exóticas.Frente a la decisión, con la sustentación documental enviada a México en junio de 2015, el Ecuador aseguró que las enfermedades referidas por la autoridad sanitaria mexicana no existían en el Ecuador. Entre esas enfermedades estaban el virus del Taura (TSV), el virus de la Cabeza amarilla (YHV) y la mionecrosis infecciosa (IMNV). En tal virtud, Ecuador solicitó a México que se revise la medida aplicada a las importaciones ecuatorianas, para lo cual remitió toda la información requerida por México necesaria para la habilitación de camarón congelado ecuatoriano, siguiendo el debido proceso.Casi cuatro años más tarde, en marzo de 2019, SENASICA, la autoridad técnica mexicana, remitió al Ecuador el informe de auditoría realizado en noviembre de 2018, el cual, concluye que, “no se encontró evidencia de la circulación del virus de la Cabeza amarilla y la mionecrosis infecciosa y se verificó la solventación y las acciones correctivas”. SENASICA también comprobó la implementación del programa oficial ecuatoriano de vigilancia epidemiológica activa y pasiva, mediante muestreos que ofrecieron resultados negativos para estas enfermedades, a la par que se llevaban a cabo acciones de prevención, vigilancia, diagnóstico, bioseguridad, trazabilidad, BPA, BPM y HACCP.Como seguimiento del informe, en mayo de 2019, mediante Oficio Nro. B00.02.04.0423.3554 SENASICA remitió la propuesta de hoja de requisitos de sanidad acuícola para la importación de camarón congelado proveniente de Ecuador y, con la contraparte ecuatoriana, se llevó a cabo un intercambio de información requerido por SENASICA. El 13 de febrero de 2020, mediante Oficio Nro. MPCEIP-SN-2020-0184-O, Ecuador aceptó los requisitos propuestos previamente por México mediante Oficio B00.02.04.-0037.-0107-2020 y, por cuanto todo estaba en orden, insistió en su pedido de la apertura del mercado mediante la publicación oficial de los requisitos. Sin embargo, los requisitos no fueron publicados.Desde febrero de 2020, México no ha respondido a los requerimientos del Ecuador respecto a la publicación de dichos requisitos y, por el contrario, ha solicitado información adicional. Ecuador ha atendido incluso la provisión de esa información adicional que le fue demandada.No solo eso, el 16 de agosto de 2023, mediante Oficio Nro. B00.02.04.1753, México solicitó nuevamente a Ecuador completar los cuestionarios sobre la situación sanitaria del Síndrome de Taura y la actualización de la situación sanitaria de los establecimientos exportadores de crustáceos. El requerimiento llamó particularmente la atención pues esa información ya fue proporcionada por Ecuador en la etapa de establecimiento de requisitos que, como he reseñado previamente, concluyó en febrero de 2020 con la entrega de toda la documentación pertinente y con la indicación de SENASICA de que todo estaba en orden, faltando solamente la publicación oficial.Seis meses más tarde, el 22 de febrero de 2024, mediante Oficio Nro. B00.02.04.320.967.2024, México solicitó adicionalmente al Ecuador completar la documentación sobre los establecimientos y las fincas proveedoras de materia prima, con referencia a los cuestionarios solicitados en agosto 2023.En una nueva demostración de su espíritu de colaboración y cooperación, el 3 de junio de 2024, mediante Oficio Nro. MPCEIP-SCI-2024-0139-O, Ecuador respondió en debida forma a SENASICA, proveyéndole con la información demandada sobre las fincas proveedoras de materia prima.Señora presidenta:El marco legal aplicable a esta situación es claro y su incumplimiento motiva esta PCE del Ecuador. El artículo 2.3 del Acuerdo MSF que señala que “Los Miembros se asegurarán de que sus medidas sanitarias y fitosanitarias no discriminen de manera arbitraria o injustificable entre Miembros en que prevalezcan condiciones idénticas o similares, ni entre su propio territorio y el de otros Miembros. Las medidas sanitarias y fitosanitarias no se aplicarán de manera que constituyan una restricción encubierta del comercio internacional”. La producción de camarones del Ecuador goza de gran prestigio y aceptación en un gran número de exigentes mercados miembros de esta Organización. La calidad y el cumplimiento de las normas fitosanitarias, con respeto a estándares internacionales, es una de las características del camarón ecuatoriano. Entendemos y respetamos la autonomía de cada miembro en la gestión de sus MSF, pero resulta evidente que las objeciones de un miembro no tienen eco en la abrumadora mayoría de importadores de la producción camaronera ecuatoriana.El artículo 5.6 del Acuerdo MSF, que señala que “Sin perjuicio de lo dispuesto en el párrafo 2 del artículo 3, cuando se establezcan o mantengan medidas sanitarias o fitosanitarias para lograr el nivel adecuado de protección sanitaria o fitosanitaria, los Miembros se asegurarán de que tales medidas no entrañen un grado de restricción del comercio mayor del requerido para lograr su nivel adecuado de protección sanitaria o fitosanitaria, teniendo en cuenta su viabilidad técnica y económica”.Señora presidenta y señores delegados:Ustedes concordarán en que resulta inexplicable que una publicación de requisitos lleve nueve años, habiendo una de las partes, en este caso el Ecuador, provisto toda la información adicional requerida por México, incluso datos demandados con posterioridad al establecimiento de requisitos, en 2019.Esta situación evidencia el incumplimiento del artículo 8 y del Anexo C del Acuerdo MSF, que con claridad disponen: “Con respecto a todos los procedimientos para verificar y asegurar el cumplimiento de las medidas sanitarias y fitosanitarias, los Miembros se asegurarán: de que esos procedimientos se inicien y ultimen sin demoras indebidas y de manera que no sea menos favorable para los productos importados que para los productos nacionales similares (…)”. A pesar de que el Ecuador ha remitido y aceptado la información y requisitos solicitados por México, todavía no finaliza el proceso de reapertura del mercado de ese país al camarón proveniente del Ecuador, con lo que en la práctica se ha restringido el comercio en contravención al Acuerdo MSF.Sobre la base normativa del Acuerdo MSF  que he referido y a la luz de la documentación e información transmitida con diligencia y oportunidad a la contraparte mexicana, Ecuador reitera su pedido a México de que se sirva proceder a la publicación oficial inmediata de requisitos técnicos en el Módulo del SENASICA, habilitando así la reapertura del mercado a las exportaciones ecuatorianas de camarón congelado con estricto apego a los mandatos del Acuerdo MSF y otras normas de la OMC aplicables al caso.Muchas gracias.
Summary: Ecuador reiterated its concern about delays in the publication of Mexico's requirements for the reopening of its market for frozen shrimp, an issue that had been ongoing for nine years. Ecuador recalled that, following the temporary suspension of shrimp imports in 2015 due to the alleged detection of diseases, Ecuador had provided information that these diseases, namely, the taura syndrome virus, the yellow head virus, and the infectious myonecrosis virus, were not present in Ecuador. A 2018 audit had confirmed the absence of the yellow head and infectious myonecrosis viruses and that corrective actions would be undertaken. Mexico had, in 2019, proposed sanitary requirements for frozen shrimp, which Ecuador had accepted. Ecuador had requested that Mexico publish these import requirements and recognize the equivalence of their sanitary systems. Ecuador regretted that Mexico had not responded to this request and had requested additional questionnaire responses. Referring to Articles 2.3, 5.3, and 8 of the SPS Agreement and its Annex C, Ecuador urged Mexico to comply with the SPS Agreement and publish the requirements to enable the reopening of the market.

Peru raised its concern about the undue delays in the procedure to authorize plants to export dairy products to Bolivia. Peru regretted the lack of response to the information submitted in February 2022 seeking to start cream cheese exports and requested that Bolivia provide an update on its request.

StatementSubmitted: El Perú desea presentar ante los Miembros de la OMC su preocupación comercial específica con relación a las demoras indebidas en el procedimiento de autorización de establecimientos peruanos interesados en exportar productos lácteos a Bolivia. Sobre el particular, el Perú lamenta que, a la fecha, no se ha recibido respuesta a la solicitud formal de información presentada en febrero de 2022 con la finalidad de iniciar las gestiones para exportar queso crema al mercado boliviano. Al respecto, el Perú desea precisar que, la solicitud es que Bolivia pueda facilitar la información actualizada sobre la solicitud presentada y, tomar conocimiento respecto a la normativa vigente en la cual se establecen los plazos previstos para concluir este tipo de gestiones.Es importante mencionar que, desde el último Comité MSF donde se expresó por primera vez esta preocupación comercial específica en marzo de este año, Bolivia indicó que se trasladaría a capital nuestra preocupación. Sin embargo, a la fecha, el Perú no ha recibido respuesta ni a nivel bilateral ni en el marco de este Comité. Por lo expuesto, el Perú solicita a Bolivia 1) se responda la Carta enviada por nuestro país en febrero de 2022 2) se nos envíe la información referida a la normativa vigente para el acceso y habilitación sanitaria para este tipo de productos 3) sostener una reunión técnico bilateral con la autoridad sanitaria competente de ambas Partes para absolver las consultas que se tuvieran sobre esta preocupación. En ese sentido, el Perú expresa su total disposición de sostener reuniones técnico bilaterales con Bolivia para absolver prontamente esta preocupación comercial.
Summary: Peru reiterated its concern about undue delays in the procedure to authorize plants to export dairy products to Bolivia. Peru regretted the lack of response to the request for information submitted in February 2022 seeking to start cream cheese exports and requested Bolivia to respond to its request, provide the legislation in force, and hold bilateral meetings between relevant sanitary authorities. Peru expressed its willingness to engage in technical discussions with Bolivia.

StatementSubmitted: The Russian Federation would like to express its concern over the European Union’s delay in updating technical information on Russian fish enterprises approved for exports to the European Union. Since 2022, the European Commission has not renewed the information in the TRACES-NT system for fish enterprises, fishing vessels, and other companies certified for supply of animal products to the European Union.  Moreover, the European Union is blocking changes to the list of enterprises that are mentioned in the document, including the correction of errors made by the competent authorities of the European Union when transferring data.The inability to apply for attestation of production facilities in the TRACES-NT module, as well as making adjustments and updating of information hinder exports of Russian fish and animal products to the European market. Thus, we consider EU delays in the renewal of authorizations for fishery enterprises and fish products as a highly discriminatory restriction of trade.We urge the European Union to base its SPS measures on the assessment of risk to life or health of people, animals and plants, on the basis of international standards, guidelines and recommendations, and not to hinder trade through technical restrictions in violation of article 5 of the SPS Agreement.*We would like to mention that the lack of answer on substance indicates EU´s low level of transparency. In a way it diminishes the authenticity of its statements that the sanctions imposed on Russia and other measures do not cover agriculture products and foodstuffs.
Summary: The Russian Federation raised its concern over the European Union's delay in updating technical information in the TRACES-NT system on Russian fish enterprises approved for exports, which hindered exports of Russian fish and animal products to the European market. The Russian Federation was of the view that the delays in the renewal of authorizations, as well as making adjustments and updating of information, constituted a discriminatory trade restriction. Referring to Article 5 of the SPS Agreement, the Russian Federation urged the European Union to base its SPS measures on risk assessment, based on international standards, guidelines, and recommendations, and not to hinder trade through technical restrictions. Further, the Russian Federation stated that the lack of answers on substance indicated a low level of transparency.

Moreover, the European Union is blocking changes to the list of enterprises that are mentioned in the document, including the correction of errors made by the competent authorities of the European Union when transferring data.Lack of opportunities to receive attestation of production facilities in the TRACES-NT module, as well as to make the adjustments and updating the information, hinder exports of Russian fish and animal products to the European market.Thus, we consider EU delays in the renewal of authorizations for fishery enterprises and fish products as a discriminatory restriction of trade.We urge the European Union to base its SPS measures on the assessment of risk to life or health of people, animals and plants, on the basis of international standards, guidelines and recommendations, and not to hinder trade through technical restrictions in violation of article 5 of the SPS Agreement.TRANSPARENCY We would like to mention that the lack of substantive answer designates low level of transparency.
